(p-55) Surat al-Baqarah

Its purpose is to establish the proof that the Book (al-Kitab) is [a] guidance [hudan] to be followed in everything it says. The greatest thing it guides to is faith in the unseen (al-iman bil-ghayb), and its comprehensive principle is faith in the Hereafter. Its foundation is faith in resurrection (al-ba'th), which is what the story of the cow (qissat al-baqarah) makes clear, and the story of the cow revolves around faith in the unseen. For this reason the surah was named after it (p-56). It was more fitting for it to bear this name than the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, because the story of the cow concerns the human species, and because of what precedes it in the story of the Children of Israel, namely the bringing to life after death by the stunning (al-sa'q), and what resembles it. The revival in the story of the cow occurs through a cause that appears weak outwardly, namely the act of one of ordinary people, so it is more indicative of power. This is especially so since it is followed by the description of hearts and stones, [a description] encompassing both those guided by the Book and those who go astray. He described [the hearts] with hardness, which necessitates wretchedness, and the stones were described with fear (khashyah), which arises in general from piety (taqwa), which grants a provision whose benefit extends to the servants of Allah. In this there is an indication that this Book, among us, is like a successor of the Messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm min al-rusul), guiding us in every matter to the right way out of it (p-57). Whoever turns away perishes, whoever hesitates nearly perishes, and whoever responds is God-fearing and excels.

It is called "al-Zahra'" (the Radiant) because it illuminates the path of guidance and sufficiency in this world and the Hereafter, and because it makes the faces radiant on the Day of Recompense for those who believed in the unseen and were not in doubting suspicion, so that they are not prevented from what they desire. And it is called "al-Sanam" (the Hump), because after tawhid, which is the foundation upon which all good is built and the ultimate end which is the goal of the journey, there is nothing in faith in the unseen that is higher, and it is elevated above every other [thing] by the highest (p-58), and there is nothing more comprehensive than faith in the Hereafter. Also, because the hump is the highest part of the belly of the carrying mount, and the Book whose surah this is, is the highest of what carries the command, which is the Law (al-shar') that their Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace (ﷺ), brought to them.

* *

"In the name of Allah" (Bismillah), who established, while being hidden, the proofs of guidance until He became manifest. "Al-Rahman" (the Most Gracious), who poured out His mercy upon all His creation after bringing them into existence, by making the path clear. "Al-Rahim" (the Most Merciful), who singled out the people of His love with success (tawfiq).

The scholar Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali said in his book "al-'Urwah li-Miftah al-Bab al-Muqfal" concerning the meaning of what he narrated from Ibn Wahb, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The first Book used to descend from one gate, upon one letter (harf). The Qur'an descended from seven gates, upon seven letters: a restrainer, a commander, the lawful, the unlawful, the decisive (muhkam), the allegorical (mutashabih), and parables. So make lawful its lawful, make unlawful its unlawful, do what you are commanded, refrain from what you are forbidden, take lessons from its parables, act upon its decisive verses, believe in its allegorical verses, and say: 'We believe in it, all of it is from our Lord.'" This hadith was narrated by Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah in his Musnad, and Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili, and from his route Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, all of them through the route of Ibn Wahb, from Haywah, from 'Uqayl ibn Khalid, from Salamah ibn Abi Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, from his father, from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and he mentioned it without mentioning the Prophet (ﷺ).

The scholar and hafiz Abu Shamah 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Isma'il al-Dimashqi al-Shafi'i said in his book "al-Murshid al-Wajiz ila 'Ulum Tata'allaqu bil-Kitab al-'Aziz," after citing this hadith from the narration of Salamah ibn Abi Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from his father, from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him (p-60):

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: This hadith, according to the people of hadith, is not established. Abu Salamah did not meet Ibn Mas'ud, and his son Salamah is not among those whose narrations are used as proof. This hadith is agreed upon to be weak as regards its chain. A group of the people of reasoning rejected it, among them Ahmad ibn Abi 'Imran, as al-Tahawi heard from him. Al-Layth narrates it from 'Uqayl, from Ibn Shihab, from Umm Salamah, [from Abu Salamah], from the Prophet (ﷺ) as a mursal (a hadith with a missing companion in its chain).

Abu Shamah said: Likewise al-Bayhaqi narrated it in his book "al-Madkhal," and said: This is a good mursal; Abu Salamah did not reach Ibn Mas'ud. Then he narrated it as mawsul (with a complete chain) and said: If it is authentic, then the meaning of his words "seven letters" is "seven aspects," and the intended meaning is not the dialects in which recitation was permitted; rather, what is intended is the types upon which the Qur'an was revealed. And Allah knows best.

I say: Our shaykh, the scholar, the reciter of his age, Shams al-Din Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Jazari al-Dimashqi al-Shafi'i, attributed it, at the beginning of his book "al-Nashr fi al-Qira'at al-'Ashr" (p-61), to al-Tabarani, from the hadith of Umar ibn Abi Salamah al-Makhzumi, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Books used to descend from the heaven through one gate, and the Qur'an was revealed through seven gates, upon seven letters: lawful, unlawful, decisive, allegorical, parables, command and restraint. So make lawful its lawful, make unlawful its unlawful, act upon its decisive, stop at its allegorical, take lessons from its parables, for all of it is from Allah, and none will remember except those of understanding." And al-Hafiz Abu Bakr ibn Abi Dawud narrated it in "Kitab al-Masahif" through another route from 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Qur'an was revealed upon your Prophet (ﷺ) through seven gates, upon seven letters, or letters; and the Book before you used to descend, or descended, through one gate upon one letter." And al-Bayhaqi narrated it in the chapter on the virtues of the Qur'an in "al-Shu'ab" from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, with the wording: "The Qur'an descended upon five aspects: lawful, unlawful, decisive, allegorical, and parables."

Al-Harrali said: In another hadith through the route of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "The Books used to descend from one gate, and this Qur'an was revealed from seven gates upon seven letters (p-62)." He said regarding its meaning: Know that the Qur'an is sent down at the completion of creation and the perfection of every matter in beginning, so the one who was formed with it (i.e., the Prophet (ﷺ)) gathered the completion of every creation and the perfection of every matter. Therefore he (ﷺ) is the qutham of existence (the one who is the totality and the summit), and he is the comprehensive, perfect one. For this reason he was the seal, and his Book was the seal, and the return (al-ma'ad) began from the limit of his manifestation. "Indeed He originates and repeats." Thus he perfected the righteousness of these three comprehensive [matters], whose beginnings had passed among the earlier ones, and whose ends were completed with him (p-63). "I was sent to complete the noble characteristics," narrated by Ahmad from Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with him, marfu' (traced to the Prophet). These [three] are the righteousness of the world, the religion and the return, which he gathered in his saying (ﷺ), as narrated by Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Allah, set right for me my religion, which is the safeguard of my affair; set right for me my world, in which is my livelihood; set right for me my Hereafter, to which is my return." In every righteousness there is advance and withdrawal, so the three comprehensive [matters] become six detailed [matters], which are the six letters of the Qur'an, which he did not cease to seek more of from his Lord, letter by letter. When he completed the six, his Lord granted him a seventh, comprehensive, singular letter with no pair, and thus its revelation upon seven letters was completed.

The lowest of these letters is the letter of the righteousness of the world, and it has two letters: (p-64) one of them is the letter of the unlawful, by which neither soul nor body is made right except by purifying oneself from it, because it is far from their correction. The second is the letter of the lawful, upon which soul and body are made right, because it agrees with their correction. The origin of these two letters is in the Torah, and their completion is in the Qur'an.

Then after these two come the two letters of the righteousness of the Hereafter: one is the letter of restraint and prohibition, by which the Hereafter is not made right except by purifying oneself from it, because it is far from its beauty; and the second is the letter of command, upon which the Hereafter is made right, because it demands its beauty. This may harm the state of the world, because it touches much of its lawful [things], since it is obligatory to prefer the Hereafter, because it is lasting and universal, over the world, because it is perishing and particular, as the good of the world is a part of one hundred, and the evil of the world is a part of seventy [parts]. None prefers this lowest part, because it is present, over that greatest whole, because it is absent, except one who has foolished his soul and whose faith is weak. So the soul's purification from the letter of the unlawful is its cleanliness, and its release from prohibition is its goodness. The origin of these two letters is in the Gospel, and their completion is in the Qur'an (p-65).

Then after these two come the two letters of the righteousness of the religion: one is the letter of the decisive (muhkam), in which the address of the servant's Lord becomes clear to him concerning the states of his heart, the traits of his soul and the deeds of his body, in what lies between him and his Lord, without turning to the aim of the soul in this world's immediate or deferred [benefit]. The second is the letter of the allegorical (mutashabih), in which the address of his Lord does not become clear to the servant, due to the deficiency of his intellect in grasping it, and the obligation to glorify his Lord above the servant's imagining, until Allah strengthens him with His support. The five letters are for use, and this sixth letter is for pausing, so that the servant may pause before Allah with his heart, from a letter, just as he had advanced before Allah with those letters; and so that, by his incapacity and faith at this sixth letter, he may negate the limit of what preceded from his capacity and knowledge in those letters at the beginning. The origin of these two letters is in all the earlier Books, and their completion is in the Qur'an (p-66).

These six letters are shared by the Qur'an with all the other Books, and the Qur'an adds to them their completion and the blessing of their gathering. The Qur'an is distinguished by the seventh, comprehensive letter, which clarifies the highest example and manifests the greatest described (al-mamthul al-a'zam): the letter of praise (hamd), specific to Muhammad (ﷺ), and it is the letter of the parable (mathal). From his gathering and the perfection of his gathering in Muhammad (ﷺ), in his heart, in his recitation upon his tongue, and in his clarification in his essence, there appeared upon him the distinguished qualities of his noble creation and his great character. It is not attained except as a gift from Allah, exalted is He, to His servant, without intermediary. The six descend through intermediaries, from the balance of nature and the purity of intellect, in the manner of the revelation to the Prophet and the inspiration to the saint (al-wali).

Since the letter of praise is its seventh, the comprehensive one, Allah, glorified and exalted, opened with it the Fatihah, the Mother of the Qur'an and the Mother of the Book, and gathered in it the comprehensive [aspects] of the seven letters which He spread throughout the Qur'an, just as He gathered in the Qur'an what He scattered in all the earlier Books. Like silver which became heavy upon one who wished to travel, so he exchanged it for gold; then the gold became heavy upon him, so he exchanged it for a jewel. That is like the Mother of the Qur'an. Thus the completion of the letters upon which the Qur'an was revealed exists in the comprehensive [aspects] of the Mother of the Qur'an (p-67).

So the first verse includes the seventh letter of praise, and the second verse includes the two letters of the lawful and the unlawful, by which the Merciful Attribute (al-Rahmaniyyah) established the world. He means, and Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best, that the Rahmaniyyah encompassed for the servants the enjoyment of created blessings and goods that agree with their natures and temperaments and the acceptance of their souls in all aspects of enjoyment. So in that there are two mercies: a mercy through permission, which is the removal of the hardship of prohibition, and a mercy which prevents the reach of the hardship of sin, or which makes the permitted pleasing to the nature.

As for the Raheemiyyah (Attribute of Mercy), it purified them from the harms to their bodies, the filth of their souls and the ignorance of their hearts. In that there is one mercy, which is the protection of the beloved from harms by the Beloved. Or he means, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best, which is closer: the Rahmaniyyah by its generality established everything that Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) encompasses of the bestowal of blessings and the removal of afflictions in a way that brings happiness or hardship; and the Raheemiyyah by its particularity established, as has preceded, what Divinity (al-Uluhiyyah) pleases: the pouring out of blessings and the repelling of afflictions in the happy way specifically. End.

The third verse includes the command of the Upright King upon the two letters of command and prohibition (p-68), whose command appears in the religion.

[p. 69] The fourth [aspect] comprises two modes of the clear (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih): the clear in His saying, ﴿You alone do we worship﴾, and the ambiguous in His saying, ﴿and You alone do we ask for help﴾. Since [the Fatihah] is built as direct address in the mode of presence (khitab muhadarah), its request is not repeated within the surah. Thus these two modes are set apart from the supplication contained in them, and the request of the fifth verse returns to the mode of praise (hamd), the request of the sixth verse returns to the verse of blessing among the two modes of the lawful (halal) and the unlawful (haram), and the request of the seventh verse returns to the verse of the King among the two modes of command (amr) and prohibition (nahy). Thus the Fatihah gathers the comprehensive aspects of the seven modes (ahruf).

When the Fatihah, the Mother of the Qur'an, began with the seventh, the comprehensive and bestowed mode, the Qur'an itself began with the sixth mode, the one that is beyond human capacity, which is the mode of the ambiguous. This is because the bestowal and support came with the manifestation of helplessness and pure faith, and so that the servant opens the Qur'an with belief in an ambiguous unseen matter, in His saying, ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾, and thus becomes most complete in submission to what follows it, and free of claim concerning what is within his capacity in the remaining modes. Then the sixth, with which the Qur'an opens, was followed by the fifth, the clear in one respect, in His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. For whoever acts upon it with a portion of faith and knowledge in his heart, it is for him from the clear; and whoever acts upon it out of compulsion and obedience to orders, without faith entering his heart, it is for him a mode of command, ﴿And if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not deprive you of [the reward of] your deeds at all﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14].

This ordering is only as it occurs in the recited Qur'an. As for its revelation in the order of exposition (tartib al-bayan), the first thing revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) was the clear mode, namely His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1] ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾ [al-'Alaq: 2] ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ [al-'Alaq: 3], the five verses. The first thing sent down to the community in the order of exposition was from the mode of rebuke and prohibition, namely His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿O you who are wrapped [in garments]﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1] ﴿Arise and warn﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 2], that is, a warner for you before a severe punishment, informing them of the consequences to be feared in the Hereafter, even though they had taken, in this world, affection for their idols. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You have taken idols besides Allah only as a bond of affection among yourselves in the worldly life; then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25], the verse. Thus, glorified and exalted is He, began the recitation of the community with the reform of the most important return, the Hereafter, for upon it the affairs of this world are set right. Whoever is sufficient in his Hereafter, Allah suffices him in the affairs of his worldly life. [p. 71] He began from it with the mode of rebuke and prohibition, which is the one with which the hadith begins. The Prophet (ﷺ) repeated the word for rebuke with the word for prohibition, because both are aimed at one thing, namely deterring from what harms in the Hereafter. However, deterrence is of two kinds: address to one who turns away, which is called zajr (rebuke), as it is also called when applied to beasts; and address to one who is attentive to understanding, which is called nahy (prohibition). Thus rebuke drives away the disposition (tab'), and prohibition drives away the intellect ('aql). End of quotation. It is clear from this what the secret is in the opening of al-Baqarah with the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah).

Since what the surahs begin with of this kind is half the letters of the alphabet, it is as if it were said: whoever claims that the Qur'an is not the speech of Allah, let him take the other half and compose upon it a speech with which he may challenge it. Al-Zarkashi transmitted this in his al-Burhan (fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an) from al-Qadi Abu Bakr, who said: some of the people of realities ('arbab al-haqa'iq) have known this, and al-Zarkashi gathered it in his saying: (a wise, decisive text, which has a secret).

And from Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: In every book there is a secret, and the secret of Allah in the Qur'an is the beginnings of the surahs.

And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him and honour his face: Every book has a choice portion (safwah), and the choice portion of this Book is the letters of spelling (huruf al-tahajji).

Since the letters of the alphabet are twenty-nine, counting the hamzah, and it was impossible to write out one half of them precisely, they were divided into fifteen and fourteen. The smaller part was taken by way of equity and distributed among twenty-nine surahs, [p. 73] according to the number of the letters; and He challenged with it in this manner.

Imam Shams al-Din Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah al-Dimashqi al-Hanbali, in a book of his like a memorandum, which he named Bada'i' al-Fawa'id, displayed a wondrous secret in the opening of the Qur'an with His saying, ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾. Its gist is that its three letters combine the three places of articulation: the throat (al-halq), the tongue (al-lisan), and the lips (al-shafatan), in order. This points to the beginning, which is the beginning of creation; the end, which is the return (al-ma'ad); and the middle, which is the livelihood (al-ma'ash) through legislation by commands and prohibitions. In this is an admonition that this Book, which is composed of these letters that do not exceed the three places of articulation by which it addresses all nations, comprises what sets right your conditions of the beginning of creation, its renewal, and what lies between them. Every surah opened with these letters mentions these three conditions.

Al-Harrali said in his tafsir: "Alif" is a name for the Highest Standing One who encompasses all, then for every one appointed to stand (as a successor), such as Adam and the Ka'bah. "Mim" is a name for the Highest Manifest One, from the most manifest of whom is the King of the Day of Judgement; it is also a name for the complete Manifest One, granted the comprehensive words, Muhammad (ﷺ); then for every manifest thing below that, such as the sky, the sphere, and the earth. "Lam" is a name for what lies between the inner (batin) of divinity, which is where minds are bewildered, and the outer (zahir) of kingship, which is the manifestation of the Day of Recompense, arising from the requirement of the Most Beautiful Names and the Lofty Attributes, which are a connection that brings down what lies between them, like the Subtle (al-Latif) and the like; then for the link that is like the angels and what they undertake of the affair of the dominion (malakut). These expressions, when their meaning is gathered, are called letters (huruf). The letter is the edge of a thing which is not taken alone, and the edge of a speech which is not understood by itself. And they are most fittingly called letters when their forms are considered and they occur as parts of words; [p. 75] and no meaning is understood from them, so that they are added to their like. A part of a word that is understood is then called letters; and when pronounced thus: alif, lam, mim, [it should be said that they are names, even though their meaning is not known, like the letters alif, ba', ta'], for all of them are names according to what al-Khalil understood. They are called letters only when they are parts of a word, either moved for the beginning or quiescent for pause and end.

As for their reality, they are comprehensive (jawami') whose origin is in a first mention from the speech of Allah, the Exalted. Then they descended into Arabic words, were translated into them, and from them this clear Arabic Qur'an was composed. They exist in the supernal, dominion-like books, arranged in summary and detail, as signs (aya), words (kalim), and possessors of a book. When they descended to the end of the detailed Qur'an, they were retained [p. 76] at its opening, to be a sign of its transmission from that Book in detail, and because they are more complete and concise in indicating the comprehensive than the detailed among them. Their indication encompasses all existence from its innermost values to its most manifest, and the most manifest of its station, and what lies between them of connection and link. They comprehend the indication of the visible cosmos seen by the eye, and the audible revelation. Because of what they require of comprehensiveness, they did not descend in any earlier book, for the book of every age corresponds to the condition of the cosmos in it; and the cosmos had not yet been completed, so its books and scrolls were according to its measure. When the cosmos was completed in the time of our master Muhammad (ﷺ), his Book was complete and comprehensive, so these comprehensive letters had to appear in it, so that the seal matches the beginning, for they are the two extremes of perfection, and what lies between them is a gradual progression toward it. It had been promised that these two would be sent down in some of those books, so their descent was the fulfilment of that. End of quotation.

[p. 77] As for the connection of what follows to al-Fatihah: when glorified and exalted is He informed that His sincere servants asked in al-Fatihah for guidance to the straight path, which is [other than] the path of those who are lost, He guided them, at the beginning of the surah that follows it, to the fact that the guidance sought is in this Book, and He explained to them the attributes of the two groups: those granted guidance, as an incitement to adopt them, and those denied it, as a deterrent from approaching it. This is among the greatest connections for following al-Fatihah with al-Baqarah, because it was brought forth to negate doubt concerning this Book, and because it is a guidance for the God-fearing (muttaqin), and for the description of the God-fearing and what they are recompensed with in the three verses, and for the description of the disbelievers who do not believe, because of the seal placed upon their hearing and the sealing for their punishment. This is so that it may be known that what the God-fearing are characterised by is the straight path, so that it is adhered to; and what is characterised by all others is the path of those who are lost, so that it is abandoned. [p. 78] In describing them as God-fearing after mentioning those who earned wrath and those who went astray, there is an indication that the station is one of fear.

If you wish, you may say: the aim of this surah is only the description of the Book, and everything else is consequences and necessary implications. It will not be established that it is guidance except by establishing that it is true, in meaning and in composition. Since meaning is more important, [the surah] put forward the proof concerning it, informing them of their persistence in disbelief by means of what their denial of it would be a confirmation of it. It followed this with mention of the hypocrites, to make known that what is negated is faith in the heart, and that there is no value in the tongue when it is stripped of it. [p. 79] It presented this in a way by which they would know that it is the truth, by exposing what was hidden in their inner selves and uncovering what was in their consciences. When that was complete, and its purpose was calling to Allah, that opportunity was seized with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21], because of the encouragement through fear that had been laid as its foundation. Then the proof of the truth of its composition was established through their failure to reach its range, so the outcome of that returned to establishing it by their inability to oppose it in its meaning by producing what it negated, and in its composition by bringing the like of it. When that was established, it was established that it is from Allah. Thus its competence to teach the laws was established, so it placed this within the debate with the People of the Book, by what they know to be true without doubt, calling them to what they had concealed of the five pillars upon which Islam is built.

When the meaning of ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:1] is "this is a Book made of the same kind of letters that you use in speech, in which you surpass all creation, yet you were unable to produce a sūrah like it, only because it is the speech of God, whose perfection brought this about," it is pointed to with the demonstrative of distance and the lām of perfection in His words, ﴿That is the Book﴾, because of the loftiness of its rank through the majesty of its effects and the remoteness of its station from being reached by the accursed. When its perfection was known, He indicated its exaltation by explicitly stating what this exaltation produces and entails, saying: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, meaning, in no part of its meaning or its composition, in (p-80) objective reality (nafs al-amr), for one who has examined it with verification. So what is negated is that it is a subject of doubt and a place where doubt could be suspected. The adverbial phrase was not placed first, because that would imply exclusivity, and it would be understood that other books are places of doubt.

Al-Ḥarrālī said: "Dhā" is a noun whose referent is the one pointed to. The lām, together with it, indicates the distance of the Book from being written (al-kitāb min al-katb), and writing is the joining of a separated thing to its origin by a hidden connection, like the beads in leather sewn with a strip from it, and like stitching in a garment with something of its own kind, so that it is closer to the form of its original connection. Thus the name was applied to what God imposed upon people of rulings, and to what was fixed by inscriptions of speech. "Lā" is for negating what is impossible absolutely or at a particular time. "Rayb" is hesitation between two positions of accusation, such that one cannot be at rest with either of them. End of quotation. Its root is the restlessness and agitation of the soul, and from it comes "the rayb of time" (p-81) for its disquieting calamities. Since this entails guidance, He said: ﴿a guidance﴾, and He specified those who benefit, because the most stubborn has no cure, and the one who seeks to trip others is turned back by nothing. So He said: ﴿for the God-fearing﴾, that is, those who were created with piety in the very nature of their creation. Understand from this that others are not guided by it, but rather doubt it, even though it is in no way a place for doubt at all.

Al-Ḥarrālī said: It is the plural of the muttaqī, who is one who holds back from proceeding with any matter, out of awareness of his own deficiency in independence and his knowledge that he is not self-sufficient. So he is God-fearing (muttaqin) by his description and the goodness of his natural disposition, and the one who is God-fearing is thus restrained for this reason. Taqwā (p-82) is a root that precedes guidance and every act of worship, because it is a natural disposition of restraint that merits guidance and every good. It is also the charge of God to the People of the Book.

Then He described them by the comprehensive qualities of their deeds, as a way of identifying them, saying: ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾. That is, in the matter that is hidden, other than which there is no benefit in faith. He expressed it with the verbal noun (maṣdar) for emphasis.

﴿and establish the prayer﴾, that is, the prayer which is the presence of muraqaba (vigilant awareness of God) and the most excellent of bodily acts, by maintaining it and by preserving it in itself and in all its states. When He mentioned the connection of the creatures to the Creator, and spending was, although it is among the greatest pillars of the religion, a connection between creatures, He followed it with spending, saying, placing the preposition first, forbidding extravagance, and by the partitive (min, "some of") alerting to the goodness of the spending, because God is Good and accepts only what is good; and commanding scrupulousness (wara') and deterring from what is doubtful, [because provision includes the lawful, the unlawful, and the doubtful]: ﴿and from what We have provided them﴾, that is, We have enabled them to benefit from it, despite the greatness of Our treasuries, and it is Ours rather than theirs,

﴿they spend﴾, that is, seeking Our good pleasure, from what is obligatory upon them, such as zakat, hajj, jihad and other things, and from what they give voluntarily in charity and otherwise. The intended meaning of these acts here is bringing their realities into existence continually.

Abu Hayyan and others said, concerning His saying in Surat al-Hajj: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [from the way of God]﴾ [al-Hajj: 25], the present tense may not be understood as indicating a specific time, whether present or future, and so it then indicates continuity. End of quote. This is something unavoidable; otherwise, in this Madinan surah it would not include those who had acquired this quality before the Hijra, and His saying: ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of God before?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91] is decisive in this regard.

(p-84) Al-Harali said: ﴿they believe﴾ is from faith (īmān), which is the verbal noun of āmanahu yu'minuhu īmānan, when someone trusts another who alerts him to a matter that he does not have, so that he does not deny it or doubt it. "The unseen" (al-ghayb) is what is hidden from the senses and about which there is no knowledge by which reason is guided, so that knowledge is attained through it. The form "they believe" and "they establish" requires continuity until the end, and the continuation of an action until the end requires that it appear from natural disposition (fiṭrah) or innate constitution (jibillah), and that it is not from artifice or ostentation; and at that point it becomes a sign of the reward. Ṣalāh is turning wholly toward a matter; so it is, from the higher perspective, an all-encompassing inclination, and from the lower perspective, fulfilling the various modes of humility and wholly turning toward receiving. Their belief in the unseen is their acceptance from the Prophet ﷺ of what he received by revelation concerning the unseen matters of this world, which is the Hereafter and what is in it, and the unseen matters of the malakut (the invisible dominion) and what is in it, up to the hidden realm of al-jabarut (the sovereign power); and what is with it, such that their action upon the unseen that their hearts received, by way of their ears, is like their action upon what their souls received by way of their eyes and all their other senses; and they persisted in that action in accordance with the ruling of their faith until the end.

Since ṣalāh is the fulfilment of the covenant of worship, founded upon the prior testimony (shahādah), completed by the totality of remembrance and all kinds of greetings to God, from standing before Him, bowing to Him, and prostrating to Him, which is the highest of them, and the greeting of peace by speech, which is the lowest of the greetings; for this reason it was a renewal and repetition of faith. Therefore, whoever does not persist in prayer, his faith weakens and disbelief covers him; there is no faith for one who has no prayer. Taqwa is the root, and faith is the branch, and prayer is its fruit; and spending is vicegerency (khilāfah), and therefore miserliness is dismissal from the vicegerency of God: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 7]. This matter in its entirety is that by which vicegerency was granted to Adam, and beyond that, the perfection of God's command, which He perfected through Muhammad ﷺ. So taqwa is an inner heart, and spending is an outward face, and faith is the prayer, a link between them. The reason for the ordering of faith in the unseen upon taqwa is that the one who is God-fearing, since he is attentive and does not hold firmly to any matter, when he is guided to something unseen that he does not know, does not repel it according to what knowledge he previously had. The reason for the ordering of spending upon faith in the unseen is that provision is unseen, because a person, since he does not perceive all his sustenance, his sustenance is unseen; so when he is certain of the replacement, he gives generously. Whenever he is supplied with provisions, his vicegerency is completed, his authority in it becomes great, and a door of supply with a higher and more perfect provision than the first opens for him. When he then exercises his vicegerency well in it by spending from it, a door opens for him to what is higher, until he reaches the point beyond which there is no further sight; and that is the Muhammadan perfection. But if he is miserly, does not spend, and is content with what he has, he does not fear God, and denies, the matter of his vicegerency diminishes and the supply from above is cut off from him. Therefore spending is rightly called zakah. At the beginning of al-Shura there is an exquisite discussion on faith from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him. End of quote.

Now when He described them with faith in general terms, He indicated some of its details in a way that includes the People of the Book, entering them at the first level. So He said: ﴿Those who believe﴾, that is, they bring this quality into existence after hearing the call, in a continuous manner ﴿in what has been sent down to you﴾, that is, of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, whether it has already been revealed or will be revealed later; ﴿and what was sent down before you﴾, that is, upon the earlier prophets. Since faith in the Resurrection (al-ba'th) is of very great importance in the religion, He specified it by placing it first, to show greater concern, and said: ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾, that is, the abode of recompense, the place where things are made manifest and the veil is lifted, and the outcome of affairs.

Al-Haralli said: "The Hereafter is the return of the affair after its completion to its beginning." End of quotation.

Because of the concern mentioned above, He expressed it with certainty (al-iqan) and brought the separating pronoun, saying: ﴿they are certain﴾, because that leads to every good and wards off every harm. Certainty (al-iqan), as al-Haralli said, is the clarity of knowledge and its freedom from the impurities of doubt and the like, derived from yaqan al-ma' (the certainty of water), which is what descends from the sky and flows into a mountain cave and does not change, neither by settling nor by flowing. End of quotation. Thus it comes after doubt, and for this reason it is not attributed to God. The description with these qualities, as you see, is an indication of the foundational bodily and financial acts, both doing and abstaining. Faith is the foundation of the matter, and prayer is pointed to as adorning oneself with every good and freeing oneself from every evil, ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45], and both are acts of the body, while spending is a financial act. Thus there is obtained a restriction of the two governing categories of action, doing and abstaining, over all deeds however they branch out. He stated the doing explicitly and alluded to the abstaining by an allusion that only the discerning understand, to ease matters for the wayfarers, because doing, in itself, even if difficult, is easier for the soul than restraining from what it desires. And in describing them also with belief in what was sent down to him and to those before him, there is a rebuke and reproach to all others, which you will see in the coming verses.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 5:

When He had told of their outward and inward acts, He told of their fruit, saying: ﴿Those﴾, that is, those described by those outward attributes, and because what preceded implied that their faith was based on the greatest form of proof, which bore for them the grasping of the most firm handholds of deeds, they deserved the description of being elevated (isti'la'), whose meaning is firm establishment (tamakkun). So He said: ﴿upon guidance﴾, that is, great guidance. He increased its magnitude by His saying: ﴿from their Lord﴾, that is, the One who bestows favour upon them by enabling them to attain it and to hold fast to it, in the manner of one who is elevated above something. Since guidance was not necessarily accompanied by success (falah), He followed it with His saying, using the conjunction to indicate the increased firmness of their establishment in each of the two descriptions:

﴿And those﴾, that is, those of high rank, ﴿they are﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿the successful﴾, that is, the perfected in this description, those for whom the faces of victory were opened. The root (f-l-h) indicates the meaning of splitting and opening, and so do its siblings made of the letters f, l and the ʿayn or others, such as falaja (with jīm), falaqa, faladha and falā.

(p-91) Al-Ḥarrālī said: The address in this verse came in the form of address to the Prophet ﷺ, and in the form of bringing the believers into presence by the place of the demonstrative, which is a station of presence lower than the station of the one addressed. End of quotation. That it is used for distance is an indication of the exaltedness of their rank. And al-falāḥ: success and victory in every desired thing, and attaining lasting survival in good.

When al-Biqa'i had followed the description of the believers with an account of the condition of the disbelievers, and they had divided into open opponents and hypocrites, and the hypocrites were of two kinds—ignorant men among the polytheists of the Arabs, and scholars among the disbelievers of the Children of Israel—it was most fitting, so that he could finish one category swiftly on its own, to begin first with the open opponents. He mentioned what he intended regarding their affair in two verses, because their affair is easier and their state is simpler, since their aim is to weaken them either by speech or by the sword. Moreover, his mention of them is in a manner that encompasses all the categories. So He said (p-92), addressing the greatest of those blessed by it, in a manner of consolation and demonstration of its inimitability, in the course of answering a question as if someone had asked: "This is the state of the Book for the believers; what is its state for the disbelievers?" ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾, meaning: He has decreed their disbelief permanently, a decree that took effect and passed, so they concealed the proofs established for the Oneness of God from the intellects prepared to perceive it and from the original natural dispositions that were free of any obstacle preventing them from submitting to it, and they persisted in that, as indicated by the context through expressing their opposites in terms that denote the renewal of faith (p-93) continuously, and the attachment to the sealing and the punishment. Perhaps He expressed it in the past tense—while the context calls for description—to warn against merely committing disbelief, even if only for a blessing, and so that it would include the hypocrites and others.

Since this state indicated that they acted contrary to what the believers did in submission, the meaning is ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them﴾, meaning: your warning at this time with this Book, ﴿or you do not warn them﴾, meaning: and your not warning them therein and thereafter. The interrogative meaning has been stripped from "am" and the hamza. Sibawayh said: "This has operated on the interrogative particle just as the vocative particle operates in your saying: 'O Allah, forgive us, O company'." End of quote. Perhaps He expressed it in the form of the interrogative while its meaning has been stripped away, for the sake of conveying that they had plunged so deeply into disbelief that one who reaches such foolishness, were he to witness the king asking you about him, would not believe.

Since it was as if it were said: "In what respect are their two conditions equal?" It was said: "In that they (p-94) ﴿do not believe﴾." This is evidence for the particularity of it being guidance for the God-conscious, and for the occurrence of obligation with what is impossible for another. For He, glory be to Him, obligated them to believe while He willed of them disbelief, so it became impossible because of His willing its non-occurrence, yet the obligation to it proceeds according to the ways of wisdom, for His willing the non-belief of them does not remove their belief from the realm of the possible, as far as is apparent, due to the lack of knowledge of what God wills for each individual person. So it follows the pattern of trial, so that the obedient is manifested from others in the world of witnessing, to establish the proof. A complement to this will come in al-Saffat at ﴿Do what you are commanded﴾ [al-Saffat: 102].

(p-95) Al-Haralli said: "Thus there was achieved, by the totality of His words ﴿It is the same for them﴾ to the end, and by His words ﴿do not believe﴾, a complete report about them regarding their prior affair and their subsequent state, so the report about them was completed by the two statements as a single report, harmonious as a prior writing and a subsequent existence." End of quote. Every place in which disbelief is mentioned, He only expressed it thus as an indication that the original proofs are so clear that they are not hidden from anyone, and none opposes them except one who has veiled the mirror of his intellect, either through obstinacy or through neglecting sound reflection and inclining to a kind of blind imitation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 7:

Since it is among the most astonishing of wonders that one and the same thing should be guidance for some people and not for others, he explained this by His words: ﴿God has sealed﴾, that is, by His majesty, ﴿upon their hearts﴾, that is, a seal that is elevated over them, so they do not comprehend with true comprehension. This is because sealing something prevents entering into it and exiting from it. He emphasized the meaning by repeating the preposition, saying: ﴿and upon their hearing﴾, so they do not hear with true hearing. He made the hearing singular because variation in it is rare.

Al-Harrali (ḥarrālī) said: He associated hearing with the heart in the sealing, because no one hears except what he understands. End of quote.

﴿And upon their sight is a veil﴾, so they do not look with contemplation.

Since here he equated warning and its absence, it was more fitting to begin with the hearts, making them equal to cattle. Since the dull-witted may hear or see and thereby be guided, and since hearing is more harmful (to them) because of its generality, while sight is specific to conditions of light, he negated hearing and then sight, lowering them further from the state of cattle. This differs from what is in ("al-Jāthiyah"), for there, when He reported misguidance, and the one who is astray is most in need of hearing the guide, He negated hearing first. And since the deaf person, if he possesses understanding or sight, can be guided, and understanding is more noble, He negated these two in that order.

When He described them with this, He reported their outcome, saying: ﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾. Al-Harrali said: In His saying ﴿for them﴾ there is an indication of the strength of the call of their condition toward that punishment, their deserving of it, and the growth of their essences toward it, until they witness with the immediate knowledge of recognition both the punishment and that it belongs to them. Their punishment is great, taking hold of the totality of their essences, because neither their bodies, nor their souls, nor their spirits are mingled with anything that would turn away any part of its punishment from them, as happens for the punished among the sinning believers of the (earlier) nations, where the punishment swerves away from their faces, the places of their ablution, and the like. End of quote.

(And it will come, at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides God, equals﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], what turns to here.)

Al-Harrali said: "Kufr" (disbelief) is covering what is due to be manifested; "indhar" (warning) is informing about what warns; "khatm" (sealing) is concealing the report of a thing by gathering its edges over it in a manner by which it is preserved; and "qalb" (heart) is the origin of a thing's being from the hidden core of its subsistence, so its state changes according to the turning of its heart in its ending, and its development and perfection occur according to its supplies in its beginning and growth. The heart of a human is like the passengers of a ship in relation to its turning; the rest of him is directed by it. By its being set for turning and making turn, it was named qalb (heart). For the subtlety of this meaning, most of his oaths ﷺ were by "Turner of hearts." "Ghishāwah" (veil) is a covering that envelops, so nothing of what is covered appears with it. "ʿAdhāb" (punishment) is pain without a finishing blow in it, and "ʿaẓīm" (great) is that which takes hold in all directions. End of quote.

In the placement of the mention of the believers followed by the mention of those whose perceptions are sealed and whose paths lead to ruin, there is an exaltation of the blessing upon the one who responds to Him, since (the believers) say: "Guide us," and He guides them, and an announcement that guidance is only in His hand, so that they persist in seeking and disavow claims of power or strength.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 2, verse 8:

When He, glorified be He, opened [the description of the believers] with those whose hearts agreed with their tongues in faith, and then followed it with the open disbelievers, whose public declaration matched their private concealment in disbelief, He then followed this with mention of the concealers, whose tongues contradicted their hearts in submission. These are the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). Their matter is more severe, because their states are confused and their statements and actions are mixed up. The most harmful of enemies is the one who shows you friendship and then takes you from a place of safety. How well what is attributed to the Imam Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi conveys this meaning:

Guard yourself against the ignorant as much as you can,
for even if they show you affection, they are enemies.

And even if among them is one whose deed pleases you,
every sweet-tasting thing, or most of it, is a sickness.

Therefore He, glorified be He, followed up by exposing their secrets and tearing away their veils, in a context that includes both of their categories. [p. 100] He condemned their affairs, weakened their aims, set forth parables for them, and expounded to them to some extent in speech. So He said, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people﴾, meaning: when We sent Our Messenger, the people divided into two groups, believer and disbeliever. The disbelievers divided into two groups: some of them openly declared, "We will never believe," and some of them said, and perhaps it was more apparent, and did not conceal, because they were separated from the open ones by some rulings. Or, because He, glorified be He, when He mentioned the two extremes of faith and disbelief, and the states of the believers and the states of those who disbelieved, He mentioned the hypocrites, who vacillate between the two extremes, with the word "people" because the meaning of swinging (nawsun) is manifest in them, due to their oscillation between the two states. For nawsun is the motion of a light thing suspended in the air, like a hanging thread with nothing heavy at its lower end, which therefore never ceases [p. 101] to oscillate between two directions. This meaning does not appear in the two other groups, because each of them leans to a single direction. This is what al-Harali said. He used the definite article for the genus, or for a specific reference, in "those who disbelieved," because they are a type of them. The reason for using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, according to this, is what has been mentioned earlier.

﴿We believe in Allah﴾, meaning: in Him alone, with all of His majesty and beauty, bringing that to mind. Since they were suspected, they emphasized by repeating the preposition, so they said: ﴿and in the Last Day﴾, which the open disbelievers denied.

﴿But they are not believers﴾, meaning: they are not people of firm rooting in faith, as they claimed, by mentioning the Greatest Name and repeating the preposition. Perhaps He negated only firm rooting, because among them were some who were wavering at the time of this statement, not firmly committed to disbelief, and who later believed. He omitted the object of belief to generalize the negation regarding them, covering what they claimed and other things. He used the plural here and the singular in "says," to indicate that disbelief is general for them, as it was for the former ones. And the scarcity [p. 102] of those among them who would make this statement indicates their harshness, their intense stubbornness, and their strength in disbelief.

In mentioning their story and condemning their states there is an admonition regarding the obligation of sincerity, and an exhortation to strive for purity from defilements in asking for guidance to the straight path.

The classification of people at the end of al-Fatihah into three categories, guided, obstinate, and astray, is like their classification at the beginning of al-Baqarah into three: the pious (muttaqun), the open disbelievers, who are the obstinate, and the astray, who are the hypocrites. Their summary in al-Fatihah and their detail here is one of the wondrous methods, and it is the custom of the Great Qur'an: summary followed by detail.

Ibn Ishaq named many of the hypocrites in the Noble Biography (al-Sirah al-Sharifah) in the early reports of what came after the Hijra (migration). Ibn Hisham said, summarizing that: Among those who joined the Jews from among those named to us as hypocrites from al-Aws and al-Khazraj were: from al-Aws, Zuwayy ibn al-Harith, Bijad ibn Uthman ibn Amir, and Nabtal ibn al-Harith, who is the one of whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to look at Satan, let him look at Nabtal!" He used to come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [p. 103] and speak with him, then carry his talk to the hypocrites, and he is the one who said: "Muhammad is only an ear." And Abbad ibn Hunayf, brother of Sahl, Amr ibn Khidham, Abdullah ibn Nabtal, and Bahzaj, who was one of those who built the Mosque of Harm, and likewise Jariyah ibn Amir ibn al-Attaf and his son Zayd, and Khidham ibn Khalid, who was the one who expelled the Mosque of Harm from his house, and Mirba' ibn Qayzi, who "said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he was heading for Uhud: 'I do not permit you, O Muhammad, if you are a prophet, to pass through my orchard!' The Muslims rushed to kill him, but the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade them and said: 'This is a blind one, blind of heart and blind of sight.'" And his brother Aws ibn Qayzi, who is the one who said on the day of the Trench: "Indeed our houses are exposed." And Hatib ibn Umayyah ibn Rafi', who was an elderly, heavy man who had become old in the Jahiliyyah, and whose son Yazid was among the best of the Muslims. He was killed, may Allah be pleased with him, on the day of Uhud. His father said to the one who gave him the good news of Paradise: "By Allah, you have deceived this poor man about himself!" And Bushayr ibn Ubayriq, Abu Tu'aymah, and in another version, Tu'mah, who is the thief of the two coats of mail, concerning whom Allah revealed [p. 104] ﴿And do not argue on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ [an-Nisa': 107]. And Quzman, an ally of theirs, who fought excellently on the day of Uhud, and "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'He is among the people of the Fire.' He was wounded and given the good news of Paradise. He said: 'By Allah, I only fought out of zealous loyalty to my people!' When his wound grew severe, he cut the tendons of his hand, and he died."

And from al-Khazraj: Rafi' ibn Wadi'ah, Zayd ibn Amr, Amr ibn Qays, Qays ibn Amr ibn Sahl, al-Jadd ibn Qays, who is the one who said: ﴿Permit me and do not tempt me﴾ [at-Tawbah: 49]. And Abdullah ibn Ubayy, the head of the hypocrites, to whom they used to gather [p. 105] and who is the one who said: ﴿The mightier will surely expel the meaner from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. Concerning him, and concerning Wadi'ah al-Awfi, Malik ibn Abi Qawqal, Suwayd, and Da'is, who were of his clan, was revealed ﴿Have you not considered those who acted hypocritically say to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾ [al-Hashr: 11], to the end of the verse, recounting what they used to convey secretly to the Banu al-Nadir when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) besieged them. So Allah spoke the truth, and they lied.

Among those who took refuge in Islam and displayed it while being hypocrites, from the rabbis of the Jews from Banu Qaynuqa', were Sa'd ibn Hunayf and Zayd ibn al-Lusayt, who is the one who said during the Battle of Tabuk: "Muhammad claims that news from heaven comes to him, yet he does not know where his camel is!" So Allah informed him of his words and of the location of the camel. Also Nu'aymān ibn Awf ibn Amr, Uthman ibn Awf, Rafi' ibn Huraymilah, who is the one to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said when he died: "Today a great one among the great hypocrites has died." And Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut, who is the one to whom "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said when that wind blew while he was returning from the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq: 'Do not fear, it only blew for the death of a great one among the great hypocrites.'" Also Silsilah ibn Barham, and Kinanah ibn Suriya. These were among the hypocrites, and whoever went in their direction; they would attend the mosque, hear the discussions of the Muslims, mock them, and ridicule their religion. The end of the quotation. There is an abridgment in it. Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed these verses concerning them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 9:

(p-106) Their story is introduced by drawing attention to the smallness of their intellects and the lightness of their judgment, in that the object of their condition is that they deceive One to whom deception cannot be ascribed. What moved them to this is that they have no kind of awareness and no portion of perception, by His saying, may He be exalted, in answer to a question as if someone had said: "What is their purpose in displaying faith and in reporting about themselves what they are not characterised by, while they know the ugliness, foulness, enormity and vileness of lying?" ﴿They deceive Allah﴾, that is, they go to great lengths in dealing with Him in this manner, by concealing the opposite of what they display, along with His comprehensive knowledge of everything. Deception (khida') at its root means concealment, and the form of the verb (mufa'alah) in its root is for emphasis, because when an action is pursued against its doer, it comes out more eloquent and more firm than when he practises it alone. ﴿And those who believe﴾, that is, they deal with them in that same manner. His command, exalted is He, to apply the rulings of Islam to them in this world has the form of deception, and likewise the believers' compliance with His command concerning them. Al-Harrali said: (p-107) It came in the form of mufa'alah because of the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah of their deception, and it was not read otherwise, nor should it be. Deception is the display of a good by which one seeks to reach the concealment of an evil to which the outcome of that displayed good leads. End of quotation.

﴿And they deceive not⦅but⦆﴾ — that is, by what they deceive the believers with — ﴿except themselves﴾. The meaning is that their minds, because of their corruption, are only called souls (nufus). Al-Harrali said: the soul (nafs) is that by which a person is covetous over others, out of self-reliance and contentment with the existing preciousness of himself over whoever else there is. End of quotation. This reading with the elision (qira'at al-hadhf) does not contradict the reading "yukhadi'una" (they deceive), because the unrestricted does not contradict the restricted by emphasis. He expressed it here with the form of mufa'alah because of their awareness, as al-Harrali said, of the corruption of their states at some times and from some persons, and with the bare form (khada'a) for their heedlessness of the corruption of their states during most of their times and the heedlessness of the common people. It is not attributed to Allah, glorified is He, except with the word khad', because they do not know what of His affair is hidden from them. For this reason it came in the verse of al-Nisa': ﴿They deceive Allah, but He is their deceiver﴾ [al-Nisa: 142]. End of quotation.

﴿And they perceive not⦅it⦆﴾ — that is, any kind of perception — due to the extremity of their ignorance that they harm none but themselves, because Allah knows their secret as He knows their open declaration. The omission of the object of perception (shu'ur) is for generality. Shu'ur, as al-Harrali said, is the first beginning of sensation with knowledge, as if it is the origin of its growth before its form is complete and distinguished. End of quotation.

Then the Exalted explained that the cause of their heedlessness of this manifest matter is that the instrument of their perception is diseased. The sickness has preoccupied it from perceiving what benefits it, so it inclines only toward what harms it, just as the sick person's soul does not incline toward anything other than what is harmful to him. So He said, as an answer to one who seems to have asked: What is the cause of their act of deception and lack of awareness? ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾, meaning from the very origin of their creation, which weakens the powers of faith within them and necessitates the weakness and corruption of their Islamic actions. For disease, as al-Harrali said, is a weakness in the powers that results in a defect in the actions. ﴿So Allah increased them﴾, meaning by what He possesses of attributes of majesty and bounty, because of their deceiving by what they see of its non-effect, ﴿in disease﴾, meaning evil belief which increases their deception, and pain in their hearts because of what they see of the frustration of their aim, so that the door of understanding and rectitude was entirely closed to them. Increase, al-Harrali said, is the bringing into being of a matter that did not exist in the existing thing. End quote.

﴿And for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7], meaning, in addition to the harm of dullness in this world which joins them to the beasts, ﴿is a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter, meaning severely painful, and pain is the constant ache. Thus said al-Harrali. ﴿And because they used to﴾ [al-Tawbah: 77]. Al-Harrali said: "kāna" (used to / was) means that when a thing "kāna" and the thing was thus, its existence has become manifest and its form is complete, or that such-and-such has manifested from its very self. End quote.

﴿they lie﴾, meaning they commit lying, which is reporting about themselves that they are believers while they are clothed in disbelief. The meaning according to the reading with the doubled letter (shaddah) is: they exaggerate in lying, or they attribute the truthful to lying, and that is the most abominable of lies.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 11:

When Allah, exalted is He, informed about their inner states, He followed it with what indicates them from the outward, showing that when they are told to refrain from general corruption, they claim general righteousness, by His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾. The passive form of its verb (qīla, "it is said") is an indication of their disobedience to every speaker, whoever he may be: ﴿Do not cause corruption on the earth﴾, meaning, by the evil deeds that we see you committing. Corruption (fasād) is the breakdown of a thing's form. So said al-Harālli.

﴿They say﴾, restricting their action to righteousness, denying all corruption of it, denying it with brazen falsehood and without concern: ﴿Indeed, we are only reformers﴾. Reform (iṣlāḥ) is the repair of a thing's defect. So said al-Harālli.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 12:

Since their condition was founded on deception, by displaying good and concealing evil, and since they considered their corruption, owing to the inversion of their perception, to be reform, they would debate about it (p-111) with all kinds of doubts. Their statement might well deceive whoever among the believers heard it, because the believer is naive and generous, while the disbeliever is deceitful and base. So God, the Exalted, said, warning against their condition, affirming for them what they had denied of corruption regarding themselves, and restricting it to them: ﴿Surely it is they who are the corrupters﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿the corrupters﴾, that is, those who are perfect in corruption, who have attained in it such mastery that the corruption of others, compared to theirs, becomes nothing, because of the ruin of relations and the seizing of the believer from his place of safety. Al-Harrali (al-Harali) said: Since the state of tranquillity through faith is reform, their agitation in it must be corruption, especially since they thought that their being with these at one time and with those at another was wisdom and reform, when in reality it is corruption itself, for it is in truth opposing both these and those. Thus they corrupted both sides of faith and disbelief. For this reason it was said: "What reforms the hypocrite?" Because he has no sincere friend and no clear enemy, so nothing is trusted from him. End of quotation.

Since this description necessitates great awe, he followed it with what lightens it, by His saying: ﴿But they do not perceive﴾, that is, they are in the utmost coarseness, to the point that they have no awareness (p-112) by which they could skilfully manage what they attempt of corruption now, as indicated by what is in the preceding verse, which shows that the present tense (al-mudari') refers to the present time, nor regarding what is to come in time, because "la" (not) does not accompany it except when it bears the meaning of the future. Therefore their corruption affects only the harm to themselves. So do not fear them, for I am sufficient for you against them.

When He had explained their condition when they were commanded to general righteousness, He explained that when they were called to the specific righteousness, which is the foundation of all righteousness, they labelled it foolishness. So He said: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾, that is, by whatever speaker it may be, ﴿"Believe as the people have believed"﴾, that is, outwardly and inwardly, ﴿the people﴾, meaning those who are (true) people, so that the fruit of that may appear upon you, namely adhering to righteousness and avoiding corruption. The belief attributed to "the people" is the lowest level of belief, as stated by al-Harrali (ʿAlam al-Harrali). (p-113) This conveys what His words ﴿And they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8] expressed explicitly. ﴿They say: "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?"﴾, that is, that belief, ﴿the foolish﴾, meaning those whom they (the ones who called them) had lured into what they entered after abandoning what their fathers had been upon, a lightness that arises from weakness of intellect. Then Glorified is He, He refuted their statement by restricting foolishness to them, so He said: ﴿Unquestionably, it is they who are the foolish﴾, not others, because of their rigidity upon their opinion, even though its falsehood is clearer than the sun and contains no ambiguity. ﴿But they do not know﴾, that is, they have no knowledge at all, neither of that nor of anything else. Knowledge cannot be conceived for them, because their ignorance is compound, which is the worst of ignorance and knowledge. Al-Harrali said: "Whatever is taken by a sign and indication that has been set up as a mark upon it," (end of quotation). Since corruption can be recognised and turned away from with only slight reflection, whereas foolishness cannot be perceived and forbidden except by the solidity of knowledge, every verse was concluded with what befits that of awareness and knowledge. And since the general is part of the specific, it was placed before it.

(p-114) When he had explained their hypocrisy, its cause, and their conduct when the one calling to the truth summoned them, with these verses, he explained their conduct in their speech and their deception, as evidence of their corruption, by His saying: ﴿And when they meet﴾. Meeting (liqa') is coming together with approach, ﴿those who believe﴾, that is, truly, outwardly and inwardly. But their belief, as al-Harrali (al-Harrali) said, is an act of theirs that has not reached the point of becoming a quality of theirs. As for the believers whose belief has become a quality of theirs, they hardly meet them in accordance with its requirement, because they find no entry for themselves with them in speech or companionship, since meeting necessarily involves some approach from both who meet. End.

﴿They say﴾ deceptively, ﴿We believe﴾, expressing it with the past verbal sentence, which suffices, for the purpose for which it is brought, for at least the occurrence (of the act).

(p-115) ﴿And when they go off﴾, arriving ﴿to their devils﴾, that is, those who are their leaders, without any believer being with them. The devil (shaytan) is the one farthest from the place of good, as al-Harrali said.

﴿They say: Indeed we are with you﴾, expressing it with the nominal sentence, which indicates constancy, emphasizing it to show their eagerness for this report, out of greater love for what it conveys, and to repel what might be suspected of a change in them in the eyes of one who sees their hypocrisy toward the believers. Then they resumed, in the position of an answer to one who said: What is the matter with you that you soften your words to the believers? ﴿We are only mockers﴾, that is, seeking mockery and persisting in it in what we display of belief. Mockery (huzu') is showing seriousness while concealing jest in it, as al-Harrali said.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 15:

Then it is answered, as if one said: "With what were they recompensed?" With His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, meaning He requites them for their deed by istidraj (gradual leading on), by displaying to them from His command what they do not perceive the reality of. So He applies to them in this world the rulings of the people of faith, and He makes them taste the utmost humiliation in both abodes, renewing this for them according to the measure of their mockery. That is more grievous than a constant thing to which the soul has become accustomed. For this reason He expressed it with the verbal sentence rather than the nominal one, although the nominal form would indicate the validity of repentance for one who repents, unlike the nominal form.

﴿And He extends for them﴾, from al-madd (extension), by what confuses them. Al-Harrali said: from al-madad (increase), which is an attached addition in a thing of its own kind.

﴿in their transgression﴾, meaning their overstepping of the limit in corruption. Al-Harrali said: it is the excess of their transgressing the boundaries of things and their measures, end of quote. This extension through respite granted to them is in a state in which they are ﴿wandering blindly﴾, meaning they stumble about like one who has no insight whatsoever. Al-Harrali said: from al-'amah (blindness), which is the obscuring of matters that contain indications by which one benefits when the sense is lost, so there remains no cause to turn him back from his transgression. Thus, whenever they overstep a limit, they become blind and do not turn back from it; so they are always increasing in transgression. End of quote.

Once all of this has been established, its summation follows without hesitation: ﴿Those﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], that is, those most remote from what is right, ﴿who have bartered﴾, that is, who persisted obstinately in their desires, burdening themselves against the disposition with which God created them, despite the proofs He had set up, until they took ﴿error﴾, that is, the thing most ugly of all things, ﴿in exchange for guidance﴾, which is the best of all things and the foundation upon which every sentient being rests. It is as if, because of the clarity of the proofs established against them, together with what He had implanted of it in their natures, guidance was in their hands, and they sold it for error. The explanation that the root sh-r-y (شرى) in all its twelve derived forms revolves around obstinacy will come in Surah Yusuf, peace be upon him. ﴿So not﴾, that is, as a consequence of this act of theirs, ﴿has their commerce profited﴾, despite their claim that they were the most knowing of people in trade, ﴿and they were not﴾ by their very natures ﴿guided﴾, for although they did not profit, they lost the capital, since nothing remained in their hands except error, whose possessor stands below the rank of beasts, while they claimed that there was no one like them in guidance.

When all of this was established, and examples were more firmly fixed in the mind and more revealing of conditions, the likeness of their state was given in terms of concrete things, because illustration through them has great power in conveying meanings even to dull minds and in fixing them there. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their likeness﴾, meaning in this state of theirs by which they sought to live, ﴿is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾, meaning he sought that a fire be lit for him, which was their guidance, so that he might walk by its light. Its root is from *nāra*, meaning to flee, because of its movement and agitation. So it blazed and gave light.

﴿When it lit up﴾, meaning the fire, and the singular pronoun is used in view of the word *alladhī* (the one who). So He said ﴿what was around him﴾, and he wanted to benefit from it in seeing what he wished. This is a *kināya* (metonymy) for the security they gained through the words of Islam which they uttered without belief. ﴿Allah took away﴾, He who possesses perfect knowledge and power. He used the plural pronoun in view of the meaning, lest it be supposed that some of them benefited and others did not, after the singular had been used. It diminishes the light, although it was strong at the start, because it was extinguished at the end. So He said: ﴿their light﴾, meaning that which arose from that fire, by His extinguishing it, and they had no light other than it. He did not say *ḍawʾihim* (their brightness), lest it be supposed that what was taken away was only the excess, since *ḍawʾ* (brilliance) is greater than mere *nūr* (light). ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾ [Yunus: 5]. So their light went away and their fire remained, so that the heat of the fire combined upon them with the heat of the loss of what would have benefited them from the light. He expressed it first with *al-ināra* (lighting up) to indicate the strength of their beginning and the annihilation of their end, because the place of their condition is falsehood, and falsehood has a momentary dominance, then it dissolves before the one who stands firm against it, so that the truthful may be distinguished from the liar. He expressed it with *al-dhahāb bihi* (going away with it) rather than *idhhābihi* (causing it to go) to indicate explicitly that He, glory be to Him, is not with them. He confirmed this by expressing *ṣayyara* (to make/render) through *taraka* (to leave), so He said: ﴿and left them in darkness﴾ (p-120), meaning with misguidance in their hearts and their sights, and their night, meaning darknesses in which no sight penetrates. Therefore its consequence was ﴿they do not see﴾, meaning they have no sight at all, neither by vision nor by insight.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 18:

When he had finished with the parable, he explained what is meant by their "darknesses": that they are the heaviness in their ears that prevents them from benefiting from hearing, and the muteness of their tongues from speaking good, which arises from lack of perception, which arises from the blindness of insight and the corruption of inner thoughts and secrets; and the veil over their eyes that prevents reflection, and the coverings over their insight that negate remembrance. So he said: ﴿Deaf﴾, that is, from useful hearing; ﴿dumb﴾, from useful speech, because their hearts are sealed, so nothing good wells up from them to be cast onto their tongues; ﴿blind﴾ in sight and insight, from seeing that guides, due to the seal previously mentioned upon their faculties. When the context was that of answering the caller to faith, he put hearing first, because it is the foundation in that matter; he placed speech second, because it enables the deaf to express what is meant; and he concluded with sight, because guidance can be achieved through it by signs. The same applies to what comes later in this surah, unlike what is in al-Isra'.

﴿So they﴾, that is, as a consequence of that, they ﴿do not﴾ [return]. Since the intended meaning is generality concerning every return, the thing returned from is not mentioned, so he said: ﴿return﴾, that is, from their transgression and misguidance to the guidance which they have sold, nor to their condition in which they were, and they do not move away from this state of theirs at all, because they are like one whose state is this, and one whose state is this cannot leave his place either forward or backward.

(p-122) "Or" [it is like] a simile for those who hear the Qur'an, which contains the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses, threat and promise: ﴿like a downpour﴾, i.e., people of a downpour, meaning a heavy rain. Al-Harrali said: a copious, pouring cloud. Then he followed it with a clarification, because the intended meaning is the literal one, with his saying: ﴿from the sky﴾. And it is, as al-Harrali said, what is high above the head; he means this is its original sense, and what is meant here is well known. The Qur'an was likened to this because of the continuous descent of its revelation, its loftiness, and its giving life to hearts, just as the downpour gives life to the earth. Then He informed about its condition with His saying: ﴿in it are darknesses﴾, i.e., because of the density and blackness of the cloud; ﴿and thunder﴾, i.e., a frightening sound that makes one tremble upon hearing it; ﴿and lightning﴾, i.e., a light that dazzles because of its flashing and its speed, as al-Harrali said. The darknesses are a simile for what they did not understand; the thunder is what calls them out with disgrace and threat; and the lightning is what gives them a glimpse of its meaning, and an opinion enters them regarding its being good.

(p-123) When the simile of the Qur'an was complete, He resumed the report about the condition of those to whom the simile is addressed and those to whom it is applied, literally and figuratively, and said: ﴿they put their fingers﴾, i.e., some of them; had they been able, they would have stuffed all of them, because of the intensity of their fear, ﴿into their ears because of the thunderbolts﴾, i.e., because of their power, for their terror nearly deafens. Al-Harrali said: the plural of ṣā'iqah, which is the sound that kills its hearer or nearly does. Then he gave the reason for this with His saying: ﴿for fear of death. And Allah﴾, i.e., while the state is that He who encompasses everything in power and knowledge ﴿encompasses the disbelievers﴾, so caution does not avail them against His decree. He stated the explicit noun in place of the pronoun because of their turning away from the Qur'an and their concealing its lights.
