The world is only a prison for the believer. If he perceives it and constricts himself within it, he seeks release from it toward the Hereafter, and so he is made happy. If he does not perceive that it is a prison, and expands himself within it, he seeks to remain in it, though it is not lasting. Horses are of three kinds: a reward for the one who fights (in the way of God), a burden on the one who boasts, and a covering (of need) for the one who seeks sufficiency through them in what concerns his affairs. Exceeding sufficiency in grazing livestock is a severance from the traces of prophethood, a constriction upon those in need, and an accumulation of wealth beyond what was set aside for sustaining livelihood, which should be taken only to the extent of sufficiency. The Prophet ﷺ said: "We have a hundred sheep; we do not want them to increase. When the shepherd gives birth to a young one, we slaughter a sheep in its place." "Food is not to be accumulated as wealth, and likewise what is prepared for sustenance is not hoarded except by a sinner." "Whoever hoards food for forty days has disowned God, and God has disowned him."

Goods are brought in and stored, and gain is sought through them with dinars and dirhams. Food and the means of sustenance are brought in but not stored, so gain is not sought through them with dinars and dirhams. Whoever stores them seeking gain in dinars and dirhams has hoarded them. What is forbidden of the glance of the eye is more fittingly forbidden in the reach of the hand: ﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given some pairs of them to enjoy﴾ [al-Hijr: 88], and the two verses that follow it. By these matters, namely faith of the heart, vision of the inner heart, patience of the soul, and restraining the hand from expanding in acquiring wealth beyond what sustains life, the recitation of the particle of prohibition is attained. And God is the Supporter of confirmation. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 43:

When He, glory be to Him, finished with the matter of the People of the Book, [commanding them] to believe in God, the Prophet, and the Book, which is of the guidance that came to them, indicated by all of that with fulfilling the covenant, He connected it with His saying: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, meaning: be steadfast in the worship known for every day, with all its conditions and pillars. ﴿And give the zakah﴾, meaning the obligatory zakah due in every year, so that you may gather the attributes of the God-fearing (muttaqun), who are guided by this Book: ﴿Who believe in the unseen and establish the prayer and spend out of what We have provided for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], those who do good in that, between themselves and the Truth and between themselves and the creation. These two acts of worship, the bodily and the financial, were singled out for mention because it is their nature to draw in and entail the rest of the acts of worship. Al-Harali said: zakah is growth, both in outward sensory form and in the inner state of the self.

﴿And bow﴾, from ruku' (bowing), which is a midpoint between standing and prostration, occurring outwardly in the stature and inwardly in the state of the heart, by which is singled out the middle community (ummah wasatah) that combines both extremes. The word "ma'a" (with) has the meaning of companionship: from above, by protection; from below, by good following; and from a peer, by good equity. End of quotation.

His saying: ﴿with those who bow﴾, together with what accompanies it, is an emphasis on the matter of prayer and a command to be among those in this religion who follow Muhammad (ﷺ), for the prayer of the Jews has no bowing in it, as its explanation will come in Surah Al 'Imran, God willing.

Al-Harali also said: What is consistent with that, that is, with what has passed, is an address of understanding which is grasped by the conjunction to establishing the prayer, which comes right after faith. So it is as if the address of understanding were: Return, make amends, declare what you have concealed, clarify what you have confused, advise those who seek your advice, establish your direction toward God through prayer, show kindness to the followers after teaching them, give zakah, and complete your prayer with what completes the prayer, the bowing that is balanced in action between the state of standing in prayer and its prostration, manifesting the sign of God's greatness, along with those who bow, who are the Arabs, for whom the first of their prayers was established in perfection. End of quotation. It is also permissible that what is meant by "ruku'" is the prayer, expressed by it because of the particular distinction of this community with it, so it is as if it were said: pray along with those who pray in congregation, for greater emphasis on the recommendation of congregational prayer.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 44:

When He commanded their scholars to adopt the noble qualities they had abandoned, namely faith and the sacred laws, after reminding them of the blessings He had bestowed upon them, and forbade them from the base conduct they had committed, namely ingratitude for blessings, breaking covenants, and what follows from these, and they were ordering others to do what they claimed to be purification, and forbidding them from what they claimed to be corruption, He rebuked them, encouraging what He had urged them to do and reproaching them for abandoning it, with His saying: ﴿Do you enjoin﴾ from "al-amr" (command), which is imposition of a judgment, as al-Haralli stated.

﴿the people to righteousness﴾, which is the extensive performance of good deeds, ﴿and forget﴾, and forgetting (nisyan) is a lapse occurring after knowledge has been attained,

﴿yourselves﴾, meaning you leave off compelling them to that, as one who forgets leaves off. Perhaps He expressed it this way to add to the aversion from this grievous matter, whose vileness reason clearly indicates, because the purpose of commanding others to righteousness is counsel or compassion, and it is not reasonable for a person to show compassion to others or counsel others while forgetting himself. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is the judgment of the Torah: they used to compel their common folk to it while they knew, unlike the common folk, that among the judgments of the Torah is following Muhammad (ﷺ). Thus they forgot themselves in commanding the foundation of righteousness, from which nothing is valid without it.

Al-Haralli said: Since among them were those who pointed the one who sought guidance toward following Muhammad (ﷺ), yet did not guide themselves to what they directed others to, He, exalted is He, declared against them with this, arranging it with what preceded of breaking their covenant, their distortion and concealment, through what appeared of the deficiency of their intellects in that they would show the path of guidance to others without following it. Thereby He removed them from the limit of reason, which is the least state of those addressed, and He increased their rebuke with a circumstantial clause depicting their being clothed in knowledge and wisdom which forbids what they were upon, so He said: ﴿while you recite the Book﴾, from "tilawah" (recitation), which is following the speech of a speaker in terms of its priority, as al-Haralli stated. This circumstantial clause is the greatest alert that among the judgments of the Torah is following him (ﷺ), and it indicates that disobedience from a scholar is more repulsive. Al-Haralli said: In it is an indication that the command of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the explicit wording of its recitation is not hidden from its understanding, so in that there is a departure from the judgment of the light of reason. End.

Since this was in their Book, and they were enjoining it while turning away from it, He, glorified is He, connected the denunciation to His saying: ﴿Will you not then﴾, that is, do you recite it and so ﴿not reason﴾, indicating that what they are upon of this is not done by one who has any sense at all. And reason is the perception of the realities of what the senses have reached in its outward form, as al-Haralli stated. It was named "aql" (reason) because it restrains (ya'qilu) one from falling into ruin.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 45:

When He rebuked them for following their desires, He guided them to its remedy through the noblest qualities of the soul and the most excellent actions of the body. So He said, linking this to the commands that preceded it. al-Ḥarrālī (ḥarrālī) said: "They were only driven to oppose the judgment of reason by what their souls had become accustomed to of leadership and precedence. Because of the hardship for them in becoming followers of the Arabs, after they had seen that the whole earth was subject to them, He connected His address on that matter with seeking help through patience, which compels their souls to become followers after having been leaders. So God, exalted is He, said." End of quotation.

﴿And seek help through patience﴾, that is, in establishing the truth and submitting to it, which is the meaning of the commands and prohibitions that preceded it, ﴿and prayer﴾. Patience (al-ṣabr) is restraining the soul from its needs and habits, and from its reform and purification. It is a light for the hearts, by which they see what the dread of departing from custom in matters the souls incline toward hides from them, as al-Ḥarrālī said. It is general to every kind of patience: fasting and others.

﴿And prayer﴾, that is, the prayer that brings one to the highest station. There is an echo here of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatiḥah: 5], and an indication that whoever's prayer does not restrain him from committing falsehood and persisting in it, and does not command him to hold fast to the truth and return to it, is not truly a worshipper. So the intended patience is freeing the soul from the snares of desire and forcing it toward sincerity. Whoever prays in this manner will undoubtedly be among the saved. He mentioned prayer second because it is a provision that makes them independent of buying a price that they used to take from their followers through confusion and concealment. ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 132]. Thus said al-Ḥarrālī. It is also valid that prayer here means supplication. Whoever is patient toward base things and in the face of hardships, and carries his patience to fasting, thereby removing from himself the turbidity of love of this world, and adds prayer to that, his heart is illuminated with kinds of knowledge. When he adds supplication and seeking refuge with God, exalted is He, to that, he reaches the utmost of righteousness.

When He had commanded and prohibited, ending with prayer, He urged them toward turning to Him, exalted is He, by singling it out with a pronoun, and said: ﴿And indeed it is heavy﴾, that is, very burdensome. The "great" (al-kabīr) is that whose rank or measure is magnificent in an apparent sense or in an inner meaning, as al-Ḥarrālī said.

﴿except for the humble﴾, that is, the lowly ones (al-mukhbitīn) who are in utmost ease, gentleness and humility before their Lord, such that there is no pride in them, and who contemplate the outcomes of the matter and the reward prepared for it. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The coolness of my eye has been placed in prayer." Others are prevented by its weight from performing it, and if they do perform it, they do so without desire. al-Ḥarrālī said: Khushū' (humility) is the stillness of the limbs and the thoughts in what is most important at the time. God, exalted is He, informed that the greatness of prayer is such that only one who is humble can undertake its practice, one who has departed from his own share and obliged his soul to the humiliation of servanthood, with which prophethood was sealed. In the indication of prayer's perfection there is a hint of the afternoon prayer, which is the prayer of the Seal of the Prophets, whose time is the time of 'Aṣr and whose state is servanthood. That is heavy for one who combines with his prophethood and his religion sovereignty, unless he humbles himself to what is heavy upon the soul. Prayer was singled out for greatness rather than patience, because patience is a diminishing for the soul, whereas prayer is a turning toward the Truth, and God is the Most High, the Great. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 46:

﴿Alladhina yazunnun﴾ (those who are certain): from al-zann (supposition), which is a preponderance in belief while an opponent to it from the opposite side remains. Said by al-Harrali.

﴿Annahum mulaqu rabbihim﴾ (that they will meet their Lord) (p-343): i.e., the One who is good to them. He expressed it with zann (supposition) rather than ilm (knowledge) in order to magnify the matter and to draw attention to the fact that it is sufficient for the intelligent person, in urging him to persevere in obedience, that he merely supposes a meeting with the obeyed King who is hoped for and feared. How much more so when the matter is certain, with no doubt about it and no possibility of uncertainty reaching it! It is also possible that what is meant is the supposition of death at every moment, for when a person keeps this in mind, it makes happiness obligatory for him.

Since this sentence, together with its warning, points those of lofty resolve, dignity and zeal away from falling into what brings shame or incurs blame, towards feeling shy before the Benefactor who has never withdrawn His kindness for a moment of time, He increased the warning by His saying: ﴿And that to Him﴾ (alone) ﴿they will return﴾. Al-ruju' (return) is the destination of one who departs, along the paths of his course, and his ascent by the ascending stairs of his descent. Said by al-Harrali. He expressed it thus, although they have never ceased to be in His grip, because His manifest name, glorified is He, will be in that abode in the utmost clarity, with the cessation of causes, such that no one will have any manifestation alongside Him at all, unlike this abode, in which the predominant meaning is that of His hidden name, except for the people of insight. In the verse there is also a rebuke to the People of the Book, that although they are certain of the Resurrection, they grow weary of the works of one who does not even suppose it, let alone one who knows it. Al-Harrali said: Since prayer contains intimate conversation with God in the unseen, it is only made easy for one who supposes the acceptance which the meeting with his Lord after his death implies, and that is the state of one whose Hereafter outweighs this world (p-345) in his deeds and condition. Thus his state and his deeds are those of one who supposes, in keeping with the conditions of those below the rank of certainty. The intended meeting is not the Resurrection itself, since they already believe in the Resurrection, but it is part of the meaning of acceptance after the Resurrection. It also contains an allusion to the state of death and the day of the barzakh, which is the first recompense, so it was joined to the other return after the Resurrection. End.

O Children of Israel (Banī Isrā'īl), [remember] the one whom I honoured and whose descendants after him I honoured with various kinds of honour. ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾, and He magnified its matter by His saying: ﴿which I bestowed upon you﴾, that is, by sending down the Books, sending the Messengers, and other things. ﴿And that I preferred you﴾. Preference (tafḍīl) is an increase, from the step (khuṭwa) of the side of nearness and elevation, in that which admits of increase and decrease. This is said by al-Ḥarrālī.

﴿over the worlds (al-'ālamīn)﴾, namely those who had come into existence in that time, singled out (bi-l-takhṣīs) (p-346) by that to the exclusion of them. What is not included in this are those who had not yet come into existence in that time, as its verification will come shortly from al-Ḥarrālī. Among the things that necessitate certainty regarding this is His saying, exalted is He, to us: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 110].

When he had reminded them of their being singled out for honour and forbidden them to oppose Him, and opposition in the face of great blessing is more abominable, more severe and more gross, He warned them of a Day in which no one will be saved except by his piety. So He said: [Fear a Day].

Al-Ḥarāllīy said: When He called them to fulfil the covenant, alerting the resolve of one who has inner excellence, which returns to the virtues of the soul, those who were granted success responded, and those who were forsaken persisted in their state. He then repeated the address to them, alerting them to the outward blessing, so that whoever fears the change of an outward blessing might take heed, since he did not fear falling from the rank of excellence in the address. So He reminded them of the blessing and the preference by which He favoured them over the worlds, and they were those whose signs of existence appeared in their time. Likewise every preference mentioned in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. The "world" is only that which existence encompasses, not what knowledge has yet encompassed, because that has not removed in witnessing the knowledge of its existence. In this there is an indication that, just as they were preferred over the worlds of their time, this is not restricted to them; rather, in the same way, God preferred the Arabs in the time of their prophethood over the Children of Israel and over all who existed in their time. Since the address reached the reminder of the outward blessing after the reminder of the inner excellence, nothing remained beyond that except the threat of the punishment of the Hereafter, as a continuation of a threat suggested to the understanding by the change of what remained of their blessing in this world. So the implied meaning of the address was: beware lest there befall you the like of what befell those who were seized in this world. End of quotation.

﴿Fear﴾. Since the thing one fears is the recompense that occurs on the Day of Resurrection, He omitted it and put the Day in its place, to magnify it and to alert that its punishment cannot be averted as things other than it may be averted by various stratagems. So He said: ﴿a Day﴾, which is of such greatness that ﴿no soul will avail﴾, that is, will suffice or be of use in it, ﴿for any soul﴾, whichever soul it may be, ﴿anything﴾ of the recompense in the same way.

Al-Ḥarālīy said: The soul of every person is possessed of a precious self-regard toward others. Those who do not benefit one another are of this kind, unlike one who prefers others and whose self-regard has departed; he benefits those below him through intercession and kindness in this world and the Hereafter. In this is the information that the humility of the soul is the origin of success, and its self-regard is the origin of abandonment. ﴿Humble toward the believers﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 54]. So the humility of the servant, with a ḍamma (dhull), is toward God, and his humiliation, with a kasra (dhill), is toward God's servants, a glad tiding of his success; and his turning away from the remembrance of God and his turning the cheek away from people is a warning of his destruction. End of quotation.

Since ransom may occur by the mere existence of the one who ransoms, and he is such that he fears that he will strive to free himself by some kind of stratagem, so hearts are moved to answer him and release his captive, and that release from captivity is taken as his liberation. And it may be sought by action, in secret, to free him by stealing him, or opening his prison, or the like. The famous kinds of ransom are three, and He conjoined them to the more general kind of ransom, so He said: (p-350) ﴿nor will any intercession be accepted from it﴾, that is, from the first soul or the second, ﴿intercession﴾, meaning it is not permitted in it. It is from shaf' (pairing), which is the supporting of the seeker by doubling his desire for what he desires, so that he becomes like an imam for him in the direction of his need. Thus said al-Ḥarālīy. ﴿nor will any ransom be taken from it﴾, which it gives other than righteous deeds. It is the equivalent of a thing, existing alongside it like two equal loads of equal weight on a beast. So ʿidl (with a kasra) applies to a tangible thing, and ʿadl (with a fatḥa) to an intangible thing. Likewise the Arabic usage distinguishes between what is perceptible and what is in meaning by a sign of inflection (iʿrāb) in the very form of the word, not at its end, said al-Ḥarālīy.

Since the absence of help for the group entails its absence for the individual by way of priority, (p-351) He said in the plural: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, meaning a help will renew for them one day from someone who rescues them by force, whoever he may be. Help is the strengthening of one who resists in a matter by something stronger than his opponent; these are two extremes, so that he becomes like one who precedes him by his independence in what the helped one is expected to be unable to achieve, said al-Ḥarālīy. Thereby all the ways of escape that the wrongdoer hopes for in this world are cancelled.

(p-352) Al-Ḥarālīy said: Since the causes of a person's salvation are one of three: either the intercession of one above him in knowledge and virtue, or the help of one above him in strength and power, or the ransom of one who frees himself, since one who is like him does not avail, and still less one below him, the address has covered all three ways, so as to block for the one who holds fast to his self-regard all three means: intercession, ransom and help. End of quotation.

Since it has been previously stated that He favoured them and made a covenant with them, and that His fulfilment of His covenant with them is conditional upon their fulfilment of His covenant, it was fitting to mention intercession first. What completes the explanation will come, God willing, in the second verse. (p-353) When He described that Day as one in which no stratagem avails the possessor of power, the one who is overcome by pride and clothed in greatness, He reminded them of the blessing He bestowed upon them by saving them through Mūsā and Hārūn, peace be upon them both, when the two of them interceded with the king who had enslaved them and inflicted upon them the evil of torment. When he did not grant them their intercession, the two of them confronted him, and they prevailed over him by the strength of their King, and rescued them from him by the might of their God.

Al-Ḥarālīy said: Since the address of calling them had fulfilled for them two aspects of reminder, the inner excellence of the soul through fulfilment, and the outward purpose of the soul in blessing and leadership, what followed of the details of the blessings came by conjunction without renewal of the call, up to the end of the concluding address with them, where He repeated to them the nearer address with the reminder of the blessing, concluding the coherence of His address with what it contained of reminding them through the repetition of His saying: "and when, and when," one after another, up to a portion of them.

When He reminded them of the apparent blessing, those whom guidance reached took heed, and those who deserved punishment persisted in transgression. He reminded those deserving of punishment of what they were punished with, of what entails the meaning of salvation, and of what He explained they were seized for, due to sins resembling their opposition to the Qur'an. When the two reminders, of the covenant and of the blessing, did not benefit them, they were threatened with being fixed upon the places of the trials they suffered from their enemy, for the sins they had committed. ﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs, but you continued in doubt about what he brought you. Until, when he died, you said: "Allah will never send after him any messenger."﴾ [Ghafir: 34] So their denial of the earlier message and their doubt were the cause of the punishment that befell them at the hands of the people of Pharaoh, until Allah rescued them through Moses, peace be upon him. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And when﴾, meaning: remember when ﴿We delivered you﴾. It is from tanjiyah (repeated deliverance), and najah (deliverance) means being raised up onto a najwah (an elevated place of ground), which is safe from the low-lying areas and the unhealthy ground, from destruction by a flood of water or the like. ﴿from the people (ālu) of﴾. Āl (people, household) of a man are those in whom his states, deeds, and actions are manifest, to the extent that they are as if he were present in their absence. It is from the meaning of ālu, which is the mirage in which what is far appears and what would not otherwise be seen becomes visible.

﴿Pharaoh﴾ is the name of the king of Egypt in the pre-Islamic era, a generic proper noun for its kings, like the names of species among animals and others. End of quote. [The meaning of ālu here is Pharaoh and his followers, for ālu is applied to the person himself, to his family, and to his followers and supporters, as stated in the Qamus, which says: it is not used except, generally, for what carries honor.] Then He clarified what He delivered them from in His words: ﴿who afflicted you with a terrible torment﴾. He named it so because it is the most severe affliction for the soul, since it involves demeaning it. It derives from al-sawm (to impose), and it is torment with contempt for the one tormented. Al-sawm is what the soul's aversion and loathing intensify. Then He explained this by His words: ﴿They slaughtered﴾, from tadhbīh (repeated slaughter), and dhabh (slaughter) is a deep cut in the neck, as al-Harrali stated.

Since the slaughter of the son and the leaving of a woman without a man are each more heinous, and since a girl, if she remains, becomes a woman, He expressed it with ﴿your sons﴾ and ﴿your women﴾. Thus ﴿your sons﴾ means driving them as one drives cattle. ﴿And spared﴾: al-Harrali said, from istihya', which is preserving life. ﴿your women﴾: from the sense of taking as a wife for marriage, touching on what had occurred from him. The derivation of insun (humankind), insan (human), and niswa (women) shares one of three letters, hamza, waw, or ya', together with the agreement in nun and sin. End of quote. Then He alerted them to the magnitude of it in His words: ﴿And in that﴾, so He pointed, using the distal demonstrative with the mim attached, ﴿was a trial﴾, i.e., a test, ﴿from your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who did good to you in both times of hardship and ease, ﴿great﴾. Al-Harrali said: balā' (trial) is testing, which is showing the reality of a thing through severe hardship and affliction. It implies that they deserved that and that they were rectified by its severity rather than by something less. He mentioned its greatness because it is widespread in bodies, souls, and spirits. He mentioned the meaning of deliverance, then detailed it, explaining its manner after that, enumerating the blessing of deliverance, which follows the mercy of favor, which follows the elevation of precedence through the covenant. Thus the address reached its end in meaning. That is, when He, Exalted, established against them what they had committed before Moses, peace be upon him, when the people of Pharaoh afflicted them with what afflicted them, He renewed for them a reminder of the blessing of deliverance from the punishment of their earlier deeds. End of quote.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 2, verse 50:

When what was done to them in the sea was the destruction of the men and the preservation of the women, he [Allah] matched with it what they did to the Children of Israel, placing it right after it. So He said, "﴿And when﴾," meaning: remember when "﴿We divided﴾," from *al-farq* (division), which is the separating of one thing from another for the purpose of showing contrast. This is what al-Harrali said. Thus there became for you paths according to the number of your tribes, "﴿for you﴾," meaning on account of you, right after Our bringing you out from the captivity of the Copts, "﴿the sea﴾." Al-Harrali said: it is the vast, wide expanse, whether of what is apparent, like water, or of what is hidden, like knowledge, from which comes *al-hibr* (ink), the two sharing the meaning through the letters of derivation.

"﴿And We delivered you﴾" from *al-injaʼ* (deliverance), which is hastening upward away from destruction to a place of safety and success. The end of the quotation. Among the wonders of this is that just as the deliverance came from it, it also came through it. Al-Harrali said: the sea was made to be divided on account of them, as if they were the cause of its division. So their deliverance is the cause, and Musa's striking of the sea with the staff is the sign and indication by which the sea split open on account of them. He made the deliverance from the tribulation of Pharaoh a rescue (*tanjiyah*) for what was gradual, and made the deliverance from the sea a quick deliverance (*injaʼ*) for what was revelation in a swift moment. The end of the quotation.

"﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾" in it and by it, "﴿while you were watching﴾," watching his hastening toward them as it closed over them. This is like what al-ʻAlaʼ ibn al-Hadrami, may Allah be pleased with him, did when he crossed the salt sea in the region of Bahrayn, or the sea receded for him, according to the two differing reports. It is also like what Saʻd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, did when he crossed the Tigris during the battles against the Persians by swimming with the horses, with all his army, who numbered more than thirty thousand, and not one of them was lost. Whenever a horse grew tired, it would leap and stand upon the surface of the water as if it were on a rock, and when it rested, it would swim again.

Al-Harrali said: "﴿We drowned﴾" comes from *al-gharaq* (drowning), which is reaching the end of a thing to its furthest limit according to its nature. If it is in destruction, then it is the extreme, and its meaning appears in water and the sea because of the depth of its bottom. In water it is like sinking into the earth. *Al-nazar* (watching) is gazing at the image without certainty and without seeing. The end of the quotation. Thus Allah, glory be to Him, reminded them of the blessing of deliverance from Pharaoh first, by their departing from him, and then of his drowning, which was greater than that, second, by that which was itself the means of their safety. And He continued to remind them of the blessings that followed for them, though they deserved vengeance. Al-Harrali said: He established them in their watching of it, and in this there is an indication of the loss of their sight due to the weakness of their insight, since He did not say "﴿you were seeing﴾." For this reason, after it they returned to similar conditions of doubt and refusal toward their prophets. The end.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 51:

When the parting of the sea was for the preservation of the body, and the sending down of the Book was for the preservation of the religion, He followed it with it. And since the sound disposition and the upright temperament call for good conduct during the time of the appointment, for showing affection to the one who makes the appointment, for being gentle with him and courting him, with the hope that his promise will be fulfilled, especially after his great kindness in rescuing them from the enemy and destroying him, He censured their conduct, which was contrary to this, by saying: ﴿And when﴾. Al-Harrali said: When Allah, exalted is He, reminded them of the matter of fulfilling the covenant, which is the final end of their affair, and of the detail that was the beginning of their affair, He arranged this together with the intermediate matter between the two extremes, the highest of which is Musa's (peace be upon him) appointment with his Lord, whose blessing upon him was a blessing upon them. So He said: ﴿And when We appointed﴾ from (p-362) the promise, which is giving hope of good, and "wa'adana" from the mutual appointment (mu'adah), which is the arranging of a meeting, a gathering, a negotiation and the like. ﴿Musa﴾ is a word arabized from the Hebrew, whose explanation, as it is said, is "water" and "tree"; he was named by it because of the chest that was placed in him, cast into the river. ﴿Forty nights﴾, which is the complete period of the night, and the night is the time when perceptible things are obscured. End of quote.

He singled out the night for mention to indicate that the most delightful intimate conversation (munajah) takes place in it, and that there was no sleep during that period, but the intimate conversation was general, covering its night and its day. "Forty" is in the accusative by being placed in the position of the second object of "wa'adna," meaning: the completion of forty, i.e., the speech, or the sending down of the Torah at the completion of the forty, and these are Dhu al-Qi'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. It was also said: Dhu al-Hijjah and ten days of Muharram. Al-Harrali said: In this there is an indication that intimate conversation is only prepared for by a set time of restraining the self from what sustains it, and the perfection of that is (p-363) fasting; and the perfection of the number, which is the stage of transition from one state to another, is forty. The mention of the appointed time in nights indicates that his intimate conversation was a dawn out of the darkness of existence, in the state of the specific creation, insofar as darkness is a sign of the loss of the aim of the light of the Truth, and day is a sign of the manifestation of the light of the Truth. The first to emerge, from the Truth to creation, was His speech to one chosen from among His creatures without an intermediary, while he was still in his worldly life and on his earth, which had been a prison. When the Truth came to one of His servants conversing with him, as it will come on the Day of Recompense after resurrection, that earth became a place of mercy, guidance and light, and that is the coming of Allah, glorified is He, from Sinai, which is mentioned in the earlier Book. End of quote. This is below the story of the Mi'raj, which was granted to our Prophet ﷺ, in piercing the lofty heavens to the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, to what none knows except Allah, the Exalted; he heard speech without an intermediary and returned to his house in the same night, having covered distances that would take fifty thousand years, as I shall explain, if Allah the Exalted wills, in the Surah of As-Sajdah.

Since noble souls and lofty aspirations call for aversion from the wrongdoer and disdain for everything attributed to him or reminding of him, and they had taken from the remnants of the people of Pharaoh some of their ornaments, by which they had entered into his bondage and servitude, and their witnessing of the signs they had seen required the utmost distance from disbelief, He expressed their engaging in it (p-364) with "thumma" (then), saying: ﴿Then you took﴾. Al-Harrali said: From "ittikhadh" (taking), which is an iftial form of that from which "mu'akhadhah" (taking to account) comes, as if it were a prick; it is making something into something in meaning, similar to "akhdh" in perception, and there is some strain in it.

﴿the calf﴾. In this account He mentioned the origin of the appointment and mentioned the appointed time, and the address passed over what came after that delay, as the word "thumma" conveys; and conveying that gave the sense of the good they had received, then they followed it up by adhering to their habit of returning to what they had been accustomed to of their deeds, down to the lowest deed of one who has no intellect and no remnant of sound judgment, namely taking the body of a calf as a god after knowing the signs of divinity regarding the unseen. In this there is an expression of wonder that Musa (peace be upon him), whom Allah had appointed for intimate conversation after the appointed time of forty days of fasting, worship, devotion and withdrawal to his Lord, and then they show themselves as having witnessed God visibly, perceptible—whereas Musa, to whom his Lord spoke, was denied the vision—so how about them? That is their wrongdoing: they placed God in the position of a perceptible thing, while He, exalted is He, is far above being seen by His chosen one who conversed with him in his worldly life, and He conversed with him only after his appointed time; and they aspire to a visible god without any appointment or special relation! In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿after him﴾, that is, after his coming to Our appointment, there is an implied mention of Musa (peace be upon him), affirming what they should have been upon of awaiting what Musa would bring them of the benefits of intimate conversation, as one whose heart is attached to his exemplar; and "al-bu'd" (distance) is a distance from a limit taken as a starting point, so that what precedes it is "before" and what follows it is "after." End of quote.

The affirmation of the particle [min ba'dihi] is because their taking that did not occupy the duration of the distance. ﴿And you were wrongdoers﴾, doing the deed of one who is in the darkest of darkness, after your rescue, Musa, by the clear light.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 52:

When that (act) necessitated the greatest wrath, which would require the One Able (to act) to hasten the seizing (of them), He reminded them of the blessing of respite after it, so He said, indicating the greatness of the sin and of the blessing by the particle of delay: ﴿Then We pardoned you﴾. Al-Harrali said: Then the address passed over the punishment that had befallen them for their taking (the calf) to the mention of pardon, affirming their repeated (acts of) making amends, state after state and time after time; whenever they committed a sin, a pardon came to them from Him. He specified it by the name "pardon" when He mentioned their sins, because one who has been forgiven does not mention his sin. Pardon (ʿafw) is the removal of punishment without removing the mention of it, whereas forgiveness (ghafr) is the extinction of the mention of the sin together with the removal of punishment. End of quotation.

﴿from you﴾, and We did not hasten upon you the seizing (of punishment). In His words, the Exalted: ﴿after that﴾, i.e., after the great sin, there is an indication of the punishment that befell them, and an address to the remainder of those who were pardoned, so that the matter among them would reach an end by which thanks might be hoped for from the rest of them. Thus said al-Harrali. The indication arises from the introduction of "min" (after/from) with the sense of time, which required an interval between the pardon and the sin, not encompassed by the pardon, but in which there was punishment. Just as His words "min ba'dihi" (after it) required an interval between their taking the calf and the first departure of Musa, peace be upon him, for the secret conversation (with his Lord). It is also possible that He used the singular form of the address to indicate that none knows the full extent of the enormity in their religion except the leader of the people of monotheism, the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿so that you might be thankful﴾, i.e., so that your state would be the state of one from whom thanks is expected.

Al-Harrali said: It is the manifestation of the blessing of the inner upon the outer, as it is said: a shakur beast is one whose fodder has yielded visible fatness. In it is an indication that among them are those who give thanks, and among them are those who persist in their error. The uncertainty conveyed by the word "la'alla" (perhaps), which indicates both possibilities and prepares for the possibility of the appearance of both groups, serves until that becomes manifest at its appointed time, for whatever is a matter of doubt on the part of the creatures is, on the part of Allah the Glorified, an ambiguity regarding what He knows about them. On this principle the word "la'alla," "ʿasā" and their like operate. End of quotation.

(p-369) Since this contains evidence of their corrupt natures, their perverse dispositions, and their inability to keep a covenant or remain on a single path, He reminded them of the blessing of the Book, whose nature is to provide firm control in all circumstances by returning to it when one goes astray. So He said: Al-Harrali said: When He mentioned the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, which was specific to them, He then detailed for them the matter of what Musa brought and what they did regarding what he brought. End of quotation. So He said, ﴿And when We gave﴾, meaning by Our majesty, ﴿Musa the Book﴾, meaning the complete one in itself, comprehensive for you along the path of truth. Since the Book, despite comprehending what was intended by it, also distinguishes between confusing matters, He described it with His words, ﴿and the Criterion﴾ (al-Furqan), meaning the one that clarifies things as they really are, without leaving any ambiguity in anything. Al-Harrali said: He established them upon two matters from the Book, in which are the rulings of actions, and the Criterion, in which is the matter of knowledge, and these two are the foundation of the state of establishing the religion through knowledge and action. Al-Furqan is on the pattern فُعْلانٌ, (p-370) an intensive form that conveys comprehensiveness, fullness, and greatness in what it is applied to. In this word it derives from the root "al-farq" (distinction), which is the manifestation of what wisdom has covered, which is apparent to the eyes, through clarification that distinguishes its confusion from what the ear hears. He used the word لَعَلَّ (perhaps) in it, to indicate ambiguity in their situation and in the division among them between one who affirms the ruling of the Book, acts by it, knows the hidden meaning of the Criterion and is informed about it, and one who abandons the ruling of the Book and is heedless of the knowledge of the Criterion. End of quotation. So Exalted is He said: ﴿So that you may be guided﴾, meaning so that your state would be that of those whose guidance is hoped for, such that their forbearance overcomes their ignorance and their intellect overcomes their desire. For this reason, after this conclusion, He followed it with what He guided them to, namely (p-371) the punishment that deters them from the like of such killing of souls. So He said:

And when Moses said to his people.

Al-Harrali said: When the turning of the address toward them had been completed several times, through what preceded of their being called and of the conjunction with what is in its relative clause, the Truth (al-Haqq) turned the direction of the address away from them toward mentioning the address of His Prophet ﷺ to them. God addresses His servants by dropping the intermediary between Himself and them, elevating their ranks before Him. So He raises whom He wills and answers him with what He wills, and He holds back whom He wills, placing between Himself and him in address an intermediary from His Prophet. When He had established them through what had passed of reminder regarding what the Truth had confronted them with, He mentioned in this verse their being established upon what their Prophet had addressed them with, when the Truth turned away from addressing them because of the ugliness of the sin they had committed. End of quotation.

Then He said: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾, meaning those who worshipped the calf and those who remained silent about it. Al-Harrali said: "The people (qawm)" is the name for those who have a favor in standing by what they are described with, and for this reason it is contrasted with the word "women," because of their weakness in what they attempt. In it there is a warning to this community that what befell them in addressing their Lord may befall them too, so that He turns away from them. End of quotation.

﴿O my people﴾. He emphasized the address because of their deep ignorance of the enormity of what they had committed and their negligence regarding it, due to what had been soaked into their hearts of desire. So He said: ﴿Indeed you have wronged yourselves﴾, a wrong for which you deserve punishment, ﴿by your taking the calf﴾, that is, as a god besides God. You made yourselves submissive to something that possesses nothing for them, and which is more noble than they are. You brought them down from the rank of their dignity, by their submission to their Master, who does not humble whoever is loyal to Him and does not honor whoever opposes Him, to a state of humiliation by their submission to one who is beneath you. This is the worst of wrongs, for a person is not fit to be humbled and to worship one like himself, so how (could he do so) for something beneath him, an animal! How much more so for what resembles an animal: an inanimate piece of gold, which is among the metals, and which is the lowest of created things in rank, since its life does not carry it to the point of appearing above the earth like plants of the herb and tree kind, and because of what benefit there is in grain and fruit, which are used as food and medicine. Metals are used only as tools and currency; their benefit lies in extracting them, not in their existence. Thus said al-Harrali. ﴿So repent to your Creator (bari’)﴾, the One who originated you before you took the calf, free from defect (bari’in min al-ayb), together with the perfecting of creation in its varied forms. Al-Harrali said: "The Creator (al-Bari’)" is a name that carries the meaning of "release" (al-bur’), which is the preparation of materials for shaping, like one who cuts leather and cloth to make a shoe or a shirt, or one who grinds wheat and kneads clay to make bread or pottery and the like. Its meaning is refining a thing according to its readiness for its form. End of quotation.

Since their repentance was by killing their relatives, even if they were fathers or sons, He referred to them by "souls" for this reason, and to indicate the vileness of what they had committed. So He said: ﴿Then kill your souls﴾, that is, the souls that He brought into being, which led you to other than Him. Al-Harrali said: Killing (al-qatl) is the cutting off of a living creature before the end of its strength, like the cutting of a crop before its harvest. End of quotation. Since what He commanded them was something that is barely permitted, He magnified the desire for it by saying: ﴿That is better for you﴾, that is, this great matter, which is killing, is better for you. Al-Harrali said: "Good (khayr)" is what is suitable in choosing among perceptible things, and what is most fitting and most excellent. Sometimes the word "khayr" is used without its comparative, so one says: "It is good in itself," meaning it is something to be chosen. And one says: "This is better than that," meaning more excellent for choosing, and likewise the word "evil (sharr)" in contrast to it. Both indicate an intermediate thing that is not chosen for the sake of additional benefit nor discarded for the sake of harm or detriment. (Al-Harrali also said:) "ʿInda (with/at)" is a word that conveys the association of what it is attached to with some general or more specific relation; "ladun" is more specific than "ʿinda," so "ladun" is its specific sense and "ʿinda" its general sense, like one who owns a thing: it is "with him" even if it is not in his presence. End of quotation.

﴿With your Creator﴾, that is, the One who is able to annihilate you as He was able to bring you into being. In the expression "the Creator" there is an encouragement for them to obey Him by reminding them of His kindness, and a warning by bringing about humiliation.

Since the implied meaning is: "So you performed the repentance that was commanded, by some of you killing others, through His granting you success, glorified is He, together with the great hardship in it," He joined to it His saying: ﴿So He accepted your repentance﴾, that is, despite the magnitude of your crime. Had it not been for His accepting your repentance, you would not have repented. Then He gave the reason for this in His saying: ﴿Indeed He﴾, that is, because ﴿He is the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾, meaning this has always been an attribute of His, not something He owed to you. Al-Harrali said: In the manifestation of "He" (huwa) separated from the pronoun it is connected with, there is an affirmation of the meaning of mercy for God, a fixed affirmation that does not change or alter, except that it is behind a veil of the unseen, with whatever God wills of discipline, trial, and punishment. For this reason He concluded it with His name "the Most Merciful," because concluding reveals most clearly the hidden meaning within what is concluded. End of quotation.

(p-٣٧٨) When they were asked to repent of worshipping the calf, to which they had bound themselves through something tangible, which is itself a proverb for stupidity, they sought to see their Creator with the senses, in keeping with the attributes of perfection that He has, which reject being made common. They forgot all the blessings and punishments, hastening into disbelief, which is characteristic of the bewildered. Yet the Criterion (al-Furqan), which leaves no doubt and leaves no confusion, stood before them. For they were in a great state of rigidity, of clinging to illusion and the senses. So He, glorified is He, reminded them of this, consoling the Prophet ﷺ regarding their refusal to believe in him, by what they did with Moses, peace be upon him, who was one of them.

(p-٣٧٩) He said: ﴿And when you said﴾, that is, after you had seen the signs and witnessed the clear matters, ﴿O Moses﴾. They called him by his name, in rudeness and harshness, as one of you calls another, and you did not single him out with anything indicating honour for him, despite what you had seen of God's honouring of him and your honouring through him. ﴿Never﴾ is a word that conveys the negation of an inner meaning; it is as if it were "lā an" (not that), with its wording made lighter by the reduction. Thus said al-Harallī.

﴿We will believe you﴾, that is, on account of your saying. Al-Harallī said: (p-٣٧٩) He used the preposition lām (for) because they had already believed in him, and then held back from believing in him in the sense that involves particulars of what would come to them from him. Whoever believes in someone has believed in matters for his sake, and whoever believes in him has accepted the essence of his message. ﴿He believes in God, and he believes for the sake of the believers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 61]. ﴿Until﴾ is a word that conveys a bounded limit, in which what follows enters into the ruling of what precedes it, in contrast to the meaning of li-kay (in order that). ﴿We see﴾ derives from ru'ya (seeing), which is a perception of the inner nature of a thing, made manifest to the one who perceives it, the manifestation being by its appearance. From this comes the word ru'yā (dream) at the beginning of sleep, because the forms of the seen in a dream are like the inner reality in the form of what is looked upon while awake. End of quote.

﴿God﴾, that is, with what He has of greatness. ﴿Openly﴾, that is, visibly, without concealment or any kind of ambiguity. Al-Harallī said: it derives from jahr (openness), which is the announcing of a thing to the point of fame, (p-٣٨٠) and its conveying to those who are not intended, in contrast to the secret that is specific to those intended by it. This thing sought is not fitting for openness, since it is established that it is specific to those whose veil is lifted, from among the special ones of those who are drawn near, from among the special ones to whom the call is directed, from among the special ones from whom turning away occurs. How then could it be sought openly, so that it would be attained by one who is in the place of distance and rejection! This is testimony to their dullness regarding the place of seeing. For Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, show me [Yourself]﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. And God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22-23]. And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Verily you will see your Lord." So the name mentioned for the meaning of seeing is only "the Lord," because of what is in the name of God, exalted is He, of the unseen, which is not mentioned for this purpose except with what is a loss, not with what in meaning is an attainment. This is because of one of the secrets (p-٣٨١) of knowledge of the places of the meanings of the Most Beautiful Names, in what suits them of the varieties of address, circumstances and actions. It is among the most noble of knowledge by which the discourse of the Qur'an is understood, so that each name is given what is most closely connected to its meaning and most appropriate to it, although all names return their meanings to one another.

﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾. Akhdh (seizing) is taking hold of a thing as a whole, with a kind of force and might. End of quote. That is, for this statement of yours, because of its monstrousness and violation of what is sacred.

﴿The thunderbolt (al-ṣā'iqa)﴾. It was said: it is a cry. And it was said: it is fire that came down from heaven and burned them. What supports this is His saying: ﴿while you were looking﴾, that is, (p-٣٨٢) the thunderbolt, and it caused you to die, because in your seeking to see Him you were in a condition resembling the worshippers of the calf, so He caused you to die as He caused them to die, by slaying.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 56:

Since their revival from that was in the extreme of remoteness and a breaking of custom, he expressed it with the particle of delay (thumma) and with the manifestation of greatness, so He said ﴿Then We raised you up﴾, meaning: by what We possess of greatness, through reviving.

Al-Harrali said: from al-ba'th (raising), which is stirring up from (p-383) a hidden and concealed state. Its most intense form is raising from the graves, and below it is raising from sleep. He said: The address has passed over what was the cause of their being raised, and likewise every place in which thumma occurs contains an address that spans a long duration and many degrees of number, understood by the one who has fully grasped the purposes of the two conjoined statements between which the word thumma stands. So within the sense of the address passing beyond is the request of Musa, peace be upon him, to his Lord regarding their being raised, so that it would not become a trial for the rest of them. End of quotation.

Since one might suppose that the raising was from a swoon or the like, he established its meaning, clarifying that it did not occupy the duration of the remoteness, by His saying: ﴿after your death﴾, meaning: this was by that thunderbolt. And He said, indicating that raising to this abode does not sever the obligation upon which they were built, because it is the abode of troubles, so there must be a purification of the secrets within it through deeds (p-384) and remembrances: ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾, meaning: so that your state becomes the state of one for whom hoping for his thanks for this great blessing is valid. Every instance of la'alla (perhaps/so that) that occurs with the acts of the Lord, blessed and exalted be He, as its causal particle, should be interpreted in a manner similar to this, for la'alla implies doubt, since it expresses hope and apprehension: one hopes for the occurrence of what follows it and fears that it may not occur. Sometimes the doubt belongs to the addressee and sometimes to the speaker. Had it been said "li-tashkuru" (that you might give thanks), there would be no doubt in it. This was stated by al-Rummani in the surah of Yusuf, peace be upon him.

Al-Harrali said: In la'alla there is the concealment of what is known to Him concerning them, that among them is one who gives thanks and among them is one who does not give thanks. End of quotation.

Sibawayh's text in his "Kitab" will come in the surah of Ta-Ha, God willing, supporting what I have mentioned.

In this verse and what precedes it, from the verse ﴿And guard against a Day when no soul will avail another soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], there is an admonition to the Arabs for their heedlessness in denying the resurrection, and a guidance to asking those among the People of the Book who deceive them into thinking they have a better claim to the truth than the Muslims about this account that befell their forefathers, of their being revived after their death, and likewise what came in their dialogues of the story of (p-385) the cow and the like, in which there is mention of revival in this abode or on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Harrali said: In it, that is, this address, is a sign of the final resurrection promised to the whole of the human race, all at once, with a sudden swoon and swift raising, for what is established for one of them or for a group among them can be generalized to all of them. End of quotation.

When the thunderbolt, which generally arises from the clouds, was mentioned, it was most fitting to follow it with mention of the clouds shading them. The warning against the punishment of being burned by the thunderbolt, and the reminder of the blessing of being brought back to life after death, were also suitably followed by mention of the favour of sustenance in preserving life, through protection from the heat of the sun outwardly and from hunger inwardly.

Al-Harrali said: "The Exalted turned, after mention of the resurrection, to mention a state like the states of the people of Paradise, which they attain after the resurrection. Thus it is as if the rest of them, who had not died, were partners with these resurrected ones, because they were as if they had died with their death and were raised with their resurrection. So He mentioned the shade of the clouds, which is among the matters after the resurrection, and the provision without toil, which is among the states after the resurrection. This implied other matters in their conditions, as it is said: their garments would grow along with them as they grew. So it is as if they were removed, in general, from the conditions of the people of this world to something resembling the conditions of the people of Paradise, in a place of their wandering and a place deserving of punishment for them, all of this as a favour upon them. Yet, despite all of that, they only increased in distance from reflection upon all the wonders displayed to them. (Speak of the Children of Israel and there is no blame.)" So He said: ﴿And We shaded you﴾, from the shade (ẓulla), which is a shelter from what descends from the sky of the one who is ever-threatening, and ﴿the clouds over you﴾, from ghamm, which is what covers the light, i.e., conceals it. (End.) That is, We did that to ease your bodies and refresh your spirits.

On the authority of Mujahid: the cloud (ghamam) is cooler, thinner and purer than the cloud (saḥab).

﴿And We sent down upon you the manna﴾. Al-Harrali said: it is what comes without toil; the mushroom (kam'a, truffle) is of the manna. (End.)

﴿And the quails﴾, that is, as food for you, given that the manna is from the clouds; and He gathered the quails to them by a wind that stirred them, so He linked them with it in the utmost suitability. Al-Harrali said: al-salwa is the name of a kind of bird; it is said to be the quail (samani) or something else. (End.) It will come, Allah willing, in al-A'raf, that it is other than the quail, and that they were singled out with it as a notification of the hardness of their hearts.

This marvel: the Companions of our Prophet ﷺ were indeed independent of it, since whenever they needed something, the Prophet ﷺ would call for what they had of surplus provisions, and he would supplicate, and Allah would multiply it until they were sufficed, from the first of them to the last. "He gave Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, some dates and ordered him to put them in a pouch (mizwad), and said to him: 'Spend, and do not scatter them.' So he ate from it for years and spent from it more than fifty wasq." He blessed another man in a little barley, and ordered him not to measure it, so he continued to spend from it on himself, his wife and his guest until he measured it and it ran out. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Had you not measured it, you would have eaten from it, and it would have remained for you." Something similar happened to Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, after the death of the Prophet ﷺ. Likewise for Umm Malik, may Allah be pleased with her, with a jar (akka) of ghee, which continued to provide her relish until she squeezed it. Many such things are in the Proofs of Prophethood (Dala'il al-Nubuwwa) of al-Bayhaqi and others.

It was said to them: ﴿Eat﴾, and this indicates that it was more than their sufficiency, by His saying: ﴿of the good things﴾, the plural of ṭayyiba. Al-Harrali said: the good (ṭayyib) is what is free of any rival that shares in it, and its goodness apart from eating is that it is not contested, and there is no right of another in it. From it is the good in taste, which is what is not contested by any aversion in its flavour. This one added to that by being not from the work of tilling or dealing with creatures. (End.)

﴿of what We have provided you﴾, that is, despite Our greatness, which cannot be matched.

When they did not heed these blessings, He turned away from them to indicate that they deserved anger. Al-Harrali said: then He turned the address away from them and directed it to Muhammad ﷺ and those with him. (End.) So He said: "And" — that is, they wronged themselves by denying all these blessings — "they did not wrong Us" in any of that, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, that is, by nature and disposition, ﴿themselves﴾ specifically, ﴿they were wronging﴾, because the harm of that is confined to them. Al-Harrali said: in this there is a signal warning to these (the present audience) that they might see something like what those (earlier people) saw, so that something like what those people suffered would befall them, because the stories of the Qur'an are not intended only for mention of the earlier people; rather every story in it was mentioned for what will befall this community in the span of its days, of similar conditions to those to whom its stories were related. (End.)

(p-٣٩١) Since both the shade of the clouds and the single food, which was unfamiliar to them, were a worldly blessing, and since familiar things are dearer to souls, He followed them with a reminder of a familiar blessing, the shelter of dwellings and eating what is desired, coupled with a religious blessing. Al-Harrali said: When the Exalted mentioned His great favour toward them, in the state in which they deserved punishment, in the shading of the clouds and the sending down of the manna and the quails, which was the beginning of the matter of their wandering (tih) when they refused to fight the tyrants (al-jabbarin), He linked to it the end of the matter of their wandering, after the death of Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, when they entered with Yusha', peace be upon him, and what they were commanded of entering the holy land, humbling themselves with prostration, which is the most specific of the ranks of worship, the perfection of the worker's deed, and nearness to the Truth. End of quotation. So the Exalted said: ﴿And when We said﴾, that is, to you, ﴿Enter this town﴾, as a sign of the blessing of victory. Al-Harrali said: Entering (al-dukhul) is penetrating into a thing wholly, physically with the body and figuratively with insight and opinion. The town (al-qarya) is from "gathering" (al-qara), which is the gathering of the benefits by which the establishment of worldly life is achieved for the towns of the people of this world, and which gathers the benefits of the people of the Hereafter for the towns of the people of the Hereafter. He, peace be upon him, said: "I have been commanded with a town that devours the towns," meaning by settling in it, as though it were seeking out the towns and gathering them (p-٣٩٢) toward itself. The letters ya', hamza and waw have alternated with qaf and ra' over the general meaning of this. End of quotation. The context of the blessings suited indicating that the entering blessing is followed by the particle "fa" in His saying: ﴿then eat from it wherever you wish﴾, and He completed the blessing with His saying ﴿in abundance (raghadan)﴾, that is, widely and pleasantly for you. Al-Harrali said: In this address there is also a repetition in mentioning the land, in reference to what preceded of its like for Adam in heaven. Their substitution for that was thus due to wickedness, not to forgetfulness as was the case with Adam, peace be upon him. It is as though they were cut off from his course toward the state of Satan, who was among the jinn and who transgressed the command of his Lord. Thus their wrongdoing was confirmed, since they did not resemble their fathers and resembled the enemy of their father. End of quotation. He commanded them to give thanks for the blessings of victory, shelter, and the abundant provision, with a small matter (p-٣٩٣) of speech and action. He placed first the entering, which delights the souls, and the prostration, which is the closest thing bringing one near to the noble presence, because it is in the context of enumerating blessings, against the saying that suggests sin. So He said: ﴿And enter the gate﴾, and it is, as al-Harrali said, the first opening of things (p-٣٩٤) and of matters that are locked, whether physically or figuratively, while you are ﴿prostrating﴾ and ﴿say﴾, combining with the regret of the heart and the humbling of the limbs the seeking of forgiveness with the tongue. Since speech is that by which sentences are related, and it takes them as its object, and it operates upon a single word when that word is a verbal noun or an adjective of a verbal noun, as in "I said truly", or when it refers to a whole sentence, as in "I said a poem", and whatever is not in this manner is a verbal (lafzi) predication without benefit beyond mere compliance, He let His saying ﴿hittah﴾ be nominative, that is, "a great [removal]" for our sins. Al-Kashshaf said: The original form is the accusative, that is, "Remove from us our sins", but it was made nominative to give the meaning of permanence. Al-Harrali said: From "removing" (al-hatt), which is (p-٣٩٥) setting down a heavy load with ease and the recovery of strength that occurs in the body. The meaning is that they were commanded to say what would remove from them their sins which had hindered them from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, together with those with him of the Emigrants and the Helpers, in one of the mountain passes, wandering between the two noble sanctuaries, that is, during the 'Umra of al-Hudaybiya. He said: Say: "There is no god but God." At that moment there was entry into the pass, which is the gate of entrance from the highlands of Najd to its plain. They said it, and he said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is! Indeed it is the hittah that was offered to the Children of Israel that they should say, but they changed it." End of quotation. He used the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama, the "we" of grandeur) in His saying ﴿We will forgive you﴾, as an indication that no sin is too great for Him, even if it is great like the taking of the calf, when it is cut off by repentance. In the reading of the one who reads with the verb in the third person masculine (ya') and the second person (ta'), in the passive voice, there is an indication of belittling sins when He wills their forgiveness, such that by a lowest command and a finest sign they are erased, and they are too little for Him to deal with them with His holy self. All of this is an appeal toward repentance. And forgiveness (al-ghafr) (p-٣٩٦) Al-Harrali said: Covering a sin is that a trace of it does not appear on the sinner, with no punishment and no mention. Then he said: In the reading "naghfir" there is a turning from the Truth and from those of His party among the angels and messengers; in the reading "tughfar" there is a conveying of the matter of their address in what the feminine form conveys of the descent of decree; and in the reading with ya' there is a middle position between the two extremes, which the height of the reading with nun and the descent of the reading with ta' imply. So in this whole there is an indication that their sins were at every level in what relates to the worship of their Lord, the states of their souls, and their dealings with others, including their prophets and their like, until their sins gathered all the directions of the three kinds of sin. It is as though they were three categories: a category that substituted, a category that was moderate, and a category that did good, and God increases for them what speech cannot contain. ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ [al-Rahman: 60]. End of quotation. Since the context here is for enumerating blessings, it was fitting to express their sins with the plural of abundance, so He said ﴿your sins (khatayakum)﴾, as an indication that they persisted in them (p-٣٩٧) to the point that they almost made, for every blessing, a sin in its place. Khataya is the plural of khati'a, from khata', which is slipping away from the limit without intention, but rather with the resolve to hit the mark or the wish not to err. Thus said al-Harrali. But the apparent meaning here is what was done deliberately, whatever it was, because that is more fitting to the context of favour and to punishment for disobedience. In the Qamus it is said: Khati'a is a sin, or what is done intentionally, and khata' is what is not done intentionally; its plural is khataya. It was read anomalously as "khati'atikum" with the sound plural, which indicates fewness, as an indication that although they are many, they are few beside His pardon. This differs from al-A'raf, since the context there is to explain their haste in disbelief, as will come, God willing, the Exalted. And enumerating the blessings suited the connection to what preceded of them with His saying: ﴿And We will increase the good-doers (al-muhsinin)﴾, that is, after the forgiveness of their sins. Al-Harrali said: The plural of muhsin is from ihsan, which is reaching the end in the goodness of action, so that with creation there is a man's seeing himself in others, so that he conveys to them the righteousness that must be done toward them, and a servant's seeing his Lord in his worship. Thus ihsan between the servant and his Lord is that he is absent from himself and sees his Lord, and ihsan between the servant and others is that he is absent from others and sees himself. So whoever sees himself in the need of another and does not see himself in the worship of the Lord is a muhsin, and that is reaching the end of goodness in action in both directions, like goodness in form. End of quotation. (p-٣٩٨)

When this exhortation to desire, which implies a warning, required the sensible person to hasten to obedience, He explained that as a consequence some of them disobeyed and rejected this great blessing. They did not stop at abandoning this command but replaced it by entering in the manner mentioned in the hadith: "They will crawl on their buttocks, saying: 'A grain in a hair.'" That is, the genus of grain within the genus of hair, i.e. in the sacks, is what we seek, not the *hittah* (the "remission," meaning the forgiveness of sins). (p-٣٩٩) Al-Harrali said: They were commanded to sincerity toward God, having regard to the life of their hearts, but they sought wheat, having regard to the life of their bodies. So He said, ﴿so those who did wrong substituted﴾, from *al-tabdil* (substitution), which is the replacing of one thing in place of another. End of quotation.

﴿Those who did wrong﴾. He omitted "from among them," because of what comes in al-A'raf: ﴿a saying﴾, that is, in place of the saying they were commanded to utter.

Since *al-tabdil* conveys change but applies even to the slightest change, even if it is only in wording while the meaning remains the same, He explained that the substituted saying is opposed to the commanded one in such a way that the two cannot coexist, by saying: ﴿other than what had been said to them﴾. For *ghayr* (other than), as al-Harrali said, is a word that conveys the negation of something and the affirmation of its opposite. (p-٤٠٠) He said: God mentioned their turning away from all of that and their preoccupation with their bellies and their immediate worldly gain. They sought food for their bellies, whose provision had already been decreed, and God showed them that they were independent of it during the wandering in the desert, by sending down the manna and quails, to manifest the dullness of their natures and the dominance of their love for the fleeting world over them. So they substituted the word of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), which is *la ilaha illa Allah* (there is no god but God), and which is the *hittah*, with the seeking of *hintah* (wheat). ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66] (p-٤٠١) ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96]. The hadith: "Whoever is occupied by remembrance of Me instead of asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give those who ask." End of quotation.

He explained that He singled out the substituters for reproach, as a favour from Him, although He could have made it general. So He said: ﴿Then We sent down﴾, that is, by Our majesty, because of that, ﴿upon those who did wrong﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿a plague﴾. Al-Harrali said: *al-rijz* is the most severe punishment, and whatever leads to it is also called *rijz*, which is what one must be restrained from, and *al-zajr* (restraint) is the holding back of beasts from their enmity. End of quotation. Since "sending down" implies a source, He confirmed it in magnification of it by saying: ﴿from the heaven because﴾, that is, because of what ﴿they used to defy﴾, that is, they continually renewed their departure from obedience into disobedience at every time. In the implication of this is that they return to obedience after departing from it, and this necessarily entails that they would do wrong to a greater degree than this, as will come. Al-Harrali said: So it is incumbent by right upon whoever enters through the gate of a mountain or a town to say at its threshold: *la ilaha illa Allah*, so that the past of his sins may be lowered from him. It is as if the mention of God at the gate of the city or the mountain pass were a slaughter (*dhakah*) for that entrance, and whoever does not enter it while slaughtering enters it as a sinner. ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned, for indeed it is a defiance﴾ [al-An'am: 121]. Therefore their mention is concluded in the verse with *fisq* (defiance). End of quotation.

[p. 403] When He, glorified is He, had shown His favour to them by enabling them to take the town, by granting them victory over its people and by letting them enjoy its benefits, and had concluded that passage with their punishment by means that cause death or burning, and it became clear from all of this that their hearts were harder than stones, as will be explicitly stated later in the words of God, exalted is He, in the story of the cow, and that the cow is of no benefit, He followed this with a reminder of His favour to them in the wilderness, with that which cools the livers and revives the bodies. He mentioned the gushing of water from the rock, whose benefit reached them all and whose spring rescued them from death, and whose root and branch point to monotheism and prophethood, through the power and knowledge of the Maker. In this way He combined for them the two favours of religion and of this world. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when he asked for water﴾, that is, he sought water. Al-Harrali said: "Al-suqya (watering) is on the pattern fu'la, a form of intensification with respect to that by which satisfaction is obtained. Al-saqy is the reviving of what is dead, and its nature is to seek revival, whether by state or by speech. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'O Allah, give drink to Your servants!' Then he said: 'and revive Your dead land.'" End of quotation.

﴿Moses to his people﴾, that is, when they feared death from thirst. ﴿So We said﴾, that is, by what We have of majesty, at the time when [the water] was hidden from them. ﴿Strike﴾. Al-Harrali said: "From al-darb (striking), which is the impact of one thing upon another with force." ﴿with your staff﴾. The "'asa" (staff) is as if it is that by which the disobedient one is restrained, and it is of the roots with waw; the waw in it indicates height, as if it were an instrument that rises above one who commits what is disobedient, whereas the yā' indicates the descent of his action into disobedience. It is as if al-'asw (the staff) is the discipline of staves. It is said 'asa ya'(w)su, meaning he struck with a staff, a second derivation; and 'asa ya'sī, when he opposed the command." End of quotation.

﴿the rock﴾, that is, its kind, so he struck a rock. ﴿and it gushed forth﴾. How appropriate is the mention of gushing here, after the conclusion of what came before with corruption, since the two share going out beyond an enclosure: [p. 405] this is an outgoing that gives life, and that is an outgoing that brings death. Al-Harrali said: "Infijar (gushing) is the emergence of a flow from something that is contained, or as if it were contained, which has split and burst open from its container; from it comes al-fajr (dawn) and the splitting of the night." End of quotation. And since this is the context of enumerating favours, He expressed it with infijar, whose meaning revolves around a splitting in which there is flowing and emergence together with spreading, expansion and abundance. Since there were not, ﴿from it﴾, that is, from the rock that he struck, ﴿twelve springs﴾, one for each tribe. The spring, al-Harrali said, is that which is manifest, sustaining, and upright, through which other things become apparent. Whatever water suffices for drinking or for crops is a spring, and what rain falls from the sky and suffices is a spring. It is said that 'ayn (spring) is the rain of days that does not cease, but rather it is rain that suffices and nourishes.
