That by which weighed things appear is a 'ayn, and that by which visible things appear from the sun is a 'ayn, and that by which objects are perceived through the senses is a 'ayn; al-rakiyya, which is a well for watering, is an 'ayn, and it is the one that some people corrupt, saying: "al-rukba" (knee) with a b, meaning the single-dotted letter, whereas it is actually al-rakiyya with a doubled yā'; so he said. The people of language have mentioned 'ayn al-rukba; and al-Qamus counts the meanings of this word at about forty, among them naqrat al-rukba (the hollow of the knee) [p. 407], that is, with the b, and among them the place where water of the rakiyya gushes forth, with a doubled yā'.

When the listener anticipated the speaker's report about whether the springs were distributed among them in a known way or in a confused way, He said: ﴿Every people knew their drinking place﴾, that is, from among them. Al-Harrali said: "It is a collective noun from al-uns (familiarity), with a damma, like al-nas is a collective noun from al-naws. He did not name them with any of the names of religion, because names follow what predominates over those who bear them, whether in states of religiosity, in natural disposition, or in acquired disposition." ﴿their drinking place﴾: their sufficiency for drinking, repeated over the days and with needs at every time, as conveyed by the form al-mash'ar, which is a second verbal noun derived from the general notion of drinking, or a noun of place that necessarily involves repetition and recurrence. So He, glorified is He, made their watering a sign from His signs through His staff, just as His sign was through His staff against His disbelieving enemy, and there was in it both punishment and mercy. Through this the perfection of His dominion, exalted is He, over Muhammad ﷺ became evident, when water gushed from between his fingers, independent in its gushing of an instrument of striking or of a rock. And the granting of dominion over water is among the greatest forms of empowerment, for it is an empowerment over that which is the seed of everything, from which every living thing comes and in which everything made and formed is contained. End of quotation. He means that this extraordinary event is less than what gushed for the Prophet ﷺ from between his fingers, and less than what gushed when his Companions placed one of his arrows into the well of al-Hudaybiyya, though it had no water in it; and there are many like this.

Since the context is one of enumerating favours, and bringing into existence does not necessarily entail permission to consume, He said, in addition to what is in al-A'raf, enumerating for them the favour of permission after bringing into existence, on the understanding that the statement is implied: ﴿Eat and drink from the provision of God﴾ [p. 409], that is, the provision that He, to whom belongs all perfection, has provided for you without toil or exhaustion. Al-Harrali said: "Since there was in their eating and drinking no continuity with the customary wisdom of God on earth, and it came from the unseen, its mention was attributed to the Name of God, which is unseen." ﴿and do not act wickedly﴾ [p. 410], from al-'athw, which is the most severe corruption; likewise al-'athy, except that this contrast between waw and yā' indicates that al-'athw is the corruption of the people of power through force, and al-'athy is the corruption of the people of deceit through trickery. End of quotation.

﴿in the earth﴾, that is, generally, because whoever corrupts any part of it in action has corrupted all of it in potential. The following of what means corruption with His saying ﴿causing corruption﴾ is evidence that the meaning is: do not hasten to do what would be corruption, intending corruption by it. For al-'athy and al-'ayth are hastening in corruption; but it may be that the good is intended through the form of corruption, so that it becomes righteousness in meaning, as al-Khidr, peace be upon him, did with the boat and the boy. The intention of "hastening" is not a restriction; rather it indicates that, because it suits desire, it will not occur except in this way. Further elucidation of this will come, God willing, in Surat Hud, peace be upon him. Al-Harrali said: "In it there is an indication [p. 411] that this occurred from them, because in every prohibition there is an indication of its violation, except what God wills, and in every command there is an indication of its compliance, except what God wills; for what a person is created upon is not commanded, since his compulsion in it by nature suffices without a command, and what he is prevented from is not forbidden, since his compulsion suffices without a command. Rather, the course of command and prohibition is a preparation for manifesting the reality of the distinction between the obedient and the disobedient. Thus there came from them, for this reason, of corruption what necessitated what the Truth reported about them of humiliation. And the gravest corruption is the corruption of the edifice of the Truth, which He created with His own hand, which are the structures of the bodies of the children of Adam; so how much more so the believers among them [p. 412], and how much more so the prophets among them." End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 1 of 6):

When Allah had bestowed upon them this great blessing, the eating of the manna and the quail and the drinking of this divinely provided water, He explained that they had ungrateful for it by being impatient with it and seeking something else, and by wandering in the wilderness while being close to it. Indeed, just as this blessing was at the utmost height of excellence, what they sought was at the utmost baseness and lowliness. So the Exalted said ﴿And when you said﴾, meaning after all these blessings, ﴿O Musa﴾, addressing him by his name without honouring him, ﴿we will not be patient﴾, meaning for a long time, ﴿with one kind of food﴾. Al-Harallī said: "Ṭaʿām (food) is that which sustains the one who eats it and becomes its substitute." Then the verse: ﴿So let man look at his food﴾ [ʿAbasa 24]. End of quote.

﴿One kind﴾ means one that does not change, even if it is of many varieties, and even if it is noble and involves no toil. ﴿So pray for us﴾. Al-Harallī said: "Duʿāʾ (supplication) is a call, implying a request, from a dependent with humility and need, to one who is in a higher position with the power to fulfil it. It is the counterpart of command from the higher, because command is a demand for what the need does not require from the one commanding, since the true commander is the Self-Sufficient, not the one in need of what he decrees." End of quote.

﴿your Lord﴾, attributing this name to him rather than to yourselves, despite its frequent manifestation to you through this attribute that looks to benevolence. ﴿He will bring forth for us﴾, meaning even though you are not paying attention to that, ﴿of what the earth grows﴾. Growing (inbāt) is nourishment and development, as al-Harallī said.

﴿the earth﴾. Then they explained what they meant by their words ﴿from its herbs﴾, meaning its green plants. Al-Harallī said: "Baql (herbs) is what is consumed in large quantity with ʾudm (condiments), and ʾudm is rich, fatty foods. Whatever grows from the earth that goes with them is baql." End of quote.

﴿its cucumbers, its garlic﴾, meaning wheat. Al-Harallī said: "It is said to be the grain that is baked into bread." End of quote.

﴿its lentils and its onions﴾. It is as if it were said: this astonishment came from them, so what did he say? It is said: He said, ﴿Said﴾, disapproving of them: ﴿Do you exchange﴾, meaning do you take, ﴿that which is lower﴾, meaning in rank, ﴿for that which is better﴾, meaning as its replacement. Here the letter bāʾ (ب) is attached to what is given up. The root of this word, namely the letters bāʾ (ب), dāl (د) (unpointed) and lām (ل), in this order, has many usages, and its meaning varies with each usage, so its understanding becomes difficult for this reason. Sometimes only the two opposites are mentioned with it, sometimes other things are mentioned with it, and sometimes it is not so. Sometimes it involves exchange and substitution, with one of the two accompanied by bāʾ, and sometimes not. Sometimes both are mentioned together with alteration and substitution. Sometimes the bāʾ is attached to what is given up, and sometimes to what is taken. Sometimes the verb is transitive to two objects directly, and sometimes it is used with only one object. Some of the usages have a meaning different from the others, and its clarification will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in Surat Sabaʾ. So it is as if it were said: Did He then answer their request? It is said: Yes. He said, ﴿Go down to a city﴾, meaning one of the cities. Al-Harallī said: "Miṣr (city) is the town that gathers what is needed for worldly affairs, which collects these desires they sought, because what is less than a city contains only some of them. From this, Egypt (Miṣr) was named, for it gathers all of worldly affairs and the strangeness of its water supply. Even if it agrees with what is said, that Egypt was named after a man, the agreement is by the wisdom of Allah, because every detail and every great thing in it proceeds by the knowledge and wisdom of Allah, whether it is behind a veil that hides it or manifest and evident to people of reflection and insight." End of quote.

﴿for you will have﴾, meaning in it, ﴿what you ask for﴾, and the manna and quail will cease for you. Al-Harallī said: "Suʾāl (asking) is seeking what need calls for and by which sufficiency is achieved." He said: "Allah the Exalted mentioned that their desire can only be found in the cities where He has established His wisdom, not in the deserts where His word manifests. For this reason, the marvels of Allah frequently occur for the saints of this community in the deserts, and rarely in cities and villages, because of what this verse implies. For this reason, the seekers have eagerly pursued wandering and separation from the settlements, because of the spirit of Allah's provision they find in that, which comes from His word without the burden of His wisdom." End of quote.

When the Exalted, through the story of Musa, peace be upon him, had arranged what occurred regarding their account with Yushaʿ (Joshua), peace be upon him, after him, He arranged in this verse, by addressing Musa, peace be upon him, what occurred among them after Yusha', peace be upon him, until the final disorder of their affairs and the reversal of their conditions, from the goodness of supporting their Prophet to the state of transgression and killing their prophets, peace be upon them. Within this there is an indication that this did not come from them except for the sake of preferring the world, its leadership and its wealth over the Hereafter, preferring the hasty over the deferred. Within it is also the strongest warning to this community against following the ways of the People of the Book in conditions like theirs. For this reason, this verse contains that comprehensive lesson, and it began by mentioning those among this community who believed, then it covered the religions that have validity, as will be mentioned shortly, if Allah the Exalted wills. End of quote.

Since the implied meaning is: they did what they were commanded regarding going down to the city, and so what they were promised came to pass, He followed it with His words: ﴿And humiliation was struck upon them﴾, clinging to them and surrounding them from all sides, as a tent struck over a person surrounds him. It is a noun from dhull (humiliation), which is a lowness of the self resulting from subjugation and defeat. Al-Harallī said: "In its connection there is an implication that the many stories exceed the limit, whose extent in clarity is what follows them, as if the address is understood as: We placed them where they placed themselves, and We withheld from them what is not fitting for their state, like their state. Thereupon various aspects of corruption appeared among them, so the enemy was given power over them, who uprooted whomever Allah willed, and those who remained among them were seized with various kinds of humiliation." End of quote.

﴿And destitution﴾, meaning similarly, appropriate to the baseness of what they asked for. Al-Harallī said: "It is the manifestation of the meaning of humiliation or of self-abasement in the outward appearance and form, in stillness and cessation of movement." End of quote.

﴿And they returned﴾, meaning they went back, and they were deserving of ﴿wrath﴾, [p. 419] from the expression bāʾa Fulān bi-Fulān, when one is deserving of being killed by another because of their equality. Al-Harallī said: "Its meaning is the unanimous decision of the Overpowering to take vengeance on a case of defiance." End of quote.

﴿from Allah﴾, the Supreme King, because of their audacity toward this supreme station again and again, repeatedly. Al-Harallī said: "In this is a warning to this community, through what has overcome the people of the world among them, of similar conditions, by exchanging the lower in meaning, which is the forbidden and the doubtful, for the higher, which is the good and the better, taken easily and contentedly." End of quote.

Then He mentioned the cause of this. Al-Harallī said: "Since anger only falls upon one who opposes the Majestic in His disobedience, and their opposition occurred in their disobedience and transgression, He mentioned their action." End of quote. So He said, ﴿That﴾, meaning the great matter that befell them of anger and what accompanied it. It is also permissible that it refers to their preoccupation with the affairs of their livelihood and their concern for the conditions of their desires in this lowest, meanest manner, ﴿because﴾, meaning the cause that [p. 420] ﴿they﴾ ﴿were﴾, meaning by nature and disposition, ﴿disbelieving﴾, meaning renewing and persisting, ﴿in the signs of Allah﴾, meaning they concealed their acknowledgment and affirmation of the signs of Allah, to whom belongs all greatness, hiding them from those who do not know the signs, and deceiving them. This renewal and persistence in it was their habit and a character established in them. Al-Harallī said: "Disbelief in the signs is the furthest rank from faith, because it is nearer to disbelief in Allah, since disbelief in Allah is disbelief in the unseen, while disbelief in the signs of Allah is disbelief in the witnessed. ﴿But those who disbelieve in Our signs are the companions of the left hand﴾ [al-Balad 19]." End of quote.

﴿And they killed the prophets﴾, meaning that was their nature and disposition. Al-Harallī said: "This is the plural of nabī (prophet), which comes from naba' (news), meaning reporting about the unseen, which the reporter was unable to achieve from the point of view of his reporting." End of quote.

Since the prophet is protected in religion and in worldly matters, He said ﴿without right﴾, meaning without the complete right, to alert that his killing never occurs except in this way. Yet this does not negate that there may be some doubt, such as the suspicion of prophethood. So the blame falls upon the act of shedding blood without complete clarity, in accordance with His prohibition: ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right﴾ [al-Isrā' 33]. So it is lighter than what is in Āl ʿImrān. Then He gave a reason for this audacity, saying ﴿That﴾, meaning the great matter of disbelief and killing, which is among the greatest disbelief, ﴿because﴾, [they] ﴿disobeyed﴾, and it is from disobedience. Al-Harallī said: "It is opposition to command." End of quote.

﴿And they were﴾, meaning by nature and disposition, ﴿transgressing﴾, meaning exceeding the limits in a manner of repetition and persistence, for whoever does that becomes accustomed to it and bold enough to commit great things. Al-Harallī said: "Iʿtidāʾ (transgression) is the affectation of hostility, and ʿadāʾ (hostility) is exceeding the limit in what has been made spacious, up to a limit for which there is no excuse for one who exceeds it, since it was made spacious in its extent and limited in what was limited for him." End of quote.

The narrative of these verses, from their stories, has come in an order other than their order in existence. In the Torah, for the great reasons I have mentioned, and Allah knows best the explanation of its matter: From the Torah, at the end of the Fourth Book in the copies existing among the Jews now, in this ninth century, as I read in a copy translated into Arabic, its script being likewise, with traces of their reading upon it and an indication of the times in which each section is read, and then I compared it by meaning, as has passed, with a person from them who was the reader, the text of which is:

"These are the stations of the children of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt with their armies under the hands of Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both. Musa wrote their exits and their stages according to the word of the Lord. They set out from Raʿmsīs (in another copy: from ʿAyn Shams) on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day after the Passover (in another copy: a day after the Passover). By the first month they mean Nisan, which is the month of the harvest. The children of Israel went out with great strength in the presence of all the people of Egypt, who were busy burying the firstborn whom the Lord had slain, and with what the Lord had avenged upon their gods. The children of Israel set out from Raʿmsīs (in another copy: ʿAyn Shams) and camped at Sukkot, and set out from Sukkot and camped at Ethām (in another copy: Ethām), which is on the far edge of the desert. They set out from Ethām and camped at the mouth of the trench which is in the mountains of Baʿal-Zephon, and camped facing Migdol (in another copy: Magdol), and set out from the mouth of the trench and crossed through the middle of the sea into the wilderness (in another copy: between the sea and the wilderness), and journeyed three days in the desert of Ethām, and camped at Marah, and came to the sea (in another copy: and camped at Marrāyir, and set out from Marrāyir and came to the sea). There were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees at the sea, and they camped there by the water. They set out from the sea and camped at the shore of the Sea of Suph (in another copy: at the Red Sea), and set out from the shore of the Sea of Suph (in another copy: from the Red Sea; in another: the Sea of Qulzum), and camped in the wilderness of Sin. They set out from the wilderness of Sin and camped at Dophkah, and set out from Dophkah and camped at Alush, and set out from Alush and camped at Rephidim (in another copy: Rephidim), and there was no water there for the people to drink. They set out from Rephidim (in another copy: Rephidim) and camped in a wilderness (in another copy: the wilderness of Sinai), and set out from the wilderness of Sinai and camped at the place known as the Graves of Craving, and set out from the cemetery of Craving (in another copy: the wilderness of the Graves of Craving), and camped at Hazeroth, and set out from Hazeroth and camped at Rithmah (in another copy: al-Ramah), and set out from Rithmah (in another copy: al-Ramah), and camped at Rimmon-Perez."

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 2 of 6):

He said in the Second Book (Exodus), when mentioning the favour bestowed on them by rescuing them from the hands of the Copts (al-Qibt) through those great signs which will be explained, God willing, in Surat al-A'raf: Moses said to the people: "Remember this day on which you went out from Egypt (Misr), from servitude and bondage, for the Lord brought you out from here with a mighty hand. Leavened bread shall not be eaten on this day. Behold, you are going out in the month of Abib (al-Fiqaq), and in one copy, al-Fareek. When the Lord brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Jebusites, the Hivites and the Perizzites, as He swore to your fathers that He would give you a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall observe this rite in this month. Eat unleavened bread seven days, and let no leaven be found among you. You shall teach your sons on that day and say to them: God did this for us when He brought us out of the land of Egypt. Let it be a sign on your hand and a memorial between your eyes, so that the law of the Lord may be on your tongue, for the Lord brought you out of Egypt with a strong and mighty hand. Keep this ordinance from year to year in its time. When the Lord brings you into the land of the Canaanites, which He swore to you and your fathers to give you, you shall set apart every firstborn male that opens the womb for the Lord, and every firstborn male of your cattle that opens the womb shall be the Lord's. You shall redeem every firstborn donkey with a lamb, and if you do not redeem it, you shall break its neck; and every firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. When your son asks you tomorrow, saying, 'What is this?', say to him: 'The Lord brought us out of the land of Egypt, out of servitude and bondage, with a strong and mighty hand. For Pharaoh hardened himself and refused to let us go, so the Lord slew all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man to the firstborn of beast. Therefore I sacrifice to the Lord every male that opens the womb, and I redeem all the firstborn of my sons.' It shall be a sign on your hand and a memorial between your eyes, for the Lord brought you out of Egypt with a strong and mighty hand."

When Pharaoh let the people go and they set out, God, exalted is He, did not lead them by the way of the land of Philistia (Filastin), because it was near, and because God said: "Lest the people see war and be afraid and turn back to Egypt." So God led the people by the way of the wilderness of the Sea of Suf (Bahr Suf), and the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt armed. Moses, peace be upon him, took the bones of Joseph, peace be upon him, with him, for Joseph had made the children of Israel swear with an oath, saying: "God will surely visit you, so carry my bones up with you from here." They journeyed from Sakhut and encamped at Atham, which is on the edge of the wilderness. The Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to guide them on the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, so that they could travel by day and by night. The pillar of cloud did not depart by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, from before the people. The Lord spoke to Moses and said to him: "Tell the children of Israel to turn back and encamp by the shore of the ditch, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon. Encamp there facing the sea, so that Pharaoh will say, 'The children of Israel are wandering in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.'" The Lord said to Moses: "I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue you, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord." They did so. Pharaoh and his servants were struck with dismay at the release of the people and changed their minds. He harnessed his horses and marched with all his people, and set out with six hundred thousand chosen riders, and all the chariots of the Egyptians also, with the men, in one copy, the commanders, over all of them. The Egyptians pursued them and overtook them while they were encamped by the sea at Pi-hahiroth. Pharaoh drew near, and the children of Israel lifted up their eyes and saw the Egyptians in pursuit of them, and they were terribly afraid. The children of Israel prayed before the Lord and said to Moses: "Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us out to die in the wilderness? Why have you done this to us, bringing us out of Egypt? Did we not say to you in Egypt, 'Leave us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians'? Would it not have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in this wilderness?" Moses said to the people: "Do not be afraid! Stand firm and see the salvation of the Lord which He will work for you today, for the Egyptians whom you see today you shall never see again forever. The Lord will fight for you, and you shall hold your peace." Moses prayed before the Lord and said: "Command the children of Israel to go forward, and lift up your staff, and strike the water of the sea, and the children of Israel shall go through the sea on dry ground. And behold, I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they will follow them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, his chariots and his horsemen. Then the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord, when I have gotten glory over Pharaoh and all his host." The angel of God, who had been going before the camp of the children of Israel, moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them, and it came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of the children of Israel. There was the cloud and the darkness that night, and for the children of Israel there was light and brightness that whole night, so that they could not draw near to them that night.

(p. 429) So Musa raised his hand over the sea, and the Lord drove the sea back with a scorching wind (in another version: a violent, whirling wind), and it became dry, and the water divided. The Children of Israel entered the middle of the sea on dry ground, and the waters became like a wall between their right and their left. The Egyptians advanced and entered in pursuit of them, and Pharaoh's horses and all his troops were in the sea. When it was near dawn, the Lord appeared to the Egyptian army in a pillar of fire and a cloud of mist. He terrified the Egyptian army and confused them, bound their chariots and held them back, so that they were made to labour with difficulty in moving forward. The Egyptians said, "Come, let us flee from before the Children of Israel, for the Lord is fighting for them against Egypt." The Lord said to Musa, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, so that the waters will return upon the Egyptians and overflow onto their chariots and their horsemen." So he raised his hand over the sea, and at the time of dawn the sea returned to its place while the Egyptians were fleeing toward it. The Lord punished the Egyptians in the sea and overturned them. The waters flowed back and covered the chariots and the horsemen and all the soldiers of Pharaoh who had entered the sea in pursuit of them, and not one of them escaped. On that day He delivered the family of Israel from the hands of the Egyptians. The Children of Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore of the Mahraqan, and the family of Israel witnessed the great vengeance which Allah had brought down upon the Egyptians.

(p. 430) The people feared the Lord, believed in Him, and affirmed the word of Musa His servant. Then Musa and the Children of Israel sang this hymn of glorification and said:

"We glorify the Lord, the Majestic One, who has exalted Himself over the chariots, and whose horsemen have drowned in the impregnable sea. The Praised One is the Eternal Lord; He became my Saviour. This is our God; let us praise Him and glorify Him. The God of our fathers; let us exalt Him and revere Him. The Lord is the Master of battles; mighty is His name, for He hurled the chariots of Pharaoh and his soldiers into the sea, and the tyrants drowned in the Sea of Suf. The waves covered them, and they descended into the depths and sank like stones. Your right hand, O Lord, is glorious in power; Your right hand, O Lord, has destroyed Your enemies by the greatness of Your might. You cast down those who hate You. You sent forth Your wrath, and it consumed them like straw by the wind of Your face. By Your command the waters were frozen solid, and their flowing stopped, as if they were mountains; and the mighty ones sank to the bottom of the sea like lead in the impregnable water. Who is like You, and who does deeds like Yours, O Glorious One in holiness, Feared and Praised, Manifester of wonders? You guided by Your blessing this people whom You delivered. When this reached the peoples, they trembled and were disturbed, and fear and terror overcame the inhabitants of Philistia. At that, the nobles of Edom were dismayed, and trembling and quaking seized the men of Moab, and all the inhabitants of Canaan melted away and fled. Let dread, anxiety and trembling fall upon them by the greatness of Your arm. They shall be still as stones until Your people pass over, the people whom You have delivered. (p. 431) You shall bring them in and plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance. The Lord shall reign forever and ever."

Musa then moved the Children of Israel from the Sea of Suf, and they went out until they reached the Wilderness of Usud. Then they journeyed in the wilderness for three days and found no water there. Then they came to Marah, but they could not drink the water of Marah, because it was bitter. So the people complained against Musa and said to him, "What shall we drink now?" Musa prayed before the Lord, and the Lord showed him a piece of wood, which he cast into the water, and the water became sweet there. There He taught him the ways and the judgments. Then they came to the oasis, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the water. Then they journeyed from the oasis and came to the Wilderness of Sin, which lies between the oasis and Sin, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had left Egypt. The whole congregation of the Children of Israel complained against Musa and Harun and said to them, "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full! But you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger!" The Lord said to Musa, "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you. The people shall go out and gather a day's portion each day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in My law and My statutes or not. On the sixth day they shall prepare what they bring in, and it shall be double what they gather each day." Musa and Harun said to all the Children of Israel at evening, "You shall know that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord, because your complaint has reached the Lord. And what are we, that you complain against us?" Musa also said to them, "The Lord has given you meat in the evening to eat and bread in the morning to satisfy you, for your complaint which you murmur against has reached the Lord. And what are we? Your complaint is not against us, but against the Lord." He said to Harun, "Tell the whole congregation of the Children of Israel to draw near and stand before the Lord." When Harun said this to the whole congregation of the Children of Israel, they turned toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud. The Lord said to Musa, "I have heard the complaint of the Children of Israel. Say to them, 'At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God.'" At evening the quails came up and covered the camp. In the morning there was a layer of dew, which dropped manna, and it surrounded the camp. (p. 433) When the dew lifted, there on the surface of the ground was a fine flaky substance, like frost on the ground. Musa said, "This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat. This is the word of the Lord, which He commanded: each one shall gather from it according to what he can eat, an omer for each person, according to the number of your heads; each man shall take for those who are in his tent." The Children of Israel did as Musa commanded, and they gathered; some gathered much and some gathered little. Yet he who gathered much had no surplus, and he who gathered little had no lack. Musa said to them, "Let no one leave any of it until morning." But they did not obey Musa; some left part of it until morning, and it bred worms and became foul. So Musa was angry. They gathered it every morning, each man according to what he could eat, and when the sun grew hot it melted. On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two omers for each man. All the leaders of the congregation came and informed Musa. He said to them, "This is what the Lord said: tomorrow is a holy Sabbath of rest to the Lord. Bake what you want to bake, and boil what you want to boil, and keep what is left over for the morning." They kept it until the morning as Musa commanded, and it did not become foul nor breed worms. Musa said to them, "Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the Lord; you will not find it in the field today. Gather it six days, but the seventh day is the Sabbath, on which there will be none." On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they found none. The Lord said to Musa, "How long will you refuse to keep My commandments and My statutes?" So the people rested on the seventh day. The Children of Israel named it manna, and it was like coriander seed, and its taste was like honey.

And in the Fourth Book it says: "The manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance was white like bdellium. The people went about and gathered it, ground it in the mill or beat it in the mortar, cooked it in pots, and made cakes of it; its taste was like the taste of bread made with oil." (Returning to the second part, it says:) "The Children of Israel ate manna for forty years, and they continued to eat manna until they reached the borders of the inhabited land, and until they reached the borders of the land of Canaan. That measure was a tenth of an ephah, that is, a tenth of a bath." The congregation of the Children of Israel journeyed from the Wilderness of Sin in their stages as the Lord commanded, and they encamped at Rephidim, and there was no water for the people to drink. So the people quarrelled with Musa, (p. 435) and said to him, "Give us water to drink." He said, "Why do you quarrel? Why do you test the Lord?" The people's thirst grew severe there, and they complained against Musa and said to him, "Why did you bring us up out of the land of Egypt to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?" Musa prayed before the Lord and said, "What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me." The Lord said to Musa, "Pass on before the people, take with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the sea and split it. Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it, and the people will drink." Musa did this in the sight of the elders of the Children of Israel. The place was named Massah and Meribah, because the Children of Israel quarrelled and contended, and because they tested God, saying, "Is the Lord among us or not?"

When in the third month after the Children of Israel had left Egypt, they reached the Wilderness of Sinai; they journeyed from Rephidim and came to the Wilderness of Sinai, and Israel encamped there opposite the mountain. Musa went up to the mountain, and God called to him from the mountain and said, "Thus shall you say to the house of Jacob: You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and I bore you as on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself. Now, if you indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you shall be dearer to Me than all the peoples of the earth." (p. 436) Musa came and called the elders of the people, and set before them all these words which the Lord had commanded him. All the people answered together and said, "All that the Lord has commanded we will do." Musa reported the people's answer to the Lord. The Lord said to Musa, "Behold, I come to you in a thick cloud, so that the people may hear when I speak with you, and believe you forever." The Lord said to Musa, "Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments, and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will come down upon Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people. You shall set bounds for the people all around, and say, 'Take heed to yourselves, do not go up into the mountain or touch its border. Whoever touches the mountain shall surely be put to death; no hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot through; whether beast or man, he shall not live.' When the trumpet sounds a long blast, they shall come up to the mountain." Then Musa came down from the mountain to the people, sanctified the people, and they washed their garments. Musa said to the people, "Be ready for the third day; do not go near a woman." On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunderings and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and a very loud trumpet sound; and all the people in the camp trembled. Musa brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain. Mount Sinai was altogether in smoke, because the Lord descended upon it in fire; its smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly, and the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder. Musa spoke, and God answered him with a voice. The Lord called Musa to the top of the mountain, and Musa went up. The Lord said to him, "Go down, warn the people, lest they break through to the Lord to gaze, and many of them perish." All the people heard the sounds, saw the lights, heard the sound of the trumpet, and saw the smoke rising from the mountain.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 4 of 6):

When the people saw that, they were terrified and stood at a distance, and they said to Musa (Moses): "You speak to us, and we will listen, but let not God speak to us, lest we die." Musa said: "Do not fear, for God only spoke to you in order to test you and try you, so that you would fear Him and hold Him in awe, and not err or sin." So the people stood at a distance, and Musa drew near to the thick darkness in which God manifested Himself. The Lord said to Musa: "Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: You have seen and known that I spoke to you from heaven. Do not make with Me gods of gold, and do not make for yourselves gods of silver." Then He said: "Behold, I am sending an angel before you, to guard you on your journey and bring you to the land which I have perfected" (in another copy: "which I have prepared"). "Beware of him and listen to him, for My name is upon him. If you accept his word, obey his command, and do everything he commands you, I will be an enemy to your enemies. My angel will go before you and bring you to the Amorites" (and he mentioned after them five groups), "and I will destroy them and annihilate them. I will send terror, fear and dread before you, and I will destroy all the peoples to whom you go. I will not destroy them in one year, lest the land become desolate, but little by little, until you grow strong" (in another copy: "until you multiply"), "until you become mighty and inherit the land. And set your borders from the Sea of Suf to Philistia, and from the wilderness to the river" (and he explained it in another place as the Euphrates). The Lord said to Musa: "Go up to the mountain, you and Harun (Aaron), Nadhab, Abihu, and seventy men from the elders of the children of Israel, and they shall worship from afar. Musa alone shall draw near to the Lord, while they shall not draw near, and the people shall not go up with him." Musa came and recounted to the people all the covenants of the Lord and all His judgments. All the people answered together with a loud voice and said: "We will do what the Lord has commanded." Musa wrote all the words of the Lord. Early in the morning he built an altar at the foot of the mountain and set up twelve pillars for the tribes of the children of Israel. (Then he mentioned sacrifices, offerings and other things, and then said:) Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it to the people, and they said: "We will hear and do all that the Lord has commanded." Musa took that blood, meaning the blood of the offering, and sprinkled it upon the people, and said: "This is the blood of the covenant which He has made with you concerning all these words." Musa went up, with those mentioned with him, then he left them in a place on the mountain and said to them: "Remain here." So Musa went up the mountain, and the cloud covered it. The glory of God settled upon Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it for six days. On the seventh day the Lord called Musa from within the cloud, and he looked upon the glory of the Lord like a fire blazing at the top of the mountain before all the children of Israel. Musa entered into the midst of the cloud and went up the mountain, and Musa remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights. The Lord spoke to Musa and said to him: "Say to the children of Israel: let them set aside for Me the tithe of their wealth, and take it from every man who has reached his maturity." (Then he mentioned the wealth that is to be given in charity, until he said:) "And let them make for Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them. In everything I show you, in the pattern of the tent and all its furnishings, so shall they make it." (Then he said:) "Make it according to the pattern which I showed you on the mountain. Let them make an ark of acacia wood, its length two and a half cubits and its height one and a half cubits. Overlay it with pure gold, inside and outside, and make for it a crown of gold around it. Put four rings of gold for it and fix them at the four corners of the ark, two rings on one side and two rings on the other side. Make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold, and put the poles into the rings on the two sides of the ark, so that it may be carried by them. The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark and shall not be removed from it. And you shall put into the ark the testimony which I shall give you. It shall be called the Ark of the Testimony. Make two cherubim, that is, two figures of gold; make them of hammered work, placed on the two sides of the mercy seat (p-440) so that the wings of the cherubim are spread out, covering from above, and they shelter the mercy seat with their wings. Let the face of each of them be toward the other, and let the faces of the cherubim be above the mercy seat." And He said: "Make a house for the Tent from the south," and He continued describing to him the making of this tent, its pillars, its curtains, its instruments, its servants, what is offered in it, the place where it is pitched among the camp, and in what manner, in about fifteen leaves. He named it the Tent of the Time (Qubbat al-Zaman). Then, at the end of this second book, He commanded him, may He be exalted, concerning matters related to its furnishings, its enclosures and other things, in more than ten leaves, as will come later. In the midst of this He said: "The testimony which I give you shall be in the ark, and I will meet with you there, and I will speak with you above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are above the Ark of the Testimony, with all that I command you concerning the children of Israel." And He said: "They shall make this offering continually, throughout their generations, at the door of the Tent of the Time before the Lord."

And I will appoint a time with you there, to speak with you, and I will appoint with the children of Israel there, and I will be sanctified by My glory there, and I will dwell among the children of Israel, and they will know that I am the Lord their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt. Then He said: Let each man among them give the zakat (alms) on his own behalf when I count them, so that the plague does not descend upon them. Then He mentioned to him the details of what is to be given, and that the zakat is for the rich and the poor. The Lord spoke to Moses and said to him: Know that I have chosen Bezalel son of Uri son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have bestowed upon him the Spirit of God, and I have filled him with wisdom and knowledge in every kind of knowledge, so that he may know the crafts [p. 441] in the making of vessels of gold, silver and copper, in the cutting and arranging and perfecting of stones, and in the trade of wood, so that he may work at every kind of work. I have also joined with him Oholiab son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan, and I have placed wisdom and understanding in the hearts of the wise and the intelligent, so that they may do all that I have commanded you concerning the making of the Tent of Meeting, the Ark of the Testimony, the mercy seat that is upon it, all the furnishings of the Tent, the table and all its furnishings, the lampstand and all its vessels, the altar of incense and the altar of burnt offerings and all their vessels, the basin and its base, the woven garments, the holy garments for Aaron the priest, that is, the imam, and the garments of his sons for their priesthood, the anointing oil and the sweet incense for the sanctuary. So they shall do all that I have commanded you. Up to his saying: And when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, there was given to Moses the two tablets of the Testimony, two tablets of stone written upon by the finger of God. The people saw that Moses had delayed in coming down from the mountain, so the people gathered together, that is, and said: Let us make for ourselves gods that will go before us, for as for this man Moses who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him. Then he mentioned their making of the calf, and that they slaughtered sacrifices to it, and sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play and to act foolishly, and that Aaron, peace be upon him, was alarmed and terrified by that.

[p. 442] I did not quote the wording of the Torah on this exactly, because at the beginning of its phrasing there is something that I consider disparaging in relation to the station of Aaron, peace be upon him, and he is far above what would suggest a deficiency. So I allowed that it may be among what they altered. Then I reflected on what al-Nasa'i, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in the hadith of al-Futun (the trial), and I found it not far from its interpretation. I have mentioned the relevant point from it in Surat Ta-Ha. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Then he said: The Lord said to Moses: Go down from here, for your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt have corrupted their conduct, and have swiftly turned aside from the way that I commanded them to follow. They have made for themselves a molten calf, and bowed down to it, and slaughtered sacrifices to it, and said: This is your god, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. The Lord said to Moses: I have seen this people, that their hearts are stiff. So leave Me now, that My anger may burn against them and I may destroy them and annihilate them, and make you into a great nation. So Moses prayed before the God and said: No, O Lord! Let not Your anger burn against Your people whom You brought out of Egypt with Your mighty power and Your exalted arm. And let not the people of Egypt say: You only brought them out to destroy them, to kill them among the mountains and to uproot their root, and to annihilate their greenness from the face of the earth. O Lord, let Your anger and Your wrath subside, and forgive the sin of Your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Your servants, and the oaths by which You swore to them, and You said: I will multiply your seed [p. 443] like the stars of heaven, and all this land which I promised to their seed, I will give it to them, and they shall inherit it forever. So the Lord relented from His people and did not bring the evil upon them. Then Moses went down and descended from the mountain, with the two tablets of the Testimony in his hand. The two tablets were written upon on both sides, and the tablets were the work of God, may His praise be exalted, and the writing of God was inscribed upon them. When he drew near the camp, he saw the calf and the dancing, and the anger of Moses burned, so he threw the two tablets from his hand and broke them at the foot of the mountain. Then he took the calf which they had made, burned it with fire, and ground it with a file until it became like dust, and scattered its dust upon the surface of the water. Then Moses stood at the gate of the Tent of the Appointed Time and said: Whoever is of the party of God, let him come to me. So all the sons of Levi gathered to him. Moses said to them: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Let each man of you gird on his sword, and pass from gate to gate, and go round the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his companion and his relative. The sons of Levi did as Moses commanded, and about three thousand men of the people were killed that day. Moses said to them: Withdraw your hands today from this, out of zeal for the Lord, so that blessing may descend upon you this day of ours. When the next day of that day came, Moses said to the people: You have sinned and committed this great sin! Now I will go up to the Lord, perhaps He will forgive you your sins and your iniquity. So Moses returned [p. 444] to the Lord and said: I beseech You with humble supplication. O Lord my God, truly this people has sinned and committed a great iniquity, and they have made for themselves gods of gold. Now, if You forgive their sins, well and good; otherwise, blot me out of Your book which You have written. The Lord said: I will blot out of My book whoever has sinned and done wrong. Now, go on with this people to the place of which I speak to you. Behold, My angel will go before you to the land that flows with milk and honey, for I will not go up with you, because they are a stiff-necked people, and lest My anger burn against them and I destroy them on the way. When the people heard this terrible word, they grieved, and no man among them put on his weapons. Moses took his tent, pitched it outside the camp, and set it far from the encampment, and called it the Tent of the Appointed Time. Whoever sought the Lord would go out to the Tent of the Appointed Time. When Moses went out to the Tent of the Appointed Time, all the people would stand, and each man would stand at the door of his tent, watching Moses from behind until he entered the Tent. When Moses entered the Tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the door of the Tent, and speak with Moses. All the people would watch the pillar of cloud standing at the door of the Tent, and all the people would stand and pray, each man at the door of his tent. The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks with his brother and companion. Then he would return to the camp, while his servant Joshua son of Nun, the youth, did not depart from the Tent. [p. 445] Moses said to the Lord: You, O Lord, commanded me to lead up this people, but You have not informed me whom You will send with me. You said: I have made You known by name, and You have found grace in My sight. Now, if I have found grace in Your sight, show me Your way, that I may know You. The Lord said to Moses: Go before Me, and I will meet with you and give you rest. He said to Him: If You do not go up among us, do not bring us up from here. For how shall it be known that I and Your people have found grace in Your sight, unless You go with us, so that I and Your people may be distinguished from all the peoples who are on the face of the earth? The Lord said to Moses: I will do this thing that you have asked, for you have found grace in My sight, and I will make your name known and renowned forever. He said: Show me Your glory. He said: I will make all My goodness and My honor pass before you, and the name of the Lord will be proclaimed before you, and I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy. And He said: You cannot see My face, for no man shall see Me and live. The Lord said to Moses: Hew for yourself two tablets of stone like the first two tablets which you broke, and be ready by the morning, and go up early to the mountain of Sinai, and stand there on the top of the mountain. No one shall go up with you, nor shall anyone be seen throughout the mountain, nor shall the sheep and the cattle graze opposite that mountain. So Moses hewed two other tablets of stone like the first two, rose early in the morning, went up to Mount Sinai as the Lord commanded him, and took the two tablets in his hand. [p. 446] The manifestation of the Lord passed before him. Moses said: O Lord! O God, my Lord, the Compassionate, the Merciful, slow to anger and abundant in patience, great in His grace and His justice, keeper of grace and justice for a thousand generations, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin. Then Moses hastened, bowed his head to the earth, and prostrated himself, and said: If I have found grace in Your sight, O Lord, then let the Lord now walk among us.

Because this is a people stiff-necked, and forgive our sins, our transgressions, and the wickedness of our intentions." He said to him: "Behold, I am making a covenant before all the people, and I will perform wonders such as have not been performed in all the earth or among all the nations, so that all this people among whom you are will see the work of the LORD, that it is awesome and feared. Keep what I command you this day. Behold, I am driving out before you the Canaanites." He named those who preceded them, and repeated the prohibition against bowing down to other than Him, glorified is He, and enjoined things among them, including the unleavened bread, saying: "And keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days, as I commanded you, at the appointed time of the month of Abib," and in one copy, "the month of Ferek," "for you came out of Egypt in the month of Abib." Then he said: "He remained there with the LORD forty days and nights; he neither ate food nor drank water. And God wrote upon the two tablets of stone the words of the covenant, which are the Ten Commandments." When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, the two tablets of testimony were in his hand, and Moses did not know that the skin of his face had become radiant with splendor when God spoke to him. Aaron and all the children of Israel looked at the face of Moses, and they were afraid to draw near to him. [p. 447] So he called them, and Aaron and all the chiefs of the congregation came to him, and Moses spoke to them. When he finished speaking to them, he placed a veil over his face. Whenever he entered before the LORD to speak with Him, he would unveil his face until he came out. He would come out and command the children of Israel with what he was commanded. He said to them: "The LORD commanded that you do your work for six days, and the seventh day shall be set apart and holy. The Sabbath is a day of rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does work on it shall be put to death. Do not kindle fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day." Then He, exalted is He, commanded them concerning the offering of gold, silver, bronze, fine linen, skins, and other things, and things they were to add to the Tent of Meeting, in more than ten sections. At the end of that he said: "The LORD said to Moses: Set up the Tent of Meeting on the first day of the first month, and place the Ark of the Testimony there, and spread the veil over the Ark." [...] He said: "And bring Aaron and his sons to the door of the Tent of Meeting, wash them with water, clothe Aaron with the holy garments, anoint him, and he shall minister to Me as priest. Bring his sons near, clothe them with tunics, and anoint them as you anointed Aaron your brother, that they may minister to Me as priests. Their anointing shall be for them an everlasting priesthood throughout their generations." Moses did as God commanded him. When the first day of the first month of the second year came, he set up the Tent on the Sunday, drove its pegs, fitted its boards, inserted its bars, raised its pillars, spread the covering over the Tent and its outer covering, as the LORD commanded. [p. 448] He took the Testimony and placed it in the Ark, put the poles on the Ark, put the mercy seat on top of the Ark, brought the Ark into the Tent, took the veil of the door and screened the Ark of the Testimony, as the LORD commanded. He set up the lampstand by the walls of the Tent on the side facing the north, outside the veil, and arranged on it rows of bread before the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses. He set up the lampstand opposite the table along the walls of the Tent on the side facing the south, and they lit its lamps before the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses. He set up the golden altar in the Tent of Meeting outside the veil, and burned fragrant incense on it, as the LORD commanded. He hung the screen at the door of the Tent, set up the altar of burnt offerings at the door, and offered sacrifices on it, as the LORD commanded. He placed the basin between the Tent of Meeting and the altar and poured water into it for washing. Aaron and his sons would wash their hands and feet when they wished to enter the Tent of Meeting, and when they approached the altar they would wash as well, as the LORD commanded Moses. He set up a court surrounding the Tent and the altar, hung the screen at the gate of the court, and Moses completed the work. The cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the Tent was filled with the glory and majesty of the LORD. Moses was not able to enter the Tent of Meeting, because the cloud had settled upon it. [p. 449] The Tent was filled with the glory and majesty of the LORD. Whenever the cloud lifted from the Tent, the children of Israel would set out on all their journeys, but if the cloud did not lift, they did not set out until the day it lifted. For the cloud of the LORD covered the Tent by day, and fire appeared upon it by night, visible before all the children of Israel throughout all their journeys. He said at the beginning of the Fourth Book: God commanded that the children of Israel be counted, those from twenty years old and upward, all who were fit to go out to war in the armies, numbering six hundred thousand, three thousand, five hundred and fifty, excluding the tribe of Levi, for they were for guarding and serving the Tent of Meeting, and their camps were to be around it, encircling it. From a month old and upward there were twenty-two thousand of them. Then he said: "The LORD spoke to Moses and said to him: When a man of the Levites reaches twenty-five years of age, and is strong enough to do the work in the Tent of Meeting, and when he reaches fifty years of age, he shall retire from the work and no longer do any work in the Tent of Meeting." The children of Israel would camp around the children of Levi by God's arrangement for them, each having a place around the Tent in a circle. Moses, Aaron and his sons would camp on its eastern side to keep the guard of holiness and the offerings for the children of Israel, and any stranger who approached the Tent of Meeting and its work would be put to death. From this, and from what precedes it, it is known that each of them prayed at the door of his tent, and that their qibla while in the wilderness was the Tent of Meeting. On the day the tabernacle was set up, a cloud from the LORD covered the Tent of Meeting and the veil of the door of the Testimony. [p. 450] In the tabernacle, from evening until morning there appeared fire blazing until dawn. So it was always in the tabernacle: by day the cloud covered it, and by night fire appeared in it. Whenever the cloud lifted from the Tent, the children of Israel would move from their places, and wherever the cloud settled, there the children of Israel would camp. The movement of the children of Israel was by the word and command of the LORD. Sometimes the cloud remained on the Tent from evening until morning and lifted after the dawn, and they would move. Sometimes it remained a night and a day, sometimes days and months, and sometimes a year. The LORD spoke to Moses and said to him: "Make two trumpets of silver, to be used for calling the assembly and for breaking camp. When they are blown, the priests shall sound them, and all the congregation of the children of Israel shall gather to you at the door of the Tent of Meeting. If one trumpet is blown, the leaders and heads of thousands shall gather to you." In the second year, on the tenth day of the second month, the cloud lifted from the Tent of the Testimony, and the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sinai.

The cloud settled in the desert of Paran. Then he said: "They set out from the mountain of the LORD a journey of three days, and the Ark of the Covenant of the LORD went before them a day's journey to find them a resting place. The cloud of the LORD was over them by day when they set out, to protect them from the heat of the sun." When the bearers of the Ark set out, [p. 451] Moses said: "Rise up, O LORD, that Your enemies may be scattered, and those who hate You may flee before You." And when they stopped, he said: "Return, O LORD, to the thousands of the children of Israel." The people complained, and it displeased the LORD, and He was angry. He heard their murmuring, and His anger burned against them, and fire from the LORD broke out among them and consumed those at the edge of the camp. The people cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed before the LORD, and the fire died down. He called the name of that place Taberah, because the fire of the LORD had burned among them and consumed them there. The mixed multitude that was among them craved a craving, and they turned to the children of Israel and said: "Would that someone would give us meat to eat! We remember the fish we used to eat in Egypt for free, and the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. But now our souls are dried up; there is nothing at all for us to eat except this manna before our eyes." Moses heard the people weeping in their families, each person at the door of his tent. The anger of the LORD burned greatly, and it grieved Moses as well. He said: "From where shall I get meat to give to all this people? They weep before me and say, 'Give us meat!' [p. 452] I cannot bear all this people alone, for they are too heavy for me. If this is how You will deal with me, kill me outright, if I have found favor in Your sight, and let me not see my wretchedness."

The LORD said to Moses: "Gather seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the officers of the people and their scribes, and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, and I will come down and speak with you there. I will take some of the Spirit that is upon you and place it upon them, so that they may bear the burden of this people with you and you will not bear it alone." Then Moses said to the people: "Prepare yourselves for tomorrow, for you will eat meat, because you wept before the LORD and said, 'Would that someone would give us meat!' Indeed, it was better for us in Egypt. So the LORD will give you meat, and you will eat it not for one day or two, but for a month, until it comes out of your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you." He gathered seventy elders of the people and stationed them around the tent. The LORD, exalted is He, descended and spoke to him, took some of the Spirit that was upon him, and placed it upon the seventy. Moses and the elders of the children of Israel entered the camp. A wind from the LORD arose, bringing quail from the sea and dropping it on the camp, a day's journey on each side around the camp, [p. 453] and it lay about two cubits above the ground. They gathered it and spread it around the camp to dry it as jerky. While the meat was still between their teeth before it was chewed, the anger of the LORD burned against them, and the LORD struck the people with a very great plague. He called the name of that place Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of craving. The people set out from the graves of craving and came to Hazeroth and camped there. It is mentioned that they remained there seven days. Then he said: "The people set out from Hazeroth and camped in the wilderness of Paran." The LORD spoke to Moses and said to him: "Send men to spy out the land that I give to the children of Israel." He then mentioned the sending of the twelve chieftains, as will come, God willing, in Surat al-Ma'idah. Then he said: "They returned to Moses after forty days, and came to Moses and Aaron and all the congregation of the children of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, at Kadesh." The end of the explanation of what was alluded to in this surah of the stories of the Children of Israel from the Tawrah (the Torah).

(p-454) When Allah, glory be to Him, explained that they, when they were stubborn toward Musa (peace be upon him), as has already passed and as will come from the texts of the Torah again and again, caused disbelief to take root in their hearts, so they persisted in disobedience and in boldly transgressing the limits, He struck humiliation and wretchedness upon them and brought wrath down upon them. In this there was a warning for whoever seeks to follow that straight path, drawn from their condition, and an announcement that the God-fearing, whose prayer for guidance is answered, are not in any of that. Rather, they said "guide us" with certainty and sincerity, free of baseless claims and of objection against the messengers. He alerted that whoever acts contrary to their deeds, whether he believes from among them or from among others of all the religious communities, will be in the opposite of their condition before their Lord. So He will not be angry with them, but will pay them their rewards and bestow upon them security and joy, which include the opposite of humiliation and wretchedness. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾.

It may also be said that when He gave the cause of the humiliation of the Children of Israel as their disobedience and transgression, it was as if it were said: "What of those who obeyed?" So He answered with a general answer for them and for others. Or it may be said that when He, exalted, informed them that they had been obliged to bear disgrace like a collar around the dove's neck, this might give the impression that there is no escape for them from it even if they repent. His custom, glory be to Him, was to follow any promise or threat with its opposite, so that the speech is complete. Know that the door of repentance is open, and the Lord is generous, in a general way.

Al-Harrali said: When the Truth, exalted is He, concluded the account of the condition of the Children of Israel, its ending, from the highest of their honor through the first address to the lowest of anger toward them in this last account, was a turning away from them in contrast to that first turning toward them. They were the first people of a Book, and by this conclusion He, exalted, made known that all who come after them will, in some measure, follow what afflicted them, from all four religious communities. End of quote. So it was said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, meaning, those who claimed belief in what Muhammad (ﷺ) called to. ﴿And those who were Jews﴾, meaning, those who claimed to be upon the religion of Musa (peace be upon him). Al-Harrali said: it is from hawd, which is a return inwardly (p-456) and steadfastness in it. End of quote. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: it is because they yatahawwadūn (يتهودون), that is, they move when reciting the Torah, and they say: the heavens and the earth moved when Allah, mighty and majestic, gave the Torah to Musa (peace be upon him). ﴿And the Christians﴾, who claim that they followed al-Masih (peace be upon him). Al-Harrali said: it is the plural of nasran; if it is from nusrah (help), then its pattern is fa'lan.

Since this surah was addressed to the Children of Israel to win them over through encouragement and warning, here He paired their two groups. And since the creed of the Sabians (al-Sabi'a) gathers what has been scattered of the roots of the religions of the polytheists, He followed them with them, intending every polytheist, and said: ﴿and the Sabians﴾, those who deny messengership in human form, who believe in heavenly idols and earthly images (p-457), mediating toward the Lord of lords. Al-Harrali said: with a hamza, from صبأ يصبأ صبأ (ṣaba'a yaṣba'u ṣaba'an), and without a hamza, from صبا يصبو صبوا (ṣaba yaṣbū ṣabwan). The hamza and the yā' interchange with the ṣād and the bā' for a common meaning, which is a return to the state of childhood after adulthood. End of quote.

﴿Whoever believes﴾, that is, from among them, by continuing in faith if he had believed before that, or entering into faith if he had been a disbeliever, so this is usage in both the literal and the figurative sense. ﴿In Allah﴾, that is, in His essence. ﴿And the Last Day﴾, whose belief includes belief in all the attributes, of knowledge, power and others, and which urges every good and turns away from every harm. ﴿And does righteous deeds﴾, that is, and makes true what he claimed of belief by following, in outward deeds, the law of the messenger of his time, and does not distinguish between any of the messengers, nor neglects anything of belief in what the Books brought of righteousness. Al-Harrali said: it is the deed observed against defect, and its origin is sincerity of intention and exerting one's utmost effort in striving, according to the knowledge and mastery of the doer. He also said: "deed" is what is planned with knowledge. End of quote.

(p-458) Since the singular indicates more specifically the individual's own share, and the plural more strongly indicates the intent of generality and cuts off obstinacy, He used the singular first and the plural here, saying: ﴿for them is their reward﴾, which they were promised for those deeds conditioned by faith. It is, in its origin, the assigning of the worker to his work, being ﴿with their Lord﹜, so it is preserved, with no fear of forgetting and no approach of loss. ﴿And no fear shall be upon them﴾ from any coming thing that overtakes them from all directions, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ over anything that has passed. Rather, they are in the greatest joy with the honor and freshness they possess, the opposite of what the transgressors have of humiliation and wretchedness.

The placement of this verse within their stories is fitting, because they were commanded to kill every male among the others, and perhaps were commanded to kill the women too, so one might suppose that whoever believes from among others is not accepted. He said in the Torah, in the story of (p-459) Madyan: "They killed every male in it," then said: "Musa became angry and said to them: Why did you spare the females? They were ten for the Children of Israel, by the word and counsel of Bal'am," meaning, by what led to fornication. Then he said: "The Lord said to Musa: speak to the Children of Israel and say to them: You are crossing the Jordan to destroy all the inhabitants of the land," and similar to this, some of which is perhaps clearer than what has been mentioned, and some of it was mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah.

In placing it within their stories there is also an indication of their lying in their saying: ﴿There is no blame on us regarding the unlettered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75], and that the basis for the protection of blood and property is faith and uprightness. That is present in the text of the Torah in more than one place, and in it is a threat to them for opposing this, with humiliation and wretchedness. Some of that will come at His saying: ﴿Do not worship except Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83], the verse. Moreover, in it is what requires forbidding the property of one who opposes in religion, for he said in the middle of the second book: "If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey going astray, return it to him; and if you see your enemy's donkey lying under its load and you are inclined not to help him, then help him and assist him." Then he returned to their stories in the best manner. When He mentioned to the believers this reward, which He magnified, encouraging with its vagueness and attributing it to the presence of the Lord, the Beneficent, with kinds of nurture, and that there is no fear with it nor grief, He followed it by saying that they did not believe after seeing the striking signs, until He lifted the mountain above them and they knew that it would bury them if they disobeyed. So accepting them was among the greatest blessings upon them, because its right is rejection, since it is like faith at the sight of punishment, not faith in the unseen.

(p-460) Then he mentioned that when He withdrew from them, they turned away from the Noble Presence to the presences of Satan, and so they honored sins. This is an indication that they are the most hard-hearted of people, and the most audacious and obstinate in opposition: they neither heed out of fear, nor remain steadfast out of desire. Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when﴾. A shorter way of putting it is to say: when Glorified and Exalted He had established His word for the learned, the active, the submissive, whoever they may be, He followed it with what the Jews had of coarseness, which calls to aversion from the traits of happiness that are the fruit of knowledge, and with the favour He had shown them, Glorified is He, by compelling them to return to Him. So He said, "And when"—that is, "remember, O Children of Israel, when" ﴿We took﴾, by the majesty that is ours, ﴿your covenant﴾ of hearing and obedience. "Covenant" (mithaq) comes from wathiqa, and it denotes the reinforcement of the pledge, as its confirmation by the Book—so said al-Harrali.

﴿And We raised﴾. Since the mountain had come to be above them like a canopy, encompassing them such that if it fell upon them no one among them would escape, He removed the particle and said: ﴿above you the Mount (Tur)﴾ (p-461) as a warning to you, so that you would accept the covenant, which is the cause of your happiness. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that every mountain that grows (vegetation) is a tur, and every mountain that does not grow is not a tur. ﴿And We said to you, while it was overshadowing you﴾: ﴿Take hold of what We have given you﴾ of the Book, for happiness, by obeying Me and adhering to My rulings, which necessitate being in My presence, ﴿with strength﴾, that is, with earnestness and diligence. "Strength" (quwwa) is the inner aspect of power (qudra), from quwan, which are the strands of a rope by which it is made firm and whose severance is guarded against—so said al-Harrali.

﴿And remember what is in it﴾ of holding fast to it, and of turning away from it when the abrogating (nasikh) one described in it comes, remembering it by heart as thought and by tongue as mention, ﴿so that you may (p-462) be mindful﴾; that is, so that you may be hopeful of guarding against the things that bring about divine wrath. Since the sense was: "So you took that and firmly bound yourselves to the covenant with it, out of fear that He would bring the mountain down upon you," He conjoined this with (the phrase) and indicated, by the particle of distance, that it is due that turning away from it be far-removed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 64:

His saying: ﴿Then you turned away﴾. And at-tawalli (turning away), al-Asfahani said: its origin is turning away from a thing physically, then it was used for turning away from a command and from religion. End of quote. And it here means turning away that is deliberate, as indicated by the form tafa''ala (taf'ul), as said by al-Harrali. That is because souls, when they become accustomed to God's command and see its excellences, and thereby return to something of the original natural disposition (fitar), do not turn back from it except through a severe struggle against desire. (p-463) And since their turning away did not extend over a long period of time, the preposition was introduced, so he said: ﴿after that﴾, i.e., after the great confirmation of the covenant and the commitment to fulfil it. ﴿Then were it not﴾, i.e., as a consequence of your turning away, were it not that ﴿the grace of God﴾, i.e., the One to whom belong majesty and honour, is upon you, ﴿and His mercy﴾ through pardon and repentance, and honouring you with guidance and victory over the enemies, ﴿you would surely have been among the losers﴾ through punishment and the everlasting of wrath. And also, since it was possible for them to abandon faith and righteous deeds, this was followed by the verse of the covenant, indicating that what saves is not faith in general, but faith in all that the covenant was taken from them to believe in, (p-464) indicating that what saves is not faith in general, but faith in all that the covenant was taken from them to believe in, namely everything God gave them in the Torah, faith accompanied by strength, and among what He gave them is the description of Jesus and Muhammad, upon both of them be peace, and the command to follow them. So it is among what the covenant was taken from them to believe in, and they disbelieved in it, so no faith or deed was valid for them, because distinguishing between what came from Him, glory be to Him, is zandaqah (heresy).

Then came the story of the transgressors concerning the Sabbath, confirming that point. Its gist is that when they neglected one of His commands and treated it lightly, namely the prohibition of the Sabbath (al-sabt), He punished them with a punishment He had not inflicted on anyone among the worlds. So He said: ﴿And indeed﴾. It is closer to this to say that when He, glory be to Him, reminded them of the blessing of pardon that preserved them from loss, He rebuked them with another act of opposition, by which He forsook a group of them until loss overcame them, so they harmed none but themselves. He swore that they knew it and had it present in their minds. Then He, exalted is He, said, connecting it to what is implied: ﴿You certainly know all of that from Our covenants and from what We mentioned of the severe punishment inflicted on whoever breaks Our covenant, and of the threat for that, by striking with humiliation and what followed it of various kinds of punishment﴾. ﴿And indeed﴾ means: by My might, indeed ﴿you know those among you who transgressed﴾, that is, who deliberately committed aggression ﴿concerning the Sabbath﴾, by making it lawful for themselves. The root of sabt is cutting off work and the like. ﴿So We said﴾, that is, as a consequence of their transgression We said, by the majesty We possess:

(p-465) ﴿To them: Be apes, despised and rejected﴾ by Our will. Khāsi'īn is the plural of khāsi', from khas' (khasʾ), which means driving away with aversion and loathing. The cause of this was that God, exalted is He, had commanded them to observe Friday, but they refused except for the Sabbath. So God imposed the Sabbath on them, made it a trial for them, and forbade them to work on it. They then hunted on it, with fear and dread of punishment. When the period of His forbearance toward them and His patience with them, glory be to Him, lengthened, and they openly committed disobedience, He transformed those among them who sinned directly, and those who remained silent about forbidding the evil.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 66:
