﴿So We made it﴾, i.e., it resulted from Our saying that they had become apes, as We said; so We made this punishment ﴿a deterrent﴾, i.e., a restraining bond ﴿for what lay before it﴾ of sins, from among the people of its own world who witnessed it, ﴿and what lay behind it﴾ from among those who came after them. Its meaning is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. (p-466) Al-nakal (deterrent) is the display of punishment for one who takes warning from it. Al-yad (hand) is that by which the essences and forms of things become apparent, their highest and lowest parts; for this reason it is dualized, since there is a higher hand, which is the right, and a lower hand, which is the left. Al-khalf (what lies behind) is what the one who turns toward something leaves behind in his turning, so that its witnessing is obliterated from the senses of his attention. This is said by al-Harrali.

And He said ﴿and an admonition﴾, from al-waʿz (admonition), which is calling things to what is in them of lesson, to submission to the true God, by means of what frightens them, in contrast to reminding by what gives them hope and expands them, ﴿for the God-fearing (al-muttaqin)﴾. This indicates that taqwa (God-consciousness) is a safeguard from every feared thing, and that retributions fall upon others as an admonition to them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 67:

When Exalted Allah had made clear their hardness toward His rights, generally and then specifically, He followed it with a clarification of their dullness regarding their own interests, so that the conclusion would be that they are the most foolish of people. So He said: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾, the Children of Israel, ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, He to whom all command belongs, ﴿commands you (p-467) that you slaughter a cow﴾, so that by it you may know the matter of the slain person whose affair has baffled you. Its ta' (ت) is not the ta' of true feminine gender, but rather because it is one of a kind within the species, so it applies to both male and female.

When it was incumbent upon them to hasten to obedience and gratitude, and they did not do so, He made clear their coarseness by way of resumption (istiʼnaf), magnifying it by His saying, relating about them: ﴿They said, "Do you take us in mockery?"﴾, that is, a place of ridicule, and making us objects of mockery, when we ask you about a slain person and you command us to slaughter a cow. So they combined, along with what was indicated of their wrongdoing, a bad manner toward one whose messengership had been established by a miracle, and rejecting his words is disbelief. So he reminded them of what they had seen from him of knowledge of Allah, which is incompatible with mockery, by saying: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah﴾, that is, I hold fast to the One for whom there is no equal, ﴿lest I be among the ignorant﴾, for indeed none mocks except an ignorant person. The ʻawdh (عَوْذ) is seeking refuge from one who is feared to a sufficient protector, and jahl (جَهْل, ignorance) is advancing in ambiguous matters without knowledge. This is what al-Harrali (الحَرالِّيّ) said.

"They said," persisting in harshness, ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾, that is, the One who has been good to you. Their singling Him out with the description of being *your* Lord was the utmost in rudeness. *Yubayyin* (let Him make clear) is from *al-tabyīn* (making clear), which means separating a thing out, and the meaning is "from what attaches to it and intermingles with it," as stated by al-Harālī. The intent is emphasis in making clear, conveyed by the form *tafʿīl* (the intensive verbal pattern). "What is it for us?" meaning that cow. "He said: Indeed He says..." Because they were being obstinate, He emphasized, so He said: ﴿Indeed, it is a cow, neither *fāriḍ* (old, past its prime, whose teeth have been worn down or shed)﴾, ﴿nor *bikr* (a young heifer)﴾, ﴿but *ʿawān* (middle-aged)﴾, which is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtadaʾ*). He clarified this predicate by His saying ﴿between that﴾, that is, between the age of the *fāriḍ* and the *bikr*. ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, for objecting to one to whom obedience is owed is disbelief. They did not comply, but instead asked for the color to be explained after the age had been explained, saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 69:

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what its colour is."﴾ (They persisted in rudeness by not acknowledging the favour), after the clarification of its age. Colour (lawn) is the manner in which the outward appearance of things is apprehended by the eye; so said al-Harrali.

﴿He said﴾ — emphasising what preceded of their vacillation — ﴿"Indeed He says it is a cow, yellow"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68] — and he emphasised (it) to indicate their increased obstinacy — ﴿"Indeed, it is a yellow cow"﴾, and he emphasised the intensity of its yellowness by departing from the word "fāqi'a" to his saying, expressing it through colour: ﴿"Its colour is intense"﴾, that is, pure in its yellowness. Al-Harrali said: it is a descriptive adjective purifying the yellow colour, in the position of qāni' (deep) in red; so it is then of a colour midway between black and white, just as it was midway in age.

﴿"It pleases the beholders"﴾, that is, it delights their souls, for when you look at it you imagine that the rays of the sun come out of its skin; so said Wahb.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 70:

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what she is."﴾ (Asking) the one who is good to you by answering you in everything you ask of Him. ﴿What she is﴾. Then they gave a reason for their repeated questioning by saying ﴿Indeed, the cow﴾, i.e., the one described by what I have mentioned before, ﴿has become confused for us﴾, i.e., its confusion (with other cows) has come to be upon us. He used the verb in the masculine form because every plural whose letters are fewer than those of its singular is treated in Arabic as masculine; this is related from Sibawayh. Then their concern overtook them, and they said ﴿And indeed we, if Allah wills, will surely be guided﴾, i.e., to what is intended, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection. They added emphasis because of what their hesitation had made necessary, from the suspicion of their obstinacy. They placed the seeking of blessing through the will (of Allah) before the predicate of "inna" for this purpose, so they sought blessing through that without which no blessing exists.

﴿He said: Indeed He says it is﴾, that is, this cow about which you have been excessively contentious, ﴿a cow neither broken to labour nor one that ploughs the earth﴾. *Dhalūl* is from *dhull* (submission), meaning good responsiveness. This is the explanation of al-Harrālī. He then described the *dhalūl* by saying ﴿that ploughs the earth﴾, meaning that its ploughing of the earth for tillage is renewed at every time of ploughing. Al-Harrālī said: *ithāra* is bringing forth something from the moist soil, as if it brings the moist soil out from the dryness within. Since *dhull* is an inherent attribute, He expressed its negation with the intensive form of the noun, meaning that submission is not an inherent attribute of it, not that there is absolutely no submission in it. For if it were like that, it would be wild and could not be controlled at all.

(p. 471) Since the description of it as free of *dhull* is not complete except by negating irrigation from it, and this is something renewed rather than an inherent attribute like *dhull*, He expressed it with a verb and linked it to it, not as a conjunction to the description or to *tuthīru* (ploughs), so that the meaning would not be corrupted. He said, describing the cow: ﴿and that does not water the field﴾, that is, its watering of the field by the *sāniyah* (water-wheel) is not renewed at every time. It is permissible that the repetition of *lā* here is a signal to its omission before *tuthīru*, so that the two negated verbs are an explanation in the manner of a resumed statement regarding *dhalūl*. And *lā* was omitted before *tuthīru* so that it would not be thought that it is a description together with *dhalūl*, which would corrupt the meaning. The intended meaning is that it has not been made docile by ploughing or watering. And it is known from the ability to purchase it and take it for slaughter that it is not in the utmost refusal, as the description *dhalūl* indicated. All of this is because of what the middle course contains of the gathering of scattered goods. ﴿Sound﴾, that is, free of defects, ﴿with no blemish﴾, that is, no mark (p. 472) ﴿in it﴾ that differs from its colour; rather it is entirely yellow, even its horn and hoof. ﴿They said: Now you have brought the truth﴾, that is, at this limit of time situated between the past and the future, ﴿the truth﴾, meaning the established, settled and clear matter from the explanation of the description of the cow, so they obtained it. ﴿Then they slaughtered it﴾, that is, as a consequence of all that preceded, they slaughtered it. ﴿And they almost did not do it﴾, that is, they were close, before this final questioning, to not doing it. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: If they had slaughtered any cow, it would have sufficed them, but they were severe in questioning, so Allah was severe upon them. That is, they were charged with the easiest, then they were severe, so it was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e. abrogation) with the more difficult. This is evidence for the permissibility of abrogation before the act is performed. Or it may be said that since the Sabbath was only made obligatory upon them (p. 473) and they were tested with severity in it through their proposing it and their asking for it after their refusal of Friday, as its explanation will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, at His saying:

﴿The Sabbath was only made for those who differed about it﴾ [al-Naḥl: 124]. It was most appropriate to follow this with the story of the cow, about which He was not severe upon them except because of their obstinacy in it and their refusal to slaughter any cow that was easily available. It is permissible to say that since among the things they treated lightly regarding the Sabbath was the hastening to take countless lives of the fish that were forbidden to them, and in the story of the cow there was obstinacy and delay in taking one soul that they were commanded to take, He followed it with that. Among the finest correspondences: in each of the two signs, the monkeys and the cow, there is a transformation of the state of the human through mixing with the flesh of some dumb animals. In the first, he was made mute after speaking, through the flesh of fish; in the second, he was made to speak after being mute, through death, by the flesh of the cow. Perhaps the specification of cow flesh for this matter is to awaken them from their slumber and alert them from their heedlessness regarding the great power of Allah the Exalted, so as to remove from their hearts the wonder at the lowing of the calf they worshipped. Al-Imām Abū al-Ḥasan al-Harrālī said: In that is a resemblance between their conditions in taking the calf and in their request for that, and in all of this there is a correspondence between their natures and the nature of the cow, which is created for toil and the working of the land, in which there is fatigue and submission, and engagement in worldly matters, sinking deeply into them. In it is the breath of their desire for what the earth grows, which is (p. 474) the effect of tillage, meaning that for which they exchanged *ḥiṭṭah* (the forgiveness-word), which is a grain in a husk. Thus they were in that earthly and dust-bound, for the natures of most of them do not rise toward lofty spiritual matters, since the innate disposition of every soul corresponds to what it inclines toward and clings to among kinds of animals. ﴿He made for you mates from yourselves, and of the cattle mates﴾ [al-Shūrā: 11]. End. Since the story was divided into two halves, as an alert to the two blessings: the blessing of pardon for hesitating over the command, and the blessing of clarification to the killer through the extraordinary matter; and as an alert that for them in this there are two rebukes: one for their bad manners in throwing mockery and hesitating to obey, and the second for killing the soul and what followed from it. Had it been arranged in its order of occurrence, this would not have been achieved. The more fitting half was placed first, the story of the Sabbath, and the other was made to follow it.

(p. 475) Al-Harrālī said: He placed the report of Moses's words, peace be upon him, before the mention of their dispute over the slain, beginning with the more noble of the two aims of legislation, which is that which is established upon acts of transgression and words of contention. End.

Then He said, the Exalted: ﴿And when﴾, meaning: remember when. He attributed the killing to all of them, though the killer was one, because that is the custom of the Arabs, since the custom of a tribe is to defend one of its members. So He said: ﴿You killed a soul﴾. He then turned to them with direct address, as a rebuke to them and an indication that those present among them were content with what their predecessors had done, and that whoever loves something is of its company.

Since they had denied the killing, He mentioned as its consequence His saying, indicating its concealment through assimilation (idghām): ﴿And you disputed about it﴾, meaning: you pushed the blame onto one another. Each party among you was returning the killing to the other. Thus you incurred three sins: the sin of the grave offence, the sin of persistence (iṣrār), and the sin of false accusation through the denial. Al-Kalbi said: this was before the revelation of the qasama (oath procedure) in the Torah, as if he is pointing to what I will mention about it shortly.

Since their conduct in evasion was the conduct of one heedless of the all-encompassing knowledge of the Creator, glorified is He, He said, relating their state at that time: ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning: and the state being that He to whom the whole command belongs ﴿is the One who brings forth﴾ by His subtle workmanship and His great majesty ﴿what you were concealing﴾. Placing it first also carries an added rebuke to them, for their hesitation in slaughtering a cow, which they were commanded to slaughter for a great benefit to them, after some of them had hastened to kill a human being like themselves, despite the strict prohibition against it. He said, drawing attention through the shift to the style of majesty, regarding the act commanded concerning it:

(p-٤٧٧) ﴿Then We said﴾, that is, by the majesty We possess, ﴿Strike him﴾. He omitted mention of the cow and did not make explicit any indication that this first part of the story, which was placed second, is one and the same story as the part before it. So He said ﴿with part of it﴾. The Imam Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said in his book *al-Hujja*: "We said: Strike the slain man with part of the cow, so they struck him with it and he came to life." He means that the evidence for this omitted element is His saying ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this great giving of life in this strange manner, ﴿God gives life to the dead﴾, that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿the dead﴾, like this giving of life which was witnessed and observed. End of quotation.

It is related that when they struck him, he rose and said: "So-and-so and so-and-so killed me," naming his two cousins. Then he fell dead, and the two were seized and executed, and no killer inherited from his victim after that. This extraordinary event is like what our Prophet (ﷺ) reported about the forearm of the poisoned sheep, that it was poisoned, when the Jewish woman who was among his people poisoned it. This verse is one such case, and this alert concerning resurrection was placed within their stories, because it is among the greatest proofs of it. Among them there occurred what made it permissible to count them as deniers, namely their saying to the polytheists: "Your religion is better than the religion of Muhammad." Alternatively, this is a deliberate alert aimed at urging the Arabs to ask those whom they sought counsel from about the Prophet (ﷺ), since they were the people of the first knowledge. Thus it obliges them either to believe in resurrection or to believe that the Jews are lying. He expressed it by the proper name because giving life is among the signs most specific to the attribute of divinity (*uluhiyya*), just as provision is among the signs most specific to lordship (*rububiyya*). ﴿And He shows you His signs﴾ concerning what witnesses to its truth, ﴿so that you may reason﴾, that is, so that by seeing those signs which bear witness to it you may hope that understanding will arise in you, and it will guide you to believe in resurrection and in other matters which the messengers report from God, exalted is He.

(p-479) Since the occurrence of disobedience from them after witnessing this extraordinary sign was hard to imagine, let alone to happen, He indicated it by His saying ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾. Qaswah (hardness) is the intensifying of firmness and stoniness. ﴿your hearts﴾. Since they had states in which they obeyed, He used the preposition and said ﴿after that﴾, meaning after what had been mentioned of the extraordinary signs in the dialogues and other events, reminding them of God's long forbearance toward them (p-480) despite their continued disbelief and obstinacy, and warning them against the like of what befell the People of the Sabbath. ﴿So they are﴾, meaning, as a consequence of their hardness, ﴿like stones﴾, which are the furthest of things from the state of the heart. For the heart is the most living of living things, and the stone is the most lifeless of the lifeless. He did not liken them to iron, because of the benefits it contains and because it can soften.

Since hearts, considered in terms of their life, are the softest of soft things, and considered in terms of their steadfastness in one state, are the hardest of things, they were such that they bewilder the observer regarding their condition. So He said ﴿or﴾. Al-Harali said: it is a word that indicates the obscurity and hiddenness of a matter, so ambiguity and confusion arise. End of quotation.

(p-481) This ambiguity is relative to the human observers who see them. As for God Most High, He is the Knower of everything, before its creation as He knows it after its creation. He added ﴿more﴾ (ashadd), with the form af'al correctly derived from qasa, to indicate the excess of hardness. So He said ﴿more severe in hardness﴾, because they do not soften when that which should soften them touches them, whereas the stone softens for that which should soften it. Every description of a living being likened to what is below it is more reprehensible in it than in what is below, insofar as the living being is prepared for the opposite of that likeness through perception.

Since the implied sense is: "Indeed stones are affected by continued handling," He joined to it, indicating their excess of hardness and coarseness through emphasis, His saying ﴿And indeed among stones﴾. He added further emphasis to this with His saying ﴿there are those from which rivers burst forth﴾, meaning they split open with abundance (p-482) and profusion ﴿from which rivers gush forth﴾, mentioning the greater part of that, and reminding them of the stone from which rivers burst forth for them by the striking of the staff. Then He joined to that what is lower than it, saying ﴿And indeed among them is that which splits open﴾, meaning slightly and with effort, indicated by the idgham (assimilation of consonants) and the tafa''ul (reflexive/intensive form) of the verb tashaqqaq (to split), which is the form of effort derived from shaqq (cleaving), meaning the thing becoming in two opposite directions, i.e. two facing sides, as said by al-Harali.

﴿So water comes out from it﴾, which is less than a river. Then He joined to this what is still lower than that, saying ﴿And indeed among them is that which falls down from fear of God﴾, meaning it moves from its place, from the top of the mountain to its base, by the command of the Supreme King to it. Yet your hearts do not submit to any of the commands. So He made the command in relation to hearts, because of the intellect in them, like the will in relation to stones, because of their inanimate nature. In this there is a reminder to them of the stones that crumbled down from the mount (p-483) at the manifestation of the Lord. Al-Harali said: khashyah (fear) is the trembling of the soul of the knower before what it magnifies. 

Since the implied sense is: "So what are your deeds, or, if read in the third person, what are their deeds, that please God?" He joined to it ﴿And God is not﴾, and it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from "your hearts," meaning they hardened while the state was that He is not ﴿unaware﴾, God, meaning He to whom belongs all perfection, ﴿unaware of what you do﴾. Heedlessness is the loss of awareness of what should be perceived. So await a punishment like the punishment of the People of the Sabbath, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

I have not found mention of the story of the cow in the Torah, so perhaps it is among what they concealed of their impurities, as indicated by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You make it into scrolls, displaying them while concealing much﴾ [al-An'am: 91]. What I have seen in it that resembles this, and could be its cause, is that in its Fifth Book it says the following text: "If you find a slain man lying in the land which the LORD your God gives you to possess, and it is not known who has slain him, then your elders and your judges shall go out and measure the distance from the slain man to the cities around him. And the elders of the city nearest to the slain man shall take a heifer which has not been worked and which has not pulled in the yoke, and the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down to a valley with running water, which is neither plowed nor sown, and there they shall break the heifer's neck in the valley. And the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward, for the LORD your God has chosen them to minister to Him and to bless in the name of the LORD, and by their word every dispute and every assault shall be settled. And all the elders of that city nearest to the slain man shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley, and they shall answer and say: 'Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it. Be merciful, O LORD, to Your people Israel, whom You have redeemed, and do not place the guilt of innocent blood in the midst of Your people Israel.' And the bloodguiltiness shall be atoned for them. So you shall purge the innocent blood from your midst, when you do what is right in the sight of the LORD." End of quotation. As you see, it resembles being a branch of this root mentioned in the Noble Qur'an, and God knows best.

﴿Then when﴾ He, glorified is He, had made clear that their hearts had become veiled by rust (al-rayn), thick in their natural disposition, from the abundance of sins and the continual audacity against their Creator, to the point that they were harder than stones, the result was that they were distant from faith. So He turned to the believers, despairing them of their success, as consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he had been earnestly desiring, namely seeking their faith, in the context of rebuking them and reproaching them, denouncing the hope of their faith after He had established that they had repeatedly disbelieved. So He said: ﴿Do you hope﴾. Ṭama' (hope) is the attachment of the heart to a thing without any prior cause for it. ﴿that they will believe﴾, i.e., these people who are among you, although you have heard what happened to their forebears of hardness, and they are (p. 486) content with that. Otherwise they would have believed merely by this report of these stories from this unlettered Prophet, of whom it is verified that he has no teacher in them except God, while acknowledging ﴿for you, and already﴾, i.e., while the situation is that indeed ﴿there was a group﴾, i.e., people intending division and dispersion, ﴿among them﴾. Al-Ḥarrālī said: "From al-farq (separation), which is the singling out of an opinion or direction from one who should be joined to it and be with it." End quote. And ﴿hearing the speech of God﴾, who deserves all attributes of perfection. And speech, al-Ḥarrālī said: it is the manifestation of what is within onto the outward, for one who witnesses that outward in every mode of manifestation. End quote.

﴿Then they distort it﴾, i.e., they remove it from its true face by returning it to its distortion. Mentioning the group together with the things coordinated with it emphasizes the magnitude of their insolence in disobedience, (p. 487) that they were, after what was described of their wretched conditions, groups in disbelief, transgression, and shedding the garment of modesty. And His saying: ﴿after they had understood it﴾, together with its being a preparation for what comes of the matter of abrogation, indicates that their distortion was not in a place of ambiguity, because it is perceived by immediate understanding. He affirmed the preposition (min) because of the difference in their states.

Since this, in addition to indicating that they are upon their innate dispositions of refusal, and that whoever dares against God, it is not fitting for the servants of God to hope for his righteousness toward them, for if he dares against the Knower of the unseen, he would be even bolder against others, indicating that no rational person would do it, He concluded it with His saying: ﴿while they know﴾, i.e., while the situation is that they, with their reason, carry knowledge, understanding it, not heedless, but rather deliberate.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 76:

Since the discourse indicates that the implied meaning is: "They, out of their audacity against Allah, when they hear your Book, distort it, and when they speak to the servants of Allah, they hardly ever speak the truth," he (Allah) follows this with His saying ﴿And when they meet those who believe﴾ in our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿they say﴾ hypocritically on their part, ﴿"We believe"﴾; ﴿and when some of them are alone with one another﴾, i.e., the hypocrites, ﴿with one another, they say﴾ rebuking them, out of their supposition, being ignorant of Allah, when they found that many of the secrets and hidden reports of theirs, of what is in their Book of subtleties and other matters, were known to the believers despite their striving to conceal them, that some of them had disclosed them, so they became known through him. ﴿Do you tell them﴾ from tahdith (telling), which is the repetition of the occurrence of speech, i.e., its happening, ﴿of what Allah has opened﴾, the Possessor of Majesty and Beauty, ﴿to you﴾, of the ancient knowledge that came to you through the tongues of your messengers, or of what He has punished some of you with. And al-fath (opening), al-Harrali said, is the widening of what is narrow, in sense and in meaning. (p-489) ﴿So that they may argue with you﴾, i.e., the believers, ﴿before your Lord with it﴾. And al-muhajjah (argument) is the establishing of intention and opinion by what corrects it. Since they considered that their disclosure of such things was the act of one who does not act (wisely), they said, in denunciation of some of them toward others, ﴿Do you not then use reason?﴾ It is possible that this is an address to the believers being addressed, who are hoping (for their faith), i.e., "Do you not have reason that would turn you away from hanging your hope on their faith?"

When their claim (that they had been given knowledge) was the foulest of corruptions, because had it not been that they knew it from God, no one else could have expressed it in words that creation could not match, He joined to it His rebuke of them with the words ﴿Do they not know?﴾ That is: do they not know that the knowledge of the believers concerning that was only from God, owing to the proof of its inimitability that stands upon it? Do they not know ﴿that God﴾, to whom belongs encompassing knowledge of everything, ﴿knows what they conceal﴾, that is, what they hide of their speech to their companions and to others, ﴿and what they disclose﴾, that is, what they make manifest of that, so that He informs His friends of it?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 78:

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned this group, which is among the greatest of them in disbelief and the most defiant in conduct, He followed it with a category that is even more defiant and harsher than it, because the learned person may be turned away from his opinion or put to shame by argument, unlike the blind follower (muqallid), who is stubborn, dense, and coarse. So He said: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones﴾ (ummiyyun). It is permissible that by them is meant those who do not know how to write, as well as those who know how to write but are coarse of nature and far from understanding. This is because the ummi (unlettered) in the language is one who does not write, or one who remains in the original creation of the nation (ummah), who has not learned writing and remains upon his natural disposition and the state of his birth. The ghabi (dull-witted) is the boorish, coarse, and sparing of speech. The meaning, then, is that they are of two kinds: scribes and non-scribes, (p-491) and the latter are the intended meaning of "unlettered ones." These, despite not knowing how to write the Book, may be taught to recite by rote without understanding the meanings. It is also permissible that the meaning is that they are of two kinds: learned experts (nahārīr) who know the meanings, and ignorant fools who have no share of the Torah except mere recitation, devoid of reflection, accompanied by wishful thinking. For this reason He said: ﴿They do not know the Book﴾, that is, in contrast to the category in which He affirmed that they were people of knowledge.

Since the intended meaning is the total negation of knowledge from them, He brought out the exception in the form of a connected exception, although it is disconnected in nature, so He said: ﴿except wishful thoughts﴾ (amani), the plural of umniyyah, which is the supposition of the occurrence of what hope reaches toward. It is said that its meaning runs in the recitation of the words, as if it were an estimate attached to the one for whom the meaning is realized, as al-Harrali said. That is, if the wishful thoughts (p-492) are of a kind that can be described as knowledge, then they belong to them and to no other kind of knowledge. Since this implied that the estimate is: they are only making estimates for which they have no knowledge, He followed it with His saying: ﴿and they are only conjecturing﴾, as an emphasis on the negation of knowledge from them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 79:

When he had established against this group that they speak against God without knowledge, and this was a matter known for its blameworthiness and certain in its sinfulness, he consequently attributed blame and sin, by way of priority, to a group that is the most wretched of them, the most harmful to the servants of God, and their greatest enemies. So He said: ﴿Woe﴾, and woe (al-wayl) comprises all evil, as said by al-Harrali.

﴿To those who write﴾, meaning from among them and from others, ﴿the Book﴾, meaning that which they know is from themselves and not from God, ﴿with their own hands﴾. He indicated the ugliness of this lie and the remoteness of its rank in wickedness by the particle of delay, so He said ﴿Then they say﴾ of what they wrote, as a lie and a fabrication, ﴿This is from God﴾, the Supreme King. Then he explained, by the cause that drives them to that, their baseness, their inclination toward impurity, and their meanness, so He said: ﴿so that they may trade it﴾, meaning with this lie that they fabricated, ﴿for a little price﴾. Then he consequently stated: ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾ of that lie against God, ﴿and woe to them for what they earn﴾, meaning they find its gain from what they have bought with it. He used the verb unqualified because its indication of wickedness is clear from the context of what preceded; and if the unqualified form is so, other forms are more appropriate. Al-Harrali said: "Kasb (earning) is what occurs from deed, speech, action and effects, with an awareness of its benefit in it and power over it." End of quotation. In this verse there is a clarification of what our Book is honored with: that, by its inimitability, no one can bring from his own making anything to insert into it and thereby confuse it. So to God belongs the favor upon us and the bounty.

And when the discourse indicated that the implied meaning is, "So they distorted much of the Book of God, adding to it and omitting from it," it followed this with what showed their audacity, their harshness, and their indifference to the crimes they commit, of which they know better than anyone that some entail eternal abiding in the Fire. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us﴾, from *al-mass* (touching), which is the contact of the surface of one thing with the surface of another, ﴿except for a number of days﴾. Since their intention by this was that they would not abide in it forever, and since the plural of paucity (*jam' al-qillah*), although it indicates this, may sometimes be used metaphorically for abundance, and so indicate what has no end or what is difficult to count, they reinforced the meaning with emphasis and explicitness by saying: ﴿countable﴾, meaning finite, because everything countable is finite. Al-Harrali said: "*Al-add* (counting) is the consideration of abundance by comparing its parts to one another. He limited the description to the singular form, since it suffices for this meaning, unlike what appears in Al 'Imran."

When they made that claim, they also claimed that the Muslims would succeed them in it afterward. Al-Bukhari, in the sections on the poll tax (*al-Jizyah*), the military expeditions (*al-Maghazi*), and medicine (*al-Tibb*), and al-Darimi at the beginning of his *Musnad*, narrated from Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, who said: "When Khaybar was conquered, a sheep containing poison was presented as a gift to the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Gather for me whoever of the Jews is here.' They gathered for him, and he said: 'I am going to ask you about something. Will you be truthful with me about it?' They said: 'Yes.' The Prophet ﷺ said to them: 'Who is your father?' They said: 'So-and-so.' He said: 'You have lied; rather, your father is so-and-so.' They said: 'You have spoken the truth and done right.' He said: 'Will you be truthful with me about something if I ask you about it?' They said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim, and if we lie, you will know our lie just as you knew it regarding our father.' He said to them: 'Who are the people of the Fire?' They said: 'We will remain in it for a little while, and then you will succeed us in it.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Be gone into it! By God, we will never succeed you in it, ever.' Then he said: 'Will you be truthful with me about something if I ask you about it?' They said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim.' He said: 'Did you put poison in this sheep?' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What led you to do that?' They said: 'We intended, if you were a liar, to be rid of you, and if you were a prophet, it would not harm you.'"

When they made that claim, it was as if it were said: "With what shall we refute them?" So He said: ﴿Say﴾, rejecting their statement: ﴿Have you taken﴾ in that ﴿with God﴾, meaning He to whom the whole matter belongs, ﴿a covenant? For God will not break His covenant﴾, meaning, as a consequence of that, He would fulfill His covenant, because He ﴿breaks﴾ not ﴿His covenant﴾, He to whom belong the attributes of perfection; ﴿or﴾ if that did not occur, then ﴿you say about God﴾, who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, ﴿what you do not know﴾. The meaning of the rejection in the interrogative is that neither of the two matters is actual: you have not taken a covenant, nor have you said this out of ignorance; rather, you said it while knowing its opposite.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verses 81–82:

When both claims were negated, it became known that what is actually the case is other than what they alleged, so He stated it explicitly in His words: ﴿Yes (bala)﴾, meaning: "Indeed you will be touched by the Fire, contrary to what you assumed." For *bala* is a word that indicates an affirmation understood from a turning away from a negation, as if it were *bal* joined with an *alif*, affirming what is being turned away from its negation. This is said by al-Harrali (al-Ḥarrālī).

*Na'am* (yes) is a response to a statement that contains no denial. When He, glory be to Him, turned away from what they had said about a predetermined number of days, judging against them with ruin, He gave the reason for that by a description with which they are characterized, informing that it is incumbent on one ignorant of the unseen to judge by the attributes upon which the Knower of the Unseen has attached the rulings. So He said: ﴿Whoever earns an evil deed﴾, meaning, a deed that by its nature is bad, ﴿and his sin encompasses him﴾, such that none of his states lies outside sin, rather it overwhelms everything else of his deeds. This is not the case except with disbelief, which demolishes the foundation of deeds, without which the continuance of deeds cannot be achieved. Since the singular pronoun states most explicitly the requital of each individual, and the judgment of punishment upon all is more grievous, more repulsive, more dreadful, and more indicative of power, He used the singular and then the plural, saying, bringing in the *fa'* (then/so) as an indication that their deeds are the cause of their entry into the Fire: ﴿Those are﴾, meaning, the distant, the hateful, ﴿the companions of the Fire; they﴾ specifically ﴿therein abide forever.﴾

(p-٤٩٨) When it became clear by this what awaits them and everyone who shares with them in this description, He joined to it what awaits those whom they claimed would replace them in the Fire, and everyone who shares with them in the description for which they deserved that. So He said: ﴿And those who believe﴾, meaning, who affirm the oneness of God with their tongues, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾, as an explanation that their hearts are at peace with that, ﴿those are﴾, the exalted in rank, the noble in virtues. He did not bring in the *fa'*, indicating that the cause of their happiness is nothing but mercy, ﴿the companions of Paradise; they﴾, meaning specifically, ﴿therein abide forever.﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verses 81–82:

When both claims were negated, it became known that what is actually the case is other than what they alleged, so He stated it explicitly in His words: ﴿Yes (bala)﴾, meaning: "Indeed you will be touched by the Fire, contrary to what you assumed." For *bala* is a word that indicates an affirmation understood from a turning away from a negation, as if it were *bal* joined with an *alif*, affirming what is being turned away from its negation. This is said by al-Harrali (al-Ḥarrālī).

When He, glory be to Him, turned away from what they had said about a predetermined number of days, judging against them with ruin, He gave the reason for that by a description with which they are characterized, informing that it is incumbent on one ignorant of the unseen to judge by the attributes upon which the Knower of the Unseen has attached the rulings. So He said: ﴿Whoever earns an evil deed﴾, meaning, a deed that by its nature is bad, ﴿and his sin encompasses him﴾, such that none of his states lies outside sin, rather it overwhelms everything else of his deeds. This is not the case except with disbelief, which demolishes the foundation of deeds, without which the continuance of deeds cannot be achieved. Since the singular pronoun states most explicitly the requital of each individual, and the judgment of punishment upon all is more grievous, more repulsive, more dreadful, and more indicative of power, He used the singular and then the plural, saying, bringing in the *fa'* (then/so) as an indication that their deeds are the cause of their entry into the Fire: ﴿Those are﴾, meaning, the distant, the hateful, ﴿the companions of the Fire; they﴾ specifically ﴿therein abide forever.﴾

(p-٤٩٨) When it became clear by this what awaits them and everyone who shares with them in this description, He joined to it what awaits those whom they claimed would replace them in the Fire, and everyone who shares with them in the description for which they deserved that. So He said: ﴿And those who believe﴾, meaning, who affirm the oneness of God with their tongues, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾, as an explanation that their hearts are at peace with that, ﴿those are﴾, the exalted in rank, the noble in virtues. He did not bring in the *fa'*, indicating that the cause of their happiness is nothing but mercy, ﴿the companions of Paradise; they﴾, meaning specifically, ﴿therein abide forever.﴾

(p-1) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to establish proof that they are among those whose sin has encompassed them. So He said: ﴿And when﴾, meaning: remember what you know in your Book about the condition of one who earned an encompassing evil, and remember when ﴿We took﴾, by what We have of that greatness of which We showed you much, [Our] covenant with you. But He made it manifest, because of the length of the separation, by mentioning an attribute that encompasses them and others. So He said: ﴿the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. It may be that it is conjoined to "my favour" in His words, ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 47], because the whole matter is in addressing them and explaining their affairs.

(p-2) Since religion is nothing but good conduct toward the Creator and toward creation, He mentioned the covenant made concerning that, arranging it from the most binding to the less binding. So He said, mentioning it in the form of a statement while intending by it a prohibition and a command, and this is more eloquent, since it is as if its fulfilment had already occurred and passed. He indicated the intention of this by conjoining "and say" to it:

﴿You shall not worship except Allah﴾, the first Benefactor, to whom all command belongs, ﴿so that you may be doers of good﴾ through this, a goodness that is all goodness. ﴿And [be good] to the two parents﴾, "be good" or "you are good," ﴿to parents﴾, even if they are disbelievers. Al-Harali said: the dual of "wālid" (parent) is from "wilāda" (begetting), to preserve what is expected to vanish by the appearance of a form from him that succeeds the form of his kind, end of quote. ﴿Good﴾ means great goodness that cannot reach its full extent, because they are in the second rank, since He, glory be to Him, made them the cause of the first creation's blessing and the direct agents of upbringing.

He changed the wording and did not say, "And you shall not be good except to the two parents," to convey that goodness to them is shared by others after them. Had the omission of this restriction been compensated by placing the two first, it would be a declaration of concern.

﴿And to the near of kin﴾, who seek a means through the two parents because of their firm kinship (p-3), ﴿and to the orphans﴾, because of their weakness. Al-Harali said: orphanhood is the loss of the father at the time of need; for this reason a male orphan is counted in the mention until puberty, and a female until she is married, because her need remains after puberty. "Al-qurbā" is a form from "qarāba" (kinship), and it is nearness in apparent or hidden lineage, end of quote.

﴿And the needy﴾, because they are broken.

Since it was not possible for people in general to do good in action, He commanded that (p-4) it be done by speech. So He said, conjoining it to the statement whose meaning is an originating command: ﴿And speak to people﴾ in general,

﴿kindly﴾, meaning "ḥasanan" with the vowel on the ḥā' (in the sense of good), which is a dialect form of it, like "bukhl" and "bakhal" (both meaning stinginess). This means that they command them with what Allah commanded and forbid them from what He forbade. Since He commanded them with what, if they fulfilled it, would unite their word, He mentioned the greatest act of worship, the most unifying of deeds before Allah, and said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾. Then He mentioned what completes the unity and sustains it, and said: ﴿And give zakāt﴾. Since turning away from these good qualities is extremely remote, how much more so when they are bound by a covenant, and how much more so when the covenant is from Allah, He indicated this with the particle of delay, and said: ﴿Then you turned away﴾, meaning from that, or from much of it. He indicated by the reflexive form that religious matters, because of their goodness, are not turned away from except through a treatment that stands between the original nature and the commanding self.

﴿Except a few of you, and you﴾, meaning, while you (p-5) ﴿are averse﴾, this being your habit. It was not from you without knowledge. "Al-i'rāḍ" (aversion) is turning a thing to its "ʿarḍ," which is its side.

Al-Samīn said: It is narrated from Abū ʿAmr and others: "illā qalīlun" with the nominative (raf'), and there are opinions about it; the most correct is its nominative as an adjective, by interpreting "illā" and what follows it as meaning "ghayr" (other than). End of quote. The grammatical analysis (iʿrāb) of this will come, Allah willing, at His words, ﴿Then they drank from it, except a few of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249]. He mentioned what bears witness to this from the Torah. In its second book, when it mentioned the matter of the secret conversation and their presence at the mountain, it said: "And God spoke all these words, saying: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them nor serve them, for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and the fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments. You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain. Honour your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour. You shall not covet your neighbour's wife, nor desire your neighbour's house, nor his field..." And all the people were seeing the voices and seeing the lamps.

(p-6) And it said in another place from the third book: "You shall not steal, nor deal falsely, nor lie to one another. You shall not swear by my name falsely, nor profane the name of the LORD your God. I am the LORD, there is no other. You shall not wrong your neighbour, nor rob him. You shall not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God. I am the LORD. You shall not render an unjust judgement, nor show partiality to the poor, nor favour the great; but in righteousness shall you judge your neighbour. You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall reprove your neighbour, lest you incur sin because of him. You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge against the sons of your people, but you shall love your neighbour as yourself. You shall not practise divination nor augury. You shall not round off the hair on your temples, nor mar the edges of your beard. You shall not make gashes in your flesh for the dead, nor tattoo any marks upon you. I am the LORD your God. You shall not follow the practices of the sorcerers or the mediums, nor seek them out to be defiled by them. Rise before the hoary head and honour the old, and fear your God. I am the LORD your God. When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong. The stranger who sojourns with you shall be to you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God. You shall do no wrong in judgement, in measures of length, weight, or quantity. You shall have honest balances, honest weights, an honest ephah, and an honest hin. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. You shall keep all my statutes and all my ordinances, and do them: I am the LORD."

And it said in the second: "Whoever follows the sorcerers and the mediums to go astray after them, I will set my face against that person and cut him off from among his people." "Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death. Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death. Whoever kidnaps a man and sells him shall be put to death." Then it said: "If a man or a woman is a medium or a wizard, they shall surely be put to death; they shall be stoned with stones; their blood shall be upon them." And it said before that: "Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall surely be put to death." Then it said: "The stranger who sojourns among you shall not be oppressed, nor shall you distress them, lest you cause them to cry out to me, and I will surely hear their cry, and my anger will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children orphans." Then it said: "If you lend money to the poor among my people, you shall not be to him as a creditor, nor shall you exact interest from him." Then it said: "You shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise in judgement and perverts the words of the righteous."

Since this matter was, with what was emphasized by the mention of the covenant in the manifestation of majesty and by attributing the offense to the very self of the offender, worthy of distance from him, he pointed to that by His saying: ﴿Then you are these﴾, the despised ones, those overpowered, the unknown ones for whom no name is known by which they are called, or those who exist now. Then he resumed the explanation of this sentence, saying: ﴿you kill yourselves﴾, without turning back to this firm covenant,

﴿and you expel a group of you﴾, i.e., people who are your full brothers, so they are more deserving of kindness from you than of expulsion, ﴿from their homes﴾.

Since it was very far-fetched, after the first far-fetching, that they would fall into that by way of transgression, he resumed the explanation of that by His saying: ﴿you support one another﴾, i.e., you help one another. It is from *tazāhur* (mutual support), which is the forced effort of *muẓāharah*, and *muẓāharah* is the reinforcing of strength, as if it were the leaning of one back against another back, as al-Ḥarrālī said.

﴿against them with sin﴾, i.e., accompanied by sin, which is the worst of transgression in speech, deed or state. A liar is called *athūm* (sinful), because he transgresses against others with speech. *Al-ithm* (sin) is also wine, because enmity and hostility arise from it, as al-Ḥarrālī said.

﴿and aggression﴾, i.e., and exceeding the bounds, ﴿and if they come to you﴾, i.e., these whom you have cooperated, or cooperated with, against them,

﴿as captives﴾, the plural of *usrā*, which is the plural of *asīr* (captive). Its root meaning is one bound with a *asr* (binding), which is the *qadd*, the strip that is cut from the hide, ﴿you ransom them﴾, i.e., you free them with wealth. From *fidā’* (ransom), which is release in exchange for a compensation. *Tufādūhum* is from *mufādāh*, which is equality in the two compensations, as al-Ḥarrālī said.

Then he emphasized the prohibition of expulsion by adding the pronoun and the nominal sentence in His saying: ﴿while it is forbidden﴾, from *taḥrīm* (prohibition). *Taḥrīm* is the repeated *ḥirmah* (sanctity), with a kasra, which is prevention from a thing because of its lowliness, while *ḥurmah*, with a damma, is prevention from a thing because of its loftiness, as al-Ḥarrālī said.

﴿upon you﴾. Since it might be thought that the pronoun refers to the ransom itself, He said: ﴿their expulsion﴾. Then He rebuked them for distinguishing between the rulings, saying: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book﴾, i.e., the Torah, which requires ransoming,

﴿and disbelieve in part﴾, which forbids killing and expulsion. Then He made the following a consequence of that: ﴿What is the recompense of those who do that﴾, the matter of great abomination,

﴿among you except disgrace﴾, the opposite of what you intended by your deed of honor. *Khizy* (disgrace) is the exposure of the vices that one is ashamed to have exposed, as a punishment, as al-Ḥarrālī said.

﴿in the life of this world﴾, hastening punishment for them in the abode that they made the target of their aim. (p-١٣) God, glory be to Him, has done that with kinds of humiliation and killing and what is less than that,

﴿and on the Day of Resurrection﴾. *Qiyāmah* is on the pattern *fi‘ālah*, in which the *tā’* conveys intensity and predominance, and it is the rising of a magnified matter. *Qiyām* is the bearing of heavy burdens,

﴿they will be returned﴾, i.e., by resurrection. *Radd* is returning to that from which the course began, as al-Ḥarrālī said.

﴿to the most severe punishment﴾, because it is the greatest disgrace.

Since direct address with threat is more indicative of anger, he turned to them in the reading of the majority, and joined to what is implied by that, that God knows what you intended in that, so He will recompense you according to what you deserve, His saying: ﴿And God is not﴾, i.e., the One encompassing in knowledge and power,

﴿unaware of what﴾, i.e., of anything, that,

﴿you do﴾, of that and of other than it. The recitation of Nāfi‘ and Ibn Kathīr is with the *ghayb* (third person), according to the past-tense style.

(p-14) Since all these verses serve as proof for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them﴾ and ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾, the summation of that is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those﴾, meaning: the distant and the hateful,

﴿who have purchased﴾, meaning: they persisted and took,

﴿the worldly life﴾ despite its baseness,

﴿in exchange for the Hereafter﴾ despite its preciousness. The word ad-dunyā is on the pattern fu'lā from ad-dunuww, which means the lower in rank, as opposed to ʿulyā (the higher). Because the immediate was attached to it, it came to be contrasted with the other, which is attached to height. So in the worldly life there is a descent in station and haste, and in the Hereafter there is a height in station and delay. The two are thus opposed, as is understood from the meaning of each of them. This was said by al-Ḥarrālī. [Thus the verse uses ihtikāk (a rhetorical device of mutual implication): mentioning the worldly life first indicates the omission of the higher one second, and mentioning the Hereafter second indicates the omission of the immediate one first.]

﴿So it will not be lightened﴾, meaning: as a consequence of that, it will not be lightened. The word takhfīf (lightening) means (p-15) the heavy and the sinking reaching the state of the floating and the rising, like the state of what is between a stone and the air. This was said by al-Ḥarrālī.

﴿for them, the punishment﴾ in either of the two abodes,

﴿nor will they be helped﴾. This is also among the greatest proofs of the abandonment of one who raids for the sake of booty or embezzles (ghulūl, the misappropriation of spoils). Many ḥadīths and reports explicitly state this. Among them is what Mālik narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Embezzlement does not appear among a people without Allah casting terror into their hearts." This is also an ancient law. In the Book of Joshua son of Nun, peace be upon him, it is reported that when he conquered the city of Jericho after the death of Moses, peace be upon him, he sent three thousand fighters to the city of Ai to conquer it. The people of Ai killed a group of them and defeated them. Their hearts trembled and became like water. Joshua fell on the ground before the Ark of the Lord, he and the elders of the Children of Israel. The Lord said to him: "Stand up." He informed him that his people had embezzled, so they could not now stand before their enemies until they removed the forbidden thing from among them. God said to him: "When it is morning, bring your tribes forward so that they may draw lots." The tribe that the Lord's lot falls upon shall advance by its clans, the clan the lot falls upon shall advance by its households, and the household upon which the Lord's lot falls (p-16) and in whose possession the forbidden thing is found shall be burned with fire, it and everything it has, because it transgressed the command of the Lord and because it committed a sin against Israel. He did what the Lord commanded, and the lot fell upon Achan son of Carmi, of the tribe of Judah. He brought him, his sons, his daughters, his livestock, his tent, and everything he had. They led them up to the valley of Achor, and all the Children of Israel stoned them with stones and burned them with fire, and they raised over him a great heap of stones, which remains to this day. For this reason that place was called the Valley of Achor to this day. Then they came the next day to Ai and killed everyone in it, of the sons of Adam, males and females, and burned it.

[p-17] When He had shown them that they had broken the covenants, so that their sins encompassed them and they deserved to abide forever in the Fire, the questioner would expect an account of the cause of their falling into this, whether it was ignorance or obstinacy. So God, exalted is He, denounced this to them by opening with the particle of expectation, and said: ﴿And indeed﴾, with the lam that is an emphasis of the content of the statement, and "qad" that is for the occurrence of something awaited, whether it was already reported or will be an established sign. This is what al-Harrali (al-Harrali) said.

﴿We gave﴾ [Ayy-2]: by Our majesty ﴿Moses the Book﴾, meaning: you broke those covenants although with you in them was the Book of God, the Torah, which you study at all times. So We did not leave you neglected after Moses, peace be upon him, but We secured your affair with the Book.

﴿And We sent after him﴾ from "taqfiyah", which is following one thing after another, as if one treads upon the other's heel. The "qafa" (back) of a picture is its back, opposite its face. This is what al-Harrali said.

﴿after him﴾: that is, after Moses.

﴿with the messengers﴾: that is, then We did not limit the securing to the Book that Moses left among you, but We made the sending of messengers after him continuous (mutawatirah), and We placed some of them following others, so that they would renew for you the affair of the religion and reaffirm the covenants upon you. Risalah (mission) is the dispatch of a command from the sender to the one to whom it is sent.

﴿And We gave﴾ by Our majesty,

﴿Jesus﴾: an arabicized name whose origin is Yasu' (Jesus),

﴿son of Mary﴾, whom We sent to abrogate part of the Torah and to renew what had faded of the remainder of it,

﴿the clear signs﴾: among the great signs about which there is no doubt for a person of intellect. A "bayyinah" is a clear proof, whether in speech or in existence, which no disputant can contest because of its clarity. This is what al-Harrali said.

﴿And We strengthened him﴾: that is, [p-19] We empowered him for all of that. It is from "ta'yid", and it is from "al-ayd", which is strength, as if one takes him by the hand in the matter in which one strengthens him, like taking the strength of support from the back, because the back is the seat of a thing's inherent strength, while the hand is the seat of its strength in grasping other things. This is what al-Harrali said.

﴿with the Holy Spirit﴾: that is, the pure Spirit, who is Gabriel, peace be upon him, just as We strengthened others of the Resolute Messengers (ulu al-'azm) with him. Al-Harrali said: The Spirit is a flash from the flashes of God's command, and God's command is His self-subsistence over all creation, both the visible realm (mulk) and the unseen realm (malakut). What sustains all creation, both visible and unseen, is the Command, as in ﴿Surely His is the creation and the command﴾ [7:54]. And what sustains a form among the totality of creation is the Spirit, which is a flash of that Command. Because the unseen realm (malakut) subsists, and especially the whole of the Throne, through the visible realm (mulk), and especially the affair of the enduring religion, God named them "spirits", and among the most specific of them is the Holy Spirit. "Qudus" is the lofty purity that no impurity can touch, as has been previously explained. Among those most specifically named Spirit is Gabriel, peace be upon him, by reason of his share of the Spirit of religious command, and Israfil, peace be upon him, by reason of his share of the Spirit of the blowing of the trumpet. End of quotation. Jesus, peace be upon him, had a greater particularity with the Spirit because of the abundance of the dead he brought to life.

The meaning is: We did this to you, O Children of Israel, and you continued in the time of all those mentioned as breakers of covenants. So none is more deserving than you of abiding forever in the Fire. Then Muhammad (ﷺ) came, and you did not believe him.

A mention of part of the Injil (Gospel) that indicates that he, peace be upon him, came with the clear signs together with his being strengthened by the Holy Spirit, extracted from the four Gospels, whose wordings have been combined. Matthew, most of the context being his, said: When Jesus heard that John, that is Yahya ibn Zakariyya, peace be upon them both, had been handed over, that is, his companions forsook him, he went away to Galilee, left Nazareth, came and settled in Capernaum, which is on the seashore in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, so that what was said through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, when he says: "The land of Zebulun, the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations, the people who sit in darkness have seen a great light; upon those who sit in the region and shadow of death, a light has dawned upon them." From that time Jesus began to preach and say: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near." Mark said: After John was imprisoned, Jesus came to Galilee preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God, saying: "The time has been fulfilled and the kingdom of God has drawn near! So repent and believe in the Gospel." Matthew said: As he walked by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew, casting their nets into the sea, for they were fishermen. He said to them: "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Immediately they left their nets and followed him. Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James son of Zebedee and his brother John, in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets, and he called them. Immediately they left the boat and their father Zebedee and followed him. In the Gospel of John, after the story of Yahya ibn Zakariyya that comes later in Al 'Imran: This happened at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing. On the next day he saw Jesus coming to him and said: "Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said: After me comes a man who is before me, because he was before me. I did not know him, but that he might be revealed to Israel, for this reason I came baptizing with water." John bore witness and said: "I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him, and I did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me: He upon whom you see the Spirit descend and remain is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. And I have seen and borne witness." The next day John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus and said: "Behold the Lamb of God!" The two disciples heard him speak and followed Jesus. Jesus turned and saw them following him and said to them: "What do you seek?" They said to him: "Rabbi (which means Teacher), where do you stay?" He said to them: "Come and see." So they came and saw where he was staying, and they remained with him that day, and it was about the tenth hour. One of the two who had heard John and followed Jesus was Andrew, brother of Simon, and he found first his brother and said to him: "We have found the Messiah (which is the Christ)," and he brought him to Jesus. When Jesus looked at him he said: "You are Simon son of Jonah, who is called Cephas, which means Peter." On the next day he wanted to go out to Galilee, and he found Philip, and Philip said to him: "The one of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the Prophets, we have found him, Jesus of Nazareth." Nathanael said to him: "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him: "Come and see." When Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, he said: "Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit!" Nathanael said to him: "How do you know me?" Jesus said to him: "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you." Nathanael said to him: "Rabbi, you are the King of Israel!" Jesus said to him: "Because I told you I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these." He said to him: "Truly, truly I say to you, from now on you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man." On the third day there was a wedding at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there, and Jesus and his disciples were invited to the wedding. When the wine had run out, the mother of Jesus said to him: "They have no wine." Jesus said to her: "What is that to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come." His mother said to the servants: "Do whatever he tells you." Now there were six stone water jars there, set for the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures. Jesus said to them: "Fill the jars with water," and they filled them to the brim. He said to them: "Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast." When the master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine, he did not know where it came from, so the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him: "Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the inferior; but you have kept the good wine until now!" This was the first sign that Jesus performed at Cana of Galilee, and he manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 87 (part 2 of 2):**

After this, he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother, his brothers, and his disciples, and they stayed there a few days. Then he said: "And the Lord Jesus knew that the Pharisees had heard that he had taken many disciples, and that he baptized more than John, although it was not he who baptized but his disciples [p. 25]. So he left Judea and went to Galilee. He had resolved to pass through the region of Samaria, and he came to the city of Samaria called Sychar, beside the village that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. There was Jacob's well. Jesus, weary from the journey, sat down by the well at the sixth hour. A woman of Samaria came to draw water, and Jesus said to her: 'Give me a drink'—for his disciples had gone into the city to buy food for them. The woman said to him: 'How is it that you, a Jew, ask me for a drink, when I am a Samaritan woman?' For the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans! Jesus answered and said to her: 'If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who said to you, "Give me a drink," you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water!' The woman said: 'Sir! You have no bucket, and the well is deep. From where then do you have living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well, and from which he drank, with his sons and his cattle?' He said to her: 'Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again. But whoever drinks of the water that I give will never thirst forever.' The woman said: 'Sir! Give me of this water, so that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw water.' He said: 'Go, call your husband, and come here.' She said: 'I have no husband.' He said to her: 'You have spoken well, "I have no husband" [p. 26], for you have had five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband. This you have said truly.' The woman said: 'Sir! I see that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshipped on this mountain, and you say that Jerusalem is the place where people must worship.' He said: 'Woman! Believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will they worship the Father. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know. But the hour is coming, and it is now, when the true worshippers will worship in spirit and truth, for the Lord only desires such worshippers. Those who worship him in spirit and truth must worship.' The woman said: 'I know that the Messiah, who is the Christ, is coming. When he comes, he will teach us everything.' He said: 'I am he, the one who is speaking to you.' At this point his disciples came and marveled that he was speaking with a woman, but no one said: 'What do you want?' or 'Why are you speaking with her?' The woman left her water jar and went into the city, and said to the people: 'Come, see a man who told me everything I have done. Could this be the Messiah?' They went out of the city and came toward him. Meanwhile his disciples asked him, saying: 'Teacher, eat!' He said: 'I have food that you do not know.' So they said among themselves: 'Perhaps someone has brought him something and he has eaten it.' He said: 'My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to finish his work. Do you not say that the harvest comes after four months? I tell you: lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are already white and ready for harvest. The one who reaps receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper rejoice together. For in this the saying is true: one sows and another reaps. I sent you to reap what you did not labor for; others labored, and you have entered into their labor.' Many Samaritans in that city believed in him because of the word of that woman. When the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days. Many more believed because of his word, and they said to the woman: 'It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves and know that this is truly the Messiah, the Savior of the world.'

After two days, Jesus left for Galilee, and departed from there, for he testified that a prophet is not honored in his own homeland. When he came to Galilee, the Galileans received him, because they had seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. Then Jesus came again to Cana, where he had made water into wine. In Capernaum there was a royal official whose son was sick. He heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, so he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for the boy was near death. Jesus said to him: 'Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe.' The official said to him: 'Sir, come down before my child dies.' Jesus said to him: 'Go, your son lives.' The man believed the word that Jesus spoke and went his way. While he was on his way, his servants met him and told him that his son had lived. He asked them: 'At what hour?' They said to him: 'Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.' His father knew that it was at that very hour when Jesus had said to him, 'Your son lives,' and he believed, together with all his household. This was also a second sign that Jesus performed when he came from Judea to Galilee."

Mark said: "He came to Capernaum, and he continued teaching in their synagogues on the Sabbath day, and they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one having authority."

Matthew said: "Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. His fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought to him all who were sick with various diseases and pains, those possessed by demons, the lunatics, and the paralytics, and he healed them. Great crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan. When he saw the crowds, he went up on a mountain and sat down. His disciples came to him, and he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted. Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God. Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when they revile you and persecute you and say all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.'"

Luke said: "So did your fathers do to the prophets. But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. Woe to you when all people speak well of you, for their fathers did the same to the false prophets"—meaning the pretenders to prophethood. In this passage there are expressions which may not be applied in our law, such as "the Lamb of God," "the Father," and "the sons of God." Its interpretation, if it is authentically transmitted from him, will come, God willing, in Surat Al 'Imran, and it is to be referred back to the clear (muhkam) texts in the clearest way, like the expressions that occur in our law, which we have referred back to the clear texts. Those who take these expressions literally, from among those who claim to be Muslims, have gone astray by them. God is the Granter of success.

Since this was their condition with the messengers, despite their familiarity with them, their knowledge of their circumstances, their connection to God, and their perfection, God knew that in their opposition to them they were slaves of desire and captives of appetites. Consequently, the rebuke against them follows, when He says: ﴿Is it that whenever a messenger came to you﴾, meaning: Do you do what you have done, breaking covenants despite the successive sending of messengers and the existence of the Scripture? Then whenever ﴿a messenger came to you﴾, meaning from God your Lord, ﴿with what your souls did not desire﴾ [p. 27]. Desire (hawa) is the soul's inclination toward the lowest of its appetites, in opposition to the elevated spirit that seeks expansion. It is as if the soul is heavy within, like water and earth, while the spirit is light within, like air and fire, and the intellect is broad within, like the spreading of light throughout the whole universe, above and below. This is what al-Harrali said.

It has been indicated that what is meant by the mention of desire and soul is falsehood. ﴿You became arrogant﴾, meaning you sought arrogance and brought it into being through your leadership over your people, refusing to accept the truth, inclining toward the way of Iblis, even though you had previously given a covenant to follow him perpetually. ﴿Some﴾, meaning [p. 32] as a consequence of your seeking arrogance, you ﴿some [of them] you denied﴾, like Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both; ﴿and some you kill﴾, meaning you killed and did not repent of their killing, but rather resolved to do the same whenever one of them came to you with what opposes your desire, though they were sent only to turn souls away from desire, because the call of the messenger is to the Higher, which is the opposite of the soul's desire. It seems clear that He, glory be to Him, by this future form, indicated their killing of the Prophet ﷺ by poison at Khaybar, as the hadith mentioned just before indicated.

When He, glory be to Him, had exposed their disgraceful conduct, concluding with their gravest crimes against the messengers, namely the figurative killing through denial and the literal killing through taking life, while knowing that they had come with clear proofs and manifest miracles, the context points to the implied sense: they said to the prophets, when these came to them with many matters that are astonishing to issue from a rational person, and in their reply to their denial and killing they uttered contradictions that no knowledgeable or ignorant person would accept. (p-33) It is conjoined either to it or to ﴿And they say: The Fire will not touch us except for a few days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], as an explanation of the extent of their obstinacy and the strength of their defiance: ﴿And they said﴾ in answer to what the prophets were presenting to them of the gems of knowledge, which are clearer than the sun.

﴿Our hearts are wrapped (ghulf)﴾. Ghulf is the plural of aghlaf, which means one whose penis is covered by the foreskin (qulfah), the skin that covers it. It is as if the foreskin were at both ends of a person, his penis and his heart, until Allah completes His word at both ends through circumcision (khitan) and faith. This is what al-Harrali stated. The meaning is: there are coverings over them, so they do not understand what you say. The intended sense is that, although they are the most knowledgeable of people, what they were saying is not fit to be directed toward understanding. (p-34) For this reason Allah, glory be to Him, turned away from it with His words: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claim, that there are truly wrapped hearts. Rather, ﴿Allah has cursed them﴾, meaning: the Supreme King has expelled them from accepting that, because they are not fit for happiness after He created them upon the original upright nature, with no wrappings upon their hearts. Cursing means distancing in meaning and status, to the point that the one cursed is like a sandal at the bottom of the body, on which the harm of being trodden upon falls. This is what al-Harrali stated.

Then He explained the cause of that with His words: ﴿for their disbelief﴾.
