Greater than that is their practice of abrogation that Allah did not permit, in their distorting of the words from their places, and their prohibiting what the rabbis and monks had not forbidden and their permitting for themselves whatever rulings they wished, a number of which has already been counted as principles and branches, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:31]. When 'Adi ibn Hatim said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of Allah, they did not worship them." He said: "Did they not make lawful for them and make unlawful for them?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then that is their worship of them." As is explained in the Sirah in the account of 'Adi's delegation. And as they did in replacing stoning for adultery with blackening and flogging; and in following what the devils recite, although in it there is much nullification of their law; and in the casting away by a group of them of the Book of Allah; and in their saying: ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:93]; and in their taking the calf despite the prohibition against it, and all that resembles it in many chapters of the Torah, and in what was alluded to by His saying: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:85], and other than that. When all of that was so, God, the Exalted, said in reply to their objection that had preceded it, in the manifestation of greatness, informing that He had clothed the Arabs, who were envied, with what the People of the Book had been adorned with for ages, and they degraded it, defiled its face, debased it, altered it and changed it, indicating that envy, being an objection to the Benefactor, becomes a cause for clothing the envied one in the garment of the envier: ﴿We do not abrogate﴾. And *naskh*, al-Harali (al-Harrali) said: it is the transfer of what has passed away, from a trace or a book or the like, from its place, by a replacement that removes it, or by a borrowing that makes its absence unnecessary, and it is apparent in both meanings in the contexts of discourse, and replacement is more apparent in this, end of quote. He stated it without a conjunction because of the strong connection of its parts with what precedes it, since we are particularizing for the sake of arranging things according to the interests, with grace and mercy. For if the intent is the abrogation of all previous laws by our Book, then this is for the honour of being singled out by mention, and the non-subordination and lightening of the burdens that were there. And if the intent is the abrogation of what was legislated for us, then it is for consideration of worldly and otherworldly interests according to what has arisen of circumstances [p. 93],

﴿from a sign﴾, that is: We remove its ruling, or its recitation after its descent, or We command that, on the reading of Ibn 'Amir, which is of *naskh*, whether it was in the law of those before us, like facing the Holy House, or not. And in the form *nafa'alu* (We do) there is an indication that those who came before may have had abrogated for them what was not replaced for them by anything better or any good; so within it is an encouragement for the believers in their own Book, that they should have a good reception for abrogation, joyful at the new or glad for what is better than the abrogated, so that their condition when the verses are replaced will be the opposite of the condition of those who refuse to accept it, who cling to the previous and fall short of the later good they have found; so said al-Harali. ''Or We cause it to be postponed'', that is: We delay it, meaning: We leave its descent upon you altogether. Likewise the meaning of ﴿or We cause it to be forgotten﴾ from *ansa*, in the reading other than that of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, that is: We command the leaving of its descent [p. 94],

﴿We bring a better one than it, or its like﴾, as We did in: ﴿Raina﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:104] and others. Or the meaning is: ''whatever sign We abrogate'', so We remove its ruling or its wording promptly, as We did in ''Raina''. ''Or We cause it to be postponed'', by delaying its abrogation or leaving it, on the reading ''nansaha'' (We cause it to be forgotten), for a time, then We abrogate it, like the qiblah. ''We bring'' at its abrogation ''a better one than it, or its like''. Al-Harali said: this is the truth, God willing, the Exalted. And *al-nasa'* is postponement from one time to another time, so in it there is a pivot between what precedes and what follows, unlike abrogation, because abrogation follows the earlier, while postponement defers the later and alternates it. This is a type of discourse, sublime, with a hidden direction, whose meaning hardly became clear to most scholars except to the Imams of the family of Muhammad (ﷺ), because of the obscurity of the distinction between what is characterized by replacement and what is characterized by alternation. Among its examples is what occurred regarding postponement, from the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition of eating the meat of the sacrificial animals, which the believers accepted as abrogation, but it was in fact a postponement and deferral of the ruling on enjoying them after three days, until the time when the influx of desert people who had come upon them from the wilderness had passed. That was not transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) until he explained it and said: "I only forbade you because of the influx (al-dafaffah)." So within the breadth of his understanding is that some rulings are deferred, resembling abrogation in one respect, then they are restored and differ from it in this respect, since the wisdom of the abrogated is cut off, while the wisdom of the postponed returns. From this is fighting the enemy when one finds power and strength, and truce when weak and unable to resist; this is among the rulings of the postponed. Every matter whose nature is to be prohibited at a time for some meaning, then returns at a time when that meaning has ceased, is of the postponed, whose knowledge most observers have neglected, and perhaps they attributed most of it to the category of abrogation because of the obscurity of the distinction between them. Truly this verse is among the comprehensive verses of the Criterion. This is the ruling of postponement and causing to be forgotten, and in knowledge it is like the succession of seasons, with what they contain of successive things in one aspect and alternating in general.

I say: its summary is the postponement of permissibility as mentioned, or of prohibition as in temporary marriage and the like, to another time. That is the meaning of *nasi'* according to what the Arabs customarily used, as will come its clarification in Surah Bara'ah at ﴿The postponement is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:37]. He said: As for *nisyan* and *tansiyah* (causing to be forgotten), its meaning is more hidden than *nasi'*, and it is what Allah manifests [p. 96] of clarifications by way of introducing forgetfulness to one who is not characterized by being postponed, like the sunnahs that the Prophet (ﷺ) made manifest by causing them to be forgotten, as came in his saying: "I am made to forget so that I may establish a sunnah." And upon him be blessings and peace, in plain statement about it, he said: "Evil is it for one of you to say: 'I forgot'; rather, he was caused to forget." And from it is his standing up after two rak'ahs and his salam after two, until Allah made manifest the sunnah of that for his community; and that prayer with its forgetfulness was not less than it without forgetfulness, but was like it or better. And of the same kind is his sleeping through the prayer, until Allah made manifest the timing of the prayer by remembrance, just as He had manifested it by the temporal time, so it came to have two times: the time of visible light from its orbit with the sun, and the time of experiential light from its orbit with remembrance. And for the validity of its occurrence at both times, the prayer timed by remembrance was performed (adda') according to it, and made up (qada') according to the passing of the temporal time. So to God, the Exalted, upon this community is great bounty in what completes for it by way of abrogation, by way of postponement, and by way of forgetfulness which is not from neglect or carelessness, but which He brings about by compulsion along with firm resolve. In all of that is information that what occurs of the command after this forgetfulness is better than the place of that command which used to occur with consensus and care, so that the conditions of this community may be equal in all the variations of its states. All of that is from the particularity of His mercy and great bounty, end of quote. And Allah, glorified is He, argued for His bringing about of that by His power, and complete all-encompassing power necessarily entails knowledge; that is: He is not like other kings, who when they command something fear the danger of their followers and subjects in breaking it. And He argued for power by the fact that to Him belongs all dominion and no one has any command with Him [p. 98]. The summary of that is: when Allah, glorified is He, mentioned this Book and emphasized its command repeatedly, and it was abrogating the branches of their law, especially what in it of burdens and shackles, He indicated that among the greatest of their misguidance, error and absurdity is their claim that abrogation is not permissible for Allah. They denied ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:23], which is present in their own Book as He commanded just before, and what they permitted for themselves through distortion and alteration. It followed from this the denial of every messenger who came to them with what their souls did not desire, and they acted contrary to the state of the believers who affirm what was sent down to their own prophet and what was sent down to others; and that comprised their fault in disparaging the religion by commanding a thing today and forbidding it tomorrow, and that if it were from God it would not change, since He knows the outcomes; and it is not free of either: that He knows the command to that thing is a benefit, so He does not forbid it afterward, or that it is a harm, so He does not command it today. Their answer to that, turning away from addressing them, indicating their dullness, was to address the most knowledgeable of creation with His saying: ﴿Do you not know that Allah﴾, that is: the one possessing all the attributes of perfection,

﴿over everything is Competent﴾, in the form of an interrogation which implies denial and affirmation, in which is an allusion to threat and warning, so He creates by His power from the causes what makes a thing at one time a benefit and at another time a harm, for wisdoms and interests He has arranged because this world is transient, and this existence requires the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of everything that has preceded and that will follow. [p. 99] And had He willed, He would have made the matter of one course and people of one heart,

﴿Had your Lord willed, all who are on earth would have believed, all of them together﴾ [Yunus 10:99]; ﴿He would have made mankind one community﴾ [Hud 11:118]. But He is the Owner of dominion and the King of the heavens and the earth, who disposes as He wills; none can repel His command or overturn His judgment, and objection to Him is in no way admissible. And is it permissible for a slave, who is never free of servitude at all, to object to the Master whose lordship is firmly established, when no obligation at all binds Him, so that the command does not bind Him according to the interests? Then He followed that with what is like a proof of the comprehensiveness of power, and said: ﴿Do you not know that Allah﴾, who combines the kinds of greatness,

﴿to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾; He does what He wills with their essences and their conditions. Al-Harali said: He, by being over everything competent, distinguishes the signs, and He, by possessing the dominion of the heavens and the earth, manages the affair, end of quote.

When He, glorified is He, had completed what He intended of displaying His power, the vastness of His dominion and His greatness by the proper name which is greater than the manifestation of greatness in ''We abrogate'' and ''We postpone'', by turning to address one whom no one but Him knows as he should be known, the hearts of the listeners were prepared and their attention inclined, so He turned the address toward them, as a warning, pointing toward encouragement, and He said: ﴿And you have not [p. 100] besides Allah﴾, the one characterized by all the attributes of greatness,

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verses 106–107 (part 2 of 2):

﴿مِن ولِيٍّ﴾ "a guardian" who will manage your affairs. It is from the root wilayah (ولاية), which al-Harrali (al-Harrali, a Qur'anic commentator) said is "standing in charge of a matter through a connecting link that joins." ﴿ولا نَصِيرٍ﴾ "nor any helper." So turn with all your hearts to Him, and do not let them turn away from Him. In this there is an indirect warning to those who believed but have not reached the rank of the believers, against opposing His command when He judges over them with what He wills, whatever it may be, lest their inner hearts be taught, in some way like what the tongues of the Jews were taught, by holding fast to the earlier revelation of their scripture, so that they become sluggish in accepting its later and completing part. Thus it follows, in keeping with the great number of the People of the Book who refuse it, that the abrogation of the rulings of their scripture that were altered is what is meant. This is the view of al-Harrali, who said: "In reality, it is an address that comprehensively covers the detailed abrogation that occurs in the particulars of rulings and circumstances, in the same way as the address mentioned at the beginning of the surah, which contains the comprehensive method of coining parables, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even of] a mosquito﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], and so on. This is because this surah is the tent-pole (fusṭāṭ) of the Qur'an (p-101), the one that gathers everything whose details are set out in it; it is the hump (sanām) of the Qur'an, and the sanām of a thing is its highest part; it is the chief (sayyidah) of the surahs of the Qur'an. Therefore it contains comprehensive principles, some of which are linked to others, and their detailed expression within it has an effect on the loftiness of its meanings and the authority of its address, somewhat like the arrangement of the verses of Surah al-Fatihah, which are arranged without any detail occurring within them, so that there may be a certain correspondence between the all-encompassing whole and the comprehensive opening." End of quotation.

He stated it without a conjunction because of the strong connection of its parts with what precedes it, since we are particularizing for the sake of arranging things according to the interests, with grace and mercy. For if the intent is the abrogation of all previous laws by our Book, then this is for the honour of being singled out by mention, and the non-subordination and lightening of the burdens that were there. And if the intent is the abrogation of what was legislated for us, then it is for consideration of worldly and otherworldly interests according to what has arisen of circumstances [p. 93],

﴿from a sign﴾, that is: We remove its ruling, or its recitation after its descent, or We command that, on the reading of Ibn 'Amir, which is of *naskh*, whether it was in the law of those before us, like facing the Holy House, or not. And in the form *nafa'alu* (We do) there is an indication that those who came before may have had abrogated for them what was not replaced for them by anything better or any good; so within it is an encouragement for the believers in their own Book, that they should have a good reception for abrogation, joyful at the new or glad for what is better than the abrogated, so that their condition when the verses are replaced will be the opposite of the condition of those who refuse to accept it, who cling to the previous and fall short of the later good they have found; so said al-Harali. ''Or We cause it to be postponed'', that is: We delay it, meaning: We leave its descent upon you altogether. Likewise the meaning of ﴿or We cause it to be forgotten﴾ from *ansa*, in the reading other than that of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, that is: We command the leaving of its descent [p. 94],

﴿We bring a better one than it, or its like﴾, as We did in: ﴿Raina﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:104] and others. Or the meaning is: ''whatever sign We abrogate'', so We remove its ruling or its wording promptly, as We did in ''Raina''. ''Or We cause it to be postponed'', by delaying its abrogation or leaving it, on the reading ''nansaha'' (We cause it to be forgotten), for a time, then We abrogate it, like the qiblah. ''We bring'' at its abrogation ''a better one than it, or its like''. Al-Harali said: this is the truth, God willing, the Exalted. And *al-nasa'* is postponement from one time to another time, so in it there is a pivot between what precedes and what follows, unlike abrogation, because abrogation follows the earlier, while postponement defers the later and alternates it. This is a type of discourse, sublime, with a hidden direction, whose meaning hardly became clear to most scholars except to the Imams of the family of Muhammad (ﷺ), because of the obscurity of the distinction between what is characterized by replacement and what is characterized by alternation. Among its examples is what occurred regarding postponement, from the Prophet's (ﷺ) prohibition of eating the meat of the sacrificial animals, which the believers accepted as abrogation, but it was in fact a postponement and deferral of the ruling on enjoying them after three days, until the time when the influx of desert people who had come upon them from the wilderness had passed. That was not transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) until he explained it and said: "I only forbade you because of the influx (al-dafaffah)." So within the breadth of his understanding is that some rulings are deferred, resembling abrogation in one respect, then they are restored and differ from it in this respect, since the wisdom of the abrogated is cut off, while the wisdom of the postponed returns. From this is fighting the enemy when one finds power and strength, and truce when weak and unable to resist; this is among the rulings of the postponed. Every matter whose nature is to be prohibited at a time for some meaning, then returns at a time when that meaning has ceased, is of the postponed, whose knowledge most observers have neglected, and perhaps they attributed most of it to the category of abrogation because of the obscurity of the distinction between them. Truly this verse is among the comprehensive verses of the Criterion. This is the ruling of postponement and causing to be forgotten, and in knowledge it is like the succession of seasons, with what they contain of successive things in one aspect and alternating in general.

I say: its summary is the postponement of permissibility as mentioned, or of prohibition as in temporary marriage and the like, to another time. That is the meaning of *nasi'* according to what the Arabs customarily used, as will come its clarification in Surah Bara'ah at ﴿The postponement is only an increase in disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:37]. He said: As for *nisyan* and *tansiyah* (causing to be forgotten), its meaning is more hidden than *nasi'*, and it is what Allah manifests [p. 96] of clarifications by way of introducing forgetfulness to one who is not characterized by being postponed, like the sunnahs that the Prophet (ﷺ) made manifest by causing them to be forgotten, as came in his saying: "I am made to forget so that I may establish a sunnah." And upon him be blessings and peace, in plain statement about it, he said: "Evil is it for one of you to say: 'I forgot'; rather, he was caused to forget." And from it is his standing up after two rak'ahs and his salam after two, until Allah made manifest the sunnah of that for his community; and that prayer with its forgetfulness was not less than it without forgetfulness, but was like it or better. And of the same kind is his sleeping through the prayer, until Allah made manifest the timing of the prayer by remembrance, just as He had manifested it by the temporal time, so it came to have two times: the time of visible light from its orbit with the sun, and the time of experiential light from its orbit with remembrance. And for the validity of its occurrence at both times, the prayer timed by remembrance was performed (adda') according to it, and made up (qada') according to the passing of the temporal time. So to God, the Exalted, upon this community is great bounty in what completes for it by way of abrogation, by way of postponement, and by way of forgetfulness which is not from neglect or carelessness, but which He brings about by compulsion along with firm resolve. In all of that is information that what occurs of the command after this forgetfulness is better than the place of that command which used to occur with consensus and care, so that the conditions of this community may be equal in all the variations of its states. All of that is from the particularity of His mercy and great bounty, end of quote. And Allah, glorified is He, argued for His bringing about of that by His power, and complete all-encompassing power necessarily entails knowledge; that is: He is not like other kings, who when they command something fear the danger of their followers and subjects in breaking it. And He argued for power by the fact that to Him belongs all dominion and no one has any command with Him [p. 98]. The summary of that is: when Allah, glorified is He, mentioned this Book and emphasized its command repeatedly, and it was abrogating the branches of their law, especially what in it of burdens and shackles, He indicated that among the greatest of their misguidance, error and absurdity is their claim that abrogation is not permissible for Allah. They denied ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:23], which is present in their own Book as He commanded just before, and what they permitted for themselves through distortion and alteration. It followed from this the denial of every messenger who came to them with what their souls did not desire, and they acted contrary to the state of the believers who affirm what was sent down to their own prophet and what was sent down to others; and that comprised their fault in disparaging the religion by commanding a thing today and forbidding it tomorrow, and that if it were from God it would not change, since He knows the outcomes; and it is not free of either: that He knows the command to that thing is a benefit, so He does not forbid it afterward, or that it is a harm, so He does not command it today. Their answer to that, turning away from addressing them, indicating their dullness, was to address the most knowledgeable of creation with His saying: ﴿Do you not know that Allah﴾, that is: the one possessing all the attributes of perfection,

﴿over everything is Competent﴾, in the form of an interrogation which implies denial and affirmation, in which is an allusion to threat and warning, so He creates by His power from the causes what makes a thing at one time a benefit and at another time a harm, for wisdoms and interests He has arranged because this world is transient, and this existence requires the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of everything that has preceded and that will follow. [p. 99] And had He willed, He would have made the matter of one course and people of one heart,

﴿Had your Lord willed, all who are on earth would have believed, all of them together﴾ [Yunus 10:99]; ﴿He would have made mankind one community﴾ [Hud 11:118]. But He is the Owner of dominion and the King of the heavens and the earth, who disposes as He wills; none can repel His command or overturn His judgment, and objection to Him is in no way admissible. And is it permissible for a slave, who is never free of servitude at all, to object to the Master whose lordship is firmly established, when no obligation at all binds Him, so that the command does not bind Him according to the interests? Then He followed that with what is like a proof of the comprehensiveness of power, and said: ﴿Do you not know that Allah﴾, who combines the kinds of greatness,

﴿to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾; He does what He wills with their essences and their conditions. Al-Harali said: He, by being over everything competent, distinguishes the signs, and He, by possessing the dominion of the heavens and the earth, manages the affair, end of quote.

When He, glorified is He, had completed what He intended of displaying His power, the vastness of His dominion and His greatness by the proper name which is greater than the manifestation of greatness in ''We abrogate'' and ''We postpone'', by turning to address one whom no one but Him knows as he should be known, the hearts of the listeners were prepared and their attention inclined, so He turned the address toward them, as a warning, pointing toward encouragement, and He said: ﴿And you have not [p. 100] besides Allah﴾, the one characterized by all the attributes of greatness,

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verses 106–107 (part 2 of 2):

﴿مِن ولِيٍّ﴾ "a guardian" who will manage your affairs. It is from the root wilayah (ولاية), which al-Harrali (al-Harrali, a Qur'anic commentator) said is "standing in charge of a matter through a connecting link that joins." ﴿ولا نَصِيرٍ﴾ "nor any helper." So turn with all your hearts to Him, and do not let them turn away from Him. In this there is an indirect warning to those who believed but have not reached the rank of the believers, against opposing His command when He judges over them with what He wills, whatever it may be, lest their inner hearts be taught, in some way like what the tongues of the Jews were taught, by holding fast to the earlier revelation of their scripture, so that they become sluggish in accepting its later and completing part. Thus it follows, in keeping with the great number of the People of the Book who refuse it, that the abrogation of the rulings of their scripture that were altered is what is meant. This is the view of al-Harrali, who said: "In reality, it is an address that comprehensively covers the detailed abrogation that occurs in the particulars of rulings and circumstances, in the same way as the address mentioned at the beginning of the surah, which contains the comprehensive method of coining parables, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even of] a mosquito﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], and so on. This is because this surah is the tent-pole (fusṭāṭ) of the Qur'an (p-101), the one that gathers everything whose details are set out in it; it is the hump (sanām) of the Qur'an, and the sanām of a thing is its highest part; it is the chief (sayyidah) of the surahs of the Qur'an. Therefore it contains comprehensive principles, some of which are linked to others, and their detailed expression within it has an effect on the loftiness of its meanings and the authority of its address, somewhat like the arrangement of the verses of Surah al-Fatihah, which are arranged without any detail occurring within them, so that there may be a certain correspondence between the all-encompassing whole and the comprehensive opening." End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 108:

When what He, glory be to Him, mentioned had settled in the hearts, concerning the completeness of His power and the greatness of His dominion, and what He had shown of the majesty of His holy Essence by repeating His proper name and affirming that all besides Him is nothing, the hearts became ready for admonition, so He startled them with a stern rebuke, saying: ﴿Or do you wish﴾, that is: do you wish to reject the command of your Creator concerning abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another), or ﴿do you wish﴾ to ﴿take besides Him a god who has no power over anything﴾, by ﴿asking your Messenger﴾ to make for you a god other than Him ﴿as Moses was asked before﴾ (that). Since their asking of this happened within a short time, He made the preposition explicit, saying: ﴿before﴾, that is: before this time, when his people said, after they had seen the signs, and when they had passed by a people devoted to their idols: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:138), and they said: ﴿Show us God openly﴾ (An-Nisa 4:153), and they said: ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:61). They also used to harass him concerning the rulings of God with various kinds of harassment, as has preceded. And "will" (al-irada) in creation is the soul's inclination toward an object it seeks to attain; this is what al-Harrali said. The clearest evidence for what I have estimated is His saying, in coordination with what is implied: "so that they disbelieve," for whoever asks for that has indeed exchanged disbelief for faith.

﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾, that is: takes disbelief in place of faith, by turning away from the signs and asking for other than them, or by clinging to what has been abrogated from it. He expressed this with the present tense to attract whoever has slipped by asking for something of that kind to return in repentance, so that the continuation of it may cease and misguidance may cease with it.

﴿has indeed strayed from the right way﴾, that is: from its evenness and its middle, so he did not find guidance to it, even though he was among clear proofs from it. For whoever swerves from the even path is close to going so far astray that no safety remains with him.

﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ (Al-An'am 6:153). Often groups of people used to waver when signs changed and rulings were forgotten, and according to what occurs in the soul of heaviness toward it or strain in accepting it, what befalls them of this straying from the evenness of this path follows. In this there is an indication that the address is to those who believed, because the believers described by this attribute do not change their state from faith to disbelief, since no one turns away from his religion after faith has mingled with the cheerfulness of his heart: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the false deity and believes in God has grasped the firmest handhold, which has no breaking﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:256), and ﴿Whoever submits his face to God while being a doer of good has grasped the firmest handhold﴾ (Luqman 31:22). The Prophet, may peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed God does not snatch knowledge by snatching it away after He has given it to you." By this the positions of the Qur'anic address become clear with those who are arranged in ranks of hearts according to their share of faith, Islam and excellence (ihsan), as al-Harrali said. He defined "the way" (al-sabil) as that which contains the sustenance of the one who travels on it and journeys along it, such as pasture and water and the like. And "the even" (al-sawa') he defined as the middle of a thing and its most suitable part for the matter intended for it. He said: it is said that it is its middle and its best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 109:

When most of those who stirred up these doubts were among the people of Islam, Allah the Exalted addressed the believers, who were among them, in order to repel them from the misguidance which in itself deserves to be repelled, let alone when it is the gloating of the enemy, its imagining and its love, warning them against mixing with them: ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish﴾. This is an explanation of the meaning of the speech, which is: "Do not exchange disbelief for faith," after explaining it by misguidance. This is the same as what passed in: ﴿What those who disbelieved wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105].

Since the polytheists were Arabs, who knew that the nature of the Arabs is steadfastness, He did not include them with them in this wish, and He said: ﴿from the People of the Scripture﴾. Thus He informed that those sincere among them are few. Glory be to Him, He gave the good news that what they wish is of the category of the impossible, by framing it in the manner of one who wishes, so He said: ﴿if they could return you﴾, i.e., all of you. Then He confirmed the impossibility of this wish, indicating by the affirmation of the preposition ("min", "after") their conviction in it, even if for a short time, so He said: ﴿after your faith﴾, i.e., the firm faith,

﴿as disbelievers﴾, i.e., so that you become like them and thus abide with them forever in the Fire,

﴿out of envy﴾ at what Allah has bestowed upon you of good guidance leading to Paradise. Envy (ḥasad) is the restlessness of the soul at seeing a blessing upon another. He expressed the extent to which envy reaches, to a point where there is no way to leave it, by His saying: ﴿from themselves﴾, i.e., that it is firmly rooted in their natures, so do not hope to turn it away by anything, for their souls overpower their intellects. Then He added emphasis to this by His saying, indicating by the affirmation of the preposition their blame, that they persisted in misguidance after the call, not seeking the truth while able to know it, until its clarity overwhelmed them and its recognition subdued them; then they did not return to it. Nor was their misguidance within themselves sufficient for them, until they wished to mislead others by turning them away from it,

﴿after the truth had become clear﴾, i.e., a clarity that is great in its own manifestness,

﴿to them﴾, i.e., concerning the validity of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), and that he is the Seal of the Prophets, sent to mankind (p-106) entirely, by the testimony of what agrees with him from the Torah, and that they will abide forever in the Fire, because they are among those whose sin has encompassed them, by what He indicated in all these verses, refuting their claim that the Fire would touch them only for a number of days.

Then He guided to the remedy by His saying, giving a reason for the report that their love is impossible and that they will not return: ﴿So pardon﴾, i.e., deal with them as one who pardons, by not mentioning to them anything of what that love arising from this envy displays, in words or deeds, and do not take them to account for it, for they will not harm you and will not return to you.

﴿and overlook﴾, i.e., show them that you have not become aware of any of that. The original meaning is turning away with the side of the neck from a thing as if one had not seen it. He commanded them with absolute overlooking and did not restrict it with the beautiful manner which was specific to the address to their Prophet (ﷺ) in His saying: ﴿So overlook with a gracious forgiveness﴾ [al-Hijr: 85], because the address descends according to its levels and the proper positions of its application. He urged them that their action in this be by relying upon His relief, by His saying: ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾, besides whom there is no command for anyone, ﴿by His order﴾. So He gave them good news (p-107) of this, by their victory over those who were commanded to overlook and pardon them. The beginning of that was and its completion occurs in the time of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him).

Since victory, while they were in a state of paucity and weakness, was a great matter, and the power and multitude of their enemy made it even more improbable, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾ — and He made the place of the pronoun manifest, to confirm the good news, by alluding to the evocation of what this greatest Name indicates of the attributes of majesty and generosity —

﴿is over all things competent.﴾ In this closing there is good news for the believers of their being empowered, just as in the closing with knowledge there is good news of their being taught; and in its implication there is a warning to the disbelievers corresponding to that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 110:

When He commanded them to have confidence in this Book, in what has been abrogated from it and what has not been abrogated, and that the taunts of those who taunt and the envy of the envious should not hinder them from it, and when He commanded them to turn away from others, He commanded them to devote themselves to reforming the self and to doing good to others, which is the attribute of the guided ones in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. Since the purpose of prayer (salah) is to restrict aspiration and intention to the Divine Presence, and to empty the heart of all preoccupations, He knew that the implied meaning, after the conclusion with the comprehensiveness of power, is: "Know that and have confidence in it."

﴿And establish prayer﴾: which, although We will test you regarding its direction with abrogation, is the foundation of the religion and the aid against all calamities, by the help of the Creator, for whom it was intended as a means of turning toward Him and drawing near to Him.

﴿And give zakah﴾, which is the companion of prayer. Whoever separates between the two has abrogated what Allah has established, and so deserves fighting, so that he may return from the error he has committed. It is among the greatest expenditures of the believers in doing good to creatures, if you are truly praying, for wealth is part of the worldly things from which prayer diverts a person.

Since His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104] and what follows it was an address to the believers, warning them against the plots of their enemies by forbidding what would destroy them and commanding what would save them, and He concluded it with this verse as a summary (fadhlakah) of all of that, gathering its meanings together, and He opened it with the foundation of the physical and financial acts of worship, and since the definite article "al" indicates the obligatory part of that, He concluded the verse itself with a general, comprehensive command, saying: ﴿And whatever good you put forward for yourselves﴾, i.e., of prayer, zakah and other things, obligatory and voluntary,

﴿you will find it﴾ with Allah. He increased the encouragement to it by His saying: ﴿with Allah﴾, i.e., the One who combines all attributes of perfection. He preserves it by His knowledge and power, and nurtures it by His generosity and mercy, and so on regarding other matters of grace.

Since a thing may be neglected because it is small, and may not be noticed because it is hidden and insignificant, He said, encouraging and warning: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, who encompasses all by power and knowledge,

﴿of what you do is Seeing.﴾ He used the noun (ism) in place of the pronoun, indicating a fresh beginning regarding the good, so that it would be a comprehensive conclusion; for if it had returned to the specific address, it would have been "innahu" (indeed He). That is because renewing the explicit mention carries the sense of returning the conclusion of the address to the encompassing of its whole, as stated by al-Harrali. The meaning is: if it had been in the pronoun form, it might have conveyed the restriction of His knowledge to the aspect of the good deeds previously mentioned. A similar point is indicated by the words of the scholar Shams al-Din al-Ghazzi at the beginning of his commentary on Isagoge: "What is dominant in the pronoun is the intention of the first meaning." As for the hadith, "Repeating a thing by its explicit name," it is a principle from which one often departs due to contextual indicators.

(p-111) When he had mentioned their claim about touching the Fire, and refuted it in many respects, since their sins had encompassed them in it, an encompassing that required their eternal abiding therein, from the aspect of their misguidance, up to the verse of abrogation (*naskh*, the replacement of one ruling by another), elevating the address from one evil to something worse than it; and then, from the aspect of their leading others astray, from the verse of abrogation onward, he turned to that claim the report of their claim concerning entry into Paradise, explicitly stating what the first claim had implied allusively. He joined to this the same thing with which he had concluded what came before it, namely that whoever does good will find it, in a clear manner, in which that good is Islam and virtue (*ihsan*).

So He, exalted, said: ﴿And they say﴾, that is, the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, out of envy toward the effect (*al-musabbab*), which is Paradise, just as they envied the cause (*al-sabab*), which is the sending down of what requires faith, the faith that leads to God's good pleasure, by which the gardens are obtained:

﴿Never will enter Paradise﴾, the one prepared for the friends of God,

﴿except those who are Jews﴾. This is the saying of the Jews among them,

﴿or Christians.﴾ And this is the saying of the Christians, spreading out what the conjunction "and" in "and they say" had gathered together. (p-112) Since they were the furthest of people from these wishes which they desired for themselves, because they rejected what they had of knowledge, and because they envied the believers in them, for that is God's bounty which He gives to whom He wills, He said, pointing to their remoteness from that, in the form of a resumptive statement, interposed between the claim and the demand for proof for it, to hasten its refutation:

﴿Those﴾, with the particle of distance,

﴿are their wishes﴾, mockingly toward them. That is, such desires as these arise from their love that no good should descend upon the believers from their Lord, that they should turn them back into unbelievers, that no one but themselves should enter Paradise, and similar of their desires.

Since every claimant to the unseen needs, in establishing his claim, a proof, and since in such a matter one is not satisfied except by a decisive word from the most knowledgeable of creation, because nothing else can silence them in their knowledge and their obstinacy, by demanding that of them, refuting their claim, He said: ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾, using the word *burhan* (proof). Al-Harrali said: it is a knowledge of decisive indication, overpowering in strength, which the form *fu'lan* conveys by the vowelling of its first letter and the added letters at its end. (p-113) This is like how He opened that discussion with the refutation in His saying: ﴿Say: Have you taken (a covenant with God)?﴾ (2:80). In this there is an informing that He, exalted, never hid anything without placing upon it a sign, so that in the observable world there is a transparency revealing the unseen world, as al-Harrali said. They said: this is the most destructive thing to the doctrine of the blind followers (*muqallidun*), and evidence that every saying without a proof is false.

When he denounced them as liars in His saying, ﴿If you are truthful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111], He affirmed for others, by His saying ﴿Yes﴾, what they had claimed to be exclusive to themselves. Then He identified the people of Paradise by His saying ﴿Whoever submits his face﴾, meaning his whole self (kulliyyatahu), because the face is the noblest part of a person that is visible. So whoever submits his face has submitted all of himself. Likewise, "faith" (iman) is the submission of the heart, which is the noblest part of the inner person, and its submission is the submission of all the limbs. As for "Islam" (islam), al-Harrali said: it is the surrender of oneself through whatever is within or without. And "the face" (wajh) is the gathering place of the senses of the animal, the best of what is in the living, as distinct from the inanimate, and the place where temptation occurs in the one who tempts. For this reason it is the first thing that one tries to display of things. ﴿To God﴾ means for the sake of Him, since He is Allah, who gathers all perfection.

Since the mention of the reward for each individual is more explicit about the intended meaning and more effective in removing obstinate disputation (p-114), He used the singular pronoun and said ﴿while he is a doer of good﴾: on the side of the Truth, by the submission of the heart; and on the side of creation, by what pleases the Lord. Thus he worships God as if he sees Him, so his inner state conforms to his outward conduct. When they had denied the reward to others, and He, glorified is He, affirmed it for whoever among them and among others is characterized by Islam, and since it might be said that He gives to others merely because He is the absolute King without any cause, He connected the reward with the particle "fa" (so), as evidence that their submission is the cause. So He said ﴿then for him﴾, specifically, ﴿his reward is with his Lord﴾, as a favor to him by affirming the benefit of his act according to what his Lord has ordained in every law.

Since one might claim that He used the singular pronoun only because the intended person is one specific individual, and that this does not undermine the claim that none will enter Paradise except the Jews or the Christians, He used the plural and said ﴿and no fear shall be upon them﴾ of anything to come, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ over anything that has passed, to repel harm from them. This is like His, glorified is He, refutation of their claim concerning the touch of the Fire in His saying ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and is encompassed by his sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 81], and so the discourse is joined by this with the strongest joining and is arranged in the finest arrangement.

When he had invalidated their claim to exclusive possession of mercy, by disparaging others, and had established it for the good-doers, he followed this with each group's disparagement of the other, and with a statement that mercy is denied to them because of their evil conduct, by invalidating each faction's claim of the other. This is accompanied by what the Book of each indicates about the invalidity of its claim. So He said: ﴿And the Jews said, "The Christians are not on anything."﴾ He made their verb feminine (*qalat*) because their statement was weak and their affair was unified.

﴿Are not on anything﴾ means: nothing that is to be counted, because it is sound. *Laysat* is not the lightened form of the *fa'ila* pattern (*fariḥa*). Its meaning is absolute negation, in contrast to a preceding affirmation or its implied equivalent. This was stated by al-Harrali (*al-Ḥarrālī*).

﴿And the Christians said﴾ likewise ﴿"The Jews are not on anything."﴾ He marvelled at them for this general claim, both for what came before the alteration (*tabdil*) and abrogation (*naskh*) and for what came after it, by His saying: ﴿while they recite the Book﴾, meaning: while the Book of each of them contains the truth of the other's religious foundation.

Then He likened to them, in this kind of statement, the ignorant who have no Book, and who have among them misguidance. In this there is the utmost reproach for them, since their state is equated with theirs, even though they know the state of the ignorant in asserting falsehood as certain in religion. Just as He equated their state with theirs in their greed for life in this world, so among these ignorant are the idol-worshippers, among whom are the Arabs who expelled the Messenger (ﷺ) from his city and prevented him from the Sacred Mosque of his father Abraham, peace be upon them both, which he was more fitting to have than they. He presented this as the answer to a questioner, as if he had said: "This is the statement of the people of the Book; what, then, is the state of one who has no knowledge?" So He said: ﴿Even so﴾, meaning: like this statement, far from the intended aim,

﴿said those who do not know﴾. Since the utterance of this by people of knowledge is extremely strange, and its utterance by the ignorant is stranger still (p-117), He drew attention, may He be exalted, to the fact that the hearer is bound to say, given that He has counted it among what is hardly believable: "How could the ignorant say such a thing?" So He said, or it may be said: since their statement is hardly believable because of its extreme strangeness, it was as if it were said: "Was this truly from them in reality, or did He use it to refer to something else?" He answered with His saying: ﴿Even so﴾, meaning: the matter is as We have mentioned concerning them, in reality and not as a metaphor for something other than it. When this settled in the soul, it was as if it were said: "Has this happened to anyone other than them?" It was said: "Yes, something more astonishing than it has happened, namely that the ignorant said, like the idol-worshippers and the deniers of the divine attributes (*al-mu'aṭṭila*)," ﴿the like of their saying﴾. So they opposed and misguided the believers, the people of knowledge of the final Book, for which there is no equal, and they misguided the people of every religion.

When the disagreement among these factions occurred, a judgement resulted from it, by the King who did not create them in vain. So He said: ﴿So Allah﴾, the Supreme King,

﴿will judge between them﴾. Judgement is restricting the one who disposes of things to some of what he disposes of and to some of what he is inclined toward; this was stated by al-Harrali. He confirmed the matter of resurrection with His saying: ﴿on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ.﴾ *Ikhtilaf* (difference) is an *iftiʿāl* form from *khilāf* (opposition), and it is a confrontation between two opinions (p-118) regarding what ought to be held as a single opinion in it; this was stated by al-Harrali.

[p. 119] When all these sects shared in wrongdoing, and the ignorant ones added to it, they prevented the party of Allah from maintaining the Sacred Mosque with what pleases Him, in word and deed. By this they increased their wrongdoing further. Whoever prevents one mosque, because it is a mosque that bars all mosques, is described as follows: ﴿And who is more unjust﴾, that is, than them. He substituted the pronoun with ﴿those who prevent the mosques of Allah﴾, that is, the one who combines the attributes of perfection, which are the gardens of this world because they are the causes of the Garden, which they restricted to themselves. Then he substituted for this, as a magnification of it, a second reminder, ﴿from having His name mentioned therein﴾. He joined with ﴿and strive for their destruction﴾, that is, by leaving them void of the remembrance of Allah, because the forms of their wrongdoing are many, as an added rebuke to them. Prevention (al-man') is restraining from what one is inclined toward. The mosque (al-masjid) is a place-noun for the place of prostration, and it is the lowest spot where a standing person rests. Striving (al-sa'y) is hastening in a matter, physically or figuratively. Destruction (al-kharab) is the departure of maintenance. Maintenance (al-'imarah) is reviving a place and occupying it with what it was made for. Thus said al-Harrali.

Then He mentioned, glorified is He, what He ordered as a consequence of their action: fear within the mosque in which they frightened His friends and all its kind, and disgrace in this world and the Hereafter, the opposite of what He arranged for those who do good. He said: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the distant and the hateful,

﴿it was not for them﴾, that is, it was not right and not fitting,

﴿to enter them﴾, that is, the mosques described,

﴿except in fear.﴾ Their safety therein was only because of the abundance of helpers for what they committed of wrongdoing and of collusion in falsehood. We will remove that. Then He generalized the ruling to include what this fear encompasses, saying: ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾, that is, a great one, by this and by other things. He increased it by joining to it His saying: ﴿and for them in the Hereafter﴾, the Hereafter which they deny by belief or by deeds,

﴿is a great punishment.﴾ So by describing the punishment, He indicated the description of the disgrace that He pointed to with the tanwin.

Al-Harrali said: In this there is an announcement of the nullifying of whatever might turn away from them some aspect of punishment, so there befell them of the great punishment what befell the disbelievers, until what they had of a religion and a scripture became as if it did not exist, and that is the worst loss. He said: Among what is promised is that among the signs of the coming of the Hour is the neglect of mosques. For this reason, every community, every group, and every specific person who commits a crime in a mosque, whose act becomes a cause of its emptiness, Allah, mighty and majestic, punishes him with terror and fear that reach him in this world, until by this there is included whoever ruins a city among the cities of Islam, or whose deeds were the cause of its ruin. Within this is what occurred from the events of those who dominated the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis) through what the deeds of the Jews there led to. He said: Thus Allah has established His way that whoever does not uphold the sanctity of His mosques, He drives him away from them and compels him to enter them under the yoke and protection of his enemies, as the witnessing of the insight of people of discernment has testified, especially in the Holy Land, where the states of dominance have alternated between this community and the People of the Book.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ [al-Rum: 1] ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum: 2] ﴿in the nearest land. But they, after their defeat, will overcome﴾ [al-Rum: 3] ﴿within a few years﴾ [al-Rum: 4]. So every group, within its few years, if its deed is bad in its mosque, is driven out of it, and enters the other one's few years in fear, and so on, until the final outcome is for the righteous, when the believers rejoice in the victory of Allah. He said: In its indication is a warning against closing mosques, shutting them, and barring from them those who seek to devote themselves to worship (tahannuth) in them and to seclusion with the remembrance of Allah. The raising of mosques is not prohibiting them; rather, their raising is that nothing other than the name of Allah is mentioned in them. He, exalted, said: ﴿In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised﴾ [al-Nur: 36]. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he built the courtyard (al-rahbah, an open space adjoining the mosque), said: Whoever wants to make noise, or to talk, or to recite poetry, let him go out to this courtyard. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Keep your mosques free of your children, your insane, the drawing of your swords, your selling and your buying, and build their doorways as places of purification." So in the permissibility of this there is an announcement that whoever acts in the mosques of Allah in a way other than what they were made for, namely the remembrance of Allah, is one who strives for their destruction, and fear will reach him in a place of safety. End.

[p-122] When the verse implied that God's friends were prevented from maintaining the House of God through remembrance of Him, and God had graciously bestowed upon this community that the whole earth be made a place of prostration for them, He consoled the believers: wherever they pray with the intention of worshipping Him, His reward reaches them, because He is not confined to one direction rather than another, since His dominion over all things is equal. It was as if it were said: "Establish the prayer, which is the greatest remembrance of God, wherever you are, for it belongs to God, just as the mosque that you prevented belongs to God." He followed this with His words: ﴿And to God belongs﴾, that is, He to whom belongs all perfection,

﴿the East﴾, that is, the place of sunrise, which is the rising point of lights,

﴿and the West﴾, which is the place of their setting. Thus He indicated, as al-Harrali (al-Ḥarālī, the Qur'an commentator) said, by attributing the comprehensive horizons to Himself, that the orientation is toward His Face and not toward a direction, inasmuch as the directions belong to Him. End of quotation.

Since these two horizons are the axes around which the heavenly bodies, the sun and others, revolve, He expressed by them all the directions, because the spheres turn, during their rotation, toward each of them. Therefore there follows from the mention of them His words: ﴿So wherever you turn﴾, that is, wherever you direct yourselves in prayer toward the qibla (the direction of prayer) to which you were commanded to turn, whether Jerusalem, the Ka'ba, or other than these in the voluntary prayer (nafila, supererogatory prayer),

﴿there is﴾, that is, that place, because "thamma" (there) indicates a place,

﴿the Face of God﴾, that is, His direction toward which He has directed you, or the place of facing Him and turning toward Him, and what confronts you of His majesty and beauty and what turns toward you of His kindness and bounty. For the relation of all places and directions, in terms of origination, nearness, distance and other things, to Him is one and the same. Al-Harrali said: He left the verb unspecified so that the turning of the heart toward the Face of God would take place when the face of the one who turns, outwardly, faces the direction attributed to God. End of quotation.

[p-124] When He had informed of the vastness of His bounty, spread throughout the breadth of His dominion, in a manner where minds fall short of the limit of His knowledge, He gave the reason by which that became small in comparison to Him, saying: ﴿Indeed God﴾, naming Him by the Greatest Name, which comprises all the names,

﴿is All-Encompassing﴾, that is, He encompasses what imaginations cannot grasp, so nothing occurs except within His dominion. The root of "wus'" (vastness) is the extension of boundaries and limits.

﴿All-Knowing﴾, so the act of any doer is not hidden from Him, wherever and however it occurs. He gives the one who turns to Him according to the measure of his intention, in accordance with the reach of His encompassing and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and power.

Al-Harrali said in his explanation of the Names: "Vastness" is an increase beyond sufficiency, from such things, extending to what lies beyond, in expansion, mercy and knowledge,

﴿My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], ﴿For those who do good is the best reward and more﴾ [Yunus: 26], ﴿They will have therein whatever they wish, and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf: 35]. Vastness occurs only with the encompassing of knowledge and power, perfect forbearance, and the outpouring of good and blessing in accordance with the requirement of perfect mercy. And because the flow of blessing is in the aspects of sufficiency, outwardly and inwardly, specifically and generally, creatures scarcely attain a share of vastness. As for the outward, it does not occur from them, or hardly so: "You will not be able to embrace people with your kindness." As for the inward, through the specific excellence of good character, it may nearly occur. [p-125] He said in his commentary: God, exalted is He, mentioned "the East" first, because it is the place where the lights appear, by which the sight of eyes is possible; and He followed it with "the West," which is the setting of the outward lights [and it is the rising of the inward lights], so that the equivalence returns to this: the rising of the outward lights is the setting of the inward lights. "Strife is here, from where the horn of Satan rises," and he pointed with his hand toward the East. "The people of the West will continue to prevail upon the truth." End of quotation.

I say: Among this is the hadith of Safwan ibn 'Assal, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, for God there is a door in the West," and in another narration: "The door of repentance is open from the direction of the West—the breadth of it is seventy years' journey—it will not be closed until the sun rises from its direction." Narrated by al-Tabarani and al-Baghawi in his Tafsir.

It has become clear that the West in the earlier hadith is, in the sound report, everything other than the East to which he pointed as the place of strife in the other hadith. So the West in that case is Medina and what is attributed to it from the direction of the East, and what lies beyond it from the direction of the South and North, and what lies beyond that from the direction of the West, to the extremity of the earth. Thus the hadith "and they are in Syria" does not contradict it, for Syria is part of the West according to this reckoning. Here, then, is a matter over which minds have long circled and thoughts have been perplexed in gatherings and lessons. And God is the Granter of success.

(p-126) When the preceding passage had established His exalted attributes of complete power, vast dominion, bounty, and all-encompassing knowledge, it became impossible for Him to need a child or anything else. He then mentioned all the followers of false religions together with their fabrications concerning offspring: the Jews regarding ʿUzayr, the Christians regarding the Messiah, and the idol-worshippers regarding the angels. He said, expressing wonder at those who dared to attribute this to Him while knowing what has been mentioned before, linking it to their earlier claims: ﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a child."﴾ He, to whom all perfection belongs, is named, and He expressed it with the word ﴿child﴾ (waladan), which applies to both male and female, so as to include the statements of all of them. Since the linking (ʿaṭf) to the statements of the People of the Book might suggest that the censure was specific to them, the conjunction waw was omitted in the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir, in the manner of a resumed statement (istiʾnaf), as an answer to someone who might be understood to have asked: "Has the rope of their fabrication been cut?" This points to the censure of everyone who says this, and it indicates the intensity of its connection with what precedes it, as Imam Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said in his book al-Hujja, because all those who band together against the people of Islam prevent them from enlivening the mosques with remembrance, their preoccupation with enmity keeping them from adhering to it. The summary is that if the conjunction is used, the speech is directed chiefly at the People of the Book, while others follow them by virtue of equality in the statement (p-127). When the waw is omitted, the speech is directed at all of them with a single direction.

He declared His noble self free of imperfection in a resumed statement with ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ (subḥānahu). He mentioned the knowledge of tasbih (glorification), which comprises the full meaning in the all-inclusive words of transcendence. Then he used the word of reversal (idrab, bal), which conveys a rejection by negation, as though the address conveyed: Allah has not taken a child, nor does He have a child.

﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever﴾ — He used the particle that is used for non-rational things (ma), which is suitable for Him, as a generalization and a belittling of them.

﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾ — of what each sect among them claimed to be His offspring and other than that.

Then He gave the reason for it, expressing with what conveys the utmost submission: ﴿All are obedient to Him﴾ (kullun lahu qanitun), i.e., sincerely devoted, humble, submissive, because of their surrender to His decree without any capacity to repel it, nor any aspiration to a kind of refusal, other than Him, so that it is as though they strive toward that and hasten to it with the eagerness of the intelligent and resolute (p-128). Al-Harralli said: He brought the plural, which indicates, as is said, rationality and knowledge, because, as previously mentioned, there is no dumbness or inanimateness between the created and the Creator; rather, inanimateness and dumbness occur only among individuals who fall short in attaining the complete perception of the created. And qunut is the steadfastness of one who stands by a matter in maintaining it, being firmly established in it. End of quote.

Then he gave a reason for that, one greater than it, saying: ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: their Creator without any preceding pattern. He originated the totality of an affair, and that which is contained within it, encompassed by it, and sustained by it, from among the things sustained by it, from its Originator. So how could a likeness of Him be ascribed to Him? For the child is something extracted, a likeness of that from which it was extracted. This was mentioned by al-Harrali.

﴿And when He decrees﴾, meaning: wills, ﴿an affair﴾ from among these two or from other than them. Al-qada' (decree) is the carrying out of what has been determined, and al-muqaddar (the determined) is what is limited from the absolute known. This was stated by al-Harrali.

﴿He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. From al-kawn (being), which is the perfection of what emerges in its outward and inward aspects. ﴿and it is﴾, so He is exalted above the need for procreation and every need. The secret of expressing it in the imperfect (mudari') will be mentioned, God willing, in Al 'Imran. Al-Harrali said: its form indicates the continuation of what exists through stages, times, and ages, whose succession extends within what is brought into being until it reaches the end of perfection. End of quotation. They said: the raf' (nominative) of ﴿yakunu﴾ (it is) is for resumption (isti'naf), meaning: "so it is," or it is for conjunction with ﴿yaqulu﴾ (He says), as an indication of the swiftness of coming into being by way of illustration. Whoever holds the first view prohibits conjunction with ﴿yaqulu﴾, because the fa' (so) requires that the saying is together with the bringing into being, and so the bringing into being would be eternal. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said in his book al-Hujja: this does not apply in a case like the second of the two verses of Al 'Imran, which is His saying: ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [3:59], because it is not good for two conjoined verbs to differ in tense or type. The beginning of his statement is the verse:

"And indeed I pass by the base man who abuses me... so I pass on, then I say, 'It does not concern me.'"

meaning: I passed by, having passed on. Abu Shama criticized this, saying that in the verse there is a past tense like it. Abu 'Ali explicitly stated, and the truth is with him, that it is on its own basis, meaning the present tense. The benefit of expressing it in the imperfect (p-130) is depicting the situation and guiding to the understanding that the estimate is: "Be, and it was," because whenever He decrees a thing, He says to it, "Be," and it is. He regarded the best reading as its conjunction with ﴿kun﴾ (Be), because although it is in the form of a command, its meaning is informative, i.e., "it is." He said: this is more consistent, since it fits with a verse like His saying: ﴿Then He said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [3:59]. This place is agreed upon for its raf'. Likewise His saying in al-An'am: ﴿The day He says, "Be," and it is﴾ [6:73]. The disagreement concerns only six places, of which Ibn 'Amir has the exclusive reading in four: this place; His saying in Al 'Imran: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [3:47]; the same in Maryam; and in Ghafir: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [40:68]. Al-Kisa'i agreed with him on two places in al-Nahl: ﴿Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [16:40], and in Ya-Sin: ﴿His command when He intends a thing is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [36:82]. They made the nasb (accusative) in these two a conjunction with ﴿yaqulu﴾ (He says), and in the first four, a response to the imperative in His saying ﴿kun﴾ (Be), taking into account the form of the wording even though the meaning is not imperative. So the estimate is: He says to it, "It shall be," and it is, i.e., it obeys. Thus the opinion of one who weakened it is refuted, that the meaning is informative and that nasb is valid only when the command and its response differ. This is not so; rather it would require that the thing be a condition for itself, because the estimate would be: "If it be, it will be." Ibn Mujahid explicitly stated the error of Ibn 'Amir and that this is impermissible in Arabic, as Abu Shama related from him in his commentary on the al-Shatibiyya. So I examined this carefully, because the correctness of Ibn 'Amir's reading is certain, its transmission being mass-transmitted from the one to whom the Qur'an was revealed. When I saw that he made nasb only for what lies within the scope of ﴿idha﴾ (when), I knew that this was on its account, because it contains the meaning of the conditional. This is like His saying in al-Shura: ﴿and that those who dispute concerning Our verses may know﴾ [42:35], with the nasb of ﴿yaʿlama﴾ (may know) in the reading other than Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, according to some interpretations. This proceeds along the path of soundness without difficulty or improbability, when the sentence with ﴿idha﴾ is considered. Al-Radi, who is the scholar Najm al-Din Muhammad ibn Hasan al-Astarabadhi, said in the section on adverbs of his commentary on the statement of the scholar Abu 'Amr 'Uthman ibn al-Hajib in his Kafiya: "Among them is ﴿idha﴾, which is for the future and contains the meaning of the condition, so the verb is chosen after it. The basic use of ﴿idha﴾ is for a time of the future distinguished from others by the occurrence of an event in it that is certain." Then he said: "The word of condition is what requires two sentences, such that from the existence of the content of the first, supposed, the occurrence of the content of the second necessarily follows. The first content is supposed and necessitating, and the second is its necessary consequence." Then he said: "And ﴿in﴾ (if) is set for a supposed condition whose existence is in the future, with the speaker not being certain either of its occurrence or non-occurrence. That is because the consequent is not certain, neither by existence nor non-existence, whether he doubts its occurrence, as in our case, or does not doubt it, as in the case of the event in the speech of God." He said: "The condition is not in a noun except by including its meaning." Then he said: "So we say: since ﴿idha﴾ is for a matter certain to exist in the speaker's belief in the future, it cannot be for a supposed existence, because certainty and supposition are contradictory apparently. So it does not carry the meaning of the conditional ﴿in﴾, because, as we have shown, the condition is what is supposed to exist. But since the situation is often revealed to us regarding matters we expect while being certain of their occurrence, contrary to what we expect, they permitted including the meaning of ﴿in﴾ in ﴿idha﴾, as in ﴿mata﴾ (whenever) and the rest of the conditional particles. So the speaker says: 'Idha you come to me, you are honored,' while doubtful of the addressee's coming, not favoring its existence over non-existence, with the meaning of 'mata you come to me,' equally." Then he said: "Since the meaning of the condition frequently entered ﴿idha﴾ and departed from its original basis of a specific time, its use is permitted even if it does not carry the meaning of the conditional ﴿in﴾. This occurs in certain matters, the use of ﴿idha﴾ containing the meaning of ﴿in﴾, because two sentences come after it in the pattern of condition and consequence, even if they are not condition and consequence." Then he spoke on the particle fa' in the verb-governing particles, saying: "The particle ﴿an﴾ (that) may be elided after the fa' and the waw occurring after the condition and before the consequence, as in: 'in ta'tini fa-tukrimani' (if you come to me and honor me), or 'law tukrimuni' (if you honored me), 'ata'ka' (I would come to you); or after the condition and consequence, as in: 'in ta'tini ata'ka fa-ukrimaka' (if you come to me I will come to you and honor you), or: 'wa-akramaka' (and I will honor you). This is because of the resemblance of the condition in the first and the negated consequence in the second, since the consequence is conditioned in its existence on the existence of the condition, and the existence of the condition is supposed, so both are not described as existing in reality." On this basis is interpreted His saying: ﴿If He wills, He stills the wind so they remain motionless﴾ [42:33] up to His saying: ﴿and that those who dispute concerning Our verses may know﴾ [42:35], according to the reading with nasb. Then he said: "They changed what follows the fa' of causation from raf' to nasb only because they intended to make explicit that it is causal. The imperfect in the raf' form, without a clear indicator separating it for the present or future, appears to mean the present, as previously stated in the chapter on the imperfect. If they had kept it nominative, it would come to the mind that the fa' is conjoining a clause of present action to the clause before the fa', meaning that the coming into being would have to be eternal like the speech. So changing it to nasb indicates apparently that it is not conjoined, since the imperfect governed by an is a single word, while before the mentioned fa' is a clause. The imperfect is freed for the future suited to the conditional, as we mentioned concerning the verb after idhan, so there were two things: removal of the aspect of the fa' being conjunctive, and strengthening its being consequential. So what follows the fa' is then a subject with an elided predicate necessarily." End of quotation.

So the estimate here, and God knows best, is: His bringing into being is a true reality, not an illusion like magic and deceptions. On this basis the nasb reading is more eloquent, since it clearly turns the meaning from the present to the future, along with (p-134) what it indicates of the swiftness of coming into being and that it is true. Then I saw that al-Burhan ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Safaqusi related in his i'rab what I drew from Ibn al-Da'i' (meaning with a dotted dad and an undotted ayn), who is the teacher Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Kutami, the teacher of Abu Hayyan. He said the following text: "Ibn al-Da'i' added a good aspect to the nasb of ﴿fa-yakunu﴾ (and so it is), which is its nasb as the response of the condition, which is idha. His intention was causation of the response, as I mentioned." Al-Safaqusi said: a third aspect is also valid according to the school of the Kufans, namely its nasb as the response to the restriction with innama (only), because they permitted: "innama hiya darbatu asadin fa-yatahattama zahruhu" (it is only a lion's strike, so that its back is broken).

When it had been established, through what He related of the wondrous signs in His scattered creations, that His greatness falls short of what imagination can grasp, and that the windows of understanding recoil dazed before it, He marvelled at their audacity toward Him. The state of the ignorant Arabs regarding the scholars of the People of the Book is the same as this, so He rebuked them and warned against them. There is no motive for them to be content with descending from the summit of knowledge to the depths of the ignorant except the pursuit of desire. So He said: ﴿And those who have no knowledge said﴾, i.e., they have no knowledge, from among the Arabs, ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us﴾, i.e., why does His speech not reach us with all of its attributes (p. 135) ﴿or a sign come to us﴾, i.e., in accordance with our demand, disregarding what He has given them of signs, including the sign of the Qur'an, to which no sign is comparable at all.

Since their saying was deserving of not being believed, He drew attention to it with His words: ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., the matter is as We have mentioned concerning them. Since it was as if it were said, "Has the like of this ever occurred?", it was said, "Yes, something even more wondrous occurred," namely that ﴿those before them said﴾. Since the intended were some of those who preceded, He introduced the preposition, so He said ﴿from before them﴾, from among those ascribed to knowledge from the People of the Book, ﴿a saying like their saying﴾. Then He gave the reason with His words: ﴿Their hearts have become alike﴾ in this, although they differ with respect to knowledge. In this is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ): just as he was subjected to obstinate demands, so were those who came before him. Since that was so, the listener anticipated information about the clarification, so it was as if it were said, "Did they say that out of ignorance or out of obstinacy?" It was said, "Rather, out of obstinacy, for ﴿We have made the signs clear﴾ in every sign in the Clear Book that is heard and in the Wise Book that is seen. Since clarification occurs specifically for people of certainty, He said ﴿for a people who are certain﴾. In this is an incitement (p. 136) for the doubter to pursue the means of certainty, which is the purity of knowledge from turbidity through the paths of doubt, by the combination of the two witnesses, hearing and sight."

Al-Harrali (al-Ḥarrālī) said: In this is an indication of the certainty the Arabs attained, as the chief of the Arabs, ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Had the veil been lifted, I would not have increased in certainty." It seeks to bring forth what is hidden of the world of malakut (the unseen dominion of the divine realm) over the apparent world of mulk (the visible dominion), completing understanding of this clear explanation which Allah undertook and whom He chose, which is comprised in the sequence of the pronoun in *bayyinan* (بَيِّنًا). And in the equality of the scholar and others in ignorance after the clarification is evidence for the content of the preceding [verse], that what He willed came to be.

When this context included the testimony to the truth of his prophethood ﷺ, and that his only duty was clear communication, [al-Biqa'i] stated both matters explicitly in His words, emphasizing them because of the large number of deniers: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾. This is on the reading that the intended referent is all nations. (p. 137) If only this nation is intended, the meaning is: We have made clear the signs that point to the path of truth, with the greatest proof and with reports of subtle matters that only the most learned of the People of the Book know, for a people for whom certainty is due because of the evidence that has become clear to them. Then He gave the reason for this in His words: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾ sent in a manner bound up with ﴿the truth﴾, that is, with the complete matter to which reality corresponds in every detail that he reports.
