Al-Harrali (al-Harrali) said: The complete truth, perfected by the definite article "al-" (ﺍﻝ, *alif-lam*), is the drawing forth of creation concerning God's command regarding them, in a manner elevated to His exalted message, specific to Him, beyond the generality of what the messages of the messengers came with apart from this specificity. That is a "truth" (ḥaqq) that is unknown, as was mentioned earlier, at His words: ﴿And it is the truth, confirming what is with them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]. For whatever reveals a hidden matter of what God has sent down is a "truth" (ḥaqq), even magic. And whatever manifests the hidden matter of decree and destiny, and makes known through displaying God's wisdom what He displayed of the execution of His will against what He displayed from His creation, is the "truth" by which the heavens and the earth were created at the beginning, and with which the message was concluded at the end, so that the first and the last correspond in perfection, while you are ﴿a bringer of good news and a warner﴾.

Al-Harrali also said: When God, glory be to Him, carried the address concerning the People of the Book and the Arabs, He announced their rejection of what He had sent down first and last, and announced what they had fabricated that has no doubt about it, [then] He turned the address away from all of them and directed it to the Prophet ﷺ, as consolation for him and as confirmation of what He had informed him of at the beginning of the sura: that the affair proceeds according to His decree and His division of creation among believer, disbeliever, and hypocrite. (p. 138) So God, exalted, informed him that the content of his message is not that he should call creation to what they were not created upon, and that the content of his message is to bring forth the hidden contents of hearts and minds through tongues and deeds, so that he gives good news to the one who is guided and steadfast upon a prior guidance, and warns the stubborn one and the one who denies what he had previously acknowledged. Thereby He included the first and the last of bringers of good news and warners. End of quotation. That is: there is nothing upon you but this, so give good news and warn, for upon you is only conveyance, and it is not upon you to create guidance in the hearts of the people of bliss. ﴿And you will not be asked﴾ may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) either from "We have sent you" or from ﴿a bringer of good news﴾ ﴿about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾. By them is meant those mentioned in the previous verse among the ignorant and those before them. That is: [you will not be asked] about their deeds, so that your soul does not go to waste over them in regret for their not believing, as He, exalted, said: ﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:134]. That is, your state is equal in relation to Us and to them, because if you convey to them all that you were sent with, We will not hold you accountable for their deeds; and if you leave out some of that to be gentle with them, they will not love you as long as you are upon your religion. So turn toward your affair and do not concern yourself with them. This is the meaning of the reading of Nafi' (Nāfiʿ), ﴿and you will not be asked﴾ as a prohibition, that is, (p. 139) regard them with contempt, for they are too few to be given attention. So convey to them the whole matter, for they will not love you unless you slip away from what you are upon. In the ruling that they are its companions is an affirmation of what they denied for themselves in His words: ﴿The Fire will not touch us﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:80], and a negation of what they singled themselves out for in their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:111], and so on. As for al-jaḥm (الجحم), al-Harrali said: it is the gathering together of a thing and its magnitude in it. Among the meanings of its letters is al-ḥajm (الحجم), which is compression and the appearance of quantity, except that ḥajm is in what manifests as bodies, while al-jaḥm, with the jīm placed first, is in what is subtle, like sound and fire.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 120:

Since it is the custom that the one given glad tidings is pleased by the bearer of them, God, exalted is He, informed that the People of the Book belong to the category of those who are warned, for they continually remain angry toward him. So He said, linking it to what the preceding verse required: ﴿And never will be pleased﴾, from al-ridā (contentment), which is the affirmation of what appears from will; this is what al-Harrali said. (p-140)

﴿with you, the Jews, nor the Christians﴾ for anything at all ﴿until you follow their religion﴾, meaning: until you become a bringer of glad tidings to them. You will never be a bringer of glad tidings to them until you agree with them in what they have introduced of their desires, by following their scripture in what they altered, distorted and concealed. This is what the attribution of the religion (millah) to them indicates, not to its owner, the infallible one, who is Ibrahim, peace be upon him. This would happen with your complete desire, as the form of al-iftiʿāl (reflexive/ infixed form) indicates, and you would abandon your own book, which abrogates the branches of their book. And millah, al-Harrali said: it is taking hold of and acting upon what is in the intellect, its guidance from informing the sensible things. (Ḥ)

When this was said, the situation required a question, which is: "So what shall I say?" Thus He said: ﴿Say﴾, and He did not restrict it with "to them", turning away from them. ﴿Indeed, the guidance of God﴾, which is all (p-141) of what He sent down, comprising the attributes of perfection, upon His messengers, from my book and your book, ﴿it is﴾, that is, the exclusive ﴿guidance﴾, meaning all of it, indicating by the definite article the perfection of its meaning, and by the restriction (ḥaṣr) that other than it is desire (hawā). He attributed it to the Greatest Name, emphasized it with inna, repeated it by its own wording, expressed it by the verbal noun, and used the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) in response to their denial of it. So if they follow it entirely, believing that their book calls to your book, then give them glad tidings. If they do not follow it, then keep to warning them. In the verse there is an allusion to that Book: "there is no doubt in it."

Then He linked to what the context implied, such as: "If you swerve from it, you will certainly abandon all of the guidance by following desire," His saying: ﴿And if you follow their desires﴾, which call them to change their book. Al-Harrali said: He thus clearly manifested what the attribution of the religion to them had implied, since it was a fabrication from desire, not a guidance of the light of intellect as it is in the case of the ḥanīfs (those who adhere to pure monotheism). End. Since the discussion here concerns the matter of the religion which is manifest to the intellect, He dropped man (مَن) and used alladhī, unlike what comes in the matter of the qibla, so He said: (p-142) ﴿after what﴾. Al-Harrali said: the word "alladhī" points to a meaning close to the apparent and sensible, as if it were a clear sign, so there is an indication that the least knowledge that came to you is a manifest proof of the invalidity of what they are upon, in their ways of deception and their desires. ﴿has come to you of knowledge﴾ that they are upon misguidance and that you are upon all of the guidance. He addressed them with this, (ﷺ), and what is meant, and God knows best, is whoever among the hypocrites followed their desires after Islam, adhering to their allegiance, hoping for their support. Therefore He concluded with His saying: ﴿you will have from God﴾, to whom belongs all the command and to whom there is no equal, no ally ﴿nor any helper﴾, and He emphasized the negation with the prepositional phrase, so He said: ﴿from any protector or helper﴾.

When he had made clear who among them deserved warning (*indhar*) for altering the religion according to their desires, he made clear who deserved good news (*bishara*). He then explicitly stated both categories: those among them who deserve good news and those who deserve warning. So He said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾, that is, the Torah and the Gospel, ﴿recite it with its due recitation﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "They follow it with its due following." This is from *tala fulān fulānan*, when someone follows another. Abū ʿUbayd narrated it from him.

This verse looks back to His earlier words: ﴿while they recite the Book﴾ [al-Baqara: 113]. That is, they do not recite it with its due recitation, but rather a recitation without reflection on its meanings or acting upon what is in it. This is if we take it as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). If we take it as a predicate (*khabar*), with His words ﴿those﴾, that is, the highly ranked specifically, ﴿believe in it﴾ as a second predicate, then the meaning is that whoever does not believe in the Book with its true belief, without distorting it or concealing anything in it, has lost the primary purpose of the Book given to them, which is benefiting from it. Thus the very act of being given it is negated from them, because it is stripped of benefit. The pronoun in *bihi* ("in it") may refer to guidance (*al-huda*).

Al-Harrālī said: The truthfulness (*ḥaqqiyya*) of a matter is its fulfilment to its end and encompassing its whole limits, so that nothing falls from it and no part of it is neglected. This points to the Book including the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

When He described the believers in it without stating their reward, He followed it with the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it﴾, that is, in the Book. Then He confined the loss to them with His words: ﴿those﴾, that is, the distant and hateful, ﴿they are﴾ specifically ﴿the losers﴾. Thus He made clear that those who believe in it are the winners. From the description of loss it is known that they were upon the truth, and upon something in which gain is possible by completing their faith in their own Book through faith in the final Book; but they wasted it, and so they lost. For one cannot lose except one who has a principal of capital ready to grow and yield profit.

And Allah knows best.

When the span grew long in thoroughly reminding them of the blessings, and then in clarifying their defects and tearing away their veils, and concluded that with a warning of their loss for having squandered their religions through their deeds, states and words, he repeated what he had opened the account of their story with: a reminder of the blessings and a warning against the descent of punishment on the Day when the nations are gathered and regret endures for whoever's foot has slipped. This was so it would be known that this is the *fadhlakah* (a summing-up or concluding recapitulation) of the story, and that the principal aim is urging the seizing of the opportunity to escape the forbidden state of deficiency toward the pleasure of profit through continuing gratitude. Al-Harrali said: "Because of its distance by earlier placement, He, exalted is He, repeated it, to show the aim of the closing of the discourse fitting together with its beginning, and so that this clarification and instruction be taken as a basis for what may come similar to it in the rest of the Qur'an, such that when discourse reaches the ultimate end of a conclusion, the heart must note the beginning of that end and follow it, so that in its recitation it gathers both ends of the structure, and in its understanding it gathers the meanings of both ends of the meaning." End of quote.

Then He said: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾. That is: O sons of the chosen prophets and parents of the prosperous prophets. ﴿Remember My favour﴾, that is, the noble one in relation to Me, ﴿which I bestowed upon you﴾ in this world. Here he limited himself to the blessing of preference and did not mention fidelity, which is the excellence of the inner self, indicating their dullness through their restricting themselves to looking at the outward. ﴿Over the worlds﴾ in all those times, through completing the blessing of this world by the legislation of religion, which entails the blessing of the hereafter. For when you remember the blessing and give thanks for it, you bind it fast, and you merit from God increase in this world and good pleasure in the next.

[p. 145]

[p. 146]

And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all. That is, [the Day] on which nothing of the recompense will be dealt with for anyone. [The verse says] "no soul will avail another soul at all," meaning [nothing] of the requital.

When the preceding verse ended by confining the loss to them, it was fitting to put first the negation of acceptance, so He said: ﴿And no ransom will be accepted from it﴾, which would be paid to redeem it apart from righteous deeds; ﴿nor will intercession benefit it﴾, [intercession] not permitted for it; ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, even if their hosts are numerous. Al-Harrali (al-Harrālī) said: God, in this repetition, let it run according to its first form, except that He varied the two presentations in His saying ﴿And fear a Day﴾ to its end, so that the report, in each of intercession and ransom, combines the totality of the two rejections, namely taking and accepting. Thus their intercession is neither accepted nor beneficial, and their ransom is neither taken nor accepted. This is because what is offered for acceptance is first taken, in accordance with its nature, by hearing or sight; then it is examined with verification in what is heard and with insight in what is seen. If verification and insight confirm it, it is accepted; if they do not confirm it, it is rejected. This happens only to one whose state has an apparent measure of soundness that does not hold up under scrutiny. God, by the content of the two verses, the opening and the closing, reported that these people have no measure of soundness whatsoever, neither in intercession nor in ransom. So it is not accepted nor taken. The report concerns one whose deceit is disguised by an appearance of soundness that would call for its being taken in some way. Therefore there is in this a clearing of those whose state is the state of what was reported about them, according to the meaning already stated in the content of the verse. For this purpose the address turned away from them to the specific matter of what they were given of the Book, which was obliging them to adhere to the acceptance of what came confirming what was with them. Yet they adopted for themselves, by their desires, a creed that their desires had fabricated. Thus God arranged by this the mention of the bearer of the creed He is pleased with, and opened with the beginning of his affair in his trial, so that the two prior proofs would converge upon them: the proof according to the upright Abrahamic creed (millah ḥanīfiyyah), and the proof that follows according to the Muhammadan religion (dīn). The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say in the morning: "We have risen upon the fitrah (innate nature) of Islam, the word of sincerity, the religion of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and the creed (millah) of our father Abraham (ﷺ)." Thus he specified the Muhammadan [community] for religion (dīn) and the Abrahamic [community] for creed (millah), so that the beginning of Abrahamic fatherhood is linked with the groups of the People of the Book, earlier and later, with the report of the beginning of the Adamic fatherhood in the earlier part of His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority (khalīfah)"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and so on, so that the heads of the addresses are linked with one another and their details with their details. And so that the manifestation of this (p-148) in the chapter that is the summit of the Qur'an may be a foundation for what is in the rest of it of this kind. He had mentioned before this that the creed (millah) is what the guidance of reason calls to, as conveyed from God, regarding His unity, from the essences of the upright monotheists (ḥanīfiyyūn); and that the religion (dīn) is Islam, and Islam is the surrender of what is in the hand, outwardly and inwardly, and that this occurs only from the beginning of the unseen of tawhid. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 124:

When He, glory be to Him, censured the people of misguidance, most of whom were descendants of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and all the sects of the religious communities venerate him, among them the Arabs, whose House which he built is their greatest pride and their most important distinction, He reminded them all of what He had bestowed upon him. This reminder leads to the establishment of this religion through the knowledge of this unlettered Prophet, who never associated with a scholar at any time, concerning matters known only to the elite of scholars. He mentioned the House which he built, and Allah made it the pillar of their righteousness, and He commanded that some of the place there be taken as a place of prayer (muṣallā), in glorification of his affair and magnification of his lofty status. In reminding them of his fulfilment after mentioning those who fulfilled the due right of recitation, and after calling the Children of Israel in general to fulfil the obligation of gratitude, there is an urging to follow his example. Likewise, in mentioning Islam and monotheism there is a stirring for everyone who venerates him to follow him in this.

Al-Harrali (Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali) said: When the Exalted Truth connected the general call of the first address, in His saying, ﴿O mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21], He mentioned the matter of Adam and the beginning of his vicegerency, so that thereby the gathering of all people would occur at two extremes: in their gathering under one father (p-149) and one religion. Thereby He arranged the connection of the address to the People of the Book with the mention of Ibrahim, so that their gathering would likewise occur under one father and one creed, specifically through being subject to the Abrahamic imamate, from the general subjection to the Adamic caliphate, as a revelation of the Book and an elevation of creation to the height of the special status of the Truth. Just as He, exalted, mentioned at the beginning a reminder coordinated with matters that the explicit statement passed over concerning the affair of Adam, He likewise coordinated the reminder with the beginning of the affair of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with matters that the explicit statement passed over, which are more specific than what the first passed over, just as their explicit statement is more specific than its own explicit statement and higher in rank, insofar as creation and command originate from a limit that has never ceased and does not cease to be perfected toward an end beyond which there is no goal. So He said, ﴿And when Ibrahim was tried﴾. The meaning is that He dealt with him by commanding him with difficult matters, in the manner of one who tests and examines. And He said: (p-150) ﴿by his Lord﴾, that is, the One who did good to him, indicating that the imposing of obligations upon the servants is the ultimate of good done to them. At the beginning of his story, with His saying ﴿with words, and he fulfilled them﴾, there is a clarification that the highest state of the servants is submission and surrender to the one whose truthfulness is established by evidence, hastening to his command without objection, hesitation, or seeking a cause. In this there is an indication of rebuking those who claim to follow him among the Children of Israel, for they objected concerning the slaughter of the cow and committed the utmost obstinacy, despite the many wisdoms in its slaughter, after they had offended manners toward their Prophet in that matter and in others, at the beginning, middle, and end of their affair, so that this brought them chastisement and distance. Thus it becomes clear that the straight path is the condition of Ibrahim and those mentioned with him of the prophets and messengers, upon them be blessings and peace, and that they are those upon whom favour was bestowed. The apparent reading is that ﴿when﴾ is coordinated with ﴿My favour﴾ in His saying ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 122], that is: and remember when He tried your father Ibrahim, and he fulfilled what he was tried with; so what is the matter with you, that you do not follow his example, and act at the time of trial as he acted in fulfilling the covenant and steadfastness in the promise, so that I may reward you for that as I reward the doers of good. Fulfilment (al-itmām) is the completion of what has a form that is composed of parts and units, as al-Harrali said.

So it is as if it were said: What was he rewarded for his gratitude through fulfilment, before? ﴿He said﴾ to him, his Lord: ﴿Indeed, I am making you an imam for the people﴾, that is, for all of them, ﴿an imam﴾, just as the caliphate of his father Adam was over his children, all of them. The imam is that which is followed as guidance toward rectitude, (p-151) as al-Harrali said. He resumed with His saying ﴿He said﴾, that is, Ibrahim: ﴿And of﴾, that is, make of ﴿my descendants﴾ imams. ﴿He said, "My covenant will not reach the wrongdoers"﴾, that is: I have indeed answered you and bound myself to you that I will do good to your descendants, but ﴿My covenant﴾, which I made with you concerning the imamate, will not reach ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ among them, because they have cut themselves off from you in the fatherhood of religion. In this there is the most complete encouragement to adopt his fulfilment, especially for those who were called before it to fulfil the covenant, and an indication that if they give thanks He will preserve their elevation just as He preserved his, and if they do wrong, his supplication will not reach them, so I will strike humiliation upon them and what accompanies it, and no one will avail them anything, nor will they be helped. The word dhurriyyah combines the meanings of scattering (dharr) and repelling (dar'). The form of dhurriyy varies in its derivation: it may be a fa'lūlah, as if it were dharrūrah, then lightened by changing the rāʾ into yāʾ to avoid the heaviness of doubling, then the letter before the two yāʾs was kasra to make both clear; because after the change a wāw and a yāʾ came together, one of them preceded by sukūn, so the wāw was changed into yāʾ. Or it may be a fi'liyyah derived from dharr with a nisba, and from dharr a lightened form of fa'ūlah, by changing the hamzah into yāʾ, then the wāw into yāʾ because it came together with it, one of them preceded by sukūn, then assimilation. Or it may be fa'īlah if it occurs in speech, because of the heaviness of combining ḍamma and kasra. This is what al-Harrali said, and in it there is some rearrangement.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 125:

When the imamate of Abraham entailed that people follow him in pilgrimage to the House which God honoured by his building it, He said immediately after that, reproaching the People of the Book for opposing him and abandoning his religion, and preparing for the matter of the qibla: ﴿And when We made the House﴾, that is, the one Abraham built, at Umm al-Qura, ﴿a place of return (mathaba) for the people﴾, that is, a place to which they return wholeheartedly. Whenever they disperse from it, they long for it, they or others, as a sign of their return from this world to their Lord. Al-Harrali said: it is a mafa'ala from the verb thawb, which is return, returning to it entirely, eagerly. In the form mafa'ala is the continuity of repeated return, persistently. ﴿And a sanctuary (amnan)﴾, because it is the House of the King, from the warfare of this world and from the punishment of the Hereafter, except for those among the disbelievers whom God excepted, in act through polytheism and in potential through atheism. Amn is the freedom of a thing from any defect of harm reaching it, as al-Harrali said. They used to see, in the Jahiliyya, a man who had killed his father within the Sacred Precinct, and he would not be touched. Al-Isbahani said: this is something they inherited from the time of Isma'il, peace be upon him, and it continued until the days of the Prophet ﷺ. Today, whoever commits a crime within the Sacred Precinct, the legal penalty is enforced upon him by consensus.

Since the presumption was: the people turned to Him, following its builder, and believed in his call concerning it, He joined to it His saying: ﴿And take﴾. And according to the reading in the imperative, the presumption becomes: So repent to Him, O people, following him, and take ﴿from the station of Abraham﴾, Our friend, ﴿a place of prayer (musalla)﴾. Musalla is a mufa''al for that in which prayer is constantly performed. The Station of Abraham is the stone on which he stood when he came to visit his son Isma'il, peace be upon them both, and did not find him. Isma'il's wife washed his head while he was leaning with his foot on it, while he was riding; she washed the right side of his head while he leaned on the stone with his right foot, then she turned the stone to the left side and washed his left side, so both his feet sank into it. For this reason there is a mark of his two feet, differing: the toes of this one are at the heel of that one. This was before he built the House, and God knows best what He intends.

﴿And We covenanted﴾, joined to His saying "We made", ﴿with Abraham﴾, the faithful, ﴿and Isma'il﴾, his son, the true of promise. In mentioning him is a clear indication of the answering of his supplication concerning it in His saying: ﴿and of my offspring﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], and an indication that among his offspring is one who will seal the nations with his nation, and that his facing his House in the most exalted of acts of worship of his law is the completion of that indication. He completed the indication with His saying: ﴿that you purify My House﴾, that is, from every filth, sensory and immaterial, so that nothing unbecoming in the Law is done in its presence. The house (bayt) is the specific place of lodging, from the specific dwelling, from the specific home, from the specific town, as al-Harrali said.

﴿For those who circle (al-ta'ifin)﴾ around it, whose action is the action of one who knows that there is nothing beyond God, no target and no refuge from Him except to Him, ﴿and those who cling (al-'akifin)﴾ within it. Al-'Ukuf is attentiveness to a thing, persistence in it, and restricting oneself to it. Al-tawaf is encircling a thing in unseen matters or for the sake of an unseen meaning, as al-Harrali said.

﴿And those who bow and prostrate﴾. Al-Harrali said: In mentioning bowing (al-ruku') is a specification of the Arabs, for whom bowing was prescribed in their religion. In this is a rebuke to whoever expelled the believers and prevented them from the House. And in repeating the detail of these verses with "when" (idh) is an alert to their reproach for abandoning His religion, which is the Friend's, and for following one who does not know, who is the enemy.

When he had mentioned the matter of the Noble House, both what He, glory be to Him, undertook for it and what He commanded the Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham) and his son, peace be upon them both, concerning its purification, he mentioned Abraham's concern for its people and his supplication for them. This rebuked those of his descendants who disobeyed him by openly disbelieving in the Day of Recompense, the One who commands every good and restrains from every harm. So He said: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord"﴾, dropping the particle of distance (أداة البعد), to indicate His nearness, as is the condition of the elite. ﴿Make this﴾, i.e., this place in which You placed Your House and commanded me to settle some of my descendants.

Since the context concerns prohibiting access to the Masjid and striving to ruin it, and since this includes, by its generality, those who dwell in the desert, he established that it is a place of return (mathabah) for people in general and a place of security. Therefore the more suitable form was to leave the word "city" indefinite, so He said: ﴿a city﴾, a place where whoever settles feels at ease, ﴿secure﴾, to make explicit what was implied by ﴿And when We made the House﴾ [al-Baqarah: 125] and so on. The meaning is that you disobeyed your greatest forefather in both of his two supplications: in making it a city, for when people cease to visit its inhabitants it falls into ruin, and in making it secure. This differs from what comes in Surat Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

When He had mentioned settlement and security, He followed it with provision and said: ﴿And provide its people﴾, and said: ﴿with fruits﴾, and did not say "with grains," because of the humiliation that engaging in them entails, which is incompatible with security. This is in line with what is related: "The Prophet (ﷺ) saw a plough share and said, 'This has never entered a house except that it brought humiliation.'" He also said: ﴿of them who believe in God﴾, the One comprising all the attributes of perfection, ﴿and the Last Day﴾, restricting the supplication for provision to the same restriction by which the supplication for leadership was restricted, showing courtesy toward Him, when He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. ﴿He said﴾, God, exalted is He, teaching that the extension of the All-Merciful quality to security and provision in this world applies to all the inhabitants of the earth: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾, i.e., I will also grant him what I inspired you to ask for, of security and provision. He expressed this by His saying: ﴿I will let him enjoy﴾, belittling him by what the word "enjoyment" conveys, since, as has passed, it is among the names of carrion, which is only what a desperate person takes while feeling aversion to it, close to one who hopes to be free of it. He emphasized this by His saying: (p-157) ﴿for a little﴾. However, there is in this an indication that he will be in a better state in this world and have wider provision than the believer. Likewise in His saying: ﴿Then I will compel him﴾, by My overwhelming majesty, ﴿to the punishment of the Fire﴾, i.e., by the blessings with which I lead him on, which carry him to acts of disobedience that are the causes of retribution. In the expression "compel," which refers to what no one would undertake by choice, there is an indication that God compels His creatures to whatever He wills of them, to manifest His wisdom, and that no one can move or be still except by His will. Compulsion (al-idtirar) is being forced toward what is harmful, with severity and constraint.

Since the implied meaning is: "Then evil is the enjoyment, namely what was mentioned for him in this world," He joined to it His saying: ﴿and evil is the destination﴾, i.e., the punishment for him in the Hereafter. It is a noun of place (maf'al) from "tasyir," which means transfer through stages and conditions that end at a goal that must differ from the thing's original state, unlike a "marji'" (place of return).

When he had mentioned what he had prepared concerning the matter of the House, both in religion and in worldly affairs, he followed it with its construction, pointing to the blessing with which He had favoured them and to their response to it with ingratitude by their own choice, so that they would be among others than the Muslim community (ummah muslimah) for which he prayed when he prayed for the Messenger. He said, linking it to "when He tried" (idh ibtala), enumerating the aspects of the blessings upon the Arabs through their greatest forefather, seeking to win them over to monotheism (tawhid): ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising﴾, meaning: remember the time when he began raising ﴿the foundations (p-158) of the House﴾. Al-Harrali (al-Harrali) said: He, may He be exalted, enumerated the aspects of His care for the Arabs' forebears in these verses, just as He enumerated the aspects of His blessing upon the Children of Israel in the earlier discourse. These were concerned with establishing the religion of God, and those were concerned with defending it, so that the difference between election (istifa') and care ('inayah) would become apparent. The qa'idah (foundation) is that upon which a thing sits (yaq'udu), that is, it is established and settled. It may also be meant as the sawaf (courses) of the building, since every saf (course) is a foundation for what is built upon it, as said al-Asbahani (al-Asbahani).

When the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, was singled out for this raising, to show his nobility by being the greatest cause of it, He joined to him his son, so He said: ﴿and Isma'il﴾, meaning: he too raises the foundations. He connected to this noble act His saying: ﴿"Our Lord"﴾, the word "say" (qul) being implied and omitted, with the particle of distance: that is, they said: ﴿"Our Lord, accept from us"﴾, meaning: we have done it by Your grace, so do not reject it from us, signalling acknowledgement of shortcoming because of the servant's insignificance, however much he strives in the face of his Master's greatness. When asking for acceptance, which suggests fear of rejection, included the knowledge of the discerning critic of shortcoming, he gave the reason with His saying: ﴿"Indeed You"﴾, and emphasised it (p-159) with His saying: ﴿"You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing"﴾, meaning: if You have heard or known from us something good, then return it with goodness; and if You have heard or known otherwise, such as a word arising from a stirring in the soul caused by weariness or exhaustion, then forgive it.

When he asked for acceptance, he asked for more along with it, saying: ﴿Our Lord﴾, following the manner of the supplications of those brought near (to God) that came before, by dropping the particle of distance. ﴿And make us﴾, that is, myself and this son of mine who helped me, ﴿submitting to You, and from our offspring﴾. Al-Harrali said: When the hoped-for faith was realized among his descendants in His saying: ﴿those of them who believe﴾ [2:126], he sought its completion through the submission of the face (of the self), and asked this for himself, for his son, and for whoever among his descendants and his son's descendants was granted faith. For Islam, when it is only the outward religion, is quick to break under the pressures of worldly affairs. Islam is only completed through the safety of creation from the hand and tongue of the servant, and through casting into the hands of his Lord everything that contends with the existence of the self and the constraints of the world. Therefore it is a goal for the elite at the end of life, so that departure from the world comes with surrender to the Truth and peace for creation, as Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Take my soul as one who submits﴾ [12:101]. And by his saying ﴿a community submitting to You﴾, he sought that they be in a state where some of them would lead others.

Since the Muslim is in need of knowledge, he said: ﴿And show us our rites﴾ (manasik, the rites of pilgrimage). In this is manifest the nobility of the act of Hajj, since it was received directly from God without intermediary, being a sign for those who come until the Day of Judgment, when there will be no intermediary between the Lord and His servants.

Al-mansak is a maf'al (place/means noun) from nusuk (acts of worship), which is what is done as an act of devotion and piety. Its letters share the letter of sukun (quiescence), said al-Harrali. Since man is the locus of incapacity, he is most in need of success, so he said: ﴿And turn to us (in forgiveness)﴾, announcing the seeking of repentance after the good deed, as is the aim of the gnostics of God who connect their good deeds by returning them to Him to whom belong creation and command. Then he gave the reason for his hope in this by saying that His custom, exalted is He, is bounty and grace. So he said: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Oft-Returning﴾, that is, the one who returns His servants to the place of salvation from His presence, after He had empowered their enemy over them through his seduction, so that they would know His favor upon them and the greatness of His power. Then he followed it with an attribute that serves almost as its reason, saying: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 129:

When he (Ibrahim, peace be upon him) asked for what belonged to him in the station of prophethood, namely that God teach him the rites (manasik) without an intermediary, he asked for his descendants something similar but through an intermediary, the way that is customary for people like them. So he said: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them﴾, i.e., among the Muslim community that is of my descendants and the descendants of my son Isma'il, ﴿a messenger from among them﴾, so that he would be gentler and more compassionate toward them, and so that they would be more fitting to follow him and to rally in support of him. That messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), for God did not send from their two lines any bearer of the Book other than him. He is thus the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), father of the Arabs and the most noble of his descendants. In this there is a great censure of them for their enmity toward him, even though he was sent to purify them by the Book, which is guidance with no doubt in it. To this he alludes with His words: ﴿who recites﴾, i.e., reads continuously and consecutively, ﴿to them Your verses﴾, i.e., Your signs that point to You, in the general sense whether they were revealed in the Book or derived from it. ﴿And teaches them the Book﴾, the complete and comprehensive one that encompasses every book, [as he said] "I have been given the comprehensive words" (ﷺ), ﴿and the wisdom﴾, which is every matter he legislates for them, whereby he protects them in the two paths of their livelihood and their return (to God), from deviation that leads to misguidance and entails destruction.

Since the apparent aim of his supplication (peace be upon him) was that the one raised up among the Muslim community (p-162) would need the teaching of what was mentioned more than purification, for its root already exists through Islam, he postponed His words: ﴿and purify them﴾, i.e., purify their hearts by what he was given of the subtle details of wisdom, so that through its clarity and refinement they rise from the peak of religion to a station where they are secure from turning back on their heels and distorting their Book as those before them did. Purification (tazkiyah) is the acquisition of zakah, which is the growth of the soul through what serves it as nourishment serves the body. So said al-Harali.

When in Surat al-Jumu'ah He mentioned his being sent to the unlettered people in general, the context required priority for purification, whose foremost part is disavowal of the greatest shirk, so that they would accept what came to them of knowledge. As for placing it first in Al 'Imran alongside the mention of being sent to the believers, that is because the situation called for rebuke over pursuing spoils, which was the cause of the defeat, since that was a pursuit of this world, which is the mother of impurities. Then He gave the reason for that with His words: ﴿Indeed You are the Mighty﴾, i.e., the One who overcomes everything and is not overcome by anything, for might (al-'izzah), as al-Harali said, is dominance that reaches the totality of the outward and the inward. ﴿The Wise﴾, i.e., the One who makes certain what He wills, so that it cannot be annulled, and no one other than You is characterized by any of that. In this there is a great demonstration of the nobility of knowledge and the purity of character, and that this is not attained except through struggles that humans cannot bear, and it is not reached at all except through earnest effort purified by might (p-163) and an arrangement established by wisdom. This is for the general case of that; how then is it for what is fit for the message? In this there is an indication that He will humiliate the enemies of the messengers, however many they become and however great their strength, and He will make their affairs firm so that no one can annul any part of them.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 130:**

Since the implied sense is: "Whoever would turn away from opposing the one who sends (the Messenger), one who has this description," he connected to it His saying: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion (millah, creed) of Abraham﴾, who was upright in his way, pure in his nature, compassionate toward his descendants, who built for them the greatest of glories, and who strove for them in noble virtues and lasting achievements, ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. That is, he degraded himself, held himself in contempt, and belittled himself; that is, he did to himself what led to this. In this there is an allusion to the stubborn People of the Book (ahl al-Kitab). Al-Harrali said: "Safahah (folly) is lightness of judgment, in contrast to what is intended from it of firmness and strength. In the construction of the verb with the object 'nafs' (himself) there is an indication that folly reaches the whole of the one who has a self, because whoever has his self made foolish, folly is confined to it. But whoever makes himself foolish (with the verb in the form saffaha nafsahu, with the object in the accusative), folly encompasses his essence and his entirety. The origin and the cause of that is from his own self, which is indicated by the accusative form of 'nafs.' This is because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made the self the source of every evil that appears in the essence of the one who has a self, for He, exalted is He, gives good through an intermediary and without an intermediary, while evil is not produced except through the intermediary of a self, so that it may be the proof of Allah against His creation. The one who turns away from the religion of Abraham deserves folly only because its evidence is manifest in reason and its great blessing is evident in experience, for whoever casts down his hand (i.e., gives up) is not excused in any rank of the ranks of this world and the Hereafter. So there is no excuse for whoever turns away from that, because it is manifest in the two witnesses of reason and the senses, which are the clearest proofs of Allah against His creation." ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people﴾ (6:83).

Since the implied sense is: "Indeed We gave him of the excellences that we have mentioned to you, which no one of sound mind turns away from," he connected to it His saying: ﴿And We indeed chose him﴾. He mentioned him with the mark of greatness, honouring him, for the servant is ennobled by the nobility of his master. And He honoured his choosing, for a craft is glorified by the glory of its maker. ﴿In this world﴾, by what we have mentioned of noble virtues, which his submission (islam) includes. The word is an ifti'al form (the eighth verbal pattern, ifti'āl) from al-safwah, which is what is pure of the subtle, free from its dense and turbid parts. In the ifti'al pattern there is an indication of deliberateness and intention, which increases the nobility referred to. ﴿And indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous﴾. In this is the greatest exaltation of the rank of righteousness, since He made him among those characterized by it. He therefore deserves the imamate (leadership), due to the height of his rank with Allah in both abodes. In this is the greatest encouragement to follow his religion and to be guided by his way, and the strongest censure of whoever opposes him. All of this is a reminder to the People of the Book of what they possess of knowledge concerning the affair of this noble Prophet and what is the cause of it, and an establishment of proof against them, because most of this is connected by 'remember' to His saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour﴾ (2:122).

When he mentioned his imamate, he mentioned what is followed in it, namely the cause of his being chosen and made righteous, and that is his religion; and what he (peace be upon him) enjoined upon his sons, and what his sons enjoined upon their sons, generation after generation, especially Ya'qub (peace be upon him), who is distinguished by the People of the Book's ascribing themselves to him. So He said: ﴿When﴾, i.e., We chose him by Our greatness, because his Lord said to him, ﴿Submit﴾, i.e., because of your Lord's favour towards you. The object is omitted so that it encompasses everything to which submission can rightly be directed, and so that it is restricted to Him alone, and the one submitting withdraws from anything else. ﴿He said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds,"﴾ i.e., the One who is good to me and to all creatures.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 132 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Wa-waṣṣā bihā﴾: that is, by this statement, or this charge, or this quality with which Allah chose him. Perhaps the pronoun was not made masculine so as not to suggest that it refers back to "his Lord." It is also read as "wa-awṣā," which is from *īṣā'* (charging), and *waṣiyyah* (a charge) is advancing toward a beneficial matter whose outcome is praiseworthy. The intensive reading is more emphatic, because it indicates repetition and multiplicity. ﴿Ibrāhīmu banīhi wa-Ya'qūb﴾: he charged his sons with it as well, and each of them said: ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah﴾, with His greatness and perfection, ﴿has chosen for you the religion﴾, which is Islam, so He spared you from seeking it and from turning it over in thought, out of mercy from Him toward you. ﴿So do not﴾, that is, as a consequence of that, I say to you: do not ﴿die﴾ in any state whatsoever ﴿except while you﴾, that is, while you are in the state that ﴿you are Muslims﴾, meaning surrendering your hands and everything attributed to you to Allah, having no share in anything at all and no turning toward other than your Master. For whoever's need of the Self-Sufficient, the Wise is perfected, He enriches him in accordance with that. By the verses that follow, He, glory be to Him, established the falsity of what the obstinate Jews and Christians hold, and He cleared His Friend (Khalīl) and the prophets of it in a manner that makes it certain that they knew of its falsity.

Mention of the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, from the Torah (al-Tawrāh): In its first book (*sifr*) it is mentioned that he was Ibrahim son of Terah, son of Nahor, son of Sarugh, son of Arghu [p-١٦٧] son of Faligh, son of Eber, son of Shalakh, son of Arfakhshad, son of Sam, son of Nuh. This is because the Torah says: When Sam had reached one hundred years, he begot Arfakhshad, and after him he lived five and thirty years, and begot Shalah, and he named him in another place Shalih. After him he lived thirty years and begot Eber. After him he lived four and thirty years and begot Faligh. After him he lived thirty years and begot Arghu. After him he lived two and thirty years and begot Sarugh. After him he lived thirty years and begot Nahor, [p-١٦٨] after him he lived nine and twenty years and begot Terah. After him he lived five and seventy years and begot Abram, Nahor and Haran. It differs from it somewhat in the Gospel (al-Injīl). In the Gospel of Luke he says: Nahor son of Sarugh, son of Arghu, son of Faligh, son of Eber, son of Sala, son of Qaynan, son of Arfakhshad, son of Sam, son of Nuh. And Nuh, according to what the Torah says, is the son of Lamech, son of Methuselah, son of Enoch, son of Yared, son of Mahalalel, son of Qaynan, son of Enosh, son of Seth, son of Adam, peace be upon him.

Thus he said in the course of the Gospel of Luke, except that he said regarding Lamech: Lamak, and regarding Jared: Yarid son of Mahlalel. (p-169)Then he said in the Torah: "Haran begot Lot, and Haran died during the lifetime of his father Terah, in the land where he was born, which is Ur of the Chaldeans." In another copy: "of the Kazdanites." "Ibram married Sarai, and she was barren, and no child was born to her. Terah set out with his son Ibram, and with Lot, the son of his son Haran, and with his daughter-in-law Sarai, from Ur of the Chaldeans, intending the land of Canaan. They reached Haran and settled there. Terah died in Haran at the age of two hundred and five years. The Lord said to Ibram: 'Go forth from your land, from where you were born, and from the house of your father, to the land that I will show you. I will make you into a great nation, I will bless you, I will magnify your name, and be blessed. I will bless your children, and I will curse those who curse you, and all the tribes of the earth will be blessed through you and through your seed.'" So Ibram did as the Lord commanded him, and Lot, the son of his brother, went with him, and Sarai his wife. He was then seventy-five years old. They took with them all their livestock and whatever servants and attendants they had acquired in Haran. They set out wanting the land of Canaan, and they arrived there. Ibram came until he reached the region of Sakham and to Bilut of Mamre. The Canaanites were still inhabitants of the land. The Lord appeared to Ibram and said to him: "I am giving this land to your offspring." Ibram built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him. (p-170) He moved from there to the mountain east of Beth-el, and pitched his tent in Beth-el, on its west side, facing the ruin, and on its east side. He built there an altar to the Lord and called upon the name of the Lord. Then he journeyed onward, and his journey was toward the south wind. There was a famine in the land, so Ibram went down to Egypt to dwell there, because the famine had become severe in the land. When he drew near to Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife: "I know that you are a beautiful woman. If the Egyptians see you, they will say, 'She is his wife,' and they will kill me. Say that you are his sister." He related the story of Pharaoh of Egypt taking her and the calamities that befell him, which prevented him from reaching her, so he released her and treated her and Ibrahim well. Then he said: Ibram went out of Egypt, he and his wife, and Lot with him, toward the land of the right hand, which in another copy is "toward the qibla," and which is the direction of the south. Ibram became very wealthy. He journeyed from the south to his dwelling place, until he came to Beth-el, to the place where he had pitched his tent before. Lot was with him, and he had flocks, herds, very much goodness, and tents. The land could not hold both of them together, because their livestock had multiplied greatly. He mentioned that Lot raised his eyes and looked at the land of the Jordan, and behold, all of it was land of watering and drinking, like the Garden of God and like the land of Egypt, at the entrance of Zoar. In another copy: Zaghar. So Lot chose the land of the Jordan, and Ibram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled in the cities of Agar and inherited, in another copy: the cities of the meadow, and pitched his tent toward Sodom. The people of Sodom were very wicked and sinful. (p-171) After Lot had separated from him, the Lord said to Ibram: "Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you are, to the north, the south, the east, and the west, for all the land that you see I give to you and to your seed after you forever. Make your seed like the dust of the earth, for if one can count the dust of the earth, your seed will also be counted." Ibram came and settled among the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, which are in Hebron, and built there an altar to the Lord. In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, in another copy: Shinwar, and Arioch king of Ellasar, in another copy: the Khazar, and Chedorlaomer king of Elam, in another copy: Khuzistan, and Tidal king of Gilan, in another copy: the nations, these gathered in the valley of the Sodomites, which is the Salt Sea, and they killed the giants who were in the ten cities, and the heroes who were there, and the Hurrites who were in the mountains of Seir, in another copy: Shurat, as far as Elparan, which is in the wilderness. They returned and came to En-mishpat, in another copy: the Judgment, which is Kadesh, and they killed all the chiefs of the Amalekites and the Amorites who dwelt in Hazezon-tamar. The king of Sodom, Bera, went out, and Birsha king of Gomorrah, and Shinab king of Admah, and Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar, in another copy: Zaghar. Five kings fought against the four in the valley of the Sodomites, so the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah fled and fell there, and the rest fled to the mountain. They plundered all the livestock of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and carried off Lot, son of Ibram's brother, and his livestock, and they went away. Then one of those who escaped came and informed Ibram the Hebrew. He mustered his young men and his trained servants, three hundred and eighteen men, and set out in pursuit of them as far as Dan, in another copy: Banias. He surrounded them at night, fought them, and defeated them, pursuing them to Hobah, in another copy: al-Mizza, which is north of Damascus, a village called Halbun. He restored Lot, his brother's son, with his livestock, all the livestock, the women, and the people. The king of Sodom went out and met him, and he returned to him everything that had been taken from him. After this, the revelation of God came to Ibram in a vision, and said to him: "O Ibram! I am your protector and helper, for your reward has become very great." Ibram said: "O Allah, my Lord! What will you give me, when I depart this world without descendants, and my heir will be Eliezer, my servant of Damascus?" The Lord said to him: "This one will not inherit you, but your son who comes out of your loins, he will inherit you." He said to him: (p-173) "Look at the heavens and count the stars, if you are able to count them." Then he said to him: "So shall your seed be." Ibram believed in God. The Lord said to him: "[I am the Lord] your God who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, in another copy: Atun of the Kazdanites, to give you this land to inherit it." When the sun set, a stillness fell upon Ibram, and a great fear and darkness overcame him. The Lord said to Ibram: "Know with certainty that your offspring will dwell in a land that is not theirs, where they will be enslaved and afflicted for four hundred years. The nation they serve, I will judge, and after that they will come out with great wealth. You will go to your fathers in peace and be buried in a good old age. In the fourth generation they will return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete." When the sun had set and it became dark and gloomy, behold, a smoking furnace and a burning lamp of fire passed back and forth between those pieces. On that day the Lord made a covenant with Ibram and said: "I am giving your offspring this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates." Sarai, the wife of Ibram, had not borne children, and she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar. Sarai said to Ibram, while they were in the land of Canaan: "The Lord has withheld children from me. Go in to my maidservant, that perhaps I may be comforted by a child from her." Ibram listened to Sarai's words and obeyed her. This was after he had dwelt in the land of (p-174) Canaan for ten years. She conceived, and Sarai said to Ibram: "You are responsible for my wrong. I placed my maidservant in your bosom, and when she conceived, I became contemptible in her eyes. The Lord judge between me and you." He said: "Behold, your maidservant is handed over to you. Do with her as you wish." Sarai, her mistress, humiliated her, so she fled from her. The angel of the Lord met her at a spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Shur, and in another narration: on the road to Hazar, and in another copy: at the spring that is on the road to al-Jifar. He said to her: "O Hagar, maidservant of Sarai! Return to your mistress and submit yourself under her hand." Then the angel of God said to her: "I will greatly multiply your seed, so that it cannot be counted." Then he said to her: "Behold, you are with child," in another copy: "You are pregnant, and you will bear a son, and you will call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heard your submission. This son of yours will be a man who dwells in the wilderness, and his hand will be against all people," in another copy: "and the wild beasts of the people, his hand upon everyone, and everyone's hand against him, and he will settle upon all the borders of his brothers." She called upon the name of the Lord who spoke to her and said: "You are God who sees and reveals," because she said: "I have seen a vision." Therefore she named that spring "the well of the living one who sees me," which is the well of Rekem and Hazar, in another copy: between Kadesh and Bered. Then Hagar bore a son to Ibram, and Ibram named him Ishmael. Ibram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him. When Ibram reached ninety-nine years, the Lord appeared to him and said to him: "I am God Almighty, the God of promises. Be well-pleasing before me and be blameless, and I will establish my covenant between me and you," in another narration: "Walk before me and be blameless, for I make my covenant with you," and I will multiply you greatly, very greatly. Ibrahim fell on his face, and God spoke to him and said: "I establish my covenant with you," in another copy: "God revealed to him, saying to him: I have made my covenant with you, and you will be a father of many nations. Your name will no longer be called Ibram, but your name will be Ibrahim, for I have made you a father of many nations, I will make you fruitful and increase you greatly, and I will make you a leader of the nations, and kings will come from your loins. I will establish the covenant" (p-175) in another copy: "I will keep my covenant" between me and you and between your seed after you, an everlasting covenant, and I will be a God to you and to your seed after you, and I will give you and your seed after you the land where you dwell and all the land of Canaan as an inheritance forever, and I will be their God." God said to Ibrahim: "Keep my covenant, you and your seed after you, throughout their generations. This is my covenant which I command you, that you keep it, so that between me and your seed after you there will be this: circumcise every male, and circumcise the flesh of your foreskins, and it will be a sign of the covenant between me and you. Every male among you shall be circumcised at eight days old, throughout your generations, whether born in the house or bought with money."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 132 (part 3 of 3):

And every male among the sons of the foreigners, who are not of your seed, shall be circumcised, the circumcision of the one born in your house and the one bought with your money. And my covenant shall be a mark in your flesh, an everlasting covenant forever. And every male with a foreskin (ghurla), whose foreskin is not circumcised on the eighth day, that soul shall be cut off from its people, because it has broken my covenant. [p. 176] And God said to Abraham: As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, because her name is Sarah. I will bless her, and I will give you a son by her, and I will bless him, and he shall be a leader of many peoples, and kings of peoples shall come from his offspring. Then Abraham fell on his face, laughing, and said in his heart (in another narration: wondering, he said to himself): Can a child be born to a man of a hundred years, and can Sarah bear, when she is ninety years old? And Abraham said to God: Oh that Ishmael might live before you! And God said to Abraham: Truly (in another copy: yes), Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac, and I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his offspring after him. As for Ishmael, I have heard you: I have blessed him, made him fruitful, and multiplied him exceedingly. He shall beget twelve great princes, and I will make him a great nation. But my covenant I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year. When he finished speaking with him, God went up from Abraham. Abraham took Ishmael his son, and all those born in his house and all those bought with his money, every male of Abraham's household, and he circumcised the foreskins of them on that same day, as God had commanded him. Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he circumcised his foreskin, and Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised. He also circumcised with him the sons of the foreigners who were attached to him. Then he completed the good news of Isaac, as will come in Surah Hud, God willing. [p. 177] He went on to say: The LORD remembered Sarah as he had said. God, may He be blessed and exalted, did for Sarah as He had promised, so she conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the time God had promised. Abraham named his son whom Sarah bore him Isaac. Abraham circumcised his son Isaac on the eighth day, as the LORD had commanded him. Abraham was a hundred years old. Sarah said: God has given me laughter, and everyone who hears will laugh with me. She also said: Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse a child, and bear a son after old age? The boy grew up and was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast on the day he was weaned. Then he repeated the account of Sarah's matter, of driving out Hagar and sending her away, and that this grieved Abraham greatly. He said: God said to Abraham: Do not let it be grievous in your eyes because of the boy and your maidservant. Abraham rose early in the morning, took bread and a skin of water, gave them to Hagar, and placed them on her shoulder along with the child, and sent her away. She went and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba (in another copy: Beer-lahai-roi... Beersheba of the oath, because Abraham made a covenant with the ruler of that land there). The water in the skin ran out, so she cast the boy under a shrub of wormwood (shih), went off and sat opposite him, distanced about the range of a bowshot, so that she would not see his death. When the boy cried out and wept, the LORD heard his voice. The angel of the LORD called Hagar from heaven and said to her: What is the matter with you, Hagar? Do not fear, for the LORD has heard the voice of the boy where he is. Rise, lift up the boy and hold him in your hands, for I will make him a great nation. Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She went, filled the skin, and gave the boy to drink. God was with the boy, and he grew up and dwelt in the wilderness of Paran, and he was learning archery in that wilderness. His mother took a wife for him. End of quotation.

Within this, the account of the expulsion of Hagar and her son appears, on its surface, to contradict what was previously stated about the circumcision of Ishmael, peace be upon him. For there it says that he was thirteen years old, whereas here it appears that he was a suckling infant. In the authentic hadith, [it is reported] that [Abraham] placed him by the House while he was nursing, and this can be reconciled with the latter account. As for the first, it does not state that he was at Bayt al-Maqdis at the time of the circumcision, so it is possible that God folded the earth for Abraham, peace be upon him, by means of the Buraq (the heavenly steed) or something else, and he went to the blessed city of Makkah, circumcised him there, and then returned.

In this passage there is also a good tidings concerning our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), more explicit than what they have mentioned, namely his saying: "And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed through you." For this did not come to pass for anyone among the descendants of Abraham, peace be upon him, except through the Prophet (ﷺ). Thus God established blessing through him (ﷺ) and goodness among the majority of the tribes of [p. 179] the earth, and what remains will be after the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him. Likewise his saying: "His hand shall be against all people," and so on, for no one has reported that Ishmael, peace be upon him, had his hand over all people, nor did his authority extend over all the borders of his brothers, nor did any of his descendants possess this quality except the Prophet (ﷺ).

Then I found, in the commentary on al-Maqasid by Shaykh Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani, and in the commentary on al-Sahaif by Imam al-Samarqandi, an indication of this text.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 133:

When Allah, glory be to Him, established for the Children of Israel that their father Ya'qub (Jacob) was among those who enjoined upon his sons the religion of Islam, He said, rebuking them: ﴿Or⦆ — and it is thus known with certainty, from the mention of the conjunction particle, that the element it is coordinated with (al-ma'tuf 'alayhi) is omitted, as the scholars said regarding one of the interpretations of this verse and of ﴿Or is one who worships devoutly during the hours of the night﴾ [al-Zumar: 9] in Surat al-Zumar. The estimate here, for their reproach and censure, is: whichever side they choose, it obliges them to what they dislike. Were you absent from this charge of Ibrahim and Ya'qub, peace be upon them, or were you present, and were you absent only regarding the matter of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, in particular? Or ﴿you were witnesses﴾, the verse, meaning: Were you absent from knowledge of that or not, when you ruled to restrict yourselves to Paradise, so that this would prevent you from such a judgment? In either case, his ignorance does not harm you, because with you in the Book of Allah revealed to your Prophet is the command of the like of it from Allah that suffices you regarding it, and it also prevents you from this judgment in a definitive manner. (p-180) In this there is an indication that it is not obligatory to be bound by the fathers, and a guidance to broaden thought to the First Benefactor, who is the Lord of the fathers, in order to be bound by His commands and to stop at His prohibitions, whether that agrees with the law of the fathers or opposes it. Since this is a necessary consequence of the content of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾ [al-Baqarah: 134], He followed it with it, meaning: What concern is it of yours to ask about them, in your claim that they were Jews or Christians? As the text will come with the reproach for that, and its being followed by a verse like this one, because the question is either about lineage or about deeds, and nothing of either will benefit you. For a person has only what he strove for. So asking about them, then, is only superfluous for one who has the knowledge of what comes and goes. In this there is a warning that they cut themselves off from them, because when they did not follow them in Islam, they severed the connection of lineage between themselves and them, and their disavowal of them was achieved, for the lineage of religion is greater than the lineage of water and clay. Or it may be said, and this is better: When the People of the Book claimed that Paradise was exclusively theirs, and Allah, glory be to Him, refuted that against them by saying that it is for whoever submits while doing good, and reminded them of the circumstances of the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, until He concluded that he was among the leaders of those characterized by this attribute, and that he enjoined it upon his sons, it was as if it were said, as a denial against them in their claim of exclusivity to Paradise and as an affirmation to them: Were you witnesses to that from him, so that you would be among those who obeyed his command in his testament and thus be worthy of Paradise? Or were you witnesses, O sons of Ya'qub, (p-181) when death came to Ya'qub, the well-known father of your lineage, ﴿when death came to Ya'qub﴾, and he was [upon] what Ibrahim had enjoined upon his sons, ﴿when he said﴾, meaning: Ya'qub, ﴿to his sons﴾.

Since his intention, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was generality in everything so that specification would fall in its place, and so that no further question would be needed, he used the term ﴿mā﴾, which is general for the rational and others, and said: ﴿What do you worship﴾. Had he used ﴿man﴾, their answer would not have yielded this explicit negation of worshipping anything non-rational. He restricted it with his saying ﴿after me﴾, because a successor often takes the place of an absent person with evil even if he was a reformer in his presence. He included the preposition because their lifespans do not cover all time. ﴿They said: We worship your God﴾ who created you ﴿and the God of your fathers﴾ who created them and remained after them, and will remain after every (p-182) thing with no end to Him, just as He was before every thing with no beginning to Him. Then they specified the fathers by saying: ﴿Ibrahim﴾, meaning your grandfather, ﴿and Isma'il﴾, because he was an uncle, and an uncle is the twin of the father, so he is a father in a metaphorical sense, ﴿and Ishaq﴾.

Since the mention of God was preceded in two idafahs, they clarified that the intended referent in both is one, establishing the disavowal of association and recording against the People of the Book the inevitability of the nullity of their claim. So they said: ﴿one God﴾. Then, after their monotheism mentioned earlier, which is the meaning of excellence in His saying ﴿and he is a doer of good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112], they reported their sincerity in worship by saying ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, meaning: to Him alone, not to the father or anyone else, ﴿Muslims﴾, meaning: we have no choice alongside Him, but we are for Him like the camel newly led, wherever it is led we follow, meaning: Or were you witnesses to this testament, so that we might bear witness for you to what we witnessed for his sons present at that time of Islam, and you would then be among the people of Paradise.

Since this contained the greatest recording against them, that they had cast aside the charge of the chosen ones (al-asfiya') of their forefathers, departed from their religion, and worshipped in opposition to them, and since it was certainly known that the answer is that they did not witness that and were not Muslims, He expressed this by His saying: ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾, i.e., centuries before you, which you did not witness. He alerted that they acted contrary to their deeds by His saying: ﴿for them is what they earned﴾, i.e., of the religion of Islam specific to them, with no partnership for you in it, ﴿and for you is what you earned﴾, i.e., of what you are upon of caprice, specific to you, and they will not be asked about your deeds. ﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾, i.e., you (will not be asked about) what they did.

The Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on 2:135

When God, exalted is He, informed that they had abandoned the sunnah (the prescribed way, practice, or precedent) in refining their souls, by following in guidance the chosen ones among their forefathers, and clarified the falsehood of what they now hold in every respect, and made clear that it is pure error, He showed that He had punished them for this by making them callers to disbelief. This is because His past sunnah had preceded, and ﴿you will not find any change in God's sunnah﴾ [33:62], that whoever causes a sunnah to die, a bid'ah (innovation) comes to life at his hands as a punishment for him.

Al-Harrali said: Because they alternate in religions as opposites alternate in bodies. God, exalted is He, said, marveling at them and linking to His statement ﴿And they say: None will enter [Paradise] except...﴾ [2:111]: ﴿And they say﴾, that is, the two groups of the People of the Book, to the followers of guidance: ﴿Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided.﴾ That is: their committing falsehood and their treading the paths of error did not suffice them, until they called to what they themselves were upon, and promised guidance that would result from it. So God commanded him to respond to them that he follows the sunnah of their father, not turned away from it as they have turned away. So He said, addressing the most noble of His creation, because of the high rank of what he reports and the difficulty of adhering to it for the self: ﴿Say: Rather﴾, turning away from their statement, meaning: it is not any of what you have mentioned; rather, we will be, or we will be closely associated, I and whoever follows me among those who perfect the people of Islam, with ﴿the religion of Ibrahim﴾, associating with it as a helper, as if we were formed from it. This is a metaphor for not separating from it, and it is more eloquent than if it were said: "Rather, the people of the religion of Ibrahim."

Al-Harrali said: In it is the perfection of Muhammad's (ﷺ) following of the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who is the first, because of the correspondence between the first and the last. He mentioned that the millah (religion, community-path) is what the light of reason manifests of guidance amid the darkness of what people have committed to of the customs of worldly affairs. So the most complete of what the light of reason has displayed is the religion of Ibrahim. ﴿Hanifan﴾ (upright, inclining toward truth), that is: gentle, pliant, easy, receptive to uprightness, inclining with the call of truth, submitting to it, yielding his affair to it, with nothing of the blindness, density, coarseness, and rigidity directed at him from which disobedience, obstinacy, and tyranny would follow. This is because the root ḥ-n-f in every arrangement revolves around lightness and delicacy, and the primary literal sense of it probably is slenderness. This meaning entails dispersal, slimness, and inclination, so it entails ease of submission and uprightness. This is revealed by the verse of Al 'Imran: ﴿But he was a hanif, a Muslim﴾ [3:67]. Thus he turned away from the crooked paths of creation in their deviation from the main road of the way of Islam.

Al-Harrali also said: The hanif is one who inclines away from what people habitually hold in flux, toward what the fitrah (innate disposition) requires, with the tenderness of a heart toward the sincerity of its inner perception.

When He established for him Islam through being a hanif, He negated from him anything else by His saying: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ (p. 186).

Al-Harrali said: In it is information that his essence is cleared of the matter of shirk (associating partners with God) in the fixed affairs, actions, and states, and in conveying that he is from the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) in final perfection, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) is from him in the opening beginning. God, exalted is He, said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Say: Indeed my prayer...﴾ [6:162] up to His statement: ﴿and I am the first of the Muslims﴾ [6:163]. This is the primacy of the rank of perfection that is specific to him, and whoever else is from him in it, because negating a thing conveys disavowal and attachment to the one rooted in its opposite. So whoever is not, for example, among the disbelievers is among the believers, because if he himself were the believer, he would have been described by the attribute opposite to what was negated from him, since in that there is the double meaning of affirming the attribute and negating its opposite. A similar pattern occurs frequently in the discourse of the Qur'an, and it clarifies who has the attribute and who is from him, with a difference between the preceding and the following in everything that comes in its manner. That is, a similar difference is apparent to understanding but hidden from the witnessing of knowledge, because knowledge from the intellect is in the position of the self (nafs), and understanding from the intellect is in the position of the spirit (ruh). So understanding has an apprehension that knowledge does not attain, just as the spirit has an elevated station that the self does not reach, because the self is directed to the apparent witnessed realm, and the spirit's direction is to the lofty existence. End.

[p-188] When this was said, the soul turned to that by which one reaches the religion of Ibrahim. So He turned the address that had been directed to the most perfect (the Prophet) into one that includes those close to him and those below him, with what includes them, because the intended meaning is generality. He (exalted is He) led it into an answer to those who seemed to say: "What should we say?" until they became like him. So He said: ﴿Say﴾, meaning: O you who believe, ﴿We believe in Allah﴾, He to whom belong all the attributes of perfection.

Since the one commanded is the believers, and since the verb "to send down" (inzal) is followed by "ila" (to), which implies reaching an endpoint, and that requires an intermediary before the endpoint, and since reaching the endpoint, which is following, is only by the secondary intention, the more fitting expression in this verse for directing the command to them is "ila", unlike the verse of Al 'Imran, as will come, God willing. So He said: ﴿and what has been sent down to us﴾, meaning from the Book which has been stated to be guidance, in whatever form it came, of rulings, abrogation (naskh), postponement (naseey), and other things. It has also been said that it means ﴿what was sent down to Ibrahim﴾, so that the path is one, ﴿and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾, his two sons.

Al-Harrali said: He thus taught the Arabs, the unlettered ones envied for what Allah had given them of His bounty, the sequence of what He had made to flow from the wording concerning the Children of Israel in His covenant with them. In it is the joining of the Arabs, who are the descendants of Isma'il, to Ibrahim and his sons, and the severing of the Children of Israel from them. In it is also a showing of the superiority of Allah's bounty to the Arabs, in that He instructs them and does not make them speak, lest they fall short in their speech. So He sufficed them with what He taught them, and they recited it, instead of what they would have said had they been left to themselves. Their Lord quieted them ... [p-189] and taught them what is fitting of speech for them. He said: ﴿and Ya'qub and the tribes﴾, a completion of what came before in the earlier covenant. End.

﴿And what was given to Musa and Isa﴾, meaning from their Lord, from what was revealed of the Torah and the Gospel and what was not revealed. He changed the style to give precedence to them, because of the two Books and the miracles they had and other powers. Then he attributed the giving to all of them, because the people of the great Books are among them, by way of taghlib (predominance, where the more prominent group gives its name to the whole).
