Since the necessary consequence of their opposition in this state is plotting and warfare, and this was on the basis of obstinacy, God, glorified is He, did not leave the sufficiency of His allies to anyone else, so this caused His saying: ﴿So God will suffice you against them﴾, that is, by a promise with no failure in it at all, even if it is delayed somewhat, by His power and His other attributes of perfection which the noble Name conveys. Sufficiency (*al-kifaya*) is making the one who resists independent of resisting his enemy, in a way that does not require him to repel it. Thus said al-Harrali. Since the one who opposes a person may plot against him either by speech or by action, and action is preceded by forming an intention in the heart, and since the one who suffices a person's sufficiency depends on knowledge of what is good for him, He said: ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾, that is, of what your enemies say, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, of what they conceal. So He causes for every word and intention of theirs something that turns back its harm upon them. Your share from them is limited to harm in speech and ill will in the heart, while their share from you is subjugation, enslavement, and seizure of their lands and property.

Al-Harrali took ﴿the dye of God﴾ (*sibghat Allah*), that is, the form of the dyeing of the Sovereign on High, which is the adornment of the Muslim and his natural disposition, just as the dye is the adornment of what is dyed, as a state required by the meaning of the speech. He reproached the grammarians for knowing a state (*hal*) only from single words and hardly understanding states from a whole sentence. He said: *al-siyigha* is a rapid transformation by the swiftness of its revelation. He also said: Since this instruction was a revealed instruction, swift in transforming from the state of manifest error in which the Arabs were in their ignorance to the state of manifest guidance in which the prophets were in their guidance, without any period of time, He, exalted is He, made it a dye, as cloth is dyed in the moment, changing from one colour to another, in contrast to what the People of the Book dye their followers with, following their desires, such as what they call the *ghitas* (baptism by immersion). ﴿And who is better than God﴾, that is, He to whom all perfection belongs, ﴿in dye﴾, because it is a dye of the heart which does not fade, since it is steadfast by the One who protects it, the All-Knowing; whereas that is a dye of the body which does not benefit. In it is conveyed what is particular to those who believe of the transformation of their essence into light, as peace be upon him said: "O God, make me light." So what the essence of the imams was transformed into, the hearts of the community were dyed with. ﴿And to Him we are worshippers﴾, that is, exclusively, as a completion of the response to the address of the covenant of the Children of Israel, where He said: ﴿What will you worship after me?﴾ [al-Baqara: 133]. However, worship in the time of the Children of Israel preceded, and submission (*Islam*) is a definitive obligation, and submission in this instruction is a beginning, so that worship may occur as gratitude. He specifically chooses by His mercy whom He wills. He brought it with the attribute that is established and permanent, so in it is an indication that none of them will turn away from his religion out of displeasure with Him after faith has mingled with the brightness of his heart. This is a general share of protection, whose particular share is established for the Prophet (ﷺ) in the highest of his affairs. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 139:

When Allah the Exalted commanded, with His words ﴿Say, "Rather, [follow] the religion of Ibrahim"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135] and what follows it, that the opponent be informed of the opposition, and that there is no agreement except by abandoning desire and following guidance, He commanded (the Prophet) to dispute with them in a way that weakens their claims and removes their doubts. So He said, turning the address away from the plural and directing it to His Messenger ﷺ, raising his station and making known his lofty rank, and informing (us) that no one else can undertake this task, because of the knowledge they have along with their argumentativeness and obstinacy: ﴿Say﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135], denouncing their argumentation and rebuking them for it, ﴿Do you dispute with us﴾. Since the more fitting approach in confrontation is to inform the opponent of the opposition (p-196), because it cuts off his greed and better enrages him, and since here it is also closer to the pleasure of the Creator, this was placed before the (mention of) disputation. The meaning of His words ﴿concerning Allah﴾ is: concerning your claim to exclusive possession of the kingdom, which has no other kingdom beside it, because to Him belongs all perfection, the nullification of which was alluded to earlier with His words ﴿Say, "If the Last Abode with Allah is exclusively for you"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 94]. That is: Do you dispute with us about this, when there is no basis for your exclusive claim to it? ﴿And He is﴾, that is, while the situation is that He is ﴿our Lord and your Lord﴾: we and you are equal in servitude to Him. ﴿For us are our deeds﴾, in which we are exclusively (independent) of you, ﴿and for you are your deeds﴾, in which you are exclusively (independent) of us. We do not fear from Him that He would single you out with our deeds or with any part of them so that you would be favored with them in His sight, nor that He would single us out with your deeds or any part of them so that we would be distanced by them from Him, either through injustice or error, because He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. ﴿And we﴾ are better in deeds than you, because we are ﴿devoted to Him﴾ alone, ﴿associating nothing with Him﴾, whereas you associate with Him ʿUzayr, al-Masih, the rabbis and the monks, and you know this in your inner reality even if you outwardly show otherwise. Therefore it is necessarily established that we are more particularly His than you. Sincerity (ikhlas) is the complete removal of the self, so a servant does not attain its reality until he does not love to be praised for a deed.

(p-197) Since there remained among their bluster the claim that their forefathers were upon their religion, so that their claim of exclusive right to Paradise would be valid, He (glory be to Him) nullified it by His saying: ﴿Or﴾, meaning: "Did you retract your saying, 'Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided' [2:135], because it is established that this contradicts the millah (religion) of Ibrahim and his family? ﴿Or do you say﴾." It is not hidden that the estimated meaning, according to the reading of Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, Hafs and Ruways (with the second-person address), is: "Did you retract your saying: 'Indeed Ibrahim,' the Khalil (close friend) of Allah, ﴿and Isma'il and Ishaq﴾, his two sons, ﴿and Ya'qub﴾, son of Ishaq, ﴿and the Asbat﴾ (the tribes), the children of Ya'qub, ﴿were Jews or Christians﴾, so that your claim that Paradise is exclusively for the people of your religion would be valid?" So it is as if it were said: What is said to them if they say that? It is said: ﴿Say: Are you more knowing﴾ about that and about other than it, ﴿or is Allah﴾, to Whom belongs all-encompassing knowledge, more knowing? So they cannot say "we," and if they say "Allah," then He has cleared Ibrahim of that, so what they claimed is void.

Since the knowledge they had from Allah was that the Khalil and those mentioned with him, peace be upon them, were upon the religion of Islam, and they used to conceal what they had of that, despite Allah's affirmation to them and His questioning them about it, and His prohibition to them from concealing it, and what is close to it, by His saying: ﴿And do not confuse the truth with falsehood﴾ [2:42]; and the estimated meaning was: "Who is more unjust than one who claims that he knows more than Allah, by his explicit claim or by its necessary implication, by reporting contrary to what is established in the Qur'an, whose truth is known by its inimitability!" He, exalted, said, conjoining this to the estimated matter: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah﴾, meaning: existing and deposited with him (p-198) ﴿from Allah﴾, meaning: he concealed it from the Supreme King, or it is with him from Him, and He asks him about it while knowing that He will expose him, for He is the Knower of hidden things. Since the estimated meaning was: "Then He knows what he did of concealing it," He conjoined to it what is more general than it, saying: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾, the One encompassing everything in power and knowledge. This indicates, by the form of the present tense, their persistence after all this in the evil of their deeds, and it is a warning against the like of that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 141:

When He left them no grounds for holding on to Abraham, peace be upon him, He followed this with an indication, on the assumption that their claim were correct, that religion revolves around God's command in every age, not around what He established for any one of His creatures. For He has no restriction placed on Him and no one may object. Rather, it is His right to command something today and its opposite tomorrow, for example, and to do whatever He wills of *ihkam* (making a ruling firm and decisive), *naskh* (abrogation, the replacement of one ruling by another), *nasi'* (postponement), and *insa'* (causing to forget). So He said: ﴿That is a community﴾, meaning Abraham and his family, ﴿that has passed away﴾, meaning: suppose they were as you claim, yet they have gone and their time has elapsed. Nothing will benefit you except what you newly acquire in this your present time, in accordance with what has been newly revealed, the inimitable revelation addressed to all the people of the earth, the red and the black among them. [p. 199]

It is also possible to say: since the content of what came before, namely the affirmation of God's supreme knowledge and their concealing of the testimony they have, establishes the truth of what God, glory be to Him, reported through the tongue of this noble Prophet, that His chosen servants followed the religion of Islam and that they are free of the Jews and Christians, the meaning becomes: if you claim falsely that knowledge came to you from God regarding what you have claimed, it is said: the prophet you attribute that to has had his miracle end with his death, and your scripture cannot be trusted against alteration and substitution because it is not inimitable. But this Prophet who brought the Qur'an stands among you now, and he informs you from God that your claim is false, and he supports his word with miracles, of which this Qur'an is one. All the Arabs were unable to produce a surah like it, and you are likewise, sharing with them in eloquence, in both verse and prose, while distinguished from them by knowledge. Therefore it is binding on you to accept him. For you do not rely, in promoting your falsehood after all your effort, except on one whose truthfulness has been established by the establishment of his messengerhood, and his messengerhood has been established by the manifestation of his miracle. So it is obligatory upon you to accept his command. This necessarily yields that it is obligatory upon you to accept this summoner with this Qur'an just as you would accept those others, equally. Otherwise, accepting some of those who possess this description and rejecting others would be arbitrariness and following of caprice, the blameworthy desire found in every law, which God condemned you for when He said, the Exalted: ﴿Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you waxed arrogant?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87]. Moreover, the refutation of your claim about them is the clearest of all clear matters, in that it is inconceivable that the earlier one should be attributed to what came to the later one only after long durations. [p. 200] The explicit text that nullifies this will come in Al 'Imran, God willing. The reference to its contradiction of reason is in His words: ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 65], so that authentic transmission and the judgment of reason agree in nullifying it. To all of this refers His words: ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾, meaning: long before you, by ages. Reports about them after such an interval are not accepted except with a decisive proof, and you have no way to it, since the decisive proof has stood against your opposition to them in this Qur'an, whose truthfulness is certain through its inimitability, as explained above, and as indicated by His words, the Exalted: ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earned; and you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ That is, for them is what they did of their deeds, and for you is what you did of your deeds, so they will not be questioned about your deeds, ﴿and you will not be asked﴾, meaning you, ﴿about what they used to do.﴾

[p-201] Since their claim was that their forefathers were upon their religion, lest their assertion that Paradise is exclusively theirs be refuted, and since this claim was an unsupported addition with no foundation on which anything could rest, they attempted to deny the permissibility of abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another). God's refutation of their claim, His reproach of them for what they had introduced into their religion, and His rebuke of them for it entailed that they had permitted themselves what they had forbidden to their Creator, who "is not questioned about what He does" (21:23). They were the most foolish of people. So He followed this with an explicit statement of their defect and an expression of wonder at them, for their denial of the abrogation of the qiblah (direction of prayer) and their hastiness in objecting to their Lord. He said, connecting it to what precedes it in a more general way: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ and so on to the end of the verse. For if they did not know the truth of that, and did not follow them, then at least they should refrain from reproaching them. How much more so when they know that it is the truth!

He said ﴿the foolish﴾ and did not say "they will say," to make manifest the attribute that led them to this statement, whose defect is apparent to the people of every religion. The foolish person is one who acts without evidence, either by not heeding any evidence and therefore not pausing until it becomes clear to him, but following his desire, or by regarding what is not evidence as evidence. He emphasized the attribute of levity by His saying ﴿among the people﴾, derived from al-naws, which means movement, without saying "among the People of the Book," "the Children of Israel," or the like. This is an explicit condemnation of them and a generalization to include everyone who supported them in this. ﴿What turned them away﴾, and they did not say "from," adding to the harm through contempt, ﴿from their qiblah﴾. Al-Harrali said: the qiblah is that which is placed opposite the face, and the qubul is the front part of the body, as opposed to the dubur, which is the back part. ﴿Which they were formerly facing﴾, that is, Bayt al-Maqdis (the Temple Mount in Jerusalem). Perhaps He omitted specifying it so that it could also apply to the intention of the Ka'bah, so that the meaning becomes: if they had shifted away from the Ka'bah by God's command, then they are in error in their return; otherwise, in every case they are followers of desire. In this there is an indication that when their proofs were cut off, they cast this doubt upon those among the hypocrites whom they had deceived, and they could not confront anyone of firm faith with it, just as they said earlier: ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾ (2:135), and similar statements, knowing that whoever argues on behalf of the believers against them has the conclusive proof.

Therefore their answer came with His saying ﴿Say﴾ without an addressee, unlike what preceded in His saying: ﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant with God?﴾ (2:80), ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾ (2:111), and similar. He, glorified is He, presented the report about them in this manner, which is among the signs of prophethood and the magnificent qualities of the message, for it is a report of what the enemies would say, and so it came from them exactly as reported. Despite the intensity of their enmity and their striving to disparage with the slightest doubt, they were unable to refute him by refraining from it. This is in addition to a preparation for it in what preceded, in five places: their distortion of the words of God; His imposition of abrogation and His use of it as evidence for the goodness of His action; His report of the wrongdoing of those who prevent access to the Masjid; His report that He is not restricted to one direction over another; and His mention of the building of the House and what He commanded regarding its veneration and its being taken as a place of prayer. Moreover, this lays a foundation in the souls of the people of Islam and honors them by teaching the answer before it is needed, so that it may be more decisive against the opponent, more breaking of his arrogance, and more effective in repelling his clamor. Their being called ﴿foolish﴾ refers to His earlier statement about those among them and others who were hypocrites: ﴿Surely they are the foolish ones﴾ (2:13), because although they openly disbelieved, the name of hypocrisy applies to them from another aspect, namely that they displayed disbelief while concealing their knowledge of faith, displaying denial while concealing what they knew of its truth. Also, if the hypocrites, who displayed good while concealing evil, were foolish, then those whom evil covered outwardly and inwardly are even more foolish. This also refers to His statement shortly before: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ (2:130), because of what was established regarding their opposition to him, even though they claimed agreement.

He said ﴿To God﴾, that is, the King who encompasses everything in greatness and knowledge, ﴿belong the east and the west﴾, specifying them because they are the two gathering points of the horizons, as has already been mentioned. Therefore no one direction is specifically the object of turning toward Him over another. Whatever He commands is the truth.

Since He established that all directions are equal in relation to Him, because they are His dominion, and that whoever turns toward any of them by His command attains His pleasure, which is reaching Him, He expressed this in a new sentence, saying, honoring the people of Islam and making known His care for them: [p-205] ﴿He guides﴾ to Him ﴿whom He wills﴾, that is, among His servants. He magnified the Ka'bah by His saying ﴿to a straight path﴾ in whatever direction it may be. Whoever follows it reaches the goal without error. He made it indefinite because what is meant by it is particular parts of the Law. As for the path defined in al-Fatihah (the opening surah), what is meant by it is the entire Law, with all the perfection indicated by the definite article "al-".

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 1 of 2):

When he had explained the rectitude of the qibla to which he had directed them, he made known that it is a middle course (wasat), with no injustice in it. He therefore followed that with His saying: ﴿And thus﴾, meaning: and in the same way as We made your qibla a middle course, because it faces the Ancient House (al-Bayt al-'Atiq), which is the middle of the earth, and it is the building of Abraham, peace be upon him, who is the most moderate of the prophets. It is also the best of houses, so it is a middle course in every sense. ﴿We have made you﴾ through guidance to it in facing it, and to other things that We command you to do, ﴿a nation﴾. Al-Harrali said: it derives from umm (origin, mother), which is the following of a sequence and a number, one part after another, until it ends at a first imam (leader). The imam and the ummah are thus like two correlates: the imam is the one aimed at by nations, and the ummah is the one aiming at its imam, who is its exemplar. The imam is what lies before the two hands, in the sensory witnessed sense and in the path of intent. End of quotation.

﴿Wasatan (middle)﴾, meaning: noble and excellent, because the wasat is the just balance, the one whose relation to all its sides is equal, and so it is the best of a thing. Abu Tammam al-Ta'i said:

"She was the protected middle; then calamities encircled her, until she became an extremity."

Whoever follows the middle of the road is protected from error, and whoever deviates from the middle falls into injustice, which causes straying from the intended path. In this there is the point that when they claimed exclusivity, they were refuted and their arguments were rejected; then the exclusivity was established for this ummah.

The wasat, with a vowel on the sin (wasat), is the name for the very thing between the two extremities of a thing, like the centre of a circle. With a sukun (wasat, with sukun on the sin) it is an indefinite name for the interior of a circle, for example. Likewise it is used as an adverb of place (zarf). The first is used as a subject, object, or predicate, and none of this is valid with the sukun form. This is what al-Asfahani said.

The root w-s-t, whether hamzated or unhamzated, with the weak (waw) and defective (ya') forms and their eleven combinations: wasata, tasa, sawata, sataw, tawasa, tasaw, tayasa, tisa, [sayata], sata'a, tasa'a, revolves around the just balance whose relation to every side is equal. It necessarily entails being higher than other things, because most created things are spherical, and whatever is in the middle of a sphere is higher. Also, because every part beyond the middle, when you compare it to the extremity adjacent to it, has less distance between it and that extremity than it has between it and the middle. The just balance necessarily entails excellence (jawda), and height necessarily entails dominance (ghalaba), power (satwa), abundance (kathra), and intensity (shidda). Height may also entail disturbance (idtirab), which brings mixing (ikhtilat), cutting off (iqtita'), and weakness (du'f).

From the original meaning, the wasat of any thing is its most just part, and the wasat of a thing is what lies between its two extremities. When the sin is vowelled with sukun, it is an adverb of place, or it refers to what is solid. When its parts are separate and distinct, it is with sukun. Wasata it: he cut it into two halves. Tawassata baynahum: he acted as an intermediary among them, and took the middle between the bad and the good. Wasata al-qawm and tawassatahum: he was in their midst, the most noble of them in lineage and the most elevated in station, and he was the one who stood between the people. Wasatat al-rahl: the part of the saddle between its front and back. Awtas: a valley in the lands of Hawazin, because of what Duraid ibn al-Simmah described it as: it is neither a hard, stony tract nor a smooth plain, meaning that walking in it is heavy, being like sand yet neither sand nor soil.

From excellence, which is necessarily linked to the goodness of the middle, comes the chapter heading. The middle prayer (al-salat al-wusta) is the best of prayers. The peacock (tawus) is a fine bird. The handsome man and silver. Land that is green, in which there is every kind of plant. The matus is like the best of a good thing. Tawas (with fatha) is the moon, and the beauty and freshness of a face after illness. Tatawassat al-mar'a: the woman adorned herself. Tawas: a night among the nights of the dark moon, as if it is from the category of removal, or with regard to the view that stars are more beautiful in the deepest darkness.

From height: sata al-faras: the horse extended its stride far. The sa'it is a horse with a long stride, one that raises its tail while standing, and the tall one. Wasit al-kawr: its front part. From intensity and dominance: sara al-ma' wasiyatahu: the water overcame the mud. Sata 'alayhi wa bihi: he attacked him or overpowered him by force. The rider of the she-camel put his hand into her womb to extract what was in it of the stallion's water. The horse: it took the bit in its teeth. Satahu: he pressed hard upon him. The sa'it is a stallion in heat, taken from one herd of camels to another; sata'aha, with hamza, meaning he mated with her. Al-wats, like al-wa'd, is a strong blow and a breaking. Al-wati is a furnace and the heat of war. Al-wati also means the intensity of an affair. Like kitab, al-ra'i. Tawati'u 'alayya: they wrestled with one another, meaning they exchanged evil among themselves. The waves clashed. Awtas: a valley in the lands of Hawazin, because it is harder than pure sand. The sawt is the whip with which one is struck, and also intensity and striking. The misawat is a horse that does not give its full speed except with the whip. The siyat are the stripes of the palm frond on which are its clusters, i.e. its bunches; and al-kirab are the thick, broad stems of the palm fronds. Sawata: he brought that out. Al-tawas, with fatha: treading; with damma: lasting of a thing, and a medicine drunk for preservation. Tawas, like sahab: a night among the nights of the dark moon. And "I do not know where he took it," i.e. where he went with it.

Tisa, like rida, tasa: fat overcame his heart so that he became stuffed, like tasa, meaning with waw. Tasi'a, also hamzated, like fariha, and the plural of tasa' and tasa'; so he is tasi', stuffed, or changed through eating fat. Atsa'ahu al-shib'a: satiety made him ill, and my soul is distressed. This falls under disturbance, mixing, and weakness.

From abundance: al-wasat, which is the she-camel that fills the vessel, and it enters into the category of the abundant. Al-tays: a great number, and everything on the face of the earth of dust and rubbish, or a creature with many offspring like flies, ants, and vermin, or fine dust like tayslan, in all of these. Also the abundance of every thing of sand, water, and other things. Sata al-ma': the water increased. Al-suwaytu': a broth with much water. From mixing: siyat, like kitab, a well-known sufficiency; and sata al-ta'am: he tasted the food. The sa'it is a stallion in heat, taken from one herd of camels to another. Sata al-ra'i 'ala al-naqa: the herdsman put his hand into her womb to extract what was in it of the stallion's water. The sawt is the whip with which one is struck, and also mixing and striking. The siyat are the stripes of the palm frond on which are its clusters. Sawt batil: a light coming out of a window. Sittu al-shay' bi al-sawt: I struck the thing with the whip. Also the sawt is what is mixed with something, like the misawat, and a child of Iblis. The misawat is a horse that does not give its full speed except with the whip, and istawata amruhu: his affair became disturbed and mixed. Amwaluhum sawiyatun baynahum: their wealth is mixed among them. Al-tus, with damma, is a medicine drunk for preservation. The peacock is a bird, and the land that is green, in which there is every kind of plant. From cutting off: al-tas, i.e. the vessel from which one drinks; and the sawt is a share and the surplus of a pool. From weakness: the wasat, the smallest part of the poets' houses (verses), which is the shortest of them. Tasa'a, like mana'a, hamzated: he was shy.

When he had established for them the middle, whoever occupies it is worthy of not being hidden from him in any of its sides, and this entails that they are the best. He said: ﴿That you may be﴾, meaning: you, not others, ﴿witnesses﴾, as the expression with this form conveys, rather than saying "that you may witness." And He said: ﴿over mankind﴾, meaning: all of them. Since the Messenger (ﷺ) was the middlemost of them, He said: ﴿and the Messenger be﴾, meaning: not anyone else, by what his exclusive status as the middle of the middle requires, ﴿over you﴾ specifically, ﴿a witness﴾ that you followed him and affirmed him, so you became "the best nation brought forth for mankind," and that he had conveyed to you during his lifetime. When he died, he left among you a book that is miraculous and mass-transmitted, which water cannot wash away nor fire burn, because it is preserved in hearts and recited by tongues until the command of God comes. For this reason He expressed it with the particle of elevation. Understand the construction of the speech thus: they gained two honours, that no one bears witness over them except the Messenger, and that they need no other testimony over the rest of the nations besides their own testimony. This forestalls the assumption that others bear witness over them as they bore witness over others, and the assumption that others are not accepted as witnesses against them except by the testimony of the Messenger, just as they were not accepted against themselves except by that.

When He had informed them about what ﴿the foolish will say﴾ and knew their reply, and explained the secret of the change, He explained the reason for directing them to two qiblas in His saying: ﴿And We did not make﴾, meaning: by Our majesty which no one can contend with, ﴿the qibla﴾. Al-Harrali said: its very formulation contains the information that the qibla is something made, i.e. appointed, from a reality beyond it, a trial through changing the rulings, so that the heart's attachment is to God the Wise and not to the firmly established action. Thus the outward direction serves as a sign of the one who follows sincerely, and he remains steadfast when the rulings change, by what is in his heart of true attachment to God and turning to Him wherever He turns him. And it serves as a sign of the one who answers for an outward purpose that is not supported by inward sincerity, so he attaches himself to what does not endure when it changes. End of quotation.

He made clear that it was the first qibla by His saying: ﴿that which you were upon﴾, and He made clear that the reason was distinction among people by His saying: ﴿except that We might know﴾, meaning: by what We have of majesty through armies, messengers and others, at the time of the command to change from it, ﴿who follows the Messenger﴾ in everything he commands, following that shows the firm establishment of his faith, ﴿from one who turns﴾, meaning: who apostatises, ﴿after having faced it﴾, turning back, ﴿on his heels﴾, a sign attached to something existing by which proof is established in the course of your customs. The 'aqib is the back part of the foot. Al-Harrali said: so that We may make a clear sign for the truthful and others, such that knowledge of it encompasses the one who knows the unseen before it happens and after it happens, and the one who does not know the unseen except through knowledge of what the nun of the plural of majesty informs him of. This is its direction and the direction of what comes similarly in the Qur'an and the Sunna. End of quotation.

Then He made clear how severe it was for those who clung to habit, because the animal and bestial power dominated them and they were not trained in submitting to divine commands by casting off familiarity and humbling the self. So He said: ﴿And indeed it was﴾, meaning the change, ﴿truly a great burden﴾, meaning heavy and very difficult, because parting from what one is familiar with, after the soul has been at rest with it, is an extremely hard matter. Then He made an exception for those whom He supported with a spirit from Himself and tranquillity, saying: ﴿except for those whom God guided﴾, meaning: God, to whom all command belongs, created guidance in their hearts, so they submitted to what He guided them to, by the share of evidences.

Because their acceptance of this command and their steadfastness when the rulings changed came from faith and all-encompassing knowledge, Almighty and Majestic God made their deeds and their turning towards the first qibla part of faith. So He said: ﴿And God would never waste﴾, meaning: the One to whom perfection is absolute, ﴿your faith﴾. Al-Harrali said: from what loss and waste are derived, which is neglect in something that has benefit and fruit, until it has no benefit and no fruit. ﴿Your faith﴾, meaning: the one declared in your saying: ﴿We believe in God﴾, the sincerity of whose claim is indicated by your saying: ﴿and we are sincere to Him﴾, in any matter, not in your prayer toward the first qibla, nor in distinguishing the truthful among you from the hypocrite through the trial of changing the rulings concerning the qibla and other things, nor in your being singled out by Him, glorified is He, over the People of the Book who deny His signs, turn away from His pleasure, and break His covenants.

When He had exalted His sacred self above all this loss, He gave the reason in a more general form, saying: ﴿Indeed God﴾, meaning: who encompasses all attributes of perfection, ﴿toward mankind﴾, meaning: those who are more general than believers and others, who waver between the state of guidance and trial, ﴿is Kind﴾, meaning: He has mercy on whom He wills, of those who draw near to Him through righteous action, out of His tenderness toward them. For tenderness (ra'fa), as al-Harrali said in his commentary, is the inclination of one who inclines toward someone who has no connection with him, so it is the mercy of one who has a bond with the one who shows mercy. He said: mercy (rahma) encompasses even those who have no bond with the one who shows mercy. He said in his explanation of the names: the one who is treated with tenderness is kept by the care of tenderness such that, in its inner secret, it preserves the appearance of what calls for pardon for its sake, in its outward manifestation. End of quotation.

This is the requirement for it being the most intense, most eloquent, and most gentle of mercies, as they have said.

﴿Most Merciful﴾ toward whomever He wills. [p. 216] Even if he had made no effort toward the union (*wuslah*), He would uproot him from his sins with an uprooting far stronger than his clinging to them, and would establish him in what the Divinity is pleased with. This agrees with what the scholars have said: "Ascend from the high to the higher." The mercy of One from whom there is no cause calls for a kindness toward him that is more eloquent in its kind, because it is an initiation (*ibtida'*). The first kind, however, is more eloquent in itself because of the cause that necessitated it.

If "the people" means the Arabs, then it is good news for him (ﷺ) that his eye will be gladdened by making them part of his party, by granting steadfastness to those who were then turning toward him, and by turning those who had been turning away toward him. If "the people" is meant more generally, then it is good news that most of creation will follow him (ﷺ). When Jesus (peace be upon him) descends, true universality will be realized along the Muhammadan path, with all of creation following him (ﷺ). And God knows best.

It is also possible that this is a justification for the whole statement from its beginning. The meaning would then be that the two attributes of His compassion and His mercy require distinguishing between the believers and others, for the sake of justice among people, because placing the reformer on the same level as the corrupter pains the reformer. What will come, God willing, at the end of *Bara'ah* (Surat at-Tawbah) of what benefits the recollection of this here.

(p-217) When the preceding discourse had signaled to the people of eloquence that a change concerning the qibla was about to occur, they anticipated news of it. Allah, having shown His compassion and mercy toward people in general, made this clear specifically through His Messenger: that turning him toward the Ka'bah was an act of compassion toward him and a mercy to him, in addition to the benefits mentioned earlier. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face﴾. Al-Harrali said: In this is a report, a kind of announcement, to one who awaits a matter or news, which conveys with the future event the rarity of its occurrence. It informs that when the Prophet (ﷺ) harbored in his heart the desire to face the Ka'bah, which is "a station for the people" (qiyam lil-nas), at a time when he was a messenger to all humankind, and when he (ﷺ) followed the religion of his father Abraham (peace be upon him), he was content with Allah's knowledge of his wish and did not ask for it outright. This is because supplication is the fulfilment of a need for those who seek, whereas being content with Allah's knowledge is an act of worship. Allah answered the turning of his face despite the rarity of its occurrence, as indicated by "qad" (certainly), which signifies diminution both of the turning and of the seeing. ﴿Toward the sky﴾: this informs that Allah made the sky the special direction of the supplicant's face, just as He made the unseen of the hearts the special direction of the worshipper's face. The one praying returns to the unseen of his heart and does not raise his gaze to the sky. "Let people cease raising their gaze to the sky during prayer, or their sight will be snatched away." The supplicant, however, turns toward the sky and extends his hands, as in the saying: "until we saw the whiteness of his armpits." End of the summary.

﴿So We shall surely turn you﴾, meaning: as a consequence of that seeing, We shall indeed turn you, without doubt, ﴿to a qibla﴾. Al-Harrali said: He made it indefinite (nakira) because behind it lies the general qibla of the one who turns in his movements. That is the qibla toward which one faces the face of Allah, not toward a visible object from among Allah's creation. Thus the scope of the qibla extends from the particularity of the Syrian qibla, to the establishment of the Hijazi qibla, to the all-encompassing universal qibla. In His saying ﴿that you will be pleased with﴾ is an indication of His approval of turning to this qibla, because contentment (al-rida) is a description of one who approves of what he wills. Everything that occurs by will is not a source of contentment until approval confirms it. If it is followed by lifting or alteration, then it is willed but not pleasing. End of quote. It is shown that the one pleasing to Him is the Ka'bah by the fa' of consequence in His saying ﴿So turn your face﴾. As for your heart, its turning is only toward Allah, the unseen toward the unseen and the apparent toward the apparent.

﴿Toward the direction (shatr) of the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning: specify the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram). Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, in al-Risalah (his treatise on legal theory), used a number of Arabic verses to prove this and said: All of this from their poetry shows that the shatr of a thing is the intention toward the very thing itself. If it is visible, then the correct orientation is by sight; if it is unseen, then it is by ijtihad (independent reasoning). ﴿The Sacred﴾: his expressing it this way rather than "the Ka'bah" contains breadth. Al-Harrali said: Allah named it "sacred" (haram) for its sanctity, since it has never been entered except by His permission, and it is entered only in a manner of devotion and humility. Thus it is forbidden (haram) to whoever enters it in the manner of an arrogant person or a bewildered one. End of quote. [From Imam al-Mawardi: every place where Allah mentions "the Sacred Mosque" the intended meaning is the sanctuary (al-haram), except here, where the intended meaning is the Ka'bah. End of quote. He expressed it in this way because the context concerns prayer, the greatest purpose of which is prostration. Further explanation will come at ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:217].] (p-220) In the Muwatta', on the authority of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed, after he had come to Medina, sixteen months facing toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Then the qibla was changed two months before Badr."

When He, glorified is He, gave him glad tidings of the change initially, and then brought about the promised matter a second time, He indicated a third glad tiding: the multiplication of his community and its dispersal throughout the regions of the earth. So He gathered them to Himself in His saying: ﴿And wherever you may be﴾, meaning: from whatever direction of the earth which He has bequeathed to you.

﴿So turn your faces toward it﴾, by directing your hearts toward Me.

When He had clarified and established this, He explained that those among the People of the Book who find fault with His religion over this matter know well the truth of this change and that it is among the signs of his prophethood. So He said: ﴿And indeed those who were given the Scripture﴾, meaning: the Jews and the Christians. He did not describe them here as foolish, in order to affirm their knowledge in His saying: ﴿surely know that it﴾, meaning this change, ﴿is the truth﴾, meaning: there is no other truth after it concerning the matter of the qibla that could abrogate it at all.

﴿From (p-221) their Lord﴾, meaning the One who is benevolent to them by sending this Messenger, who relieves them of their burdens, and whose message they had been awaiting. Yet when he came to them, they rejected his mercy. Allah, glorified is He, placed this within a context that both warns and gives hope, to console them, to strengthen them, to fortify their resolve, and to establish them. He concluded the verse with: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾, meaning He who encompasses everything in power and knowledge. Al-Harrali said: With the letter ya' (the third person), meaning turning away from them; with the letter ta' (the second person), meaning addressing them. In this is an announcement of their persistence in their evil states at two levels: one persisting in an evil for which He threatened them when they approached it, and another persisting in something worse, for which, in the threat, turning away from them and addressing others was required, others who had not reached the same level of evil and distress as those who turned away (p-222).

When the opening of the verse gave hope regarding the People of the Book, and its ending cut that hope off from them, it stated plainly what the ending had hinted at. It informed him (ﷺ) of the outcome of their affair: that there is no agreement between him and them at all, nor agreement between the two groups of them, even though all of them are from the Children of Israel. This was to relieve him (ﷺ) of longing for the guidance of some of them. So Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Book﴾. It is phrased in the passive to alert to their humiliation. ﴿the Book﴾ means: from the Jews and the Christians. ﴿every sign﴾ means: of the signs that are heard, encouraging and warning, and of the signs that are seen, showing what is distant and what is near. ﴿they would not follow your qibla﴾ means: this one to which you have been turned, and for which you were the most worthy, since it is the means of standing for mankind, just as you are a messenger to all mankind. Their turning away is not due to doubt, which would disappear if the doubt were removed, but due to obstinacy. Then He indicated to him that they would set traps for him, hoping that he might return, even for an hour of the day, to their qibla, so that they could use this to discredit him. So He said: ﴿And you are not one who follows their qibla﴾. Then He pointed to their fault in their disagreement and division, together with their prohibition of it, saying: ﴿Nor are some of them followers of the qibla of others﴾, meaning the People of the Book, despite their closeness in lineage. This is an incitement to the Arabs to remain steadfast in keeping away from them and to beware of being deceived by them.

Since their religion had been abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a earlier ruling by a later one), Allah, glorified is He, informed that their steadfastness upon their qibla, despite this, was merely caprice. He spoke to the head (of the community) directly, to make the community averse to them and to warn them against them, so that this would be more likely to win acceptance of the following: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾. Since this context concerns the qibla alone, He said: ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾. Al-Harrali said: He left it indefinite, and did not say as in the first instance "after that which," because what was mentioned in the first was evident, while what this refers to is hidden. The word "min" (from) is used, which denotes the starting point of origin, because the origin of the knowledge that came here is hidden, while in the first case it is manifest. That was concerning the religion whose source is reason, whereas this concerns the direction of prayer, whose source is religious law and the unseen. Al-Harrali said: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers﴾, according to the principle already mentioned: whoever glances at any quality of something is subject to it in its most subtle form, and he describes each rank according to its measure. So what raises the Prophet (ﷺ) above this is that it is a matter of displaying his desire and eagerness for the guidance of creation, which he was created with, mercy within him, and seeking to be lenient in falling short of it, out of regard for the right of Allah, exalted is He. The substance of Allah's command to him, when He instructed him without interpreter or intermediary, was that he should pardon those who wronged him and join ties with those who severed them. Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) would seek reconciliation with those who cut themselves off from him, until He made it binding upon him to abandon that and leave it, and he would comply with the ruling even though he had knowledge. From this is his saying: "O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know." So within every address to him, Allah, mighty and majestic, manifests His compulsion upon him to adopt the judgment of truth and to carry out justice, which is the greatest praise for him and an upholding of His command to him. He is praised by being addressed with the discourse of compulsion to carry out justice and to limit himself in the matter of his mercy to the worlds. Thus He elevated him above being one who places mercy in a place deserving of retribution. So what unites the meaning of the opposite wrongdoers is this: whoever places retribution where mercy belongs commits the lesser wrong, or whoever places mercy where retribution belongs, changing the order by putting grace in the place of justice. Upon this is everything that comes in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾ [Yunus: 94], meaning: in carrying out justice, ﴿do not be among the doubters﴾ [Yunus: 94] in seeking grace for the people of justice, for Allah carries out His justice just as His grace overflows. Likewise His saying: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ [Abasa: 1] ﴿because there came to him the blind man﴾ [Abasa: 2]. This contains a manifestation of his praise through his eagerness to win over the more distant and to join those who had cut themselves off, until he turned away from them by the ruling and the enforcement of compulsion upon him in that. So he did not turn from the command of the charge to the judgment of the Book in truth, except by being compelled to it. Thus he is praised for what he was forbidden, because his address in that matter in the Qur'an is always between grace and justice, while the address to the rest of creation is between justice and injustice. Between the two addresses lies the distance between the ascending degrees and the descending depths, in the requirement of the two similar addresses that differ in knowledge. End. What clarifies this will come later in His saying: ﴿Allah pardon you. Why did you give them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43], in Surat al-Tawbah.

When He concluded the address with the allusion in His words, "their desires" (2:145), indicating implicitly their knowledge of the truth of this change (*tahwil*, the change of the qibla), just as He opened it by informing about it explicitly, He returned to emphasizing the information about what they were in regard to its certainty. This indicated what they concealed of obstinacy, which necessitates persistence in corruption. He then said, implying it in a manner that may apply to the Prophet ﷺ, glorifying this recognition by ascribing the giving to Himself, glorified is He: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾, meaning, by the majesty We possess, which they recognize, ﴿know it﴾, meaning the change (*tahwil*), which includes an increase in their certainty of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ and the completeness of their knowledge of it, ﴿as they know their sons﴾, meaning they have no doubt about the truth of that in any respect, because its evidences are manifest to them. For they know the Messenger ﷺ through all his attributes, [a knowledge] about which they have no doubt, because it comes from Allah, in whose word there is no inconsistency. Thus they came to know the soundness of this change with this knowledge. This is as they have no doubt about anything by which knowledge of their sons is attained, due to the intensity of their closeness to them. The summary is that their knowledge of his prophethood increases them in knowledge of the truth of the change [with insight, because it is part of his description, and their knowledge of the matter of the change] firms them up in the truth of his prophethood, since it is among what is established from it. For this reason al-Harrali (al-Ḥarrālī) said: in His informing about their certainty by direct observation of what was mentioned to them about his matter, because (p-227) the one who recognizes a thing is the one who had a clear perception of it through evidences, then denied it due to its confusion for him, then recognized it through a certainty he recalled, because of what preceded of its manifestness in his perception. Therefore this is the meaning of recognition (*ma'rifah*), since it is tied to the senses, and the sight of the heart is more complete than knowledge taken from reflection (*'ilm*). It is not permitted regarding the attributes of the Truth because its meaning includes the condition of indefiniteness. For this reason it is said: recognition is a boundary between two knowledges: a knowledge through witnessing things in their appearances, and a lesser knowledge that infers things by their signs. In it, that is in the comparison with sons, there is an indication of the continuity of their recognition of him, existence after existence, until his manifestation. Even if his witness against them were only their migration from their lands in Syria to the place of hardships in the land of the Hijaz, to await and expect him.

﴿But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ (2:89). He made the example through mention of sons because of the intensity of a father's care for his son, due to its being attached to his heart. So in it is an indication of the intensity of their attachment to him before his coming. ﴿Indeed, a party of them﴾, meaning of the People of the Book, ﴿conceal the truth﴾, meaning they hide it and do not make it known.

Since it does not necessarily follow from this that they know it, and their knowledge of it does not necessarily entail its being present to them at the time of concealment, He said: ﴿while they know﴾, meaning that it is true and that they are sinners by concealing it. Thus He made them categories: a category that recognized it and followed it, a category that recognized it and denied it, as is implied in its meaning, and (p-228) a party that knew it and concealed it. In singling out this party with knowledge there is an indication of the difference between the state of one who recognizes and the state of one who knows. For this reason they were three categories: a steadfast recognizer, a denying recognizer who is the worst of them, and a knowing concealer who is attached to him. In the pattern of "they conceal" and "they know" there is an indication of their persistence in knowledge and their persistence in concealment.

And because this whole (combination) indicates the dominance of the Truth over creation, guiding whomever He wills of them and testing whomever He wills, so that His mercy and His vengeance may become manifest through it. This is the Truth, the judgment that has been carried out, and the disposition of Muhammad (ﷺ) would tend to pause over it because of his desire for mercy and his adherence to the ruling of the command. So the Truth addressed him with His saying: ﴿The truth﴾. That is, this distinction and classification, which necessitates the levels of the degrees of Paradise and the levels of the depths of Hell, is the Truth. Or the meaning is: the Truth about which you were informed in this surah or these verses, or the kind of truth that exists ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to you by driving away those whose following would harm, just as He does good to you by drawing near those whose following would benefit. ﴿So do not be among those who doubt﴾ regarding what he explained of its like: the confusion of the two levels that occurs from him between grace and justice, and that which occurs from others between injustice and justice. [End of quotation from al-Biqa'i's source.] In it there is addition and alteration. In emphasizing the matter sometimes by knowledge, sometimes by recognition, and sometimes by other things, there is an emphasis on the obligation of following him (ﷺ) and a removal of the doubts that the foolish people, who know it, cast forth.

Al-Harrali said: The mumtari (one who doubts) is from imtira' (disputation/doubting), which is the affectation of mirya (doubt), and mirya is a dispute that draws out the evil hidden within the disputant, from imtira' ma fi al-dar', which is milking it completely. And because it is the state of the one in doubt, it is sometimes applied to him.

When he had explained that none of these groups follows the qiblah of another, which implies that each of them has a qiblah of its own, and had established that the People of the Book did this out of obstinacy, he affirmed what the preceding discourse contained in a more general form, and derived the conclusion from it. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿For each there is a direction﴾, i.e., for each group of those mentioned and for others, ﴿towards which he turns﴾, i.e., an aim that he intends, turns his face towards, and inclines his heart towards, whether it is the qiblah for prayer or any other of all the objectives. ﴿He is turning towards it﴾. If the lam is kasrah (muwalliyhā), the meaning is huwa mutawalliyhā, i.e., he is the one performing the act of tawallī (turning), that is, inclining towards it with his face. This is because the root (māddah) revolves in every arrangement around the sense of inclination, as will come, God willing, at the end of al-Anfāl (p-230). Thus wallā would mean tawallā, just as qadima means taqaddama. It is well known that there is a difference between tawallāhu (to turn to it) and tawallā ʿanhu (to turn away from it). If it is read with a fatḥah (muwallāhā), the meaning is: he is made to incline towards it.

Al-Harrālī said: In the reading muwalliyhā with a kasrah there is an indication of the difference in the natural dispositions (jibillāt) of the people of the religions, and of each group being established in what it was naturally disposed to. In the reading muwallāhā (with a fatḥah) there is a manifestation of the reality of this, namely that this is not from them, but by that which the one who turns them (al-Muwallā lahum) has established them in, wherever He wills. The one who turns is left unspecified (ubhima) because among some of them there was a share of desire. It is from tawliyah, which is what is placed on the part adjacent to the body, or it is the intention, i.e., he is inclined in front of himself, adjacent to it. End of quotation.

Since their act was only for the sake of purifying the soul and freeing it, and this is not attained except by doing good and avoiding evil, He made the following statement its consequence: ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾, i.e., make the goods of every kind your aim, including the qiblah and other things, and compete in your aiming towards them. That is, they were to be quick to do acts of goodness, like one who races against an opponent and strives to outpace him, for istibāq (racing) is the effort to attain precedence (sabq), and sabq is the emergence of one of two combatants. Then He urged them to this and warned them against abandoning it, saying, by way of causal explanation: ﴿Wherever you may be﴾, i.e., from the directions towards which you have raced, the sensory and the spiritual ones, ﴿God will bring you all together﴾, i.e., the Supreme King, ﴿all of you﴾ from them, to Him, on the Day of Resurrection. Then He gave the reason for this cause by saying: ﴿Indeed God﴾, i.e., He to whom all command belongs, ﴿is over all things Competent﴾.

Mention of the Resurrection here establishes an equivalence between the two qiblahs: the qiblah of the people of excellence, the middle community (al-ummah al-wasaṭ), which was made the place of security, and the first qiblah. Al-Harrālī said: from the point of view that creation, at the Resurrection, returns to the site of the earlier qiblah in the land of al-Shām. Thus the site of truth and justice is the first of the two qiblahs in this respect, because the highest of the two qiblahs is a site of security, in that whoever enters it is safe. So the gathering (al-maḥshar) is towards their first qiblah, which is the beginning of the matter, in order to correspond with the other of the two qiblahs, the first in that the other was in this world for excellence (al-faḍl) and the first in the Hereafter for justice (al-ʿadl). And of the two calls, in that the first call was in the beginning by judgment and knowledge, and the other coming in the end is by subjugation and dominion.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 149:

When the spread of their statements concerning the qibla became great, in their diversified clamour and disputation, and they were people of knowledge and of the Book, and centuries had passed during which they were marked as being upon the right course, hypocrisy (nifaq) was emboldened by this, the wheel of falsehood and dissension turned, and the market of wickedness (fusuq) was set up on its legs there. The situation required further emphasis on the matter, magnifying its importance and disarming the doubts of the foolish. So He, exalted is He, said a second time, using an expression that conveys his (ﷺ) leadership and the waiting of those who pray behind him:

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾, that is: for the obligatory prayer, by following from this direction in which you now are, in the blessed city of Madinah, which lies to the north of the honoured Ka'bah, or from other directions, east, west, or south. ﴿then turn your face toward﴾, that is: precisely toward ﴿the Sacred Mosque﴾. As for your heart, it is toward God.

Since the implication is: you are commanded to this so that it is not supposed that this was done out of his (ﷺ) eagerness for it while he had the choice in the matter, and so it is not supposed that returning to the first qibla is a benefit because of what spread in that talk, which penetrated the hearts like the penetration of arrows, He joined to it His saying: ﴿And indeed it is the truth from your Lord﴾, affirming it with various kinds of emphasis, and attributing it to the quality of beneficence through the beneficence of nurture and the consideration of the final outcomes of affairs and their rulings.

Since the implication is: "And indeed your Lord is aware of what they say of the doubts that circulated among the people and whose consequences were feared," He joined to it what is more general than it, saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what﴾, that is, of anything of what ﴿they do﴾, that is, the foolish among the Jews and others, in the future of time, so that He weakens it, nullifies its harm, repels it and removes it far away. And according to the reading in the second person, "you" (in this pause and after it), so that He overcomes it, establishes it and keeps it, if it is sincere for His face, and otherwise makes it scattered dust. Al-Harrali said: Whoever turns his heart during his prayer toward other than his Lord, the facing of his body toward the Ka'bah will not benefit him, because that is a true ruling whose reality is the turning of the heart. And whoever turns his heart toward something of creation during his prayer is like one who turns his face away from the direction of his qibla. Just as the validity by jurisprudential standards is undone by turning one's back to the Ka'bah in the sensible sense, so acceptance is undone by turning the face of the heart away from the Lord in the unseen sense. Therefore this address is directed to those who believe and those who submit, because he (ﷺ) is free of the like of that. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 150:

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾, that is, from the regions of the earth, for the prayer, on behalf of your community. ﴿Then turn your face﴾, that is, make it face ﴿the direction of﴾, that is, exactly toward ﴿the Sacred Mosque﴾.

When it has been established, by what has been repeated, that this change of direction is an obligation regarding him (ﷺ), a definite command with no slackening from it and no concession in it, except for what was excepted in voluntary prayer, he included his community with him so that the ruling would encompass them. He also exalted his lofty station and noble rank above having anyone able to raise against him what would be called a proof (ḥujja), whether rightly or wrongly. So He said: ﴿And wherever you are﴾, that is, O community, from all directions of the Ka'ba, in all the regions of the earth, near and far. Al-Ḥarālliyy said: By mentioning his community with the word "being" rather than "setting out," there is an indication that the community falls short of the exalted states of the leaders, and that the state of the community in their seclusion is like their state in their wandering. End.

﴿Then turn your faces﴾, that is, make them face ﴿its direction﴾ for the prayer. Al-Ḥarālliyy said: In this there is an indication that recognises the validity of your prayers whether performed alone or in your homes, as He said: "When you come, pray with the people, even if you have already prayed in your household." This is unlike his own case (ﷺ), for his prayer is only valid in congregation, insofar as he leads them in prayer, and as an imam his prayer is never valid when performed alone. End.

Since it might have been thought that returning to the first qibla would nullify the matter, He, glorified and exalted, made clear that the matter is otherwise, and said: ﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾, that is, none of them, ﴿except those who do wrong among them﴾. The argument would be that they say: the Prophet who was foretold faces the House of Abraham, peace be upon him, and then does not turn from it, yet this one has not done so; or they say: he brought nothing new, and is merely a follower of us in our qibla.

Since an argument is a statement arising from certain premises properly composed, the exception was made in terms of the excepted party being involved with a part of the meaning negated of the excepted-from by way of implication (dalālat al-taḍammun). Thus it is close to what is called istikhdām (a rhetorical device). So He said: ﴿except those who﴾, that is, the people who ﴿did wrong among them﴾. For, due to their obstinacy and contentiousness, they do not return to the truth that they know; rather, for them against you there is merely a mere statement which is the material of an argument, not an argument in itself. Their description as wrongdoers, which is placing a thing in other than its proper place, as is the nature of everything that proceeds along the derivation of the root (ẓ-l-m) meaning darkness, indicates this. On this reading the exception is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), in the sense: so that no one may argue against you; but those who did wrong say, or display, wickedness and contentiousness in this, statements which they call an argument. Perhaps the secret in portraying it, on the supposition of disconnection, in the form of an exception is to urge steadfastness in the command of God, glorified and exalted, and to turn away from whoever opposes it, considering what is rooted in its refutation and bringing to mind what has become evident of their corrupt states, even if they put forward doubts whose matter is obscure and which are hard for some of the sincere to resolve, to the point that they may be thought to be an argument. It is also permissible that by "argument" is meant something more general than the certain and the conjectural, in which case the exception is connected (muttaṣil). Al-Safāqisiyy said: The source of disagreement is whether "argument" means a sound proof, in which case the exception is disconnected, or argumentation and dispute, in which case it is connected. End. Describing it as having ascendancy over them is because of the harm it produces, by its indication of enmity and dissension, not because it alters anything of the proofs. As for ﴿those who did wrong﴾: if by them are meant the Jews, they say: he only turned back to the Ka'ba out of love for his own land; had he been upon a command from God, glorified and exalted, from our qibla, he would not have changed from it. If the polytheists are meant, they say: he has faced your land and your mosque, so he is about to adopt your religion.

When He negated from the people of this qibla, through their steadfastness in it, every path to argument, there followed from this His saying: ﴿So do not fear them﴾, that is, in this matter or any other, for I will ward off their scheme from you and weaken their affair. When the rulings of His act had been made clear and what He intended of binding and loosening had passed, He urged them to hold fast to this qibla, warning against opposing it in anything at all, and said: ﴿And fear Me﴾. Then He joined to the reason for facing it His saying: ﴿And that I may complete﴾, that is, through this religion which brings the honour of both abodes and their bliss, of which this facing is part, ﴿My favour upon you﴾, by empowering you with proofs and other matters of religion, when He sent down upon you the verse: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 3], just as I completed it upon Abraham, My intimate friend, the owner of this House toward which I have directed you. Al-Ḥarālliyy said: Within this is good news of the conquest of Mecca and his taking possession of the whole Arabian Peninsula, and his thereby gaining power over all the rest of the people of the earth, through Islam's pervading all the Arabs, by whom God opened for him the eastern and western regions of the earth, reaching which the sovereignty of his community extended. End.

﴿So that you may be guided﴾, that is, and so that you may be in hope, in your own selves and in the eyes of those who see you, of those who do not know the outcomes, that you will be guided to steadfastness on this qibla and on other matters of this religion, the cause of my fear, for it brings every good and repels every harm. Al-Ḥarālliyy said: In the word "la'alla" (perhaps), as previously stated, there is an ambiguity which indicates that they are classified into two categories: one guided to steadfastness upon the Sunna, and one who deviates in it in some respect of innovation, because what belongs to the creatures is subject to wavering, while what is from the Truth is a division, and the ambiguity lies in specifying that division and classification. Therein is an announcement to one people of the lasting guidance indicated by the form of permanence, and an indication of the cutting off of another people from that persistence through what the word of hope in the verb implies. Within this is also an indication of their independent control of the matter after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), and of their division in it between one who remained upon it, constantly guided in it, and one who deviated from it, as became evident in the steadfastness of those who remained after him and the apostasy of those who apostatised. End.

﴿Just as﴾: that is, We directed you to the Ka'bah for these reasons. ﴿We sent﴾: that is, by Our majesty. ﴿among you﴾: for that very purpose, and so that you would not say what they used to say, that you have no sanctity because of your polytheism and no sin attaches to whoever harms you. Thus He completes His blessing upon you by sending one whose following will rescue you from ignorance and humiliation in this world and from punishment in the Hereafter. ﴿a Messenger﴾ characterized by being ﴿from yourselves﴾, whom you know through his lofty qualities and his exalted aspirations, which move you to follow him and to seek blessing through his opinion, things that no one other than you knows. ﴿who recites to you (p-240) Our verses﴾, which preserve whoever observes them with due observance upon the straight path, in place of your exchanging poetry with one another. Al-Harrali (al-Harrali) said: In this there is a taking of them by what is innate in their nature, namely preferring what is heard over what is seen, which is the disposition the Arabs were created with, for they are a people who prefer praise and commendation spoken by people over the comfort they might gain. So they strive to seek praise from people more than any other nation strives. How much more so when what they are called to is the praise of the Truth upon them and the perpetuation of that for them in a speech which is the speech of their Lord. Thus they attain, through this, what is beyond their intended goal, from what they were created to prefer, namely hearing over sight, unlike the rest of the nations. He then said: In this there is also a sufficiency for the Arabs from exerting their minds in acquiring knowledge and wisdom so as to extract rulings from it. Thus in the recitation of the verses to them there is a sufficiency from their relying on proofs and taking matters by evidence, and God and His Messenger undertaking their instruction, so that the honor of the learner is in proportion to the eminence of the one who teaches him. Hence the superiority of the scholars of the Arabs over all other scholars is like the superiority of the Prophet (ﷺ) over their teachers from among others. End of quotation.

(p-241) Since the context concerns an action, namely turning toward the House for prayer, and since prayer is the greatest purifier for acceptance from the filth of impurities, His saying ﴿and purifies you﴾ is placed first: that is, He purifies you in your statements and actions and causes you to grow by reviving your hearts, so that they may be exalted by good meanings and pure characters, which bring about lasting success and salvation from that which defiled the Jews and made them err, namely the disease of the heart through denying abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by a later one), concealing the truth, and spreading falsehood, which bears fruit together with error, leading others astray. Al-Harrali said: He informed them that this revelation for their souls is like nourishment for bodies. Just as their bodies grow by rain water and what comes from it, so their souls grow by the rulings of the Book and the recitation of the verses. This is their purification and growth, so that their desire for it becomes firm, because the one who is nourished has a desire for food once he realizes it. Whoever knows that adhering to the rulings is nourishment for his soul will be eager for them. When the soul grows and is purified, it becomes strong for what its faculties are meant to attain, just as the body, when strengthened by food, is enabled to do what its work requires. End of quotation.

﴿and teaches you the Book﴾, which establishes the religion and the world. Al-Harrali said: that is, the understanding (fiqh) of it. ﴿and the wisdom﴾, the subtle allusions that heal the diseases of the hearts and prevent one from following desire. Al-Harrali said: He singled out the teaching of wisdom from the general teaching of the Book, because seeking through the rulings is an effort of action, whereas seeking through the knowledge of wisdom facilitates the attainment of intellect, since wisdom is the grasping of a matter that is difficult, through a cause that is easy. Thus the wise person, by his wisdom, grasps the connection of the causes established by one another, between the causes of the immediate world and the effects of the deferred Hereafter, which the striving laborer's effort cannot reach. In completing "the Book and the wisdom" with the word "al-" (ألْ, the definite article), there is a referral to the ultimate goal which encompasses every book and every wisdom, with what the first and last generations know. He then said: (p-243) Accordingly, he (ﷺ) used to speak about the sciences of the earlier people with words that the perception of creation cannot grasp, such as his saying (ﷺ): "Use the miswak (tooth-stick) with every wood except the myrtle (ālas) and the pomegranate, for these two stir up the vein of leprosy." This is because creatures cannot restrict all the universals of sensible things; the utmost of their perception is restricting the universals of intelligible things. Whoever examines his state (ﷺ) knows that his sense perceived the encompassing of sensible things and the encompassing of their wisdoms and their tongues, the speaking and the dumb, the living and the inanimate, all together, since in ordinary custom there is wisdom, and in what breaks custom there is a sign. He then said: According to the measure of intellect that Allah, glorified and exalted, has granted the servant, He teaches him from the Book and the wisdom. It is reported from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to speak with Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), and it was as if they were speaking in a non-Arabic tongue; I did not understand anything of what they said." Since the end of what is in the Book is at this goal, He informed that His Messenger (ﷺ) (p-244) teaches them what was not in their Book, the example of his knowledge. In this there is an indication of the opening and renewal of a natural disposition by which they ascend to what was not in their Book as knowledge. End of quotation. That is because employing wisdom necessitates ascent. Thus He, exalted, said: ﴿and teaches you what you did not know﴾, that is, by way of inference from the Book, of the knowledge by which He makes you aware of statements and actions, and leads you in it along the paths of good that uncover the darkness of injustice and make visible to the sight of thoughts that are illuminated for the insights of reflection.
