This verse includes all that al-Bayhaqī related in his book al-Asmā' wa'l-Ṣifāt from al-Ḥalīmī, that what must be believed about God, glorified and exalted is He, is five things. The first is His affirmation, glorified and exalted is He, so that the denial of His existence (ta'ṭīl) is excluded. The second is His oneness, so that disavowal of association is established. These two are from His saying: ﴿And your God is one God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163]. The third is affirming that He is neither a substance nor an accident, so that disavowal of anthropomorphism is established. This is from His saying: ﴿There is no god but He﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163], because whoever cannot be replaced by another has no likeness. The fourth is affirming that the existence of everything other than Him came about through His originating it and His bringing it into being, so that disavowal of the view of those who speak of cause and effect is established. This is from His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163], ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. The fifth is that He is the Manager of what He originated and the Director of it as He wills, so that disavowal of the view of those who speak of natures, or of the management of the stars, or of the management of angels, is established. This is from His saying: ﴿and what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾ [and so on to the end of the verse].

Al-Bayhaqī said: The names of God, glorified and exalted is He, and His majesty, with which the Book and the Sunnah came, and upon which the scholars agreed (ijmā') to name Him, are divided among the five beliefs. So each of them should be joined by some of them. Some of them may be joined to two meanings and enter two or more categories. End of quote.

The reason for multiplying the proofs is that people's intellects differ. So God, glorified and exalted is He, made the world, which is the contingent existents, and which is the totality of what is other than Him, indicating His existence and His voluntary action, into two kinds. One kind is such that it can be perceived by the outward senses, and in the usage of the people of the Law it is called the witnessed (shahādah), the creation (khalq), and the dominion (mulk). The other kind is not perceived by the outward senses, and it is called the unseen (ghayb), the command (amr), and the malakūt (the dominion of the unseen). The first is perceived by common people, and the second is perceived by those of sound minds whose intellects are free of illusion and whisperings. So God, glorified and exalted is He, in the perfection of His care, compassion, and mercy, made the world with both its kinds contain totalities and details from many aspects and by many paths, which the human faculties are unable to master, by which His oneness is inferred. Some of them are clearer than others, so that all may share in the knowledge, and each attains according to what has been prepared for him. Except for one who has been sealed upon his heart. That, by God's refuge, glorified and exalted is He, is the wretched one.

When the proofs rose up, the evidences shone forth, and the doubts and causes of error were removed, He censured whoever worshipped other than Him and turned to other than Him. This is like His forbidding rivals (*andad*) right after the first verse that calls to worship, and by ending the previous verse with ﴿they reason﴾, He indicates that these people are ones whose minds have gone astray and whose opinions have gone wrong. He also made clear that some of them will disown others on the Day when the veil of heedlessness is lifted from the canopy of greatness and the Compeller appears in the attribute of retribution. So He, glorified and exalted be He, said, conjoining it to what I have estimated from what the meaning indicates, "and": or the estimate is: "So among the people is one who reasoned about those signs, believed in his Lord, and was annihilated in His love. ﴿And among the people is one who takes﴾," and these are the ones who do not reason, ﴿besides God﴾, the One for whom there is no equal, despite the clarity of the proofs, ﴿rivals﴾ from among what He created. They claim that these are His partners. This is more general, whether they are idols or leaders whom they follow in disbelief in God and in declaring things forbidden and permitted without any command from God. ﴿They love them﴾, from love (*hubb*), which is a sensing of a connection whose reality is not known, ﴿as they love God﴾, who possesses majesty and honor, by doing toward them the obedience and veneration that the lover does, as is done toward God, beside whom there is no greatness. This is if it is in the passive form. It may also be in the active form, meaning "as their love for God", because they are polytheists. ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾, who possesses all perfection, than the love of the polytheists for their rivals. He therefore poured upon them some of His perfection, because they do not equate anything with Him in any circumstance, whether in hardship or ease, on land or at sea. In contrast, the polytheists equate others with Him in times of hardship, but when in ease they see a better stone, they abandon the first and worship the second. Their love is one of desire, while the love of the believers is rational. Al-Harrali said: When the people who stand firm in God's command deserved this consideration through the intellect God gave them, whoever takes rivals besides God is not called a "people", but is reduced to the name of *nawas*, which is wavering and bewildered. It is as if He, glorified and exalted be He, was astonished at the one who did not join these people in this consideration, whose clear signs are manifest. He then informed that a group of people, in contrast to that manifest consideration of the light of reason, takes up the opposite of reason, the sharpness that advances where it should hold back and holds back where it should advance. Then this overcame them until it reached their inner selves and became love, as if it were a connection between their inner selves and their hearts and what they took as rivals besides God. Within this is an indication of something like what was made explicit to the Children of Israel, that their hearts became like stones or even harder. In the nobility of this address concerning the Arabs there is a veiling over them, out of regard for their Prophet, so that he would not state explicitly about them what he stated about the Children of Israel. In its implicit meaning there is an indication that whoever takes a rival besides God, that is due to a connection between the state of his heart and the state of what he took besides God. So whoever worships a stone, his heart among hearts is a stone; whoever worships a plant, his heart among hearts is a plant; and likewise whoever worships an animal.

﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief﴾ [2:93]. Similarly, this extends to everything that is worshipped besides God, from the highest of the two luminaries, which is the sun, down to the lowest idols, and to what occurs among creatures in the worship of some of them by others, such as the worship of the Pharaohs and the Namrudites. It also extends to what is connected to that, such as the rank of worship through following the desire that is widespread among the nations and in this nation, because whoever is overcome by the desire for something has worshipped it. So the worshipper of the sun has a heart that is a blaze, the worshipper of fire has a heart that is fire, and the worshipper of the moon has a heart that is frigid. Whoever worships the like of himself among creatures has worshipped his own desire. ﴿Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god?﴾ [25:43]. Whoever worships God is the one who has risen above others among created beings. Thus He, glorified and exalted be He, equated the address to the earlier ones, who were considered reasonable, with this category, whose state in disbelief reached the point of love, since their inner selves became bound to them in what should be exclusive to God: fear, hope, support against enemies, and aid to allies. When they imagined in them the hoped-for divinity and the feared one, they loved them for that reason, as one loves God. This is because the devoted worshipper is one who obeys commands and hastens to them; the one who hastens before the command is a lover, and the one who answers the command is obedient, so the lover is higher in both respects. End of quotation.

When He wondered at their state, He warned about the evil of their outcome and their fate, and said: ﴿If only those who wronged would see﴾, that is: if only they would see, namely those who take rivals, but He made apparent, for the sake of generality, the attribute for which they deserve what is mentioned, which is placing a thing in other than its proper place, like the one who walks along the root of derivation, which is darkness. Here it means equating those who own nothing at all with the One who owns everything. ﴿When they see the punishment﴾, that is, when they take rivals, while if they knew at the time of their humiliation and the softening of what had been hardened in their hearts, and in seeing what does not deserve anything other than Him in relation to Him, it is called a punishment. ﴿That power belongs to God﴾, who possesses all the qualities of perfection, ﴿entirely﴾, when they witness the punishment that has encompassed them, ﴿and that God﴾, who has no sovereign besides Him, ﴿is severe in punishment﴾, they did not take rivals and did not equate anyone with God. Or the estimate may be: "If you see," with the *ta'* or with the *ya'*, meaning: if you had seen, or if those who wronged themselves had seen by taking rivals, and so on. Al-Harrali said: The Almighty said: ﴿If only he would see﴾, as a continuation of matters beyond their requital, of what befell them of punishments resulting from their disbelief in this world. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "When the servant commits a sin, a black spot is made upon his heart" [hadith], up to the furthest extent of their seeing the punishment. In His saying "you see" with the *ta'*, there is turning toward the Prophet (ﷺ), a marvel for him at what befalls them of what they had inflicted. In it is an indication that this is a matter whose significance rises to the level of its vision, which is the most complete vision. In His saying "he sees" with the *ya'*, there is a sorrow for them, indicating that what they would gain from seeing the punishment, which would have restrained them from what they were upon, if they had seen it. End of quotation.

﴿When they see﴾, that is, the time at which they perceive the punishment, that is, the greatest punishment, than which there is no punishment like it, as its definite article indicates. Then He clarified it by His saying ﴿that power﴾, which is the inner strength that the capable one finds as the source of what his outward self displays, [and what his outward self displays] is the power of the faculties, their gathering and their root, while power is their outward manifestation, and the detailed formation of their creation, ﴿belongs to God entirely﴾. For there is nothing more difficult for a person than seeing his adversary's command prevailing, standing alone in might in every respect, especially [if he is an overbearing, arrogant one, severe in seizing those who disobey him, as indicated by His saying ﴿and that God is severe in punishment﴾, and especially] if the one who disobeyed Him has wronged Him by harming His allies and has gone to such lengths that he has left no room for reconciliation. Al-Harrali said: The place of the vision, in reality, is that power belongs to God entirely, stripped from all their rivals whom they loved, and from themselves, as their speaker said: ﴿We are possessors of strength and possessors of mighty might﴾ [27:33]. But since their seeing of this came from witnessing the punishment that is the most complete punishment, He mentioned the punishment, which is the outwardly visible sight, along with the statement that power belongs to God entirely. In ﴿that power﴾ there is an announcement that on the day of this sight they become aware of the inner reality of their rivals, and of their stripping of what the inner reality should be adorned with of power, since their describing them with inner love made them aware of the stripping of their inner powers through the sight that is the inner aspect of seeing, which is the inner aspect of looking. When He mentioned the matter of power, He conjoined to it what concerns might, saying ﴿and that God is severe in punishment﴾, completing the address with its outward meaning. He resumed with the great Name to show what lies between the two extremes of inner and outer, in the matter of might and power, so that with the outward sight of might there is a name that He made manifest, resumed, and placed first, just as with the inner sight of power there is a name He added and attached to it, so that what came first in the address corresponds to what ended the address, and its beginning is conjoined with its end and its end with its beginning, inward to outward and outward to inward, in both conjoined parts, in ﴿that power belongs to God entirely and that God is severe in punishment﴾. End of quotation. Or it may be said: ﴿when they see the punishment﴾ which they are now threatened with, because ﴿power belongs to God entirely﴾, so there is nothing to prevent Him from bringing it upon them, as was shown in the two preceding verses, that He has no equal, and that He is perfect in power and comprehensive in knowledge. The answer is omitted to magnify its terror, so that the mind of the one threatened goes to every kind of threat. If one kind of it were mentioned, one could settle oneself to face it. So the estimate is: if you saw, or if they saw, that time in which they witness that majesty, you would see, or they would see, a dreadful, overwhelming matter, which would occupy them from taking rivals, loving them, and other injustice. The answer is omitted because it is known, as it is omitted in similar constructions. Then He made ﴿when they see﴾ a substitution.

﴿Idh tabarra'a﴾ (when they disowned). It is from the tabarru'," which means seeking to be free of something and carrying that out earnestly and with effort. It is the manifestation of disengaging from a connection or entanglement. ﴿Alladhina ittubi'u﴾ (those who were followed) means: along with others following them. They are the leaders. ﴿Mina alladhina ittaba'u﴾ (from those who followed) means: even though the followers benefited from them in this world by following them and defending them.

Al-Haralli said: He said that to manifest the clarification of what the meaning of the first address implied, so that the verses align with one another, and the verse makes clear what is within its preceding verse, and gathers what is in the detail of the verse that follows it. It also elevates the address to what is intelligible by reason, whose knowledge precedes what the news of faith concerns, so that the light of reason is completed, by which consideration occurs, through the light of faith, by which acceptance occurs, for what is in the Hereafter is witnessed directly. Whoever understands the lesson of the visible universe deserves to hear the news of the unseen that is to come. Then he said: By this, the one who is followed is disowned in the mention, because he is last in the existence, so the meaning is as if to say: the follower clung to the one followed only so that he would protect him in the Hereafter, just as there had been a pact from him [that he would protect him in this world, and then he disowns him]. When the Exalted mentioned ﴿that all power belongs to God﴾ (Q 2:165), the mention of disowning was connected to the mention of the seizing of power and might from them. End.

Almighty God said: ﴿wa ra'aw﴾ (and they saw), that is, all of them, ﴿al-'adhab﴾ (the punishment), that is, from which there is no escape for them. Al-Haralli said: He said this as a response to the pronoun referring to all of them, and it implies that this is before the punishment overwhelms them, and during the state of seeing it. So it conveys that between their seeing the punishment and their being seized by it there is a respite in which their disputing, their disowning, and their realization of the truth, which had been hidden from them in this world, take place, through the way some of them tempted others. End.

﴿Wa taqatta'at﴾ (and were severed), that is, it was forced and deliberately caused to be cut, and cutting is between what is connected. Al-Haralli pointed to this, and its meaning is that it was cut with great force. It is also possible that the form tafa''ala indicates the repetition of the cutting over a period, so that the severance of the causes becomes apparent to them little by little, increasing their regret and their pain. ﴿Bihim﴾ (for them), that is, all of them, ﴿al-asbab﴾ (the causes), that is, all of them, which are the bonds that existed between them in this world. The sabab is that by which one reaches an attainment; originally it is the rope, then it was applied to every purpose. Al-Haralli said: This implies that their inner selves were empty of piety and of relying upon God, may He be glorified and exalted, in their worldly life, and that they had only understood the causation of some of them by others, so the causes were severed for them and were not theirs, because that happens to them in their own selves, not as something that belongs to them in others. It is as though they were a system of causes that was cut apart, so they were scattered from them. Their causes, the connections between them in this world, did not endure into the Hereafter, because they belonged to the perishable connections, not the enduring ones. For what is in this world, insofar as it was in truth, is among the enduring good deeds, and what was from desire is among the perishing and corrupt. End.

﴿Those who followed (others) said﴾: they are the followers, wishing for the impossible out of regret at having followed those who cannot benefit them, at a time when regret benefits no one. ﴿If only we had a return﴾, that is, a return to the world. Al-Harrali said: it is a returning and a coming back at the extremity of a crisis.

Since "law" (if only) here carries the sense of wishing (tamanni), its answer is in the subjunctive, so He says: ﴿we would disown them﴾, that is, the leaders there, and we would humiliate them, ﴿as they have disowned us﴾ and humiliated us here.

Al-Harrali said: In this there is an announcement of their regret over following those who were taken in place of their Lord, and a depiction of their regret as being based on a supposed benefit that is not certain, just as their clinging to those leaders was based on a supposed benefit that is not certain. Thus it affirms for them, in the Hereafter, the condition they had in this world: grasping at what is merely imagined and being heedless of what is known. End of quotation.

Since some of these things are the fruit of their deeds and others are the report of their statements, Almighty God said, by way of resumption (isti'naf, a new sentence that answers an implied question), in reply to one who asks: "They have already seen the consequence of their beliefs, so do they also see the consequence of their bodily actions?" ﴿Thus﴾, that is, this dreadful and awesome matter, ﴿God shows them﴾, He who possesses complete power and perfect majesty, ﴿their deeds﴾, the evil ones and others, ﴿as anguish upon them﴾, that is, as a sighing over what has passed. He uses the general for the specific, the effect for the cause. By using the preposition of elevation ("upon") He indicates their domination and the severity of their humiliation, so He says ﴿upon them﴾.

Al-Harrali said: Since their beliefs were, for them, sources of anguish, He showed them their deeds, which they had done seeking good in this world, as sources of anguish. ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make it scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23], just as the deed of one whose heart loves and devotes itself to what is other than God. In this there is an indication that the deed of every doer is returned to that in which his heart rests, in which his soul is calmed, and to which his fear and hope are attached. Whatever has come to dominate his inner self is his lord, to whom his deed is directed. So he finds no reward from him, because he has disowned him, and so it becomes anguish for him. Thus He, glorified and exalted, informed that they will not help them in the Hereafter nor repay them for their deeds, so their devotion to them did not benefit them. The one who was followed among them was himself devoted to his own self, and so he found no reward for his deed in it, and therefore each of them sighed over the good deeds he had done, because they were nullified. ﴿And it has been revealed to you and to those before you: if you associate (others with God), your deed will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. Anguish (hasrah) is the most intense regret over what has been lost, which causes the one who grieves to be cut off from what he laments. End of quotation.

They will enter the Fire with their deeds. ﴿And they are not﴾, that is, they are not those who have missed out on exiting, but even if they come out of the blaze into the frigid cold, they will return to it ﴿as ones who will come out of the Fire﴾ on any day of the days or any hour of the hours. Rather, they will remain in it forever, through the length of ages and the passing of eons. This is unlike the disobedient believers, for when they come out of it they do not return to it. Al-Harrali said: In this there is an indication of their intent to flee from it and to get out, as He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Whenever they wish to come out of it, they are returned into it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. He informed that their aim of coming out does not benefit them. So no hope remains for them that could raise them out of it, until the cutting off of their hope in their own selves is joined with the cutting off of their hope in those whom they clung to among their associates. ﴿And they are not from it be brought out﴾ [al-Hijr: 48], as He said about the people of Paradise, to indicate that despair and severance come upon them from their own selves. Just as the course of their deeds in the world proceeded from themselves in their own view, the report of their recompense has proceeded in the same sense, as He said: the deeds of the people of Paradise, in their view, are from the guidance of their Lord, and the mention of their recompense has come in the same sense, according to what the difference of the two expressions requires. End of quotation.

Perhaps the verse also looks back to His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. That is, just as among the People of the Book there are hypocrites and open opponents, so too among the Arabs. Thus His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6] comes to include the four categories. Then He followed this with the hypocrites among the Arabs, then the hypocrites and dissenters among the People of the Book, then the open disbelievers among the Arabs. So the two Arab categories frame the two categories of the People of the Book, as an indication that they are the primary intended audience, that most of them will believe, and that they will overcome the People of the Book and slay them like dogs are slain.

[p-315] When the Exalted and Glorified One had marvelled at those who went astray, and had made clear the outcome that would restrain anyone with even minimal intellect, they thereby belonged among those who turn back after turning away, and who submit after arrogance. He addressed all of them, as He did in the first verse of divine oneness (tawhid), saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:21], addressing them with gentleness, by the general permission to partake of what He has originated for them and bestowed upon them in mercy. This is in this dominion (malakut) that was mentioned within the proofs He set up, as a reminder of the blessing and as an expression of affection toward them, with everything that calls for love, and as an indication that He is the One who created for them what they drew near to others with, claiming those others as rivals (andad), such as the baheerah, the saa'ibah, the waseelah, and what resembles them. So He said: ﴿O mankind﴾. If you wish to be brief, say: When the Exalted and Glorified One had established the proof of His oneness through the benefits He created, and had divided mankind into two categories, the astray, whose connection is implied by a conjunction referring to something unmentioned, and the guided, which is conjoined to it, and He had concluded with the everlasting punishment of the astray, He addressed both categories with gentle and tender address, inviting them, with an everlasting benefit for them, saying: ﴿O mankind﴾, meaning all of them.

Al-Harali said: When the Exalted and Glorified One had completed the mention of the matter of religion, reaching the level of the religion of Islam that He has approved, and since religion is the nourishment of hearts and the purification of souls, He linked to it the mention of the nourishment of bodies through food, so that the mention of the two growths would be complete: the growth of the self, its outward bodily part and its inward religious part. When He made clear the nourishment of bodies and the sustenance of religions through cooperation in gathering the two matters of the righteousness of action outwardly and its acceptance inwardly, the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him said: "God accepts no deed except with the protecting scrupulousness (al-wara' al-shafi)." As it is said: The foundation of religion is scrupulousness, its ruin is luxury, and its deficiency is excess. Thus, just as the Book arranged the restriction of creation to the best of their dealings in religion, it connected to it their restriction to the best of their food in sustenance. When He mentioned religion in the level of the two categories of people and those who believe, He linked to it the mention of food in both categories. So He said: ﴿O mankind﴾, and thereby linked the address to His words, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:21], because of the bond between worship and eating. End of quotation.

Since the rank of mankind is among the lowest levels in their address, He granted them general permission, out of gentleness toward them, and did not startle them with restriction. So He said, granting them permission for what He has bestowed upon them: ﴿Eat﴾. And since on earth there is what is not eaten, He said: ﴿of what is in the earth﴾, meaning of what We have made clear to you is among the proofs of His oneness.

Since in this permission there is a reminder that everything belongs to Him, and benefiting from it depends on permission from Him, He showed them that within it there is what He has permitted and within it what He has forbidden. So He said: ﴿lawful﴾ (halalan). Al-Harali said: It is what is free of the ruling of prohibition, so that what is disliked and what is not disliked are both included. Prohibition (tahreem) is the forbidding of what, if eaten, harms the body, like carrion, or harms the self, like the flesh of swine, or places a rust (rayn) on the heart, like what is slaughtered in the name of other than God. Then He indicated that what is forbidden is foul, by His words: ﴿good﴾ (tayyiban), meaning not foul or loathsome, and its basis is what is pleasant to taste; it is described in this manner by way of the comparison of purity, because the soul dislikes what is impure because of its filth, and the lawful is what the intellect does not find repugnant, since the Law has restrained it from the forbidden. Al-Harali said: The lawful is sought to be acquired, not merely to be eaten, so that it is good, and the good is what contains no contention. End of quotation.

Since this category is the lowest of the religious, the Exalted and Glorified One joined to their feeding on what is in the earth, because they are earthly, the prohibition against following the enemy, whose affair is built upon hostility. So He said: ﴿And do not follow﴾. By the form of the reflexive (ifti'al) He indicated that this category is absorbed in clinging to him, and that they will not reach complete repudiation of him as long as they remain in this station. Their effort is necessary, because opposing him is not possible except through great striving, which they are not capable of as long as they remain at this level. ﴿steps﴾ (khutuwat) is the plural of khutwah, which is the distance between the two feet in walking. ﴿of Satan﴾, meaning his paths in his whisperings, in taking rivals and forbidding the lawful, like the saa'ibah, and permitting the forbidden, like carrion, for all of that is from his command, as will come in His words: ﴿And I will surely command them, and they will slit the ears of cattle﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:119], and so on. The word is from shatana, meaning he went far away, and shat, meaning he burned; he distances them, as al-Harali said, from the homeland of what they are upon, of conformity in their foods, to indulgence in their appetites, so that he may lead them step by step, from the step of eating from desire to eating from caprice, whereupon they are drawn from it to the forbidden things. [p-319] End of quotation. Then He justified this by His words: ﴿Indeed, he is to you an enemy﴾, by his arrogance toward your father, his deception toward him, and his request for respite to mislead you, ﴿clear﴾, meaning manifest in enmity. So do not follow the enemy in repudiating the Friend.

Then he gave the reason for explaining his enmity and for the prohibition against following him by His words: ﴿Innama﴾ ("only"), which restricts, so that the command to something good is negated from him. In His words ﴿yamurukum﴾ ("he commands you"), as al-Harali said, there is information about what Allah, glorified and exalted, empowered him with until it became a command ﴿to evil﴾, which is the corruption of the inner souls whose doing brings about harm, and ﴿to indecency﴾. Al-Harali said: it is what the nature dislikes of outward vile deeds, which the intellect also rejects and the Sharia finds repugnant. Thus the three signs of Allah, from the Sharia, the intellect and the nature, agree in its judgment, and by this the act becomes indecent. (p-320) ﴿And that you say about Allah﴾, who possesses the highest degrees of greatness, ﴿what you do not know﴾, of what you begin to speak about even the least of existing things, such as associating partners with Him, claiming a son for Him, or declaring lawful and unlawful, or other than that. Allah, glorified and exalted, has indeed gone to great lengths in this verse in beautifully calling His servants to Himself, out of His gentleness toward them and mercy for them, by reminding them, in the context of argument for His oneness, of what He has bestowed upon them: first, by creating them; second, by making the earth suitable for them; third, by permitting it to them; and fourth, by warning them against the enemy, along with other subtle kindnesses and great favours, in a context that points to all kinds of what is lawful and the reason for its being made lawful.

Al-Ustadh Abu al-Hasan al-Harali said in the book Al-'Urwa, in the section on the letter of permissibility (ḥalāl): The purpose of sending down this letter is to broaden the enjoyment of what Allah has created on earth of His bounties and goodness, (p-321) suited to their natures and temperaments, and acceptable to their souls in all aspects of enjoyment: food, drink, clothing, mounts, shelter, and all other things that are of benefit, whether Allah brought them forth or scattered them on the earth, and what their hands have made of craft, composition and mixing, so that they may witness the continual renewal of creation in every creature according to what He originated His creation. Since man was created from the purest essence of everything, enjoyment was broadened for him in every direction of benefit from everything, except what was excluded from it by the letter of prohibition and its aspect, just as the eating of the tree was excluded for Adam from the wide abundance of the Garden. So for him was the enjoyment in its entirety, except what harms his body, or corrupts his soul, or stains the knowledge of his heart. This is by its being agreeable to him in nature, its outcome being good in the morals of his soul, and his heart attributing it to its Benefactor, whom he witnesses through its beginnings and perfections by experience. Then the Qur'an completed this by sincerity toward the Benefactor, without any trace of anything else in it, and by gathering its place according to the order of the Qur'an: the words of the Exalted, ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqara: 29], and from its beginnings according to the order of the exposition. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best. ﴿It is He who sent down from the sky water; from it is drink for you, and from it are trees in which you pasture [your animals]﴾ [al-Nahl: 10]—the verse, and the rest of the verses found in Surat al-Nahl and Surat Ya-Sin, for they are the heart from which the ink of the whole Qur'an flows, in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth which We have brought to life and produced from it grain, and from it they eat﴾ [Ya-Sin: 33]—the verses, and to the rest of what is in the Qur'an of the like. Within the broad scope of this letter, the trial fell upon creation through what was adorned for them from it: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires from women and children﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14]—the verse. The manner of its trial is that in proportion to one's expansion in it, one is deprived of the goodness of the Hereafter: ﴿You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20]. "Only one who has no share in the Hereafter wears these." ﴿So you enjoyed your share﴾ [al-Tawba: 69]. From seeing the evil of this outcome arose the abstinence of the ascetics; and from seeing the goodness of the trade, its profit, its multiplication to a degree beyond reach, and its bliss, in exchanging the worldly share for the share of the Hereafter, arose the scrupulousness of the scrupulous. Thus their hearts found rest through renunciation, they withdrew from toil through scrupulousness, their hearts and deeds were freed to exert effort in the path of praise, and the wretched was distinguished from the happy by desire for it or aversion from it: whoever desired the lawful became wretched, and whoever turned away from it became happy. This is the letter (p-323) whose expansiveness was restricted by the letter of prohibition, until no portion remained for the son of Adam in what exceeds the coarse food, which is a morsel and a garment to cover him and a house to shelter him. Whatever exceeds this is a trade: if he spends it, he profits and advances it; if he hoards it, he loses it and regrets it. For this reason Allah, glorified and exalted, did not permit anyone to eat it until he is characterized by goodness toward people—those who are the lowest of the addressed, as most of them have lost reason, gratitude and faith: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqara: 168]. And He erased its name from those who believe, who are those who neither remain steadfast nor persist in the best of their states, but rather become sincere; this is in His words: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you﴾ [al-Baqara: 172]. This is what the letter of prohibition made good in knowledge, and it was free from the agitations of hearts in tranquility, and it completed and made pure for the messengers, so He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 51]. It came as an answer to their question in His words: ﴿They ask you what is made lawful for them. Say: The good things are made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 4]. So whoever prefers the letter of prohibition over the letter of permissibility has purified himself, followed the best, and his guidance is sound and his core is clear. (p-324) Whoever prefers the letter of permissibility over the letter of prohibition has corrupted himself, is deprived of the guidance of the Books and the knowledge of wisdom, and of the greater permanence that he has lost through the purification, and has fallen into the corruption. Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.

Then he said, regarding that by which its recitation is attained: Know that man, since he is comprehensive, benefits from everything. As for the state of abundance, with the exception of a few things that harm him, either in himself or in others or in his Lord, as mentioned in the first chapter, that is, the letter of prohibition: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqara: 29]; ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 145]—the verse. As for the state of necessity, then without any exception whatsoever: ﴿But whoever is forced, neither desiring nor transgressing, then there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqara: 173]; ﴿But whoever is compelled by severe hunger, not inclining toward sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]. What attains the recitation of this letter is, on the side of the heart, knowledge of Allah's wisdom in what is consumed of His creatures, and knowledge of the most specific benefits of what He created, so that it may serve as nourishment in abundance or necessity, and as condiment, fruit, or medicine likewise; and knowledge of weighing the benefit of a thing against its harm, and using it according to the predominant judgment of its benefit, or avoiding it according to the predominant judgment of its harm: ﴿Say: In both there is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ [al-Baqara: 219]. This is apprehended from Allah, glorified and exalted, by considering reason and the perception of the senses in His creatures, as the monotheists (ḥanīfiyyūn) have perceived it. Al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, had forbidden wine to himself in the pre-Islamic period, and when he was questioned about this he would say: "By Allah, if I found something to buy with all my wealth that would increase my intellect, I would do it. So how could I buy with my wealth something that diminishes my intellect!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would often draw attention to the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted, in the things by which one takes or avoids, acting upon His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 169 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And He purifies them and teaches them the Book and the Wisdom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164]. "He said to Talhah, may Allah be pleased with him, when he offered him a quince: 'It drives away the bleakness of the heart.'" "He said to Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, when he had an eye inflammation, regarding barley bread and silq (chard): 'Eat of this, for it is more suitable for you.'" "He said regarding dates and cucumbers: 'The heat of this breaks the cold of that.'" And he said to a man with an eye inflammation: "Do you eat dates while you have an eye inflammation?" "He said to 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, regarding sun-heated water: 'Do not do that, O Humayra! For it produces leprosy.'" And he said: "Use the miswak with every kind of stick, except myrtle (al-aas) and pomegranate, for they stir up the vein of leprosy (judhām)." "He said to a woman who had suffered diarrhea from shubrum: 'It is hot and it is harmful. Why did you not purge with senna? For if there were anything that removes the disease, senna would remove it.'" And there is much else of this kind, which, whether he permitted or prohibited it, he drew attention to its wisdom. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, used to say to the sick: "Prepare for him khaziral, for it soothes the heart of the sick person and removes some of the sadness." Much like this is found in the sayings of the scholars, may Allah be pleased with them all, and in the tested remedies of the wise and the knowledge of the upright sages.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding His words, glorified and exalted be He, ﴿and He makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the wicked things﴾ [Al A'raf: 157]: "The good things (al-tayyibat) are what the souls of the Arabs find pleasant, and the wicked things (al-khaba'ith) are what the souls of the Arabs find repugnant." This is from the side of [the heart]. As for the side of the soul (al-nafs), its generosity is with what is shared in, [of] the lawful benefits, because withholding lawful things from their rightful recipients is forbidden. It is incumbent upon the one who possesses them to offer hospitality to the people of the Wabar (Ahl al-Wabar, i.e., the Bedouins): ﴿And when the division takes place, if relatives, orphans, and the needy are present, provide for them from it﴾ [al-Nisa: 8]; ﴿And give the relative his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Isra: 26]; ﴿So eat from it and feed the contented one and the beggar﴾ [al-Hajj: 36]. Likewise is his patience in refraining from what he desires of harmful things, in the aspects mentioned: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants and gambling...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90], up to His words ﴿so that you may prosper﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90]; ﴿And do not consume their wealth along with your own﴾ [al-Nisa: 2]; ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, it is those who are the successful﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. Likewise is mutual consent and contentment of the soul in what is shared: ﴿except that it be a trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [al-Nisa: 29]; ﴿And if they give you willingly something of it, then consume it with satisfaction and pleasure﴾ [al-Nisa: 4]. These are the three conditions of generosity, patience, and contentment in the soul. As for action and the handling of the hand, the first of these is the mention of Allah and saying the basmalah at every taking, because everything belongs to Allah. Whatever is taken in His name is taken with His permission, and whatever is taken without His name is taken as theft, not in its proper manner, and Satan shares in its taking; the one who takes it follows him in his steps and shares with him in wealth and children. A bedouin and a child came to eat food before the Prophet ﷺ without saying the basmalah, so he took their hands and said: "Indeed, Satan came to make this food lawful for himself through the two of them. By Him in whose hand my soul is, his hand is in my hand along with theirs." Then the Prophet ﷺ said the basmalah and ate, then released it and said: "Eat in the name of Allah." And he said to a young boy who was eating: "O boy! Say the name of Allah."

The second is taking with the right hand, for Satan eats with his left hand and drinks with his left hand. The right hand serves the upper part of the body, and the left serves the lower part.

The third is that one takes in a manner of modesty and dignity, avoiding grabbing like plunderers. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to eat with three fingers, and drink in three sips, and said: "It is more healthful, more wholesome, and more pleasant." And he said: "Liver disease comes from gulping."

The fourth is contentment with less than being full, because in that there is good nourishment of the body and preservation of the outer and inner senses. Among the signs of the Hour is the appearance of fatness among men from eating too much. And: "The son of Adam has never filled a vessel worse than his stomach." And: "Wisdom does not enter a stomach that has been filled with food." And: "The believer eats in one intestine, and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines," because the believer trusts in what sustains him, while the disbeliever relies on food for his strength. "A few morsels suffice the believer to keep his back upright. If he must do it, then a third for food, a third for drink, and a third for breath." End of quotation.

I say: Perhaps what is meant is that the disbeliever eats to satiety, so he fills his belly, because the intestines, as they have said, are seven; while the believer eats to sustain himself, so he eats in one intestine, which is a seventh of his belly. If not, then in two intestines and a part, which is a third. And Allah, glorified and exalted be He, knows best.

Al-Harrali said: The fifth is praising Allah, exalted be He, at the end, for whoever does not praise Allah at the end has disbelieved in His blessing, and whoever praises other than Allah has believed in His tyrant (taghut). Thus, by these matters of knowledge in the heart, states in the soul, and etiquette in action, the recitation of the letter of lawfulness (harf al-halal) becomes sound, the good of this world is attained, and the foundation for building the good of the Hereafter is extended. And Allah, glorified and exalted be He, is the Guardian of success. End of quotation.

[Page p-330] When Glorified and Exalted is He forbade them from following the enemy, He censured them for following him, even though he is an enemy without proof, merely through blind imitation of the ignorant. So He said, linking to ﴿And among the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165], marvelling at them: ﴿And when it is said﴾, i.e., by whatever speaker it may be. Since the address was to people in general, and most of them were imitators, especially of their fathers, He repeated the pronoun, meaning most of them, and said: ﴿to them, "Follow"﴾, i.e., exert yourselves in restraining yourselves from the desire that Satan has breathed into them. In His saying to them ﴿what God has sent down﴾, i.e., the One who possesses all-encompassing knowledge and perfect power, there is a turning toward that Book, "in which there is no doubt" [2:2] and what is similar to it. ﴿They say, "No, [we will follow]"﴾, i.e., we will not follow what God has sent down; rather ﴿we will follow﴾, i.e., we will strive to follow ﴿what we found﴾, i.e., what we found [our fathers doing]. Al-Harrali said: it derives from *al-ilfa'*, which is finding a matter in accordance with what the one who reflects upon it or looks at it is accustomed to. ﴿Our fathers upon it﴾, i.e., upon what they were in ignorance and incapacity. He said: In this there is an indication that the customs of the fathers are forbidden unless a witness of the fatherhood of religion testifies for them. Thus there is a warning, through the degrees between the state of disbelief and the lesser trial, in which people are inclined to follow the customs of their fathers. End of quotation. [Page p-331] When they refused anything but the familiar valleys of blind imitation, and so drew back from rising to the rank of those of knowledge who reflect rightly, Glorified and Exalted is He rejected this from them, rebuking them, saying: ﴿Even though, [would they follow them] while their fathers did not reason at all [2:170]?﴾, i.e., would they follow them while their fathers did not understand with the insight of their hearts ﴿anything﴾ of intelligible things ﴿and were not guided﴾ by the sight of their eyes to anything of sensible things.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 171:

Since the implied sense was: "Their likeness, then, is that of one who follows a blind man on a rough, hidden path, through vast, very dangerous wastelands," He added after it what guides to its supposition, from His saying, drawing attention to the fact that by this they have become like cattle, nay more astray, because although cattle do not understand, they hear and see, and so they are guided to their benefits: ﴿And the likeness of﴾ and He clarified the attribute that led them to this ignorance by His saying: ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, meaning: they concealed what they knew of the greatness of God, glorified and exalted is He, and His power, knowledge and wisdom, through what they held of caprice, in that they hear from the summons nothing but the jingle of the tone and the echo of the voice, without casting their minds or seeking insight. ﴿Like the likeness of﴾ (p-332) al-Harrali said: The mathal (likeness) is what is obtained within perception from the realities of sensible things, so that it is finer than the sensible thing, and thus it occurs as a clarifying image of a meaning like the intelligible meaning, and the more apparent of the two becomes a likeness for the more hidden. Therefore the clarification of a likeness comes through a likeness, so that there is in it a refinement of the apparent sensible and a bringing-down of the absent known. In this verse, the clarification occurs between the two likenesses, not between the two things likened, because of the closeness of the two likenesses, meaning the point of resemblance, and the distance between the two things likened. In the mention of these two likenesses there is a correspondence that conveys two other likenesses, so this required two depictions in one likeness, as if the fullness of the expression that conveyed this concision is: "The likeness of those who disbelieve is the likeness of their shepherd who calls, like the likeness of the shepherd and the likeness of what is pastured of cattle." This is among the highest forms of address of eloquent Arabs, and whoever's understanding does not reach the gathering of the two likenesses restricts it to an interpretation by a single likeness, so he supposes in the speech: "The likeness of the caller of those who disbelieve is ﴿like the likeness of one who shouts﴾," meaning: cries out. That is because interpretation is carried by implication and supposition, whereas understanding prevents it and requires understanding the Qur'an's revelation according to its own limit and manner. He said: ﴿with what﴾, meaning: by means of something of the cattle which have no intellect, so it ﴿hears nothing but a call﴾, meaning: from the speaker concerning what is summoned to it, of the sustenance of its food and its offspring, ﴿and a cry﴾ concerning what it is driven to by the place of its calling, since the cry indicates distance and the call indicates beginning to head toward a goal. End.

So the disbelievers, in that they do not turn back from their error because of the proofs they hear, while they are people of intellect, hearing and sight, are like the cattle which hear (p-334) and see, but because they do not understand, they [do not turn back] by speech, for they hear only the apparent sound and do not grasp what lies beneath it, but rather by the stone and the staff. When the shepherd wants them to turn back from a direction, he shouts at them and throws a stone at what is in front of them, and they turn back. So they are the locus of their likeness, which is the lack of perception. And the cattle, in that they do not turn back by the call but only by a striking blow, are like the deaf, dumb, blind person who turns back only when struck in the face, so he recoils on his heels; so they are the locus of its likeness. Their caller, in that he speaks yet his speech has no effect despite great exertion, is like the shepherd of the cattle, so he is the place of its likeness. The shepherd of the cattle, in that his cattle turn back only by a blow of a stone or other, like the whip with which the deaf is driven, or like the striker of the deaf man mentioned, is the locus of its likeness. Therefore the outcome of the likeness is His saying: ﴿deaf﴾, meaning: they do not hear; ﴿dumb﴾, meaning: they do not speak; ﴿blind﴾, meaning: they do not see. It is known from this that the verse is of the type of ihtibak, in which the likeness of the caller is omitted from the first, indicated by the one who shouts, and the one shouted at is omitted from the second, indicated by those being summoned. Since the existing faculty of intellect's perception is the realities of sensible things, and He has negated from them the sense that perceives sensible things, there follows from it His saying (p-335) ﴿so they﴾, linked with the fa' of consequence, sequence and causation: ﴿do not understand﴾, because they do not benefit from their intellects, just as this deaf one is likewise. He negated it with the negating "lā" for what is impossible, and with the imperfect form, which indicates continuity, as al-Harrali said.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 172:

When Allah, glorified and exalted be He, informed that calling them does not increase them except in aversion, the address was elevated [from the people] to a higher rank than them. So He said, commanding them with a command of permission as well, which is in fact an obligation, regarding the consumption of what sustains the proof and preserves it: ﴿O you who have believed, eat﴾. Al-Harrali said: Since the address concerning matters of religion had come on two levels, the first being ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21], and the second being ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104], He commanded mankind therein to worship, and commanded those who believed to good observance toward the Prophet ﷺ. Likewise here, He commanded mankind (p-336) to eat from what is in the earth and forbade following the steps of Satan, and the address indicated that they are among those toward whom Satan turns, for commanding evil and indecency and speaking according to whim. And He commanded those who believed to eat ﴿of the good things﴾, so in their address He omitted mention of the earth, since they take their provision from the heaven. For the lowest level of faith is worshipping the One who is in the heaven and seeking provision from the One who is in the heaven, as He said to the slave woman: "Where is Allah? She said: In the heaven. He said: Free her, for she is a believer." The Exalted said: ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 22]. So He fed the earthly ones, who are mankind, from what is in the earth, and fed the heavenly ones, who are those who believed, from the provision of heaven, likewise. This address was specified by the word "lawful" since it takes its provision from heaven, partaking of what is good, being free from any state of what is in the earth that is by nature harmful outwardly or injurious inwardly. And for this reason [it is said]: "Were the world blood pure and fresh, the sustenance of the believer from it would be lawful." Thus the one who seeks provision from heaven makes what is forbidden to him lawful by taking it in case of necessity, for sustenance and not for desire, and makes what is lawful to him good by being content with what suffices, without craving (p-337), ﴿They ask you what is made lawful for them. Say: The good things are made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4]. In the locus of these two addresses is an explanation that the word "for mankind" applies to one tier of the tiers of hearts, while the phrase ﴿those who have believed﴾ applies to a tier above it, and it does not apply to a generality encompassing all the tiers of hearts. Whoever imagines otherwise is misled by the locks upon hearts that prevent contemplation of the Qur'an, for the address of the Qur'an is directed to every people of tiers according to the tier of their hearts. The address of each tier suits only it: that which falls short of it does not reach it, and that which is above it has no need of it. These tiers are many: the tier of man, then the tier of people, then the tier of those who believed, then the tier of those who (will) believe, then the tier of believers, [then the tier of believers] in truth, then the tier of the doers of good. These are seven tiers whose addresses are arranged, one above another. Beyond them are tiers above them, the tier of the certain ones, and beyond that to the states between these tiers: the state of those who submitted and the Muslims, and those described by intellect, remembrance, reflection, and hearing, and other descriptions that accompany those tiers in ascending ranks, where the lower does not encompass the higher and the lower does not rise to the address-level of the higher (p-338), to what lies beyond that, namely the particular address of the Prophet ﷺ with what befits none but him and whoever is of him from the Divine. In the orderly arrangement of these ranks there is a comprehensive summary of what occurs of their meaning throughout the Qur'an. End. And since this rank, as has preceded, is higher than the rank of people, He specified in their address, after explaining that what is not lawful is impure, by saying: ﴿of the good things﴾, and He did not come with that generality with which people are familiar.

And since they were at the first levels of faith, He alerted them to gratitude by His saying in the manifestation of majesty: ﴿what We have provided you﴾, and [We have] made it pure for you from doubts, and do not expose yourselves to what contains filth, as the polytheists made lawful of the forbidden things, nor forbid what they made lawful of them, such as the sa'ibah and what accompanies it. Then He made it explicit in His saying [commanding with a command of obligation]: ﴿and be grateful to Allah﴾, i.e., dedicate your gratitude to the Benefactor, than whom there is no blessing except from Him (p-339). This is in contrast to what comes in Surat al-Mu'minun, an address to the highest tier of the sincere ones, who are the Messengers.

And since gratitude is not valid except with monotheism, He tied it to their singling Him out in worship, saying: ﴿if you are indeed Him you worship﴾, i.e., alone, ﴿worship﴾. For His being singled out in that is a cause of gratitude; so when the singling out, which is the cause, is absent, gratitude is absent. Also, when the caused thing, which is gratitude, is absent, the singling out is absent, because the cause is one; so they are equal, each one being removed by the removal of the other. Al-Harrali said: Since this address comprises the taking of the good and gratitude, and its reality is giving from the good, the gratitude for every blessing is its manifestation according to its measure, whether of wealth, rank, knowledge, food, drink, or other things, and the spending of its surplus, contentment with the least from it, trading with its surplus seeking reward, and conveying it to its people for one who fulfills the trust, for the hands of servants are treasuries of the Generous King: "Leave people, Allah provides some of them from others." So since that is not complete except by knowing Allah, glorified and exalted be He, the Restorer to whoever spends, as He said: ﴿And whatever you spend, He will replace it﴾ [Saba': 39], they were alerted to their covenant which they were taught in Surat al-Fatihah in His saying: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5]. So it was said to them: Eat and be grateful, if you are indeed Him you worship. Whoever knows Allah as Generous finds it easy to be generous, and whoever knows Allah as Bestower and Benefactor finds it easy to be beneficent, and that is his gratitude to Allah. Whoever is certain of the replacement gives freely in giving. End.

[p. 341]

When He restricted the permission granted to them to the good of the provisions, it became necessary to explain what was foul among them so that it might be avoided. So He explicitly stated what was forbidden to them out of what the polytheists used to consider lawful, while they forbade other things. He also made understood that everything else is lawful, and that it is very abundant, so that the one addressed might increase in gratitude. Thus He said: ﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only﴾.

Al-Harrali (al-Harali) said: Since the believers' comprehension of what the address requires surpasses that of other people, the Exalted addressed them by mentioning what was forbidden to them. This corresponds to what He prohibited people from, namely following the steps (khutuwat) of Satan. So He said: ﴿Indeed, He has forbidden﴾. He made the pronoun (idmar) refer back to the first, great Name, to inform that the One who permitted them to eat has forbidden them only what is unfit for them in every respect, because of its severe harm to them in their whole being, outward and inward. When he mentioned that the forbidden thing is either forbidden because of its exalted sanctity, like the Sacred Land (al-Balad al-Haram) and the prohibition of certain matters, or forbidden because of its baseness, like the prohibition of these forbidden things, then the word "innama" (only) contains a negation of the imagined things that might be subject to prohibition, other than what is mentioned here. As if someone were to say: "This is forbidden, and that is forbidden," of the sort that the earlier scriptures forbade, or that divergent desires forbade, or that some intellectual speculation forbade, like what Israel forbade for himself. So the indication served to refute all those prohibitions. End of quotation.

The meaning, and God, glorified and exalted, knows best, is: You have forbidden the she-camel that is set free (wasilah), the free-roaming one (sa'ibah), and other things that God had made lawful, and you have declared lawful carrion (maytah), blood, and other things that God, glorified and exalted, had forbidden. God has not forbidden you from the sa'ibah and what is with it of what you have forbidden, nor anything else that you have declared lawful, except what this verse mentions. If you refer to what He, glorified and exalted, said in al-An'am: ﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am 6:118], and His saying: ﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned﴾ [al-An'am 6:121], and His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am 6:145], from My Book, you will know the intended meaning of this verse.

[p. 342]

He said ﴿carrion (al-maytah)﴾, meaning: that which people of common usage call by that name, namely that from which the spirit has departed without lawful slaughter, and it is of that which is ordinarily slaughtered. Al-Harali said: It is that which death has overtaken among animals, from the weakening of strength and the extinction of life. It is the most corrupting thing for the body, because of the corruption of its composition through death, the passing of the pleasure of its parts, its rot, the departure of the spirit of life, and the loss of purity from it.

﴿And blood﴾, meaning: that which flows, because it is a substance that has fallen back from the state of food and has not yet reached the state of the organs. It is therefore dead in terms of its specific life, degraded in its substance, except for those whom God has purified in their entirety, as in Muhammad (ﷺ), and those who have removed from themselves the impurity of the outward and the inward, by nature and by soul.

﴿And the flesh of swine﴾, because of its harm to the soul, just as what precedes it was forbidden because of its harm to the body. For among the wisdom of God in His creation is that whoever's body is nourished by the material substance of a thing, his soul is nourished by the psychic quality of that thing. "Pride and arrogance are among the coarse, the people of camel-hair (the herders of camels, al-fadaddin), and tranquility is among the people of sheep." Since the swine has been given blameworthy qualities, it is forbidden to whoever guards his soul against blameworthy character traits.

[p. 343]

Flesh (lahm) is that which covers the innermost part of the animal, from the middle of its bone, and what its outer surface reaches of the skin's surface. The use of the word is known to be predominantly applied to fresh red meat. Here it is in its original linguistic sense, comprising red meat, fat, sinews, and veins, up to the limit of the skin, and what lies between the two extremities of moist parts. And if its flesh, which is the intended object of eating and is the best of what it contains, is forbidden, then its other parts are more deserving of prohibition.

Since He forbade what harms the body and injures the soul, He forbade what stains the heart. So He said: ﴿And that over which other than God has been invoked﴾. The "ihlal" (invocation) is the raising of the voice upon seeing a matter of great importance. ﴿Over which﴾, meaning: the raising of the voice of the one raising it because of it, slaughtering it, ﴿for other than God﴾, meaning: the One who has no equal in any respect. Al-Harali said: Because what the name of God has not been mentioned over is taken from the hand of the one over whom His name was mentioned, and that is not its Creator and Owner. Its Creator and Owner is God, who made the mention of His name over it a permission for benefiting from it. And He mentioned over the ending of life those who are of His breath, not those who find no way to claim any part of it among creatures. [p. 344] The mention of the invocation (ihlal) is an informing that what is proclaimed over it by other than God's name is the most severe of the forbidden things. Its indication also serves to lighten the address concerning what is not known from hidden mention. They said: "O Messenger of God! Indeed, some people bring us meat, and we do not know whether they mentioned God's name over it or not." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Mention God's name yourselves and eat." So the forbidden thing is not what is not known to have had God's name mentioned over it, but rather what is known to have had the name of other than God proclaimed over it. In the placing of the pronoun for the forbidden thing before the words "over it" (bihi), there is an emphasis on its meaning, because they put first what matters to them most and what they are most concerned to explain. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Begin with what God began with." So, since this verse comprises the prohibition, the emphasis on the forbidden thing appears in it by giving it precedence. And in terms of conveying meaning, this is more complete than the pronoun which is delayed in it.

Since this religion is ease, with no hardship, no constraint, and no blame, He lifted the ruling of this prohibition from the one in necessity. And since the condition of necessity is that it encompasses a group of creatures, He informed them that this which has been lifted from them of the prohibition does not free them [p. 345] from the totality of the rulings. Rather, along with this concession, there remains the place of the rulings concerning transgression and aggression. So He said: ﴿Whoever is compelled﴾ [meaning: whoever is made to need by one who makes him need, and is driven by whatever necessity it may be], to eat something of what has been forbidden, to the point of being on the brink of perishing, and so eats some of it, ﴿without being rebellious﴾, meaning: intending corruption by a plot with which he schemes, out of his weakness, taking from that carrion something stronger than himself, such as diverting him to something else by deception so as to monopolize the best of it for himself; ﴿nor transgressing﴾ against others, by being stronger than them and thus repelling them from it, nor exceeding what is needed to stave off hunger and remove the necessity. The verse also includes that whoever rebels against an imam, or intends by his walking on the earth to cause corruption, or transgresses against anyone unjustly, and as a result of that suffers a state of extreme hunger, it is not lawful for him to eat what was forbidden, because that would be helping him in his disobedience. If he repents, he may then permit it: ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾, neither from the first prohibition nor [p. 347] from the second ruling. Had the removal of sin been without these two conditions, there would have occurred among those in necessity such rebellion and domination that would not be lawful for anyone other than those in necessity. So sin is removed on the basis of two correct conditions and the lifting of both rulings. Thus in ease one avoids what is harmful, and in necessity the preservation of the body's life for its sustenance is given precedence over the ruling of the Book on its prescribed observance. In its indication also is that whoever is compelled to something forbidden to him and eats it will not suffer harm, because God, glorified and exalted, when He permits something, removes its harm. "Indeed God has not placed the cure of my community in what He has forbidden to it." So there is an allusion to the transformation of these substances for the one in necessity from what they were, so that they become a concession in the outward and a purification in the inward. Just as He lifted from him their legal ruling, His favour is completed, and He lifts from him their natural harm.

Then He explained this ruling, inducing both fear and hope, by saying: ﴿Indeed, God﴾. He used this all-encompassing Name to indicate the generality of this ruling for the one in necessity and the one in ease. In His saying ﴿Forgiving﴾ there is an indication that no one reaches the state of necessity regarding what is forbidden to him except because of a sin he has committed. Were it not for forgiveness, He would have completed His punishment upon him, because the believer or the one of certainty is not overtaken by necessity, since God, glorified and exalted, is not overcome by anything, and the servant of God is not overcome by what does not overcome his Lord. ﴿And even though they were, before it was sent down to them, certainly in despair﴾ [al-Rum 30:49]. So despair, which leads to necessity, occurs only to one who is below the rank of certainty and below the rank of faith. [p. 348] The Messenger of God (ﷺ) equipped an army, and their provisions ran out, so they remained for days subsisting on little, until they sustained themselves with a single date each, and God brought forth for them the ambergris (anbar), a creature from the sea. So He did not compel them in their necessity to what was forbidden to them, but brought them in their necessity what is the best of their foods in times of ease: the game of the sea, whose "water is pure and whose carrion is lawful." And in His saying ﴿Merciful﴾ there is an informing that whoever is compelled and obtains from what he was compelled to something without rebelling or transgressing, God's mercy reaches him in its breadth, so that he will not be compelled again to its like; He forgives him the earlier sin that caused the necessity, and reaches him with the expansive mercy by which He reaches the one who has not committed what the compelled person committed, [p. 349] the one who was compelled to its like. End of quotation. I have exercised some latitude in it.

When the explanation of these prohibited foods included a reproach to those among the Arabs who made them lawful and abandoned what they were commanded to take as good things, out of ignorance and blind imitation, he followed it with a repeated reproach against those who conceal what they possess of the truth that is in their Scripture, concerning the description of the Prophet ﷺ, the rites of the Hajj, the direction of prayer (qiblah), and other matters that confirm this Book, about which there is no doubt. This was out of fear that what used to be given to them, for their leadership over their religion, would be cut off. It was a reproach in a manner that exposed them, because they made lawful the eating of ill-gotten gain (al-suht) while knowing clearly. They deserved blame on two counts. The first is the act of eating itself in this manner, which leads to turning away from the good things and conforming to the Arabs. The second is that it was done by concealing the truth they knew. So He said: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ (p. 350), emphasizing their blame with various kinds of emphasis. The placing together of the two attributes, forgiveness and mercy, is remarkable, just as He concluded the first verse on concealment with the two attributes of repentance and mercy. Thus it was, together with what it contains of encouragement, a form of precaution (ihtiras), meaning: it is a help, since such people will not be forgiven unless they possess the qualities indicated by the first verse, namely repentance.

His saying ﴿what Allah has sent down﴾ attributes the sending down to His greatest Name, because the Book encompasses varied rulings. ﴿from the Book﴾, meaning: from its limits, its rulings, and other things indicated by the first verse with the clear proofs and guidance of wisdom and rulings.

Since concealment may be for a good purpose, and how many a word of truth has been intended for falsehood! He restricted it by His saying ﴿and take for it a price﴾. Al-Harali said: "The price is that which is not benefited from in itself until it is exchanged for other compensations. The threat is therefore upon what includes the ignorance of the concealer and his greed in seeking gain through knowledge, and in using it (p. 351) for other than what Allah the Exalted has decreed upon the tongues of His prophets: ﴿And I do not ask of you any wage for it﴾."

Since everything that does not remain from the goods of this world in the Hereafter is worthless, however great it may be, He said ﴿a little﴾. This indicates that the intended meaning is not restricted to the small amount.

Since they had gone far from the places of mercy by their stinginess with what spending does not diminish, He pointed to them with the particle of distance and said ﴿those﴾. The address to the Prophet ﷺ with this indicates that such conduct occurs among a group of his community out of greed for this world. ﴿They consume﴾, meaning: in this state, as indicated by ﴿what﴾. Since eating is sometimes used for mere corruption, He clarified its meaning by His saying ﴿in their bellies﴾. Plural of belly (baṭn), which is the hollow space of a hollow thing, because it is hidden from its outer surface, which is the back of that belly. ﴿but the Fire﴾. Just as His knowledge, glorified and exalted, encompasses the unseen, this is in reality, and His sight reaches the eyes of the people of unveiling (ahl al-kashf), who see the outcomes at their beginnings and the unseen in the visible. In His mention of it in the form of restriction there is a negation of an interpreter's reading that it is merely a cause, and a turning of it toward the reality that is attained by unveiling and beyond the reach of the senses. They were therefore like one who cautiously puts his hand into hot water and does not feel it, so that his feeling is numbed; this is like the death of the senses of these people in the state of what they took.

Since He placed the threat concerning the price first, because it is what drives them to concealment, He followed it with the threat concerning concealment itself, and said: ﴿Allah will not speak to them﴾, meaning: the Sovereign, the Greatest, whom everything turns to when He speaks, with speech indicating displeasure, because they did not speak to people of what was written for them. He said ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, as an emphasis on what the preceding indicates, that what is meant by the previous clause is the state. ﴿And will not purify them﴾, meaning: He will not cleanse them from the filth of sins, nor praise them, nor cause their deeds to grow with what they would have gained of the covenant on the Day of Meeting, just as He purifies with that whomever He wills of His servants. This is because they concealed from the servants what would have purified them. In this there is a magnification of the sin of concealing knowledge. ﴿And for them﴾, along with this punishment, ﴿is a painful punishment﴾, for what they caused the people of hardship through their concealment from them of what would have set them upon the easy path.

(p-353) When He mentioned their recompense, He followed it with a description of their state, emphasizing their remoteness (from guidance), so He said: ﴿Those are the ones who have purchased﴾ — that is, out of obstinacy and persistence in misguidance — ﴿the error﴾ in place of the path of good, ﴿at the price of guidance﴾. When He mentioned their state in this world, He followed it with the matter of the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿and the punishment﴾ for their committing this destructive act, ﴿at the price of forgiveness﴾, which would have saved them, erasing their minor sins, had they been spared from this obstinacy that was the cause of the misguidance of a great many people, so that its burden fell upon them. When Glorified and Exalted is He made the first of their consumption fire and the last of their affair punishment, and the description of their state the absence of forgiveness, then this was likewise the midpoint of their state regarding fire. From this He drew the consequence of wonder at their affair, in their confining themselves to that which is the meaning of patience (ṣabr), since they are involved with the fire in reality or with its requisites, without concern. So He said: ﴿How patient they are﴾ — that is, how intense is their confining of themselves, or how bold they are ﴿toward the Fire﴾ which they consumed in the world, so they will feel it in the Next. Al-Harrali mentioned much of this, though I have altered it. (p-354) If you take it as a figurative usage, it is like your saying to one who opposes the sultan: "How patient you are under the long imprisonment and the heavy chain!" as a threat to him.

That is, the Book of God revealed with truth (ﷺ)... I have to translate the passage faithfully, so here it is.

When He mentioned their recompense and described their condition, and marveled at their affair, He mentioned the cause that necessitates this great exclusion and this severe threat, so He said: ﴿That﴾, using the distal demonstrative particle, ﴿because Allah﴾, and He mentioned the Greatest Name here too, whose meaning is that He possesses all the attributes of perfection, glorifying the station. ﴿Sent down the Book﴾, i.e., the one comprising all kinds of guidance, ﴿with the truth﴾, revealed in installments to bring it closer to understanding and to train both the elite and the common people. It is suitable for the meaning of the Qur'an and the Torah alike, i.e., the one that is firmly established, perfect in its firmness. Whoever conceals it has attempted to negate what Allah has affirmed, and has thus opposed Allah in His dominion. Whoever disagrees about it, and it is the one to whom no doubt attaches, has considered the clear to be obscure, and has thus gone far from the target.

Since the implied meaning was "so they disagreed," He followed it with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who differed﴾, i.e., some of them opposed others, ﴿concerning the Book﴾ itself, i.e., not concerning its understanding. This expression indicates that [the] disagreement, whether it is someone's saying about the whole Book or about some part of it that is false, and acknowledging some of its rulings while denying others, and distorting words from their places, and the like, ﴿is indeed in extreme dissension﴾, since each one of them is on one side, ﴿far﴾ indeed from the side of the people of truth.
