The "guidance" (al-huda), defined as revelation, is more general than the Book and the Sunnah, or the Mother of the Book, or other than that. According to what al-Harali said, it is valid that it be meant as the Qur'an, which gathers all the books, so it includes the earlier books of the days. And the Criterion (al-Furqan) is that which is specific to the Arabs, which expressed the unity of the month.

When he had completed what is in the mention of the month of encouragement following the specification, he mentioned what in it is of the firm rule ('azimah) and the concession (rukhsah), so He said: ﴿So whoever witnesses﴾, that is, is present in full presence by clear sighting, the sky being clear without cloud, or by completing the count of Sha'ban if there is cloud, and is not sick or on a journey.

Al-Harali said: In (p-60) its being widely known is an obligation upon whoever sees the crescent alone to fast.

His saying: ﴿of you﴾ is an address to people and those above them, when fasting was elevating for them. ﴿the month﴾ is the witnessed, according to the principle the grammarians state, an object (maf'ul) in the broad sense, for what it contains of the goodness of the report and the conveying of the meaning. What clarifies its meaning is His saying: ﴿let him fast it﴾, making it fall upon the month, not falling upon a meaning "in it," since it was not: "let him fast in it." In its announcement is the validity of fasting a night, so that the latitude that existed in the first fast between fasting and breaking it for the one able becomes here, between the fast of the night and its breaking, for one granted strength by a spirit from God, exalted is He. End of quotation.

Since by this the earlier choice was abrogated, He repeated what applies to the sick and the traveller (p-61) lest it be thought that it was abrogated, so He said: ﴿And whoever is sick﴾, that is, whether he witnessed it at the outset, ﴿or on a journey﴾, that is, whether he is sick or healthy; and it is clear that what is meant is his witnessing it in the place of residence. ﴿then a number﴾

Al-Harali said: The return of this address is from the content of its beginning, so its meaning is: then his fast is a number, from the point that in this address He did not mention the books, so that the return of every address proceeds according to the principle of its origin.

In His saying: ﴿of other days﴾ is an indication that making up (qada') does not proceed by the unity of a month, since the unity is specific to the month of Ramadan, and the descent of its making-up takes the place of the first fast. In its number and in its unrestricted form is an indication of the validity of its occurring consecutively and non-consecutively. End of quotation.

When He granted this concession, He gave the reason in His saying: ﴿God desires﴾, that is, the One whom no one can measure at His true measure (p-62) ﴿ease for you﴾, that is, He legislated ease by permitting the sick and the traveller, and by limiting the fast to one month; ﴿and He does not desire hardship for you﴾ in making it an obligation upon all and extending it beyond one month.

Al-Harali said: Ease is an action that does not exhaust the self nor weigh upon the body, and hardship is what exhausts the self and harms the body. He said: In it is an announcement of God's kindness toward the bodies for whom He eased things by breaking the fast. And in the inner meaning of this outer meaning is an indication to the people of strength that ease is in their fasting and that hardship is in the breaking of the breaker's fast, so that the outer meaning proceeds according to its wisdom in what is manifest, and the inner meaning proceeds according to its wisdom in what is hidden, since for every verse of it there is an outer and an inner. For this, and God, glorified and exalted is He, knows best, "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to fast in Ramadan while traveling, and would command the breaking of the fast," and the people of strength among the scholars would fast and not object to breaking it. End of quotation.

Al-Sha'bi said: When two matters are before you, the easier of them is the nearer of them (p-63) to the truth, by this verse.

Since the cause of the emphasized facilitation, expressed by the negation of hardship, was ability (ita'ah), the sense was: so that you may be able to do what He commanded you and that its command may be light upon you, so He joined to it His saying: ﴿and that you complete the period﴾, from completion (al-ikmal), which is the reaching of a thing to the limit of its boundaries in measure or in counting, sensibly or in meaning, ﴿the period (al-'iddah)﴾, that is, the number of the days of Ramadan, up to the sighting of the crescent if you see it, and up to the end of thirty, beyond which the month cannot be extended, if the sky is overcast so that you do not witness it. For if He had obligated you to more than that, or if its obligation were in every state, it would have been fitting that you diminish some of its days, either in essence, by reducing its count, or in attribute, by eating during it as the Christians do, which would lead to its annihilation altogether.

Al-Harali said: The sense is: that you may fulfil the fast by sighting, and that you may complete it if it is clouded over. (p-64) In this address there is an equivalence of the mention of clear sky at the beginning with His saying ﴿witnesses﴾, and the mention of cloud at the end with completion. End of quotation.

In this there is an indication of ihtiba' (a rhetorical balancing, where one part is left implicit and understood from the other): the mention of witnessing first indicates its absence second, and the mention of completion because of cloud second indicates clear sky first.

Since the great, when his matter is made easy, is more fitting for his magnification, He said: ﴿and that you magnify﴾, and magnifying (al-takbir) is the elevation of rank or of measure, sensibly or in meaning, as al-Harali said. He joined to it the Greatest Name, since the context requires it, so He said: ﴿God﴾, that is, the One before whose majesty understandings fall back in confusion and before whose perfect beauty necks bow, so that you may believe in His greatness in your hearts and mention it with your tongues at the festival and otherwise, so that this may be more fitting for the lasting of submission from the hearts.

Al-Harali said: In it is an indication of what is obtained by the fasting person through the purity of his inner self, of witnessing what shows him the trace of his fast, from the crescent of His lofty light. Just as he magnified at the beginning of the month upon sighting the crescent, he magnifies at its end upon seeing, in his inner self, a sight of the crescent of his Lord's light. So this action was the prayer of the forenoon of the festival day, and it was proclaimed in it with magnification and repeated (p-65) for that purpose, and it was placed in an open space of the wide earth for the aim of magnification, because God's magnification, glorified and exalted is He, is only by what is exalted of His creatures. So in its wording there is an indication of what the Sunnah has shown: the festival prayer is specific to the magnification of two rak'ahs and to being said aloud, for the aim of agreeing with the meaning of magnification, which is only done openly. End of quotation.

**Part 2 of 2**

One of the greatest secrets of this is that, since the festival (ʿīd) is a place of joy and happiness, and since it is in the nature of the soul to exceed limits because of its innate greed, sometimes through heedlessness and sometimes through transgression, He commanded the takbīr on it so as to remove its heedlessness and break its fierce rush. And since oddness (al-witriyya, the quality of being odd-numbered) has a great effect in reminding of the Odd, the Eternal Refuge (al-Samad), the One, the Unique (al-Aḥad), and since the number seven has a great place in the Law (sharʿ), He made the takbīr of his prayer odd and made it seven in the first (rak'ah) for this reason, and as a reminder of the seven acts of the Hajj: the circumambulation (ṭawāf), the running between Ṣafā and Marwah (saʿy), and the stoning of the pillars (jimār). This is to create longing for them, because the gaze is more often directed toward the Greater Festival (al-ʿĪd al-Akbar). It is also a reminder of the Creator of this existence through reflection on His well-known acts: the creation of the seven heavens and the seven earths and what is in them, in seven days, since He created them in six and created Adam on the seventh day, Friday.

Since the custom of the Lawgiver was to be gentle with this community, and among that is the lightening of the second (rak'ah) relative to the first, and since five is closer to seven in oddness than what lies below it, He made the takbīr of the second (rak'ah) five for this reason. Also, since the greatness of the Creator is evoked by the indication of the first (rak'ah), for the knowledge that He alone is distinguished by greatness, majesty and dominion over all affairs, so hearts turned toward Him and aspirations were confined to Him, the takbīr of the second (rak'ah) indicates worship of Him through Islam, which is built upon the five pillars, and especially upon its greatest pillar, the five daily prayers. And Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, is the One who grants success.

Since guidance (hidāyah) is sometimes applied to mere clarification (bayān) and sometimes to clarification together with the expectation of adherence to what is clarified, and since lightening the commanded duty and facilitating it is a greater help toward adhering to it, He said: ﴿Alā﴾, meaning, giving thanks to Him for ﴿what He has guided you to﴾, meaning, He made easy for you the laws (sharāʾiʿ) of this religion, and so prepared you to adhere to them and to continue holding firmly to their handles. Perhaps this is the secret of the great concern with fasting among the elite and the common people, to the extent that almost no Muslim neglects it except rarely. And Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, is the One who grants success.

Al-Ḥarālī (al-Ḥarālī) said: Indeed, guidance is an indication of that finding (mawjidah) which the fasting person experiences, and of what Allah witnesses of His blessings, such as seeing the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) through a special unveiling for the people of seclusion, or through clear signs for the people of insight, or through a manifest sign for the people of watchfulness (murāqabah), each according to a state he finds from being wholly absorbed in his self-restraint, his seclusion, and his absorption in remembrance during his fasting. The greatest guidance is therefore a person's guidance to having his body and soul wither and his essence pass away in the right of his Lord, as He says: "He leaves his food and his drink for My sake." Every act is a doing and a fixed reality, except fasting, which is an effacement and an annihilation. Thus it fits the realization of what Islam and piety truly are, by casting off the burden of outward appearance and the strength of the inner self. Here ends his words.

Since gratitude (shukr) is spending what the Bestower has bestowed in His obedience, and since when an act is light it is closer to adhering to obedience by continuing it, whereas if it were heavy one would almost disobey by abandoning it, He said: ﴿And that you may be grateful﴾, meaning, and so that you may be in a state in which there is hope of adherence to obedience and avoidance of disobedience.

Al-Ḥarālī said: In it there is a refinement of gratitude at its end, just as in it there was a refinement of piety at its beginning, as He says: ﴿That you may become pious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]. Whoever has piety sound at the start has gratitude sound at the end. In its implication there is also an announcement of the manifestation of Allah's blessing and of the thanks for beneficence, which is the content of the obligation of the Zakāt al-Fiṭr on behalf of every fasting person and on behalf of whomever the fasting person feeds. Thus, in gratitude there is his giving out his fast-breaking (fiṭr) by concluding his fast and receiving his breaking of the fast by his Lord's command, and the manifestation of his gratitude through what He has entrusted to him of feeding his dependents. For this reason it applies both to the one who fasts and to those whom the fasting person supports. Here ends his words.

[p. 69] Since the supplication of the fasting person is not hindered, and since this month in particular is a time when supplications are likely to be answered, both because of fasting and because of the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), and since the mention of God's greatness, exalted is He, prepares His servants to feel distance, a thought might arise that He is like the arrogant, who are distant from the places where servants dwell. Someone might think that if He is so distant, no one may ask Him except through an intermediary. To remove this thought, He says: ﴿And when﴾, which by its conjunction indicates an unmentioned omission, meaning: "So when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I, despite My exalted station, am watchful over those who obey Me and those who disobey Me." ﴿And when﴾.

Al-Harali said: When the Truth, exalted is He, prescribed fasting for His servants, He did so because of what He willed for them of elevation toward the hidden reward of fasting. He let them see, in their fasting, something of His dominion through the presence of the Night of Power. Then He directed them to magnify Him for the great guidance He gave them, and He made them successors in His bounty, and He thanked them for His blessing by what He bestowed of His great favor. He manifested upon them, from the abundance of His blessings, what would move onlookers [p. 70] to ask them about what they had obtained from their Lord. Thus they would make clear to those below them what suits them, rank by rank. It is related from Umar, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ would speak with Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, and it was as if the two were speaking in a non-Arabic tongue; I did not understand anything of what they said." This continues until the matter reaches the lowest of the askers, who are still in the rank of nearness, and they are given the good news of beholding closeness. So He said: "And when" as a conjunction with matters that exceed (what has been mentioned), as if He were saying: "When you leave your seclusion and pray, and the adornment of God appears, with which He takes pride before His angels, which is not the adornment of this world that the people of His presence among His angels despise; so when someone whose condition is such asks you, inform him of such; and when someone whose condition is such asks you, inform him of such. And when ﴿My servants ask you about Me﴾," meaning: "Am I like the arrogant kings of this world, distant from those beneath them? Inform them that I am not like that."

Since one is not asked about a thing unless it is great in one's sight and one longs to hasten news of it, the most fitting for the context, the most comforting to the eyes of the servants, and the most effective in restraining the stubborn, is that the answer be brought near and that He, exalted is He, inform them Himself, with His noble Self and without an intermediary, to signal the abundance of His nearness and His presence with every asker. So He said: ﴿Then I﴾, rather than "say: I," because if He had mentioned "say," it would have suggested distance, and the situation does not call for that. And "I" would have caused a misunderstanding, requiring one to say that it is God or something similar. Even so, it would not be free of ambiguity. If this gentleness is shown to those who ask, what do you think of those who travel and journey (on the path)! Al-Ustadh Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri said, in meaning: Those who ask about mountains, orphans, menstruation, the crescent moons, and the like, are answered through an intermediary; but as for those who ask about Me, I remove all intermediaries between Myself and them. Imam Qadi al-Qudat Nasir al-Din ibn Maylaq said, in meaning: Since He, exalted is He, had made Himself known to His servants through His acts and His signs and what He had placed in their intellects of knowledge of Him, it was more fitting to omit the intermediary in speaking of Him. This is unlike the crescent moons and the like, for intellects cannot independently grasp knowledge of them. So reporting about them through the Messenger, through whom alone they are known, was more fitting.

﴿Near﴾ is an intensive form (fa'il) from nearness, which is the beholding of a thing, sensibly or in meaning. That is: whoever seeks Me with his intellect will find Me and know Me. I sent the messengers only to increase knowledge of Me [p. 72] and to remove hardship through the secret of gentleness. Dropping "say" is faster in making Me known, and so it is more worthy of magnifying the intermediary, because haste in answering is a closer indication of the truthfulness of his message.

Al-Harali said: Give good news to the people of the presence of distance of nearness, for those who have ascended to the arrival at nearness were made into those who reach it, and those who fall short of nearness became those who are given the good news of it. It is known that the nearness of God and the distance of created beings from Him is not a distance of space, nor a nearness of space. What can be indicated from the meaning of nearness is that whoever hears, in what is addressed to him, the address of his Lord, is near to the One from whom that address comes. Whoever hears the address only from one who addresses him in his sensible and perceptible reality, and hears it from someone other than his Lord, is distant in accordance with that intermediary, a distance below distance, down to the furthest distance. For this reason, the Prophet ﷺ was told: ﴿Your duty is only to convey﴾. And since what he recites to his community is the speech of his Lord, he recites to them the speech of their Lord so that they may hear it from their Lord. Thus he ﷺ is not an intermediary between the servant and his Lord, but rather he brings the servant to his Lord. In indication of this meaning, the word "say" is recited in the Qur'an so that it may be a clear statement for hearing the speech of God, exalted is He, from whoever hears it, whoever he may be. In its implication is the stirring of hearts and ears toward the call to Hajj right after fasting, for He made the first day of the months of Hajj come right after a day of the days of fasting. It is as if God's caller calls on the day of Fitr for Hajj. In the hidden allusion of this is the elevation of the call of Abraham, peace be upon him, on whose foundation the matter of Islam, its monotheistic uprightness (hanifiyyah) and its religion, was previously established. This comprehensive verse prepares for the mention of Hajj, because this surah has comprehensive matters that are arranged within its details in a wondrous arrangement, which makes the meaning evident to people of understanding, details it for people of knowledge, and then judges by it upon those who judge. He said: ﴿I answer﴾, from "answer" (ijabah), which is meeting by speech, the beginning of the commencement of the complete meeting by direct confrontation, [p. 74] ﴿the call of the caller﴾. In this is an indication of answering the caller, that is, for Hajj at the end of fasting, meaning because of the complete relation between the two acts of worship. The state of fasting, which follows the verse of death, is a wiping out of the state of the barzakh, and the state of Hajj is a journey to a specific place in the state of detachment, like the state of gathering. He said: And Fitr came, meaning after completing the fast, with what helps in answering the call of visitation to God, exalted is He, following seclusion in God's House, so that their movement from the house of their seclusion in retreat moves to the place of His manifestation in Hajj. In this is a verification of the caller from his own state: the caller is not one of His own purposes or desires. God, exalted is He, answers the supplication of the servant if there is rectitude in it; otherwise He stores it up for him, or expiates by it for him, as the Prophet ﷺ explained.

[p. 75] Since every creature is calling out for its need, even if it does not speak of it, God, exalted is He, pointed to the purpose of manifesting supplication, both by speech and by humble entreaty, and so He said: ﴿When he calls Me﴾, so that his state may be truthful by conforming his state to his speech. In the recitation that omits the two (final) yā's, reading "the caller" with a kasra and "calls Me" without their full forms, and the recitation that keeps them fully, there is a broadening of recitation to suit the tribes of the Arabs according to what is on the tongues of some of them, namely full pronunciation, and what is on the tongues of others, namely elision. ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ In His answering is a proof against them: when a master commits himself to answering his servant, the servant's answering his master is more binding, since the master is self-sufficient and the servant is in need. So when the Self-Sufficient answers, the one in need should more fittingly answer. Therefore He attached to this, as an indication of the condition of answering, His words: ﴿So let them answer Me﴾, informing them of what He has called them to of His nearness and intention for His House, through what He has made them naturally needful of it. [p. 76] He used the form of the (tenth-stem) conjugation, which indicates drawing out an answer from what by nature refuses, because of the aversion in souls toward what it bids them: reaching a house they would not reach except with difficulty to the souls. End of quotation, with some alteration.

When He made His answering obligatory in everything He called to, and answering was by faith, the first and foremost of stations, and the stations of faith in its strength and weakness are nearly endless, He said, addressing those who believe and others: ﴿And let them believe in Me﴾, that is, absolute faith or the true faith. Then He gave the reason for this in His words: ﴿so that they may be rightly guided﴾, that is, so that they may be hopeful of persisting in attaining their aims and being guided to the path of truth.

Al-Harali said: Rushd (right guidance) is the good management of a matter, sensibly or in meaning, in religion or in worldly affairs. From the requirement of this verse, all the states of the wayfarers to God, exalted is He, are conveyed: from the repentance of the penitent, from the limit of his distance, to following the way of His nearness, to what God grants of the servant's arrival at his Lord. End of quotation.

(p-77) When they contemplated this noble verse, its closeness and love despite His greatness and exaltedness, they recalled the sweetness of His address before this, and they longed for it. He had made the matter of fasting easy for them in quantity for all of them, and in manner for those among them who were in necessity. It was as if they had asked Him for ease for those in comfort regarding what had been forbidden to them, as it had been forbidden to the People of the Book: intercourse during the month of fasting and eating after sleep. So He said, confirming the response and the nearness: ﴿It has been made lawful for you﴾, which indicates that it had been unlawful. ﴿The night﴾, meaning throughout the whole night, ﴿of the fast, the sexual intercourse (al-rafath)﴾. Al-rafath is what is addressed to women regarding the matter of marriage. If it is changed, there is no rafath according to the scholars of the language. This is indicated by its being connected with the preposition of termination (ila), as a clarification of the implication of ifda', meaning ﴿going in (mufdina) to your wives﴾ with intercourse, in word and deed. By the addition (of "your"), the wives of others are excluded.

(p-78) Since rafath and wiqa' (intercourse) are generally concomitant, He said, emphasizing the intention of the reality of rafath and explaining the reason for its permissibility: ﴿They are a garment for you﴾, meaning your wives, ﴿and you are a garment for them﴾, which you wear. The meaning is: that was permitted in the state of mutual covering or its suitability. This implies that it is not permitted by day, and Allah the Glorified and Exalted knows best. It may also be a justification, because garments are indispensable, and patience weakens against them in the state of closeness and mixing.

Since the fasting was general to both kinds, He said: ﴿and you are a garment for them﴾, meaning they wear you. Then He gave the reason for that by His saying, showing the greatness of this nation in His sight in His intention (p-79) of kindness toward it: ﴿Allah knows﴾, meaning the One whose knowledge and mercy encompass all things, and He has complete encompassing, as He mentioned previously regarding His being near, which necessarily entails His being watchful, ﴿that you were deceiving yourselves﴾, meaning you were acting treacherously in that matter by hastening toward it, as one who compels himself to it. Khiyanah (betrayal) is failure in trust, and amanah (trust) is what is placed to be preserved. Al-Bukhari related in the Tafsir from al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the fasting of Ramadan was revealed, they would not approach women the whole of Ramadan, and some men were betraying themselves, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves﴾."

Al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i related from al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him, also, who said: "When a man fasted and slept, he would not eat until the next (night). Sirmah ibn Qays al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him—" and he mentioned his story regarding sleeping before eating, and that he (p-80) fainted before midday, and then the verse was revealed."

Since the harm of that does not extend beyond them, He said: ﴿yourselves﴾. Then He made the following statement a consequence of it: ﴿so He turned to you in forgiveness﴾.

Al-Harali said: In it there is ease, in that they were not held accountable for the sin of a ruling that contradicted the law of their natures. He excused them by His knowledge of them, and He did not hold them accountable through His Book. In repentance there is a return to a state like that before the sin: "The one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin." This incident concerned a man from the Muhajirun and a man from the Ansar, so that the ease might be combined in both groups. Indeed, the most auspicious of people in their dealings is the one who falls into a violation, and Allah makes its judgment easy through the means of his violation. As in this verse, in which Allah the Glorified and Exalted manifested kindness toward this nation, in that He legislated for it what accords with its constitution, and turned away from it what He knew they would betray because of what they had been created to oppose. Likewise is the case of a commander who, if he wishes his subordinate to obey him, commands him with matters which, if left to his own inclinations, he would do, and forbids him from things which, if left to his own inclinations, he would avoid. Thus the portion of preserving the subordinate from violation is attained. When Allah the Exalted wishes to be strict with a nation, He commands it with what He created it to abandon and forbids it from what He created it to do, so violation spreads among them because of that. This is among the heaviest burdens that were upon past nations. So He lightened this nation's burden by making its legislation accord with its natures. Allah the Glorified and Exalted hastened to them with a portion of what they desired, as "A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Indeed your Lord hastens to what you desire.'" This is so that they may have a share of what their Prophet had in totality. As he, upon him be prayers and peace, said to Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Allah! Turn the truth with him wherever he turns." He (ﷺ) would command the brave to fight and restrain the coward from it, so that violation would not appear among those with him except from bad (p-82) disposition that the restraint of kindness does not hold back. That is the intent of the rabbani scholars who direct the experienced and the trained toward what is most befitting to their state, their natural disposition, and what best suits their creation and character. In this is the greatest gentleness to this nation from its Lord, from its Prophet, and from the imams of its time. From it is his, upon him be prayers and peace, saying: "I had almost forbidden ghilah (nursing while pregnant), until I heard that Persia and Rome do it, and it does not harm their children at all." So that the rulings proceed in accordance with natural dispositions and the temperaments of nations, because he was a messenger to all people despite their differing temperaments. What is in the Sunnah and jurisprudence of that is among the derivatives of this exalted principle, by which Allah the Glorified and Exalted made the ruling for the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) proceed in accordance with what their trust is firmly established upon and their betrayal is repelled from them.

In His saying ﴿and He pardoned you﴾, meaning by erasing the trace of the sin, there is an indication of what would have deserved such purification from it, like expiation or the like. Since what the address of fasting was directed to was the fasting of the month, according to the ruling of its unity that comes after, covering its night and day, elevated above the rank of the earlier Books, in which the days are numbered and their days are separated from their nights, so that the day operates by the ruling of worship and the night by the ruling of nature and need, in this elevation there was the feeding of the weak with what Allah feeds and waters him, not because he takes it by nature, but because it is a ruling upon him by legislation, when He made the law according to the rulings of their natures. As He said regarding the forgetful one: "Only Allah has fed him and given him to drink." In it there is also the sufficiency of the strong from food and drink, as he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "Indeed I am not like your condition." So he would continue fasting without break, and he permitted continuous fasting until the pre-dawn meal. Just as they were fed and given drink by legislation along with the continuation of the ruling of fasting, so likewise they were permitted marriage by legislation along with the continuation of its ruling. Thus their marriage became obedience to Allah's ruling, not a response to nature or a purpose of the self. So He said: ﴿Now (fa-al-ana)﴾, meaning when He manifested to you the manifestation of the law upon the knowledge of Him regarding you and what your natures were created with, (p-84) the doors of violation that had been opened to others were closed to you. ﴿Go in to them (bashiru-hunna)﴾ by ruling, so much so that a group of scholars recommended marriage for the fasting person at night, since it becomes an act of obedience. It is from mubashara, which is the contact of two skins intentionally. ﴿And seek (wa-btaghu)﴾, meaning pursue with diligence and desire, ﴿what Allah has decreed (kataba)﴾, meaning He who has complete power, so nothing comes out of His command, ﴿for you﴾, meaning of offspring or the lawful place of enjoyment. In it there is an indication that the offspring decreed during the nights of Ramadan partakes of the blessing of its creation, through a marriage that was commanded, to the extent that some of the scholars among the Companions would break their fast with marriage.

﴿And eat and drink﴾. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would break his fast with fresh dates; if he did not find them, then with dates; if he did not find them, he would take a few sips of water, and said: 'Indeed water is pure.'" In placing eating first there is an application of this legislation's ruling in accordance with nature. End.

And because it is the cause of thirst, and it indicates the obligation of making intention at night, and the permissibility of delaying the ghusl (major ritual washing) until the day, by His saying ﴿until﴾. In making (p-85) the appearance of dawn the limit for the lawfulness of the things that break the fast, there is an obligation of vigilance in abstaining from them, and that is the reality of intention. Whoever continues in intercourse until dawn cannot perform ghusl at night. He said: ﴿becomes distinct (yatabayyana)﴾.

Al-Harali said: In the form of yatafa''alu, where the observer strains his looking, as if the one rising strains to rise. He did not say yabin (becomes clear), because that occurs after clarity. End.

In His saying ﴿for you﴾ there is an explanation that the rulings are according to the apparent, and that obligation is according to capacity. ﴿The white thread (al-khaytu al-abyadu)﴾. Al-Asfahani said: It is the first thing that appears of the dawn, spreading across the horizon like a stretched thread.

Al-Harali said: So it is extended until the limit of the end of the night, and the boundary of the day is made distinct by the finest thing resembling a thread. ﴿From the black thread (al-khaytu al-aswadu)﴾. Al-Asfahani said: It is what extends with it from the dimness of the night, that is, what remains of the night, (p-86) and it has been said: the darkness of the end of the night, by analogy with two lines, one white and one black. Al-Harali said: In it there is an incitement toward good insight at the meeting of night and day, until the servant attains the light of goodness by making that distinct despite its fineness and delicacy. This parable was revealed without explaining what it represents, until a Bedouin began looking at two perceptible threads, and then He revealed ﴿from the dawn﴾, meaning He clarified the white. Thus He removed it from metaphor (isti'arah) to simile (tashbih) by mentioning the thing compared, because among the conditions of metaphor is that a state or speech indicates it. This metaphor, although it was common among them, and their poets used it, and their eloquent and noble ones discussed it, was not limited to that, and clarification was added because it was obscure to some people among them, such as Adi ibn Hatim, may Allah be pleased with him. So the verse was not mujmal (general and unspecified), nor was clarification delayed past the time of need. Had the matter been so, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have censured Adi, may Allah be pleased with him, for not understanding it.

Al-Harali said in a book of his on the principles of jurisprudence, based on the premise that it is mujmal (general): The address by generality (ijmal) is possible, and it is not necessary to act upon it. Imposing obligation is imposing what cannot be borne, and imposing action requires clarification; otherwise that impossibility returns. Delaying the clarification of the mujmal until the time of obligation is possible, because in that there is the harmony of the wisdom of revelation with the wisdom of the created world. The generality in the Qur'an is like the speech of the cosmos, and the clarification in it is like the drawing of pictures, and that is evident to one who has practiced it. In that case it is not said that general address is futile, because it conveys the gradual wisdom of revelation and the attainment of the blessing of recitation. In restricting it to its clarification there is a pattern of the eloquence of Arabic address, in that the two things compared are not both mentioned, being satisfied with one of them over the other. In it there is a rooting of the principle of clarification as conveying understanding, in that He did not say "from the night," as He said "from the dawn," being satisfied with what is understood from the mention. In the placement of the clarified after something other than its like there is another pattern of the eloquence of Arabic address, because the Arabs return the third to the first, not to the second, so that it is connected to the first in meaning and aligned with the second in wording, so that the place of understanding is secured and returns to the first in meaning. End.

The clearest proof that the night must be spent in intention is His command to complete. When the beginning of the fast has occurred, the reckoning is: when the dawn that you were commanded to watch for becomes distinct, being the limit for what was made lawful for you, then fast, that is, abstain from what breaks the fast. ﴿Then complete (thumma atimmu)﴾ that ﴿fast until night﴾. The expression "then (thumma)" indicates the distance between the two ends of the time in which breaking the fast was permitted.

Al-Ḥarālī said: The fast of the day was thus a completion of a beginning made in the night. So the fast in the night is, as it were, not complete, because it is broken to the senses, though in meaning it is a fast. From this same meaning, some scholars held that one may begin i'tikāf (seclusion in the mosque) before sunset, because of the entry of the night into the complete fast through seclusion, and the attribution of the night to the day in the ruling of a single fast. The day is complete both in meaning and in the senses. He (Allah) obligated the completion of the fast by day and counted it valid by night, and eating and intercourse were permitted in it by command, because the day is the time of livelihood, so eating in it is eating at the time when people are dispersed and deal with one another, and the one awaiting it would be averse to it. And because the night is a time of sleep and of withdrawal and obscuring, so in it there began from the command of Allah what is veiled from view in the day. It is as if the one who eats at night is eating from his Lord, who is in the time of His manifestation: "Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven." It is as if the one who eats at night is only fed and given drink by Allah, and this does not detract from the meaning of his fasting, (p-89) even though the outward form of its occurrence appears in his senses, like the one who forgets. Rather, the one who is permitted is of higher rank than the one who forgets. End of quotation.

Since fasting is closely connected with the mosques and i'tikāf, and the mosques are the place suited to i'tikāf, and since He, glorified be He, had at the beginning of the verse granted general permission for intercourse in all places and states other than the state of fasting, He singled out from among the states i'tikāf and from among the places the mosques, and followed this with His saying: ﴿And do not have intercourse with them﴾, meaning in any place, ﴿while you are staying in the mosques﴾, meaning remaining, abiding, or in seclusion. The root ʿ-k-f revolves around confinement, meaning that you are confining yourselves for God ﴿in the mosques﴾ from their desires with the intention of worship. The phrase ﴿in the mosques﴾ is an adverbial complement to ʿākifūn ("staying"). Thus intercourse is forbidden during i'tikāf even outside the mosque. Restricting i'tikāf to the mosque does not imply that it is valid elsewhere, for it was mentioned only to describe the actual situation and to make understood the prohibition of intercourse (p-90) in the mosques. For if it is forbidden out of honor for that which is the cause of its prohibition and what validates it, its prohibition is more fitting as an honor for the mosque itself. Or it may be said, and this is the better view: since the meaning of ʿukūf is absolute confinement, He restricted it to the mosque so that the specific i'tikāf, which is confinement as an act of worship, would be understood. It is as if He had said: "while you are in i'tikāf." This is the meaning of the subject and predicate and what is connected to them. It is as if He stripped the verb of restriction so that it would include the case where one remains in the mosque without intention. The summary is that He, glorified and exalted be He, equated the state of fasting with the state of i'tikāf in the prohibition of intercourse, and if the two combine, it is more emphatic, for i'tikāf is part of the perfection of fasting. This is by way of prohibiting intercourse in the mosque absolutely.

Al-Ḥarālī said: The one who stays in the mosque completes his fast because the reality of fasting is restraint from everything over which a person would normally act, such as buying, selling and all his aims, so the one in i'tikāf is restrained from all activity except what is necessary for his needs. The fasting person who completes his fast, and who acts while guarding his tongue, and who does not take retribution against one who has wronged him, is the one who completes the fast. Whoever falls short of this and takes his rights from one who has wronged him is not completing the fast. Whoever lets loose his tongue and his actions has no need from God that he abstain from food and drink. So the reality of fasting is fasting itself, not its outward form, until its meaning is established even when eating by night and by day. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever fasts Ramadan and follows it with six of Shawwal, it is as if he had fasted the whole year." And he (ﷺ) said: "Three days of every month constitute fasting the whole year." Some of the people of the Qibla among the Companions would say, "I am fasting," and then he would be seen eating at that time, and when he was asked about it he would say: "I have fasted three days of this month, so I am fasting in the bounty of God, and breaking my fast in the hospitality of God." All of this reflects the consideration by people of insight and understanding of the reality of fasting more than the consideration of its outward form. End of quotation, in meaning.

Since He, glorified and exalted be He, had mentioned these sanctities first, He included what He had mentioned in (p-92) the rulings: the prohibitions explicitly, and the commands by implication. This was placed first because His carrying His prohibitions upon the earth alerts to their exaltation and the emphasis on their prohibition. He resumed with His saying, using the demonstrative of distance: ﴿Those﴾, that is, these rulings, wondrous in their order and lofty in their aims, ﴿are the limits of Allah﴾. The mention of the greatest name serves to emphasize the exaltation. The reality of a limit (ḥadd) is a barrier between two opposites that prevents one from entering the other. Here it is applied to the ruling by naming the whole by a part, through the implication of inclusion. He returned the pronoun to its direct referent, using the plural form, saying: ﴿so do not approach them﴾, expressing it with approach, because the context is fasting and abstinence, and this fits better, since its subject is weaning the self from desires. So it is a prohibition against doubtful matters, from the saying: "Whoever grazes around the protected pasture is likely to fall into it." Thus it includes the preliminaries of intercourse, and abstaining from them is scrupulousness.

When this explanation rose to a level that a human being cannot fully grasp, it was as if he said in amazement: "Does the explanation of something like this happen for anything other than this?" So it was said, as explanation of the reality, and as an encouragement to recitation, and as an incitement to reflect upon the Book, which is guidance with no doubt in it: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this explanation of lofty status, ﴿Allah makes clear﴾ (p-93) because of His greatness, which cannot be confined by any limit nor reached by any counting, ﴿His signs﴾, which, because of their greatness, rightly are attributed to Him. He said: ﴿to the people﴾, a reference to generality, indicating the completeness of His power through the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, until the explanation reaches a level at which there is no difference in basic understanding between the dull and the intelligent. He explained this by His saying: ﴿so that they may be mindful of God﴾, that is, so that their condition becomes that of one from whom fear of God Most High is hoped for, because of what they know from this explanation of His greatness. This vagueness also indicates that among them are some who do not fear God.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 188:

When Allah, glory be to Him, permitted what He had forbidden to the fasting person, namely eating and intercourse, He mentioned intercourse first, because it is more desirable, since the natural inclination toward it is stronger. And because the prohibition on it applied throughout the whole month, the harm of refraining from it is greater. He then followed it with permission to eat, because eating sustains the body. He had given priority to the prohibition on intercourse in some circumstances, and in the same way He dealt with wealth, from which eating comes. This is because among the things the People of the Book had betrayed in the covenant of their Book, and for which they "exchanged a small price," was much of His command, especially the prohibition of bribery (rashwa). They concealed it and made it lawful for themselves, until it became among them an accepted practice.

Good food was urged, especially during fasting. So He forbade certain means of acquiring wealth, whether they were bribery or something else, and said: ﴿And do not consume﴾, meaning that some of you should not take the property of others. He expressed it as "consuming" because it is the greatest purpose of wealth.

Since wealth is changeable, it may be in one person's hand today and in another's tomorrow. Whoever is patient reaches what has been decreed for him from what is in another's hand by right. Whoever hastens reaches it by falsehood, incurs wrath, and does not gain more than what has been decreed for him. He said: ﴿your wealth﴾ and said: ﴿among yourselves﴾, to make this sin repugnant and to stir people toward enjoining what is good. ﴿By falsehood﴾ (bil-batil) means what Allah has not permitted in any way, whether in its origin or in its attribute.

One of the ways of consuming wealth falsely is to seek a ruling from a judge through a false argument that the opponent cannot repel, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, so I judge for him according to what I hear from him. Whoever I give him something of his brother's right, I am cutting for him a piece of the Fire."

Thus the sin belongs specifically to the one who consumes, not to the judge. Then He connected to it what the judge shares in. He said, linking it to ﴿do not consume﴾: ﴿and do not send it﴾ (wa-tudlu), meaning do not convey it, keeping it hidden, ﴿to the judges﴾ (ila al-hukkam) through bribery that blinds insight. It comes from idla' (letting down), like the lowering of a bucket secretly into a well to draw water from it. The one who bribes lowers his bucket of bribery to the judge secretly, to draw out his injustice so that he may consume property thereby. End of quotation.

﴿So that you may consume a portion﴾ (fariqan), meaning some property that separates one party from its owner, ﴿of the property of people﴾, from whatever group they are, ﴿with sin﴾, that is, deliberate injustice. Among its meanings are wrongdoing and doing what is not lawful. ﴿While you﴾, that is, while you know, ﴿know﴾, that is, you are among the people of knowledge in general, for falsehood is more heinous coming from them. It also implies knowing that such a means does not make it lawful. Perhaps this also hints at the permissibility of recovering one's property from a denier who has no way to recover it except by this means.

Al-Harali said about the connection of this verse to what precedes it: Since the revelation of the Qur'an was to establish three matters by which those addressed by it stand: the sound state of their religion, which is what lies between the servant and his Lord in terms of action or submission to Him; the sound state of their worldly life, which is what sustains a person's livelihood; and the sound state of their hereafter, which is where their return lies. For this reason the Qur'an was revealed in detail, with rulings for these three matters. It became a fragment for religion, a fragment for the world, and a fragment for the hereafter. When the beginning of this address was ﴿O people, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:168], which addresses kings and those who follow them among chiefs of tribes and those who follow them, there followed after that a ruling concerning the scholars and those who follow them in His words: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:174]. Then the mention of bequest from the wealthy was included, and then the mention of the conditions of bribery from the giver and the taker. So the arrangement of the revelation comes between a command concerning religion and a prohibition concerning worldly life, so that this is more complete for the heart in accepting the worldly ruling after the religious ruling, and the state of the hereafter is understood from the lesson of the worldly matter. Therefore these verses bring these meanings together, and some of them follow others and are distinguished by others, just as is the state of a person in his day and throughout his life, where the conditions of his religion, his worldly life, and his hereafter come upon him. The command corresponds to the creation in revelation and in development. End of quotation.

When Allah, glorified and exalted, had completed the explanation of what He willed from what He legislated concerning the month of fasting, by night and by day, and some of what follows from that, and since many rulings revolve around the crescent moon, especially the Hajj, one of the pillars of Islam, which is the brother of fasting, and the crescents act like judges, making some things obligatory and negating others, such as fasting, debts and zakat, and wealth is consumed through them, rightly or wrongly, and since the mention of the month and the completion of the count (al-'iddah) had stirred the desire to ask about it, He explained this with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you﴾. He made this a resumption (isti'naf, a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes it), an answer to one who seems to have said: "Did they ask about the crescents?" So it is said: "Yes." This is because what precedes has stirred the desire to ask about them explicitly, so it was a cause for asking about asking about them. Likewise is what comes after, His saying ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215], ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], in contrast to what is conjoined to what precedes it with "and" (waw), as will come. And, if Allah the Exalted wills, in Surat al-An'am will come what is fitting of the knowledge of the stars and what is not fitting.

﴿About the crescents﴾, that is, those of which it has been said that righteousness is not turning your faces toward their east and west: what is the reason for their increase after being like a stalk or a thread, until they become complete and even, and their decrease after that, until they become thin (p-99) and vanish?

Al-Harali said: "It is the plural of hilal, which is what raises the voice upon seeing it, and it came to be applied to the sighting of the month, which is the crescent." End.

Since it was as if it were said: "What is their answer?" it was said: ﴿Say﴾, turning away from the question because of the trial it contains for them, since it is based on observing the movements of the celestial sphere, and that leads to the knowledge of the courses of the stars and what follows from it of effects that lead to speech about the rulings attributed to them, and thus it drags one toward heresy. Many of the earlier nations and past generations went astray through this, believing that the stars themselves have influence. The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, forbade this, saying: "Whoever acquires a branch of knowledge of the stars has acquired a branch of magic; he has increased as much as he has increased." Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah related it (p-100) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whoever seeks the knowledge of the stars has become a soothsayer." Guiding them, Exalted is He, to what is good for them: ﴿They are times﴾. Mawaqit is the plural of miqat, from waqt, which is the limit lying between two matters, one of which is known and prior, and the other is known and subsequent to it.

Al-Isfahani said: "The difference between waqt (time), muddah (period) and zaman (age) is that the absolute muddah is the extension of the movement of the celestial sphere from its beginning to the end, while zaman is a divided period, and waqt is the time appointed for a particular matter."

﴿For the people﴾, in their fasting as has preceded, and in their dealings, so that they may know the number of years and the reckoning, ﴿and the Hajj﴾. He mentioned it explicitly because it is among the greatest (p-101) of the entries into them.

Al-Harali said: "It is the gathering of the servants to the place of standing (al-mawqif) in the months at the end of the year, so it is a religious matter indicating the closing of time and its passing, because of the sign of the return (al-ma'ad) in it." End.

Since they had become accustomed in the Hajj to a reprehensible practice, and abandoning what is habitual is the hardest thing for souls, the people of the path and the masters of the people of realization said: "The essence of intending Allah, Exalted is He, is to strip off habits and to renew readiness to accept what is sent down from the Sustainer of the heavens and the earth." By this the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, became the masters of the people of Islam. Allah, Exalted is He, said, connecting it to ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], condemning that practice upon them and alerting that they reversed in their question as they reversed in their conduct. It is also permissible that it be conjoined to a state indicated by the context, its estimate being: "and the state is that it is not righteousness, your asking this about them." ﴿Nor is righteousness﴾, and He emphasized the negation by adding the letter bi in His saying: ﴿that you come to the houses﴾, that is, neither the sensory nor the figurative, ﴿from their backs﴾ upon arrival from the Hajj or other than it, just as (p-102) it is not righteousness that you reverse your speech by abandoning asking about what does not concern you and asking about what does not concern you, rather what concerns you.

When He negated righteousness from that just as He negated it in the first, He corrected along the method of the first, saying: ﴿But righteousness is﴾.

Al-Harali said: "With the nominative and the lightened form, it is a corrective statement of what righteousness is, and a turning away from the first. With the accusative and the doubled form, with attention to the first, for the purpose of discarding it." End.

﴿The one who fears﴾, so He made the one who fears the very essence of righteousness, as an incitement toward turning to piety, since piety, when it carries one to all that has passed of the praiseworthy qualities of faith, it sufficed with it. Since the estimate was: "So fear Allah, and do not ask about what does not concern you in your religion," He conjoined to it: ﴿and come to the houses (p-101) from their doors﴾, sensorily in action and figuratively in receiving. The door (bab) is the entrance to a thing enclosed by a wall that restrains and surrounds it. So said al-Harali. He had defined it previously in another way.

Since the command to piety had been preceded implicitly and allusively, He brought it expressly, indicating its great benefit in mention and clarity, as a proof of emphasis upon their abandoning that custom, since the situation required it, for whoever is accustomed to something rarely abandons it, and if he abandons it, his thought strikes him at some time. So He said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King in all that you do and leave undone, and settle your souls and bind your hearts to the conviction that all of Allah's actions, Exalted is He, are wisdom and rightness, without the flutter of doubt or the objection of suspicion in that, so that one does not ask about it, since asking involves the suggestion of parting from certainty. Then He gave the reason with His saying: ﴿so that you may prosper﴾, that is, so that your condition may be the condition of one whose continued renewal of success is hoped for, and prosperity is attaining all one's aims of righteousness and other than it. The context of the verse indicates the dislike of this kind of question. Al-Harali mentioned that most of what falls into questioning is what has been clothed in trial, or drunk as affliction, or followed by punishment, and for this Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not ask about things﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked questions and found fault with them, and said: "Leave me as I have left you, for those before you were destroyed only by the abundance of their questions," and so on in the hadith. From this comes the dislike of opinion and the imposition of generating questions, for it is an occupation away from the knowledge of foundations, and an exposure to their occurrence, like the one who asked about a man who would be tested in his family, and he was tested with it. It is said: the abundance of generating questions of doubt led to doubt.

He said: This verse is like a comprehensive preface to what is mentioned after it concerning the timing of fighting, which they practised as they practised in the age of ignorance, where the ruling was to refrain from fighting in the sacred months and to be lax about it in the months of permissibility, though it was a transgression without a true ruling, so there was in it an act of corruption and the shedding of blood. End, with some alteration. So Allah, glorified is He, erased what they had established of that by what He legislated concerning fighting, since it is holy struggle (jihad) for a portion of the portions of this world.

(p-105) When He (glory be to Him) mentioned the Hajj in this Madinan surah, its path was at that time blocked to the people of Islam by the people of war who had expelled them from their land and prevented them from the Mosque, though they had a greater right to it than others. The Hajj is also a form of jihad. Each of fasting and jihad is a withdrawal from worldly life: "The tourism (siyahah) of my community is fasting, and the monasticism (rahbaniyyah) of my community is jihad." The principal acts of worship are time-bound: prayer, zakat, fasting and Hajj. Others are not time-bound: remembrance (dhikr) and jihad, which is fighting the people of war. This is unlike the practice of the people of the Jahiliyyah, who fixed its time and place differently: its place was outside the Sacred Precinct (Haram) and its time outside the Sacred Months (al-ashhur al-hurum). Fighting in the Sacred Months and in the Haram was strictly forbidden, so how much more so near the Mosque. Having mentioned the time-bound acts of worship, He (glory be to Him) followed them with the one that is not time-bound, namely jihad, which is the enclosure (hazirah) of the time-bound acts, for they have no safety without it. This is in response to the wrongdoers who blocked access to the Sacred Mosque and expelled from it. So He commanded that they be treated in the same manner as they treated them, with fighting and expulsion, in the manner of a wise person who recommends a great matter: he delivers it gradually through the methods of eloquence and the varieties of expression, arousing desire for it and encouraging it. This came after He had first indicated to the people of this religion that their oppressors would be disgraced; secondly, that whoever among them was killed is alive and provided for (p-106) ; and thirdly, by praising them for their patience in times of severity, saying that they are "those who are truthful" and "the God-fearing." When He had stirred their desire for jihad against the rebellious and obstinate, He obligated them to fight in the form of a command, to ease the path of the Hajj which He had made obligatory and whose path was blocked by the people of war. So He said, the Exalted: ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾, meaning the way that has no equal, as a signal of its mention in absolute terms after the time-bound by the crescent, indicating that it is not bound by it. It is said that this is the first verse revealed about fighting; this was stated by al-Isfahani.

al-Harali said: Because it is an enclosure for the religion of Islam, which is bound by times, whereas the defense of it is not bound by any time. Rather, whenever harm befalls the structure of Islam, it is repelled, as is the ruling on repelling in religious matters. Thus prayer is tied to the times of the day and night, fasting and Hajj to the times of the crescents, zakat to the time of the sun, and jihad to absolute time, wherever it occurs in place and time, looking in some respect to what corresponds to it from the pillar of Islam, which is the statement of sincerity, "There is no god but God," constantly: ﴿O you who believe, remember God with much remembrance﴾ [al-Ahzab: 41].

﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. End of quote.

He said: ﴿those who fight you﴾, meaning those whose nature is to fight you, not those whose nature is not so, such as children. In it is an indication that fighting has a cause for which it is waged, so it is done for a cause, not for a time. The use of the present tense is intended only to express the occurrence of the act without regard to a specific time, as they have said regarding similar forms.

Since God, glory be to Him and exalted, has made justice obligatory in every (p-108) matter, even with regard to His enemies, He said: ﴿and do not transgress﴾. Thus He arranged that this applies to initiating fighting against those with whom initiating it is not permitted, either by a covenant, or without a call for those who have not received the message of the religion, or by other kinds of treachery and deceit, and killing women, children and old people who are decrepit and have no power or opinion; and it applies to continuing fighting against one who has offered peace after it was initiated against him. So He omitted the object for brevity, which conveys an increase in meaning. This is one of the rare varieties of eloquence. It seems that the form of the reflexive verb (ifti'al) conveys restriction to deliberate intent. Then He gave the reason with His words: ﴿Indeed God﴾, meaning, by virtue of His attributes of perfection, ﴿does not love the transgressors﴾, absolutely in this and in other matters, meaning He does not treat them with the goodness that a lover shows.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 191:

When He forbade aggression, He explicitly permitted the fundamental act of fighting, saying: ﴿And kill them﴾, meaning those who fight you, ﴿wherever you encounter them﴾, meaning wherever you find them while you hope to prevail over them, or wherever you are able to kill them. This is what al-Asfahani said, because "thaqifa" (with a damma, "thaqafa") means to be overcome and captured, and "thaqifa" (with a kasra) has the same meaning. It also means to become skilful and perceptive. "Thaqaftu al-shay'" means "I took the thing," and "thaqaftu al-shay'" also means "I came upon the thing." This is what Ibn al-Qatta' said.

Al-Asfahani also said: "Al-thaqf" is finding someone in a way that involves seizing and overpowering. He used the general term "wijdan" (finding), which includes the sanctuary (al-hill) and the sacred precinct (al-haram), in terms of both place and time, because they behaved in this way toward the Muslims. They used to harm and persecute them at the House at every time. The use of the verb indicates the victory of the party of God and gives good news of the weakness of the enemy in sustaining continuous resistance against the fighters. Experience has shown the same thing, and at the very least, if they flee, they do not return to fight.

Since the verse is concerned with retaliation (qisas, the principle of equal retribution), He said: ﴿And expel them﴾, meaning, if they do not fight you, ﴿from where they expelled you﴾, meaning Mecca, which is the place of the Hajj and the 'Umrah and the centre of the rites intended by the people of Islam.

Since this indicates that they did not fight the Muslims in Mecca except by harming them in a way that compelled them to leave their homes, the implied meaning is: expulsion from one's dwelling is more severe in persecution, and they did persecute you with it. So He joined to this His words: ﴿And persecution﴾, meaning punishment by expulsion or other kinds of intimidation, ﴿is worse﴾, meaning its softening effect on them toward Islam, ﴿than killing﴾. This is general, whether the intended killing is your killing of them within the sacred precinct or elsewhere, or their killing of you, or something else, because it involves continuous distress that restricts the soul from its desires. For this reason, We permitted you to kill them as retaliation for their expelling you. The primary aim was their expulsion, so that the Hajj and 'Umrah could be carried out, but since this could not be achieved except by fighting and killing them, permission was given for both. The reality also revealed this in the cases of Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, Safwan ibn Umayyah and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'a: expulsion from Mecca softened them toward Islam more than killing would have. They embraced Islam when they were about to leave Mecca, after Islam had become dominant there, whereas none of the Quraysh embraced Islam out of fear of being killed. Because the context concerns their expulsion, the expression here is stronger.

Since permission to expel implies, as is customary, permission for fighting, and permission had already been given to begin fighting wherever they were found, He restricted this and, looking also to reciprocity and pointing to what would happen in the Conquest of Mecca (ghazwat al-Fath), referred to later in His words: ﴿and disbelief in Him and in the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], He said: ﴿But do not fight them﴾, meaning these people whom you were permitted to expel, ﴿at the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning the sacred precinct, if you intend to expel them and they resist you, ﴿until they fight you therein﴾, meaning in that place which is at the Mosque. It seems that He used "fihi" (in it) in the second clause and "'inda" (at) in the first, and the intended meaning in both is the sacred precinct. The prohibition is to refrain from fighting there for as long as there is any way to refrain, as a sign of its glorification and the honour of its place, because it is the place of prayer, whose greatest purpose is prostration and to no other, let alone fighting.

﴿If they fight you﴾, meaning in that place, ﴿then kill them﴾, meaning do not limit yourselves to repelling them, but strike them with full force. There is no blame on you on account of the Mosque, for the violation of its sanctity is attributed to the one who initiates it. The use of the verb in the answer to the reciprocal form (mufa'ala), in the reading of the majority ("qatalukum"), or the verb in the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i ("yuqatilukum"), gives good news of the victory of the one who has been wronged and the strength of his triumph over his enemy. Since this might suggest that the ruling applies only to them, He generalised it by saying: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning such a deed of great benefit, ﴿is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾, all of them.

Since withdrawing after having begun is difficult for noble souls and lofty resolves, especially when the moment of victory is near, He said: ﴿So if they desist﴾, that is, from fighting and its preliminaries. In this there is an indication that some of them will desist, for the One who knows all things does not use the particle of doubt except in this way. (p-113)

Since the implied sense is: "Then refrain from them and do not confront them, for Allah has forgiven them," He gave a general reason, saying: ﴿indeed Allah﴾, that is, the One encompassing all attributes of perfection, ﴿is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾. That is, He possesses these two attributes eternally and everlastingly, so whoever repents, this is His manner with him.

When the intended meaning of their fighting in what preceded was restraining their harm by whatever act it took, he confirmed it with His words: ﴿And fight them﴾, meaning these people whom we have attributed to fighting you, expelling you, and tempting you, whether they are disbelievers or not, ﴿until there is no more fitnah﴾, meaning that fitnah (persecution, trial) ceases to exist, in that they are unable to harm anyone of the people of Islam in order to turn him away from his religion, or to expel him from his home, or to strip him of his wealth, or to overpower him in his right. So fighting is directed at everyone who commits any of that, whether as disbelief or as transgression, in the way of Allah, ﴿until it returns to the command of Allah﴾. ﴿And religion be for Allah﴾, meaning obedience and worship.

Since this was in the early period after the Hijrah (emigration), before they had seen the help of Allah that would strengthen their resolve, He stripped it of emphasis and said: ”Allah”, meaning the One who has no equal, specifically, so that the affair of the Muslims would be manifest, with no share for Satan in it, and no one among the people of disbelief or the people of transgression would be able to display harm against any of them. This would happen when no polytheist remains at all, and no People of the Book remains except that he is obligated to pay the jizyah (poll tax, a gloss) in humiliation. The wisdom in sparing them and not the polytheists is that they have books, and they were given respite out of respect for them, so that they might look into them and arrive at the truth in them. For although distortion has occurred in them, there remains in them what guides the one who is granted success, since distortion did not encompass them entirely. As for the people of idols, they have nothing that guides them to the truth, so granting them respite would be an increase in their polytheism, certainly without any expected benefit.

Al-Harali said: Within this is an indication of what has occurred, what is occurring, and what will occur of fighting between the party of truth and the party of transgression throughout the Muhammadan era, until the fitnah is removed and religion becomes purely for Allah in monotheism, contentment, and steadfastness upon the state of the righteous predecessors and the time of the caliphate and prophethood. End of quotation.

﴿But if they desist﴾, meaning they have obliged themselves to return from what made fighting obligatory for them, then they have abandoned wrongdoing and the forbidding.

Al-Harali said: The ruling that prevents an action, which is directed at it, is like the effect of intellect called nuha (restraint, sound judgment), because it restrains one from what the self inclines toward, in matters in which nuha is sought. The prayer and peace of Allah be upon him said: «Let there come close to me from among you those possessing understanding and restraint (ulu al-ahlam wa-al-nuha)». So whoever is not among the people of nuha, the nuha that restrains him is the ruling mentioned. End of quotation.

﴿Then there is no hostility﴾, meaning there is no path in which the severe enemy would fall into fighting against them, for there is no hostility ﴿except against the wrongdoers﴾.

Al-Harali said: He mentioned wrongdoing in its comprehensive sense, referring to all the ways of placing a matter in other than its proper place, from the highest of religion to its lowest. End of quotation.

It is also possible that the sense is: if they desist from polytheism, then the name of wrongdoing has been removed from them, so do not transgress against them. If you transgress against them, you will be given authority over you because of your wrongdoing toward them, so that someone will transgress against you. For there is no hostility except against the wrongdoers, those whom you have entered into their designation and who have left their designation by desisting. So there is no hostility except against you, not against them. The meaning of ʿudwān (hostility) is fighting with the utmost of the enemy's intensity, strength, and determination.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 194:

When Allah, exalted is He, permitted fighting in every place, even within the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and this was, in their view, something very grave, namely fighting during the Sacred Months, the resolve to ask about it arose. So He said, instructing them concerning what they should do in the 'Umrat al-Qada' (the lesser pilgrimage made in the year after the Treaty of Hudaybiyya), if they needed it, in a general manner: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾, which is Dhu al-Qa'da of the year seven (AH), if you fight them in it, because they fought you in a sacred month ﴿for the sacred month﴾ in which they fought you, which is Dhu al-Qa'da of the year six, when they barred you in it from the 'Umra of al-Hudaybiyya.

When what preceded had indicated retaliation (qisas), He made it explicit in a more general form, so He said: ﴿And the sacred violations﴾, meaning all of them. It is the plural of hurma, which is that which is protected, safeguarded, and not violated. (p-117) ﴿is subject to retaliation﴾, meaning it is subject to following equality and parity. ﴿So whoever﴾, meaning, consequently, from this: whoever ﴿transgresses against you﴾, meaning deliberately harms you in any matter, at any time or place, ﴿then transgress against him﴾, meaning, go beyond him. It was called "transgression" by way of correspondence (mushakala), to strengthen their resolve and to settle their aspirations, meaning: act, even if the aggressor names it by something other than what is due to him. ﴿In like manner as he transgressed﴾, meaning his hostility ﴿against you﴾, meaning in the same manner as he transgressed against you with it. Perhaps He repeated the adverbial phrase, although the first already conveyed it, to repel the captiousness of one who might say: the statement includes his transgression against me and against others, so I may retaliate against him with the greatest of what befell him from that. For the intent is to deter him, and if the ruling were not so restricted by a qualifier that negates this, it would not be meant as such.

When He made equivalence the limit, and its matter was subtle, and standing at it after the soul has run free by releasing it was difficult, He warned against exceeding it after permission to retaliate was granted, which had drawn most people into it by calling it transgression, in a manner urging the discerning toward pardon. So He said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, meaning the One who encompasses all things in knowledge, by being scrupulous in retaliation so that you do not exceed (the limit). ﴿And know﴾, and He stated it explicitly and did not leave it as a pronoun, lest it be restricted to piety in matters of transgression, for example. So He said: ﴿that Allah﴾, meaning the One who possesses all attributes of perfection, is ﴿with you﴾ if you are mindful, by being scrupulous in it or by pardoning, for indeed Allah ﴿is with those who are mindful﴾. And whoever has Allah with him attains success in its entirety. "Allah has not increased a servant in forgiveness except in honor."

Al-Harali said: Within this is an indication and a pathway to the aim of forbearance, which is the best of virtues, namely maintaining ties with one who severs them and pardoning the wrongdoer. And since in this piety there is a departure from the portion of the self, He informed them that He, exalted is He, would be a substitute for them in place of their own selves, for what they feared and persisted in piety until it became an attribute of theirs; so He informed them of His companionship with them. — End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 195:

When spending (infaq) was among the greatest pillars of jihad, and life at the beginning of Islam was narrow and wealth scarce, it was natural for each person to cling to what was in his hand, thinking that clinging to it was salvation and spending it was destruction. So He informed them that the matter is contrary to what Satan embellishes to them in this regard: ﴿Satan promises you poverty﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268]. Al-Harali said: Because of the honor that accompanies pardoning, which comes contrary to the aim of the self, Allah arranged with it what comes contrary to the perception of the senses in spending, through which purification (zakah) and increase (nama') are obtained. Also, when Allah established the ruling of jihad, which is the most difficult of deeds for the self, He arranged with it the matter of generosity and spending, which is even more difficult for souls. And since fighting is a defense that requires equipment and provision, its matter could not be completed except (p-120) by the deeds of the two dispositions: courage and generosity. For this reason, the gravest afflictions in religion are stinginess and cowardice. End of quote.

So Allah said: ﴿And spend﴾, and He stated it explicitly rather than leaving it implicit, to show concern for the matter of spending, and so that it would not be restricted to any particular aspect, and He said: ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, i.e., the King under whose domination everything is, as He said: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190]. It is everything Allah has commanded, although its use is most frequent in reference to jihad. That is, do not fear poverty and loss, for Allah, your Lord, is the One who commanded you to that. ﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty﴾ [al-Baqarah: 268].

Al-Harali said: So the consideration is toward wealth by spending it, not by preserving and maintaining it. Thus the two addresses are united: the honor in pardoning and the growth in spending. He reinforced this by informing them of what the perceptions of souls do not reach: that preserving and holding back wealth is destruction. End of quote.

Allah said: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾, i.e., do not hasten to place them (in the sense of) hurrying as one who throws something away by not spending (p-121) ﴿into destruction﴾, from perishing (halak), which is the collapse of a thing until it becomes void and vanishes. In that is inclination toward ease and reliance on others, so the enemy becomes bold against you and nothing of yours stands. Stinginess is the swiftest thing to bring about destruction. The word is "tahlukah" (tahlukah, a form with a dammed 'ayn), the verbal noun of halaka. It is said that it has no second instance in their speech.
