Literally, He attributed the throwing to the hands for what benefits a person, both himself and others, by his hand, that is, by himself, and so He made destruction seize them and possess their owner.

Al-Harali said: The comprehensiveness of the address requires that destruction is the neglect of fighting and spending, by abandoning which domination falls upon the foundation of Islam, so it reaches its demolition. Since the matter of spending was especially (p-122) for the Ansar, who were the people of wealth, because the Muhajirun were stripped of it, it was implied within it that most of the decisive address concerning it is for the Ansar. End of quote.

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, and this wording is his, and he said: hasan sahih, and al-Nasa'i, related from Abu Ayyub, may Allah be pleased with him: "This verse was revealed concerning us, the company of the Ansar, when Allah honored Islam and its supporters multiplied. Some of us said to others in secret, without the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knowing: Indeed our wealth has been lost, so let us stay with our wealth and repair it! So Allah revealed this verse. Thus the destruction was staying with wealth and repairing it, and abandoning the raid."

Al-Bukhari related in the Tafsir book, from Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning ﴿And spend in the way of Allah and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾, that he said: It was revealed concerning spending.

Since latitude in the matter of fighting may draw one into aggression, He concluded it with the prohibition against that and with the statement that Allah does not love the aggressors. And since latitude in spending in the way of Allah is among the highest qualities of faith, Allah said: ﴿And do good﴾, i.e., perform good in general, by what the restriction of the verb and the omission of its object conveys regarding abundance of spending (p-123), and think well of Allah. He stated it explicitly without implicit reference because of the long separation and for the reason previously mentioned: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, the King, the Mighty, ﴿loves the doers of good﴾, i.e., He does with them everything that the lover does with the one he loves of honor, exaltation, support, enrichment, and other things, of all that they need, just as He does not love the aggressors.

Al-Harali said: The conclusion of the two addresses is united: that aggression not occur in killing, and that goodness occur in wealth. In its implication is an urging of the Ansar to spend their wealth, following the state of the Muhajirun in being stripped of it. Just as the command to the Muhajirun was not to undo the emigration, the command to the Ansar was not to turn toward worldly life. So when the Muhajirun departed from its origin, the Ansar, by holding to it, departed from its attribute, so their turning away (p-124) was consequent upon the Muhajirun's abandonment of their wealth.

[p. 125] When he had concluded the verses on fighting with the command to spend in the way of God, owing to the great need of jihad for that spending, and since "the way of God" (sabil Allah) is a term that applies to the Hajj as it applies to jihad, as in the hadith, "The Hajj is part of the way of God," he returned to the Hajj and the 'umrah (the lesser pilgrimage), which he had alluded to with ﴿a place of return for the people﴾ [2:125], and ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah﴾ [2:158], the verse, and ﴿the times are for the people and for the Hajj﴾ [2:189]. This is especially so since these verses on fighting were arranged here only because of those two, as a connection leading to them. Some of them have as their occasion the 'umrah of al-Hudaybiyah, from which the polytheists barred the Muslims. So it was as if it were said: "The times are for the people and for the Hajj, so perform the Hajj and the 'umrah," meaning, "engage in them, even if you are prevented from them, and fight in the way of God against those who fight you in that direction, so that the way may be opened for you." Since that was possible after the conquest with no one to obstruct it, he expressed it with completion, saying: ﴿and complete﴾, meaning, after the way is opened by conquest [p. 125] ﴿the Hajj and the 'umrah﴾, with their rites, their limits, their conditions, and their sunan (recommended practices).

Since spending in the way of God and fighting in the way of God had been mentioned earlier, he drew attention here to the fact that all of that is only so that the acts of worship, which are the foundation of Islam, may be established for Him, glorified and exalted be He. So he said: ﴿for God﴾, the King who has no equal, meaning for His own sake. He did not use a pronoun so that it would not be restricted by a condition.

Since God, glorified and exalted be He, had honored this community for the sake of its Prophet (ﷺ), so that He would not destroy it with a general punishment and would not give an enemy from outside power over it, but made the expiation of its sins to lie in the infliction of its violence upon itself, He indicated that perhaps something would cut it off from completion. He did so by saying, building the verb in the passive because the ruling revolves around the existence of the act without regard to a specific agent, and expressing it with the particle of doubt to indicate that this is something that rarely occurs: ﴿But if you are prevented﴾, meaning, you are barred and held back from completing them, from ihsar (encirclement or restraint), which is the enemy's prevention of the one restrained from his freedom of action (p. 126), like illness that restrains a person from acting in his affairs; so said al-Harali. ﴿then whatever﴾, meaning, then what is obligatory upon the one restrained who is prevented from completing it, as an amends for the deficiency that befell his performance of the two, is ﴿what is easy to obtain﴾, meaning, what he finds ready with the greatest ease, as if he were seeking ease for himself. Yusr (ease) is the attainment of a thing without effort or hardship. ﴿of the hady (sacrificial animal)﴾: when he wishes to exit the state of ihram from the Hajj and the 'umrah, it is of camels, cattle, or sheep, which he slaughters where he was restrained, and gives in charity; and he has then returned to a state of lawfulness (p. 127).

Since the pilgrim is the one with disheveled hair and unkempt body, he drew attention to the sanctity of interfering with his hair by saying: ﴿and do not shave your heads﴾, meaning, do not shave their hair if you are in the state of ihram for Hajj or 'umrah, from halq (shaving).

Al-Harali said: It is the removal of what can be removed by cutting with the instrument that is used in its work. The head is the gathering place of creation and the gathering place of every thing is its head, and the discussion ends.

﴿until the hady reaches﴾, from balagh (arrival), which is reaching the goal, ﴿its place of sacrifice﴾, meaning the place where it is lawful to slaughter it. If you are restrained, then where you were restrained; otherwise, at al-Marwah or in Mina or the like.

Al-Harali said: The hady is what the lower brings near to the higher, and it is the name of what is taken as ransom from the livestock by offering it to God, glorified and exalted be He, and directing it to the Ancient House. In following the shaving with the hady there is an indication that the two share a single meaning, which is ransom. The hady is originally a ransom for the pilgrim's slaughter of himself for God, the sunnah of Abraham concerning his son, upon them both be peace; and the removal of hair is a ransom for a head, for God. For this reason, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about putting one of them before the other, he said: "Do it, and there is no blame" (p. 128), because the whole is a goal in the comprehensive sense that includes ransom. The discussion ends.

Since man is a locus for the accidents of hardship, and God, glorified and exalted be He, had lifted from us the burdens through the blessing of the chosen Prophet (ﷺ), making His religion ease, He said: ﴿So whoever is﴾, and restricted it by saying: ﴿among you﴾, O muhrimun (those in ihram), ﴿ill﴾, for whom a good outcome may be hoped by shaving; ﴿or has an injury﴾, even a slight one, and adha (injury) is that whose effect touches the self; ﴿on his head﴾, from lice or other things; ﴿then a ransom﴾, meaning a choice of action by shaving his head or treating himself with what the muhrim is forbidden, as a fidyah (ransom) ﴿of fasting﴾ for three days, ﴿or charity﴾ of three sa' (measures) of food for six needy persons, because charity, as al-Harali said, is the equivalent of fasting when it is absent, as (p. 129) has been mentioned earlier. For each day there are two meals, one for breaking the fast and one for suhur, each meal being two mudd, so each day has one sa'. ﴿or nusuk (sacrifice)﴾, meaning an act of drawing near by slaughtering one of the livestock. This ransom is optional.

Since God, glorified and exalted be He, with the breadth of His forbearance, the greatness of His power, and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, had established causes that prevent the corrupters, despite their numbers, from gaining the ability to corrupt, He indicated this by the particle of realization after expressing the ihsar with the particle of doubt, and said: ﴿So when you are secure﴾, meaning, when you have come into security, so the ihsar and the illness are removed (p. 130). The verb is here built in the active, to indicate that it is as if the one secure comes of his own accord, as an alert that this is the original state, unlike ihsar, as an exhortation to gratitude. ﴿then whoever performs tamattu' (combined pilgrimage)﴾, meaning, enjoys the permission to enter the Haram, by his ihram in the months of Hajj, at the distance of qasr (shortening of prayer) from the Haram, ﴿with the 'umrah﴾, so that he obtains lawfulness upon his arrival at the House and remains lawful during that journey; ﴿until the Hajj﴾, meaning his entering ihram for it from the general time of that, from Mecca the honored, without returning to the miqat (ritual boundary); ﴿then what is necessary﴾, meaning, upon him is what ﴿is easy﴾, what he finds ease in, ﴿of the hady﴾, of the livestock. This hady is for what he enjoyed between the two rites, of lawfulness while traveling. This is for the mutamatti'. As for the qarin (one combining both), it is because he combines the two rites in a single journey, and their nature is that they occur at two times, a time of lawfulness and a time of ihram. In the expression there is an indication of the validity of following the Hajj upon the 'umrah, because it is an ascent from a lower ihram to a higher ihram.

Since restriction to ease implied a state of hardship, he explained it by saying: ﴿So whoever does not find﴾, meaning a hady, from wujd (finding), which is ability and capacity; ﴿then fasting﴾, meaning upon him, as a substitute for the hady, is fasting ﴿of three days during the Hajj﴾, meaning during the days of his being in its state, so it is not valid before that, and it must be before the day of 'Arafah, such that he is not fasting on it; and "and" (wa), ﴿seven﴾, meaning of days, ﴿when you return﴾ to your lands, so it is not valid before arrival. He did not specify it individually, so that it would be understood that the criterion is the possibility of returning, not the actual return. So if he stays in Mecca, for instance, he fasts there. And if he missed the three during Hajj, he separates them from the seven at home by the length of time needed for the possibility of return, plus the four days of tashriq and the 'Id, so that the making-up imitates the performance on time.

Al-Harali said: So fasting is the equivalent of the hady that the offerer feeds, just as feeding was the equivalent of fasting in the verse ﴿and upon those who are able to do it﴾ [2:184]. The discussion ends.

Since explicitness has a distinction that others do not have, he said: ﴿That﴾ (p. 132), meaning, that prescribed count of fasting, ﴿is ten﴾, to remove the possibility that wa (and) means aw (or), or that seven is intended as hyperbole rather than literal, and so that the number is brought to mind as a whole just as it was brought to mind in detail. And ten:

Al-Harali said: It is the return of the counting of units to its first.

Since the time of the two fasts differs, he said: ﴿complete﴾, negating the assumption that fasting after release from ihram is less than what is in ihram. And completeness:

Al-Harali said: It is reaching the goal beyond which there is no further increase in every respect. He also said: Just as the state of the hady is equal in its arrival at the sacred or the lawful, so the state of fasting is equal in the sacred city and the lawful city, so that in its indication there is an alert that the earth is a masjid for God just as the Sacred House is a masjid for God. Thus he made manifest the meaning of their equality in completeness in the ruling of reward for those of reward, acceptance for those of acceptance, and approval for those of approval (p. 133), and attainment for those of direction, each acting according to the rank of his deed. The discussion ends.

If he had said "perfect" (tammah), this meaning would not have been conveyed, because perfection may exist in number while some attributes are deficient.

Since this ruling might come to mind as a question, whether it is particular or general, he began by specifying it for one who is absent from the Haram of Mecca at the distance of qasr, saying: ﴿That﴾, meaning the aforementioned ruling, exalted in its benefit and wise in its placement, ﴿is for one whose family is not﴾, from his wife, his relatives, or the inhabitants of his homeland.

Al-Harali said: The ahl (family) is the dwelling of a man, from a spouse and one who dwells with him, ﴿present﴾, at the distance of hadar (residence), by being a resident (p. 134) in the Haram or from the Haram at less than the distance of qasr. Whoever is like this is ḥāḍir (present), from hudur (presence), which is staying in one's homeland, not at the distance of travel from ﴿the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning the Haram; rather, his family was at the distance of absence from it, which is the distance of qasr.

Al-Harali said, explaining what the meaning of tamattu' implied: That is because God, mighty and majestic, when He undertakes to clarify an act, carries it to its ultimate explicitness. The discussion ends.

He expressed the Haram as "the Mosque" out of reverence and magnification for what is near the Haram, just as the Haram is magnified by its nearness to the Mosque, and the Mosque is magnified by its proximity to the Ka'bah; for it is the custom of the great that their houses have courtyards, their courtyards have enclosures, and around those enclosures are the houses of their special attendants. As for those present at it, there is no sacrifice (dam) upon them in tamattu' or qiran, a distinction between the king's special people and others.

Since the commands in these verses were many, and only taqwa (God-consciousness) carries one to comply with them, God, exalted be He, multiplied in them the command to it.

Al-Harali said: Because the souls drag entry points of deficiency into intentions, deeds, and transitions from rulings to their substitutes; so whatever is built upon taqwa is purified, even if it is short. The discussion ends.

Since among the commands there are those whose meaning is rational and those that are devotional, and since understanding the meaning assists the soul in complying with the command, it was fitting that the command be coupled with encouragement, as He said: ﴿And fear God and know that God is severe in punishment﴾. Since complying with what is not rational in meaning, from His saying ﴿and complete the Hajj and the 'umrah for God﴾, is heavy on the soul despite its resistance to all commands, it was fitting that it be coupled with a threat. So its conclusion was with His saying: ﴿And fear﴾, meaning, do all of that, strive to be careful in it, and stand at its limits outwardly and inwardly; and fear ﴿God﴾, meaning, place between yourselves and the anger of this greatest King a shield. He emphasized the greatness of the station with the command to knowledge and the repetition of the greatest Name (p. 136), and so that the pronoun would not imply a restriction of the severity of His punishment to fear of what has passed. So He said: ﴿And know﴾, as an alert that what motivates fear is only knowledge, ﴿that God﴾, meaning, the One whose greatness nothing approaches, ﴿is severe in punishment﴾, and it is the infliction that follows a prior crime. This is along with the appropriateness of this conclusion to what follows it, the prohibition against obscenity (rafath) and what is within its scope. Whoever reflects on the beginning knows the end, and whoever considers the end perceives the beginning.

Ustadh Abu al-Hasan al-Harali said in the Kitab al-Miftah, in the fifth chapter on the descents of the Qur'an according to the Names: Know that God's address comes with its explanation according to His Names, and it gathers them in comprehensive ways, the most apparent of which is what you see of His verses, which is His Name al-Malik (the King), and what is detailed from the Names that are upright for the matter of ruling, judgment, and recompense, such as al-'Aziz al-Hakim (the Mighty, the Wise), with which He concludes the verses of rulings: ﴿a deterrent from God, and God is Mighty and Wise﴾ [5:38]. Then what you hear of His verses from His Name al-Rahman al-Rahim (the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate), and what is detailed from the Names of the meaning of mercy, which announces pardon and forgiveness, with which the verses of mercy are concluded (p. 137).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And Allah turns in forgiveness toward the believing men and the believing women, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73]. So for every detailing within the domain of the two aspects, justice and grace, there are names whose structure is specific to it. For this reason, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "As long as he does not conclude a verse of mercy with a punishment, or a verse of punishment with mercy." Then, [there are the verses] whose signs are found directly within the soul, which is the Rububiyyah (lordship), and what its meaning reaches regarding its equal affair, from "All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds," and what it details of the names that occur in concluding the comprehensive encompassings, such as "al-Wasi' (the All-Encompassing), al-'Alim (the All-Knowing)." Whoever is attentive to this will draw clarity about the conclusion from the detail, and will seek elucidation of the detail from the conclusion.

This was clear among the Arabs, but it became obscure among the non-Arabized (those who learned Arabic as a foreign language), except for what was very evident of it. And the repetition of the names, by explicit mention and by pronoun, is a firm clarity of understanding in the Qur'an. End of quotation.

(p-138) When the Exalted and Glorified One mentioned that the Hajj is fixed by the crescent moons, but did not specify for it a time within the months of the year, and concluded that matter with the distinction made in some of the rulings of the Hajj according to places, the soul longed to know the specific time of it, and whether it is like the place (p-138) or of general application. So He said, ﴿The Hajj﴾, meaning its time, ﴿is in known months﴾. He mentioned it with a form of the plurals of paucity (jumu' al-qilla), the least of which is three, and it is three (in the genitive, with the broken plural being in the genitive). They are: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and nine days of Dhu al-Hijjah, along with the night of the 'Id, by the evidence that it (the Hajj) is lost with the break of dawn on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). When it was left vague, He specified, so He said: ﴿known﴾, meaning known before the revelation of the Shari'ah. This indicates that the matter after the Shari'ah is as it was before. There is no doubt that in mentioning it vaguely and then specifying it there is glorification and magnification of the one spoken of.

When He concluded the preceding verse with a warning against His punishment, He commanded the sincere dedication of the Hajj free from impurities, forbidding it through the form of negation, to magnify it and to emphasize the prohibition. Since the Hajj does not take place except as an obligation, He said: ﴿Whoever imposes upon himself﴾, meaning makes obligatory by entering the state of ihram. It derives from al-fard (obligation), which is cutting into a thing so that something may enter it to fill its notch, physically (p-139) or figuratively. From His glorification of it, the Exalted and Glorified made it below the rest of the acts of worship, in that there is no supererogatory performance (nafl) in it after one has entered into it.

Al-Harali said: "Because obligations, whoever does not perform them, the pillar of his religion collapses limb by limb; just as supererogatory acts, whoever does not perform them, he is deprived of their adornment. So obligations are soundness and supererogatory acts are adornment."

In His saying ﴿in them﴾ there is an indication that the Hajj may validly take place within some of them, and that the Hajj is not like fasting in being exactly coextensive with its time. Thus among acts of worship there is that which is exactly coextensive with its time, like fasting; that which has a range within it, like prayer; and that which must reach its conclusion, like the Hajj, and latitude is allowed in beginning it. — End. ﴿The Hajj﴾, meaning whoever enters into it in any manner.

Since in man there are four powers: the appetitive, which is animal; the irascible, which is predatory; the illusory, which is satanic and, with the assistance of the two other powers, arouses contention and dominance in everything; and the intellectual, which is angelic. The purpose of all acts of worship is to subdue the three powers, because the source of all evils is confined to them, while the intellectual one is what is sought. He said, indicating it and warning against them in order: ﴿So there shall be no lewdness﴾, meaning no approaching women with anything of the matters of marriage.

Since lewdness (al-rafath) is what calls to intercourse (p-140), which is sinfulness through leaving the valid state of ihram, He said, adding to it everything that falls under this term: ﴿nor wickedness﴾.

Al-Harali said: "It is leaving the encompassment of knowledge, intellect, and nature." — End.

Since contention (al-miraa') may lead to wickedness through what it stirs of rancor and inflaming of hearts, and it is a particular, great sin whose harm is immense, He said: ﴿nor disputing﴾, meaning contending by speech, twisting away from the intent, like the repelling of an executioner by hand or sword. Perhaps He expressed it with this verbal noun (masdar), whose pattern is usually an augmented form, rather than al-jadal (disputation), whose meaning is repelling in litigation, so that the negation would fall upon the exaggeration (p-141), and thus pardon of its root would be understood, because hardly anyone is safe from it. The same applies to wickedness ﴿in the Hajj﴾. So wickedness became an intermediary between two matters connected to it. Disputing, because it may corrupt relations between people, is the greatest in danger, and it combines the desire found in lewdness, and it may be wickedness; thus it includes the foulness of all of them. For this reason the seven readers (al-Qurra' al-Sab'ah) agreed on its being built (with fathah) with "la" rather than with raf', unlike what precedes it. This is because building (bina') indicates negation of the quiddity, and negating it necessitates negating all its instances. Whereas raf' only indicates negation of one indefinite instance of that quiddity, which does not necessitate negating all instances. Also, because the Arabs used to build the Hajj upon intercalation (al-nasi') and would differ concerning it at the station (of 'Arafah). So disputing about it was removed after the clarification in every respect, whether concerning servants, dependents, and others, or intercalation, the station, and other things, since its sacred places (mash'ir) have become known (p-142), its laws are established, its rites are fixed, and all its landmarks are made clear. Thus contention concerning its matter is entirely removed.

Al-Harali said: "He forbade, in the Hajj, turning toward creatures with what is repugnant of lewdness, abuse, and disputing, so that creatures would not turn toward creatures during the Hajj except with what in turning is turning toward the Truth in reality. Thus what the Truth, exalted be He, is distant from being confronted with, is protected against in the time of Hajj, just as what pertains to the self of impurities is guarded against in the performance of prayer. In His coming as negation and not as prohibition is an indication that it contradicts the state of Hajj, since negation is the proper form for what contradicts, and prohibition is the proper form for what can be contradicted and opposed, as He said concerning what is open to disputation: ﴿And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in the way that is best﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 46] (p-143). Between the address of prohibition and that of negation there is a loss in the legal rulings, since jurisprudence in rulings is built upon realizing it in their foundations and derivations." — End.

Since these negated matters are evil, and the sense is: whatever you do of these forbidden things in this most emphatic manner, you will be punished for it, He connected to it: ﴿And whatever﴾. Al-Harali said: "Since He protected against the evil treatment of creatures toward creatures, He alluded to placing oneself in the position of that goodness, so that one falls into the place of bringing forth souls to be drawn to them by bestowing good, which is goodness from the good of this world. So in His informing us there is an encouragement to goodness in the Hajj for one another, because of what its delegation gathers of the weak and the one cut off. So He said: ﴿whatever you do﴾." — End. That is, whatever good act occurs for you at any time ﴿of good﴾ in the Hajj or otherwise, with reliance in detachment (p-144) or provisioning in asceticism, or other than that, of good speech, replacing lewdness, righteousness and piety in place of wickedness, and good character, ease, and harmony in place of disputing. ﴿Allah knows it﴾, He who possesses all attributes of perfection, so He will reward you for it; thus this is the strongest encouragement and warning.

Since He generalized in urging toward good in a comprehensive manner that includes provisioning, and then left it after specifying, He pointed out that good is provision in a way that encompasses the sensory and the spiritual, as an increase in urging toward it, since nothing is more harmful than the lack of provision for most servants. So He said: ﴿And take provision﴾, meaning piety, for your return, which compels sensory provisioning for your livelihood, which compels asceticism regarding what is in people's hands, and consolation for their needy, protecting the servant from the punishment of Allah.

"Guard yourselves against the Fire, even with half a date." That is the fruit of piety. Provision is the enjoyment of the traveler. Then He gave the reason for that by what it produced, with His saying ﴿For indeed the best provision is piety﴾. It is possible that the sense is: "And take provision and fear Allah in (p-145) your provisioning, ﴿for indeed the best provision is piety﴾." In detachment there are entryways of corruption in some intentions of those mixed with the reliant, from dependence upon creatures. So He commanded all to take provision, to conceal the two categories, since every gathering must have both sides. — Al-Harali said this, and said: "Within this is their classification into three categories: the one who relies on Allah with no provision, for him is the best of the two provisions; the one who enjoys without realizing his piety, for him there is in reality no provision; and the one who combines piety with enjoyment, this is in perfection of the Sunnah, as the Prayer and Peace be upon him said: 'Tie it and rely upon Allah,' because that conceals both sides more completely. The reality of piety in the matter of provisioning is looking to Allah, exalted be He, in establishing His creation and command." One of the people of gnosis (ahl al-ma'rifah) said: "Whoever Allah, glorified and exalted, has accustomed to the continuous contemplation of Him through absence from all else, has possessed the provision; so let him go wherever he wishes, for he has found a way." — End.

(p-146) Since it is known from this that the sense is: "So increase in provision accompanied by piety," and since man is a locus of deficiency, increase in it usually drives him toward transgression, except those whom Allah protects, and they are few. The Exalted and Glorified said, emphasizing the matter of piety and honoring it by attributing it to His noble Self, as an alert to sincerity for the sake of His exalted essence, not by considering anything of hope, fear, or association with Hajj (p-147) or other than it, and linking it to what the context has guided to in its implied meaning: ﴿And fear Me﴾, meaning in your piety through provisioning. He increased the encouragement toward it by His saying: ﴿O people of understanding﴾, meaning the pure intellects and the clear, sincere, luminous minds that are detached from all bodily ties, so that they perceive the majesty of piety and adhere to it.

The Qur'an reading in this translation is my rendering of the meaning. Where the commentary is a quotation, I have kept the ﴿ ﴾ markers.

When the people of intelligent resolve, whose souls are pure and capable of detaching themselves from transient worldly concerns, understood from this exhortation to take abundant provisions, their souls were stirred to ask about trade, namely whether it is disliked in a particular time or place, for the purpose of spending its profits on good causes. This was especially so when they recalled that some people in the pre-Islamic age (al-Jāhiliyya) used to dislike trade for pilgrims. So He answered with His words, informing them that severing ties is better for one whose resolve is sincere and whose aspiration is noble: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, that is, no sin, ﴿in seeking﴾, that is, in striving earnestly and diligently to seek, ﴿bounty﴾, that is, gain through trade during the seasons of the Ḥajj and other times, ﴿from your Lord﴾, the One who is good to you in every state. So do not rely for bounty on anyone but Him. Al-Bukhārī related in his Tafsīr from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: ʿUkāẓ, Majanna and Dhū al-Majāz were markets in the pre-Islamic age, and they regarded trading in the seasons as sinful, so there was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord﴾, during the seasons of the Ḥajj.

Since accumulating wealth is disliked only because it distracts from the remembrance of Allah, He made the command to remember Him a consequence of this, in His words ﴿then when﴾, that is, seek bounty from your Lord through trade, ﴿you pour forth﴾, that is, when you carry out the outpouring (al-ifāḍa). The object is omitted because it is known, meaning: when you urge your mounts forward at sunset, and they pour forth into those valleys as water flows down the slopes of ravines. The root meaning of al-ifāḍa is pushing forward in large numbers ﴿from ʿArafāt﴾, the mountain on which you stood, at the gate of your Lord, at the Greatest Standing, without which the Ḥajj is not attained. The word is definite in the sense of knowledge (min maʿnā al-taʿarruf), since it was preceded by an indefinite noun. Its tāʾ is not the feminine marker, which would prevent it from taking tanwīn (ṣarf). Rather, it is the sign of the feminine plural, the pilgrims heading to spend the night at Muzdalifa. It is a proper name for the standing place, and it was named Jamʿ. ﴿Then remember Allah﴾, the One of majesty by His essence, with all kinds of remembrance, ﴿at﴾, that is, near, ﴿the Sacred Monument﴾, that is, the landmark. Since it is within the Ḥaram, He said ﴿al-Ḥarām﴾, and it is the mountain called Quzaḥ. It is from al-shuʿūr, which is hidden to the inner perception. Thus the first standing is a sign of the decline, effacement and passing away of this world, and the second indicates, by its dawn and its sun, the Resurrection, for the recompense of creatures for their deeds. The use of ʿinda (at/near) indicates that all of Muzdalifa is a standing place, not only the valley of Muḥassar, for all of it is near to it. This implies that standing there is valid, a fortiori.

Al-Ḥarālī said: This is a portion of standing for a brief period, fixed in the sacred land at the approach of day, as an equivalent to standing at ʿArafa within the non-sacred land from the sun's decline until nightfall, so that standing may be accomplished both in the non-sacred land and in the sacred. Thus there was a standing in daytime that ends at night at ʿArafa and a standing at night that ends at day at the Mashʿar. He, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, stood there after the dawn prayer and before sunrise. This is the remembrance of Him in that place, because remembrance depends on the one who remembers. The remembrance of the tongue is speech, the remembrance of the body is action, the remembrance of the soul is state and affect, and the remembrance of the heart is knowledge, certainty and the like. Everything has its remembrance according to its nature. In the combination of the two standings, in the sacred and non-sacred lands, at the landmark of the Ḥajj, which is a sign of the Gathering, there is an announcement and glad tiding that the people of standing are of two kinds. One kind stands in a place of terror and fear, standing for a long time, taking as an example the standing of those at ʿArafa from the sun's decline until its setting, six hours. Another kind has its share of standing in repose in the shade of the Throne, which is the sacred precinct of the Day of Resurrection and its Kaʿba. The lightness of standing at the Sacred Monument indicates that the span of that long day passes over those who take shade under the Throne as the easiest of periods, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said, as long as an obligatory prayer. So there was in that a superiority of the standing in the sacred land over the standing in the non-sacred land. End of quotation.

Since it is known from the mention of the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-Aʿẓam) that the sense is: as He deserves to be remembered for His essence, He follows it with His words ﴿and remember Him﴾, that is, at the Sacred Monument and elsewhere, ﴿as﴾, that is, according to what and for the sake of what, ﴿He guided you﴾, O people, all of you, to Islam, and O the five (tribes) in particular, to abandon standing there apart and to stand with the people at the standing place of ﴿your father Abraham﴾, peace be upon him.

Since the sense is: indeed He has made clear to you a clarity that He did not make clear to anyone before you, and He has granted you success in acting upon it, He follows it with His words: ﴿And indeed﴾, that is, you ﴿were﴾, and since they were upon guidance before ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy, and among them after that were those who were guided, such as Zayd ibn ʿAmr and Waraqa ibn Nawfal, their time was not wholly consumed by error. So He affirmed the preposition, saying ﴿before it﴾, that is, before the guidance which Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him, brought to you, ﴿surely you were among the astray﴾, astray from the paths of guidance and the stations of the prophets, in knowledge and in action, since you used to pour forth from the Sacred Monument.

When al-Biqa'i had condemned the deviation they were engaged in regarding the standing (at Muzdalifah), describing it as misguidance with a nominal sentence emphasized by several forms of emphasis, and since what had preceded, the mention of *al-ifadah* (the outpouring), was not decisive in establishing obligation, He pointed them to the magnitude of the guidance He had granted them in the agreement (with the Prophet's practice), using the particle of delay (*thumma*). So He said, linking it to what is implied: "So do not pour forth from al-Mash'ar al-Haram (the Sacred Monument) with the outpouring you used to make in opposition to the people," indicating the difference between the two outpourings and the great distance between them, in a manner that makes the obligation known.

﴿Thumma﴾ (then) means: after your long immersion in misguidance, "I sent down to you in this wise remembrance" (p-153) "which you rejected, and which is your might and your honor, not what you assumed to be honor for you through exalting yourselves over the people by opposing the guidance in the standing at Muzdalifah and in the outpouring from it." ﴿Pour forth﴾ means: when you have completed the standing.

Al-Harali said: Since address has an ordering of the more important before the less important, just as existence has an ordering of the earlier before the later, the particle of succession, which is *thumma*, occurs sometimes to order existence and sometimes to order reporting. So a speaker says, for example: "Go to such-and-such a need," placing the more important matter first in the report, "then let your departure be from such-and-such a place." So what is prior in existence is later in the report by way of succession. From this meaning is His saying. End of quotation.

Then, "pour forth, O Hums!" ﴿from where the people pour forth﴾, that is, most of them, and they are at ʿArafat, to al-Mash'ar al-Haram so that you may spend the night there. Al-Bukhari reported in the Tafsir chapter, from ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "Quraysh and those who followed their religion used to stand at Muzdalifah, and they were called al-Hums, while the rest of the Arabs stood at ʿArafat. When Islam came, Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to go to ʿArafat, stand there, and then pour forth from it. That is His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿Then pour forth﴾," the verse.

﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾, that is, ask the Possessor of majesty and honor to forgive you what you used to do in the days of your ignorance, of opposing the guidance in the standing, and what remains in the souls of the traces of that custom, and other shortcomings besides that which Allah knows of you.

Al-Harali said: Customs are the most difficult thing for those who worship, and the path to Allah the Exalted is by casting them off. Their disputation, that is, in their standing in the Sacred Precinct, was without knowledge, because knowledge requires that the one standing be fearful, and the one who is fearful does not feel fear in the Sacred Precinct, since Allah, glorified and exalted, made the Sacred Precinct a place of safety. So it is right that the standing be outside the Sacred Precinct; when one feels safe, one enters the Sacred Precinct, and when one enters the Sacred Precinct, one feels safe. End of quotation.

He made the noble Name manifest, to establish the station and to inform that He is (p-155) described by what describes Him in a general manner, without regard to any restriction or aspect. So He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, the Possessor of perfection, ﴿is Forgiving﴾, that is, veiling the sin of whoever seeks His forgiveness, ﴿Merciful﴾, that is, abundant in mercy, who admits the one who seeks forgiveness into the company of those shown mercy, those in whom no sin has appeared. So He treats them with honor in the manner of the merciful toward the one shown mercy, so that the one who repents from sin becomes like one who has no sin.

When He had commanded them to remember Him during the rites (al-manasik), and since a person is inclined to remembrance during them, He commanded them to remember Him after completing them, because one who has finished worship is apt to rest, and so lapse from remembrance to other things. Their custom was to recount the glories of their forefathers after finishing. So He said: ﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾, that is, finished them with clear completion, without any doubt about it, ﴿your rites﴾, that is, the pillars of the Hajj. He repeated the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam) with the same veneration as before and generalized the remembrance in all aspects, saying: ﴿then remember Allah﴾, who is the One from whom alone every blessing comes to you, and who is the One who guided you, ﴿with remembrance﴾ ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾, because they showed you kindness through upbringing, which in reality is from the grace of Allah the Exalted. Yet they inflicted upon you every trial for which no blessing could compensate, for they led you astray. Glory be to the One who is pleased, who is the Absolute Bestower and the Guide, that He should be remembered in the manner of one who was a means of a particular blessing, when He is the One who bestowed it upon him, despite that man having been a cause of misguidance!

Al-Haralli said: Thus the mention of their being sent forth from their customary speech is joined with their being sent forth from their customary station, a sending-forth from their habits in their deeds and states. In this announcement is a taking of creation to treat the Truth in the manner of those whom they esteem among creation, and this is because of the affliction of what dominated them of being bound to what they see, and the weakness of faith in what they have heard or known.

Since this upbringing contained a deficiency, this address was directed to it, as has been reported: "Be shy before Allah as you would be shy before a noble man of your people." The Exalted said: ﴿or with a more intense remembrance﴾. End of quotation.

That is: remember Allah with a higher remembrance than that, by remembering Him with a remembrance more intense than your remembrance of your fathers, due to His general bounty. What enters under this remembrance is that one should be too proud to have a partner with Allah in His worship or in any of His affairs, just as a son is too proud to have a partner in his father; rather, he should be even more proud in the matter of shirk.

Al-Haralli said: So the raising of the address to what is more fitting for the Truth, preferring what returns to Him over what returns to creation. End of quotation.

When the Exalted had commanded what He commanded of remembering Him for His own essence, then for His bounty in absolute terms, then restricted it to His singling out with that, and left out mention of others, He thereby made a division of people in accepting the command. So He said, turning the speech away from direct address to indicate generality: ﴿Among the people is one who﴾ has the world as his greatest concern, so he pays no regard to anything else; he ﴿says﴾ (the pronoun is singular in observance of the word "man"), which gives good news that the one destroyed in this nation, if Allah wills, is few: ﴿Our Lord﴾, O You who are good to us, ﴿give us in this world﴾, its object omitted, its estimate being: what we want, while the state is that he has "no share"; it may also be an conjunction to what is estimated: so He gives him what He wills of it, not what he asked for himself. And he has ﴿no share in the Hereafter﴾, that is, no portion, because he has no desire for it; he does not seek it nor strive for it as it should be striven for.

Al-Haralli said: Al-khalaq is the portion suited to creation and to disposition.

﴿And among them is one who﴾ makes his worship and his Hajj a means to desire his Lord, and remembers Allah the Exalted as He commanded, so he ﴿says: Our Lord﴾, by Your goodness, ﴿give us in this world﴾ a state and a living ﴿good﴾, by which we are not made to reach the Hereafter in a manner that pleases You not.

Al-Haralli said: It is sufficiency of food, drink, clothing, (p-159) shelter and wife, as they are, with no nobility in them. End of quotation.

﴿And in the Hereafter, good﴾, that is, from Your mercy by which You admit us into Paradise. Since hope is not fitting except with fear, and giving a good does not negate touching by an evil, he said: ﴿and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, that is, by Your pardon and Your forgiveness.

When He had commanded them to remember Him during the rites (al-manasik), and since a person is inclined to remembrance during them, He commanded them to remember Him after completing them, because one who has finished worship is apt to rest, and so lapse from remembrance to other things. Their custom was to recount the glories of their forefathers after finishing. So He said: ﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾, that is, finished them with clear completion, without any doubt about it, ﴿your rites﴾, that is, the pillars of the Hajj. He repeated the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam) with the same veneration as before and generalized the remembrance in all aspects, saying: ﴿then remember Allah﴾, who is the One from whom alone every blessing comes to you, and who is the One who guided you, ﴿with remembrance﴾ ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾, because they showed you kindness through upbringing, which in reality is from the grace of Allah the Exalted. Yet they inflicted upon you every trial for which no blessing could compensate, for they led you astray. Glory be to the One who is pleased, who is the Absolute Bestower and the Guide, that He should be remembered in the manner of one who was a means of a particular blessing, when He is the One who bestowed it upon him, despite that man having been a cause of misguidance!

Al-Haralli said: Thus the mention of their being sent forth from their customary speech is joined with their being sent forth from their customary station, a sending-forth from their habits in their deeds and states. In this announcement is a taking of creation to treat the Truth in the manner of those whom they esteem among creation, and this is because of the affliction of what dominated them of being bound to what they see, and the weakness of faith in what they have heard or known.

Since this upbringing contained a deficiency, this address was directed to it, as has been reported: "Be shy before Allah as you would be shy before a noble man of your people." The Exalted said: ﴿or with a more intense remembrance﴾. End of quotation.

That is: remember Allah with a higher remembrance than that, by remembering Him with a remembrance more intense than your remembrance of your fathers, due to His general bounty. What enters under this remembrance is that one should be too proud to have a partner with Allah in His worship or in any of His affairs, just as a son is too proud to have a partner in his father; rather, he should be even more proud in the matter of shirk.

Al-Haralli said: So the raising of the address to what is more fitting for the Truth, preferring what returns to Him over what returns to creation. End of quotation.

When the Exalted had commanded what He commanded of remembering Him for His own essence, then for His bounty in absolute terms, then restricted it to His singling out with that, and left out mention of others, He thereby made a division of people in accepting the command. So He said, turning the speech away from direct address to indicate generality: ﴿Among the people is one who﴾ has the world as his greatest concern, so he pays no regard to anything else; he ﴿says﴾ (the pronoun is singular in observance of the word "man"), which gives good news that the one destroyed in this nation, if Allah wills, is few: ﴿Our Lord﴾, O You who are good to us, ﴿give us in this world﴾, its object omitted, its estimate being: what we want, while the state is that he has "no share"; it may also be an conjunction to what is estimated: so He gives him what He wills of it, not what he asked for himself. And he has ﴿no share in the Hereafter﴾, that is, no portion, because he has no desire for it; he does not seek it nor strive for it as it should be striven for.

Al-Haralli said: Al-khalaq is the portion suited to creation and to disposition.

﴿And among them is one who﴾ makes his worship and his Hajj a means to desire his Lord, and remembers Allah the Exalted as He commanded, so he ﴿says: Our Lord﴾, by Your goodness, ﴿give us in this world﴾ a state and a living ﴿good﴾, by which we are not made to reach the Hereafter in a manner that pleases You not.

Al-Haralli said: It is sufficiency of food, drink, clothing, (p-159) shelter and wife, as they are, with no nobility in them. End of quotation.

﴿And in the Hereafter, good﴾, that is, from Your mercy by which You admit us into Paradise. Since hope is not fitting except with fear, and giving a good does not negate touching by an evil, he said: ﴿and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, that is, by Your pardon and Your forgiveness.

When these people were upon the path of the Messengers, because they worshipped God first, as the context indicates, their souls were broken [in humility]. Then they remembered Him through those three stages, so their hearts were stirred by the manifestation of the light of His majesty, glory be to Him and exalted. Thereby they became qualified for supplication, and their supplication was complete, as the Friend (Khalil), peace be upon him, did when he said: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 78], through the verses, until he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me judgment and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 83]. So he placed the remembrance before the supplication. This is also what He indicated at the end of Al 'Imran in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we have believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins﴾ [Al 'Imran: 193], through the verses. So they gave precedence to obedience. He magnified their status by His saying, as a resumptive statement (istinaf), which carries the meaning of good tidings of the abundance of those who are saved in this community. Or the plural is for the greatness of their attributes: ﴿Those﴾, i.e., the people of elevated ranks and great aims, ﴿for them﴾, i.e., this category only, because the first [category] has informed that the matter is against them, not for them.

Since most of the actions of servants are not upright, and the least that can be said of them is that they are free of a good intention, He said, indicating this: ﴿a share﴾. It is a noun for the portion that falls to each member of a group when a division is made, being ﴿of what﴾ [they have earned]. Had He said "they sought" (talabu), for example, it would not cover all their actions. Had He said "they did" (fa'alu), it would have been thought to exclude speech, so He turned to His saying: ﴿they have earned﴾ (kasabu), i.e., they sought, obtained, managed, and strove in it, and gathered from the essence of their actions, both verbal and physical, including the doctrinal. This is what they were sincere in, and it is what they are rewarded for, and it is little in comparison with the rest of their actions.

Since the swiftest of people in reckoning is the one most knowledgeable of its branches, in both error and correctness, and since the implied meaning is: God knows the hidden and the apparent of their actions, and distinguishes the good from the bad, and therefore He recompenses them according to that, He followed this with His saying: ﴿And God﴾, i.e., the One encompassing in knowledge and power, ﴿is swift in reckoning﴾. He has counted the actions and clarified what is due for each of them as recompense, and it reaches the doer, because of His vast knowledge and comprehensive power. It was said to one of them: "How does God reckon the creation at one time?" He said: "As He provides for them at one time." In this is an encouragement, that He does not forget any deed, and a warning, that falsehood does not prevail over Him, and no delayer can resist Him.

[p.162] Since He had commanded them to remember Him at the completion of the rites, and it might be understood that their remembrance was to be confined to the time when they used to mention their fathers, He spoke in general terms. The exhortation to remembrance is made more emphatic by repeating the recommendation to it in the form of a command, so that its importance is magnified. ﴿And remember﴾ with stoning. He commanded stoning but expressed it as remembrance, so that it encompasses every form of remembrance, whether by the tongue or otherwise. ﴿Allah﴾, that is, for what He deserves in His essence of perfection. ﴿During numbered days.﴾ Since these days need nothing beyond counting, being few in number, and since they follow the days in which one must be careful about matters through deliberation and other means so that they become known, He spoke, combining the description of the non-rational noun with the feminine plural ending (alif and ta') which is regularly used when its referent is a plural of paucity: ﴿numbered﴾. These are the days of your stay at Mina as guests of Him, glorified is He, in order to perform the remaining completions of the Hajj rites that are incumbent upon you. The first of them [p.163] is the Day of Qarr (settling), which is the eleventh, so that people may settle at Mina on it. The second is the first Day of Nafr (departure). The third is the greatest Day of Nafr. These three are called the Days of Tashriq (drying of meat), and together with the Day of Sacrifice they are called the Days of Nahr (sacrifice). The four days together with the Day of 'Arafah are the Days of Takbir (proclaiming Allah's greatness) and remembrance.

Since it was understood from this that residence there is necessary throughout the three days, He negated this, making things easy, because the Hajj gathers the strong and the weak, the servant and the served, and the weak in this religion has precedence over the strong. He therefore said, indicating that in that great gathering a person has two inclinations: one inclines him to remain in those pleasing places and forgiven gatherings, and the other draws him to his family, homeland, tribe and brethren. ﴿Whoever hastens﴾ among you in departing to return to his homeland ﴿in two days﴾ [of them], ﴿there is no sin upon him.﴾ Haste is doing a thing [p.164] before its most suitable time. He restricted it to two days to inform that whoever is still in Mina when the second day sets is obliged to spend the night of the third night and to stone on the third day; but if he departs before its sunset, the obligation of spending the night and stoning falls from him. Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: without disagreement. Likewise, if sunset overtakes him while he is on the way out before he has separated from it [p.165] from it, and he did not specify the delay because its limit at the third day is well known, since the days are three.

Since this might have suggested that one who delays incurs sin, as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to say, and since the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were a people who raced toward lofty deeds, and since He, glorified and exalted is He, desired to show leniency to the people of this religion, He concealed explicit encouragement to delay. He therefore expressed it also by negating sin, as in the first case, after indicating encouragement to it by describing the first departure as hastening. He said: ﴿And whoever delays﴾, that is, remains in Mina until the completion of the three days and stones on the third day, ﴿there is no sin upon him.﴾ Delay is moving an action away from the present moment.

Shaykh Muhyi al-Din (al-Nawawi) said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and the scholars of his school said: departure on the second day of Tashriq is permissible, and departure on the third is permissible. This is agreed upon, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever hastens﴾ – the verse. They said: delaying until the third day is more excellent, based on the authentic hadiths that

"the Messenger of Allah ﷺ departed on the third day."

[p.166] Since the basis of physical acts rests on intentions, He restricted this by His words: ﴿for whoever﴾, that is, this negation of sin applies to both categories, for whoever ﴿fears Allah﴾ among its people, thereby directing his actions toward what pleases Allah. Since the implication was: do whatever you wish of hastening or delaying, He followed it with what is known to be its spirit, saying: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, that is, the One who has complete encompassing knowledge.

Since the Hajj is a gathering (hashr) in this world, and departure from it resembles the departure of the people of the place of standing after the Gathering away from this world, a group to Paradise and a group to the Blaze, He reminded them of this by His words: ﴿And know that you﴾ all together ﴿to Him﴾, not to other than Him, ﴿will be gathered﴾ after resurrection. Hashr is gathering by compulsion, and it applies from the first emergence of them from their graves until the end of the place of standing. So know what will be the cause of your departure from it to the abode of His honor [p.167], not to the abode of His humiliation.

Al-Harali said: the universality of the Hajj and its rites corresponds, in what it signifies, to the matter of the Day of Resurrection and its stations. The pilgrim's departure from his homeland, provisioned, is like the departure of the dead from this world provisioned with the provision of deeds; his arrival at the miqat and his ihram, stripped bare, is like his rising from the grave, naked; his talbiyah during his Hajj is like his talbiyah at his gathering: ﴿hastening toward the caller﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. Likewise, his standing at a place until the end of the ifadah, and his residing in the sanctuary of Allah, correspond to the Hereafter, which is Paradise; and drinking from the water of Zamzam, which is a sign of the provision Allah gives the people of Paradise, has many aspects that those of understanding and certainty perceive. For this reason, the most complete conclusion to the rulings of the Hajj is the mention of the Gathering. End of quotation.

Here is complete what He, glorified and exalted is He, intended to explain of the five pillars of Islam: faith, prayer, zakat, fasting and Hajj. The first three of them were alluded to at the beginning of the surah in His words: ﴿who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]. The mention of Hajj is for greater emphasis on it, placing it after fasting, which was mentioned earlier. Perhaps this is the reason for placing fasting before Hajj in some narrations and after it in others, in the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, in the Sahih: "Islam is built upon five."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 204:

Since He, glorified and exalted is He, had mentioned the one who desires only the worldly life and the one who desires both abodes, and there remained from the rational divisions the one who turns away from both, and he is non-existent, so He did not mention him, and [there remains] the one who desires only the Hereafter. Each of these divisions is sometimes secret and sometimes open. The one to be feared among them is only the one who is secret, desiring the worldly life while showing [the appearance of] desiring the Hereafter. This is the hypocrite (munafiq). He began with him after the mention of piety (taqwa) and gathering (hashr), so that he would be struck and be the first to be addressed with that matter, targeted with the threat of gathering. He brought him in the form of what is at the beginning of the surah concerning the mention of the hypocrites, so that the listener would recall those accounts and summon them with those conditions. The long separation and the distance of time made this fitting. So He said: ﴿And among the people is one who﴾ (p-169) meaning, a person or the one who ﴿pleases you﴾, i.e., pleases you and captivates the core of your heart, O addressed one, ﴿with his speech﴾. As we mentioned at the beginning of the surah, he deceives. And "yu'jibu" (pleases/impresses) is from i'jab, and it is from 'ajab (wonder), which is a thing being outside its counterparts of its kind to the extent that it is a rarity in its making, as said by al-Harali.

Al-Isfahani said: it is a state that overtakes a person upon perceiving a perfection whose cause is unknown. From al-Raghib that he said: it is not something that has a state in its essence, but rather it is according to relations to one who knows the cause and one who does not know it. The literal meaning of "a'jabani kadha" (this pleased me): (p-170) it appeared to me in an appearance whose cause I did not know.

Since the mention of this came after the mention of gathering, it might have been thought that the speech or the pleasing occurs in that state, so He restricted it by His saying: ﴿in﴾, i.e., existing in ﴿the life of this world﴾. His lengthy duration in it only increases his speech in beauty and what is hidden of his deed in ugliness. As for the Hereafter, his speech is neither good nor pleasing. ﴿And he calls God as witness﴾, the One who combines the attributes of perfection (p-171) ﴿to what is in his heart﴾, that it corresponds to what he displayed with his tongue. ﴿And he is﴾, i.e., while the state is that he is ﴿the most contentious of opponents﴾, i.e., he persists in quarrelling with falsehood, his disputation never ceases; all of this while he shows that he is upon goodness and beauty, and he directs every part of his dispute toward an aspect that turns it from what he intended of ugliness to comeliness. Ladd (ladad) is the intensity of enmity, and khisam (dispute) is the speech that strikes the ear of the one who listens and enters into its canal what restrains him from his claim and his assertion, as said by al-Harali. Al-Isfahani said: it is going deep in investigating a thing and pressing into it; and it is permissible to make khisam the superlative "ألد" as an intensification, ending.

When he had mentioned that he is the most hostile of adversaries, he began to state the reason for his hostility. He said, coordinating with what is implied by the preceding clause: "If he confronts you, he strives to show that he is a reformer." Or the clause may be circumstantial (ḥāliyyah): ﴿And when he turns away﴾, meaning he turns away in his heart, or he says this about the one he deceived with his words. He used the expression "striving" (sa'y) to indicate hastening to bring about strife with the utmost effort, and so he said: ﴿he strives﴾. He drew attention to the extent of his corruption by saying: ﴿in the land﴾, meaning all of it, through his deeds and his words among those who agree with him. ﴿To cause corruption﴾, meaning to bring about corruption, which is a term for all acts of disobedience, ﴿therein﴾, meaning in the land, in relations among people, for the purpose of destruction. People are the thing he hastens to most, so they become his partners in acts of corruption. When he does what he intends, he becomes known among them, and so he has helpers against it. He made clear that by his corruption he reaches his goal, saying, naming the tilled field a "tilth" (ḥarth) for emphasis: ﴿and destroy the tilth﴾, meaning the cultivated land by which living beings sustain themselves. Al-Ḥarālī (al-Ḥarālī) said: he called it ḥarth because it is what he attributed to creation, and he did not call it zar'(crops) because that is attributed to the Real (al-Ḥaqq). End of quotation.

And because when the cause is destroyed, the caused thing is destroyed, but not vice versa: ﴿and the offspring﴾, meaning the progeny by which the species of living beings continues.

Al-Ḥarālī said: it is the extraction of the subtle part of a thing from its whole. End of quotation. His doing this is for the sake of corruption. The verse was arranged in this way for clarity, because the meaning is that his aim, first, by causing strife among people, is to reach destruction, and second, by destruction, to reach corruption. ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning while the Greatest King ﴿does not love corruption﴾, meaning He does not act toward it as one who loves; so He does not command it but forbids it, does not approve of it but changes it, however long the time, and punishes for it. He did not say "destruction" (halāk), because destruction may be merely outward, and so it may be righteous, as when it is retribution (qiṣāṣ). Nor did He say "corruption" (ifsād) in the sense of including cases where the corruption is unintended. The verse is of the type called iḥtibāk (a rhetorical device in which two opposites are mentioned and each omits what the other supplies). He first mentioned corruption to indicate its omission the second time, and the second time he mentioned destruction to indicate its omission the first time. He mentioned the tilth, which is the cause, as an indication of the progeny, and the progeny, which is the effect, as an indication of the crops. So this is a second iḥtibāk.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 206:

Since there are people who commit corruption, and when they are told to desist they stop, he (God) made clear that this (the case of the corrupt-minded) is otherwise, to confirm the severity of their hostility (al-ladadiyya). So he said, giving good news with the particle of emphasis (tahqiq) that there will always remain among people those who uphold enjoining good and forbidding evil: ﴿And when it is said to him﴾ by whichever speaker it is said, ﴿"Fear God"﴾, that is, the Greatest King under whose domination everything is, ﴿and leave off what you are upon of corruption,﴾ ﴿pride takes him﴾, that is, overpowers him, because of the faculty of arrogance he has, ﴿in his self-esteem﴾ (al-izza) (p-175) because of the haughtiness it contains and the contempt for the command of God. It is not the nature of creation to be characterized by that, for ﴿honour belongs to God entirely﴾. ﴿With sin﴾, that is, accompanied by wrongdoing, namely the base and vile deed, and that which is not lawful and necessitates punishment, by despising others and being arrogant toward them.

Since this vile matter is always his habit, by which he prepares for himself the means to achieve what he desires, the statement follows: ﴿So Hell is sufficient for him﴾, that is, his adequacy is ﴿Hell﴾, which will be a resting-place (mihad) for him just as he prepared himself for corruption. The specification of this name, which indicates grimness, is in confrontation, that is, meeting with a disagreeable face, in response to his having confronted someone like himself who commanded him.

Al-Harali said: "So for the meaning of what pertains to judgment, the Exalted names the Fire by one of its names." (end)

﴿And wretched is the resting-place﴾, it and the resting-place being the place of calm and what is pleasant among what is spread out and trodden upon. Al-Harali said this, and said: In it is an indication of God, Mighty and Majestic, granting respite to this nation out of consideration for its Prophet, so He deferred the punishment of the Hereafter for its wicked and its disbelievers. Had He hastened the punishment of the world for its believers, He would have made worldly punishment the lot of its disbelievers and the Hereafter the lot of its believers, and this indicates a long stay and eternal abiding therein.

When he had finished reporting on this category, which is the worst of the categories, he followed it with its best, so that it would serve as a conclusion. Between the two there is a contrast: the first is one who destroys people to preserve his own self, while this one destroys his self to set people right. So He said: ﴿And among people is one who﴾, i.e., any person, or the one who, ﴿sells﴾, i.e., does this act whenever the opportunity presents itself, which is that he sells with the utmost desire and eagerness ﴿himself﴾, so he proceeds to destroy it. Or he buys it with that which will be the cause of its emancipation and revival, through striving in the commands of Allah, by forbidding such a stubborn person from his wicked deed, commanding him to piety, and reminding him of Allah.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Suhayb, may Allah be pleased with him, because when he emigrated, the Quraysh wanted to return him, so he gave them his wealth until they let his way free. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "The sale has been profitable." According to this, the verb *shara* (شَرى) has the meaning of *ishtara* (اشْتَرى, "bought").

Then he gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿seeking﴾, i.e., pursuing, striving for, and aiming with the utmost possibility at each of these, ﴿the pleasure of Allah﴾, i.e., the pleasure of the One who encompasses all attributes of perfection, and of the time and place of pleasure, as indicated by the noun being of the *mīmī* form (a *maṣdar*, verbal noun, beginning with *mīm*), and that being the utmost in its category, as indicated by its being pronounced with the extended *tā'* (ت) in pause, due to what is known of the intensity of Allah's mercy toward it. ﴿And Allah is Compassionate⦆ i.e., of far-reaching mercy, (p-178) and He made explicit the place where a pronoun would have been expected, indicating generality and the attribute that calls for mercy and nobility, so He said: ﴿to His servants﴾, all of them, in that He has lavished His blessings upon them, both apparent and hidden, despite their disbelief in Him or their negligence in His command. He made the path clear to them in the fullest clarity: first by reason, then by the Messengers, third by the laws, and fourth by the books that preserve them.

Perhaps the separation between the four categories by the ﴿numbered days﴾ was to emphasize its importance, since it belongs to the acts of the Hajj, and its delay after its counterparts is an indication that it is not among the pillars of the rites, but rather is compensated by a sacrifice (*dam*).

Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on Surah 2, verse 208:

When He concluded these two categories with the one who strives for the pleasure of Allah, in correspondence with the first ones, it was very fitting to follow it with His saying: ﴿O you who believe﴾ (p-179), so that this call would fall immediately upon the ear of this attentive listener, just as the hypocrite was shattered by what preceded it of piety and gathering (to the Resurrection). Along with that, it is an indication of the attribute of compassion. Repeating the command to faith among the various categories of deeds is among the greatest proofs of the wisdom of the One who commands it, for, along with it being more emphatic for His command and more fitting for His glory and honour, it makes clear that faith is the pillar of right guidance, which brings about felicity on the Day of Mutual Recrimination. So He said: ﴿Enter into submission﴾ (al-silm), that is, faith, which necessitates ease of compliance with every good. Al-silm, in origin, with a fatḥa or a kasra, means peace and truce, outwardly, by word and deed. That is: O you who have believed with your tongue like this obstinate one, let faith or submission be by the entirety of the inner and outer self, as an all-encompassing vessel from all sides, so that it surrounds the heart and the body just as it has surrounded the tongue, and there will be no path for the burden of ignorance and the coarseness of disbelief to reach you. ﴿Entirely﴾ (kaffah), that is, let all of you in that be one way (shar‘an wāḥidan) (p-180) like this one who sells himself, and do not divide, so that some of you are like this and some of you are like that obstinate one, for that is a proof of the falsehood of the claim to faith.

Since refusal and obstinacy, which are driven by arrogance and pride, are the act of Satan and the fruit of his being created from fire, He said: ﴿And do not follow﴾, that is, do not burden yourselves with matters of error, contrary to what Allah Most High has innately created them upon and facilitated for them of guidance, ﴿the footsteps of Satan﴾, that is, the paths of the distanced, burnt one, who through pride is far from the truth.

Al-Harali said: In its implication is that the authority in this day belongs to him, and in it is an indication and a warning of what has occurred in this Ummah and is occurring and will occur, of their departure from peace into fighting, through the outbreak of strife in tongues and spears over matters of this world, and their return to the affairs of their pre-Islamic ignorance, because this world is the fief of Satan just as the Hereafter is the essence of the Most Merciful. So the beginning of the strife was from the breaking of the door closed upon peace, and that was ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. Thus the turmoil has not ceased and does not cease until the war lays down its burdens.

(p-181) Then He, glorified and exalted, gave the reason for that in His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, that is, by what We have informed you of in the matter of your father Adam, upon him be peace, and other than that, of which the evidences are manifest. How excellent is this ending, opposed to the ending of the one before it! For remembering the compassion from Him, glorified be He, despite His greatness, and servitude from us, which is the meaning of walāya whose spirit is submission to all that the Beloved loves, and remembering the enmity of the misleader is the greatest deterrent from him and a call to Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 209:

When Allah, glorified and exalted be He, had established the proofs of His greatness, among which is His oneness, removed doubts, erased suspicions, and reminded (them) of the various kinds of kindness and beneficence, until He concluded the two verses with what He mentioned of His guardianship and of the enmity of the one who misleads from His path, He caused His saying ﴿If you slip﴾ to follow from that. By the particle of doubt (in "in," "if") He indicates that they had come to a state of such clarity of the path, the broad, the most secure place, the most trustworthy, the most straight and the safest, that it is far, very far, that they should slip from it. For this reason He said: ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾ (p-182), that is, through this Book about which there is no doubt.

Al-Harali said: The clear proofs are the witnessing of experience, and the report of what has passed, and the verification of what has occurred. He also said: The expression "in" (if) indicates that they are liable to slip, and the expression in the past tense indicates a turning back from it, as a mercy from Allah toward them, like His mercy earlier toward their two parents when Satan made them slip. Just as he made their two parents slip in the Garden from the forbidden tree, he made them slip in this world from the tree of forbidden things: blood, property and honor. End of quote.

Since fear impels one to adhere to the path of safety, He said: ﴿Then know﴾, for knowledge is the greatest helper toward objectives, ﴿that Allah﴾, who encompasses the attributes of perfection, ﴿is Mighty﴾, whom none who slips can overcome and from whom none who strays can escape, ﴿Wise﴾, who ordains what no one can annul any part of.

(p. 183) Since this sealing (*khatm*) signals punishment, and since punishment coming from a place where mercy is expected is more dreadful, and since the most beneficial of things is the clouds, which carry the rain, and the angels, who are pure good, and since those who witnessed the punishment came from the cloud, which is the expected place of mercy, the punishment is more terrifying. It is so that the 'Ad and the Children of Israel would be more awe-inspiring. The 'Ad had passed away, so it is customary that they cannot be questioned. Whoever slips after this clarification has come to resemble the Children of Israel in this condition, so he is deserving that his end should resemble theirs, in what they came to: being struck with humiliation and wretchedness, the descent of wrath, and falling into ruin. God the Exalted said: ﴿Do they await﴾, i.e., do they wait, when they have slipped. This is driven in the style of denial. The form of the third person, stripped of *ifti'al* (reflexive form), is to alert that the wrongdoers are at the furthest distance from the places of compassion and deservingness, with the appearance of arrogance and vengeance, with the Lord turning away from addressing them and turning toward their punishment in ways they did not reckon. ﴿Unless God comes to them﴾, i.e., the glory of the One (p. 184) that nothing can bear, the manifestation of His majesty and the appearance of His splendour, His glory being ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾: a canopy within a canopy. It is what screens the sun, so it is in the utmost darkness, terror and awe, because of its density, which overwhelms the one who sees what is in it and destroys whatever it reaches. And beyond this there are other kinds of glory which no one can measure as it truly deserves except God. ﴿And the angels﴾, i.e., and His army will come, those who do not disobey God in what He commands them. This is according to the reading of the majority (*qira'at al-jama'a*, the widely transmitted recitation). According to the reading of Abu Ja'far, with the genitive case (*bi-l-khafd*), the meaning is: and shadows of angels, i.e., groups that fill the horizons so that they may hasten to carry out His commands. ﴿And do they await﴾ (p. 185) from the Mighty, the Firm in what He does, the Almighty whose command overrides every command except His coming with might when He is angry after long forbearance and prolonged patience, so that His might is not repelled and His command is not opposed. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And the matter is decided﴾, i.e., and the state is that the matter has been decided, ﴿the matter﴾, i.e., it has been carried out by their swift destruction. Thus they returned to God, the Exalted, all of them, having no power over themselves for anything. ﴿And to God﴾, Who alone has complete encompassing, ﴿all matters are returned﴾, both worldly and otherwise, for His judgment cannot be reversed and His power cannot be limited.

Al-Haralli (al-Harrali) said: God's coming (*ityan Allah*) in the place of faith is an ambiguous matter that the knowledge of the knowers cannot reach, and the faith of believers stops before it; they neither grasp it by a modality (*kayf*) nor imagine it by any imagining. God's coming in the first understanding of the understanders is the emergence of His command and His address in some place of the heavens or the earth, or the Throne, or the Footstool, or whatever of His creation He wills. He, the Exalted, is too majestic to be veiled by any created thing. So wherever His address begins face to face, without intermediary, there He is: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the Mount﴾ [Maryam: 52], to: ﴿Indeed, I am God﴾ [al-Qasas: 30]. In the first Book it is said: God came from Sinai. He concluded: and He shone forth from Seir, and appeared to us from the mountains of Paran.
