[p. 251] *Al-Hils* (with a kasra on the unpointed letter, a sukun on the lam, then an unpointed letter, in the pattern of *kataf*) is the fourth of the arrows of the *maysir*. *Al-Nafis* (with a nun, a kasra on the fa, and an unpointed letter, as an active participle) is the fifth of the arrows of the *maysir*. *Musbil* (with an unpointed sin and a ba, in the pattern of *muhsin*) is the sixth or fifth of the arrows of the *maysir*. In Majma' al-Bahrayn he says: it is also *al-musaffah*, meaning with a fatha on the fa. *Al-Mu'alla* (in the pattern of *mu'azzam*) is the seventh arrow of the *maysir*. *Al-Manih* (in the pattern of *amir*, with a nun and ending in an unpointed letter) is an arrow with no share. *Al-Safih* (in the same pattern, with an unpointed letter, then a fa, and ending in an unpointed letter) is an arrow of the *maysir* with no share. *Al-Wagh* (with a fatha, then a sukun on the dotted letter, then an unpointed letter) is the foolish, weak, base, lowly man, and an arrow with no share. The author of al-Zina says: They used to buy the she-camel and guarantee its price, then they would strike the arrows over it, then slaughter it and divide it into ten parts, according to what most scholars of the language have related. Then they would turn the arrows over it. If *al-Mu'alla* came out, its owner took seven shares and was saved from paying. Then they would turn them a second time, and if *al-Raqib* came out, its owner took three shares and was saved from paying. Then they would turn them a third time, and if *al-Darib* came out, its owner took ... and was saved from paying, and the parts of the she-camel were exhausted. The rest paid according to the number of their shares. So the owner of *al-Fadhdh* paid one share, and the owner of *al-Tawam* paid two shares. In this way they divided the payment among themselves. [p. 252]

It is reported from al-Asma'i that he said: They used to divide the she-camel into twenty-eight parts: for *al-Fadhdh* one part, for *al-Tawam* two parts, for *al-Raqib* three parts. On this basis, until it reaches twenty-eight parts. Most scholars disagreed with him on this and rejected him, and said: If it were so, and each one took the share of his arrow, no payment would remain, and there would be neither a gambler nor one who is gambled against. For this reason they called the parts of the she-camel *a'shar* (tenths), because they are ten parts. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Your eyes shed tears only so that you may strike with your two arrows
for the tenths of a slain heart."*

He made the heart a substitute for the tenths of the she-camel, and made the two eyes a figure for the two arrows, meaning: she captivated his heart, and so she won it, as the owner of *al-Mu'alla* and *al-Raqib* wins. Al-Qazzaz said, in the chapter on the letter *ta'* in his Diwan: *Al-Tawam* is one of the arrows of the *maysir*, and it is the second of them. It was called *tawam* (twin) because of the two portions it carries: it has two shares and it has two portions of the she-camel. If the portions of the she-camel are exhausted, whoever the *tawam* came out for pays two portions. This is because there are ten arrows, the first of which is *al-Fadhdh*, which has one obligation and one share. The second is *al-Tawam*, which has two obligations and two shares. The third is *al-Raqib*, which has three obligations and three shares. The fourth is *al-Hils*, which has four obligations and four shares. The fifth is *al-Nafis*, which has five obligations and five shares. The sixth is *al-Musbil*, which has six obligations and six shares. The seventh is *al-Mu'alla*, which has seven obligations and seven shares. Among them are three that have no shares: *al-Safih*, *al-Manih*, and *al-Wagh*. Perhaps they called them by names other than these, but we have mentioned here those in use, and we will mention them by their names in their places in this book, if God Most High wills. These which have no shares have no obligation, and for this reason they are called *aghfal* (unmarked), because the unmarked animal is one without a brand.

The manner of what they did in gambling was this: the she-camel was slaughtered and divided into ten parts. One of the two haunches was one part, the other haunch was one part, its rump was one part, the shoulder was one part, the chest, which is the breast, was one part, the *milha* (the spine between the shoulder and the rump) was one part, the two shoulder blades, with the upper arms in them, were two parts, and the two thighs were two parts. The neck and the *tafatif* (the flesh around the bones) were divided equally among these parts. What remained of bone or morsel [p. 254] was the *rim*, which originally derives from the increase over the load, and it is what is called *'ilawa* (surplus). The butcher took it. Sometimes the seller of the she-camel reserved some part for himself, and most often what is reserved is the extremities and the head. When the she-camel was in this state, they brought a man to strike with it among them, called the *hurdah*. His eyes were bound, and a garment was placed over his hands so that he would not feel the arrows. Then a bag was brought in which were the arrows, wide at the bottom and narrow at the mouth, just wide enough for one or two arrows to come out. The arrows in it were like the long dice of the backgammon game, except that they were rounded. The bag was placed over the hands of the *hurdah*. A man was brought who was appointed trustee over it, called the *raqib*, and he was told: "Shake the arrows," and he shook them in the bag twice or three times. When he had done so, he poured them out, meaning he threw them with a single push, so that they fell out through that narrow opening. When an arrow came out, the *raqib* took it. If it was one of the three which have no obligations, he returned it to the bag and said: "Again." If it was one of the seven that carry shares, he gave it to its owner and said: "Step aside from the people." That is because each of those who gambled had taken an arrow according to what he liked. [p. 255] If the one that came out was *al-Fadhdh*, its owner took one part and was spared from paying, and the *hurdah* repeated the pouring. If the one that came out was *al-Tawam*, its owner took two shares, stepped aside from the people, and was also spared from paying. Likewise, each of them took what came out for him, stepped aside from the people, and was spared from paying. When an arrow came out in the second round, its owner took what came out for him; likewise the third takes what came out for him and steps aside from the people, so long as the first and second have not exhausted the shares of the she-camel. For example, if *al-Raqib* came out for the first, he takes three shares, then *al-Mu'alla* comes out for the second, and he takes seven shares, and the rest pay the price of the she-camel. Or *al-Fadhdh* comes out first, *al-Tawam* second, and *al-Mu'alla* third, so that all the other shares are also gone, and the rest of the people pay the price of the she-camel. Likewise in any case similar to this. If the arrows of the one who came out exceed what remains of the she-camel, the rest pay him for what his arrow exceeds. For example, if *al-Mu'alla* comes out first, he takes seven shares, then *al-Nafis* comes out for the second, whose portion is five, but only three remain of the she-camel, so he takes these, and the rest pay him two-fifths of the she-camel. Likewise if *al-Nafis* came out first and took five shares, then *al-Hils* came out second and took four shares, and *al-Mu'alla* came out third, he takes the share that remains, and the rest pay him three-fifths [p. 256] of the she-camel. This is the case in all their gambling. If you consider it carefully, you will know how the whole of it proceeds, and the people pay what is due from them according to the number of their remaining arrows. They assess what is due from them according to the number of obligations in their shares. It has been mentioned that the she-camel was divided according to the number of obligations in the arrows, which are twenty-eight parts. There is no sense in this statement, because it would imply that in this there would be neither gambling, nor winning, nor loss, since each one chooses for himself whatever arrow he likes, then takes what comes out for him, and the parts of the she-camel are not exhausted except when the arrows are exhausted, so there is no point in gambling over them. The first view is more correct, and the poetry of the Arabs indicates it. This is because a man might take two arrows in the *maysir* and win the parts of the she-camel. For example, he takes *al-Mu'alla* and *al-Raqib*. When the *hurdah* strikes for him, one of them comes out, and he wins his share. Then when he strikes the second time, the other comes out for him, and he wins the rest of the she-camel. If the arrows and shares were as they mentioned, the owner of two arrows would not win all [p. 257] the shares, since the shares do not go except with the exhaustion of the arrows. Among what indicates that the owner of two arrows wins all of it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Your eyes shed tears only so that you may strike with your two arrows
for the tenths of a slain heart."*

He says: she strikes with her two arrows, *al-Mu'alla* and *al-Raqib*, and so she takes the whole heart. From this is the saying of Kuthayyir, describing a she-camel whom travel had emaciated until it removed her flesh:

*"And she is praised, from the exhaustion of the noon heat and night travel,
for two arrows that won from the arrows of the one who shakes them."*

He says: this she-camel was emaciated by travel until no flesh remained on her, as if he had struck the arrows over her, and two arrows won from her, and they took possession of her tenths, namely *al-Raqib* and *al-Mu'alla*. End of quotation.

Thus the commentator on Kuthayyir's verse mentioned it. But I have seen in the margin of a copy of his book what is perhaps more apt. He said: that is, she is thought to excel the camels in her travel after the exhaustion of the noon heat and night travel, for her patience, her nobility, and her strength, as the excellence of a man whose arrow won twice over the arrows of his companions. The *muqa'qa'* is the one who shakes the arrows. End of quotation.

This is closer to what he said, because his statement "he is dragged with two arrows and wins" clearly indicates that the two arrows belong to him and that he is the winner. And God, glorified and exalted, is the one who grants success. This is it.

As for his statement, "there is no meaning to gambling over them on the assumption of division into twenty-eight," that is not so. Rather, its fruit appears in the unequal distribution of shares. This is because the arrows, which are the qidāḥ (arrows used in the lot), are ten. When he said that the parts are twenty-eight, he did not say that they are equal in number to the arrows, so that the arrows would be twenty-eight. Rather, he said they are equal in number to the shares (furūḍ) that are in the arrows, and he knew that these are ten. The author of al-Zīnah and others have explicitly stated this on the authority of al-Aṣma'ī, as has already been mentioned, and he is among those who held this view. Accordingly, whoever receives the al-Mu'allā (the best arrow), for example, takes seven shares out of twenty-eight, and so he has a greater portion than one who receives an arrow marked with six shares or fewer, for the strikes (ḍarabāt).

His statement, "a man may take two qidāḥ," and so on to the end, indicates another aspect of the disparity. A man may draw only one arrow because the arrows are obstructed and deviate from the straight course at the moment of drawing. At other times he may draw two or three arrows in a single casting, because the arrows are straight and balanced for drawing, so he wins the greater part of the camel. This occurs when the men are fewer than the arrows. At other times he may draw more than that, while the price is still fully covered and shared among them equally. This aspect also applies on the assumption that the arrows and the men are equal in number to the parts, since the counting is restricted to those who draw arrows, whether they are equal in number to them or more, and the obligation to pay is restricted to those who do not draw an arrow, on the assumption that a number of arrows are drawn by others. And on the assumption that not every individual draws an arrow, it is still gambling, because each of them is not certain of winning. In that case the benefit goes to the poor. As for the one who said that whoever draws any of the three blank arrows (al-aghfāl) must pay, for him gambling is necessarily present in every case and under every assumption.

In al-Kashshāf it is said that they used to give the shares to the poor and take nothing from them. This has already been quoted from the author of al-Zīnah. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best.

When He mentioned what removes the light of the soul and the sustenance of the body and censured spending on them, the situation required a question about what praises spending on the good. So He said, linking it to the question about what prompts the squandering of wealth: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾. The repetition of the question about it indicates the repetition of the events that call for it, and this indicates the great importance of the matter, because it is among the greatest pillars of jihad. God, glorified and exalted, arranged this in the manner of conjunction (ʿaṭf) because the question and the answer had already preceded in His saying: ﴿Say: whatever good you spend is for parents﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215], which prevents the expectation of another question. As for orphans and menstruation, nothing preceded that would necessitate the expectation of a question about them at all. The claim that the reason for conjunction is that the revelation came all at once, and the reason for disjunction is that it came in parts, while not sufficient to explain the matter since it does not clarify the wisdom, is refuted by what has been transmitted: that the last verse revealed was ﴿And fear a day when you will be returned to God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281], and it is with a conjunction (wāw). This was reported by al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalā'il and al-Wāḥidī through two chains in the introduction to the Asbāb al-Nuzūl (occasions of revelation), and al-Bukhārī included it as a chapter heading in the Ṣaḥīḥ. Whoever traces the occasions of revelation will find much of this.

Al-Ḥarālī said: In the conjunction there is an indication of the strengthening of hesitation twice, as in the story of the Children of Israel. But perhaps this community feared a third instance, so their silence about asking in the third case occurred because what happens in this community is less than what happened among the Children of Israel in some respect.

God, glorified and exalted, said in the answer: ﴿Say: the surplus (al-ʿafw)﴾. This is what the soul is willing to give without hardship. He said: So it is as if He obliged the soul to spend the surplus, and encouraged it to spend what it disputes over, without obliging it to do so, so that it would not be burdensome to it, because of His desire for ease for this community. So the spender has three ranks: a rank of an obligatory right which must be given, which is the obligatory charity (ṣadaqah mafrūḍah), whose withholding is destruction in this world and the next. Opposite it is the surplus, which one should not hold onto, since the soul is willing to let it go, so whoever withholds it has forced himself to withhold it. Between these two is what the soul disputes withholding, so it struggles to spend it, and this is her trade, through which she buys the Hereafter from her worldly life.

A woman said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "What is lawful for us from our husbands' wealth?" She was asking about spending from it. He said: "The fresh dates (al-rutab), with the rāʾ vowelled with a ḍammah and the ṭāʾ with a sukūn: eat them and give them as gifts." This is because it is from the surplus, whose withholding harms it through spoilage, since al-rutab is what changes if kept from one day to the next, like grapes and watermelon. Similar to it are cooked foods and all other things that change by being left overnight. End of quotation.

In restricting the spender to the surplus there is a prohibition (p-262) against one who indulges in wine before its prohibition from disposing of property. This is because most of his dispositions were not in this manner, since the state of intoxication is not considered valid, and any disposition made in it usually leads, when he comes to his senses, to regret. The same applies to gambling, and it is even more severe. Perhaps the delay in clarifying that what is urged in spending is only the excess until this place is so that the people of the religion, despite the hardship they were in, would be inclined to prefer others over themselves without being commanded to do so, out of mercy for them. Among the most evident indications of this is that in one of the verses that mentioned it earlier: ﴿And he gives wealth though he loves it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. Al-Iṣfahānī said: The people of tafsīr (exegesis) said: After the revelation of this verse, when a man possessed gold, silver, crops, or livestock, he would look at what would suffice him and his dependents for a year, keep it, and give the rest in charity. If he was one who worked with his hands, he kept what would suffice him and his dependents for that day and gave away the rest, until the verse of zakāt was revealed, and this verse abrogated (naskh) it.

When He had clarified the previous rulings in this surah in the best explanation, and had detailed what He had related of everything He intended in the most wondrous detail, especially the matter of spending, for He had explained it from the beginning of the surah until here, in various kinds of clarification with the utmost wisdom and perfection, it became a matter of question: Does our Lord clarify for us other verses besides these in the same manner? So He said: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like what has passed of this exalted clarification (p-263) remote from the stations of the base. ﴿God makes clear﴾, He to whom belong all attributes of perfection, ﴿to you﴾ all ﴿the verses﴾.

Al-Ḥarālī said: He gathered them because they are verses from different aspects concerning what relates to the heart, the soul, the body, and the person's state with others.

He used the singular address first and the plural second, to indicate the grandeur of this speech, directing it to the head (of the community), and as a hint that he (ﷺ) had already been filled with knowledge before this, such that he does not need more, and that this clarification is for the followers, who understand it according to their levels of comprehension and aspirations. It is also possible that the speech was complete with "thus," meaning the clarification, and then began what follows, so the clarification would be mentioned twice: once in His address to him, implicitly, and once in His address to them, explicitly. Or it may be said: He indicated the elevation of the address through the singular, and its generality through the plural.

﴿So that you may reflect﴾, that is, so that you may be in a state in which reflection is hoped for from you. Reflection (tafakkur) is the seeking of thought, and it is the hand of the soul by which knowable things are attained, just as sensible things are attained by the hand of the body. Thus said al-Ḥarālī.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 220:

Since the clarification from the beginning of the question up to here has fully healed matters of both abodes and has made clear the fruits of each of them, and since the Arabs denied the Hereafter, he (God) brought up its mention in the manner of what is beyond dispute, because of the abundance of what points to it. So He said: ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾, meaning, concerning their affairs, so that you may know, through what God, glory be to Him and exalted, has opened for you of the doors, and what I have attained for you of the principles, what is good and what is better, and what is evil and what is worse, so that you may do good and avoid evil, and that this may lead you to success in both abodes.

Since pardon is not confined to wealth but encompasses the bodily and intellectual faculties, and since benefiting the orphan is among the greatest things that reflection on the affairs of the Hereafter guides to, and since fighting (jihad) is among the causes of killing that necessitate orphanhood, and since they were in charge of their orphans, the severe prohibition regarding consuming their property came down, so they kept away from them, and this became very hard upon them. They asked about them, and God, glory be to Him and exalted, gave them a ruling concerning them, and urged them to mix with them in the manner of reform, which is not possible for one who indulges in wine and gambling. So He said: ﴿And they ask you about the orphans﴾ (p. 265), meaning, concerning their guardianship over them, their handling of their property, their eating from it, and similar matters that are too numerous to enumerate. He commanded him to answer with His words: ﴿Say: Reforming them is good﴾, meaning, better than leaving it. Reform is not hidden from one who has understanding. Thus, by this brief statement (p. 266), governed by the discipline of reason, which He established as a proof over His creation, He gathered what can hardly be counted. And in His words ﴿for them﴾ there is an indication that encourages devoting attention to their conditions, even if that leads to hardship for the guardian.

Since that may occur together with keeping away from them, and since they were sometimes inclined to marry their orphan girls, He said: ﴿And if you mix with them﴾, meaning, by marriage or otherwise, so that consideration of what is good becomes shared between you and them, because their interests have become as one.

Al-Harali said: "This is a rank below the first. The mukhalatah (mixing, a form of mufa'alah) derives from al-khulṭah, which is the release of things whose nature is to be separated, so that some of them are mixed into others, as if he removed the barrier between what is by nature of that kind. ﴿Then they are your brothers﴾: the plural of akh, which is one who grows up with his brother from a single origin, in equal footing, in some respect." End of quotation.

That is, you owe them the sincere counsel that natural feeling leads you to give to brothers, and it is permitted for you to eat from their property in a reasonable way, and what is permitted from the property of your brothers. A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, said: "I dislike that the property of an orphan should be with me like a ghuddah (a swelling or gland), so that I mix his food with my food and his drink with my drink."

They said: If this is broad regarding the property of orphans, it is broader regarding others. This is a principle that supports what travelling companions do on journeys: they bring out their expenses equally and differ in how much they eat. This was transmitted by al-Asbahani.

Since that is something into which the evil may enter, whose doer appears to intend only good while the reverse is the case, He said, encouraging and warning: ﴿And God﴾, He to whom belongs comprehensive knowledge of everything, ﴿knows﴾, meaning, in every movement and stillness.

Since scrupulousness (wara') is recommended and urged, especially in the matter of orphans, and so warning in this context is more fitting, He said: ﴿the corrupter﴾, meaning, the one whose nature is corruption, ﴿from the reformer﴾. So fear God in all matters, and do not make your mixing with them a means to consuming their property.

Since this is a matter for which there is no better or easier ruling within its own domain, He granted them favour through His law in His words: ﴿Had God willed﴾, meaning, by the greatness of His perfection (p. 268), ﴿He would have burdened you﴾, meaning, He would have imposed upon you, in their affair and in others, what is hardship beyond endurance. So He set for you limits and specified them, at which it is difficult to stop, and obliged you to obligations that are hard to undertake. From al-i'nat, which is causing ruin, the worst destruction, whose description is grievous. Thus said al-Harali.

Then He gave the reason for that with His words: ﴿Indeed God﴾, meaning the Greatest King, ﴿is Mighty﴾, able to do whatever He wills, ﴿Wise﴾, who makes things so firm that no one can undo any part of them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 2, verse 221:

When God, exalted is He, mentioned earlier the permissibility of sexual intercourse during the nights of fasting, and followed that with some of His commands that He willed, until He mentioned mixing (*mukhalatah*) in a manner that includes marriage, within a context that restrains from corruption and calls to righteousness, and concluded with the attribute of wisdom (*hikmah*); and since marriage is among the greatest forms of mixing, in matters of maintenance and other things, and since man is ignorant, He, glorified and exalted is He, took upon Himself in His wisdom the task of informing him what is suitable for him and what is not suitable in that regard. He deferred the matter of marriage from the explanation of what was mentioned alongside it, namely eating and drinking during the nights of fasting, because the necessity for those two is greater. And He placed it first in the verse about fasting because the soul is more inclined towards it. So He said, conjoining (*'atifan*) to what the conjunction indicates of an unmentioned element, indicating that its implied sense is: "So mix with them, and marry those orphan girls under your guardianship, in a manner of reform, if you intend it." ﴿And do not marry﴾

Al-Harali said: "From it (*mimma minhu*) is marriage (*al-nikah*), which is the insertion of a *nahd* into a *farj*, so that the two become thereby like a single thing." End of quote.

This is its linguistic origin, but what is meant here is the contract (*al-'aqd*), because it has been used for the contract in the Sharia and its usage became frequent and dominant until it became a technical Sharia usage (*haqiqah shar'iyyah*, a term denoting a meaning fixed by Sharia usage, distinct from its original linguistic sense). Thus in the Sharia it is literal for the contract and figurative for intercourse, while in the language it is the reverse. It will come at the words ﴿until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:230], from al-Farisi, a qualifier by which the intended meaning of the lexicographers is known. ﴿The idolatresses﴾, that is, the women worshippers of idols. Most scholars hold that the women of the People of the Book are included in what the verse covers, but then they were specified by the verse ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:5]. ﴿Until they believe﴾, for idolatresses are pure evil. ﴿And a believing slave-woman﴾, a female slave, ﴿is better﴾, because the benefit of faith is a religious matter that returns to the enduring Hereafter, ﴿by way of concession﴾, ﴿than an idolatress﴾, a free woman, ﴿even though she pleases you﴾, that is, the idolatress, because the benefit of her lineage, her wealth and her beauty returns to the base, transient, perishing world.

Al-Harali said: "These verses are thus arranged to clarify the better of the two goods, and to prefer the matter of the unseen in the matter of religion, and the outcome in the lowest of the believing slave-women in creation and existence, and in outward form in terms of what is visible in the immediate matter of this world, over the highest of the free idolatresses in character, outward form and nobility of house." End of quote.

﴿And do not marry﴾, O guardians, ﴿idolaters﴾, that is, disbelievers of any kind of disbelief, ﴿any of the Muslim women﴾, ﴿until they believe﴾, for disbelievers are pure evil. ﴿And a believing slave﴾, that is, a male slave, ﴿is better﴾, by way of concession, ﴿than an idolater﴾, a free man, ﴿even though he pleases you﴾, that is, the idolater. This indicates the superiority of the believing free woman and the believing free man by way of a stronger argument (*min bab al-awla*), together with their great honour through the omission of mentioning them, to inform that their superiority is a settled matter with no dispute in it, and that the comparison is only between those whom they used to regard as lowly, whom faith elevated, and those whom they regarded as noble, whom disbelief debased. Likewise He mentioned the one described by faith in both places, to indicate that although he is lowly, the place of preference is due to the elevation of his attribute; and He established the attribute of idolatry in both places, restricting it to it, because it is the place of contempt, even if its bearer is exalted in customary estimation.

Since mixing with the people of idolatry is a likely cause of corruption, which may lead to laxity in religion, and the husband may then invite his wife to disbelief, drawing her by inclination to follow him, He said, drawing attention to that and giving the reason for this ruling: ﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾, that is, those who are deserving of distance from every good, ﴿invite to the Fire﴾, that is, to the actions that lead to it, inevitably. For love may lead a Muslim husband to disbelief, and no consideration is given to the possibility that the disbelieving spouse may abandon disbelief and embrace Islam in agreement with the Muslim husband, because the averting of corruptions takes precedence. Further explanation of this will come in al-Ma'idah at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become void﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:5].

Since He warned against the people of idolatry, urging hatred of them, He encouraged turning towards Him, glorified and exalted is He, by turning towards His friends with love for His sake and otherwise. So He said: ﴿And God﴾, that is, by the might of His majesty and the greatness of His perfection, ﴿invites﴾, that is, by what He commands, ﴿to Paradise﴾, that is, to the actions that lead to it, ﴿and forgiveness﴾, that is, until they do what leads to His forgiving them and refining their souls to the point that they reach a lofty state in which they forgive people for what they have done to them.

Since the calling may be by compelling someone toward a thing, and may be by explanation, to the point where the one called becomes prepared to reach it, He said: ﴿by His permission﴾, that is, by His enabling of it for whoever He wills his happiness, ﴿and He makes His signs clear﴾ in that and in other matters, ﴿to the people﴾, all of them, whoever wills their happiness and whoever does not, ﴿that they may remember﴾, that is, that they may be in a state in which there becomes apparent to them, through the understanding that their Lord created in them and the natural dispositions He impressed upon their souls, the goodness of what He calls them to and the ugliness of what He forbids them from, in the utmost clarity, through what the manifest declaration makes understood.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 222:

When the mention of this verse was a return to completing what had been made lawful of intimacy (al-rafath) during the nights of fasting in the best manner, He followed it with the question about approaching a menstruating woman. And since marriage has an aspect of intercourse that stirs questions about its circumstances, and an aspect of enjoyment and benefit that turns away from that, the arrangement of the verse of tilth (al-harth) with the verse of the marriage contract by way of conjunction (al-'atf) was more fitting than by way of fresh beginning (al-isti'naf). So He said: ﴿And they ask you about menstruation﴾, meaning about marital relations with women during it, and there is in this a contradiction of the Jews.

Al-Harali said: "Al-mahid is a noun of place from menstruation (al-hayd), which is the flowing out of the corrupt blood that is in the blood, in the same position as urine and feces are to the waste products of food and drink, from the vagina. ﴿Say: It is a harm﴾, meaning it is harmful to the body and the soul, because in it the sperm mixes with the corrupt, putrid blood." This is the statement of al-Harali, who also said: "To the extent that it is said that the one who is intercourse with while she is menstruating will suffer various calamities in her offspring." End of quotation.

For this reason, Glorified and Exalted be He, made the command ﴿So keep away from women﴾ follow it as a cause. That is, impose upon yourselves the abandonment of intercourse with them. I'tizal (keeping away) is the seeking of separation, which is being alone away from what is shared; this is the statement of al-Harali.

﴿During menstruation﴾, meaning its time. He made it explicit lest it be ambiguous had He used a pronoun, so that it might be taken to refer to the general sense of harm from blood, which would include istihadah (irregular bleeding). Istihadah is sound blood that flows from a vein that bursts from the neck of the womb, so it is not harm like menstruation, which is corrupt blood generated from the woman's nature through the womb; were it retained, the woman would fall ill. Thus it is like urine and feces, so intercourse is permitted with it, unlike menstruation, to remove hardship. This is the statement of the Imam.

﴿And do not approach them﴾, meaning at the place of entry for intercourse, nor for mere physical contact below the waist garment; physical contact is only in what is above the waist garment. ﴿Until﴾ And since it contained what was pointed out of the putrid corruption, He said: ﴿they have become pure﴾, meaning by its cessation, the passing of its time, and bathing from it. What indicates that this is intended, together with the reading with the emphatic consonant, is His statement, exalted be He: ﴿and when they have purified themselves﴾, meaning have bathed. So intercourse has two conditions: the cessation and the bath. Perhaps the reading without emphasis indicates the permissibility of approaching, but not penetrating, and that is by physical contact below the waist garment. ﴿Then go to them﴾, meaning in intercourse and mixing, beginning ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾, meaning the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, and this is the front passage, in whatever state that may be. And since what is in the context indicates an emphasis that some of them had resolved or loved to do some of what was previously forbidden, He gave the reason with His statement: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, repeating the Greatest Name to magnify the occasion, and not using a pronoun, to inform that this is a general ruling for whatever lapse occurs due to menstruation or otherwise. ﴿Loves﴾, meaning by what He has of the specific quality of encompassing generosity, even though He is specifically encompassing in majesty. ﴿Those who are constantly repentant﴾, meaning those who return from what they had resolved upon and from every sin that caused them a deficiency of humanity, especially the lust of the private parts, whenever a lapse occurs from them they renew repentance for it, because that is among the causes of His manifesting the attributes of forbearance, pardon, generosity, mercy, and noble kindness. "If you did not sin, Allah would bring a people who sin, then they seek forgiveness, and He forgives them." Related by Muslim and al-Tirmidhi from Abu Ayyub, may Allah be pleased with him.

When He loves one who repeatedly repents through repeated sins, then this applies to the penitent who, after his repentance, commits no further lapse, if that is found; He is more loving, more inclined, and more merciful to him. And since this is something hard to be free from being associated with, whether in exceeding what is permitted in physical contact or in intercourse, at first or at last, He used the form of intensification.

Al-Harali said: To reassure the hearts of those who scruple about returning to sin after repentance from it, and about returning to repentance after falling into a second sin, since the sinner fears that his lying will be recorded against him whenever he renews repentance and then slips after it, so he is counted as mocking, falls from the eyes of Allah, and then He pays no attention to him, and this stops him from repenting.

Since intermingling in the manner Allah has forbidden is extremely foul, He indicated this by His statement: ﴿And He loves﴾. Since the desire of marriage and the intensity of lust are worthy of overpowering a person unless he exerts great effort against it, He manifested the taa' of reflexive form and said: ﴿those who purify themselves﴾, meaning those who compel themselves to what is difficult regarding matters of purity, from this and other things. They are those who, out of scrupulousness, exceed in keeping far from every doubtful matter, so they do not approach a menstruating woman except after complete purification. That is, He treats them with the honor of one who loves, and likewise everything that requires purity, whether physical or spiritual.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 223:

When He, glorified and exalted is He, had explained the "coming" (al-ma'ti) in the preceding verse, He explained it in a manner that clarified it, indicating the fruit of marriage, which forbids every person of intellect from fornication (sifah). So He said: ﴿Your women﴾, i.e., those who are lawful for you by contract or by right of possession (milk yamin) (p-280). Since the casting of the seed from which offspring comes is like the casting of the seed from which crops grow, He likened them to a tilth (mahaarith), indicating that the essential purpose is the seeking of offspring. He then named the place of tilling by its name, using the name of the part for the whole, and in the singular because it is a genus, saying: ﴿a tilth for you﴾, and thus He clarified that.

Al-Harali said: So that the address would fall by allusion in the first verse, i.e., for people of understanding (ulu al-fahm), and by explicit statement in this one, i.e., for people of knowledge (ulu al-'ilm), because tilling, as some scholars have said, takes place only in the place of sowing. End of quote.

In the specifying of tilling by mention, and the generalizing (p-281) of all the modes that lead to it, by His saying: ﴿So come to your tilth﴾, i.e., to the place suitable for tilling, ﴿as you wish﴾, i.e., from wherever and however, indicating the prohibition of anything other than this, because it involves futility through the absence of benefit. Al-Tha'labi said: The backsides are the place of excrement, not the place of tilling.

Since these are hidden matters that cannot be interpreted in their good sense nor restrained from their corrupt sense except by pure scrupulousness (wara'), He said: ﴿And put forward [for yourselves]﴾, i.e., perform the advancing. Since the context is plural and this is among the desires of the self, He said, indicating a restraint from following it in everything it desires: ﴿for yourselves﴾, i.e., from this act and others, from everything connected to desires, that if it were presented to those you stand in awe of and whose goodness you believe in, you would take pride in it before them. This is by directing, for example, this act away from mere desire toward the intention of chastity (i'faf) and seeking a child through whom good deeds endure, so that the reward is continued. Among the "putting forward" is saying the basmala at intercourse, as the Sunnah has transmitted and as the scholar Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, stated, according to what is reported from him (p-282).

Since the actions of a person in matters of desire come close to the act of one who has doubt, further admonition was needed, so He said: ﴿And fear Allah﴾, i.e., make between yourselves and what the Supreme King dislikes, of that and other things, a shield against the lawful or the doubtful.

Glorified and exalted is He increased in admonition and warning by alerting to the seeking of knowledge and depicting the presentation, so He said: ﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾, and He is the One who will call you to account for all that you have done, both subtle and great, good and otherwise. So do not fall into what you would be ashamed of when He asks you, for He is greater than every great thing.

Al-Harali said: In it is an indication of the rulings that occur in the course of this, which the rulings of the judges of this world cannot reach, matters whose decision takes place only in the Hereafter, inasmuch as the affair between the spouses is a secret that is not disclosed. The Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "A man is not asked why he struck his wife," and he said: "I do not like for a woman to complain about her husband" (p-283). Thus Exalted is He informed that the affair between the spouses has its judgment deferred until the meeting with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as a safeguard over what is between the spouses, so that it remains a secret whose affair none reveals except Allah, exalted is He. In this indication is a preservation of manliness, in that the spouses do not go to judgment before a judge in this world, and that each of them returns to the fear of Allah and knowledge of meeting Allah. End of quote.

Since this is not fully comprehended by everyone, He pointed to it by turning to the most perfect of creation, saying, joining it to what its sense implies: "So warn those who deny," in deed or word, the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, i.e., those for whom faith has become a firmly established attribute, by which they are prepared for vigilance (muraqabah). This is an indication that such a matter, being among the trusts, is held back only by sincerity in faith and firmness in it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 224:

When He permitted intercourse with women in the place of tillage (*mahall al-harth*) in whatever manner was possible, and forbade what was other than that, and forbade the place of tillage during menstruation (*hayd*), He then distinguished the ruling for when a person restrains himself from this by *iyla'* (a vow of abstention from intercourse) or by an unrestricted oath, even if not in the manner of *iyla'*. This is because he reported from many of them an intense inclination toward marriage, so they feared sexual intercourse during the time of abstention. The intensity of their scrupulousness (*wara'*) would lead them to restrain themselves by a barrier of *muzaharah* (*zihar*, likening one's wife to one's mother), as explained in Surat al-Mujadilah or elsewhere, or by other oaths. So He forbade them from that with His words, the Exalted, turning away from addressing His Prophet ﷺ out of exaltation of his station: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle﴾, that is, the One to whom nothing compares in His majesty, greatness and perfection, ﴿a target for your oaths﴾, that is, something exposed to them. Thus He would be placed in a position of being degraded and made common, for when this is prolonged it leads to boldness in lying, which drags a person to the most vile [p-285] of things.

Al-Harali said: *al-'urdah* is the mention of a thing and taking it up without intending it and without aiming toward it, rather there is another aim beyond it. ﴿That﴾, that is, for the sake of your ﴿being righteous﴾ regarding the wealth of orphans and other matters previously commanded or forbidden, ﴿and being God-conscious﴾, that is, your oaths should not lead you to righteousness, which is expansiveness in every good character, and God-consciousness (*taqwa*), which is immersion in the fear of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, ﴿and reconciling between people﴾. You should not make oaths a habit for yourselves, so that you swear at one time that you will do something and at another time that you will not do something, to bind yourselves to those things. For whoever is not led to good except by a driver of an oath or something else is not one of true resolve. And in the proverbs: "A horse that does not run except with a spur is a bad horse."

Since the context and the conjunction, with an unmentioned element, indicate that the implied sense is: "So Allah is [p-286] Majestic and Great," He followed it with His words: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, with what He possesses of might and greatness, ﴿is All-Hearing﴾ of everything that happens of that and other matters, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what He conceals and what He makes known. So beware of Him in all that He commands you and forbids you. It is permissible for the clause to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the waw of ﴿you make﴾, in which case there is no implied element, and the explicit mention stands in place of the pronoun in order to glorify the station.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 225:

Since He, glory be to Him and exalted, had already laid down the ruling on this matter, and since their tongues had been trained to utter oaths without intention, to such a degree that they could not abstain from that except through great discipline and lengthy treatment, and since among the things with which Allah has shown mercy to this Ummah is pardon for what it errs in and does not intend, He said, in answer to one who as it were asked about this: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable﴾, that is, He will not punish you. Its reality is that He treats you in the manner of (p-287) one who disputes with a person over the claim that each of them wants to seize the other for a sin the other has committed against him. ﴿Allah﴾: thus, in the context of pardon and leniency, He repeated the Greatest Name, which He had mentioned in the context of restriction and prohibition, to signal that His greatness does not prevent forgiveness. ﴿For idle words﴾: this is what the tongues run to of speech without a resolve that was intended, as al-Harali said.

﴿In your oaths﴾: for that does not indicate contempt; rather it may indicate love and glorification.

When He had explained what He had left unrestricted, He explained what He had prohibited, saying: ﴿But He will hold you accountable﴾. The expression is suitable both for sin and for expiation. Since the motive for swearing is mostly worldly benefits, which are provision, and since earning (kasb) is applied both to seeking provision and to intention and deliberate purpose, He expressed it with this word, saying: ﴿for what your hearts have earned﴾, that is, what your hearts have intended (p-288). Thus intention is combined with the utterance.

Al-Harali said: That will be an inner resolve and an outer utterance, so one is held accountable for the combination of both. Within this is an elevation of the one who does not swear by Allah either in resolve or in idle speech, and this is the one who has preserved the sanctity of swearing by Allah. Opposite to him is the one who swears to do good that he will not do it. End of quote.

He did not state the expiation here explicitly, as an indication that they should be more God-conscious than to be prevented from something and then commit it; and He alluded to it in the discussion of ila' (vow of abstention), as will come.

Since mention of accountability cuts to the hearts of the fearful, He calmed them with His saying, using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun to indicate that His mercy precedes His wrath: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, together with His greatness, ﴿is Forgiving﴾, that is, Concealing of the sins of His servants when they repent.

Since the context concerns accountability, which is the treatment by each of the two disputants of the other by seizing him, forbearance was the most fitting of things for this, so He said ﴿Forbearing﴾ (p-289), not hastening to seize them. Forbearance is the endurance of the superior toward harm from the inferior, and it is also the lifting of accountability from one who deserves it for a crime against a great right, as al-Harali said.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 226:

Since the ila' (oath of abstention from intercourse with one's wife) is a restricted oath, and [the verse before it] had explained the ruling on the unrestricted oath, because the unrestricted precedes the restricted by being separate from it, he explained it as evidence of His forbearance (ḥilm), in that He did not hold them to account for it. For they used to harm women with it in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) by swearing never to have intercourse with them, so that the woman would be neither a widow (ayyim) nor one who has a husband (dhat ba'l). He also made for them in this a point of return to which they could come back. So He said, in answer to a question that is implied by what preceded: ﴿For those who take an oath﴾, that is, who swear an oath beginning [anew], ﴿against their wives﴾, within the bond of marriage or within a revocable divorce, as the idafah (possessive construction) indicates, that they will not have intercourse with them ever, or for more than ﴿four months﴾. The use of min (from) therefore indicates a beginning of distancing from them.

Al-Ḥarālī said: The ila' is the strengthening and tightening of an oath, whether they are free men or slaves, or some of them [are free and some slaves], whether in a state of contentment or anger, whether the wife is beloved or not, because the harm is achieved by his oath.

﴿A waiting period (tarabbuṣ)﴾, that is, a respite and a remaining in which one bears patience, which is the inverted form of its own word (ṣabr, patience) — end of quotation.

﴿Four months﴾, in which he awaits their return to them, [this being] forbearance from God, glorified and exalted is He, in that He did not make the matter, at the time of the oath, dependent on separation or reconciliation.

Al-Ḥarālī said: Since the woman's release from the husband requires a term of 'iddah (waiting period), its term together with the duration of this tarabbuṣ was as if—and God knows best—it were the measure of what a woman can endure away from her husband. It is mentioned that ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, asked women about the measure of what a woman can endure away from her husband, and they informed him that she can endure six months. So he made that the limit of the military expeditions. Thus the tarabbuṣ and the 'iddah became the measure of what a woman can endure away from her husband, and God, glorified and exalted is He, thereby cut off the harm of the Jahiliyyah in ila' that had no fixed limit — end of quotation, and there is some paraphrase in it.

Since their condition after that was uncertain, God, exalted is He, explained its two divisions, saying, elaborating on it: ﴿And if they return﴾, that is, they go back within the months, and it resulted from separation to connection, from fay' (return), which is returning to that from which one had departed. ﴿Then indeed God﴾ forgives them the sin they committed in that, and has mercy on them by granting their aims, for He is ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾. He possesses these two attributes, by which He looks upon those who deserve them, so He forgives the offence on the part of either or both of them if He wills, and they are treated with honour thereafter.

Al-Ḥarālī said: In the address being directed to the husbands, with its attribution to them, there is what supports the meaning that the affairs of marriage are conducted under a covering and aversion from the judgment of the judges, in that the tarabbuṣ and the fay' are assigned to the husband. So the ruling of the judge only falls upon the one who violated the sanctity of the covering of the rulings of spouses, which must operate between the two spouses behind a veil, as is the secret of marriage, which is the cause of their union, so that the ruling of what is secret remains secret and the ruling of what is open remains open — end of quotation.

The circumstances during the period of ila' (oath of abstention) resembled those of divorce without being divorce itself. He said, clarifying that divorce does not take effect merely by the passing of the four months, but rather that the husband either returns (yafi'u) or divorces; if he refuses, the judge divorces on his behalf: ﴿And if they are resolved upon divorce﴾. He attached the resolve (al-'azm) directly to the divorce without a preposition, meaning that they abandoned the wavering they had been in, and made divorce a firm resolution taking effect without hesitation or concealment. (p-293) Al-'azm is the determination to carry out an action, and divorce, in meaning, is like releasing a thing from the hand, which can be taken back after it has been released; so said al-Harali.

Since the one divorcing may regret it, and passion may lead him to deny the divorce, He warned him with His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the King to whom belong majesty and honor, ﴿is Hearing﴾, that is, of their expression concerning it.

Al-Harali said: In this indication is the notice that divorce must have an apparent utterance that is heard, and so it takes effect. End quote.

﴿Knowing﴾, that is, of it and of their intention regarding it.

Al-Harali said: In this is a warning of what occurs within the souls and inner selves of harm and irritation between spouses in matters that the rulings do not seize and that the judges cannot reach knowledge of; so He made them trustees over their own selves in what is hidden and what is apparent. For this reason the scholars held that divorce is a trust in the hands of men, just as the 'iddah and the istibra' (waiting period and clearing) are a trust in the hands of women. Therefore the verse about the woman's waiting through her 'iddah is joined with the verse about the husband's waiting through his ila'. End quote.

There remains from the rulings of ila' a third category, which He left unstated, indicating that they should be in the utmost purity from it, namely persistence in harm (al-israr 'ala al-idrar). By attaching the two attributes of forgiveness and mercy to the doer, He indicated that its perpetrator is treated with their opposites, a matter whose ruling is known in jurisprudence. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 228:

When he had concluded the two verses on *ila'* (the oath of abstention from intercourse) with divorce, he explained its waiting period, saying:

Al-Harali said: "When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the waiting of the husband in the matter of divorce, which is his trust, He mentioned the waiting of the woman in the matter of the *'iddah* (the waiting period), which is her trust; end of quote." So He said: ﴿And the divorced women﴾, i.e., those who have been consummated with, as is understood from the *ila'* context that the discussion concerns those other than the pregnant, whose *'iddah* ends with childbirth, and other than those who do not menstruate due to youth or old age [p-295].

When the emphasis on their *'iddah* was intended, it was preceded, after its emphasis by being built on the subject, by the form of a report whose nature is that it has already occurred and concluded, as a hint toward hastening to comply with it. So it was said: ﴿shall wait﴾, i.e., shall observe the *'iddah* by waiting.

Since the soul is inclined toward desires, especially women's souls toward men, and since waiting applied generally to the soul by contracting marriage with another husband, and by exposing oneself to him through applying kohl, adorning oneself, and hinting at speech, along with separation and other things, He specified the first [contracting marriage] and expressed it through the soul, stirring them to caution in complete waiting and to modesty regarding what gives the impression of haste. So He said: ﴿themselves﴾, so that they do not lead anyone to hope for union with a man before the *'iddah* ends.

Since *qur'* (a term meaning either the period of purity or the menstrual period) is shared between purity and menstruation, and since its plural *aqra'* is shared between the plurals of each of them, and since purity, according to a group of lexicographers, is specific in being pluralized as *qurū'*, its number was made masculine, while menstruation is feminine and its number is made masculine. This indicates that what is intended is the manifest sense, through what is specific to it in plural form and in the feminine form of its number. So He said, mentioning the time frame of waiting: ﴿three *qurū'*﴾, i.e., three gatherings of blood. It will come in the beginning of surah al-Hijr that this root, in whatever arrangement it occurs, revolves around gathering, and that what is meant by *qurū'* is the periods of purity, because they are the actual time when blood gathers. As for the time of menstruation, it is called so only because it is the cause of the gathering being realized. The well-known statement of the lexicographers is that the plural of *qur'* in the sense of purity is *aqra'* and *qurū'*, and that its plural when used for menstruation is *aqra'* only. That is because the root is for gathering, so the days of purity are what realize this, and since the plural of multitude is more familiar in the plural, it is more appropriate to apply it to purity [p-297].

Al-Harali said: "*Qurū'* is the plural of *qur'*, which is the dividing boundary between purity and menstruation, and which admits of being attributed to each of them. For this reason the interpretations of the lexicographers conflict regarding its language, and the scholars differ about its meaning, because its meaning is obscure as the boundary between two states, like the dividing boundary between shade and sunlight. So *qurū'* are boundaries. That occurs when a woman is divorced before the beginning of her *'iddah* during a period of purity in which she was not touched, so that he divorces her in a state of clearance from their bond, lest he divorce what has not yet been released from him. When the purity ends and menstruation begins, what is between them is a *qur'*, because the *qur'* is the completion of the gathering of menstrual blood when it ferments; so as long as it has not reached the point of expulsion, it is not completed as a *qur'*. When she becomes pure a second time and it reaches menstruation, they are two *qurū'*. When she becomes pure a third time and it reaches menstruation, witnessing the completion of the *qur'*, it is three *qurū'*. Therefore its meaning indicates the woman's release when she sees blood from the third menstruation, for the completion of the three *qurū'* waiting period. Thus it agrees with the meaning of those who interpret *qur'* as purity, and it is closer than interpreting it as menstruation. The apparent duration of purity is the duration of inferring the blood internally, so interpreting it as menstruation is far from what is the realization of the meaning of boundary, to a certain extent." End of quote.

[p-298] Since marriage is the most desired thing for living beings, and since love for something blinds and deafens, and since women are more eager for it, along with their deficiency in intellect and religion, this might have led them to conceal a child in order to desire another husband, in order to shorten the *'iddah* and attribute the child to him, or to conceal menstruation out of desire to return to the one who divorced them. The Glorious and Exalted said: ﴿And it is not lawful for them﴾, i.e., the divorced women, ﴿to conceal what Allah has created﴾, i.e., He to whom all command belongs, of a child or of blood, ﴿in their wombs﴾, the plural of *raḥim* (womb).

Al-Harali said: "It is that which contains the child from the organs of reproduction, in which it develops from being a drop of fluid into being another creation; end of quote." There is no evidence in it that pregnancy is known; only its signs are known.

Since the meaning of this report is a prohibition, so that it negates permissibility in its wording and establishes prohibition in its meaning as emphasis on it, the sense was: "and they must not conceal." He said, encouraging compliance and warning against its opposite [p-299]: ﴿if they believe in Allah﴾, i.e., He who possesses all greatness, ﴿and the Last Day﴾, in which His greatness appears most fully, and in which the servants will be judged for what they did. That is: if they conceal any of that, it indicates the absence of faith.

Al-Harali said: "In its implication is the establishment of a kind of hypocrisy upon the one who conceals what is in her womb; end of quote." There is some alteration in this.

Since the revocable divorce is the lightest of divorces, He explained the taking back, as an alert that if divorce must occur, then let it be revocable. So the Exalted said: ﴿And their husbands﴾, i.e., their spouses, the plural of *ba'l* (husband).

Al-Harali said: "It is the man prepared to marry the female, to whom that is possible, and it is applied to the husband and the master; end of quote." Since the divorced woman has a right in herself [p-300], He said: ﴿have more right to take them back﴾, i.e., to return them to what was theirs over them of the marital bond, to nullify the waiting period. So he has the right of enjoyment over divorced women by intending reconciliation, ﴿during that﴾, i.e., during the days of the *qurū'*. When it ends, she becomes more entitled to herself than he is to her, since his right has ended. The discussion concerns the revocable divorcee, as indicated by the verse that follows.

Since the right was established for them, and since some of them intend harm, He restricted it by His saying: ﴿if they desire﴾, i.e., by taking back, ﴿reconciliation﴾. This is an alert that if he does not desire reconciliation, and she desires separation, then in the inner reality he is an adulterer.

Al-Harali said: "Reconciliation of some defect between them is more worthy in Allah's knowledge and wisdom than opening a second union, because remembering the past harms the present. This is what the Prophet ﷺ warned against: marrying the *lafūt*, who is the woman who has a child from a previous husband. Therefore reconciling the first is more appropriate than initiating a union with a second; end of quote."

[p-301] When He removed the matter of taking back from them, He consoled them by His saying: ﴿And they have rights﴾, i.e., of the rights ﴿similar to what is incumbent upon them﴾, i.e., in that it is good in itself, according to what is fitting for ownership between them, not in kind. So just as men have the right of taking back by compulsion, women have companionship with kindness; and just as they have the right to hold them back, women have what removes loneliness through one who provides companionship, and similar things. Since each of them may wrong the other, He said: ﴿according to what is reasonable﴾, i.e., according to the circumstances of each of them.

Al-Harali said: "The reasonable is what the Law approves, the intellect accepts, and noble disposition agrees with; end of quote."

When He mentioned their taking back in the form of *al-aḥaqq* (more entitled), and clarified the right from both sides, He explained the superiority of men by His saying: ﴿And men have a degree﴾, more general than whether they are husbands [p-302] ﴿over them﴾, i.e., over their wives, ﴿a degree﴾, i.e., a superiority in ways that are not hidden, such as provision and dowry, because *daraja* is the rising to a height.

Al-Harali said: "Because of what they were given preference in, of soundness of intellect and completeness of religion; end of quote." Thus a man exceeds a woman by one degree out of three, because every two women are equivalent to one man.

Since the Glorious and Exalted honored the man, He described Himself with might, beginning with the Greatest Name, which indicates every perfection. So He said, connecting to what is implied by: "Because Allah has given them precedence over them by His wisdom": ﴿And Allah﴾, i.e., He who possesses perfect greatness, ﴿is Mighty﴾. This is an indication that He is mightier, indeed there is no mighty one except Him, so that everyone who lends him the garment of might fears His authority. And He said: ﴿Wise﴾, as an alert that He did this only for a profound wisdom [p-303], a consolation to women, and that what He brought into being by His might and perfected by His wisdom cannot be annulled.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 229:

When he mentioned the return (al-raj'ah, taking back a divorced wife) without specifying an end point at which it terminates, the verse became like something unspecified (mujmal), and a question arose: Is it extended indefinitely, as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic Age of Ignorance), so that whenever he returns to her during the 'iddah (the waiting period) he may divorce her again, as long as he keeps doing this, even a thousand times? Or is it discontinuous? So He said: ﴿The divorce is twice﴾, meaning the divorce that has been spoken of, which is the one in which he may take her back.

Al-Harali said: Since divorce is for that which can be reversed, the Truth, exalted is He, restricted it to the two occasions in which it is possible to remedy the marriage through return. End of quote.

He said, exalted is He: ﴿twice﴾ rather than "two pronouncements," as an admonition that it should be one time after another, each pronouncement at a separate time, and not that he combine them into one time. [p. 304] Since, after the second divorce, he has two states during the 'iddah: exercising (his right, i.e., retaining her) and neglecting it. The exercising is either by return or by divorce. He began with exercising, because it is more deserving of explanation, since it is closer to harming her by it. The neglecting was deferred until the 'iddah expires, because although it is understood from the verse about the periods (al-aqra', menstrual cycles), he will state it explicitly in the coming verse, His saying: ﴿or release them with kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:231]. So He said, following with fa (then), ﴿then retention﴾, meaning, if he returns to her during the 'iddah of the second divorce.

Al-Harali said: It comes from imsak (holding), which is an encompassing that restrains a thing; from it comes the miskah (a leather water-container, pronounced with a fatha). ﴿In good fashion﴾.

Al-Harali said: By this He turned them away from the harm of the Jahiliyyah in which they had been, by repeating divorce without limit, and He made for it a limit that cuts off the intention of harm. End of quote.

﴿Or release﴾, meaning, if he divorces her a third time. After this release, he does not possess the right of return over her, as was the case in the state of the people of the Jahiliyyah.

Al-Harali said: He called the third (divorce) a release (tasrih), because it is a sending off without the intention of retaking, like releasing a thing that is not intended to be brought back. He also said: It is letting a thing go in a manner that does not permit return. So whoever sends off a falcon (al-bazi) [p. 305] in order to retrieve it is one who divorces, and whoever sends it off not intending to recall it is one who releases. End of quote.

It is possible that by release is meant non-return after the second (divorce), not that it is a third pronouncement. Since the purpose of marriage is good companionship, and from the man there is enjoyment (al-imta') through self and property, and divorce is a prevention of enjoyment through the self, He said: ﴿with kindness﴾, as an allusion to not forcing her out through weariness, lest two prohibitions combine: the prohibition of the self [p. 306] and of what is in the hand (i.e., property). Al-Harali explained this and said: So in it, in some respect, there is an allusion to what the verse of mut'ah (provision), which comes later, states explicitly. End of quote.

Among this is giving the full dowry (al-sadaq) and not haggling with her over anything in which she has a right, together with good speech and noble conduct.

Since He, glorified and exalted, had given him the choice between two matters, the return and the release, as described, and return was closer to good, He began with it. But since it may be for the sake of ransom (al-iftida') by what the woman has given, and taking it, or some of it, shares with release the fact that it cuts off what he had of the right of return, and he does not possess the right of return over her after this release, as was the case in the state of the people of the Jahiliyyah, and since ransom may occur in the first (divorce), He did not make it dependent on the later one. He said, pointing out that part of the goodness of release is that the husband permits what he has given her, linking to what is implied as: "Then it is not lawful for you to harm them": ﴿And it is not lawful for you﴾, meaning, O you who divorce, or those who intervene [p. 307] among the rulers and others, since they were the ones commanding, they were counted as takers. ﴿To take﴾ in release, out of goodness, ﴿of what you have given them﴾ of dowry and other things, ﴿anything﴾, meaning without violation.

Al-Harali said: Because a man giving a woman is a gift of nihlah (a voluntary gift), to show the distinction of rank, not in exchange for benefit. Therefore He let it stand and did not require any of it back. For this reason, the dowry became obligatory in marriage, so that the man's distinction through what is in the hand might appear, as it appeared in what is in the self. End of quote.

Since attributing fear to a plural pronoun might be ambiguous, He said: ﴿unless they both fear﴾, explicitly stating the intended meaning by attributing it to the spouses. He expressed suspicion (al-zann) by fear, as a warning against the punishment of God. In this exception, if we say it is disconnected (munqati'), He used the particle of the connected (muttasil) to express aversion to taking. The meaning of the passive form in the recitation of Hamzah, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub (variant readings) is: unless some matter arises for both of them from desire or appetite that compels them to fear falling short of the limits. There is no implication (mafhum) in the restriction by fear, because it cannot be imagined that a sane person would ransom himself with property without a pressing matter that compels him. And whenever the compelling matter occurs, there is fear. And whenever one of them fears, both fear, because whenever the other opposes, dispute arises, which stirs up appetites that lead to doing what is not permitted. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best. ﴿That they not keep﴾, meaning in living together, ﴿the limits of God﴾, the Mighty, so that each of them does what is obligatory upon them of right.

Al-Harali said: In its implication is that ransom, under the ruling of the Book, is from what the wife took from her husband, not from anything else of her property. The limits (hudud) are the plural of hadd, which is the end in a disposal that prevents excess beyond it. End of quote. Then the matter was made clearer, because it is in the context of [p. 309] delimitation. So He said, attributing it to a plural pronoun to urge verification, so that ransom may be permitted as a complete resolution removing all hardship: ﴿And if you fear﴾, meaning, O you who intervene between them, from among the rulers and others, and the leaders, regarding what you see from them and what they tell you about themselves, ﴿that they not keep the limits of God﴾. The repetition of the Greatest Name indicates an additional elevation for this station, great exaltation of these rulings, and a strong urging to adhere to these regulations with observance and commitment. This is because every person is naturally inclined to prefer himself over others, and the whole Law is built upon justice, which is equity, and a person's loving for others what he loves for himself. ﴿Then there is no sin﴾, meaning no inclination with wrongdoing, ﴿upon them both﴾. What permits this is that suspicion is a doubt, for you do not fear what you do not suspect. [p. 310] ﴿Concerning that by which she ransoms herself﴾, meaning there is no blame upon the husband for taking, nor upon her for giving, whether it is of what he gave her or of something else, more or less than it. Because khul' (the wife's divorce by ransom) is a contract of exchange, just as it is permissible for her to refuse at the beginning of the contract until she is content, even with more than the usual bridal price (mahr al-mithl), so likewise in khul' it is permissible for him not to be content except with what is in his self, whatever it may be. And that would be from what he possessed over her of the right of return. So when he takes it, the woman becomes separated, and she becomes more entitled to herself, so there is no way over her except with her permission.

Since the rulings concerning women are sometimes by companionship and sometimes by separation, and were built upon desires, sometimes upon the bestial and sometimes upon the predatory, and since He, glorified and exalted, had set limits in them by which benefits are realized and corruptions removed, He forbade, glorified and exalted, whoever transgresses those limits, meaning the rulings He explained in that matter, and did not mention approaching them as He did in the verse on fasting. So He said: ﴿Those are﴾, meaning the rulings [p. 311] that are great, whose explanation God has undertaken, of the rulings of divorce, return, khul' and others, ﴿the limits of God﴾, meaning the laws of the Greatest King, to whom belongs all might, of commands and prohibitions that He explained, so that they became like the known boundaries in lands.

Since God's laws are suited to the original pure nature, free from the impulses of deficiencies and the pulls of vices, He indicated this, glorified and exalted, by the form of the reflexive (ifti'al) in His saying: ﴿So do not transgress them﴾, meaning do not burden yourselves with exceeding them. In it there is also an allusion to pardon for exceeding them without intent.

Since He emphasized the command at one time by explanation and at another by prohibition, He added emphasis by threat, so He said, linking to what is implied: "Whoever transgresses any of them has wronged": ﴿And whoever transgresses﴾, meaning exceeds, ﴿the limits of God﴾, meaning the encompassing one with the attributes of perfection that He explained [p. 312] and emphasized the matter of, and increased its magnificence by repeating His Greatest Name.

Al-Harali said: In it is a hope regarding what occurs of transgression of limits outside those of the people of knowledge and the aspects of the sunan (prophetic practices); and in its information there is notice that the reckoning on the Day of Recompense will be according to the limits of the Qur'an, from which no one has any escape in any way of latitude in violating them. For this reason, piety and guardianship are realized together with adherence to the varying sunan and the varying opinions of the scholars. End of quote.

To this the restriction in His saying points: ﴿Those﴾, meaning those deserving of distance, ﴿they are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning those deeply immersed in wrongdoing by placing things in other than their proper places, as if they walk in darkness.

Al-Harali said: In its implication is the classification of limits into three kinds: the limit of God, glorified and exalted; the limit of the Prophet (ﷺ); and the limit of the scholar. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What comes from God is the truth, what comes from me is the Sunnah, and what comes from my companions is latitude." So the one among the servants most free from wrongdoing is the one who guards himself against going beyond the limits of the scholars, so that he is further from going beyond the limits of the Sunnah, so that he is further from going beyond the limits of the Book. Thus the wrongdoer whose wrong reaches its end, outside the three limits, is the one who exceeds the limit of the scholar, the limit of the Sunnah, and the limit of God. End of quote.

(p-313) When he had explained the two kinds of irrevocable divorce, and since the concern of divorce is more with the number [of pronouncements] than with the compensation, he placed its kind first in His words, ﴿or release with good treatment﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:229]. Then he built on it, saying, using the singular, so that the ruling is not understood as conditional upon plurality: ﴿So if he divorces her﴾. The repetition also conveys the intensity of blame for what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, beyond these rulings. That is, ﴿if he divorces her﴾, meaning the third time, which was previously mentioned with the word release (tasrih). It is as if He said: if he chooses the final irrevocable divorce after the two [pronouncements], either during the waiting period of a revocable divorce, or after a return (ruj'ah), with or without compensation. There is no difference in counting it as the third whether the woman has married another husband or not.

Al-Harali said: He repeated the meaning of release, which he had explained in its place, with the word divorce, because he had directed it toward the return (to the first husband). This concerns what is said about the particularity of this Ummah: that the ruling of the first Book was that a woman divorced three times never returns, and so because of this return after another husband, release became divorce. End of quotation.

(p-314) ﴿Then she is not lawful to him﴾. Since omitting the particle and the adverbial phrase might suggest that the prohibition is confined to the whole span of the separation, and so one might understand that marrying her during part of that period is lawful, he said: ﴿after [that]﴾, meaning at any time, however brief, after the completion of the cycle, which is three, as indicated by the affirmation of the preposition. The prohibition continues ﴿until﴾, meaning until ﴿she marries﴾, meaning has intercourse, through tasting the honeymoon (ʿusaylah), which the Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly stated. Al-Farisi said: When the Arabs say "So-and-so married So-and-so," they mean he contracted marriage with her; and when they say "He married his wife," they mean he had intercourse with her. The Imam said: What Abu ʿAli said accords with the principles of legal theory (usul), and it is not valid to intend anything else; he proved this by a rank-based analogy. The verse indicates that for making her lawful again, a mere contract is not sufficient without intercourse, as the Sunnah has clarified; otherwise the Sunnah would be abrogating (naskh) the Qur'an, since the end of the prohibition in the verse is the contract, while in the report it is intercourse, and a single-transmission report cannot abrogate the Qur'an. By His words ﴿a husband﴾ he indicated that the condition for this intercourse is that it be lawful, within a valid contract. ﴿Other than him﴾, meaning other than the divorcer. Making this the limit of lawfulness serves as a deterrent for anyone who has some aim regarding his wife of divorcing her three times, because every man of honor dislikes that another should take his wife as a bedfellow. Mere contract does not achieve this wisdom.
