Since whoever is granted something has the choice of assigning it to another, He said: ﴿And God﴾, meaning who chose him, while the true King, to whom no one else has any command, ﴿grants His kingship﴾, meaning that which belongs to Him, and to which no one else has any share, ﴿to whomever He wills﴾ (p-٤١٩), as He gave it to you after you had been enslaved by the household of Pharaoh. ﴿And God﴾, to whom belongs complete encompassing knowledge, so objection to Him is not permitted, ﴿is All-Encompassing﴾, meaning in the comprehensiveness of His power, the vastness of His majesty, the abundance of His armies and His provision, ﴿All-Knowing﴾, meaning of perfect knowledge. Whatever He chooses is the chosen, and no one has any choice alongside Him. He acts with His vast power and knowledge in ways that minds may not grasp, and intellects and understandings cannot bear to describe. He gives to whoever has no wealth from the treasuries of His provision whatever He wills.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 248:

Since most of them were attached to what they could witness and their feet were not firm in faith in the unseen, He said: ﴿And their prophet said to them﴾, affirming the matter of Talut, ﴿Indeed, the sign﴾, i.e., the proof, ﴿of his kingship﴾.

Al-Harali said: Few are those who, in their faith, needed a miraculous sign without their faith being, if they believed, a case of overpowering that departs from them at the slightest trial. Whoever's faith is based on insight remains steadfast in it and has no need of a sign. If there is a sign, it is a blessing for him and not a trial upon him. ﴿And We do not withhold the signs from sending, except that the former peoples denied them﴾ [al-Isra' 59], ﴿And We send not the signs except as a warning﴾ [al-Isra' 59]. For signs are the vanguard of retribution, and being convinced through reflection is the vanguard of acceptance and steadfastness. End of quotation.

﴿That there should come to you﴾, i.e., without anyone bringing it, which you see, ﴿the Ark﴾.

Al-Harali said: Its status is great. End of quotation. And Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best: it is the chest in which were placed the two tablets on which the Ten Commandments were written, whose relation to the Torah is like the relation of the Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha) to the Qur'an. It is called the Ark of Testimony (tabut al-shahada), as its mention was previously made in describing the Dome of Time at the beginning of the story of the Children of Israel. Whenever they went to war, a group among them appointed to carry it would bear it and go before the army, and that would be the cause of their victory. When the Amalekites, the companions of Goliath, overcame them, they took it along with the rest of their precious possessions. Their covenant with it seemed to have been long ago, so He reminded them of its glories, encouraging them toward it and urging them to submit to Talut. So He said: ﴿In it is tranquility﴾, i.e., something that brings calm and steadfastness in places of fear.

Al-Harali said: Its meaning is steadfastness in the hearts, which has a form in the realm of the dominion according to the state of the one who is made firm. It is said: the tranquility of the Children of Israel was the form of a cat of ruby, pearl and chrysolite, its limbs composed of these, from which a gentle wind would issue, which was a sign of victory for them. End of quotation.

He increased its praise by saying: ﴿from your Lord﴾, i.e., the One whose kindness to you has been long and whose nurturing you with gentleness has been constant.

Al-Harali and others said: In the Ark there was a figure from which, at the time of victory, a wind was heard.

Al-Harali said: Just as the eastern wind would blow for this nation with victory, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been given victory by the eastern wind" (ﷺ). Its tranquility was universal to its horizons, and its ark was universal to its heavens, so that it needed no carrier to bear it nor preparation to equip it, because it is an unlettered nation, for whom Allah took charge of establishing their knowledge and their deeds. End of quotation.

Since Moses and his brother, upon them be prayers and peace, were the greatest of His prophets, He said: ﴿and a remnant﴾.

Al-Harali said: The remainder of a whole, most of which has gone. ﴿of what was left behind﴾, from leaving behind, which is that it is not presented to the matter in sense or meaning. ﴿of the family of Moses and the family of Aaron﴾, i.e., they are the two tablets of the covenant.

Al-Harali said: In the repetition of the mention of "the family" there is an indication, which is known, of the distinction of Moses, upon him be prayers and peace, with a quality not shared by Aaron, upon him be peace, namely the severity he had in the matter of God; and of the distinction of Aaron, upon him be prayers and peace, with what he had of gentleness and forbearance, since "the family of Moses and Aaron" does not apply here, because "family" in its true sense is the one in whom the qualities of the one whose family he is become apparent.

He also said: "Al-al" (family) originally means the mirage in which distant things appear, as if it were a mirror that makes things clear. So the family of a man are those who, when they are present, make it as if he has not been absent. End of quotation.

Then he stated explicitly what the attribution of the coming to it had implied, saying: ﴿carried by the angels﴾. "Carried" is from carrying, which is what one bears alone. This is no stranger than the story of Safina, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out with his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and their goods became heavy for them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Spread your cloak.' I spread it, and they placed their goods in it and carried it upon me. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Carry it, for you are a ship!' He said: So from that day I carried a load of a camel, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven, and it did not weigh heavily upon me." As for the fighting of the angels, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, at the Battle of Badr, it is a well-known matter: a Companion would be heading toward an unbeliever to fight him, and his head would have fallen before he reached him. Since this was a striking matter, He pointed out its greatness, saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾, i.e., in this matter of great importance, ﴿for you, if you are believers﴾, for admonitions do not benefit others.

Al-Harali said: When their acceptance of looking and insight weakened, their condition took the form of weakness, of which it is said: "If it be so..." So in its indication lay their deficiency and their trial, except for a few. End of quotation.

In this story there is a preparation for the Battle of Badr, a training for those upon whom fighting was prescribed, though it is hateful to them, a discipline and refinement for them, and a great and clear indication toward the caliphate of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, by what it indicates of the matter of his appointment as imam in the prayer, which is the essence of this religion, just as what was in the Ark of Testimony was the essence of that religion. It is also a warning to whoever might oppose him in this, or say that he is not of the Banu Hashim nor of Abd Manaf, who are the house of imamate and leadership, and similar things from which Allah protected the believers, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah refuses that, and so do the believers." In directing the address to the Prophet (ﷺ) there is an announcement that the first intended by it is the closest to him (ﷺ), then the closest. And in it is encouragement for the Companions, may Allah's good pleasure be upon them, in what al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, urges them to, namely fighting the apostates and what follows, and other indications that words fall short of. And Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is the Granter of success.

(p-426) Since the intended sense is: the Ark came to them in the described state, they obeyed their Prophet concerning it, they made [Talut] their king, and they volunteered with him, so he set out with them toward the enemy and departed from the place of residence with the troops, He then said: ﴿When he set out﴾, from *fasl* (separation), which is the cutting off of a part from a whole. Its underlying form is "he separated himself or his troops" or something similar, but the object was frequently omitted because it was known, so it came to be used intransitively. ﴿Talut﴾, that is, the one whom they had made king, ﴿with the troops﴾, that is, those whom he had chosen, and they went out to meet the one whom they had asked to fight, because of his disbelief in Allah, together with the various kinds of subjugation that he had inflicted upon them.

Al-Harali said: It is the plural of *jund* (troop), and they are followers who serve as a support to the one they follow. ﴿He said﴾, that is, their king, ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, that is, the One than whom there is none greater, while you are going out seeking His pleasure, ﴿will test you with a river﴾ of water, which He, glorified and exalted, made a life for every (p-427) thing. He thus made it a parable for this world, for whoever inclines toward it is humbled, and whoever turns away from it is honored.

Al-Harali said: Allah made manifest upon his tongue what He had informed His Prophet of, in His words ﴿and has increased him broadly in knowledge﴾ [al-Baqara 2:247]. End of quote.

﴿So whoever drinks from it﴾, that is, fills his belly, ﴿is not of me﴾, that is, is like one who has immersed himself in the world, so the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped. ﴿And whoever does not taste it, then he is of me﴾, like one who has entirely turned away from it. Then he recited this lofty rank (p-428), which had been placed first out of concern for it, followed by the moderate course, and so he said, making an exception from ﴿whoever drinks﴾: ﴿except one who scoops with his hand a scoop﴾, that is, one who makes an effort to scoop. In the reading with a fatha on the ghayn, there is an indication of the sense of taking it as a single act of taking whatever was taken, whether little or much. With a damma, there is an indication of filling it. *Al-gharaf* with a fatha is taking with the whole hand, and *al-gharfa* is a single act of that. With a damma, it is the name of what the scoop contains. So among those who scooped there were those who took a full scoop and others who did not take a full one. This was said by al-Harali, who also said: In it there is a notification of their division into three categories: those who did not taste it at all, and these are those who held firm and thought that they would meet Allah; those who drank from it, and these are those who were tested and cut themselves off from jihad in the way of Allah; and those who scooped a scoop, and these are those who held firm but were shaken until those who had not tasted it made them firm.

Since the story of the Children of Israel is an example for this community, the one tested by the river in this community is tested by the river of this world flowing through it. Therefore their armies, by the rule of this inferential allusion, when they passed by a river of the people's wealth, their lands, their crops, and their regions on their way to fight them, whoever took any of the people's wealth without permission from Allah was cut off from that army even if he was present with it. What occurred to the Children of Israel (p-429) openly occurs in this community as insight, a veil for it and a disgrace for those others. And whoever took nothing from it at all remained among the steadfast of that firm army. It was said to Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Commander of the Believers! Why has your horse never thrown you?" He said: "I have never trodden with it on the crops of a Muslim."

Whoever took what he had a necessity for, from a dwelling in which he stayed or from a habit that overcame him and which he would wish did not happen, these accept the steadiness from those who were scrupulous to the utmost degree. The foundation of this religion is asceticism in the heart and scrupulousness in what is taken by the hand. The Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"You are only victorious through your weak ones." In the clarity of this parable and this lesson is that the greatest army is one in which there are people of scrupulousness equal in number to the steadfast companions of Talut, and by their number were the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Badr, who were three hundred and thirteen, the number of the messengers in comparison with the great number of prophets. He said: In the singling out of the hand there is an indication that it is the right hand, because it is the special hand (p-430) for distinction. So in his reasoning, taking from the world happens with one hand, not two, since the two hands include the two sides of good and evil. End of quote.

So the river presented itself to them as he had informed them, ﴿and they drank from it﴾, exceeding the limit of moderation, ﴿except a few of them﴾. Those who obeyed were refreshed by Allah, and He strengthened their hearts. Whoever disobeyed in drinking was overcome by thirst and became too weak for the encounter, so he remained on the bank of the river.

Al-Harali said: It is reported that it was read in the nominative, which takes them out from the drinkers by way of following, as if the speech was built upon that exclusion, since it became a follower. Its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is among the things the grammarians neglected, so they did not establish it. Its rule is that what is built upon an exclusion is made to follow, and what is not built upon its exclusion... as if he only turned to it after the preceding speech was cut off and it was put in the accusative. End of quote.

The meaning in the accusative is that when the verb had settled for all, the exception returned to a part. In the nominative, by following, he intended the exception from the first, so it became like the *mufragh* (construction without a stated antecedent). This reading was attributed by al-Ahwazi in his book *al-Shawadhdh* to al-A'mash, and al-Samin in his *I'rab* attributed it to Abdullah and Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with them both. Sibawayh, may Allah have mercy on him, devoted about half of his book to the following of such a construction, titling it: "Chapter on what has *illa* and what follows it as a descriptor in the position of *ghayr* (other than) and *mithl* (like)," and he supported it with many verses, among them:

"Every brother who parts from his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqadan [stars]."

He said, as if he had said: "Every brother other than the two Farqadan." He equated this with the verse ﴿The believers who sit at home, other than those with a harm, are not equal﴾ [al-Nisa 4:95] in the nominative, and ﴿other than those who have earned Your anger﴾ [al-Fatiha 1:7]. He permitted in "what the people stood except a *zabad* (a foam)" both the substitution and the descriptor in the nominative. Al-Radi said, relying on his verse "Every brother..." and on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "All people are destroyed except those who have knowledge, and all those who have knowledge are destroyed except those who act, and all those who act are destroyed except the sincere, and the sincere are in great danger." Al-Samin said: The difference between a descriptor with *illa* and a descriptor with other particles is that it is not used to describe definites, whether proper nouns or pronouns. Some said: It is only used to describe indefinite nouns and definites with the article of genus, since it has the force of an indefinite.

When he mentioned their test with the river, he followed it with the test of the encounter with the sea of the army and the great danger in it that shakes hearts, urging them to ask for well-being and defining its great rank, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) said on the day when he presented his noble self to the people of al-Ta'if and suffered from them the great harm that he suffered: "If there is no anger from you upon me (p-433), I do not mind, but well-being is wider for me!"

So He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿When he crossed it﴾, that is, the river, without drinking, from *al-mujawaza* (crossing over), a form of *mufa'ala* from *al-jawaz*, which is passing from the near bank to the far bank, ﴿he and those who believed﴾, that is, those who affirmed faith and crossed, ﴿with him﴾. And when the two groups faced each other, ﴿they said﴾, that is, most of them.

Al-Harali said: He returned the pronoun in a general way, to indicate the great number of those who scooped and the small number of those who did not taste, just as the pronoun in "they drank" indicated the great number of those who drank from it. End of quote.

﴿No power﴾ from that for which there is capacity, which is what the doer can carry out without being unable to do it, ﴿for us today﴾, that is, in the state we are in, ﴿against Jalut and his troops﴾, because of their strength and great number.

Al-Harali said: In this there is something like their saying ﴿and he has not been given abundance of wealth﴾ [al-Baqara 2:247], relying on the notion that victory comes through the abundance of wealth or power, whereas it is only by the victory of Allah. Then he said: When this report from them and the request is examined, as will come in ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾ [al-Baqara 2:250], along with what Allah took charge of regarding the affair of this community in their army which was the example for this army in the Surah of al-Anfal, such as His words ﴿When He covered you with drowsiness as security from Him﴾ [al-Anfal 8:11] and the verses following, there is a great knowledge which Allah bestowed upon this community, and it senses what will be for them at its end of what is even greater news and fuller manifestation. So to Allah belongs praise for His great favor and kindness. End of quote.

When He reported this statement of theirs, He pointed out that it should not come from one who believes that his term is fixed, which is not increased by cowardice and hesitation nor decreased by boldness and advance, and that he will meet Allah, Who will reward him for his deeds, and that victory is from Allah, not from strength and number. So He said: ﴿Those who are certain﴾, that is, who know, but He expressed it with *zann* (supposition) when He mentioned ﴿that they will meet Allah﴾, that is, He who has majesty and honor, indicating that for fear of Allah and hope in Him, supposition suffices, because it necessitates fleeing from what one supposes Allah dislikes, sanctified and exalted is He, so as to save oneself from destruction by that. Just as these people had indulged in drinking because of the supposition of destruction by its absence, they turned back because of the supposition of destruction by the encounter. It is also possible that *zann* is in its own sense, and "meeting" is interpreted as a good state: ﴿How many a small company has overcome a large company﴾, as happened for this community on the day (p-435) of Badr, ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾. Then He pointed out that the cause of victory is obedience and remembrance of Allah, by His words ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, that is, by the empowerment of the One for whom there is no equal. So one who knows this should not slacken in remembering Him, and should be content with His decree.

Then He explained that the basis of all this is patience, by His words ﴿And Allah is with the patient﴾, that is, the Supreme King, and He does not abandon whoever is with Him.

Then he explained that they confirmed their words before actually engaging in battle. He said, connecting to what is implied: "When they told them this, Allah unified their word, so they relied on Him and came out to fight before Him": ﴿And when they came forth﴾ while they were in their state of weakness and scarcity. Al-buruz is going out into an open place of the earth, the kind of ground where there is nothing to hide behind from the eye of the observer. ﴿Jalut﴾ (Goliath) is the name of a king among the Canaanite kings who was in al-Sham at the time of the Children of Israel. ﴿And his hosts﴾ in their state of strength, numbers, and boldness, having become accustomed to victory. ﴿They said: "Our Lord, pour upon us﴾ from ifrigh, which is pouring out abundantly so that it covers the whole of what is poured upon. ﴿patience﴾ until we attain by striking what we love in such a situation. ﴿And make firm﴾ from tathbit, which is a form of intensification from thabat, meaning to be established in a place where the danger is slipping. ﴿our feet﴾ plural of qadam, which is that upon which a thing stands and rests. That is, by strengthening our hearts so that we do not flee, and so that our blows are heavy and painful. And by their saying ﴿and help us against the disbelieving people﴾ in place of their saying "against them," they indicate that they fight them only because of their neglect of His right, glorified and exalted is He, and not for any of the desires of the self, as was the case for most of them at the first request, and they indicate that they are weak, so they must have His aid against them, glorified and exalted is He.

[p-437] Then he made this outcome a consequence of that, urging people to follow their example so as to attain what they attained. So he said, conjoining it to what is implied: Allah, glory be to Him, answered their supplication: ﴿So they routed them﴾, from which comes the rout (al-hazimah), which is the fleeing of one whose nature is steadfastness. This is what al-Harali said, and he added: Allah did not "rout" them, as He did for this Ummah in ﴿But it was Allah who killed them﴾ (Al-Anfal: 17). End of quote.

﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, that is, the One to whom the command belongs entirely. Then he explained what was specific to the one who took charge, owing to the magnitude of the matter, by exposing himself to destruction for the sake of Allah, glory be to Him, from the noble qualities that bring about the perfection of life and lead to eternal everlasting survival. So He said: ﴿And Dawud killed﴾, and he was in the army of Talut, ﴿Jalut﴾.

Al-Harali said: This is a counterpart to His words ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ (Al-Anfal: 17), and ﴿And the favour of Allah upon you has been great﴾ (An-Nisa: 113). End of quote.

In the Zabur, in Psalm one hundred and fifty-one, which is its last: "I was small among my brothers, a youth in my father's house, tending his flock. My hands made the organ, and my fingers fashioned the lyre. From now on the LORD, my God, has chosen me and answered me, and He sent His angel and took me from my father's flock, and anointed me with oil, the oil my brothers anointed, handsome ones, and He honoured me, and the LORD was not pleased with them. I went out to meet the Philistine, the mighty stranger, and he cursed me by his idols. I struck him with three stones on his forehead by the power of the LORD, and I felled him, drew his sword, cut off his head with it, and removed the disgrace from the children of Israel."

﴿And Allah gave him﴾ with His majesty and greatness ﴿the kingdom﴾.

Al-Harali said: Dawud, peace be upon him, was among them of the tribe of the king, so there came together for him two excellences: the entitlement of the house and the manifestation of the sign at his hands in killing Jalut. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿and wisdom﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 151), to purify the kingdom from what would befall it through the loss of wisdom, namely transgressing the limits. End of quote. Thus Dawud, peace be upon him, was the first to whom kingship and prophethood were combined. ﴿And taught him﴾, that is, in addition to what the two of them needed, ﴿of what He willed﴾, such as the craft of making coats of mail, the speech of birds, and other things.

[p-439] When Allah, glory be to Him, had explained this event at such length, with this explanation which humans and jinn cannot match, He explained the wisdom of jihad and of enjoining good and forbidding evil, and even what is more general than that: the empowering of some people over others. This is because He created humans with dispositions that lead to tyranny and to seeking to be unique in exaltedness, which leads to disagreement. So He said, building it upon what is implied: Thus Allah repelled from the children of Israel what He had afflicted them with: ﴿And if not for Allah's repelling﴾, who encompasses all with wisdom and power, by His might and His capacity, ﴿the people﴾. It is also read as "difa'" (defence).

Al-Harali said: It is fi'al (a form) from two, and what occurs from one of them is daf' (repelling), which is turning a thing back from its direction, towards which it is set in motion, by overpowering and subduing it, at the utmost extent. It is more emphatic than the first, indicating that He, glory be to Him, acts in this matter as one who magnifies. End of quote.

When Allah, glory be to Him, had established that the act belongs to Him in creation and origination, He explained that it belongs to His servants by acquisition and direct engagement. So He said: ﴿some of them by means of others﴾. Sometimes He gives victory to their strong over their weak, as the analogy requires; and sometimes He gives victory to their weak over their strong, as He did in the story of Talut, so that the protection that remains among them through the awe some have for others continues to exist. ﴿Otherwise the earth would be corrupted﴾ by the strong devouring the weak until no one remains. ﴿But Allah﴾, the Exalted, by His greatness, majesty, might and perfection, restrains some people by means of others, and sets some wrongdoers over others. Religion may even be supported by a dissolute man, under a system He arranged and a law He decreed in eternity, which becomes a cause for the strong to refrain from the weak, to preserve this existence upon this order up to the limit He set. Then He removes the enmity at the time of Isa, peace be upon him, [p-441] so that knowledge of His complete power and choice is completed. This is from His grace upon His servants, and He is ﴿full of bounty﴾ immensely great ﴿to the worlds﴾, that is, to all of them, first by origination and second by repelling. He restrains the oppression of oppressors, either some of them by means of others, or by the righteous, and few are they, and He bestows upon them other than that of the garments of His blessings, outward and inward.

Among what is closely connected with this story is what the memorizer Abu al-Qasim ibn 'Asakir reported in al-Kuna from the Tarikh of Damascus, in the biography of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', from al-Asma'i, who said: Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' recited to us, saying: I heard a Bedouin reciting, and I had gone out to the outskirts of Basra for relief from what I suffered at the hands of al-Hajjaj and from hiding from him:

Patience of the soul at every affliction, indeed in patience is the stratagem of the strategist.
Do not be constricted in matters, for their troubles are relieved without scheming.
Often souls recoil from a matter, yet for it there is an opening like the untying of a knot.
The coward may be struck at the back of the line, while the one who fights the heroes survives.

I said: What is behind you, O Bedouin? He said: al-Hajjaj has died. I did not know which of the two I was happier about: al-Hajjaj's death, or his saying "for it there is an opening!" Because I was seeking a witness for my choice of the reading in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿except one who takes a handful in his hand﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 249). End of quote.

Perhaps the conclusion of the stories of the children of Israel with this story is because of what it contains of clear indication for the Prophet (ﷺ) of the truth of his claim to messengership, since it is among what only a few expert scholars of the children of Israel know. Then He followed it with the Verse of the Throne, which is the greatest sign among the proofs of Tawhid. This was most fitting, given what is at the beginning of the surah in His words: ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 21), to the end of those verses, which are proofs of Tawhid including the proofs of prophethood, with which the stories of the children of Israel were opened. Thus the proofs of Tawhid enclosed their story, at its beginning and its end, along with what lies within it, following the wise method in disputing with scholars and debating with eminent people. The essence of this is as if it were said: "Alif Lam Mim" to alert souls to what the All-Knowing, glory be to Him, has kept to His knowledge alone. When the hearing is given over and the minds are present, it is said: "O people." When the eagerness is great, He said: ﴿worship your Lord﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 21). Then He specified Him after describing Him with what He explained in His words: ﴿Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 255), as this will be gathered without separation at the beginning of the surah of Tawhid, Al 'Imran, which was revealed concerning the debate with the People of the Book, including the Christians and others. Their stories end with His words: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord"﴾ (Al 'Imran: 193), meaning by the caller, and Allah knows best who the speaker is: ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 21), to its end.

Among what must be heeded from their story is what it contains, for it is training for those upon whom fighting was prescribed, and discipline in facing men. It guides to the fact that most of the self's talk and wishes are falsehood, especially regarding steadfastness on slippery footing. So a person grows bold, but when he is caught up, fear overtakes him, until they do not wish to meet the enemy, as their Prophet (ﷺ) taught them. That is because the children of Israel, despite being uncountable in number, asked their Prophet (ﷺ) to send a king for the jihad. When he was sent, and he opposed their aims, they did not meet him except with objection. Then, when the situation settled after the establishment of proofs and the showing of signs, he summoned them, and an army of immense number responded. He stipulated on them that a young man who was free should build a house and marry a woman. Those present who met the condition were only eighty thousand. Then they were tested at the river, and of them there remained only three hundred and thirteen, who were less than a third of an eighth of a tenth of those who met the condition, of those who were less than the least of those who had volunteered, who were less than the least of those who had asked for the sending of the king. So those sincere with him were as they were, as one of the later saints said at the end of his journey for visitation:

Do you not know that I am a money-changer, testing friends on a touchstone?
Among them is the base, with no good in it, and among them is one I might accept with doubt.
And you are the pure refined gold, by my certifying, and one like me certifies.

This is the secret of the saying of the Truthful one, upon him be prayer and peace: "My Ummah is like a hundred camels, among which you can hardly find a riding camel." And his (ﷺ) saying: "Do not wish for meeting the enemy, but ask Allah for well-being; and when you meet them, be patient." So the conclusion is that the intelligent person who believes in his own ignorance of outcomes and in the all-encompassing power of his Lord should not trust himself in anything at all. He should continually describe himself as powerless, even if the self claims otherwise, and he should disown his own strength and power in favour of the strength and power of his Master, and never cease to ask Him for pardon and well-being.

When these verses rose above the highest level that discerning and eloquent people know of the aims of speech, and went beyond a limit that minds cannot reach, and the capacities of understanding shrank from producing anything like them, God, glory be to Him, drew attention to this with His words: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the verses that are miraculous for whoever's noses are held high and whose aspirations and souls are lofty in the degrees of arrogance. The reference is to what was mentioned in this sura, especially this story from the reports about the Children of Israel, and the expression of it in these dazzling styles and miraculous, overpowering modes of expression. ﴿are the signs of God﴾, that is, of Him whose greatness is exalted and whose power and might are perfect. Since the Majesty (al-jalalah), inasmuch as it is a name for the Essence comprising the attributes of perfection, beauty, and the qualities of majesty (p-445), he turned the speech to the locus of greatness, indicating their incapacity to produce this composition by the qualities of arrogance and exaltation, and so He said: ﴿We recite them﴾, that is, We send them down one thing after another by virtue of the greatness We possess, ﴿to you﴾, to establish the pillars of the Book, which is guidance, and to fortify its foundations, ﴿in truth﴾. The Imam Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani said in his commentary on al-'Aqa'id: al-haqq (truth, the correct) is a judgment that corresponds to reality. It is applied to statements, beliefs, religions, and doctrines in respect of their including that, and its opposite is al-batil (falsehood). As for al-sidq (truthfulness, sincerity), it is commonly used of statements specifically, and its opposite is al-kadhib (lying). It may be distinguished between the two by saying that correspondence is considered in al-haqq from the side of reality, and in al-sidq from the side of the judgment; so the truthfulness of a judgment means its correspondence to reality, and its being true (haqqiyyah) means reality's correspondence to it. End of quotation.

The meaning of the verse on this basis is: We know the reality of these verses, so We have brought an expression to which that reality corresponds, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. That expression is fixed as firmly as reality is fixed, and no fair-minded, knowledgeable person can deny it or deny any part of it, just as he cannot deny a known reality whose occurrence is known. The report about it is truthful because it corresponds to that reality without addition or deficiency. The summary is that al-haqq is considered from the side of the one who reports, for he brings an expression equal to reality, and thus it is true; and that al-sidq is considered from the side of the listener, for he looks at the report, and if he finds it corresponding to reality, he says: "This is truthful." (p-446) It is not far-fetched that among the evidences for this are this verse and His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And he who brought the truth and confirmed it﴾ [az-Zumar: 33], and His words: ﴿He said: "Then the truth, and the truth I say"﴾ [Sad: 84], ﴿Nay, he brought the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ [as-Saffat: 37], and ﴿It is the truth, confirming what is before it﴾ [Fatir: 31]. Likewise ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ [al-Hijr: 85], meaning: this act, which is Our creating them, is one in which We have not overstepped, and this reality corresponds to their creation, neither exceeding it, in the sense that it was incumbent upon Us to add something to them and We had no right to be content with what came to be, nor falling short of it, in the sense that it was incumbent upon Us to make them deficient from what they are and it would not have been for Us to complete them thus. Or it means "with the truth," which is Our power and choice, not as the philosophers claim of an act by the essence without choice. Or it means "for the sake of truth," that is, to establish and confirm it and to nullify and negate falsehood. And His words: ﴿We have brought you the truth, and indeed We are truthful﴾ [al-Hijr: 64], meaning: We have brought you the report of their punishment, and it is established, for its content, when it occurs, its attribution to the report (p-447) is known as its correspondence to it, i.e., the correspondence of reality to it and of our reporting about it as it is; so We are truthful in it. That is, We attributed the occurrence of the punishment to them with an attribution of correspondence to reality, so when it occurs, one looks at our report and finds it corresponding to it, and thereby knows our truthfulness in it. What leaves no ambiguity in this is His words, glory be to Him, recounting of Joseph, upon whom be peace: ﴿My Lord has made it true﴾ [Yusuf: 100]; he brought about the correspondence of reality to its interpretation. As for the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ, it is by attributing the report to reality, namely that he saw what he reported, and that exists from the time of his reporting, for his report at the time of its telling corresponded to reality. As for the truthfulness of the dream, it is by considering that it had a reality to which its interpretation corresponded. If it is said: the foundation of al-mufa'alah (the verbal form indicating reciprocity) is that it occurs between two or more, where each does to the other what the other does to him; so suppose we consider correspondence from one side, that does not negate considering it from the other side, so what is the use of what you claim? It is answered: although it necessarily requires taking both sides into account, it conveys that the one to whom the verb is attributed is the seeker, unlike the pattern al-tafa'ul (the form indicating mutual action), whose verb has no indication of that. The sum of the matter is that reality has more right to the name al-haqq, because it is the established, and the report has more right to the name al-sidq. Reality (p-448) seeks a report that corresponds to it so that it may be known as it is, and the report seeks the correspondence of reality to it so that it gains honor by being named truthful.

The first established thing in the reality of the matter is reality itself, for it precedes the report about it as having occurred. So when the origin of seeking is from reality, the report is named by its name; when the origin of seeking is from the report, it is named by its proper name. Perhaps, if you consider the verses of the Book, the speaker of what is right, you will find them all in this style, and God, glory be to Him, is the Granter of success.

Since it has been established that the recitation upon him ﷺ is truth, God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed you﴾, that is, while the state is that you ﴿are among the messengers﴾, by what these verses indicate of your knowledge of them without a human teacher, and then by their miraculousness that endures throughout the ages.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 253 (part 1 of 3):

(p-١) When this surah had mentioned many messengers, and the preceding verses had concluded by stating that the Prophet (ﷺ) was among them, the soul yearned to know their states in excellence: whether they are equal in it or differ in rank. So He pointed to the exalted standing of all of them in His words, ﴿Those messengers﴾, using the demonstrative of distance, to inform that their ranks are far above and their stations lofty, and that they are in a place that cannot be reached and a rank that cannot be attained. Al-Harrali (al-Harrali) made the expression with ﴿those﴾ (tilka), which is the feminine demonstrative, rather than ﴿those﴾ (ulaika), which is the masculine demonstrative, a preparation and an indication of what is mentioned after it concerning the divergence of nations after their prophets. He said: The grammarians say that it is a demonstrative for a feminine plural group, but in Arabic it is for a second group in rank, because the feminine is the taking of the secondary from a primacy that corresponds to it in meaning (p-٢) and is opposed to it in its approach. He said: Among the eloquence of the Arabs and the indication of the foundation of their speech is that when the meaning is intended to be elevated, it is stated without the sign of the second in rank and its indication; and when it is intended to be lowered, it is restricted by the sign of the second and its indication. Then he said: Within this indication, for those who are attentive, there is an intimation of what this verse contains of information descending from the rank of permanence and continuance to the rank of divergence and cessation. Just as, when the mention occurred in a place of elevation in the verse of the cattle, it was said: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. And since the matter of divergence and cessation is not strange in a place of deficiency and difficulty, he prepared for this event after the messengers by stating that it is not of that kind, and that it is of what happens after the manifestation of the preference and the conveying of the clear proofs, according to what He wills of His command. End of quotation. Then he followed this indication, as a circumstantial clause or as a new sentence, with His words: ﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾, that is, by specifying them with merits not gathered for anyone else after We had preferred them all with the messengership.

(p-٣) Since most of the surah concerns the Children of Israel, and most of that concerns the followers of Moses, peace be upon him, He began with describing him and followed with Jesus, peace be upon him, because he abrogates his law and is the last of their prophets. So He said, clarifying what was summarized of that preference, beginning with the rank of speech because it is among the greatest ranks, turning the word to the manifestation of the Essence with all its attributes, because that is more suitable for speech that gathers completeness: ﴿Among them are those to whom God spoke﴾, that is, without an intermediary, with His majesty, such as Moses, Muhammad, and Adam, peace be upon them all. ﴿And He raised some of them in rank﴾, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ) above the others. And among (p-٤) the benefits of leaving it ambiguous is that deduction by evidence is drawn, so that what is ambiguous, though clearer, is more fit to be memorized. That deduction is that it may be said: He, glory be to Him and exalted, has generally honored them all with preference by the messengership first, then He clarified that He preferred some of them over others. All of that is elevation. If this were merely another elevation, it would be a repetition, so it must convey that it is an elevation above the highest of them. He omitted the word "over" here out of honor to the messengers, unlike in Surah az-Zukhruf. So He said, specifying (p-٥) some of what the preference requires: ﴿degrees﴾, that is, great degrees by the general call, the enduring miracles, the numerous followers over long periods without alteration or distortion, by the abrogation of his law of all laws, by his being a mercy to the worlds, by his nation being the best nation brought forth for mankind, and by his being the seal of the prophets whom God, glory be to Him and exalted, sent as bearers of good tidings and warners and sent down the Book with them, at the time of divergence. So there is no prophet after him to abrogate his law. Rather, the prophet who abrogates the law of Moses, peace be upon him, comes confirming his law and renewing what had been effaced of it, as happened with the prophets of the Children of Israel who were between him and Moses, peace be upon them all. Since a person's excellence is not made clear except by his signs, and the signs of Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, were more numerous than those of anyone who preceded them, He singled them out for mention to indicate that. This entails the manifestation of excellence for our Prophet (ﷺ), because there is no comparison between what any of the prophets was given and what was given to him. And the ambiguity of the expression indicates this in that it points to the fact that (p-٦) its ambiguity in clarity and manifestness is like its mention, because what is described by it refers only to him.

Since people are bound to the senses, except for the rare individual, and Jesus (ﷺ) had repeated sensible signs such as raising the dead and healing the blind and leprous that were not given to anyone else, [and yet] most of them apostatized after his ascension, peace be upon him. He said, turning the word to the manifestation of majesty, as a threat to whoever disbelieves after seeing or hearing those great signs: ﴿And We gave﴾, by what We have of majesty, through power over every thing, of creation and fashioning however We will and otherwise. ﴿Jesus﴾, and He attributed him to his mother, to indicate that he had no father. So He said: ﴿son of Mary﴾, that is, whom We created from her without any male intermediary at all. ﴿The clear proofs﴾, such as raising the dead and other things. Al-Harrali said: A clear proof is that whose evidence is manifest in nature, knowledge, and intellect, such that there is no escape from witnessing its existence. That is in what God, glory be to Him and exalted, made manifest through his hands of giving life and causing death, which is among the highest of God's signs. For every thing that appears in creation and descends in command is one of God's signs, so whatever is closer to what God has exclusively reserved for Himself is higher and more dazzling, and whatever occurs at the hands of His creatures is more hidden and more obscure, except for those whom God has alerted in heart to perceive it. ﴿And We strengthened him﴾, that is, with Our mighty power, ﴿with the Holy Spirit﴾, in making known the mention of what God placed between him and Jesus, peace be upon him, in his being, so that his action moved toward him through the intermediary of the Spirit, as He, glory be to Him and exalted, said: ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾ [Maryam: 17]. Thus was his action along with his strengthening. In this there is an initial parallel between him and Moses, peace be upon them both, since Moses' matter began with the matter of speech, which is the ultimate removal of the intermediary, while Jesus' matter, peace be upon him, began with the matter of giving life, which is the ultimate of the actions of those who act. End of quotation.

Mention of some of what is in the Gospel of its clear proofs, its wisdoms, and its signs.

Matthew said: "You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has lost its taste, how shall it be made salty? It is no longer good for anything but to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by men."

Luke said: "Salt is good; but if the salt has lost its taste, with what shall it be seasoned? It is fit neither for the land nor for the dunghill; it is thrown out. He who has ears to hear, let him hear." (p-٨) Matthew said: "You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a lampstand, and it gives light to all who are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill. For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. Therefore whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches men so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." Then he said: "And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Truly, I say to you, they have their reward. But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly. And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. Pray then like this: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen." (p-٩) Mark said: "And when you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your trespasses." Matthew said: "For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses." Luke said: "And he was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.' And he said to them, 'When you pray, say: Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.'" (p-١٠) Then he said to them: "Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, 'Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey and I have nothing to set before him'; and he will answer from within, 'Do not bother me; the door is now shut and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything.' I tell you, though he will not get up and give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 253 (part 2 of 3):

Matthew said: "When you fast, do not be like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces and change them so that they may show people their fasting. Truly I tell you, they have already received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that your fasting may not appear to people." Luke said: "Which of you, if he has a servant who plows or herds, will say to him when he comes in from the field: 'Come at once and sit down'? Will he not rather say to him: 'Prepare my supper, gird yourself and serve me until I have eaten and drunk, and afterwards you may eat and drink'? Does he thank that servant for doing what he was commanded? So also you, when you have done everything you were commanded, say: 'We are worthless servants; we have only done what was our duty.'" He also said: "One of the crowd said to him: 'Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.' He said to him: 'Man, who appointed me a judge or divider over you?'" He said to them: "Look and guard yourselves from all greed, for a person's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions." He told them a parable: "A rich man's land produced abundantly, so he thought and said: 'What shall I do, since I have no place to store my produce? I will tear down my granaries, build larger ones and store my goods there, and I will say to myself: O soul, you have much good laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink and be merry.' But God, glorified and exalted be He, said to him: 'O fool! This night your soul will be taken from you, and what you have prepared, whose will it be? So is the one who stores up treasure but is not rich in God.'" Matthew said: "Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and thieves break in and steal. Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where there is no moth or rust to destroy and no thieves to break in and steal." Luke said: "Sell your possessions and give alms; make for yourselves purses that do not wear out, and a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief reaches and no moth destroys." Matthew said: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The lamp of the body is the eye. If your eye is sound, your whole body will be [bright, and if your eye is evil, your whole body will be] dark. If then the light within you is darkness, how great is that darkness! No one can serve two masters, for he will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth. Therefore I tell you: do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink, nor about your body, what you will wear. Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?" Luke said: "For the soul is better than food, and the body than clothing. Look at the birds of the sky, which do not sow or reap or gather into barns, yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much more valuable than they?" Luke said also concerning you: "You are better than the birds. Which of you by worrying can add one cubit to his stature? Why do you worry about clothing? Consider the flowers of the field, how they grow, without toil." Luke said: "Consider the flowers, how they grow without labor or effort." End of quotation. I tell you that Solomon in all his glory did not dress like one of these. If the flower of the field is alive today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, God will clothe it thus; how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith! So do not worry and say: 'What shall we eat, drink or wear?' All these things the Gentile nations seek, but your Father knows that you need all of these. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself; each day has enough trouble of its own." Luke said: "Let your waists be girded and your lamps lit. Be like people waiting for their master, when he will return from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks they may open to him immediately. Blessed are those servants whom their master finds awake when he comes! Truly I tell you, he will gird himself, have them recline, and come and serve them." Then he said: "Peter said to him: 'Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for everyone?' He said: 'Who then is the faithful and wise steward whom the master sets over his household to give them their food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master finds doing so! Truly I tell you, he will set him over all his possessions. But if that evil servant says in his heart: 'My master delays his coming,' and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat, drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in two and assign him a portion with the unbelievers. As for the servant who knows his master's will but does not prepare or act according to his will, he will be beaten severely; and the one who does not know but does things deserving of a beating will be beaten lightly. For to whom much is given, much will be required; and to whom much is entrusted, much will be demanded.'" He said in another place: "One who is faithful in little is faithful in much, and one who is unjust in little is unjust in much. If you have not been faithful with unjust wealth, who will entrust you with the true? And if you have not been faithful with what is not yours, who will give you what is yours? I came to cast fire on the earth, and I desire nothing but that it be kindled. I have a baptism to be baptized with, and I am anxious until it is accomplished. Do you think I came to bring peace on earth? I tell you, from now on there will be division: five in one house will be divided, three against two and two against three; father against son, son against father, mother against daughter, daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law." Matthew said: "Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; for with the judgment you judge, you will be judged, and with the measure you measure, it will be measured to you." Luke said: "Do not love judging anyone, so that you may not be judged. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Give, and you will be given good measure, pressed down, shaken together and running over, poured into your laps, for with the measure you measure, it will be measured to you. Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will not both fall into a pit?" Matthew said: "Why do you look at the speck in your brother's eye and not notice the log in your own eye? How can you say to your brother: 'Let me take the speck out of your eye,' when there is a log in your eye? O hypocrite! First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces. Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to whoever knocks it will be opened. Which of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake? If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! So whatever you want people to do for you, do the same for them; for this is the Law and the Prophets." Luke said: "It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one letter of the Law (nāmūs) to be abolished." He also said, and told them a parable: "That they should always pray and not lose heart. He said: There was a judge in a city who did not fear God nor respect people, and in that city there was a widow who kept coming to him and saying: 'Give me justice against my opponent.' For a while he refused, but afterwards he said to himself: 'Even though I do not fear God or respect people, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will grant her justice, so that she will not wear me out by continually coming.'" The Lord, glorified and exalted be He, said: "Hear what the unjust judge said. Will not God vindicate his chosen ones who cry to him day and night? I tell you, he will vindicate them speedily." Matthew said: "Enter through the narrow gate, for the gate is wide and the road that leads to destruction is broad, and many enter through it. How narrow is the gate and how hard the road that leads to life, and few find it! Beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits. Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? So every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears evil fruit. A good tree cannot bear evil fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit." Luke said: "Every tree is known by its fruit; figs are not gathered from thorns, nor are grapes picked from a bramble. The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings forth evil, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks." Matthew said: "Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. So by their fruits you will know them. Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father in heaven, that is, his command. On that day many will say to me, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many miracles in your name?' Then I will declare to them, 'I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity.'" Luke said: "One said to him: 'Lord, will few be saved?' He said: 'Strive to enter through the narrow door, for I tell you that many will seek to enter and will not be able. When the master of the house rises and shuts the door, then you will stand outside and knock on the door and say: "Lord, Lord, open to us." He will answer: "I do not know you, where are you from?" Then you will say: "We ate and drank in your presence." He will say: "I do not know you, where are you from? Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity." There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there.'" Matthew said: "Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock." Luke said: "He built a house, dug deep and laid the foundation on rock. When the flood came, the rivers burst against that house, and it could not be shaken, because it was founded on the rock. But everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them is like a foolish man who built his house on sand. When the flood came and the rivers burst against it, it fell, and its fall was great." When Yashu' had finished these words, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one having authority, and not as their scribes.

In it, the use of the words "Father" and "Lord," which are forbidden to be applied in our law, occurs; and what will heal the sick person in interpreting such a thing will come in Al ʿImrān, establishing its soundness. And whatever is mentioned of the prophets being described as "liars," what is meant by it is one who falsely claims prophethood.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 253 (part 3 of 3):

Since it was previously stated that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, sent messengers and sent down with them scriptures, and that they endured hardship, suffering and adversity, and were shaken until they gathered the people upon the truth, and that their followers disagreed after the clear proofs had come to them, the soul would naturally turn to ask about the cause of their disagreement. So He made clear that it is solely His will, glorified and exalted be He, in order to inform that He is the Doer who chooses. The sense is therefore: "Had Allah, glorified and exalted be He, willed, He would have made the messengers equal in excellence; and had He willed, He would have made their followers equal in accepting what they brought, so that no two of them would have disagreed. But He did not will that, so they disagreed among themselves while they were witnessing the clear proofs." He linked to this His saying, as consolation to His Prophet ﷺ, turning the speech to the expression of majesty (al-jalalah, the Name Allah), indicating that disagreement, together with the evidence of reason that there is no good in it, is a witness to the Creator with all attributes of majesty and beauty. ﴿Had Allah willed﴾, i.e., He to whom belongs all command. Al-Harrali said: This is a comprehensive Qur'anic, Muhammadan phrase which testifies to Allah alone and erases from the establishment (of existence) whatever is other than Him, end of quote.

﴿Would not have fought one another﴾, i.e., would not have undertaken fighting, even though it is hateful to souls, ﴿those who came after them﴾, because of their agreement upon what they had separated from their Prophet of guidance. Al-Harrali said: He mentioned fighting, which occurs only after the trial of speech, which follows the trial of states, through grudges and rancour, after the loss of peace, after the loss of affection, after the loss of the love [that unites] the community with its Prophet, end of quote. ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, i.e., through the hands of their messengers. Al-Harrali said: In this is a notice that the means and causes do not necessitate their effects except by the execution of Allah's word through them, end of quote.

﴿But they differed﴾, because He, glorified and exalted be He, did not will their agreement upon guidance. ﴿So among them﴾, i.e., as a consequence of their disagreement, there were among them ﴿those who believed﴾, i.e., those who remained steadfast upon what their Prophet had departed upon, according to what the clear proofs called for; so this belief of theirs is faith in truth, because it is more firmly rooted in the matter of the unseen. ﴿And among them are those who disbelieved﴾, either through error concerning it or through obstinacy.

Since there are among people those whom Allah has blinded in heart, and who attribute the acts of choosing creatures to themselves independently, He, exalted be He, stated, informing that the whole is by His creation, as emphasis upon what has passed of that, repeating the Greatest Name to indicate the greatness of the matter concerning fighting, which exposes whoever engaged in it to error regarding the most reprehensible of qualities: ﴿Had Allah willed﴾, who has no equal, ﴿they would not have fought one another﴾ after their disagreement over belief and disbelief. He repeated the Greatest Name to add notice of the greatness of the station. ﴿But Allah﴾, i.e., by His majesty and the might of His perfection, willed their fighting, ﴿for He does whatever He wills﴾. So they disagreed and fought, in obedience to His will, contrary to their natures and to what contradicts the knowledge and wisdom they possess.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 254:

Since disagreement over the prophets was a cause of jihad, which is the enclosure of the religion (ḥaẓīrat al-dīn), and since the pillar of jihad is expenditure (nafaqah), He followed that with His saying, returning to the beginning of the surah from here to its end, and with emphasis by means of the imperative form, because of the urging to expenditure that had preceded: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, meaning those who affirmed with their tongues (p-22) the faith, ﴿spend﴾, confirming your claim in all the avenues of the lesser and greater jihad, and do not be stingy, for what disease is more harmful than stinginess? Whoever is protected from the avarice of his own self, those are the successful.

When He commanded this, He made it easy for them by informing them that it belongs to Him, not to them, so He said: ﴿from what﴾, that is, the thing, and He returned the speech to the locus of majesty, urging haste in complying with the command and disparaging the state of whoever delays in it, so He said: ﴿We have provided you﴾ (p-23) with what We possess of majesty. He made the command a jussive here, because when He had encouraged expenditure from the beginning of the surah until here, time after time, in varied styles, the motives of intelligent people reached the degree of acceptance of what is recommended in it, even though departing from what is in hand is most hateful to the soul. He directed the command toward partiality, to lawful and good things, thereby preventing the Mu'tazilah from using it as proof that provision can only be lawful because it is commanded. He followed this with what entices and warns concerning the state of the Day of Mutual Calling (yawm al-tanād), on which the means that He, glorified and exalted, established in this abode are cut off, so He said: ﴿before there comes a Day﴾ described as ﴿in which there is no trading﴾ existing, ﴿nor friendship﴾. Al-Ḥarrālī said: it is of that from which comes mutual intimacy (al-mukhālallah), which is interpenetration in what admits interpenetration, until each one is within the other; and its locus of meaning is agreement in the attribute of approval and anger, so the close friend's approval is the approval of his friend and his action is of his action. End of quote.

﴿Nor intercession﴾. The meaning is that no captive is ransomed with wealth, nor is anyone shown consideration out of friendship from an equal, nor intercession from a great one, because Allah, glorified and exalted, (p-24) does not will any of that, and nothing happens except what He wills. In the verse there is a strong allusion to the beginning of the surah, where He described the believers as those who spend from what He provided them and who are certain of the Hereafter, and a clarification that expenditure in general is more inclusive than zakat, and that this includes all forms of expenditure from all kinds of resources and fortunes that acquire lofty status and deliver from ruin. What will come in the verses urging expenditure guides to this, such as His saying, ﴿If you disclose the charities﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271], and others. Al-Ḥarrālī said: Thus this conclusion in address is joined to what is at the beginning of the surah, from ﴿those who believe in the unseen and establish prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] to His saying ﴿the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. Therefore after this conclusion there occurred the opening of a verse which is the chief of the verses of this surah, unified with its beginning by a semantic unity, with the head of ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1] ﴿This is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. So in the indication of this unity there was a preparation for what the address made plain at the opening of the surah of Āl ʿImrān, because the Qur'an is repeated (mathānī) in understanding and praise. Its beginning is praise and its end is praise, and what lies between the two praises turns back upon its beginning, as He said: "My servant has praised Me, My servant has extolled Me." So its totality is praise and its details are glorification. End of quote.

When He, glorified and exalted, urged expenditure, He concluded the verse by censuring the disbelievers, because they did not adorn themselves with this quality, due to their being empty of faith, their distance from it, and their denial (p-25) of that Day. So they do not spend, neither out of fear of it nor hope in it. So He said, in place of "nor is there support for a disbeliever": ﴿And the disbelievers﴾, that is, those whose disbelief is known on that Day. This conjunction indicates that the implied sense is: those who believed do what We commanded them, because they are the ones who are right; and the disbelievers ﴿they﴾ are the ones specifically described as ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, that is, the complete ones in wrongdoing, and no others. It is known that the wrongdoer is a loser, and that he is forsaken, not supported, because he places matters in other than their proper places; whoever is such, no affair is firm for him and no station is raised for him, but rather he is always on the brink of a crumbling precipice. For this reason, Allah, glorified and exalted, concludes many of His verses with His saying, "And the wrongdoers have no helpers." Thus all the kinds of deliverance customary in this world are negated on that Day: ransom with wealth, consideration for friendship or the greatness of an intercessor, or support through strength.

When Allah, glorified and exalted, began al-Fatiha as He has already done, He began with mention of the Essence (dhat). Then He made Himself known through His acts, because these are things that are witnessed. Then He raised the address to make Himself known through the Attributes. Then He ascended further, returning to the Essence, so that the hearer would be fit for knowledge. He began this surah with the attribute of Speech, because it is the greatest and clearest of the miracles, the most indicative of the unseen Essence, and the most impressive to souls, especially to the Arabs. Then He made Himself known through acts, and He gave more of them. [p-26] When no confusion remained, He established Divine Oneness through its preceding verse, weaving that together with the varieties of wisdom, the excellences of rulings, and the kinds of encouragement and warning, in a firmly ordered description and arrangement.

When the commands were complete, and those warnings had alarmed the hearers, [and the souls yearned,] and the minds longed to know the cause of the severance of connection, with the cutting off of all means and the negation of intercession on that Day, [p-27] since it is customary among the kings of this world that they can hardly exercise any matter fully without many intercessors and willing friends. For the king's assembly is never empty of a group, each of whom is fit to stand in his place. If they abandon him, or turn their hatred against him, his affair is weakened and his strength is undermined, so he needs to keep their favour, win their approval, and manage them. Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear the attribute of the One who commands, through what He is of majesty and greatness, the authority of His command, His exaltedness above obstruction, His transcendence above disbelief and rivalry, His singularity in all perfections, and the awe that prevents, which, once it is fully revealed there, [p-28] prevents hearts from turning to other than Him, prevents tongues from speaking without His permission, and prevents anything from being other than what He wills. This makes His command more likely to be accepted and His prohibition and restraint more likely to be heeded. For these purposes He placed the speech in the manner of an answer to a question, as if it had been said: "This is what is not known of the states of kings. Who then is the King on that Day?" So He mentioned Ayat al-Kursi, the chief of the verses of the Qur'an, which no other scripture has matched. He opened it with the proper, singular, all-comprehensive Name, which no other has been named by. This was because the hearer, after becoming acquainted with the speech and being drawn by the acts, became fit for the station of knowledge, and so ascended to the peak of watchfulness and the presence of witnessing. Then He said, returning to the manifestation of majesty, which gathers the attributes of majesty and generosity, since it is among the greatest of His stations: "Allah," meaning: He is the King on that Day. Then He affirmed for Him the attributes of perfection, [p-28] free from any taint of deficiency, opening them with singularity, and said: "There is no god but He," establishing the perfection of Oneness, for it is the greatest aim of all the laws. But because humankind is created with deficiency, it needs encouragement to draw it on, warning to turn it back, admonitions to soften it, deeds to make it sincere, and character to realise it. So Allah, glorified and exalted, interwove the verses of Oneness with rulings and stories. Rulings produce righteous deeds, which lift the veils of heedlessness from the eyes of the hearts and bestow noble character to polish the rust from the mirrors of the souls, so that the realities of Oneness appear in them. Stories bind through their admonitions and lessons with the rulings, and establish the proofs of knowledge, so that Oneness takes firm root. This detailed arrangement was for the sake of the soul's vigour, through moving from one kind to another, along with the stirring of the beauty of the composition, the eloquence of coherence, and the kindling of the wondrous connection and the skill of interlocking.

Al-Harrali said: When He had delivered the address on the explanation of comprehensive principles of the religion, the aspects of contemplation, and the explanation of the rulings of jihad [p-29] and spending in it, and the religion was thus complete within its enclosure, the markers of Islam, the rites of faith, and the glimpse of excellence (ihsan), He raised the address to explain the matter of ihsan, just as He had fulfilled the explanation of the matter of faith and Islam. He thus opened this lofty address, which masters every address, so as to exalt by it those who believe, bringing them out by it from the darkness of faith in the unseen, whose light removes the darkness of doubt and disbelief, to the clear radiance of certainty, in relation to which the light of faith becomes darkness, just as the light of the moon becomes darkness in the presence of the sun's brightness. Thus the relation of this verse to the verse of divinity in His saying, glorified and exalted, "And your God is one God" [al-Baqarah: 163], and what follows it of contemplation on the creation of the heavens and the earth, is like the relation between the exaltedness of His Name Allah, in which no association has occurred, whether rightly or wrongly, and His Name al-Ilah, in which association has occurred falsely. Thus He, exalted, transfers the believers who have settled in the faith of contemplation, through the verse "And your God is one God" [al-Baqarah: 163] and what follows it of contemplation on the creation of the heavens and the earth, to the certainty of direct witnessing through His Name "Allah" and what accords with its meaning of His great attributes. End.

When He, glorified and exalted, declared His noble Self one, He established His right to this through His life, and made clear that the meaning of the everlasting life is through the attribute of self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah). So He said: [p-30] "The Ever-Living" [i.e., the One to whom life belongs, which is an attribute that necessitates the soundness of knowledge and power, i.e., the One who can know and can power], "the Self-Subsisting" [i.e., the One who subsists by Himself and sustains others constantly, at the highest degree of standing and sustaining].

Al-Harrali said: The form fa'ul (qayyum) has the letter ya' added to its roots so that the word gathers what is of its meaning, which is standing by the affair, together with its waw, which is from qama yaqumu. Its form conveys the intensity found in qayyam and qawwam, in the manner of what the meanings of the letters convey when addressed by them, from the leading scholars who enter the city of Muhammadan knowledge through its Alawid gate. End.

Then He made clear His self-subsistence and the perfection of His life by His saying: "Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him." Al-Harrali said: Drowsiness (sinah) is the region of slumber in the two eyes, before it overwhelms the senses and enters the heart. "Nor sleep" is what reaches the heart from slumber, so that it covers it [p-31] in the case of one whose heart sleeps, while what overwhelms the senses is in the case of one whose heart does not sleep. End. Since He expressed it with "overtakes" (al-akhdh), which means subduing and overpowering, it was necessary to put drowsiness first, as if it were said: "No commander or ruler overpowers so-and-so." Then He explained this clause by His saying: "To Him belongs" [meaning: in His hand, under His disposal and His exclusive control] "whatever is in the heavens," of which the earth is part, "and whatever is on the earth" [meaning: of drowsiness, sleep, and other things, whether in origination or in continuance, and whatever is in His grip and disposal, which none can overpower.

Al-Harrali said: By the first clause He removed the affair of the dominion of the angels from their hands into the subjugation of His might, and the effects from the stars of the spheres into His restoration. By the second clause He removed the effects and crafts from the hands of His vicegerent and His creation into His decree and destiny and the manifestation of His power. Thus this address, with what it reveals to understanding, establishes His self-subsistence over the created order of the earthly and heavenly wisdom, which is the veil of His self-subsistence, negating the subsistence of all else. End.
