﴿Those who spend their wealth﴾, meaning: the likeness of their expenditure, free of any worldly cause or any soul-based admixture, but ﴿seeking the pleasure of God﴾, meaning He who possesses majesty and honour. Therefore it is entirely sound, free of reproach (mann), harm (adhā) and other flaws that cause defect. Al-Harrali said: al-marḍāh (pleasure) is on the pattern of mafʿalah, indicating the repetition and continuance of satisfaction. End.

﴿And as a strengthening from themselves﴾: by considering the correction of the deed and its sincerity, by compelling the self to forbearance, pardon and patience with all the hardships of obligations. For whoever trains his self by forcing it to give up wealth, which is the twin of the soul, and it becomes submissive to him and its craving for following its desires diminishes, it becomes easy for him to compel it to all other acts of worship. Whereas when he leaves it while it is inclined toward deficiencies, its craving for following desires and adhering to baseness increases. Here min is partitive (lil-tabʿīḍ), functioning as an object, like their saying: "he softened from his bending" (layyana min ʿaṭfihi) and "he moved from his vigour" (ḥarraka min nashāṭihi). ﴿Like the likeness of a garden﴾, meaning an orchard and the likeness of its owner. Al-Harrali said: Since the cultivation of this world consists of grain and fruit, He made the expenditures for the Hereafter likewise grain and fruit. Whoever spends in the way (of God) has his likeness as grain; whoever spends seeking the pleasure of God has his likeness as the garden which has a firm root, around which fruits revolve while it remains established, and which is independent of water in ways that cultivated crops are not, because cultivation needs renewal at every time, just as jihad occurs when there is need for it, whereas one who spends seeking God's pleasure spends in every direction continuously. So his likeness became the likeness of the lasting garden, so that the two parables correspond to the two things paralleled. Thus this expenditure encompasses all the directions of giving in all the paths of goodness. End.

﴿On a height﴾, meaning a elevated place that is not a mountain. Al-Harrali said: in informing that the best gardens are those on a height, so that the sun reaches them and the fertilizing winds pass through them. As for gardens in low valleys, the fertilizing winds pass over them from above, so their life weakens, because the winds are the life of plants: "The wind is from the breath of the Merciful." End. Then He described it by saying: ﴿Heavy rain struck it﴾, meaning abundant rain, ﴿so it yielded its produce﴾, meaning it brought it forth by God's permission, glorified and exalted, until it became as if giving ﴿double﴾, meaning as much as it would have produced had it not been struck by heavy rain. So they said "double," but the apparent meaning is that it is four times that, since by "double" is meant the thing's amount plus its like with it, so the two doublings amount to four. And God knows best. The verse contains ihtibak (a rhetorical device of omission): mention of the spender first indicates the omission of the owner of the garden second, and mention of the garden second indicates the omission of the expenditure first.

Since heavy rain may not always occur, He said: ﴿But if heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain (ṭall)﴾, meaning that a light rain reaches it because of its height. The ṭall is the dew that falls in mist. Al-Harrali said: the ṭall is one of the kinds of rain, subtle, not perceived by the senses until it gathers; rain descends imperceptibly to the senses, which is the ṭall, then appears gently, which is the ṭashsh, then strengthens, which is the rashsh, then increases and becomes continuous, which is the hatl, then becomes abundant and close together, which is the wābil, then its pouring grows great, which is the jūd. So it has kinds, from what the senses cannot reach because of its subtlety, up to what the senses cannot bear because of its abundance. End. The meaning is that the people of this category are not subject to corruption in their deeds; at most the deficiency may reach them in terms of weakness of intentions. For this reason the implied sense as a consequence is: "So God is Knowing of what you deserve for your intentions." Then He joined to it: ﴿And God﴾, meaning the One who encompasses in knowledge and power, ﴿of what you do﴾, meaning of what appears from you, ﴿is Seeing﴾, as He is likewise of what is hidden. So strive to perfect both the outward and the inward. He placed the parable of the one who gives without condition before it, because averting harms takes precedence over securing benefits.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 266:**

When Glorified and Exalted is He had first mentioned that reminding of favour (al-mann) nullifies charity, and gave it the likeness of showing off (al-riya'), and set forth a parable for both, and encouraged sincere giving, and concluded that with what is suited to instilling fear of both reminding and showing off, He returned to them, indicating concern with them. So He set forth for them a parable clearer than the earlier one and more forceful in repelling from them and keeping away from them. He said, and al-Harrali said: "When the report of the two kinds of spending and its opposite came back around, their likenesses came back around too. So He struck, for the one who spends in contrast to the one who seeks the pleasure of Allah, a parable of the abandoned garden." End of quotation. Then He said, denouncing the one who nullifies his deed, like the people of the parable of the smooth rock after the condition has been uncovered by striking these parables: ﴿Would any of you like﴾, that is, loves intensely (p. 86) ﴿to have a garden﴾, that is, an orchard that covers what is inside it. Here He specified what He had left vague in the first parable, and said: ﴿of palm trees﴾, plural of palm (nakhla), which is the tree standing on a trunk, the most similar of trees to a human from its top; its leaves are firm, its fruit nourishing and savoury, and in its entirety its benefit is complete, even its wood is food for a human, unlike other trees. Its likeness is the likeness of the believer, from whom every part is benefited. ﴿And vines﴾, plural of vine ('inab), which is a tree of generosity whose growth is not confined to the direction of height the way the palm's is, but branches upward, downward, to the right and to the left. Its likeness is the likeness of the God-fearing believer who is honoured by his piety in every direction. Thus said al-Harrali.

Since gardens cannot stand and endure except with water, He said: ﴿Beneath them rivers flow﴾, that is, because of the generosity of their land. Al-Harrali said: In its implication is the burden of that in them, unlike the first, which is rain-fed (ba'l), for the calamity in irrigation is greater for the owner than in rain-fed land, due to the lightness of cost in rain-fed land and the heaviness of costs in irrigation. End of quotation.

Since He described it with abundance of water, He mentioned the outcome of that, and said: ﴿For him in it is of every kind of fruit﴾, that is, along with the palm and the vine. Since He mentioned its generosity, He mentioned the intensity (p. 87) of the need for it, and said: ﴿And old age has struck him﴾, that is, while the state is that old age has struck him, so he is no longer able to earn; ﴿and he has weak offspring﴾, weak through youth, just as he is weak through old age; ﴿then it is struck﴾, that is, the garden, at some point ﴿by a fiery whirlwind (i'sar)﴾, that is, a very violent wind. Al-Harrali said: The form denotes intensification by the addition of the hamza and the alif in it, from 'asr (pressing), which is the intensity that brings out what lies hidden in things. The i'sar is a violent wind within a cloud in which there is a sharpness from the cold of the zamharir, and it is one of the two kinds of fire; its counterpart from the blaze is the samum. Al-Isfahani said: It is a wind that whirls on the earth and then rises toward the sky like a pillar. ﴿In it is fire, and it burns﴾, that garden, and its owner remains in ruin, with his weakness, the heaviness of his back from dependents, and the scarcity of wealth. Al-Harrali said: From burning (ihtiraq), which is the departure of a thing's spirit and form, departing and dying out by the striking of a subtle, scorching agent that spreads through its entirety, destroying it and annihilating it. So He made the first parable concern the seed upon the smooth rock, because of a blight from beneath it, and made the parable of the garden concern a calamity from above it, as though they are the two directions from which ailments and afflictions arrive, from the side of root or branch. End of quotation. Thus the state of one who shows off in his deeds, or causes harm in the charity of his wealth, on the Day of Resurrection and its terrors, is like the state of this man in himself and his dependents when his hopes are disappointed. (p. 88) Al-Bukhari, may Allah be pleased with him, related in the Book of Tafsir from Ubayd ibn Umayr, [he said: Umar said] may Allah be pleased with him, to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "On what do you think this verse was revealed: ﴿Would any of you like...﴾" until he said: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It was struck as a parable for a deed." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What deed?" Ibn Abbas said: "For a deed." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "For a rich man who works in obedience to Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, then Allah sends Satan to him, and he works in acts of disobedience until he drowns his deeds."

When He had made this explanation clear to them, which overwhelmed the eloquent among mankind and the jinn, He alerted them to its magnitude for honouring and exalting it, by saying, beginning a new sentence: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this explanation, ﴿Allah makes clear﴾, that is, He to whom all perfection belongs, ﴿the signs for you﴾, that is, all of them, ﴿so that you may reflect﴾, that is, so that your state may be the state of one from whom reflection is hoped, and one who is like that benefits from his reflection. Al-Harrali said: So you build affairs upon firm foundation; there is no good in worship except with reflection, just as the builder must reflect on his building, as the wise man said: "The beginning of thought is the end of action, and the beginning of action is the end of thought." Likewise, it is among the requirements of the deeds of religion that they not occur except with reflection upon correcting their earlier beginnings and their later ends. Thus they were, in that regard, two categories, indicated by the word "so that you may," corresponding to the parable: one who reflects, whose seed and garden are multiplied, and one who acts without reflection, whom the whims of his soul seduce, so the blight reaches him in his work, in his seed and his garden, from what came before or after him. End of quotation. (p. 89)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 267:

When he (Allah) desired the act of giving and its purification from impurities, He followed it with the wealth that is spent from it, and commanded its goodness, saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, that is, who have affirmed faith, ﴿spend from the good things you have earned﴾, that is, as a confirmation of your faith. He placed the act (of spending) first because it is closer to the human being, while making it good is more beneficial in its generality. When He, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned what He had permitted of the profits of trade and the like, He followed it with what He had permitted of the benefits of plants and the like, thereby alerting that everything that servants turn over in themselves and in other than themselves is a blessing from Him, which He brought into being from the earth that He originated from non-existence, encouraging generosity with it and making it a good and lawful thing to be chosen, and warning against stinginess with it and making it a debt or a prohibited thing. So He said: ﴿And from what We have brought forth﴾, that is, by Our majesty, ﴿for you﴾, a blessing from Us upon you, ﴿from the earth﴾. Al-Haralli (al-Ḥarālī) said: He placed first the address to those who earn by their deeds, as if they were the Muhajirun (emigrants), and he joined to them those who spend from the tilling and the sowing, as if they were the Ansar (helpers). End of quotation.

When He had commanded this, He reinforced the command by prohibiting its opposite, saying: ﴿And do not aim at the bad of it﴾, that is, do not take pains to intend ﴿the bad of it﴾, that is, exclusively (p-90) ﴿to spend﴾. Al-Haralli said: "The khabith (bad) is an intensive form with the addition of a yā' from khubth, which is what repels the sense of the soul, outwardly and inwardly; opposite to it is what the soul finds at ease with from the good, which it opens to outwardly and inwardly. In its allusion there is a sense of restriction, as if they spend only from it, so that the prohibition passes over those who spend from their good and their bad alike, without intending to restrict spending to the bad." End of quotation. Then He clarified the ugliness of that by His saying: ﴿And you would not take it yourselves﴾, that is, if someone owes you a right and gives it to you, ﴿except that you overlook﴾, that is, you show leniency ﴿in it﴾, with shame together with dislike. Al-Haralli said: from al-ighmāḍ (overlooking), which is ignoring a defect in what is used; its root is from al-ghumḍ, which is a sleep that covers the sense and then clears. He said: Since the one who takes is Allah, glorified and exalted is He, He concluded with His saying: ﴿And know﴾. End of quotation.

He expressed it with the Greatest Name, saying: ﴿that Allah﴾, the One who has perfected all attributes of perfection, of majesty and of beauty, ﴿is Rich﴾, who is above anyone who sends forward good, desiring what is with Him, and who has no need that would prompt Him to take the inferior, nor did He encourage you to the principle of spending out of any need of His for something of what you have; rather, that is a kindness from Him toward you, so that He may bring about reward and punishment upon it. ﴿Praiseworthy﴾, who rewards the doer of good with the best reward, on the basis that He has never ceased to be praised and never ceases to be (so); He punishes or rewards. Al-Haralli said: It is an intensive form with the addition of a yā' from praise (ḥamd), which is the matter of Allah that admits no variation in terms of its manifestation, whether it agrees with the souls or opposes them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 268:

When Allah, glorified and exalted is He, had encouraged spending and concluded His verses with what implies the promise, from the most truthful of speakers, of wealth and reward in both abodes, He followed it with what the lying enemy has of the opposite of that. So He said, warning against stinginess, in answer to one who seems to have said: "This is beyond doubt, so why is it that souls are generally found only stingy with spending?":

﴿The Shaytan (Satan)﴾, that is, the one whose name is the worst of names, for it implies ruin and distance. Either of the two attributes is sufficient to keep one away from him, so how much more when they are combined! ﴿Promises you poverty﴾, which prevents spending. Al-Harrali said: "It is because of fear of him that the people of this world sever ties, turn away from one another, covet, and hoard. None of that removes poverty: every greedy person is poor even if he owns the world, and every contented person is rich. It is the right of one who is a slave to a rich master to be certain that he is rich, one who enriches his master. So in the fear of poverty lies the runaway of the slave from his Lord." End of quote. Poverty is the lack of what one needs at a time, in the outer and inner existence of a person.

﴿And commands you to indecency﴾, which nullifies it, such as reminding of favours and harm, and other pleasures of the self. It may involve the destruction of wealth and the loss of lives. Al-Harrali said: "Everything on which the rejections of reason, the Law and natural disposition agree is indecency, and the greatest intended meaning here is stinginess, which is the most grievous disease, owing to the mention of poverty. Upon it the worst of this world and the Hereafter is built; it is accompanied by greed, followed by envy, and all evil follows it in succession." End of quote, with some alteration.

When He mentioned what the enemy has of evil, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, followed it with what He has of good, saying, explicitly stating what was previously alluded to: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses the Most Beautiful Names and the Highest Attributes, ﴿the Merciful, the Loving﴾, ﴿promises you forgiveness from Him﴾ for the shortcomings that have occurred from you. This implies that no one can measure Allah with His true measure, because of the comprehensiveness of His attributes of perfection and because of the deficiency with which man has been created. ﴿And bounty﴾ through increase in both abodes; every blessing from Him is a bounty. Then He emphasised that with His saying: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One encompassing every perfection, ﴿is All-Encompassing﴾, because it includes the meaning of ﴿Forbearing﴾ and ﴿Self-Sufficient﴾. He followed it with ﴿All-Knowing﴾, indicating that He does not lose anything, however minute. Al-Harrali said: "In its implication is a weakening of the plot of Satan and a generous promise to the one deluded by fear of poverty and the doing of indecency, because He knows the weakness of souls and how quickly they accept whisperings." End of quote. Thus He concluded the last of the verses of parables with what He concluded its first with, as encouragement and warning.

When al-Kalām concerning spending and the wealth spent had concluded in this wise manner, both explicitly and allusively, and [Allah] concluded that with these two attributes, and included with the explicit statement that He is All-Knowing, that He is All-Wise, He followed that attribute with [the statement] that, out of His vastness, knowledge and wisdom, He bestows of His attributes what He wills upon whom He wills, by granting him *al-ḥikmah* (wisdom), so that He makes him comprehend the knowledge of what is hidden in these well-crafted parables and good sayings, explicitly and allusively, and enables him to act upon that, both in its composition and its correction. So the Exalted said, alerting to the preference of acting upon the command of the All-Merciful and accepting His promise, that it accords with reason and wisdom, and that the command and promise of Satan accord with desire and appetite:

Al-Ḥarrālī said: When Glorified and Exalted He manifested the matter of the Hereafter, made apparent what is in it, and clarified the matter of this world in terms of its order and causation, and the return of some of it upon others, a returning upon a beginning, He informed that this is from His wisdom, and that wisdom (*al-ḥikmah*) is ended in it, because of what it contains of the fulfilment of the wisdom of the two abodes. The wise person is not the one who knows the matter of this world, but the one who knows (p-94) the matter of what lies between this world and the Hereafter, so he treats the ailments of this world with the remedy of the Hereafter, and treats the soul with the remedy of the two abodes, and gathers its comprehensive principles into the facilitation of speech, just as He gathered them for the one He chose: ﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾ [al-Isrā' 17:39]. So He, Glorified and Exalted, said: ﴿He gives wisdom﴾. End of quotation.

In its arrangement, after ﴿Wise, Mighty﴾ [being] ﴿All-Knowing, Vast﴾, and ﴿Praiseworthy, Self-Sufficient﴾ after ﴿Mighty, Wise﴾, there is a warning against exposing oneself to spending that He rejects because of His might, self-sufficiency and vastness, and for which He censures, since He knows its baseness or corruption in intention, even if it is hidden. For that is outside the path of wisdom on our part, and the requirement of wisdom from Him, Glorified and Exalted, as occurred with Qābīl when he offered something inferior, as is well known in his story. Perhaps He alluded to this by the mention of *al-tadhakkur* (reflection) at the close of this verse, and then by His saying: ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:270]. It becomes as if He, Glorified and Exalted, said: Know that Allah is Mighty, Wise, who gives wisdom [and it is knowledge] of things as they are, adorned by action, and action perfected by knowledge, ﴿to whom He wills﴾ of His servants. Then He praised the one adorned with it, saying, indicating by the passive construction of the verb that it is sought for its own sake: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom﴾, i.e., that which is an attribute of His, and by the definite article He indicated its perfection (p-95) according to what the powers of the servants can bear. Wisdom is a power combining two things: correct knowledge and the performance of justice, which is acting in accordance with knowledge. Al-Aṣbahānī said: The Qur'an is full of verses indicating that the perfection of the human being is nothing but these two powers. ﴿Then he has indeed been given much good﴾. Al-Ḥarrālī said, in substance: it is indefinite because of what wisdom contains of causation, which involves hardship even if made easy; so the much good is definite in the word because of the ease, the protection, and the sustaining that it contains, which cannot be attained by a cause, but is only His bounty, which He gives to whom He wills, so that Glorified and Exalted He becomes his hearing and his sight. To its end.

Since the intended meaning is: that one who has been given wisdom becomes one of understanding, and thus is fit to be reminded by what Allah, Glorified and Exalted, casts of His word, what He has spread in the souls and horizons of His wisdom, He connected to it His saying: ﴿And none will be reminded﴾, i.e., by the speech of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, of His wisdoms, ﴿except the people of understanding﴾ (p-96), i.e., the possessors of pure intellects, free from the impulses of desire arising from the illusions produced by whispering. They ascend through reflection, knowing that they have no power over the causes, to their means, until they reach their Causer, and so know Him with the true knowledge of Him. Al-Ḥarrālī said: Those who possess the kernel of intellect, which attains the kernel of sense, [know that] the world is like a husk, attained by the outer intellect, while the Hereafter is a kernel, attained by the kernel of intellect, outwardly to outwardly and inwardly to inwardly. Whoever reflects from the initial beginnings that preceded and to which Allah's bounty came to him, whoever returns from his sense to his self, there grow in him the attributes of the soul's virtues, and he rises above what is in his sensed realm of the abysses of appetite. Whoever is freed from his self to his spirit senses the connection of the All-Merciful and the divine love. Likewise, whoever ascends from his spirit to his command is realized by the unitary encompassing, and whoever penetrates from his command to his secret is gathered into the singular primacy. This order is among the perfections of this bestowed wisdom, revealed by inspiration in this Book, which gathers the news of what came before, the account of what follows, and the inner dimension of what is manifest. Glorified and Exalted has directed, in mentioning it, the works of creation, especially in the generosity of bringing into existence (p-97), just as He directed the establishment of the edifice of religion through the manifestation of its existence. So He directed the descent of His command through the manifestation of its existence, and directed the vicegerency of His servants through reaching the flow of His generosity. Thus the highest of wisdom is generosity [in bringing into existence]. By this, and Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows best, the mention of the verse of wisdom became connected in arrangement with the spending, and in parallel with the Verse of the Throne. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 270:

Since the context, both before and after, concerns spending (infaq), it is understood that the implied sense is: whatever you gather of anything, God will hold you to account for its placement and its gathering, in accordance with wisdom, and will call you to account for that. He then joins to it an exhortation to give charity secretly, and to fulfil vows, and a warning against spending in disobedience, even in the most subtle of ways, by informing them that He knows all of that and will repay for it. [He says]: ﴿And whatever expenditure you spend﴾, meaning in any of the ways, so there enters into it all the permissible expenditures made at marriages, circumcisions, births, the acquisition of a dwelling, and in the invitations of brothers, and other than that.

Since a person often fears the loss of something, so he vows that if it is attained he will spend in a good cause and the like; but perhaps he thinks that the encouragement to spending applies only to what God has recommended from the outset, not to what a person has obligated himself to. (p-98) [He says]: ﴿or whatever vow you vow﴾, and the insertion of "min" (from) is for emphasizing comprehensiveness. Al-Harrali (al-Ḥarrālī) said: the vow (nadhr) is the firm binding of a promise to a good act that is to be done in the future, or for which one awaits something, and to which one commits oneself; and it is the lowest level of expenditure, especially if it is made as a condition. He, ﷺ, said: "It is only extracted by it from the miser." End of quote.

﴿Indeed, God﴾ magnifies the matter by this greatest name, ﴿knows it﴾. He mentioned the pronoun because, although its reference to what came before is clear, it is more emphatic in magnifying the vow, given that there may be suspicion of falling short of what the Sharia recommends. So be scrupulous in the goodness of that, in fulfilling it, and in all that falls under it of commands and prohibitions, like one who seeks to please a great king with what he gives to him and presents to him. Therefore whatever you dispose of with wisdom, whether by expenditure or otherwise, God, glorified and exalted, will repay you for it according to the measure of the multiplication He has mentioned to you. And whoever among you does something [of it] not in accordance with wisdom is a wrongdoer, placing a thing in other than its place, so it is returned to him and he is punished for it, and ﴿for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾, meaning those who place a thing in other than its place (p-99). Al-Harrali said: in its implication is that God takes by the hand the generous and the noble whenever they stumble, so they find a helper for them, and the wrongdoer who places oppression where righteousness belongs finds no helper; and in it is a comprehensive negation expressed by the word "min" (from). End of quote.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 271:

Since the state of spending, which is urged upon them, differs according to whether it is done secretly or openly, and since this is among the matters they would be asked about, the Exalted and Glorified One said, urging charity in both states while giving preference to secrecy because of what it contains of distance from showing off: ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾, i.e., the voluntary ones. Al-Harrali said: "They are among the lowest of spending, and for this reason they are not permitted to Muhammad or to the family of Muhammad, because they are a purification and a washing which the people of exalted rank and chosen status shun." He also said: "The gift (hadiyyah) is the most noble kind of wealth-right, because it is for one who is above the rank of the giver, and the gift (hibah) is for one who is equal." ﴿Then how excellent it is﴾. So He gathered for it the unspecified praises, because ni'ma is an intensive word that comprises all praise, and má is an unspecified word that comprises the one praised, so the two agree in being unspecified. Abu Talib al-'Abdi said in his commentary on al-Idah: "Ni'ma and bi'sa are for intensification, so what is meant by them is the utmost in praise and blame. Because they are restricted to this meaning, they are denied inflection, and they are limited to the meaning, because praise and blame apply only to what has been established and settled; a person is not praised for what has not occurred from him." (p. 100) End.

﴿And if you conceal them﴾, so that no one knows of them except the one for whom you did them. Since the purpose of them is to fill the need, He said: ﴿and give them to the poor, that is better for you﴾, i.e., that concealment and directing it to the needy ﴿is better for you﴾, because it is further from showing off and nearer to sincerity, which is the spirit of acts of worship. In defining them and putting them in the plural there is what may perhaps indicate the generality of obligatory and voluntary charity, because of the exposure of hidden wealth to the risk of injustice and envy; and in the implication of the context, charity is permissible even to the wealthy. Since the implied sense is: "Indeed, We raise your ranks by means of them," He followed it with His saying: ﴿and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾, i.e., those between Us and you.

Since the implied sense is: "So do not fear that anything of them will be lost to you by concealing them, for Allah is All-Knowing of everything you have done of them," He followed it with a general statement, encouraging and warning: ﴿And Allah﴾, i.e., the One who possesses every perfection, ﴿is Aware of what you do﴾, i.e., of that and of other things, ﴿All-Aware﴾. He leaves no need at all for public display. So upon you is concealment, for it is nearer to the welfare of both religion and worldly life; so be sincere in it and let your eyes be comforted by the reward for it.

[p. 101] When He, glory be to Him and exalted, urged the ways of goodness and encouraged adherence to guidance, and most of them turned away, because what He called them to tears down what they were created to love, namely the love of amassing wealth and the zeal for self-preservation, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was intensely grieved over them and constantly anxious on their account, out of his great mercy and compassion towards them, he found their reluctance to what He called them to, that exalted state which is the wisdom of God, whose foundation is faith in God and the exchange of this world's entirety for the Hereafter, a source of intense sorrow. So God, glory be to Him and exalted, lightened the matter for him and eased his condition, and said: ﴿It is not upon you﴾, that is, in your power, ﴿their guidance﴾, so that you would be able to bring it about. Your duty is only to convey the message. As for creating guidance in them, it is not upon you, and you have no power over it. ﴿But God﴾, who has no equal, ﴿[alone] has power over that﴾, and so ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾. From this it becomes clear that ʿalā must necessarily be understood here in the sense of ʿindaka ("with you"), ma‘aka ("in your company") and similar, because lākinna is used for istidrak (corrective contrast), which is that the ruling after it is contrary to what came before it, and the statements of the lexicographers support this. The Imam ʿAbd al-Haqq said in his book al-Wā‘ī: In the hadith of ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, may God be pleased with them both: "I used to sacrifice with a trunk, and we had a thousand sheep," meaning: "and with us a thousand sheep." The Arabs say: "ʿalaynā kadhā wa kadhā," meaning "we bestowed such and such." Qāsim explained it so. End of quotation. It returns to the sense of capacity, as one says: "ʿalayya riḍā fulān," meaning "I am able to do that, I am capable of bearing it." So the meaning is: [p. 102] you are not able to bring about guidance in them at all; that rests with God, glory be to Him and exalted, and He guides whom He wills, so He does what He decrees for him of the ways of guidance, such as spending and other things. Al-Harrālī said, in substance: The Anṣār, may God be pleased with them, were the first intended by this sentence, because God, glory be to Him and exalted, placed among them the support of His religion.

Since the greatest aim in this wisdom and this guidance is only guidance towards reaching the Generous One through generosity with self and wealth, which bestows generally upon the near and the distant, the believer and the disbeliever, like the bountiful rain that reaches the plain and the mountain, this address came to turn away a people who had scrupled at giving charity to the poor among the disbelievers and at maintaining their kinship ties with them, so they were directed towards general spending. End of quotation. Then God, glory be to Him and exalted, said: ﴿And whatever good you spend﴾, that is, wealth and kindness, upon a believer or a disbeliever with whom it is permissible to do this, even if it is little. "Let no female neighbour belittle a gift to another female neighbour, even if it is a sheep's trotter." ﴿it is for yourselves﴾, as when it was said to him (ﷺ) about a sheep that had been slaughtered: "It has all gone, in the form of gifts and charity, except its neck!" He said: "All of it remains except its neck!" So this implies that if you are stingy or you bestow favours, you are only doing that [p. 103] to yourselves.

Since the discourse concerned spending among the believers [who spend] and in the way of God, and expressed it as "good", and all of this points to the sincerity appropriate to the state of the believer, He said: ﴿And not﴾, that is, while the situation is that you ﴿spend except seeking﴾, that is, desiring.

Since remembering the Face, because of its nobility, is more conducive to striving to ennoble the deed through its excellence and sincerity, He said: ﴿the Face of God﴾, that is, the Supreme King, by filling the need of a poor person, or maintaining the ties of kinship with a Muslim or a disbeliever to whom charity may be given, not for your own sake nor for anyone else's, but to rid yourselves of withholding wealth by discharging the trust in it to God's servants, because they are His servants. This is what faith calls for, so it should not be thought that a believer would do otherwise. That demands great distance from harm, ostentation, and every defect, and the presence of everything that makes acceptance due, of sensory and spiritual perfection.

Since certainty in fulfilment encourages excellence and keeps one far from harm and reproach, out of fear of the reward of the Sovereign, the Judge, He said: ﴿And whatever good you spend﴾, [that is], in whatever manner and whatever description the almsgiving and the recipient of it may be, ﴿it will be repaid﴾, that is, it will be fully paid back with multiplication, [p. 104] ﴿to you, and you will not be wronged﴾, that is, no injustice will befall you by withholding anything of what you have spent, nor by any diminution of what you were promised of multiplication if you do good, nor of recompense in kind if you do evil.

For the poor who are confined in the way of God, who cannot travel about the land (for trade), the one who knows nothing of them thinks them wealthy because of their restraint. You will recognize them by their marks; they do not beg of people with importunity. Whatever good you spend, indeed God knows it.

Wait, that is not a faithful translation. Here is the full translation of the passage:

When the greater part of these rulings mentioned concerning spending for the sake of the needy was given, and what had preceded was inclusive of the believer and others, he made clear that the focus of exhortation to them is the believer. The Exalted and Glorified said: ﴿For the poor﴾, i.e., these rulings are for them, ﴿who have been confined﴾, i.e., prevented from earning a living. By his words ﴿in the way of God﴾, i.e., the One to whom belongs majesty and honor, he indicated that what keeps them from that occupation is their engagement in establishing the religion through jihad and other means, ﴿they cannot go about in the land﴾ for trade for that reason. He indicated the intensity of their contentment with God, the Exalted and Glorified, by their not complaining, so he said: ﴿The ignorant one thinks them rich﴾, i.e., the one who lacks the discernment of the sincere ones, ﴿because of [their] restraint﴾ from asking and hinting at it, out of contentment with what God, the Exalted and Glorified, their Master, has given them, and satisfaction with Him, and nobility of soul. Restraint (al-ta'affuf) is the effort to be chaste, and chastity (al-'iffah) is restraining what the human appetite extends toward for desire except for its right and proper manner, as al-Harali said.

When he mentioned their concealment from the ignorant, he mentioned their manifestness to the discerning, so he said: ﴿You recognize them﴾, i.e., O you most insightful of the certain and most perceptive of them, you and whoever's foot is firmly planted in following you, ﴿by their mark﴾. Al-Harali said: it is an intensive form from al-simah and al-wasm, which is the hidden sign that appears to the one who discerns. End quote. And that sign, and God, the Exalted and Glorified, knows best, is tranquility, dignity, a low voice, humble condition together with high aspiration, and freedom from arrogance, haughtiness, insolence, pride and the like. ﴿They do not ask﴾, because the eyes of their insights are aspiring from the creation to the Creator, ﴿people﴾, whether a king or anyone else, ﴿with importunity﴾, i.e., asking with compulsion, taken from the blanket (al-lihaf) with which one covers oneself, because of its clinging to what it covers, and from it "laḥafahu," meaning he clung to him. Al-Harali said: it is persistence and continuity in a matter, from the letters of al-hilf, which is ending a report at its limit; likewise al-laḥf is ending the request at its limit. End quote. Their asking, if they ask, is only in the manner of presentation (al-'ard) and subtle hinting, as Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, would ask another to recite the verse so that he might host him, though he knew it better than the one he asked, and none understood his intention except the Prophet ﷺ. So the expression "restraint" indicates diligence in chastity and exaggeration in it, and the restriction "with importunity" indicates that asking occurs very rarely or in the manner of hinting, not explicit declaration, as the recognition by their mark supports and confirms.

When the Exalted and Glorified mentioned the most hidden places of spending, He indicated its concealment, especially in that place, so He said: ﴿And whatever good you spend﴾, i.e., at whatever time you spend it, ﴿indeed God﴾, i.e., the One combining all attributes of perfection, ﴿knows it﴾, even if you strive to conceal it by giving it to one who does not ask, such as by not being recognized or otherwise. Mentioning knowledge in the place of recompense is the greatest motivation and the most fearful warning, as this is realized by deep reflection on it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 274:

When he (Allah) urged spending in abundance, struck examples for it, extended his discourse, and did not specify a time for it, it was as if a questioner had asked: "At what time is it to be done?" So in one comprehensive verse, encompassing the types of wealth, times, and circumstances, He made clear that it is good at every time and in every state. He said: ﴿Those who spend their wealth﴾ (p-107), that is, in the righteous causes already alerted to. He mentioned first, among the contrasting pairs, what was closer to sincerity, giving it attention and showing its excellence. He said: ﴿by night﴾, if that circumstance calls for it, ﴿and by day﴾, if the course of right guidance prompts them to it, ﴿secretly and openly﴾, likewise.

When refraining from reproach (al-mann) and injury (al-adha) is, in some circumstances, the hardest thing for the soul, because of what it sees from the recipient of spending in terms of lowering of the gaze and the like, it is hardly possible for anyone [to be spared] from it.

He began the reward in the verse without linking it with the particle fa' (then), as an indication of pardon for what overcomes the soul from it, treating it as if it were non-existent, and as a hint at magnifying it by making it the beginning of a gift from the King, encouraging refraining from it, since it is looked upon in general. He linked the reward in this case, to inform that it is caused by these circumstances, because actions are easier than abstentions, so attaining it depends on their attainment, urging the performance of them all for the ease in that. For one who permits spending for Allah, glorified and exalted is He, the times are equal to him in it. So He said: ﴿then for them is their reward﴾. Its being causative (sababiyyah) (p-108) consists in it being a sign of the attainment of the reward, not that it is a true cause. The true cause is the mercy of Allah through granting success for the deed and taking account of it. He informed that it is protected, multiplied, and increased, never lost at all, by His saying: ﴿with their Lord﴾, [meaning] He increases their expenditures and purifies them as He nurtured them. Then He concluded the verses on expenditure with what He began them with of security and joy. He said: ﴿no fear shall be upon them﴾, as they rejoiced in it over others, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾, because there is no reward greater than that, for there is no life for one who grieves or fears. And because of the severity of the hardships of spending on oneself, especially at the beginning of Islam, given the hardship they were in, He, exalted is He, emphasized this emphasis in it with its whole, and explained it with this clear explanation, until no aspect of it remained hidden without His making it manifest, warning against it, and establishing it. Ustadh Abu al-Hasan al-Harralli indicated this, saying: "The most excellent of them is the one who spends by night secretly, and the lowest of them is the one who spends by day openly; thus they are four categories." End.

[p. 109] Since Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, has mentioned spending from what He has bestowed upon them as provision in more than one verse from the beginning of the surah until here, encouraging it with various kinds of exhortation and in many modes of expression, and since provision includes both the lawful and the unlawful, and since among the means by which they sought provision before Islam was [[p. 109]] *riba* (usury), which is taking without compensation. In form it is an increase, but in reality it is a loss and a defect, the opposite of what was previously urged, namely giving without compensation, which outwardly is a loss but inwardly an increase and goodness. He forbade them from engaging in it and made them averse to it, and He explained its ruling, that it is *khabith* (foul) and not fit for eating or for charity. He put this in the form of an answer to someone who asked: Can the beloved spending that is urged be from every kind of wealth? So He answered with His saying:

Al-Harrali said: Since the state of the one who spends, especially one who seeks the face of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is the best of states, and it is the state to which they were called, He set alongside it the lowest of states, which is the one by which wealth is sought through *riba*. So the best of people is the one who spends, and the worst of people is the one who practices *riba*. Thus He set against it the address concerning *riba*, and said:

﴿Those who﴾. And since some of the Companions had consumed *riba*, He expressed it in the present tense, indicating [that] this punishment is specific to the one who persists, and said: ﴿consume riba﴾, which is the increase, of the same kind as that on which the increase is made, being defined in some respect. End of quotation. So he followed the customary way of this wise remembrance, mentioning one of two opposites after the other, and he expressed "consuming" in place of "taking," because it is the greatest of aims and the most harmful, and it runs through a person as blood does, like Satan. [p. 110] ﴿do not stand﴾, that is, at the Resurrection, their weight appears in their bellies, so it prevents them from alertness, and this will be their mark by which they are known among the people of the place of standing, as a disgrace and a scandal to them.

Al-Harrali said: In its absoluteness there is an indication of their state in this world, in the intermediate state, and in the Hereafter. In its announcement there is a notice that the one who consumes it is stripped of his reason, and his remaining in this world is with foolishness rather than intellect; he turns toward what calls for turning away, and turns away from what calls for turning toward. End of quotation. This is confirmed by observation, for we have never seen or heard of a consumer of *riba* who speaks with wisdom or is renowned for virtue; rather they are the lowest and most defiled of people.

﴿except as one stands﴾, the one struck down, ﴿whom the Satan has driven to madness﴾, that is, who strains to be driven mad, and [Satan] imposes it upon him and makes it hard for him, ﴿the Satan﴾. And since this might be thought to mean that he confuses the mind through whispering, for example, He said: ﴿from﴾, that is, a derangement beginning from ﴿the touch﴾, that is, madness. Thus Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, indicated by this the prohibition of spending from unlawful wealth, especially *riba*, and that the foul thing from which the choosing of spending is forbidden is of two kinds: the sensory and the immaterial, [p. 111] and the prohibition regarding the immaterial is stricter.

Al-Baydawi, following al-Zamakhshari, said: It [i.e., the derangement and the touch] is in accordance with what they (i.e., the Arabs) claim, that Satan strikes a person so that he is thrown down, and that a jinn touches him so that his intellect is confused. End of quotation. Its apparent meaning is a denial of this, and it is not to be denied; rather it is the truth about which there is no doubt. Al-Mahdawi said in his tafsir: This is evidence against whoever denies that the seizure is from the jinn and claims that it is an act of the natural temperaments.

Shaykh Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani said in his commentary on *al-Maqasid*: In sum, the affirmation of the existence of angels, jinn, and devils is among the matters on which there is consensus of opinions and which the speech of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, and the speech of the prophets, peace be upon them, have spoken of. The seeing of jinn has been reported by many of the intelligent and by people of unveilings among the saints, so there is no basis for negating it. He also said: The jinn are subtle airy bodies that take on different forms, and strange conditions appear from them; and the devils are fiery bodies whose nature is to cast people into corruption and error. Because air and fire are in extreme subtlety and transparency, the angels, jinn, and devils enter narrow openings, even into the bodies of [p. 112] people, and are not seen by sight except when they acquire something from the mixed substances. End of quotation.

It has been reported in many hadiths from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "Satan runs through the son of Adam as blood does." And it is reported that "the Prophet (ﷺ) expelled the jinn who was seizing the afflicted person from his belly in the form of a dog," and similar things. In the earlier books of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, there is an uncountable amount of such things. As for the observation of the afflicted one who gives information about unseen matters while he is afflicted and his sense is absent, and sometimes he is thrown into fire and is not burned, and sometimes he rises into the air without anyone lifting him, there are very many who witnessed this, not to be counted—along with other matters that make it certain that this is from the jinn or the devils. And here I shall mention to you from the hadiths of the Prophet (ﷺ), [then] from the earlier books of Allah, what is sufficient for whoever reflects on it, and Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is the Granter of success.

Al-Darimi narrated at the beginning of his *Musnad* (a collection arranged by narrators) with a good sanad (chain of narration) from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "A woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) [p. 113] with a son of hers and said: O Messenger of Allah! My son has madness, and it seizes him at our lunch and dinner times, and it grieves us." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wiped his chest and supplicated, [then he vomited a vomit], and there came out of his chest something like a black puppy. [Thaʻa thaʻah: with a triliteral and an unpointed letter, meaning he vomited.]"

Al-Darimi also, and 'Abd ibn Humayd, with a sound and good sanad, from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey, and we rode with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was among us as if birds were over our heads shading us. Then a woman met him with a child of hers and said: O Messenger of Allah! Satan seizes this son of mine every day three times. So he took the boy and placed him between himself and the front of the saddle, then said: Begone, enemy of Allah, I am the Messenger of Allah, three times! Then he gave him back to her."

Al-Tabarani narrated it through another route and clarified that the journey was the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa', and that this was at the lava field of Waqim. Jabir said: [p. 114] "When we finished our journey and passed by that place, the woman met us with her child, and with her two rams she was driving. She said: O Messenger of Allah! Accept my gift from me. By the One who sent you with the truth, he has not returned to what he was after that! So he said: Take one of them from her and return the other to her."

Al-Baghawi narrated it in *Sharh al-Sunnah* (Explanation of the Sunnah) from Ya'la ibn Murrah, may Allah be pleased with him.

In the Gospel there is much of this, very much. In the Gospel of Matthew, Luke, and Mark, one of them exceeds the other, and I have combined their wording: "And he (i.e., Jesus, peace be upon him) came across the sea to the country of the Gergesenes." And in the Gospel of Luke it says: [which is] opposite the Galilee. When he came out of the boat, there met him [a madman; Luke said: from the city, with him were devils; and Matthew said:] two madmen coming from the tombs, very fierce, so that no one could pass by that way. They cried out, saying: What have we to do with you, O Jesus! Have you come to torment us before the time? Luke said: [p. 115] He was bound with chains and fetters and held, and he would break the bonds, and Satan would drive him into the wilderness. Jesus asked him: What is your name? He said: Legion, because many devils had entered him. Mark said: He said to him: Come out, unclean spirit, come out of the man. Then he asked him: What is your name? He said: My name is Legion, for we are many, and he begged him to send them out of the country. Now there was a herd of many swine feeding on the mountain at a distance from them, and the devils begged him, [saying]: If you are casting us out, send us into the herd of swine. [He said to them: Go. Mark said: Jesus permitted them, and immediately the unclean spirits came out and entered the swine.] And Matthew said: When they came out and went into the swine, behold, the herd of swine rushed down a steep bank and plunged into the sea, and all of them died in the waters. [p. 116] And the herdsmen fled and went to the city and told them everything and about the two madmen, so everyone in the city came out to meet Jesus. Mark said: They saw the madman sitting, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. When they saw him—meaning Jesus, peace be upon him—they begged him to leave their borders. Luke said: For they were greatly afraid. Mark said: When he got into the boat, the madman begged him to be with him, but Jesus did not allow him, but [said to him]: Go to your home and tell them what the Lord has done for you and His mercy to you. So he went and proclaimed in the ten cities and told everything Jesus had done to him, and all of them marveled. [In Luke's Gospel it has the same meaning, and at its end: So he went and was proclaiming throughout the whole city everything Jesus had done for him. And in Matthew's Gospel: When Jesus went out from there, they brought to him a mute who was possessed by a devil. When the devil was cast out, the mute spoke, and] everyone marveled, saying: Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel. But the Pharisees said: He casts out devils by the prince of the devils. [p. 117]

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 275 (part 2 of 3):

Then he said: "At that time there was brought to him a blind man who had a mute demon, and he healed him, so that the mute man spoke and saw. The whole crowd [all of them] were astonished and said: 'Perhaps this is the son of Dawud (David).' But the Pharisees (al-Farisiyyun) overheard and said: 'This man casts out demons only by Ba'il Zabul (Beelzebul), the chief of the demons.'" And in it, after that: "When he came to the crowd, a man came to him, prostrating himself before him and saying: 'O Lord!' And in the Gospel of Luke: 'O Teacher! Have mercy on my son, for he is tormented at the new moons, and many times he wants to throw himself into the fire, and many times into the water.'" And in the Gospel of Mark: "I have brought you my son! He has an unclean spirit, and wherever it seizes him, it throws him down, foams him at the mouth, and damages his teeth, and he becomes rigid." And in the Gospel of Luke: "I beg you to look upon my son, for he is my only child. A spirit takes hold of him, and he suddenly cries out, and it throws him into convulsions with foaming, and it gets worse when it leaves him, and it crushes him. I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not." And in the Gospel of [Matthew]: "I brought him to your disciples, but they could not heal him." Yasu' answered: "O faithless and crooked generation! How long shall I be with you! And how long shall I bear with you! Bring him here." And in the Gospel of Luke: "While he was coming, the devil threw him down and convulsed him." And in the Gospel of Mark: "When the unclean spirit saw him, at once it threw him into convulsions, and he fell to the ground, writhing and foaming. Then he said to his father: 'How long has this been happening to him?' He said: 'Since his childhood.' Then he said, in meaning: 'Do what you can for him and have compassion on us.' Yasu' said to him: 'All things are possible for the one who believes.' The boy's father cried out and said: 'I believe; help my weakness of faith!' When Yasu' saw the crowd gathering, he rebuked the unclean spirit and said: 'O deaf and mute spirit! I command you to come out of him and never enter him again.' It cried out, convulsed him greatly, and came out of him, and he became like a dead man. Many said: 'He has died.' But Yasu' took him by the hand and raised him, and he stood up." And in the Gospel of Matthew: "Yasu' rebuked him, and the devil came out of him, and the boy was healed at that hour. Then the disciples came to Yasu' privately and said [to him]: 'Why could we not cast it out?' He said to them: 'Because of your little faith. Truly I say to you, if you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain: Move from here to there, and it would move, and nothing would be impossible for you. But this kind does not come out except by fasting and prayer.'" Mark also said: "It cannot be driven out by anything except prayer and fasting." And he said in the Gospel of Mark: "He was teaching in Capernaum, a town in Galilee. And in their assembly there was a man who had an unclean demon, and he cried out in a loud voice saying: 'What have we to do with you, Yasu' of Nazareth! You have come to destroy us! We know who you are, O Holy One of God!' Yasu' rebuked him, saying: 'Be silent and come out of him!' The unclean spirit convulsed him, cried out in a loud voice, and came out of him." And in the Gospel of Luke: "The devil threw him down in their midst and came out of him without hurting him. The crowd was afraid and said to one another: 'What is this new teaching? With authority he commands the unclean spirits, and they obey him!' And his report spread throughout all the region of Galilee." And in it: "Then he rose from there and went to the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and he entered a house and wanted no one to know about him, but he could not remain hidden. A woman whose daughter had an unclean spirit heard about him, came to him, and fell prostrate at his feet. She was a Greek, a Syro-Phoenician, and she asked him to cast the demon out of her daughter. He said to her: 'Let the children be satisfied first. It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs.' She answered: 'Yes, Lord! Even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from the children's table.' So he said to her, because of this word: 'Go, the demon has gone out of your daughter.' She went to her daughter and found the girl lying on the bed, and the demon had gone out of her." And at the [end] of the Gospel of Mark: "He cast out of Mary Magdalene seven demons." And in the Gospel of Luke: "After that, he traveled through every city and village, preaching and proclaiming the Kingdom of God, and with him were the Twelve and some women whom he had healed of diseases and evil spirits: Mary who is called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, Martha the wife of Khuzi, the steward of Herod, Dassa, Susanna, and many other women." And in the Gospel of Luke: "While he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, and she was bent over and could not straighten up at all. When Yasu' saw her, he said: 'Woman, you are freed from your sickness.' [He laid his hand on her, and she immediately stood up straight and glorified God. The ruler of the synagogue, being indignant, answered] and said to the crowd: 'There are six days on which work should be done; come on those days and be healed, but not on the Sabbath!' He said: 'Hypocrites! Does not each of you untie his ox or his donkey from the stall on the Sabbath and lead it to water? And this daughter of Ibrahim (Abraham), whom Satan has bound for eighteen years, should she not be released from this bond on the day of the Sabbath?' When he said this, he put to shame all who opposed him, and all the people rejoiced at the glorious deeds done by him." End of quotation.

I have written this [quotation] although what has been transmitted from our Prophet (ﷺ) is sufficient, because it does not prevent it from containing consolation for him and a corroboration that increases faith; and in it there are also proofs that refute the Christians in their claim of the Trinity and incarnation (al-ittihad), and the best refutation of a person is with his own words and with what he believes. In Surah al-Ma'idah, at His words, glorified and exalted be He: "There is no god except Allah" (5:73), God willing, he will turn to some of this and explain it in a good and beneficial way. Likewise in all that I quote from the Gospel, as you will see, God willing, in its places. Whatever ambiguous material in it you are not familiar with, which suggests incarnation or trinity, do not let your aversion to it increase, and review what will be established in Al 'Imran and elsewhere; it will return you to the clear muhkam (decisive) texts with plain clarity. Moreover, most of it, when its details are considered, you will find to have no doubt at all in it, even if you are not qualified to run in the field of what is attributed to the Commander of the Faithful, 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "Be among those who know men by the truth, and do not be among those who know the truth by men." So look at the book "al-Radd al-Jamil li-Ilahiyyat 'Isa bi-Sarih al-Injil" (The Beautiful Refutation of the Divinity of Jesus by the Explicit Gospel) of the Proof of Islam, Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, and you will find that it interprets much of what I have mentioned, in the same manner as my interpretation or close to it. I did not see his book except after I had written this.

And Allah, glorified and exalted be He, is the Granter of success.

In the verse there is an indication that He, glorified and exalted be He, decreed the removal of the light of reason from the one who consumes riba, and He pointed to this by His words: "That" [i.e., the remote matter, far from correctness] "because they" [i.e., those who consume riba] "said" [in disputation with the people of Allah]: "Trade is only like riba" [i.e., the trade you restrict to lawful means, O people of Islam, is like riba], in that each of them is an exchange; so we engage in riba just as you engage in trade, so why do you deny it to us? Their making riba the basis is a departure from what Allah placed in the light of reason, the judgment of the Law, and the soundness of nature from wisdom. Trade, as the jurists define it, is the transfer of ownership for a price. Al-Harrali said: it is the desire of the owner for what is in his hand in exchange for what is in the hand of another, and buying is the desire of one who takes possession of what is in another's hand by an exchange with what is in his hand, which he desires less; therefore every buyer is a seller. "And Allah has made" [i.e., while Allah has made] "trade" [lawful], that is, because of what it contains of the justice of benefit, since it is an exchange in the manner of fairness by mutual consent from both sides, because the loss in it is not certain for either of them; for whoever buys what is worth one dirham for two dirhams may sell it afterward for its marketability or because there is a buyer for it who is attracted to it for a reason that makes him pay three. "And He forbade riba," because in it one of the two parties is singled out for harm and loss, and the other for certain gain; for whoever takes two dirhams for one has no hope of recovering what he lost in that way at all. Likewise is riba al-mudá'afah (doubling riba), which is when he demands his debt, and the debtor is insolvent, and he forces him to pay or to increase the debt; for there is nothing in return for this extra that the debtor benefits from. Al-Harrali said: thus preference occurs by compulsion, and that is the injustice to which justice is opposed, whose aim is grace. The most unjust of injustices in property is riba, and the most unjust of injustices in riba is like one who kills two people for one victim. Every one who cheats in a scale, his cheating is riba in some respect. Therefore the forms of riba have multiplied and increased. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Riba has seventy-some kinds, and shirk is like that; and this is its root" (ḍ, cf. the sense of the hadith). It was the practice of the people of the Jahiliyyah, in their saying: "Either you pay the increase or you settle the debt." Then the rest of its forms attached to it. It is a benefit to the one who takes riba and a harm to the one who gives riba, and this is the greatest injustice among servants, whose share is equality in a matter according to worldly language. So just as He, glorified and exalted be He, informed them of the effect of the wisdom of good [in spending], He informed them of the effect of the wisdom of evil [in riba, in the Hereafter and in the unseen of worldly affairs]. Just as He hastens a replacement in this world for the one who spends, so too He hastens the eradication (mahq) of the one who takes riba in this world, as the address expressed after this notice. End of quotation.

The root b-y-‘ (ب ي ع) and all its nine permutations (بيع، وعيب، ...), whether with a yā’ or a wāw and whether hamzated or not, revolve around the notion of expansion (ittisā‘). Al-bay‘ (sale) revolves around full disposal (al-taṣarruf al-tāmm), sometimes in potential (bil-quwwa) and sometimes in actuality (bil-fi‘l). What is in actuality may be through ownership (bil-milk) or otherwise. What is through ownership may be by acquisition (al-taḥṣīl) or by removal (al-izālah). It is evident that all of this is from expansion.

From what is in potential: "bā‘ahu min al-sulṭān" (he sold him to the ruler), meaning he informed on him to him. A woman is "bā’i‘" if she is in demand (nāfiqah) because of her beauty. Al-biyā‘ah is the merchandise (al-sil‘ah), and al-bayyi‘ (on the pattern of sayyid) is the one who bargains (al-musāwim). "Abā‘tuhu" means I put it up for sale (‘aradtuhu lil-bay‘).

From what is in actuality without ownership: "bā‘a ‘alā bay‘ihi," meaning he stood in his place in rank and eminence and gained it. Likewise "abā‘tu al-rajula faraskan," meaning I lent him a horse so that he might raid on it.

From what is through ownership by removal: "bi‘tuhu" and "abā‘tuhu," meaning I removed my ownership of it for a price. "Istabā‘ahu" means he asked him to sell it to him. "Inbā‘a" means it was exhausted (nafaqa). "Inbā‘a lī fī sil‘atihi" means he was lenient in selling it and extended to agreeing to it.

From what is through ownership by acquisition: "bā‘a al-shay’" in the sense of "ishtarāhu" (he bought it). Al-Farabi said in Diwan al-Adab: Abū Tharwān said: "Bi‘ lī tamran bi-dirham" (sell me dates for a dirham), meaning "ishtari" (buy). This word is among the contranyms (al-aḍdād). "Ibtā‘ahu" means "ishtarāhu."

Al-‘ayb (defect) in the sense of al-waṣmah (blemish): the widening of speech regarding a person's honor (ta­wassu‘ al-kalām fī al-‘irḍ), and its cause is a person's expansion in speech or action beyond the path of reason. Al-‘aybah is a container of leather in which goods are placed, and it also means the chest, the heart, and the place of secrets. Al-‘ā’ib from milk is that which is sour, i.e., one that has taken on a sour taste, either from "al-‘ayb" or because it has spread away from its original taste. Al-‘abā’ah is a type of cloak, because it is wide compared to the waist-wrap and the like in length and breadth; and a rough, heavy man is likened to it in coarseness and heaviness. Ta‘bi’at al-jaysh (arraying the army) is preparing it from its place, as if its divisions were containers (‘iyāb) for it, each unit placed in its container. ‘Aybuka min al-jazūr is your share of the slaughtered camel. Al-ta‘ābī is that a man inclines with one group and another with another group, because that is an expansion of both parties and a dispersal of both men.

From the hamzated (forms): al-‘ib’ (with kasra) is a heavy burden of any kind, because it is according to the capacity (wus‘) of the bearer or beyond it, and it is wider than what is less than it of loads. It also means equal weight (al-‘adl), because it contains what is placed in it, and a like (al-mithl). It may be vocalized with fatḥa (al-‘ab’), because two are wider than one. Al-‘ab’ with fatḥa is the light of the sun, and it is clearly in expansiveness. ‘Abba’a al-matā‘ wa-al-amr [like manaʿa] means he prepared; ‘abba’ahu ta‘bi’atan, because he gave it what contains it and placed it in places that contain it. He prepared the perfume: he made it and mixed it, so it expanded through the mixing and its fragrance spread through the making. Al-‘abā’ is a known cloak, and it contains what is wrapped in it, like the ‘abā’ah. Al-aḥmaq al-thaqīl al-wakhim (the foolish, heavy, sluggish one) has had its derivation already mentioned, and it is possible to make it from al-‘ib’ in the sense of burden and in the sense of heavy. [Al-mi‘ba’ah] like mikhnasah is the rag of a menstruating woman, because it is according to what the vagina can contain. Al-ma‘ba’ (on the pattern of maq‘ad) is the way (madhhab), because of its expansiveness for the one who goes in it. "Mā a‘ba’u bihi" means "mā aṣna‘u" (what I do). "Wa-bi-fulān: mā ubālī" means I do not give thought to it, i.e., I do not extend my thought to it. This concludes the hamzated forms.

Al-bā‘ is the measure of the extension of the two hands, and also nobility and generosity. Al-bawʿ is the distance of the stride of the horse in its running, and the spreading of the hand with wealth. Al-makān al-munhadim, i.e., the low-lying place in the crevice (liṣb) of a mountain; al-liṣb with kasra is a small ravine of a mountain, narrower than al-lihb and wider than al-shiqb. Al-lihb is the gap between every two mountains, or a crack in a mountain, or a small ravine. Al-shi‘b with ‘ayn is a path in a mountain, or a watercourse in the bottom of a land, or what opens between two mountains. Al-shiqb with qāf is a crack that occurs in the ridges of mountains and the valleys' slopes, short of a cave, where birds nest. Bā‘at al-dār is its courtyard. Al-bā’i‘ is the young of a gazelle when it walks with a swaying gait. Inbā‘a al-‘araq means the sweat flowed. The snake spread itself out after coiling, in order to strike. Al-wabbā‘ah is the anus, because of its expansiveness through what comes out of it. "Kadhabat wabbā‘atuhu" means it broke wind, i.e., it farted. Al-wabbā‘ah of a child is what moves from his fontanelle, because it extends to movement. Wa‘abahu, like wa‘adahu, means he took it all; like aw‘abahu and istawʿabahu. Aw‘aba means he gathered. Al-shay’ fī al-shay’ means he entered it entirely, i.e., he widened it until it entered into it. Al-wa‘b from roads is the wide one; and bayt wa‘īb means a wide house. Al-ba‘w is the crime and offense, because that widens speech regarding a person's honor. It is also a loan (al-‘ārīyah). Ba‘āhu qamaruhu means he [the moon/a person] was affected by it and took from it. Ba‘āhu bil-‘ayn means he struck him with the evil eye, as if he gave his eye a share in him.

Since waʿẓ (admonition), as al-Ḥarrālī said, is calling things to what is in them of lesson, for submission to the true God, by what frightens them and restrains them, in contrast to reminder (tadhkīr) by what gives them hope and expands them; and since what He, glory be to Him and exalted, reported about the state of the one nurtured (al-murbī) was the most complete restraint, because the greatest thing for a human after his spirit is his intellect, He based on that His saying: ﴿So whoever receives it﴾. Al-Ḥarrālī said: He released the word from the sign of the feminine, the lowly in rank, to elevate the status of this hidden admonition, great in its effect: ﴿an admonition﴾ [built on] the pattern of intensification and exaltation, for what the augmented form (al-maf‘alah), with its additional letters, indicates beyond the root of the word waʿẓ, with what the mīm indicates of completeness and the hā’ of endpoint. So laying down rulings is wisdom, and informing of their fruits in the Hereafter is an admonition that makes the soul yearn for its desire and its dread. End of quotation.

Since fear from the benefactor is more effective in restraint, because the soul accepts it more readily, He said: ﴿from his Lord﴾, i.e., the one who nurtures him and is good to him in all the good he has.

Al-Ḥarrālī said: in its indication [that] a fundamental of nurturing is protectiveness from this usury. End of quotation.

﴿So he desists﴾, i.e., from what was the cause of the admonition. Al-Ḥarrālī said: He used the particle fā’ of immediate consequence, and did not allow in it any respite or settlement upon it, because of what is in it of corruption of intellect, which [is the root of] the distinction of humanity, even if the wise men and physicians of this world do not perceive it. End of quotation.

Since the context, by what the causal clause ﴿That is because they said﴾ indicates, shows that the verse concerns the disbelievers and that "eating" means considering it lawful, He confirmed that with His saying: ﴿then his past is his﴾, i.e., of the vile things he committed after he had been upon them, and nothing of his offense follows him, because Islam erases what came before it, and the repentance of a believer does not erase wrongs (al-maẓālim). Al-Ḥarrālī said: al-salaf is the matter past in its totality, remaining with its successor. He said: In His informing is a notice of permitting what had become firmly in their hands of the usury of the Jāhiliyyah, by the blessing of their repentance from resuming dealing in it in Islam, since Islam erases what came before it; and within the implication of His informing is an allusion to rejecting it for one who takes for himself the better, and His saying strengthens its indication: ﴿and his affair is with God﴾. End of quotation, i.e., He deals with him by what is His due of majesty and honor, according to what He knows of his intention of sincerity or otherwise.

Since those who nurture themselves after these rebukes are far from the mercy of God, He, glory be to Him and exalted, expressed them with the particle of distance in His saying: ﴿And whoever returns﴾, i.e., to permitting usury after abstaining from it, rebelling against the wisdom of his Lord. ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those far from God, ﴿are the companions of the Fire﴾. And since the consequence of companionship is constancy, He said: ﴿they therein abide forever﴾.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 2, verse 276:**

Since what encourages usury is the immediate, visible profit it brings, and what discourages charity is that it appears as a concrete, sensible loss, he clarified that usury, even though it takes the form of an increase, is in fact a loss, and that charity, even though it takes the form of a decrease, is in fact an increase (p-134), because that is in the hand of God, glorified and exalted. He deprives whatever He wills of increase, however great it is, and makes grow whatever He wills, however small it is. He said, as a justification for the command to give charity and the prohibition of usury, and for the fact that its practitioner is among the people of the Fire: ﴿God deprives usury of blessing﴾, that is, by His majesty and power, ﴿usury﴾, through the means He opens up to it from the doors of expenditure. Al-Harrali said: "Mahq (deprivation) is removal entirely, with force and dominance. ﴿And He causes charities to grow﴾, that is, He increases charities by providing in place of them the like of that, and yields profit in their fluctuations." It is also permissible that this be a new, independent statement. This is because, once it was established that its practitioners are among the companions of the Fire, it was brought in the manner of an answer to someone who seemed to say: "And if you give charity from usurious wealth and spend it in the ways of goodness!" This informs that usury is incompatible with goodness, so it is among what becomes ﴿scattered dust﴾.

When their being placed among the companions of the Fire indicated that whoever does not desist from usury at all, or desists and returns to its practice, is entangled in the snare of associating partners and faces obstacles: two of them in violating the sanctity of God (concealing His signs by not desisting, and treating them lightly by returning to it), and a third in violating the sanctity of God's servants. Thus his sin is repeated and exaggerated, and it does not occur except in this way. God, glorified and exalted, expressed this with the form of intensification (p-135) in His words, coordinating it with what is implied as a justification for what came before: "So the one who gives charity is a believer and generous, while the one who practices usury is an ungrateful, sinful wrongdoer." ﴿And God﴾, who is characterized by all attributes of perfection, ﴿does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾, that is, in what is due by right, by denying what He has legislated of His signs, concealing them, and treating them lightly; or, [ungrateful] for His blessing, glorified and exalted, by exalting oneself over what He gave, by taking away what He gave His servants. ﴿Sinful﴾ in what is due in conduct, that is, one who is absorbed in engaging in what He forbade of their particular dealings in usury and other things. Therefore, He, glorified and exalted, does not treat them as one who loves, neither with blessing in their wealth nor with prosperity in their circumstances. This negation falls under the generality of negation (ʿumum al-salb, the scope of negation), and its method is that you consider the negation first and then attribute it to the whole. The meaning then is: love is negated from every ungrateful sinner. Likewise, everything that comes to you of its like: if you consider the attribution to the whole first and then negate, it is for the negation of generality; and if you consider the negation first and then attribute it to the whole, it is for the generality of negation. The same applies to all restrictions. A statement that includes a negation and a restriction may be for negating the restriction, and it may be for restricting the negation. For example, "I did not strike him as discipline" (that is, rather to humiliate him) is a negation of the justification, and so the action is negated; "I did not strike him out of honor for him" (that is, I left off striking him out of honor) is a justification for the negation, and so the action is negated; "He did not come to me riding" (that is, rather walking) is a negation of the manner; and "He did not perform the pilgrimage while able" (that is, he abandoned the pilgrimage despite having the ability) is a specification of the negation. Shaykh Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani, may God have mercy on him, extensively discussed this in his commentary on al-Maqasid, in the section on vision, in the context of the Mu'tazila's (the Muʿtazila, a rationalist school) use as evidence of the words of God, exalted: ﴿Eyes do not perceive Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103].

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 277:

When the Exalted (ta'ala) had explained what He withdrew from the disbelievers of His love, He followed it with what He established for the believing, affirming ones, of mercy, the One who beckons to them in what came before, by way of conjunction without an apparent conjoined element, as has been mentioned just now, in a manner that did not leave it free of mention of spending. So the Exalted said, indicating the counterpart of ﴿And whoever returns﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]: ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, that is, who affirmed the truth of all that the Messengers, may God's blessings and peace be upon them, brought from God, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, as a confirmation of their faith, ﴿the righteous deeds﴾, by way of obedience (ita'mar) and abstention (intiha'), especially abandoning usury (riba).

When prayer was the essence of religion in what lies between the Truth and creation, He singled it out for mention, saying: ﴿And they establish the prayer﴾ with all its limits, ﴿Indeed, the prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45].
