And since generosity (al-iltha') is the most sublime of what lies between the Truth and creation, and its essence is paying the obligatory portion of wealth willingly, He said: ﴿And they give the zakat﴾, let alone that they be stingy, let alone that they take usury. He indicated that their reward is according to their intentions, through their steadfastness in the trial of apostasy (al-riddah), by His saying: ﴿For them is their reward﴾; He informed of its preservation and its growth by His saying: ﴿with their Lord﴾; and He announced the complete benefit by His saying: ﴿and no fear shall be upon them﴾, that is, from any visitor who comes to them with what does not suit them, because they are under the protection of the Mighty, the All-Knowing; ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ over anything that escaped them, so they are in the utmost contentment with what they have. And because of the great benefit in this, He repeated it in these verses more than once, and drew attention to it again and again, one after another.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 278:

When the outcome of the preceding verse was reliance on what is with Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, of reward, and not grieving over what had passed of riba and other things, and not fearing something coming of poverty or other things, He abandoned everything that is attributed to riba. Between the People of Islam and the People of Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance), and between some of them and others, there were transactions of the Jahiliyyah involving riba that had not yet been completed. He clarified their matter, negating what might be imagined from His earlier saying ﴿So he will have what has passed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275] regarding the remnants of riba, and that the prohibition is specific to what was newly contracted from it. So He said, addressing those closest to whom He had mentioned among those who had adopted faith, and not turning to others, honouring them: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, meaning, who have affirmed the attestation with their tongues.

Since riba may be deferred, so that its holder has passed periods of time while he has resolved his soul to taking it, and refraining from it becomes equivalent to death for him, He, subhanahu wa ta'ala, emphasised in the strictness of these admonitions and said: ﴿Fear Allah﴾, meaning the One to whom belongs all greatness, confirming your affirmation. ﴿And leave﴾, meaning abandon, with whatever abandonment it may be, ﴿what remains of riba﴾, meaning that in which you were dealing, so do not consider it lawful and do not consume it.

When He hinted at the beginning of the verse that whoever persists is not truthful in the claim of faith, He declared that explicitly at its end, saying: ﴿If you are believers﴾, meaning, characterised by what you have mentioned with your tongues. Al-Harrali said: So He made clear that riba and faith do not coexist, and most of the afflictions of this Ummah, until there befell it what befell the Children of Israel of severe calamity and retribution by years of drought, come only from the work of those who practise riba. This verse is a great foundation in the rulings concerning disbelievers when they embrace Islam: what passed of it is not reversed, and what has not yet passed is not to be done. Al-Asbahani drew attention to this.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 279:

Since it is right that one who opposes the Lord (al-Sayyid) should be seized, he links to that His saying: ﴿But if you do not do it﴾, that is, abandon usury (riba). Al-Harrali said: In its implication is that a group of them will not abandon it after its prohibition, since they are not among those who were believers. End of quote.

﴿Then be informed of a war﴾, that is, a great one. Al-Harrali said: War is a forceful repelling that comes from expansion; the one repelling, when asked to leave something, does not allow it and defends it with the utmost strength. Then He magnified its matter by mentioning the Greatest Name, saying: ﴿from Allah﴾, the Mighty, the Majestic, ﴿and His Messenger﴾ (ﷺ), who is the greatest of creation by the honor of being attributed to Him. Al-Harrali said: He who prepared him for mercy, so the Prophet of mercy was at war with it, and its connection to the Merciful and the Intercessor was severed. End of quote.

﴿And if you repent﴾, that is, you do what Allah has commanded you, after the permission to fight or before it, by abandoning what remains of it, ﴿then for you is your principal (ru'us amwalikum)﴾, that is, as is the case in sale. Since that is the just (al-'adl) because it is the truth, He said: ﴿You will not wrong [others]﴾, that is, by taking anything of what remains of usury, ﴿nor will you be wronged﴾ by a decrease from the principal or by delay in payment, because that is the truth.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 280:

[When] people are divided into the affluent (*mūsir*) and the poor (*mu'sir*), that is, the wealthy and the destitute, it is as if it were said: "This is the ruling concerning the affluent," ﴿and if there is one of hardship﴾, that is, if there is found among the debtors one who is in hardship and cannot pay at this time, ﴿then let there be a respite﴾, that is, then it is incumbent upon you to grant him respite. Al-Ḥarrālī said: This is the postponement whose reward is expected, ﴿until a time of ease﴾, if you will not accept anything but taking your wealth. Nāfi' and Ḥamza read *maysara* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. Al-Ḥarrālī said: It indicates the dominance of ease, and it is the wider of the two respites. The rest read it with a *fatḥa*, indicating its being in the middle, so that ease is in two stages. Whoever waits until the wider of the two eases, his repentance is more excellent. End of quotation.

﴿And that you give charity﴾, that is, your charity to the one in hardship by forgoing it for him, ﴿that is better for you﴾, in this world by what Allah, glorified and exalted, blesses you with and compensates you, and in the Hereafter by what He bestows upon you of abundant reward.

Since everyone claims knowledge and is extremely disdainful of being associated with ignorance, He said: ﴿if you know﴾, that is, if you are among the people of knowledge, then you recognize the soundness of what I have called you to, which requires turning away from or turning toward something. When you have verified that, then act upon it, for it is ugly for one who knows the ugliness of a thing to persist in it. Otherwise, make clear that it is not good; otherwise you are among the people of crookedness through ignorance, fighting, striking and stabbing like ravenous beasts and howling wolves. Al-Ḥarrālī said: He, glorified and exalted, informed that whoever directs his being toward knowledge, so that he is among those whose knowledge endures, is alerted, because the goodness of abandoning [something] is better than the goodness of taking [it], so he does well by abandoning all of it. End of quotation.

Al-Bukhārī narrated in the Book of Tafsir (commentary) from ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "When the last verses were revealed" — and in another narration: "from the end of Surah al-Baqara, concerning usury" — "the Prophet ﷺ recited them" — and in another narration: "to the people in the mosque" — "then he forbade trade in wine." He also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The last verse revealed upon the Prophet ﷺ was the verse of usury." Abū ʿUbayd narrated from Ibn Shihāb, who said: "The last of the Qur'an to be revealed before the Throne was the verse of usury and the verse of debt." He also narrated, from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The last verse revealed of the Qur'an was ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 281]." He said: "They claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained nine nights after it, and it was begun on a Saturday, and he died on a Monday." End of quotation. There is no contradiction, for these are both from the verses of usury and debt. Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī narrated the hadith in his book *al-Bayān fī ʿAdd Āy al-Qur'ān* (The Clarification on the Count of the Verses of the Qur'an), and said in it: "The angel said: Place it at the end of two hundred and eighty [verses] of al-Baqara."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 281:

Since it is well known that no argument repels it, the implied sense is: "So comply with what you have been commanded and avoid what you have been forbidden." He then followed this with a warning of the Day of Presentation before Him and of being requited in His presence, and so said: "And al-Harrali said: When the address had finished with the matters of the religion, its outward and inward aspects, and the matters of the Hereafter in all their modes, and had shown its wisdom as linked to the affairs of this world, and had explained the matter of spending and usury, which is the ultimate concern of religion and of this world in their righteousness, and had brought all that to an exhortation with the promised recompense in this world and the Hereafter, it summed up the exhortation with the fear of the Day of Return to the comprehensiveness of His command, so that the conclusion would fall upon the most excellent and most comprehensive exhortation. Its ending would be a warning that stirs the souls, so that their resolves would gather around what is the foundation of their affairs: the acceptance of the righteousness of their religion, their worldly life, and their return, from the address of God, glorified and exalted be He, to them. So He concluded that with the full meaning of this verse, just as it is the verse with which the revelation was concluded. It was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ in his illness, and it is the last verse revealed to the Prophet ﷺ, in contrast to ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1], which is the first station of prophethood, and ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1], which is the first station of the mission. Thus the beginning of the matter was warning, and its end was admonition that moves the soul to fear and moves the heart to longing, in line with the meaning of what the address of God, glorified and exalted be He, concluded with in the verse ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Fatiha: 4]." End of quotation.

Then He, exalted be He, said: ﴿And fear a Day﴾, meaning one of utmost greatness, ﴿in which you will be returned﴾, physically in your very selves as you are in this world, and in meaning, with respect to all your affairs, a manifest return that nothing veils, and no doubt of any kind prevents. ﴿To God﴾, [who] is not confined in His greatness by any attribute, nor encompassed by any limit. So your condition after your transfer from this world will be like your condition before you emerged from the womb: you will have no control at all, and no one will control you except God. Your condition on that Day will be one of helplessness, because no one can repay what God, glorified and exalted be He, has bestowed upon him of blessings. Whoever is strictly reckoned is punished. So if you wish to be pardoned by Him on that occasion, then pardon your brothers today, and give charity while you are still able to give charity, and guard yourselves against the Fire on that Day, even with half a date. God, glorified and exalted be He, indicated the length of their standing at that station, in the position of awe, and the prolonged detention in the scene of majesty and greatness, by the particle of delay in His saying ﴿then﴾. Al-Harrali said: And it was said:

"O Messenger of God! Where will people be on the day ﴿when the earth will be changed to other than the earth, and the heavens﴾ [Ibrahim: 48]?" He said: "In darkness, short of the Bridge."

He ﷺ also said: "They will remain in darkness for a thousand years." And it has been related from Ali, may God be pleased with him, in detailing the stations of the Day of Recompense, that the creatures will be made to stand at their graves for a thousand years, then driven to the place of gathering for a thousand years, and they will be made to stand in darkness for a thousand years. Then will come the splitting of the seven heavens, the changing of the earth, and whatever God, glorified and exalted be He, wills of His command, awaiting its coming. In the lesson of his statement, and God, glorified and exalted be He, knows best, that this will be six thousand years, and just as it was built in six days, it will be demolished in six days, ﴿As We began the first creation, We shall return it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104], so that will be nine days. And its coming will be on the tenth day, which is the Day of 'Ashura', the day on which the arrival of His command was repeated in the day of this world. Then the Prophet ﷺ described the stations to their end. End of quotation.

Since placing a person under account for everything he did, secret and open, is extremely hateful to him, let alone being requited for everything, and not merely in relation to a specific station, He used the passive form in His saying ﴿is paid in full﴾, meaning is given in full measure, ﴿every soul for what it has earned﴾, of good and evil. Al-Harrali said: He came with the form fa'ala, which implies that deeds flow without strain or exertion. In this implication, every soul is paid in full for what it has earned of good, and for what it has brought about of evil. Whatever it has strained itself to do of evil, and whatever it has done with reluctance, perhaps God pardons it, since it is not paid in full for what it has earned and acquired, as He said in the verse that follows: ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has acquired﴾ [al-Baqara: 286]. So what it has acquired is against it, and perhaps He pardons it, because what it has earned of evil, which its outward and inward aspects encompass, is paid in full, until it is made easy for it. End of quotation.

Since it is the custom of people that when a small amount remains, it falls into the realm of leniency, and since the small amount varies with the principal (for example, a thousand may be tolerated with a hundred), He made clear that the matter with Him is otherwise, and so He said: ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ in anything at all, even if it is little. This is an indication of His justice among His servants.

Al-Harrali said: This verse is the seal of the revelation and the seal of the completeness of the meaning in this surah, which is the summit of the Qur'an and its tent-pole, and the seal of every exhortation and every conclusion. It is among the special qualities of the Muhammadan community, the all-encompassing and detailed one, from the Surah of al-Hamd, which points to the details of God's great command concerning His right, concerning His creation, and concerning what lies between Him and His creation. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glorified and exalted, forbade riba, and it was one of their forms of debt-dealing, while other kinds of debt were permitted, and it is a type of spending (infaq) that also involves demanding repayment of the principal, He followed that with the verse of debt. Also, when Allah, glorified and exalted, mentioned two things regarding wealth that diminish it outwardly but purify it inwardly, namely charity (sadaqah) and abandoning riba, and He permitted the principal sums, commanded granting respite to the one in hardship, and concluded with a warning, this might have led the debtor to hope for some relief from the debt, even by claiming hardship. The state of man, because of his deficiency, required guidance toward preserving lawful wealth and protecting it from corruption, and an alert to how to secure it (tawaththuq). So He said: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, as in the verse before it, ﴿when you contract a debt﴾. Tadayantum (contracting a debt) is a reciprocal form (tafa'ul) between two parties from ad-dayn (debt). In its apparent sense, ad-dayn is a transaction on the basis of deferral, just as ad-din (the religious obligation) between the servant and Allah, glorified and exalted, is a transaction on the basis of deferral. This is what al-Harrali said, meaning: you have brought that about between you. Ad-dayn is wealth set down as an obligation upon the person, whether it is deferred or not, and it is the opposite of the present and the specific (al-'ayn). He said ﴿with a debt﴾, although the verb already implies it, to exclude the sale of debt for debt, since that is a transaction of debt for two debts. Al-Harrali said: In His informing by the use of the particle idha (when), there is [an indication] that they must contract debts, because it is a time that is expected in most of its meaning. End. He guided to specifying it by a time, indicating that it may be immediate, and that the term (ajal), which is a defined period and whose origin is deferral, if it is unknown, would be invalid, by His saying: ﴿for a specified term﴾. Al-Harrali said: from tasmiyah, which is presenting a thing by its name to the hearing, in the sense of the pictured, which is presenting a thing by its form to the eye.

Since Allah, glorified and exalted, who is All-Knowing, All-Aware, had established His practice in His religion through writing, and commanded His angels, who are trustworthy and upright, to record the deeds of creation for purposes and benefits that are not hidden, and sent down His noble Book as a testimony for them and against them regarding what they will be recompensed for on the Day of Religion, of reward and punishment, decisively cutting off their proofs, He commanded that their conduct in debts be as His conduct in religion. So He guided them to recording what passes between them of transactions, lest that lead to disputes. Allah, glorified and exalted, said, as a command of guidance and not of obligation: ﴿So write it﴾. The mention of the term is an indication of the resurrection, in which the promise of fulfillment was made: ﴿Did you then think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115] ﴿Then He decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 2]. Since He commanded writing, and the intent was its achievement in general and not from any specific person, because most people do not do it well, He followed it with guidance to choosing the scribe, by His saying: ﴿And let a scribe write between you﴾, that is, the aforementioned debt, ﴿a scribe﴾, even if he is a child or a slave, writing accompanied by ﴿justice﴾, following the example of Allah, glorified and exalted, among His angels: ﴿Indeed, over you are guardians, noble and recording, who know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 10-12] ﴿in the hands of scribes, noble and dutiful﴾ [Abasa: 15-16].

Since He guided to choosing the scribe, He preceded that with a prohibition, to ward off corruption before the command, saying: ﴿And let not a scribe refuse to write﴾, that is, what he has been recommended to write of that, ﴿as Allah has taught him﴾, that is, for the sake of the One who is independent of Him and of His other creatures, ⟨thanks to Him⟩ for that blessing, and writing the like of the writing that Allah, glorified and exalted, taught, without diminishing anything from it. ﴿So let him write﴾. In this is an alert to the hardship involved in striving to give sincere counsel.

Since that is so, and since dictation is necessary in it, He explained who may validly dictate what is written, saying: ﴿And let the one who owes the debt dictate﴾, from al-imlal, which is casting what the hearts contain upon the tongue in speech and upon the book in writing. Al-Harrali said this. ﴿the one upon whom is the obligation﴾, so that the one hearing the dictation and whoever is present may bear witness to it.

Since souls are naturally inclined to love monopolizing things at others' expense, He warned them against what is not lawful of that, saying: ﴿And let him fear Allah﴾, and He used the greatest Name so that it would be more restraining to the one commanded. Then He said: ﴿his Lord﴾, as a reminder that He, out of His benevolence, commands only good, and as a hope for compensation in that when he discharges the trust in quantity and quality, including the term and other matters. He emphasized this by His saying: ﴿and let him not diminish﴾, from bakhs, which is the worst deficiency, that souls do not tolerate, because it is far from the place of leniency and reaches the level of injustice, ﴿from it anything﴾.

Since this dictator may be incoherent in speech, and dictation is not within the power of everyone, Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿But if the one upon whom is the obligation is weak-minded﴾, so his acknowledgment is not considered, due to the weakness of his judgment and reasoning and the deficiency of his share of worldly wisdom, ﴿or weak﴾, unable to dictate at that time, due to illness or other causes, such as childhood, insanity, or senility, from weakness, which is the enfeeblement of the powers, sensory or intellectual, ﴿or he is not able to dictate himself﴾, such as through muteness, shyness, a foreign tongue, or the like, ﴿then let his guardian dictate﴾, the one who attends to his affairs, whether a father, a legal executor, a judge, an interpreter, or an agent, ﴿with justice﴾, so that he does not deviate in it nor against the rightful claimant. Al-Harrali said: He made the guardian's tongue the tongue of the one under guardianship, and there is in this a likeness to what the Book has revealed of the placing of Allah's speech upon the tongues of His creatures, as in the previous saying: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5], and what is detailed from it, ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who have believed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. He dictated to them what rights they owe to Him, and made it a speech from His speech which they recite. So the dictation from Him to them is because of their shortcoming in the duty owed to Him, just as the foolish one and whoever is with him fall short in dictating to his guardian because of his maturity, strength, and the firmness of his capacity. End.

Since there was no necessary connection between writing and testimony, He stated it and specified its people, saying: ﴿And call upon two witnesses﴾, that is, seek testimony and establish it along with writing and without it. ﴿two witnesses﴾. Al-Harrali said: He made the testimony for debt two, just as He made the witness in religion two: the witness of reflection on visible signs and the witness of contemplation of heard signs. And in the form fa'il there is an intensification of the meaning in the realization of the attribute of insight and experience. End.

Since He specified the number of witnesses, He specified their type, saying: ﴿from among your men﴾. By the attribution, He indicated the condition that he be a Muslim. The unrestricted use of this term, which refers to the complete (male adult), together with what supports it in the verse, implies freedom, as in His saying: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾. The use of the intensive form for the witness, restricting it with approval, and defining the witnesses and the like, [all show this]. Al-Harrali said: Because debt is frequent and general, He broadened the testimony in it, ⟨saying⟩: ﴿But if they are not two men﴾ [that is, the two witnesses] ﴿then a man and two women﴾. In the generality of the meaning of being there is an indication of admitting the testimony of two women, together with the possibility of requiring a man in some respect, since they were not found. ⟨But⟩ if you do not find them, there is in it an aim at disagreement in some respect, since the inclusiveness of the Book is a broadening in knowledge, whether it is on equal footing or in a sequence. And since they are deficient in intellect and religion, two of them were made in place of one man. End.

Since He explained the number, He explained the attribute, saying: ﴿of those whom you approve﴾, that is, in uprightness, ﴿of the witnesses﴾. This applies to debts and the like. Al-Harrali said: In the concept of testimony is the insight of the witness's gaze, for the witnesses have the perception of a hidden meaning in an apparent form, toward which penetrating vision guides. End.

Since He stipulated for the standing in place of one man a number of women, He gave the reason by something that points to deficiency in their precision, saying: ﴿that if one of them errs﴾, that is, the testimony escapes her and she forgets it or some part of it, ﴿then one of them may remind the other﴾, so that she is guided to what she had forgotten through the aid of memory. Al-Harrali said: because they are more knowledgeable of the entrances of error upon them, since those who are close are nearer in cooperation. In the two readings, the light and the heavy, there is an indication of dividing women into two categories in the rank of this testimony: one who suffers error about some of what she witnessed, until she is reminded, with the light reading, and this does not recur for her; and one whose nature is that this recurs for her. In the use of the indefinite word "one of them" (iḥdāhumā), without restricting it to a pronoun that specifies what it refers to, there is an indication that this occurs between them alternately, so that perhaps one errs in one respect and the other errs in another respect, and each one reminds her companion. For this reason, one reliable witness stands with them together. End. In the mention of reminding there is a prohibition of testimony without remembrance, and the verse is of the type called ihtibak (interlocking). Since this understanding encourages testimony, He stated it in His saying: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse﴾, that is, to bear testimony and to render it after bearing it, ﴿when they are called﴾, a firm calling, as indicated by the added ma.

Since all this was complete, and small rights and large rights are sometimes neglected, the small through carelessness and the large through weariness, He warned against that. He did not place it within the core of the command before the witnessing, but singled it out for mention, magnifying its importance, saying: ﴿And do not be weary﴾, from as-si'amah, which is the intensified form of weariness. Al-Harrali said: it is a form of intensity, and it is the greatest weariness, ﴿of writing it﴾, that is, do not act as one who is bored and so leave off its writing, ﴿whether it is small﴾, the debt, ﴿or large﴾, whether the writing is long or short.

Al-Harrali said: He did not say "little or much," because multitude and paucity apply in relation to the counted thing in itself, whereas small and large apply in relation to the debtor. Thus a large number may be of small value to a man of great standing, and a small number may be large relative to a stingy man concerned with it. So smallness and largeness are more comprehensive and more closely tied to the state of the debtor, who is the one addressed to write. End.

﴿to its term﴾, that is, the one upon which you have agreed and covenanted.

Since it was as if it were said: what is the benefit of that? It was said: ﴿That﴾, indicated by the distal demonstrative and the plural mim, to point to the great value of it. Al-Harrali said: Because of its clarity and evidence among them, it was not an address to the Prophet ﷺ, to whom one turns in hidden matters. End.

﴿more just﴾, that is, more equitable. It is related from Ibn al-Sayyid that in his book al-Iqtidab he said: qasata means both "he oppressed" and "he was just." Al-Harrali said: ﴿aqsat﴾ is from al-iqsat, which is establishing qist, and qist is preserving balance so that it does not go out into fraud. He then increased its magnification by His saying: ﴿with Allah﴾, that is, the One who encompasses the attributes of perfection in relation to each of His attributes, because it leads to justice by preventing deception and inconsistency in any of the circumstances of that debt. ﴿and more upright for testimony﴾, that is, more just in establishing testimony when the witness is asked to establish it by what is recorded for him and against him. ﴿and nearer to preventing doubt﴾, that is, nearer to your not doubting anything of the matter that occurred. Al-Harrali said: In its indication is that it may happen that a man or two men are confronted by something like what confronted the two women, so the writing establishes their testimony. Thus He removed doubt from men by the writing, just as He removed error from women by the reminder. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 2 of 2):

Since the deferred debt is more general than being a loan or a trade, through which wealth is increased, the wealth that is commanded to be spent in the beneficial ways of goodness on the Day of Judgment, and since he (God) had emphasized the matter of writing it down with an emphasis that might lead one to think it was urged, even though there was no term (ajal), he drew attention to the reason for it, which is the term, the thing that is the seat of forgetfulness that dominates man, by His saying: ﴿except when it is﴾, i.e., the transaction, ﴿a present trade﴾. This is according to the reading of ʿĀṣim; in the reading of others it is complete: ﴿which you conduct among yourselves﴾, i.e., hand to hand, from the verb "idārah" (conducting/circulating). Al-Ḥarālli said: it derives from the root "dawr," which is the return of a thing to its starting point. ﴿Then there is no blame upon you﴾ at that time, ﴿if you do not write it﴾, i.e., there is no objection, because it is an immediate exchange, and it is a passing commodity that hardly stays in anyone's hand, since the purpose of it is trade [not retention], so the fear of mutual denial is remote.
Since sale is more general than being intended for trade, or other forms of benefit, he said: ﴿And call witnesses﴾, whether it is writing or not, ﴿when you trade with one another﴾, i.e., for the purpose of trade, immediately or deferred, or not for trade, because calling witnesses is further from dispute and closer to mutual trust, given the fairness it contains. The command is one of guidance, so it is not obligatory.
Since at the beginning of the address He obligated the scribe to write and the witness to respond and not refuse, and He confirmed that with a form that includes the one who is asked to write and the one who is asked to witness, He said, forbidding: ﴿Let no harm be done to scribe or witness﴾. It may be read with the verb in the active or passive, and the meaning is sound in either case: ﴿no harm be done to scribe or witness﴾, i.e., no harm should come from them or to them. Al-Ḥarālli said: in its implication there is an allusion to kindness on his part toward the witness and the scribe, so that he will answer his need and help him to comply with the command of his Lord, by protecting him from the harm of his idleness and of being employed in a matter of his worldly affairs. So in this allusion there is a permission for what the scribe takes, and for whoever is called upon to provide assistance of this kind to one who is in need, when abandoning him would harm him. End of quote.
﴿And if you do so﴾, i.e., what you have been forbidden of harm and other things, ﴿then it is indeed wickedness﴾, i.e., a departure ﴿in you﴾ from the Law which God has laid down for you. Al-Ḥarālli said: in the form "fa'ūl" there is emphasis and intensification in the warning. End of quote.

The closing of the verses of these transactions with the attribute of knowledge, after the command to piety, is most fitting for what the dealers do of stratagems by which each of them seeks advantage for himself, and it is an encouragement to comply with what He commanded them in these clauses, by stating that it is from His knowledge and His teaching. So He, exalted is He, said, conjoining it to what preceded of command and prohibition, or to what is implied: "Do what you have been commanded and refrain from what you have been forbidden": ﴿And fear God﴾, i.e., beware of Him to whom belongs all greatness, in what He has commanded you and forbidden you of this and other things. Since the implied sense is [a resumption to explain the grandeur of these admonitions]: "God guides you to such guidance for the reform of your mutual relations," He conjoined to it His saying: ﴿And God teaches you﴾, i.e., He makes you aware, He to whom all perfection belongs, of that by way of knowledge. Al-Ḥarālli said: in His saying "yuʿallimukum" (He teaches you) in the form of continuity there is an indication of what the teaching continues to be, apart from this attainment. [End.]
He mentioned the noble Name here and in what follows, to magnify the station and to generalize the teaching, so He said: ﴿And God﴾, i.e., He to whom belongs complete encompassing ﴿of all things is Knowing﴾. This closing combines the glad tidings of teaching and the warning of threat.

When the implied sense was: "This applies if you are present, where it is easy for you to bring a scribe and a witness," he conjoined to it His saying: ﴿And if you are﴾, and since a person on a journey is gathered in strength, complete in his faculties and fully equipped, he used the particle of elevation (ʿalā) and said: ﴿on a journey﴾, in which bringing a scribe like it is difficult, ﴿and you do not find a scribe, then a pledge in hand﴾. That is: a pledge that serves as a substitute for it will suffice you in place of writing. It is also read *fa-rihānun*, and both forms (*rihān* and *rahān*) are plurals of *rahn* (pledge), with a fatha or with sukun, meaning securing something by a thing that equals it in some respect. He indicated that its serving as a substitute is beneficial only through what he described it with in His saying: ﴿taken in possession﴾, that is, in the hand of the creditor as a security for his debt.

(p. 161) When the implied sense was: "This applies if you fear [being unable to repay] in dealings of debt," he conjoined to it His saying: ﴿But if one of you trusts another﴾. Since trust may come from the creditor and at other times from the one who gives the pledge, he said: ﴿one of you trusts another﴾, that is, you did none of that. ﴿Then let him who has been entrusted﴾, that is, let him give, from *al-adāʾ* (rendering), which is bringing a thing at its appointed time. Since the purpose is to remind of the favour of trust so that it may be thanked, and no aim is tied to its being from a particular benefactor, he put the verb in the passive, saying: ﴿who has been entrusted﴾, from *al-ʾitmān* (entrusting), which is seeking trust, and it is the depositing of a thing for safekeeping until it is returned to the one who entrusted it. Al-Harali said: ﴿his trust﴾, which is [the debt] that the one who entrusts has left unsecured from the debtor, out of kindness to him and good opinion of him. Likewise if the trust comes from the side of the pledge-giver. ﴿And let him fear God﴾, who possesses the attributes of greatness, ﴿his Lord﴾, that is, the One who nurtured him with His favours and protected him from His harshness and retribution. He also conjoined to it the heart of the one who gave and entrusted him, so that he would render the right in the manner in which he received it, and thus not betray anything of what he was entrusted with.

(p. 162) Since writing is for the sake of establishing testimony, and since souls are naturally disposed to stinginess and founded on love of taking for oneself, disputes arise from this and enmities grow intense. Perhaps some of the disputants are those whose affairs are feared and whose goodness is hoped for, so this leads the witnesses to silence. The Most Glorified and Exalted said: ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾, that is, whether the owner of the right knows it or not. When He forbade it, He followed the prohibition with a threat, saying: ﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾. Since its seat is the heart, which is the foundation of the body, He said: ﴿his heart﴾. Whoever's heart is sinful [is corrupted, and whoever's heart is corrupted, his whole being is corrupted, because the heart is the stability of the body; when it is corrupted, the rest of the body is corrupted].

Since the implied sense was: "Indeed God, the Most Glorified and Exalted, knows that he concealed it, and the witnesses have aspects by which testimony may be turned away from the manner of its establishment," He conjoined to it His saying, so that the threat would encompass those actions through comprehensive knowledge: ﴿And God﴾, that is, (p. 163) the One encompassing all attributes of perfection. Since man is the greatest object of concern among all created beings, and his states are [governed] by kinds of regulation, as though perfect knowledge were restricted to him, He therefore placed first His saying: ﴿of what you do﴾, that is, all of it, however minute, whether it is an act of the heart alone or not, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾. Al-Harali said: Thus He has concluded the matter of what lies between the Truth and creation in the form of an exemplar, and the matter of what lies between creation and creation in the form of a parable. End.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 2, Verse 284**

When He informed about the vastness of His knowledge, He indicated it by the vastness of His dominion, which necessarily entails the vastness of His power, so that this would indicate all perfection. For, as al-Asfahani said, it is established that the attributes which are true perfections are none other than power and all-encompassing knowledge. He then said, promising the obedient and threatening the disobedient, and declaring explicitly that the actions of the servants and other things are created by Him:

Al-Harrali said: Since the beginning of the surah was the manifestation of the Book of Decree in the First Reminder, its conclusion is the manifestation of the effect of that (first) Book in deeds and recompense, which are the ultimate end in the beginning of the matter of decree. Thus the conclusion came with His taking away from creation [whatever] is in their hands, of what they have revealed and what they have concealed, from the people of the heavens and the earth. End of quotation.

He said: ﴿To Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King. Since "mā" (what) is used for one who is heedless, and since most existing things [and inanimate things] are of this kind, He expressed it with "mā," saying: ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, that is, all of it, with their height and vastness, of dominion and other things, ﴿and whatever is on the earth﴾, of what you spend and other things, of rational and non-rational beings. He commands in them and from them what He wills, forbids what He wills, gives to whom He wills, withholds from whom He wills, and multiplies for whom He wills.

Since the sense was: "So He knows all that is in them of your concealment and other things, and disposes of it as He wills," He followed it by warning whoever conceals testimony, or harbours evil other than that, or displays it, with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you show﴾, that is, make apparent, ﴿what is in your souls﴾ of testimony or other things, ﴿or conceal it﴾ of what you have settled in the soul and resolved upon. It is not among the passing thoughts which you dislike and have not resolved upon. Al-Harrali said: From concealment, which is hiding a thing and not placing any sign by which it may be found from its direction. ﴿He will call you to account for it﴾. "Muhasabah" (reckoning) is a form of "mufa'alah" from "hisab" (calculation) and "hasb" (sufficiency), which is the exact enumeration of what is due to a person and upon him of deeds, outward and inward, meaning, so that He may recompense for them. ﴿Allah will call you to account﴾, that is, by His mention of it to you, while you know what He possesses of attributes of perfection. Al-Harrali said: Within this address to those who have understanding is an announcement that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, if He hastens to reckon with the servant according to what the arrangement of reckoning following the occurrence of the deed makes understood, where there is no [reckoning], such as "He will call you to account," then He has greatly bestowed kindness upon him. For whoever is reckoned for his deed swiftly in this world, his recompense lightens upon him, since he is expiated by a thorn that pricks him, even by a pen that falls from the scribe's hand. Thus the believer is expiated for everything that befalls him in his worldly life, until he dies in purity from his sins [and free of his reckoning], like one who regularly cleans his body and garment so that it does not become soiled or stained and remains always clean. End of quotation, with some alteration.

Since the true meaning of reckoning is the mention of a thing and the recompense for it, and since what is intended here is presentation, which is mere mention by implication, He indicated it with His words, placing first the postponement (tarji'ah, deferring of judgement) to balance what the beginning of the verse had made understood of intimidation: ﴿So He forgives whom He wills﴾, that is, He will not requite him for it, whether it was a major sin or not, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾, by expiation or recompense.

When Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, informed by this that He has absolute disposal, He concluded the speech, indicating that by His words, explicitly stating what necessarily follows from the completeness of His knowledge of His complete power: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One with whom no command belongs to anyone, ﴿is over all things Competent﴾, that is, He is not [like] the kings of the world, between whom and some of what they wish is placed a barrier by intercession and other means. Al-Harrali said: By this verse He negated power from all creation. End of quotation.

Some scholars held that this verse is specific to the matter of testimony, while most said it is general, as the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, understood it, regarding whisperings, self-talk resolved upon, and other things; then it was lightened by what follows it. Muslim related in his Sahih from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the words of Allah's Messenger ﷺ were revealed: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ up to ﴿Competent﴾, it weighed heavily upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Then they knelt upon their knees and said: O Messenger of Allah! We have been charged with deeds we can bear: prayer, fasting, jihad and charity, and this verse has been revealed to you which we cannot bear. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Do you wish to say as the People of the Two Books said before you: ﴿We hear and disobey﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 93]? Rather say: ﴿We hear and obey; (we seek) Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the (final) destination﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 285]. They said: ﴿We hear and obey; (we seek) Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the (final) destination﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 285]."

When the people recited it and their tongues were humbled by it, Allah sent down after it: ﴿The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and [so have] the believers﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 285] up to ﴿the final destination﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 285]. When they did that, Allah abrogated it (naskh, abrogation) and sent down: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 286] up to [﴿or if we have forgotten or erred﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 286]]. He said: "Yes." Al-Baghawi said: In a narration from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "I have done so." And it continued to the end of the surah, whenever they recited a sentence he said: "Yes."

Thus it has become clear from this the coherence (tanasub) of these verses. As for its connection to the beginning of the surah, returning the end to the opening, it is that when He began the surah with describing the believers as those who believe in the Book in which there is no doubt, in the manner mentioned earlier, He concluded it with that after detailing the spending by which He had described them at its beginning, in a way that joins what precedes it, of commands, prohibitions, and attribution of the qualities of perfection, in the closest connection. He made their head the Messenger, upon him be the best of prayers and the purest of peace, to exalt the praise and to encourage that description. So He informed of their belief in what was sent down to him specifically and in all the Books and all the Messengers, and of their saying, which indicates complete desire and utmost supplication and humility. He said, beginning a reply to one who seems to have asked: What did those to whom these commands and prohibitions and others were sent down do?

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 285:**

﴿The Messenger believes﴾ meaning: in what became manifest to him of the miracle establishing that the one who comes to him with this revelation is an angel from Allah, glorified and exalted be He, just as the angel believed in him through what became manifest to him of the miracle indicating that what he brought is the speech of Allah, which Allah, glorified and exalted be He, commanded him to send down. [The Messenger] knew him, as an indication that he is the most complete of the messengers in this attribute, in terms of his being sent to all creation (p-169) who belong to Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and that he gathers what was dispersed among them of perfection, and that he is singled out with what none of them was given of excellences and bounties. ﴿in what was sent down to him﴾ meaning: that Allah, glorified and exalted be He, calls to account by what was mentioned and other things he was commanded to convey, and what he was specifically singled out with, and He encouraged belief in what he believed in through His saying: ﴿from his Lord﴾, that is, the One who bestows good upon him with noble upbringing, who purifies [him] with beautiful purification. So He does not send down to him anything except what is utmost in goodness, and among it is what befell him in his worldly life of hardship.

Al-Harrali said: The Messenger accepted this first, swift, facilitated reckoning, so that he would receive his due and his share of it in his worldly life. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, when Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her) said to him at his death: "Oh, my distress!": "There is no distress for your father after today." And the Prophet (ﷺ) said, as narrated by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "No one has been harmed for the sake of Allah as I have been harmed." Thus he received his share of the wisdom of his Lord in his worldly life, to the point that he would be feverish as ten men are feverish, and he did not eat his fill of wheat bread for three consecutive days swiftly until he met Allah. Likewise, the believer has no rest apart from meeting his Lord, and no imprisonment (p-170) upon him after he leaves his worldly life. "Fever is the share of every believer from the Fire." End of quote. When he (Allah) informed about the head, He informed about those who follow him, so He said: ﴿And the believers﴾, describing them with the attribute that indicates firmness, meaning: they believed in what became manifest to them of the miracle which established that it is the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, by what indicated that the one who brought it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

When He stated in summary, He detailed, saying, beginning: ﴿Each﴾, meaning: of them. Al-Harrali said: He gathered them into a totality, as if their hearts were one heart, not differing, because acceptance is one, while rejection occurs in varied ways. End of quote. Then He informed about that subject with His saying: ﴿believes in Allah﴾, meaning: in what is due to Him by virtue of His essence, because of His encompassing of all perfection; ﴿and His angels﴾, those among whom are the ones who descend with the scriptures, because belief in what was sent down necessitates that; ﴿and His books﴾, meaning all of them; ﴿and His messengers﴾, all of them, whether from mankind or from the angels, for in what was sent down to him (ﷺ) is the information (p-171) about that. Al-Harrali said: In compliance with the command of humans.

Since among people there are those who believe in some of the prophets and disbelieve in others, He said, emphasizing what the plural construction with a possessive pronoun conveyed of comprehensiveness, meaning: they said: ﴿We make no distinction﴾, as the People of the Book did, and He expressed it with what encompasses two and more, so He said: ﴿between any one﴾, meaning: one or other ﴿of His messengers﴾, meaning: we do not make any one of them in a state of extreme separation from his companion in this matter, but we believe in each one of them. What indicated the supposition of "they said" rather than something else is that, when He completed their statement regarding the theoretical faculty, which is sufficient for belief in the origin, He followed it with their statement regarding the practical faculty, which lies in the middle, conjoining it to what precedes: ﴿And they said: We hear﴾, meaning: with the ears of our intellects, all that can be heard from You, and we knew it and submitted to it; ﴿and we obey﴾, meaning: to everything in it of Your command.

Al-Harrali said: They shared with the People of the Book in the forefront of refusal, and differed from them in hastening repentance and acknowledgment with hearing and obedience. So for these there is what belongs to the penitent, and upon those there is what is upon the persistent. End of quote.

(p-172) Since man is a place of slips and deficiency, they indicated this with humility on their part, as is most fitting for them in the station of divinity. So they said, along with their obedience, acknowledging the return (ma'ad): ﴿Your forgiveness﴾, meaning: forgive us, or we ask You for Your forgiveness, which is fitting to be ascribed to You because of its perfection, nobility, and majesty, for what we fell short in, and do not take us to account for it, for if You do that, we would be destroyed. The summary is that they asked that He treat them with what He is worthy of, not with what they are worthy of, so He responded with what He had made them bold to ask in His saying: ﴿He forgives whomever He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. Al-Harrali said: This statement from the Messenger (ﷺ) is an unveiling by direct witnessing, and from the believers it is a budding of faith, and from those who say "we hear and obey" it is a statement of submission. It encompasses all, each according to his rank. End of quote. They added flattery in their saying: ﴿Our Lord﴾, mentioning the attribute of beneficence in the station of seeking forgiveness. Al-Harrali said: This is an address of nearness, inasmuch as no particle of calling appears in it, and Allah, glorified and exalted be He, has never, in His Mighty Book, made the believers' speech a call of distance at all. Forgiveness (ghufran) is on the pattern fu'lan, an intensive form that gives fullness, so that it is a covering for the outward and the inward. It is a verbal noun of encompassing meaning, standing in the place of seeking forgiveness, comprehending what the outward and the inward encompass of what the souls deposit, which are the locus of the manifestation of Allah's wisdom, glorified and exalted be He, in which the totality of forgiveness and punishment occurs: ﴿He forgives whomever He wills and punishes whomever He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284]. Thus within it is good news of the identification of those who say and submit, and those who follow them, with the statement appropriate to the state of forgiveness, because these closings are accepted from the servant in the position of the Opening (al-Fatihah), since both are from the treasure beneath the Throne. This is in accordance with what has come in the saying: "My servant has praised Me... up to His saying: and for My servant is what he asked." And in accordance with what has come in the supplication of this closing in His saying: "I have done, I have done," and with what Exalted He began the verse of this reckoning with and concluded it with: the removal of command at first and the removal of power from other than Him at the end. In the beginning and the end there was an establishment of the excuse of those who speak, so forgiveness became binding for them, just as it was for their father Adam when he received words from his Lord. End of quote.

Since the estimate is by what He guided to with ﴿Our Lord﴾, for it is from You that our origin is, He conjoined to it His saying, urging striving in everything He commanded and forbade, in the manner of sincerity: ﴿And to You is the destination﴾, meaning: not to other than You, ﴿the final return﴾, meaning: absolutely, for us and for others. Ibn al-Zubayr said: When Allah, glorified and exalted be He, made clear that the Book is the Straight Path, He mentioned the divergence of nations as He willed, and the states of those who deviate and turn away, as a warning against their condition and a prohibition against their wrongdoing. This occurred (p-174) shortly before the descent in its entirety and the confinement of those who abandon it. He followed this with mention of the obligations of the pious and what befits them to comply with and adhere to of commands, rulings, and limits. He followed that with the fact that a person must embrace all of that and surrender the matter to its Owner, so He, glorified and exalted be He, said: ﴿The Messenger believes in what was sent down﴾. He made known that this is the belief of the Messenger and those with him in his belief, and that they said: ﴿We hear and we obey﴾, not as the statement of the Children of Israel: ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93]. He also rewarded them for their belief with the lifting of burden, hardship, and blame for error and forgetfulness, so He said: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. Thus there resulted from this surah in its entirety a clarification of the Straight Path in full and completion, in what to take and what to leave, and a clarification of the nobility of one who takes it and the evil state of one who turns away from it. When the servants knew ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], to the end of the surah, it was said to them: "Hold fast to the Book," in answer to their request. Then He clarified for them the state of one who follows what they sought, so it was said to them: the people of the Straight Path and its followers are those whose matter and affair He has clarified; and those who have incurred anger among those who turn away are the Jews, whose matter and affair He has clarified; and the astray are the Christians, whose (p-175) matter and affair He has clarified. Therefore, whoever desires to follow the Straight Path must beware of what befell these people, from what He has warned about, must discipline himself accordingly, must let his faith extend over all of that, and must surrender the matter to Allah, from whom guidance is sought, and entreat Him not to take him to account for what error and forgetfulness produce, not to burden him with what is beyond his capacity, and to pardon him. (And so on) to the end of the surah. End of quote.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 2, verse 286 (part 1 of 3):

When they were inspired with faith in asking for forgiveness, they justified the request by saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾, that is, the Greatest King, the Most Merciful, the Most Generous, to whom belong all attributes of perfection. ﴿A soul beyond what it can bear﴾ means what it can contain and is able to do, and in which it is not incapable. This is the possible in itself (al-mumkin li-dhatihi), the matter over which the servant's choice relates to his act. Allah, exalted is He, did not inform us that He does not bring about either the impossible in itself or the possible in itself, whether it is something in which a person has no part in choosing, such as sleep, or something in which he has a part. The eternal knowledge (al-'ilm al-azali) has determined the non-occurrence of the first kind, and Allah, glorified and exalted, has informed us of its non-occurrence as a help to the one addressed. So the first kind is not a matter of obligation (taklif), but the second kind may be imposed as an obligation. This statement is part of their supplication in the form of praise, seeking fulfilment of what the Messenger (ﷺ) had told them from Him, glorified and exalted, out of fear that they might be charged with what is beyond their capacity, as the verse indicates, and as the believers said when it was revealed, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) answer to them: that they would be held accountable for the whisperings which the heart does not resolve upon, because these are things that the souls conceal and there is no power to repel them. This falls under the saying:

*When a man praises you one day,*
*the praise itself suffices him from seeking your attention.*

Perhaps the shift from direct address to the third person, by mentioning the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-A'zam), is a form of flattery, implying that He has attributes of greatness which call for pardoning their weakness, and attributes of forbearance, mercy and compassion which ease their burden. It is also possible that this is part of Allah's own words, as a reward to them for their saying ﴿We hear and we obey﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285] and the rest of the verse. Thereby He informs them that He will not call them to account for the stirrings of the soul in which there is no resolve. Thus what had troubled them from His words ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284] is removed. This is unlike the Children of Israel, whose saying ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93] brought them burdens in this world and the next. In that case, the sentence is a fresh statement answering one who might ask, "Did He answer their supplication?" It also explains His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. This interpretation is supported by the following of the ruling on what is within capacity by way of a fresh statement or an opening with His saying ﴿It shall have what it earned﴾, that is, specifically for it. The mention of the verb in its bare form for good deeds indicates that merely its occurrence suffices for it to be counted, even with laziness, and indeed even by merely intending it. Al-Harrali said: The bare form of the verb (fa'ala) indicates the lowest degree of earning, and therefore whoever intends a good deed but does not do it, it is written for him as a good deed. End of quotation.

﴿And against it what it has earned﴾, that is, specifically against it. For evil, he used the form of the reflexive verb (iftaʿala), which indicates effort and striving, pointing out that the nature of the soul is to incline entirely toward desire, and that sin is not recorded except with determination and strong resolve. If such resolve produces an outward act, it is done with diligence, energy, desire and enthusiasm. Therefore whoever intends an evil deed but does not do it, it is not recorded against him. Sometimes the expression is different for a meaning required by that context and the situation.

When He gave them this good news, He made them aware of the places of His favours in a supplication arranged from the lightest to the heaviest, in ascending order, to inform them that He does not hold them accountable for what they committed through forgetfulness, nor for what they did by error, nor did He place upon them a heavy burden. Rather, He made their law upright (ḥanifiyyah), easy and tolerant, and did not burden them beyond their capacity, although all of that is in His power. He also pardoned them from punishment and then concealed them, not exposing them by mentioning their faults. Then He showed them mercy by placing them in a position of nearness, making them fit to be successors (khilafah). From this it becomes clear that He will exalt their affair above every affair and make their religion prevail over every religion, since Allah, exalted is He, is the one who supports them. Thus the whole supplication is carried toward being correct and is accompanied by being answered. So He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task﴾, that is, do not treat us as one who argues with an opponent and scrutinises him over every small and great matter, ﴿if we forget﴾, that is, so we do what You have forbidden us, ﴿or err﴾, that is, we do it while remembering it, but we did not intend any evil. Al-Harrali said: Error is slipping away from the limit without intending it, rather with the intention of being correct or the wish not to err. The fact that it is recited from the words of Allah, exalted is He, upon the tongues of His servants indicates its acceptance. End of quotation. The repetition of "Our Lord" at the beginning of each clause of this type, as has been indicated earlier, serves as a reminder of the greatness of the station, in the goodness of upbringing and the gentleness of kindness and compassion.

Since this might happen, He has the right to impose whatever He wills, even heavy obligations that are very difficult, for He is not questioned about what He does. They said: ﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden (iṣr)﴾, that is, a heavy load.

Al-Harrali said: It is a heavy covenant, meaning one in which the bearing of it involves the greatest hardship. End of quotation. Then they magnified the favour by saying: ﴿as You laid it upon those before us﴾, indicating that He had laid upon those who came before them rulings that would break the pillars, as a reinforcement of what should move them to gratitude for lightening these for us. The root of iṣr is a bend or curve. It is said that a thing "aṣara-hu" (bent it) and "ya'ṣuruhu" (bends it), meaning he bent it. It implies heaviness, because when a branch becomes heavy it bends and curves, and this is the intended meaning here. These burdens referred to are very many. Among them is what is in the second book of the Torah concerning offerings: that the blood of the sacrificed animal is sprinkled on the corners of the altar. Then it says: Whoever draws near by slaughtering a bull or other animal in a place other than the door of the Tent of Meeting, the House of the Lord, that man shall be punished with the punishment of one who has killed a person, because he has shed blood, and that man shall perish from among his people. Whoever eats blood, wrath shall come upon him and he shall perish, because the souls of animals are the blood. [They were commanded to bring it to the altar for the forgiveness of their sins and the purification of their souls, because the soul is forgiven only through blood.] Whoever offers a sacrifice shall eat of it on the day of its slaughter and the next day, and what remains until the third day shall be burned with fire, and whoever eats of it shall perish from his people. Among these are the afflicted with disease: whoever among humans is leprous shall sit alone and not mix with people, and his dwelling shall be outside the community of the Children of Israel. The leprosy is also mentioned in garments, houses and other things. If leprosy appears in leather or garments, the place of the leprosy shall be cut out of it, and if it appears again after cutting, all of it shall be burned with fire. If leprosy appears in a house, it shall be demolished, and its stones, wood and dust gathered and taken outside the village and burned with fire. Likewise, in the case of the discharge (salas), there are many severe rules, among them that whoever sits on a garment upon which a person with the discharge has sat shall wash his garments, bathe in water, and remain unclean until the evening, and similar. Then he said: The Lord spoke to Moses and said to him: This is the law for the leper who is cleansed: he shall be brought to the priest, who shall take him outside the camp, and the priest (ḥabr) shall look to see whether the leprous wound has healed, and when he is cleansed of it, the priest shall command that he be brought forward, and two live clean birds shall be brought, and cedar wood, and scarlet yarn, and he enumerated other things, and an offering in a specific and difficult manner by a spring of water. He shall wash his garments and his body, shave the hair of his head, beard, eyebrows and all the hair of his body, and remain outside his house for seven days. On the eighth day he shall bring another offering, which shall be presented in a specific manner, and the priest shall sprinkle some of its blood on the garments and body of the one who has been cleansed of leprosy, and likewise some of the oil of the offering, and the rest shall be poured on his head. Likewise, in the case of the discharge, when the one with the discharge is healed, he shall remain for seven days, then be purified, wash his garments, and offer an offering at the door of the Tent of Meeting. He also said: Any man who emits seminal discharge or has an emission of semen shall wash his whole body with water and remain unclean until evening. Whoever touches a menstruating woman shall be unclean until evening, [and whatever garment or bedding is touched by an emission of semen shall be washed with water and remain unclean until evening], and any garment on which she lies while menstruating shall be unclean, and whoever touches her bedding shall wash his garments, bathe in water, and remain unclean until evening; likewise the woman with an irregular flow of blood. Also in it: The Lord spoke to Moses and said: Speak to the Children of Israel and say to them: When a woman conceives and gives birth to a male, she shall be unclean [for seven] days, as in the days of her menstruation, and on the eighth day the boy shall be circumcised, and she shall remain in her state of impurity for thirty-three days, touching nothing holy and not entering the House of Allah, exalted is He, for prayer is forbidden to her until she completes the days of her purification. If she gives birth to a girl, she shall be unclean as in the days of her menstruation for fourteen days, and remain in her state of impurity for sixty-six days because of the pure blood. When she completes the days of her purification, whether she has borne a son or a daughter, she shall bring a lamb in its first year, and he mentioned an offering in the Tent of Meeting to be offered by the priest so that she may be cleansed of the blood that flowed from her. Among the burdens also mentioned in the second book: when they reaped a field or gathered grapes, it was forbidden to them to gather everything, and they were commanded to leave it for the poor. Then he said: Do not gather what falls from your olive trees, but leave it for the poor and for those who come to Me, because I am the Lord your God. Then he said: When you enter the land and plant in it every tree that bears fruit for food, leave its fruit for three years and do not eat of it. In the fourth year, all its fruit shall be holy, a consecration to the Lord and a glory to His honour, and in the fifth year you may eat its fruit, for it will grow and its produce will increase for you. I am the Lord your God! At the end of the fifth book, which is the last of its books, he said: Do not oppress the poor, the orphan, or the stranger among you in judgement, and do not take the widow's garment as a pledge. Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt and the Lord redeemed you from there. Therefore I command you and tell you that it is obligatory upon you to do the same. When you reap the harvest of your field and forget a sheaf, do not go back to retrieve it, but let it be for the stranger, the orphan and the widow, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the work of your hands. When you shake your olive trees, do not seek what you have forgotten in your field, but let it be for the orphan, the stranger and the widow. When you cut your vines, do not strip them completely, but leave what the stranger, the orphan and the widow may live on. Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt; therefore I command you to do this. As for what is upon the Christians of this, much of it will come, God willing, in al-Ma'idah at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed in it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 47].

When they prayed with what included faith in what had been revealed to them, of the burdens borne by those before them, they followed it with what indicates their belief that this is justice from Him in judgement, and that He has the right to do more than that, imposing upon them what is beyond their capacity, because He is the absolute Owner and the King who alone possesses dominion. They asked for lightening by removing this, saying: ﴿Our Lord, and do not﴾. He used the intensive form (tafʿil) because of what it conveys of treatment, in keeping with the imposing of what cannot be borne, and so He said: ﴿burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾, that is, power, ﴿for﴾

When the human being sometimes deliberately commits a sin out of desire that calls him to it and a purpose that drives him to it, they followed this with a general supplication, saying: ﴿And pardon us﴾, that is, lift from us the punishment for all sins, ﴿and forgive us﴾, that is, do not mention them to us at all. The first is pardon from the punishment of the body, and the second is pardon from the torment of the soul. (p. 186)

Al-Harrali (al-Harrali, Abu al-Hasan) said: Since one who is pardoned and forgiven may fall short in rank and thus fail to attain his share of mercy, God, exalted is He, joined the one pardoned and forgiven to the one shown mercy from the outset, with His saying: ﴿And have mercy on us﴾, that is, so that the sinner who repents and the one who never sinned are equal in attaining mercy.

When God, exalted is He, doubled for them His pardon, forgiveness and mercy, He brought them through this to the station of the preserving caliphate: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of God except for him on whom He has mercy﴾ [Hud: 43]. When they became caliphs, jihad against the enemies of God, standing up for God's command, and opposing whoever takes other than God as ally were realized in them. So it was established that enemies would necessarily oppose and confront them. Therefore He, glorified is He, who had shown them mercy, taught them to attribute their affair of guardianship to Him, saying about them: ﴿You are our Mawla (Protector)﴾. The mawla is the walī (guardian) who is constant in guardianship, who stands by it and perseveres in it for the one who entrusts his affair to him in matters he is not able to manage. End of the meaning. Its true reality is the one who effects the fruit of guardianship, which is nearness and turning toward. This is because when they asked for pardon from the punishment of body and soul, they asked for their rewards: the reward of the body is Paradise, and the reward of the soul is the delight of witnessing, and that is the fruit of guardianship, namely full turning toward the Guardian. Then He made the conclusion of the believers' turning to their Lord a supplication for the fruit of guardianship, saying: ﴿So help us﴾ with the tongue and with the spear, and He pointed to the strength of (p. 187) the opponents, urging them to sincere reliance and truthful desire, with His saying: ﴿against the disbelieving people﴾, and He pointed out that the proofs for Him, glorified is He, are at the utmost clarity for every intelligent person, with His saying: ﴿the disbelievers﴾, that is, those who conceal the proofs that point them to their Lord, which were mentioned at the beginning of the surah. This thus includes the obligation to fight them, and that they are the worst of enemies. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 256] does not prohibit that; rather it indicates that the religion has reached such clarity that compulsion cannot be conceived in it. Rather every intelligent person ought to enter it with the utmost desire, let alone needing intimidation. Whoever advises himself enters it by what his intellect guides him to; whoever refuses is forced into it by the counsel of God, which is striking with the sword and the piercing arrow.

Since the closing with this indicates that He, exalted is He, when He doubled His pardon for them from the sin, so He does not punish for it, and His forgiveness for it, such that He makes it as if it had not been, so He does not mention it at all nor punish for it, and His mercy in bringing the sinner who is pardoned and forgiven to the lofty stations, He brought them to the rank of the caliphate in standing by His command and in jihad against His enemies. And although their affair is great and their enumeration difficult, it serves as an alert that the beginning of this surah is guidance and its end is caliphate. Thus it completed the clarification of the matter of prophethood up to the limit of the manifestation of the caliphate, so it became the hump (sanam) of the Qur'an. The sum of what is in the Qur'an was joined to its meanings, either by what it stated explicitly or by what it hinted at and what was understood from one of its explanations, just as it is joined with the rest of the Qur'an to Surah (p. 188) al-Fatihah, so that it becomes a mother for all. This was stated by the Ustadh Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali.

It has become clear, by mentioning what was revealed, belief in it, and victory over the disbelievers after the detailed treatment of spending and the wealth from which it is spent, that its divided parts return to its opening and its end returns to its beginning. Among the great comprehensive features of its matter, and the breadth of its meaning that shows the height of its status, is what al-Harrali said: when the Revealer of this Qur'an, which is specific to the Seal of the Prophets, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him and upon all the prophets, revealed letters whose meanings encompass, addressing with them the Prophet and the imams, and detailed [verses] addressing with it the common community, this surah combined the two kinds of address. It opens with (Alif Lam Mim) as letters announcing comprehension of what its meanings contain: the comprehension of the one who stands (qā'im) from the meaning of the alif, the comprehension of the station from the meaning of the mim, and the comprehension of connection from the meaning of the lam. Since comprehension is on three levels, divine comprehension of self-subsistence (qayyūmiyyah), scriptural comprehension, and detailed comprehension, the particular comprehension of these letters with which this surah opens was a middle-level scriptural comprehension. So the opening fell, in what the Qur'an's command fell upon in its recitation on earth, at the intermediate rank, since it is closest to the two extremes and easiest for knowing the higher and acting upon the lower. Thus what occurs in the Qur'an of ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [Luqman: 1], ﴿Those are the verses of the wise Book﴾ [Luqman: 2], and the like, is a detailed comprehension of the comprehension of the [Book] in which Surah al-Baqarah was revealed. So it included the comprehensions of the four Books: the Book of Decree (taqdīr), which God, glorified is He, wrote before He created creation, with what God willed of duration [and] number. It is reported that "God wrote the Book and decreed the decree, and His Throne was upon the water," and "God, glorified and exalted is He, measured the measures of creation fifty thousand years before He created them," and that He measured the provisions two thousand years before He created the forms. Much of that is among what is reported in the traditions. Opposite this earlier Book of decree is the later Book of recompense, which God, glorified and exalted is He, wrote and writes, the trace of the complete manifestation through preserving the deeds apparent at the hands of creatures, upon whom bliss and hellfire, security and terror, unveiling and veiling are bestowed. This other Book corresponds to the first existence. Through the passage of these two appears the Book of rulings, which includes the matter of religion and the call, in which guidance and trial occurred. Then the Book of deeds, which God, glorified and exalted is He, wrote in the essences of the responsible (p. 190) persons, concerning their actions and the states of their souls, and what He wrote in their hearts of faith, or what He sealed upon them or stamped upon them with wickedness or rebellion. Thus the first and last agree, while the Book of rulings and the Book of deeds differ, by what God, glorified and exalted is He, manifested from behind a veil of the meaning of guidance and trial, advance and retreat. So Surah al-Baqarah included the comprehensions of all these Books and fulfilled the Book of destinies through what is in its beginning of clarifying the matter of the believers, the disbelievers and the hypocrites; and the Book of acts, as God, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the seal upon the disbelievers and the sickness in the hearts of the hypocrites; and what is detailed throughout the surah of religious rulings, and what is mentioned with them of what is suitable to them of recompense, from the beginning of faith to the furthest point of certainty, which the meaning of the surah reached concerning the matter of religion between the Truth and creation, and between creation and creation concerning transactions and opposition, and between a person and himself concerning oaths and covenants, up to the limit of its ending with what is due from the Truth to creation in the installation of the caliphs, whose mention ended this surah, who said: ﴿Forgiveness, our Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285] until its end. Since the purpose of this surah is scriptural comprehension, that was its explicitness and most of its verses, and divine self-subsisting comprehension (p. 191) was its hint and the light of its verses. So that was explicit in the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi), and in its other verses it was a hint, according to the nearness of scriptural comprehension to divine comprehension, and in an earlier beginning, a later closing, or a comprehensive wisdom. Therefore, the surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned was joined with the surah in which Al 'Imran is mentioned, because of what was revealed in Surah Al 'Imran of divine comprehension, to the point that at its opening is the Greatest Name of God. So what was in al-Baqarah was explicit in Surah Al 'Imran as a hint, and what was in al-Baqarah as a hint was in Surah Al 'Imran explicit, except what was observed in each of them of the explicit statement of the other. Therefore these are two linked surahs, two shades and two clouds that will shade their companion on the Day of Resurrection.
